So far, I have to say that I am incredibly impressed.
I waited anxiously for the game to release, and I was happy to see all the positive reviews. I'm also happy to add my own extremely positive review to the game.
I initially started playing as Ki, due in part to the skin and the fact that she was the first character I got to play as. Started messing around with the 5 turn games, and got my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me by everyone else. I thought that it surely had to be the character. Unlocked 1 or 2 other characters, and tried them as well. Still got my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me. Then, I decided to try the Trials. Went back to Ki.
First 4 fights were easy, and then the last 1 took me 3 or 4 tries. And that's when the magic happened. Instead of actively trying to make random matches, I started playing to the strengths of Ki's abilities. And lo and behold: it worked!
Unlocked a few auras, messed around a bit, got 1 I liked up to level 2, and practiced a bit more in Trial mode and  that 5 turn mode. What a blast! Moved on to Ranked matches, and managed to get up to Silver Rank 1, with a win streak of about 7 or 8 matches, I think.
With the initial 500 Gem allotment, and the fact that the game is liberal in giving you these Gems for victories, and even a few for defeats, unlocking the Auras and Skins doesn't require godlike skill, just some perseverance. And perseverance is always made easier if the game is fun, which it sure as hell is! I've seen no bugs or crashes, and the artwork in the game is beautiful on all characters.
A special mention to the community so far, as well. Every opponent I've played against so far, has been gracious in defeat, and humble in victory.
The game has a solid base for what it is, and can easily be transformed into a massively engrossing affair. An absolute steal at the current price, and worth it if you enjoy the Match-3 gameplay style. Wicked Fun: you really live up to your name with this one so far! Keep it up!

This has to be one of the best games i've ever played, the atmosphere it builds makes you feel REALLY trapped on the space station where the game takes place, it feels like being on the Alien movie but at the same time it innovates in various ways, it doesn't just stick to the movies but also builds its own story. This is the scariest game I've ever played. I actually had to take breaks just to let the heart pounding taper down a bit.
If you watch any "Let's Play" videos, don't over do it, or you'll numb the experience. This one is best played fresh. And, you will, of course, get *used* to the alien after a while, but do cherish the terror. No game will instill it in you quite like this.
Graphics: are fantastic on my crappy old GT 560.
The sound: ...the sound MAKES this game. If you play in a building with another story above you, the thudding of someone walking around above will never be the same after you play this.
The story: They found a clever hole in the original Alien film, and expounded on it. Very nice.
Gameplay: There's some quirky console controle stuff in this game, but it's really minor. Full of typical game plot tropes, like "go get this thing, but then realize you have to get this other thing to get the first thing..." but I didn't mind. Savor the terror and you should be "ok". Some of the puzzles take a moment and some observation (wich always comes at a risk), but they aren't terribly hard. That said, this game is pretty hard. The AI is incredibly unpredictable. You don't realize it until your veteran-gamer blood expects some kind of routine and doesn't get it. You can reload your game a few times at a checkpoint and it won't do the same thing every time. Oh, and it will learn. Don't repeat the same tricks ;) Don't say I didn't warn you.
Summary: 10/10 -you should play this game. Not for the impatient.

Have you ever wondered what it would be like to be on a spaceship and hide from a xenomorph? Well, Alien: Isolation serves as the perfect simulator for that. I was very hyped for this game when it came out and I am so thankful that Isolation delivered. This game is perfect for me as I love both stealth games and the Alien series. Contrasting from most modern AAA games, Isolation refuses any handholding and instead requires you to learn on your own. One of my most memorable moments was when I sat in a locker with my motion tracker out, hiding from the Xenomorph. It walked in front of the locker, then suddenly pried open the door and devoured me. At that moment I realized that the xeno could hear the tracker, and I ended up relying on the tracker far less throughout the game, to a point where it almost felt as a burden to pull out that beeping machine. As someone who is often cynical towards things that claim to be “scary”, I can honestly that Alien: Isolation is definitely scary. This is no mainstream pretender like Slender or Paranormal Activity, this is legitimately scary. Isolation is a kind of stealth game where you are almost never safe. In the early game, I relied heavily on moving through vents because, foolishly, I thought it was safe. The A.I. must have picked up on this as it started to check by vents more frequently. Eventually it started moving in the vents itself, and hearing those footsteps while in those cramped metal pathways was horrifying. Unlike so many other stealth titles where enemies feel preprogrammed, the xenomorph in Isolation feels like a living breathing enemy out to get you. Its paths don’t feel scripted but also don’t feel random, making all of its movements seem like they have purpose, and that purpose is obvious. It truly feels like it is out to get you, as opposed to the standard stealth foe that walks in distinct lines and has obvious cones of vision. If you’re into that kind of thing, Isolation offers the average stealth gameplay through the Working Joes, robots that are going haywire System Shock style and are also out to get you. I liked the addition of these as it kept the game feeling familiar and gave a good change of pace from the difficult xenomorph sections. Even with all that stealth, Isolation understands that hiding from enemies can be tiresome, so there are down time sections where you simply walk around to do basic tasks. That may seem boring but it actually functions as a good refresher so that the game isn’t just all tension all the time. With all of my compliments to Isolation’s gameplay and horror, I do have gripes with its story. Amanda Ripley is a great character in her own right, and any concerns of her being a lazy ripoff of Ellen were thrown away. However, her relationships with her teammates are not explored much and frankly most of the people outside of Amanda feel boring. When a key person dies and I don’t feel much, then you know your game did a poor job at creating characters. My greatest complaint goes towards the game’s ending. If you know Alien lore, then you know what happens to Ellen (go rewatch Aliens if you want to know). After the many hours I put into getting away from the xenomorph, I was hoping to finally find some peace and quiet for Ellen Ripley, but unfortunately the game gives us a somewhat ambiguous and unsatisfying ending to such a long story. There lies another issue: the game felt too long. I know, that might sound strange in a medium where games are often scolded for being too short. Isolation on the other hand is one of the few examples of games that dragged on too long. The story is filled with many “oh wait” moments, where you think your struggle against the xeno is finished only to find that it is still a threat. While this is in line with the franchise’s fashion, it can get tiresome especially with how long the game turned out to be. While I prefer a game to be too long than too short, the Isolation developers tried a bit too hard in putting things into their game. I appreciate the efforts they put into making this game but they did overdo themselves a bit.
Wow, this turned out to be a pretty lengthy review but that's because I have so much to say about this wonderful game. At the end of the day, this is a game that was evidently made by Alien fans for Alien fans. Even if you aren’t big on the franchise, buy this game if you enjoy stealth gameplay or are just wanting a good scare.

Solid stealth game. Nothing too major has been changed since the first game. Just a whole lot of minor details which make the game much more smooth and enjoyable. (being able to knock out people from every angle imgainable, that sort of thing)
First two missions like to show off a lot of npcs which can really stress out the engine and possibly your rig if it's lower end. Just download the demo if your worried about it not running on your machine well. (The devs have put out a decent amount of patches and they have all drastically improved the game from my experience)
Story isn't much of an improvement from the last (besides several more endings) but the level design is the best it's ever been in the series. The levels are very open and free. A few even feel like the hub areas in deus ex. Watch a gameplay video of the clockwork mansion if you want to get an idea for how free the levels are.
Gameplay is fantastic. Uses significantly more animations than the last one (opening doors and interacting with buttons) but they are all "over before you know it" so they don't hinder the freedom of movement that was in the first. This one is pretty difficult compared to the last installment so it isn't as easy to go on a rampage or get that precious ghost rating. The new equipment and powers are really exciting to use and allow a lot more room for how you want to play.
Good sequel to a good game just not exactly the sequel some fans and media outlets imagined.

This game was a great experience and is one of my favorites to this date. It does so many things right to an extent that other farming games could never imagine. A truly breathtaking experience, the game gives you freedom to move at your own pace. You can spend your days on the ranch, taking care of the adorable slimes you captured, or set off into the surprisingly large open world to explore. Farm, adventure, experiment, or build. No matter what you do you can always find a way to have fun. The differences thematically in areas that you unlock (in very unconventional ways) are astounding and provide unique experiences. The soundtrack sets the tone for the entire game with its relaxing, smooth instrumentals. The textural design is both visually appealing and fits the motive of the game. And finally, with the latest addition of a story, you can begin to feel emotionally attached to simplistic narrative. While the true nature of the game is stated in its name, Slime Rancher is so much more than ranching slimes. Everything from the freedom to roam to the magical and memorable places to discover fits the game perfectly. I would recommend Slime Rancher to any who enjoy indie games, want a truly unique experience, or just want to mellow out and meet some cute creatures.

This game is absolutely magical, until it isn't. It just becomes a boring grind after you unlock slime science, and at that point you're not accomplishing much else except walking to the end. I did not hate this game. I loved it for a while, but you quickly run out of things to do, and upgrade, and everything optional feels like an absolute chore. For example, you can craft pumps to get exclusive materials, but they are limited use, so you need to spend more and more stuff in order to get the most out of the system, you can build a teleporter but you're still limited by how much items you can hold at a time. Something as simple as a FIFTH item slot would have dramatically improved this game. The lack of inventory space makes this game a chore. Another great example is how you can build a silo, but the silo can only hold four items, you have to waste a precious plot on your ranch just to hold FOUR items, and not even in an unlimited capacity. The truly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing about this system is everything you'd want to save goes right into the forge, and the only thing worth storing in the silo is extra fruit. If the silo let you store an unlimited capacity of different items up to a set amount this frustration would have been alleiviated immensely. The entire game is full of contradictory systems like this.
I still liked it though.

In a future
Where man lives in constant fear of slavers and mechs
An unlikely duo can make a difference
Trip is a young woman, her skills include: hacking, giving orders, and causing distractions.
Monkey is a bit of an enigma, and thanks to a headband, is under Trip's control. He's the character you play as, and you'll spend much of the game climbing around, keeping an eye out for Trip, and crushing mechs with your staff. There are even rare moments where he can use a hoverboard (which he refers to as a "cloud") to cross over lakes and such.
The parellels to the classic Chinese novel "Journey to the West" are pretty obvious.
As an action-adventure game, Enslaved leads towards the simplistic side of things. Well, perhaps simplistic isn't the word I'm looking for. Overly approachable, casual, automated, ehhh I'm better off just explaining it. Enslaved is one of those games that would have been very difficult a generation or three ago. Let's use Tomb Raider for comparison. The original game featured some difficult platforming segments. You had to account for several different possibilities. Is Lara moving fast enough? Did she jump at the right moment? Are there obstacles nearby? Fast-forward through numerous sequels and now you don't have to worry about where and when to jump. If you're facing the right direction, Lara will always make the jump. Enslaved pushes this game-design even further. You can't die from falling even if you wanted to, Monkey won't allow it. I think I managed a falling death once, and that was by getting zapped out of the air by a Mech. It was more of a fluke than anything.
There is a lot of fighting to be done in this game, but it's typically very trivial. I have to wonder how Capcom decided Ninja Theory was a good fit for Devil May Cry after playing through this game. While not quite a button-masher, Enslaved's combat doesn't require much effort. Enemies fall into certain camps. There are the close-range slashers, the long-range shooters, shockers have some mid-range ability, sometimes they have shields. The strategy rarely deviates from "hit them really hard" or "blast them with plasma and/or stun shots". Also, there's not much in the way of stylish maneuvers. Monkey does some flipping and spinning around, but he's not pulling off any Dante-esque combos. None of the mechs survive long enough anyway. I made the mistake of playing this game on the easy difficulty. Not only did Monkey never die (in combat), he never lost more than 1/5th of his health. It's best to jump straight to the hard difficulty, which doesn't make much of a difference aside from everyone doing a bit more damage. Most of my deaths came from mines.
With easy combat and platforming, Enslaved thrives almost entirely on its other aspects. The locales in this game are pretty neat to visit, and there's some nice attention to detail in this post-apocalyptic land. The pacing is also effectively done, with a nice balance between combat, puzzle-solving, and a hint of exploration. Some credit should also be given to the chapter setup. This game is broken up into 14 chapters, and most of them can be completed in 15-20 minutes. You can play for a fairly short amount of time, and still make quite a bit of progress. I prefer this over having something like 5 chapters that take an hour or more to get through.
As an action game, Enslaved is bound to disappoint. It does work as more of an adventure game though. The world is impressively-realized, the characters (all three of them) are well-done, and for the most part it's a breezy experience that you just take in.
Three characters? Oh right...can't forget about Pigsy.
This dude is another reference to Journey to the West. While human, Pigsy is also part...mecha pig. He's a fat slob with an eye for Trip, and he wears socks with his sandals. Unlike his inspiration, this little piggy prefers a sniper rifle over an 11,000 pound rake. In the latter half of the game he's the comic relief, and he ain't too bad at it. He also has his own quest. This was originally DLC in the console version of Enslaved. Pigsy's Perfect 10 follows his misadventures in building a new friend. As I said, Enslaved has three characters, it's a pretty lonely world.
Unlike Monkey, Pigsy isn't very tough, punch or stab him a couple times and he's a goner. In order to survive, you have to sneak around, make your shots count, and take advantage of various gadgets. Unlike the main game, there's actually a bit of creativity and depth that goes into each encounter. Simply blasting everyone is never the answer, but you can distract them, stun them, seduce them(?!) to fight your enemies, or simply destroy them with a bomb. While this quest does run a bit long, I think it does a good job at providing something different from the rest of Enslaved. The similarities to cover-based shooters are apparent, but PP10 does enough to stand out. This is pretty impressive for a DLC adventure.

I'd heard lots of things about Dark Souls 2 before going into it. I'd heard things like it not being worth the full price, but worth it with any discount. I'd heard things like that the pc-controls were horrible, and yes they were, (if you don't use some autohotkey script for these pc-controls I feel sorry for you) but once that problem was fixed, I was mostly impressed. The game makes some bad decisions that shouldn't be made after the game's predecessor, and ultimately it felt easier, and a little bit cheaper (the bad kind of cheap).
However, its length is impressive, and the amount of exploration you can do in this game is amazing. Shortcut placement on the other hand, is horrible here compared to Dark Souls and Demon Souls, and the number of bonfires in the game is mostly ridiculous. (Especially considering you can warp to every single one...)
On the birght side, Dark Souls 2 gets atmosphere right, and has its own moments like the memorable silver knights on the outside of Anor Londo. And some of the areas are really impressive from a gameplay PoV. Most notably the Lost Bastille and the DLC area. Also, there's weapons. TONS of weapons. And most of them have something special about them if you look carefully. Sadly, the concept of secret tail-drops and the like has been completely abandoned, and shows that this game was made with less attention to detail in bossfights than its predecessor, however that is only a small problem.
If you want to buy this game, don't you dare to play the game without the DLC! The Crown of the sunken King gets so many things right (although there's still no tail-drops) its almost scary. If it was just the base game, you should probably wait for it to be on sale, however if you want the DLC as well, its probably worth the full price.

Being a major fan of the series, It was a must for me, but even so, let's keep an analytical point of view on this.
The transition between Dark Souls and Dark Souls II, it's huge, simply put.
The devs promissed a good port, on time for the PC release this time around, and they delivered.
60 fps, constant, I have no troubles running this. My hat is off to you, developers.
In terms of story, it's pretty gripping as the last one and it's told to you in a discreet manner. Note that you do not have to play the first game to understand the second, yet, there are references made and characters that "live on", sort to speak.
The combat this time around is way more fluid and less staggering. You've got more ways to fight your opponents now, as dual wielding swords, wich is the new addition to the game.
You also have, instead of 7 New Games as the old Dark Souls, you've got 15 this time around, to more and more baddy baddy action. (Note : You can do New Game+ on each game as much as you'd like, but the cap is 15 and from there on out, the difficulty will no longer escalate.)
You've got alot of ways to customize the game in graphical terms now, the access around the game is way less clunky than the first game.
And now, finally, even though the most optimal way is to play with a controller, you can play with the keyboard and mouse if you wish. You can rebind keys and much as you'd like.
There's also a new adition wich is Regional Play and Non-Regional. You can enable and disable this at any given time aswell as the inbuilt voice chat in the game.
As for bad points, the game promissed one thing in it's trailers, and that was interaction with light in dark places. You can even notice throughout the game, several places to light a torch. I do believe it was due to problems with the aesthetic of the game that this was cancelled out. Light still makes alot of difference in some places, but you can do just fine without.
The infinite spawning of the enemies as it was back in Dark Souls, it's no longer present. They still respawn, but after about... 15 times or more, they will eventually disappear. This can be considered a "medium" point. I actually thought it would ruin most of the game, but turns out, you won't actually feel any difference at all. There's always the factor that you can just add in Bonfire Aesthetics to a certain bonfire and they will respawn again. So, I consider this a neutral point.
Overall, the game is great and as always, a pain in your backside. I guarantee you will enjoy it.

Originally, I played this on the 360 when it first came out and thoroughly enjoyed it, despite a few odd decisions concerning the plot and the pacing in the latter third of the game.  I'm glad to say I'm enjoying it just as much this time round too.
I was worried that knowing exactly where to go and what to do would take some of the game's bite away, but so far, this hasn't been the case.  This is undoubtably thanks to the alien AI and the intelligent score that ramps up the music and makes subtle changes to the background noise whenever the alien is nearby.  The environment and VFX add to the replayability too. It looked better than it had any right to on the 360, but even running on my modest PC (Sapphire R7 260x 2gb) it looks beautiful. The lighting is perfect and the artists really did their homework when they were desiging the environments.  If you loved the look of the 1979 film, you will love the look of this game.   It's well optimised too, all the settings bar AA are turned up to 11 and it rarely drops below 55fps, usually staying at a flat 60.
Like I said, later in the game, there are a few plot points, mainly based around the alien's life cycle, that will have you scratching your head.  The mission design is sketchy at best too, by this point.  CA did a great job of building tension initially, scaring the living p*ss out of you with some great set pieces, followed by AI driven, barely scripted hunt sections, then taking their foot off the gas at the right moment to give the player a break.  Somewhere around two thirds in, however, this goes a bit wrong.  The missions become slightly irritating fetch-and-fix quests, some of which require A LOT of backtracking.  While this is going on, the tension/relief balance goes out of the window (airlock?), so the end of this game can be a little frustratng to get through.
That said, the failings of this game are minor, when taken in the context of its whole.  Simply being in that beautifully designed environment, with this singularly challenging, pseudo-intelligent enemy, is enough to justify the great reviews this game recieved.

Borderlands 2 was initially released in 2012, and I haven’t played it until now in 2016. Purchasing the Game of the Year edition, all the DLC included except for a few customize heads, which may or not be worth the purchase if you desire. Each are about $1 a piece, more or less. But that is depending on how far you want to take your customization and uniqueness for your character.

Now, as I said, I am playing this game years after its release, and I am thoroughly enjoying it! From the story to optional side missions, to exploring, to finding those perfect weapon combos, to customizing skins for the vehicles and player, and of course to the intense combat. The game just seems to keep me entertained, and I keep finding reasons to keep going. The game is very good at getting you hooked, and retaining your attention.
Story 10/10-
You are a notorious vault hunter, in search of treasures on the planet Pandora. You will be prompted to help the Crimson Raiders in the city of Sanctuary, and make some quirky, yet useful allies to aid you with your struggle against a powerful enemy, “Handsome Jack”, and the billion dollar corporation, Hyperion.
Gameplay 8/10
The game is a first person shooter, and the environment is vividly immersive. I find myself thinking I will do just more mission, and suddenly find that time had escaped me. Seriously, there’s so much to do in the game. The main story, side missions, collectibles, different weapons with different abilities. Each character has their own perks and different play styles. While I have test played a couple of the characters out, I find myself building and focusing on decking out my main character.
Mind you, I have just recently started playing Borderlands 2… and I have dumped hours into it, and I feel I have come close to completing the game. And things that I have already done, I don’t mind doing another run by myself or with others.
NOW- the only reason why I am not giving the game play a perfect 10, is because some of the side missions can be a bit tedious. Going back n forth from point to another… much like how most MMORPGs are done. It’s not often but it does happen. Also, I felt the quest tracking could have a been a bit better or improved, instead of manually having to track and follow your quests for the regions- I feel like a log would have been much more efficient and less time consuming.
Visual/Sound 10/10-
The graphics are not realistic but rather have its own original art style which can best be compared to comic book art. It is beautiful. It is unique. It fits the game perfectly. The music is pretty dope and fits whatever seems to going on at the moment. Sounds, narration & dialogue are awesome, witty, and comical. I don’t care what anyone says, Claptrap is cool asf. Lol.
The environments are fun to explore, and with how big each free roam map is;  I often forget how detailed and active the camps and dungeons can be.
Multiplayer 10/10
One of the coolest features is being able to run with a pack in the search of loot, dungeon crawling and mission completing. The difficulty increases, and the loot (allegedly) gets better. I say allegedly, because I definitely found my rarer items on solo play through. But still its awesome to team up with a squad and mow through bandits, fight over loot, and duel to see who is the better vault hunter
----------------------------------------
The game is very fun, action packed, has absolutely no pacing problems, and I imagine will keep me entranced for a extensive time in the future.
Recommend? Y/N?
Of course, I recommend the game. Buy it full price, or buy it on sale. Buy it for yourself, or get a pack and play with friends. Just get it, and enjoy it.
Happy Vault Hunting,

So, I hated this game at first...
I've never been into a MMO before, and I went into it with a mindset of "♥♥♥♥ YEAH! MULTIPLAYER SKYRIM LETS GO" - In short don't do that. This isn't going to be like playing Skyrim, Oblivion, Morrowind.
It is when it all comes down to the core an MMO, it's set in Tamriel, it sounds like Tamriel and the storylines feel like an Elder Scrolls game. However being an MMO, it has a lot of grindy MMO style quests. And don't get me wrong, it's bewildering at first, all these mechanics, all these places to go....and before the 'One Tamriel' update if you chose the wrong faction, you were screwed, in a place all on your own surrounded by all these people who are WAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAY higher level than you. But thankfully they changed all of that. The game scales now, so you can rock up to a dungeon with your level V300 mate, and still have some fun slicing up enemies.
So I saw a friend playing the other day, and spent a few hours installing this to join him (By the way its like 70 Gig...If you have slow internet prepare for a few days of download), I got back on it after not playing for 14 months, but this time I was playing with a friend who was already Veteran Level 250, So I was in luck, he introduced me to everything and I got used to all the deconstructing of equipment to get my blacksmithing up, showed me about dungeons and bascially got me to enjoy the grind. I think my previous time was a bit lackluster because I got dropped in the middle of the Aldmeri Dominion on my own, without any of my friends. So I left.
Now I know what I'm doing, and keep in mind I usually hate MMO's never played WoW or anything like that, this is the first one. I'm enjoying myself, I'm triple digits into this game time-wise and I don't see it stopping now. We've made a guild for noobies. To help them out, and get them to enjoy the game also. Because the community is nice...but you still get the elitist ♥♥♥♥s from any competitive game kicking you out of dungeons because you're only level 14. But you won't get that when you're in a guild, having people to play with and explain all the mechanics did help, a lot. I've even gone as far as to buy this AGAIN on steam just to collect my hours and so on.
Add-ons are awesome being able to mod basic features of the game to help with information and quality of life improvements is a must. I'll provide an essential mods pack if any of you wish to know.
For those of you who actually got this far into this, well done. I didn't think I'd keep you captivated long enough to get to the end.
If any of you are new to the game, on EU server and would like to join a guild to show you the way, add me or visit our
and join us on teamspeak, or just message us in game @diseasedcrow.
But all in all if you like Elder Scrolls and you think you want to try this, just do, I'm glad I gave it a second chance.

The testosterone rich action films of the 1980s and early 90s have no doubt inspired generations of game developers, providing a metric ton of material to repackage into shooters and hack and slash titles both contemporary and classic. Of course, over time those sources of inpiration have become fodder for parody and irrevrent jabs at what was once considered the pinnacle of awesome. Broforce has risen like a phoenix from the faded pixels of Contra and Metal Slug wearing the war paint of Stallone and Schwarzenegger. This side scroller cropped up on steam's early acces page three years ago and has finally emerged as a finished product, poised to flex it's biceps and set the world on fire in the name of bromance.
Broforce places you in the boots of any number of parodies of iconic action film characters from the past 35 years of action and sci-fi cinema. There is Brochete, Rambro, Snake Broskin, Brobocop and 26 other bros ready to burn, blast and blow through any anti 'Merican, ski mask wearing, AK wielding meat bag. Select a level, warm up you hammies, decorate the environment with lead and get to the chopper—wash rinse and repeat until every American can sleep soundly at night knowing that the bros have mulched every terrorist on earth.
Broforce plays like a mash up between Metal Slug, Contra and Terraria, forcing players to blow through various enemy types and rescue hostages in a completely destructable environment. Each time you spawn you take control of a random Bro. Rescuing hostages unlocks additional characters and each one has a unique weapon and a special attack with finite uses. The Brominator wields a mini gun that has to wind up before it fires and has nasty recoil that sends the player backwards. Ash Broliams has his short range boom stick that excels at shredding the environment and terrorist scumbags. Taking control over random Bros keeps players on their toes but it can also be annoying when you have character that is ill suited to the task at hand. Fighting bosses with melee focused characters can get irritating and some characters can completely break levels by making them too easy. Cherry Broling for instance has an assault rifle for a leg which can be used to fly short distances. This allows her to fly over enemys in relative safety giving enemies a lead shower or simply skipping obstacles altogether. Also, when in multiplayer, randomly swapping between character can make it difficult to keep track of who you are controlling. This leads to unnecassary deaths and some frustration. As it should be, broforce is a chaotic game and this is only magnified by adding more players to the mix. The end result is that anything more than two players becomes a handicap since your real life Bros will  be too busy felxing to notice they are blowing up barrels right next to you or causing large rocks to collapse on your player's dome. Also, when cutscenes displaying newly unlocked characters pause the action mid game ruining your rhythym and ultimately getting you killed. It's all good fun, but don't expect to progress as a well oiled unit. Also, initiating a multiplayer bromance involves navigating a terrible lobby that doesn't display the host nor who is currently in the lobby.
The real problem with Broforce is that it's mechanics are more flaccid phallus than bulging biceps and when the novelty of it's screaming rock soundtrack and goofy characters wares off you have a game that doesn't offer any challenge in terms of platforming, the gunplay has little variety since enemies are not very dynamic and  the destructible environments allow you to cheese you way through the game if you feel inclined. The main campaign I only lasts a few hours and there is a map editor to tinker with and other players creations can be downloaded but there just isn't much to ensure that the gameplay remains compelling. It's not kind of stuff that will make a god damned sexual tyrannosaurus out of anyone...
The visuals in Broforce do a great job of keeping the tone light and when all hell breaks loose, it looks fantastic to see a Jackson Pollack painting of bloody and fiery pixels engulf the screen. Vehicle designs have the same stubby cartoonish quality as the art in Metal Slug characters are also cartoony and awesomely ridiculous. It's a shame that the game offers so few environment types. The rock tunes give the game that 80's action film feel but over extended gameplay sessions they can be obnoxious.
Broforce is a solid title that is good for a few laughs and will tickle the nostalgia bone of players who grew up on games like Contra and Metal Slug and please movie buffs with it's large cast of action flick inspired bros. However, it relies too heavily on it's novelty offering up mediocre gameplay. Anyone looking for a game relying on the cheesy testosterone fueled attitude of 1980s action cinema would probably be better served by paying Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon. Broforce is a solid game that just doesn't have what it takes to live up to the classics it tries to emulate.

TL:DR For $15.00 I got about 17 hours of gameplay before I beat the game and I enjoyed every minute of it.
Try out the expendebros (I think it's free). The gameplay is the same. If you like expendebros, you will enjoy Broforce. Wish it was a little bit longer though and many people online tend to shy away from custom made maps unless it's password only, so create levels within the editor with that in mind. Once you beat normal mode, you can play a harder difficulty where enemies take more damage and react faster (more fun and more incentive to play stealth when solo). Ironbro mode is also a fun timekiller and forces you to learn the ins and outs of the character (which is not too hard of a task.. Except Anderbro... He takes a while to learn) because once your character dies, it will either switch you to a reserve character or if you don't have one, it's game over. It's extremely fun and when you play it on the harder difficulty, it forces you to think outside of the box instead of running in and unloading. I can't beat the hard difficulty on ironbro mode, maybe you can.

This game is a long time favourite of mine. I've played it on and off, since it's release. I know some people complain about it being 'absolutely broken' bla bla bla... booring.. boring.. boring.. I wonder how much they actually played HW1 in particular? Because the UI in the first version annoys me terribly, and have done so since it came out. This remastered UI is much improved. So much so, that I don't actually mind the odd misses here and there. Seriously, if you want to complain about the UI, play the original version again. Let's be honest here.. the first version UI is really not good. Switching screens entirely for one.. etc.. I won't engage in that debate. It is focusing on the entire wrong thing.
Many of the bugs other complain about are also present in the original. Why? Because believe it or not, they deliberately minimized changing things in the game. Bugs included.. just because some people just can't take a breath without complaining about things being totally 'broken', 'unfinished', 'total letdown' etc.. those people are as expected as the sun rising up in the morning.  So, let's forget about that nonsense, and actually talk about the game..
The story is fantastic, the game was graphically stellar when it came out, and what they have done now, is to lift it back up to a similar level again. If you read books with art from Chris Foss etc.. you know what to expect, It is that good. I know of very few games that stood the test of time like this game. They are: Tron V2.0, Supreme commander, Quake 2, Medal of Honor, Doom, Fallout 1 and 2, Knights of the old republic, Master of Orion 2,  Nexus : The jupiter incident (A true gem, if you missed this, pick it up. It makes me incredibly sad that people entirely missed the opportunity to back a sequel by the original team and actors.. just recently) Half life and of course Homeworld. There is only one game out there that even comes close to Homeworld, and that is Nexus (possibly one of the most underrated games in history of gaming, and nearly as great looking)
But the story holds well, today. So much so, that in all this time (about 18 years now) hardly any RTS game have come close to this game. 18 Years?? It boggles the mind to even think about. I won't talk about the story, I would spoil it if you haven't played it. But you really owe it to yourself to play this game. There are so few good games coming out in all these years (and yes, I am talking about story) that I can mention them by heart. The most recent example being 'The vanishing of Ethan Carter' (absolutely brilliant) but I digress, look at this game (if you already played the original) as a graphical update. Because this is essentially what it is. Like I mentioned, you will find bugs from the orginal game still present. And I hope they don't fix those, because for better or worse, those bugs are part of the game now.
If you haven't played the game before, pick it up at once, and enjoy a good piece of gaming history. Try the original if you so please, but the art, and especially sound quality, is so much better that it probably won't take too long before you return to the updated version. Some of the original developers were involved in making sure this update stayed as true to the original as possible. The only thing I really miss is the orginal soundtrack by Yes (the Ladder) but you can blame the music industry for that one (who else is so stuck under a rock, that they don't mind messing up a piece of history for an extra dollar. Pray to Mammon gents!)
I also won't have a pro and cons list, it is pointless in this case. The game is 18 years old. It got reviewed enough. Now, get it and enjoy a good game. Load up some favourite beverage, and commit the hours to play this game. You won't regret it.

Black Mesa has potential but the design flaws are just too much for me.
(I've never played any Half Life game before, so I judge this game without any nostalgic factor.)
PROs:
- Production value is good. The graphics are starting to look dated but they still hold up pretty well.
- The set pieces are interesting enough to keep you engaged (if you're not turned off by the design flaws, which I'll explain).
- No game breaking bugs. The performance is good on Win10.
- It also supports controller, in case you prefer controller. No button prompt for controller though.
NEUTRAL:
- There's no character progression or weapon upgrade of any kind. You just pick up new weapons along the way, but this is actually an old game so that's acceptable.
- The story doesn't go anywhere or answer anything much.
CONs:
I read that it follows HL1 very closely; therefore, the old FPS design flaws are also there.
I can see why HL1 was considered ground-breaking back in the old days but some of the designs just don't hold up well now.
***
First:
The visual indication for interactive objects aren't clear and there's no waypoint system.
To quote the Angry Video Game Nerd, "This is one of those Where-the-♥♥♥♥-Do-I-Go kind of games." It's often unclear where to go and what to do. FPS games have evolved pass this, and that's for the best. I don't consider waypoint system in newer FPSs hand-holding. It saves you from wasting your time and spare you some serious motion sickness.
***
Second:
Soldier programming.
While you get all the distracting screen effects when shot, enemy soldiers don't even flinch. Your bullets have no impact at all. Enemies just take it like Terminators on steroid and keep shooting at you. I'm totally okay with bullet-sponge enemies in Shooter/RPGs like The Division or Borderlands, but generic human soldiers that take a shotgun shell in the chest at point-blank range and still stand just won't do in a traditional FPS.
Talk about shooting, those soldiers shoot like Hawkeye. Their MP5s hit you with the accuracy and precision of sniper rifles from far across the scene.
Switching the difficulty to easy doesn't help much since soldiers still behave the same, except doing less damage.
Plus, those tiny jumping aliens that try so hard to hump Gordon's face are annoying as ♥♥♥♥.
***
Third:
There are platforming and underwater sections. That's never a good idea in an FPS.
***
CONCLUSION:
Is Black Mesa a bad game? No, but it doesn't offer anything extraordinary that would make me want to sit through the pain either. So I can't recommend it.
If you're dying to know what all the fuss is about with HL1, I recommend getting the original HL1 instead. It goes on sale for only a dollar or less.

particularly with the lack of any multiplayer at all, it can quickly become repetitive, you can vary the number of AI but all that really does is vary the amount of action going on at one time, rather than promoting larger movements of groups and different tactics.
further more veteran FPS players may often find the game not challenging at all, with everything from infantry to tanks pretty much a breeze to take out.
The UI is forgivably simplistic, although sometimes has no reticle to aim a vehicle weapon with (see heli gunner), no indicator of vehicle integrity and a few other minor issues.
Some of the most irritation comes from the match settings constantly resetting, with no way to dynamically generate a game, you always have to punch in the settings and remember what works best for each map.
The summary of my complaints: Vehicle combat, especially air combat is too easy, occasionally infantry combat is to easy with enemies almost never seeking cover, finally there is no depth to gameplay, ultra simplistic vehicle mechanics that take no time to learn (for veteran FPS players) and no variety in vehicle weapons.
I understand custom maps lend a large part to the game, but even the modding doesn't stretch far, with maps having to stipulate settings for optimal gameplay, with no significant changes beyond cosmetic.
This game has great potential but at the moment its overpriced, for the amount of re-playability and the lack of multiplayer it should be half its current price.

I keep on reading reviews about how hard Fuse is to navigate, but I've found it to be very simple and straight forward to use.
However the character import features is virtually useless because Fuse won't load most non-Fuse .obj character files.
The software also has very limited hair and clothing options available, and not a whole lot of sbsar texture options either.
While it's very easy to create a custom face and body, it's seriously let down by not being very compatible with files from other related software.
But it is FREE at the moment, so it's hard to complain about something that costs nothing to try.

In Fuse you get a bunch of pre-made body parts and clothes that you can (mostly) mold and modify, including those of a couple TF2 characters.
Without some prior modeling experience (or Sims 4 experience I suppose) the push-pull method of changing the model parts you hash together can be confusing. I feel having a secondary camera view instead of having options take up half the screen would help with this immensely, as would having some built-in lighting and background options. The default clothing options are well-made and can also help see abnormalities when editing the model.
While I think Fuse is good for making the pre-made models resemble a character or person, it's not going to help anyone much if they're looking for something accurate. I found the limitations to the stretching of the models unsatisfying, and the built-in options for hair and skin abnormalities very finite.
If you're looking to mess around for a while or to get a good 3-D reference to aid you in your own modeling, Fuse is good for you. Otherwise, I don't think it's all that worthwhile.

Originally, I played this on the 360 when it first came out and thoroughly enjoyed it, despite a few odd decisions concerning the plot and the pacing in the latter third of the game.  I'm glad to say I'm enjoying it just as much this time round too.
I was worried that knowing exactly where to go and what to do would take some of the game's bite away, but so far, this hasn't been the case.  This is undoubtably thanks to the alien AI and the intelligent score that ramps up the music and makes subtle changes to the background noise whenever the alien is nearby.  The environment and VFX add to the replayability too. It looked better than it had any right to on the 360, but even running on my modest PC (Sapphire R7 260x 2gb) it looks beautiful. The lighting is perfect and the artists really did their homework when they were desiging the environments.  If you loved the look of the 1979 film, you will love the look of this game.   It's well optimised too, all the settings bar AA are turned up to 11 and it rarely drops below 55fps, usually staying at a flat 60.
Like I said, later in the game, there are a few plot points, mainly based around the alien's life cycle, that will have you scratching your head.  The mission design is sketchy at best too, by this point.  CA did a great job of building tension initially, scaring the living p*ss out of you with some great set pieces, followed by AI driven, barely scripted hunt sections, then taking their foot off the gas at the right moment to give the player a break.  Somewhere around two thirds in, however, this goes a bit wrong.  The missions become slightly irritating fetch-and-fix quests, some of which require A LOT of backtracking.  While this is going on, the tension/relief balance goes out of the window (airlock?), so the end of this game can be a little frustratng to get through.
That said, the failings of this game are minor, when taken in the context of its whole.  Simply being in that beautifully designed environment, with this singularly challenging, pseudo-intelligent enemy, is enough to justify the great reviews this game recieved.

Homeworld Remastered Collection is a modern HD remake of two classic sci-fi real-time strategy games, Homeworld 1 and 2. Homeworld played like many other RTS games at the time: you'll command your star fleet, harvest resources, research technologies to build more ships, and attack other enemy fleets. However, in Homeworld, the game took place entirely in three-dimensional space, resulting in units not just moving horizontally, but also vertically, adding an extra tactical layer to the combat. Watching the combat between large groups of spaceships flying around each other was a sight to behold back then and now it looks even more amazing in the Remastered Collection. Gearbox has updated the visuals to modern standards and ships now have an incredible amount of detail. Even with the enhanced graphics, the game still manages to not be too demanding on hardware and it runs smoothly without any major stability issues. The user interface has also been updated for both games and it feels cleaner and more usable now. They even remastered the audio and the cutscenes with voice overs and music sounding much clearer and the animations looking more high-definition. The entire package isn't without its faults, however.
The remastered version of Homeworld 1 feels like it was ported over to the enhanced Homeworld 2 engine without properly adjusting and balancing the campaign for it. Ships won't stay in formation when attacking (might be just a bug for now), researching technologies costs resource units now, some prices for constructing ships have changed,  ship AI behavior seems to glitch out at times, and other minor differences. Worst of all, the remastered campaign seems to have borrowed the auto-balancing difficulty from the Homeworld 2 campaign. This might result in frustratingly difficult situations in some missions if you did too well in the last mission. Still, none of this is game-breaking and some might still enjoy the game and only have a few problems with it (especially those who have never played the game in the first place). All of this is sure to annoy veteran Homeworld players and hopefully Gearbox can fix some of it soon. At least the package inculdes the original "Classic" version of Homeworld 1 which is still very playable and fun by today's standards, even with the dated visuals.
Homeworld 2 Remastered seems to be pretty well intact, but that's not really a surprise given the fact that it's running on an enhanced version of the same engine. You can play the "classic" version of Homeworld 2 if you want, but considering the remastered version is the exact same game with better graphics and presentation, there's not much of a reason to go back now (except for some Skirmish mode differences).  It's pretty much there for preservation and it's still a nice thing to have in the package.
Which Brings me to the multiplayer mode. It's a good thing the multiplayer still has a "BETA" label attached to it because it does feel a bit unfinished. The multiplayer suite for the Remastered Collection is a mixture of the multiplayer modes from Homeworld 1 and 2. You can pit the two Homeworld 1 factions against the two Homeworld 2 factions now, but this results in some balance issues. The HW1 factions are underpowered compared to the HW2 factions right now and the game feels more like HW2 multiplayer with HW1 factions patched in rather than a true mix of the two games. For right now, just use HW2 factions until Gearbox decides to fix the balance issues.
Despite some blemishes in the Homeworld 1 Remastered campaign and the multiplayer mode, I'd still recommend the Remastered Collection simply because there's nothing quite like Homeworld on the market right now and it's the first time the series has been on a digital platform. The gameplay still holds up very well to this day and the storylines for both games are still just as good as they once were. I'd even say this package is worth it just for Homeworld 1 Classic and Homeworld 2 Remastered alone. If you've never experienced either game and you have an interest in story-driven RTS games or massive space battles in general, you owe it to yourself to play Homeworld.
Just like the original only better looking.  Highly recommend!

The testosterone rich action films of the 1980s and early 90s have no doubt inspired generations of game developers, providing a metric ton of material to repackage into shooters and hack and slash titles both contemporary and classic. Of course, over time those sources of inpiration have become fodder for parody and irrevrent jabs at what was once considered the pinnacle of awesome. Broforce has risen like a phoenix from the faded pixels of Contra and Metal Slug wearing the war paint of Stallone and Schwarzenegger. This side scroller cropped up on steam's early acces page three years ago and has finally emerged as a finished product, poised to flex it's biceps and set the world on fire in the name of bromance.
Broforce places you in the boots of any number of parodies of iconic action film characters from the past 35 years of action and sci-fi cinema. There is Brochete, Rambro, Snake Broskin, Brobocop and 26 other bros ready to burn, blast and blow through any anti 'Merican, ski mask wearing, AK wielding meat bag. Select a level, warm up you hammies, decorate the environment with lead and get to the chopper—wash rinse and repeat until every American can sleep soundly at night knowing that the bros have mulched every terrorist on earth.
Broforce plays like a mash up between Metal Slug, Contra and Terraria, forcing players to blow through various enemy types and rescue hostages in a completely destructable environment. Each time you spawn you take control of a random Bro. Rescuing hostages unlocks additional characters and each one has a unique weapon and a special attack with finite uses. The Brominator wields a mini gun that has to wind up before it fires and has nasty recoil that sends the player backwards. Ash Broliams has his short range boom stick that excels at shredding the environment and terrorist scumbags. Taking control over random Bros keeps players on their toes but it can also be annoying when you have character that is ill suited to the task at hand. Fighting bosses with melee focused characters can get irritating and some characters can completely break levels by making them too easy. Cherry Broling for instance has an assault rifle for a leg which can be used to fly short distances. This allows her to fly over enemys in relative safety giving enemies a lead shower or simply skipping obstacles altogether. Also, when in multiplayer, randomly swapping between character can make it difficult to keep track of who you are controlling. This leads to unnecassary deaths and some frustration. As it should be, broforce is a chaotic game and this is only magnified by adding more players to the mix. The end result is that anything more than two players becomes a handicap since your real life Bros will  be too busy felxing to notice they are blowing up barrels right next to you or causing large rocks to collapse on your player's dome. Also, when cutscenes displaying newly unlocked characters pause the action mid game ruining your rhythym and ultimately getting you killed. It's all good fun, but don't expect to progress as a well oiled unit. Also, initiating a multiplayer bromance involves navigating a terrible lobby that doesn't display the host nor who is currently in the lobby.
The real problem with Broforce is that it's mechanics are more flaccid phallus than bulging biceps and when the novelty of it's screaming rock soundtrack and goofy characters wares off you have a game that doesn't offer any challenge in terms of platforming, the gunplay has little variety since enemies are not very dynamic and  the destructible environments allow you to cheese you way through the game if you feel inclined. The main campaign I only lasts a few hours and there is a map editor to tinker with and other players creations can be downloaded but there just isn't much to ensure that the gameplay remains compelling. It's not kind of stuff that will make a god damned sexual tyrannosaurus out of anyone...
The visuals in Broforce do a great job of keeping the tone light and when all hell breaks loose, it looks fantastic to see a Jackson Pollack painting of bloody and fiery pixels engulf the screen. Vehicle designs have the same stubby cartoonish quality as the art in Metal Slug characters are also cartoony and awesomely ridiculous. It's a shame that the game offers so few environment types. The rock tunes give the game that 80's action film feel but over extended gameplay sessions they can be obnoxious.
Broforce is a solid title that is good for a few laughs and will tickle the nostalgia bone of players who grew up on games like Contra and Metal Slug and please movie buffs with it's large cast of action flick inspired bros. However, it relies too heavily on it's novelty offering up mediocre gameplay. Anyone looking for a game relying on the cheesy testosterone fueled attitude of 1980s action cinema would probably be better served by paying Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon. Broforce is a solid game that just doesn't have what it takes to live up to the classics it tries to emulate.

TL:DR For $15.00 I got about 17 hours of gameplay before I beat the game and I enjoyed every minute of it.

Black Mesa has potential but the design flaws are just too much for me.
(I've never played any Half Life game before, so I judge this game without any nostalgic factor.)
PROs:
- Production value is good. The graphics are starting to look dated but they still hold up pretty well.
- The set pieces are interesting enough to keep you engaged (if you're not turned off by the design flaws, which I'll explain).
- No game breaking bugs. The performance is good on Win10.
- It also supports controller, in case you prefer controller. No button prompt for controller though.
NEUTRAL:
- There's no character progression or weapon upgrade of any kind. You just pick up new weapons along the way, but this is actually an old game so that's acceptable.
- The story doesn't go anywhere or answer anything much.
CONs:
I read that it follows HL1 very closely; therefore, the old FPS design flaws are also there.
I can see why HL1 was considered ground-breaking back in the old days but some of the designs just don't hold up well now.
***
First:
The visual indication for interactive objects aren't clear and there's no waypoint system.
To quote the Angry Video Game Nerd, "This is one of those Where-the-♥♥♥♥-Do-I-Go kind of games." It's often unclear where to go and what to do. FPS games have evolved pass this, and that's for the best. I don't consider waypoint system in newer FPSs hand-holding. It saves you from wasting your time and spare you some serious motion sickness.
***
Second:
Soldier programming.
While you get all the distracting screen effects when shot, enemy soldiers don't even flinch. Your bullets have no impact at all. Enemies just take it like Terminators on steroid and keep shooting at you. I'm totally okay with bullet-sponge enemies in Shooter/RPGs like The Division or Borderlands, but generic human soldiers that take a shotgun shell in the chest at point-blank range and still stand just won't do in a traditional FPS.
Talk about shooting, those soldiers shoot like Hawkeye. Their MP5s hit you with the accuracy and precision of sniper rifles from far across the scene.
Switching the difficulty to easy doesn't help much since soldiers still behave the same, except doing less damage.
Plus, those tiny jumping aliens that try so hard to hump Gordon's face are annoying as ♥♥♥♥.
***
Third:
There are platforming and underwater sections. That's never a good idea in an FPS.
***
CONCLUSION:
Is Black Mesa a bad game? No, but it doesn't offer anything extraordinary that would make me want to sit through the pain either. So I can't recommend it.
If you're dying to know what all the fuss is about with HL1, I recommend getting the original HL1 instead. It goes on sale for only a dollar or less.

The character creation is extremely basic. You don't get to edit it completely, only what the sliders say you can. Although there is plenty of sliders for different sections of the body, such as the fingers and teeth, it lacks the freedom of creating your character from scratch. You can only make humanoid characters as far as I am aware.
There's a feature to upload characters made to the Mixamo website for rigging and animating. This sounds fantastic on paper, but you really need to make sure this actually works. I managed to get one character rigged and exported to Gmod, but if I tried to upload another character I would upload it half-way before it suddenly stops and tells me I'm not connected to the internet with a error 99. I've tried to get help with this, but there is absolutely nothing telling me how to resolve this.
That continued for two days solid. The Mixamo website was still up and operational, so it seemed to be a client-side issue. I can't tell if this is a line of script not responding, a missing file or simply the fact I'm running Vista. I meet every system requirement except for the OS which doesn't seem to impede the software in any way.
In conclusion, I don't recommend this. If you want to design a character but have no knowledge on how to make one from scratch I'd recommend learning how to instead. Trust me, making a model from scratch will not only work out better most of the time, it will also be more satisfying.

Ok before anyone reads, know that I have never played Demon Souls, or Dark Souls 1.  DS2 was given to me as a gift or I likely would never have played this one either.  I had always heard that these games were very hard and I usually do not equate fun with hard to play.
Anway...
The first couple of hours on this game were a true test to my commitment.  I think I died in the first 30 seconds (fell off a cliff damnit!).  It was extremely frustrating, and challenging, to figure out how to safely move and how to fight.  I have never played a game where everything can kill you so easily and the environment is so deadly.
As I said above though, this was a gift, and I was not going to waste someone elses generosity by quiting.
It took me a bit to get used to.  Clumbsy turning, slow recovery from weapon swings, and more.  I would recommend to anyone picking this up for the first time, run around for a few minutes, get used to how your character moves.  Especially practice stopping and quick direction changing.
Once you have it down, continue.
The combat is every bit as hard as you have heard.  For a novice such as myself, it was extremely unforgiving.  However, once you learn HOW to fight, it is one of the most rewarding experiences in recent gaming memory.  Going back and totally dominating something that basically has humiliated me on prior attempts is nothing short of pure joy.
And it only gets better.  As you adapt to the controls, and the enemie behaviors, you get bolder.  You get aggressive.  And, you get dead.  hehe.  The game will always remind you if you get to cocky.
I will be honest, I focussed more on the gameplay than the story.  The story is good, but feels a little tacked on.  Lots to listen to and read though.

This game transformed not only my life, but my own soul and being. Let me start from the beginning.
On a normal Tuesday afternoon, I was browsing through the free to play Steam games in searches of some mind blowing new software to absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing blow my mind. After hours of searching to no avail, I click on something called "Fuse". I explore the ratings, reviews, videos, screenshots; I am intrigued. This game was something I had never seen before. To have the power to mold human flesh, create my own beings like I was God in the living flesh. I couldn't turn down the opportunity, so I indulged my curiosity. Closing my eyes, breathing in deeply, I clicked download. My heart pumped faster and I could feel my blood coursing through my veins as I waited for it to complete downloading. When it did, I felt my palms moisten as I reached out and pressed play.
My life was forever changed.
I created hundreds of creatures, from breathtaking beauty to utter desolate beings. From humans, to the darkest monsters ever to be imagined. It was paradise, to be able to form my greatest dreams and most terrifying nightmares. It had me hooked.
Soon, I found myself on a mission. To create the most perfect body, and make it my own. It took months. Each curve and shadow was specifically molded by me for hours at a time before I deemed it good. I didn't sleep, eat, I barely breathed in fear of breaking my steel concentration through this quest that would change the course of my life as it was. When I was finished, my hands were shaking and my bowels released themselves from pure exhaustion. I uttered the satisfying words, "It is finished."
I uploaded the model body to my email and send the 130GB file to my doctors email, hastily typing up a scatterbrained message of my request of him. I needed to have this body. If I did, I would be indestructible. I told no one of the true motives behind my plans.
My doctor agreed. The date for the surgery was set. A 62 hour surgery. A slim chance of living. But I needed it, I needed this chance to change into my final form.
The morning of my surgery rolled around. My will was written, tacked to my refridgerator in case of my almost certain demise. Everything went to my cat, Gertrude.
My palms sweaty, knees weak and arms heavy, I drove to the surgery with hope and determination in my heart. I would not let myself fail, not this time, not when it mattered most.
Sign the documents, change into a gown, IV drip, I was almost there. I could taste the success on my tongue already. I fell asleep with dreams of breath taking perfection tickling my scalp.
When I woke up, venom ripped through my veins. Fire tore through my throat and I felt poison blur my eyes. Voices, hands touching me, I flinched in response. Did the surgery succeed? Was I finally my true form? I lurched out of bed, ripping tubes out of every one of my orifices, pushed nurses aside and stumbled to the bathroom. My eyes met with the mirror, and I knew it was complete. Fuse had not failed me, my doctors had not failed me, I had not failed me. Delicious brown hair parted to the side, a small brown mustache and a magnificent build. I was ready.
Through sheer will power and utter satisfaction, I escaped the hospital with hospital personnel close behind. I jumped into my car; no need for a seatbelt, I was invincible. I drove back to my house to pet Gertrude, then to in-act the second part of my plan: world domination.
Booting up my computer, I clicked and dragged all my Fuse character files to my 3D printer file, and they began uploading. I awaited nervously, combing my fingers through my hair and stroking my mustache with impatience. Then, I heard my printer start. The time had come. Through many perilous hours of planning, waiting, surviving, I was here. My Fuse creations were here. They began printing and one by one came out of my 3D printer. I cried over their beauty, they were all utter perfection. Blonde hair that swayed with any small gust of wind, and eyes bluer than the ocean itself. Soon, I found myself among an army of thousands of beautiful, uniform creatures. After so many failed creations, my satisfaction laid in them.
"Soldiers!" My deep voice boomed from my lungs. "Our mission: person uniformity, then onto world domination itself! It all starts with you. . . Onward!"

Video game movies tend to suck, but Alien: Isolation is a great example that movies can make great video games. I've spent many hours exploring Sevastopol, the desolate and isolated space station where the inhabitants that have survived for several weeks are worse at hiding than someone who just got there. Visually, Alien: Isolation is stunning. The enhanced graphics combined with the retro-futuristic style from the original Alien movie make for a visually appealing experience. The gameplay is another strong point of this game, pitting you against different types of enemies: the paranoid humans, the tyrannical androids, or the predatory alien. Different enemies require different approaches, and most situations require you to think ahead rather than act on impulse. There are some parts of the game that seem off: the alien seems to have a delayed raction to being set on fire and ignores other survivors in the room that are weeping loudly in favor of randomly searching the locker that Ripley happens to be hiding in. Overall, Alien: Isolation is a fun, tense experience that was well worth the money I paid for it

It's been a long while since I played this game--without any of its expansions--and the amount of time I spent is realistic of my first playthrough. Let me justify those ~16 hours by saying I spread them over a fortnight of gaming, basically waiting until nighttime when it was dark enough that I could turn all the lights off in my house and play it like I felt it needed to be played...
... and what an amazing experience it was. I'm a fan of the original Alien film, and all the lore and miscellany that went into the beginning of the franchise, Giger, the works. To digress from the game for a moment: What disappoints me the most about the Prometheus prequel is Scott's lack of attention to even the most basic of details. Chunky keyboards. Green Text. Technology that feels like the era it was originally shot in. All missing. But not in Alien: Isolation. Even if you're just looking for a nostalgic walk in the proverbial park, Isolation is the game for you. Environmentally, it's spectacular.
The first ten minutes of the game, not knowing what to expect--other than the fact that behind every corner, every dark space, every air-vent, the possibility of some sort of Alien encounter was more than likely--I was crawling around on all fours praying not to be heard. I didn't have anything. I only knew that my character didn't know what she was getting herself into, and her lack of insight made me borderline hysterical WAY before anything Xeno ever happened. That's a level of player involvement I have yet to experience in a game, where I genuinely feel myself transposed into the station's corridors, almost like Amanda's helpless subconscious.
I mean to impose with this wall of text, because the phenomena of this game still lingers with me after all the time I haven't played this game until I've written this review (release until now). The game feels more like a film than it does a game. The story is compelling, but it's made more-so by the environment than it is its characters; the downside is you're basically re-enacting a plot you couldn't change even if you wanted to, besides how you go about executing it. You want to explore, and there's nothing quite like gallivanting about an empty space station without knowing why it's empty until you do; but it's no sandbox. Without giving away any of the specifics, story does drop off a bit towards the middle of the game, where it honestly feels like the transition from Alien to Aliens, and feels a bit rushed, while the ending (unfortunately) tapers off into ambiguous sequel territory.
It's definitely worth it for that first thrill, though, not of coming face-to-face with the Xeno itself, but feeling the hot of its breath against the cold of your cheek; that eyeless grimace, that insatiable, whiplash tongue, debilitate you into your last save.

Homeworld is two games I have spent hours and hours playing. From the (incredible) main campaigns to the excellent mods for them. So Remastered comes and polishes them up (and ports HW1 to the HW2 engine) which seems like the perfect of perfects. Except its not. Except it is.
HW1 mechanics are flawed. Badly. Sometimes hilariously. The port of the game over to the HW2 engine is not as smooth as I hoped it would be. They nerfed the salvette everything strategy, but the HW2 AI is kind of laughable in HW1's tactical situations anyway, plus the addition of default "jump with all map resources" from HW2 takes out the need for fleet tooling and resource op micromanagement which was kind of a staple for me in the first game.
But it does (largely) function like it should. Homeworld 1 still feels like Homeworld 1. And it. is. glorious.
But where remastered really shines is with Homeworld 2. Designed for the engine already the gameplay and visuals are just absolutely flooring if you've played the game back in the day. It's easily the best looking space RTS. Even beating out Sins. Gearbox nailed the graphics and sound for both packages and the game is gorgeous and plays very well on my system, even in large engagements.
There's rough areas, MP is broken, it took a while for me to even get the game to launch, and HW1's mechanics are iffy at parts. However this is still the Homeworld I remember, redone in highest quality that could command AAA prices. I have no personal ties to Cataclysm though, so I can't comment on that too much. I know its some kind of hugemassive problem for some people.
They shouldn't look this gifthorse in the mouth though. 10/10 AI still reks me at mission 3 of HW2 :|

Well, I can safely say that that was the worst Freddi Fish game I've played yet. I know, it's a bold claim with Freddi Fish 1 and 2 being so bland and terribly-made but I legitimately think this is the worst of the bunch.
Freddi Fish 4 starts you up on the traditional Freddi Fish plotline- you're going to some event, when it's been postponed due to a problem that's been incited by someone (either singular or plural) having done something that's "just plain wrong" in the eyes of our titular character, and you decided to go beyond the boundaries of the law to stop that plain wrong thing from continuing. And like the first two games there isn't a whole lot of mystery. It's just finding a rustler disguise. You know where the hideout is and who stole the hogfish. It's just getting in that becomes the bulk of the story- not the mystery of who stole it, but how to get in and free the hogfish.
The story goes by so alarmingly fast and has so many faults in it, that it's hard to find anything I really liked in it, apart from the unintentionally funny one-liners and horrible presentation quality. I've never played a Humongous game with such a lack of focus on detail. Sure, I like to insult Putt Putt and the last few Freddi Fish games, but they still animated their games well and didn't have glitches or issues with characters and their backgrounds. Freddi and Luther oftentimes appear beneath an object, but still are swimming as if they're in front of it, and sometimes characters that are standing with their legs look like they're floating above the ground.
Even the lip-syncing is thrown way off; making the ending espcially funny. During the scene where you discover who stole the hogfish with a final clue (Freddi Fish 3 style) Freddi and Luther keep moving their mouths, but its Freddi's voice that's coming out of both of them. Uncanny and creepy, but still hilarious to no end.
Honestly, what I hate the most about Freddi Fish 4 is that it doesn't really progress forward from the last few games. There was a rise in quality from Freddi Fish 1-3, though it wasn't astounding. Freddi Fish 3 actually had a mystery, and I genuinely wanted to find out the answer behind it. Freddi Fish 4 just borrows the drab backgrounds that plagued Freddi Fish 1 and 2, and steals the cheap final clue and culprit ending of 3 without doing anything to improve itself in that regard.
I know this sounds oddly sophisticated for a review on a game intended for 5-year-olds, but I still appreciate the Humongous games that have enough quality and polish in them for both kids and adults. And the only 3 games that have enough polish in their library to be recommended are still only Pajama Sam 1 and 3, and Spy Fox 3. While the rest of their games have been slightly charming, Freddi Fish 4 just feels astoundingly lazy. Very little time or effort was put into this installment, and it really shows unfortunately. I'm giving Freddi Fish 4 a 2/10.

Alien: Isolation is one of the best games I have played in recent memory, and one of the best horror games of all time, if not the best. Featuring a (mostly) well-paced campaign, gorgeous visuals and level design, crisp gameplay and controls, absolutely hair-raising sound design and music, and one of the most devious, adaptive an all-around terrifying unscripted AI's ever, it's an experience you won't forget soon. This is an absolute recommendation to anyone who feels that they can handle the trauma of being stalked and repeatedly dragged screaming and crying from under desks and out of lockers by HR Giger's nightmarish creature.

I'd give this game a thumbs up all day along if it wasn't for a single near game breaking issue: PVP Matchmaking.
This game relies upon a new system called soul memory, instead of matching players based on their soul levels (which basically is the accumulation of all the status points you've spent souls on upgrading). In Dark Souls 1 there was a glaring issues where newbs would be faced off against other players who spent their souls on gear and upgrading, leaving their status points alone and breaking PVP for the first 50 levels or so. Past that, everything slowly comes into balance.
In the old system if you lost souls that was really the only consequence, it set you back slightly but really didn't inhibit matchmaking. Now? If you lose souls often you cripple your character in any future PVP endeavor. This is thanks to soul memory, the new matchmaking tool that fixes the PVP issue in the first game but in the long run will cripple or empower players. Soul memory is just the number of souls you've accumulated throughout your character's history. Doesn't matter if you spent them on soul levels, gear, upgrades, etc, all that facilitates PVP matching is the number of souls you've collected.
So if you're new to this series, and it takes you a while to make it through the game becuase you die often while getting used to the game. Despite how good you become, the souls you've lost getting to this point will not be subtracted from your soul memory. This means you'll be matched against other players who've had more souls overall to put into their character, slowly creating greater and greater disparity between players as the overall memory count gets higher.
Additionally, there are serious issues with latency. Often you'll die not because you weren't good enough, but because the guy who invaded you had such a high ping that both of you will be playing 'chase the lag' and what you're hitting in front of you might really be the guy who is a second from pulling a critical backstab on your bum. If they at the very least were more selective with matchmaking and filtered players from interacting with excessive ping, that'd be fine.
Honestly I want to recommend this game, depsite these issues it is a lot of fun and enjoyable. But PVP wise this game is pretty broken.
