Fuse is a child's game; unless you have loads of cash.
What you get is the ability to make a 3D model and give it a couple of animations. Beyond that, Fuse is only gateway software. Here's how it works. You create a 3D model in Fuse. You must go to the Mixamo website for free rigging (skeleton). Now you have a character in a T-pose that needs to be animated.
If you're not an animator, you need a wallet, preferably a fat one. Animations are $15* each per character. Every unique movement constitutes an animation. Stand Idle; $15. Draw Sword; $15. Swing Sword; $15. To properly animate a character for use in a game would cost $300-$400. Or there's an option to subscribe monthly for a few hundred dollars.
(Currently, animations are unavailable as Adobe is redesgining the product.)
The characters don't just drop into a game but have to be run through plugins specific to the game engine.
All you get at the moment is free electronic "paper dolls". Later, you'll be able to animate them for a (what the market will bear) price.
*prices shown are prior to Adobe takeover

A nice, relaxing and well-priced farming/exploration game.
In slime rancher you alternate between tending to your slimes in your ranch and exploring the world around said ranch. These two mechanics work in pair. Tending your slimes will generate revenue, items and tools you need for exploration and exploration allows you to expand your ranch by providing new (and more valuable) types of slimes. At some point in the game, a crafting system is also unlocked, providing you with more utilities (teleporters, turrets,...) and cosmetics.
It's never too challenging. Perfect for these moments when you feel like playing but you can't/don't want to spend too much energy in it. Yet, farming has a small bit of depth to it. The environments you are to explore are well worked with secrets to find. The crafting system adds gameplay value in an unartificial way. All in all, it's a very fair game if you are into that sort of thing. Definitely worth its 20 bucks.

WARNING!!! This review contains information that could be construed as a spoiler!!!
Background:
I've played ESO Tamriel for about 500 hours with the ESO Premium monthly subscription.
Pros:
* Is it worth the money? Yes, absolutely.
*The micro-transactions? I like them because you can't buy OP weapons, skills or mounts to ride. You can buy more storage to haul and bank. You can buy new side-worlds. You can buy things that make playing more convenient.
* The world? Good production values in voice actors -- especially the Main Story's actors are top-notch. The non-Main actors are good on average.
* The Main Story line is very satisfying (there are Cons about this later)
* The crafting and trading is interesting and helps rank up your player.
* PVE is satisfying.
* Multi-player is satisfying. I played with an experienced player as a guide.
* Side quests are satisfying. Good stories with good acting that are sometimes comical and other times tragic -- if not, at times, horrific.
Cons: SPOILER ALERT!!!!
* Perhaps I'm naive, but the Main Story should have had resulted in a changed world that I have come to expect from other completed side quests. Instead, once you kill Molag Bal, and the cut scenes are done (and they are satisfying, by the way) you essentially exit into an *unchanged* world where Molag Bal still is a threat. It is either that, or get recast as a new soul into a different faction, to begin your quest over again, but at a higher challenge level.  You don't get that "ticker tape parade" you expected. To me, this was a great disappointment, made all the more so as earlier, there was a side quest where your victory had consequences and changed the world by working with Argonians to free trapped souls caused the gloom of Davon's watch to be replaced by sunshine and plant growing.
I stopped playing the game after achieving the goal of the Main Story for this reason.
* Training up and tutorials: They leave out a ton of stuff you need to know to avoid rage-quitting at the beginning. I had an experienced player guide me through those stages, until I could become self-sustaining.
* The Main Story you are forced to go through in Solo Mode rather than be able to have your friends join you.
*PVP: This is just me, but you do get a chance to fight other players in Cyrodil. As a mostly solo player it is an exercise in frustration because, by the very nature of the design,  you will frequently encounter vastly higher-level players who will make short shrift of you. Some, I'm sure, will enjoy that kind of punishing game -- I don't.
* The ethical choices you make didn't have a global impact to the degree I hoped for. They, at times, did change a locale, but not the whole game world. I understand that could be difficult to program.
* Having completed a locale-changing side-quest made multi-player difficult if another player hadn't played through that side-quest. For example, my evacuating Bleak Rock, when my friend hadn't yet, prevented us from playing together.
Still, I found the game well worth spending 500 hours and $150 on, as it was like a good novel with whichI could interact and affect the plot outcome to a minor degree.

Broforce is a game I can’t believe didn’t already exist – South African developer Free Lives has righted a mighty wrong here. Bursting at the seams with veiny biceps and draped in American flags, Broforce is a love letter to action cinema carved into lead, fired into the corpse of the nearest copy of Contra, and then brought to life via dark magic. It’s so obvious, really; a squad of Earth’s greatest heroes (and heroines)  – most of whom are only a typo away from a thick wad of cease-and-desist letters – against the worst that international terrorism, the galaxy, and the underworld itself can throw at humanity. Frankly, it’s bloody fantastic (and spectacularly bloody).
Unforgiving but (mostly) fair, frantic yet tactical, and oozing with 16-bit 2D charm, if Broforce had been released two decades ago I expect it probably would’ve been the greatest thing to happen to me since puberty. In 2015 the effect is a little less life-altering, but Broforce remains an incredibly confident, refined, unique, and content-rich run ’n gun shooter for up to four co-op players.
The objective of most levels is simple; you just need to blast and/or dart your way through several different locations and very literally get to the chopper. Some of the later levels change this up somewhat as the enemies segue from enemy soldiers to aliens, and later again to supernatural nasties, but that’s the general gist. I love how hilariously dim-witted the regular enemy mooks are but, as just one shot will kill you, you still need to play with precision. The difficulty spikes a few times across the final campaign stages, but it’s certainly in step with the sorts of games that have clearly inspired it. My only major criticism is that I noted some odd slowdown during a couple of periods where a great many alien enemies had pinned themselves in a small area on screen.
Broforce’s nearly completely destructible environments put a creativity-enabling twist on proceedings. Blast through walls to access buildings and get the drop on the baddies inside, or fire through the ground itself to tunnel beneath potential engagements. I found that particularly useful against the large, fire-spitting, worm-like bosses; you can create tunnels to get right up against the still-buried parts of their bodies and use the intact terrain above to temporarily protect you from their ranged attacks.
"The bros are quick and nimble and there’s a good level of nuance in the controls."
The sheer amount of explosive objects on screen means destruction gets pretty wild with other players involved so I’ve actually found myself preferring to play it solo, where you control the pace yourself. There’s also a dedicated deathmatch mode for those of you who’d rather work against one another than together; it’s perhaps a little too chaotic for my tastes, but it’s a laugh in short bursts. Beyond that there’s even an intimidating level editor, but if you’re too daunted to try that out you can simply browse through and quickly and easily load community-made levels. The large team of varied bros themselves are the big stars, and there are plenty of them. Rambro, Brommando, B.A. Broracus, Double Bro Seven, The Brofessional; by now you’re probably picking up on the theme. The bros are quick and nimble and there’s a good level of nuance in the controls; bros can grab walls and climb indefinitely, and automatically execute a handy flip when you’re trying to jump up and around a ledge above. They’re little more than small blobs of pixels, but the way in which each has been lovingly imagined and crafted is evident in the art that splashes on screen each time you unlock a new bro and the quaint little animated profile pics.
What’s particularly great about Broforce is that every time you die you’re forcibly swapped to a random new bro, and each of them has distinctly different weapons and abilities and require a different approach. Some are melee-focused, some have powerful, short-range weapons, some can fire longer distances, and at least one seems completely useless (yes, I’m speaking about you, Brocketeer). Some are better at using their speed to scamper past clumps of enemies, and some have the firepower to duke it out with the baddest of bad guys. Some are faster at chewing through the destructible scenery to create new paths and avoid conflicts and traps, and some have incredibly potent secondary abilities that beg to be exploited at every opportunity.
“Every time you’ll spawn as a new bro who might be better suited to the challenge ahead."
Several of my favourite bros are amongst the latter; Time Bro can slow down time to a crawl (extremely handy against bosses), Brominator has an endoskeleton form that makes him temporarily invulnerable, and Bro Heart’s “Freedom” battle cry sends enemies running (perfect if you’re being swarmed). I often wished I could swap to my preferred bro at will, especially prior to some of the tougher bosses, but I do concede that tougher bosses, but I do concede that making do with the abilities of your given bro is part of the fun. It certainly takes the edge off of repeated failures, knowing that every time you’ll spawn as a new bro who might be better suited to the challenge ahead. The fact that rescuing hostages gains you an extra life but changes your on-screen bro (and is the way you unlock new bros) also creates an interesting risk-reward dynamic; do I trade Time Bro for the extra life and a random new character, or do I stick it out?
I gleaned a great deal of joy discovering the more subtle characteristics of the bros, too. The way the Brodator’s spears stay lodged in the environment for you to jump on, or the way his body explodes if he’s defeated in battle. The way the death of one of the Boondock Bros (who come as a pair, or a trio alongside their father if you activate him) enrages the surviving brother and causes him to flash red and fire his pistols far more rapidly. The fact that the Chuck Norris-inspired Brodell Walker’s melee attack is a roundhouse kick, or that Time Bro’s is a classic JCVD split kick. Broforce is a parody done with a lot of reverence.
I also really love Broforce’s attention to the smaller details of its presentation, from the way the profile pics of each bro bounce as they run and are lit up with muzzle flashes as they fire their weapons, to the enemy kill count at the end of each level (which is usually a conga line of exploding bodies, like nuking a large group of tightly-packed Lemmings). I highly rate the sound, in particular the pitch-perfect glam rock guitar score and hilarious enemy squeals and death gurgles and its constantly screaming narrator.

I've lost progress several times just because of that - having to play through the same part of the story (without being able to skip cutscenes)
because the gamemakers decided to sharply rotate (requiring directional adjustment) or completely swap camera angle in high-action spots ruins the game. It's a common mistake made in these kinds of games, unfortunately.
Overall? A mediocre, linear platformer with awkward controls, not offset enough by a story but with nice visuals makes this a game that could be enjoyable to watch someone else play (who already knows what to expect) but not to play yourself. It's a decent buy if you can get a big discount on it and don't mind some frustration, but certainly not being worth the full price.

$6.22 for the premium edition. Will post more as I play. Does not port over properly as the instructions for Focus Attack are "Press Y+B" which does not exist on the PC version.
PROS
1. Cloud Travel
Loved the cloud movement levels. High speed, high jumps and lot of room to explore. Boss Hound fight was great too.
2. Combat system
Very interesting fighting system. Love the power of range weapons and how they function very similarly to reality. Distracting is a new mechanic, simple but it adds a different method of playing.
I was a bit disappointed that the bosses tend to be killed with a similar pattern e.g. Stun, Heavy Attack, Stun, Heavy Attack, Takedown Move, Rinse, Repeat.
You can't target lock/focus on an enemy making it hard to aim your shields with the lousy camera movements.
3. 2-person puzzle
It is interesting but it gets kind of repetitive. E.g. Piggyback, Toss Trip, Open Security Door/Push Blocks, Rinse, Repeat.
4. Dragonfly View
Interesting but it would be better if you could control and fly the Dragonfly yourself instead of a controlled cutscene. If control was allowed, you could design hidden areas in the map, plant ambushes, plant mines, hide paths and switches etc etc and the player would have to use Dragonfly view to find them. Like hide-and-seek.
5. Puzzles
Quite fun relative to plain old switches E.g. Drawbridge
CONS
1. Porting
Did not port over properly from Playstation. Viewing mode is horrible at certain areas. Worst, they are bugged and you can't reach certain areas.
Refer to my screenshots for more information.
2. Jumping Off/On
Certain ledges are really silly. While I appreciate not being able to fall off an edge, I really hate having  to find specific ledges just to jump off E.g. Theatre with the hound reaquires you to jump off at the first prop stage in order to reach the stage floor.
Jumping off into a 90 degree corner can create a bug where you keep falling infinitely, so you look like you're swimming in mid air.
Refer to my screenshots for more information.
Very linear. There is no wrong pathway to jump to. Just keep pressing an obvious direction key and the jump button to proceed. You just need to be fast.
3. Storyline
Very meh. It's not exactly engaging. You have Slavers, Earth 200 years in the future, evolutionary robots, etc etc, but they don't come together to form a concrete story. They seem to be modularised instead of being integrated into a complete story.
4. The Staff
Absolutely horrible to switch between Plasma and Stun on the PC. You have to Right Click, go into First person mode, then press the Left Arrow and Right Arrow key while holding down Right Click in the middle of battle.
5. Upgrades
Only Staff, Combat, Health and Shield to choose from, yet you can't use WASD to choose them. You can't mouseover the correct wheel to choose the specific upgrade properly as there seems to be a bug.

This deserves more than I'm going to write for now, so I'm going to add more later. But for now:
If you enjoy RTS games, games set in space, or amazing science fiction storylines (especially space operas), buy this. Buy it so hard. You will thank me.
Homeworld as a series has always been both thematically and mechanically beautiful-- I remember being in a trance watching the gameplay at a friend's house in 1999. From the agile and sleek scout ship to the mile-high Pride of Hiigara, no detail was spared. Combat was believably realistic and yet maintained a magical feeling of watching a high-tech waltz of destruction. Massive capital ships ran broadsides against each other while strike fighters battled in furballs. Flak exploded, plasma lanced, and ions beams sliced through space leaving a hot afterlight in your vision. It was everything I'd dreamed about for space battles, and Homeworld delivered above and beyond.
The story is nothing short of masterful. Narration both actively and passively help to build a universe where you truly feel for the people you are guiding. You feel their motivation, their need to complete their mission, and it is hard to pull yourself away from the game-- an active effort is required.
The Remastered collection is superb. Clearly, heart, soul, blood and tears went into the production, and it shows. You know how your mind's eye for the first games that you played always sharpened and enhanced as time went on? The story and graphics that you saw in your thoughts, instead of what was on screen? Remastered takes it from your head and puts it on screen. It looks, feels, and plays that well. This is what "HD Remakes" should consider the master model, the bar to reach for. But man, they're going to have a really, REALLY tough time grasping it at the height Gearbox/Blackbird hung it at.
There are a few gripes, albeit extremely minor-- the new UI is a bit goofy, and balance in the extremely clearly Beta multiplayer is totally nonexistent. But these are vices that are both fixable and forgivable, especially in the light of what I personally feel is one of the best games to be published, ever.
Homeworld is a bona fide classic. Homeworld 2, although slightly weaker in storyline, is a great follow-up. The Remastered pack is without a doubt a top tier, GOTY candidate work. If any of these words even remotely stuck with you, buy the game. Gearbox and Blackbird deserve every cent they get.

If you haven't played A:I yet, here's the quick and dirty: It's Bioshock 1, but there's only one Big Daddy and he's indestructible.
You play as Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen, who has come to the station Sevastopol to follow a lead in her mother's disappearence fifteen years before (during the events of the first few Alien films). Of course, the alien shows up on Sevastopol and you have to figure out how to avoid it, how to find other survivors, and ultimately how to escape.
This involves traversing a series of interlinked levels. The station is broken up into three towers which are connected by a transit system. This means you can backtrack and travel to places out-of-sequence, which you may want to do if you're short on ammo or supplies. The levels themselves are big and usually non-linear, with multiple paths available to you. You do backtrack a decent amount, but usually with a very different set of equipment, so the annoyance is minimal.
Typically, what you are tasked with doing is standard FPS fare: find a key card, fix a comm station, get medical supplies. What makes the game great is how you get there - by avoiding the Alien, which cannot be killed, only avoided, distracted, or annoyed. You can hide under tables, in lockers, in vents, or behind walls. You can distract it by throwing noisemakers or temporarily disable it with a flamethrower or molotov cocktails. No technique is perfect though, as the Alien learns from its encounters with you: If you frequently hide in lockers, it will start ripping lockers open looking for you. If you burn it with the flamethrower and it sees you carrying the same weapon, it will rush at you and then halt, forcing you to use up your flamethrower fuel, and then attack again. You always have to be thinking one step ahead, and that's what makes the game so enjoyable. You never have enough resources, either ammo or crafted items, so you have to be choosy about what you use.
The other station residents can be dangerous, as well - humans and malfunctioning androids. There's no easy way to tell if a person will be hostile or not, so encountering other humans can be a game of chance. You can't just assume they are friendly, be wrong and die, and play the section over, either, as their hostility towards you may be affected by how you approach them. The human AI is almost as good as the alien AI in that regard.
The save system also adds a high degree of tension to the game. You have save points, not quick save, but not checkpoints either. You can manually save at the save points, but the save game animation takes several seconds, and you are vulnurable to being killed during or immediately after a save, which means you can make mistakes about when to save. Thankfully, you are given three save slots - the current save, save immediately previous, and beginning of mission - but the save points are far enough apart that saving at the wrong time can lose you a huge amount of progress.
The game's overall design is gorgeous - visually and aurally. The alien makes terrifying sounds, skitters and thumps, as it chases you through the station. You can frequently hear it but not see it. The game's lighting effects and dramatic space visuals are incredible, especially considering how well it runs - well over 100 fps on max settings on my i5-3470/gtx 970 rig. I suppose the confined areas and limited number of NPCs helps keep the game less demanding.
Overall, a definite buy now.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Borderlands 2 was initially released in 2012, and I haven’t played it until now in 2016. Purchasing the Game of the Year edition, all the DLC included except for a few customize heads, which may or not be worth the purchase if you desire. Each are about $1 a piece, more or less. But that is depending on how far you want to take your customization and uniqueness for your character.

Now, as I said, I am playing this game years after its release, and I am thoroughly enjoying it! From the story to optional side missions, to exploring, to finding those perfect weapon combos, to customizing skins for the vehicles and player, and of course to the intense combat. The game just seems to keep me entertained, and I keep finding reasons to keep going. The game is very good at getting you hooked, and retaining your attention.
Story 10/10-
You are a notorious vault hunter, in search of treasures on the planet Pandora. You will be prompted to help the Crimson Raiders in the city of Sanctuary, and make some quirky, yet useful allies to aid you with your struggle against a powerful enemy, “Handsome Jack”, and the billion dollar corporation, Hyperion.
Gameplay 8/10
The game is a first person shooter, and the environment is vividly immersive. I find myself thinking I will do just more mission, and suddenly find that time had escaped me. Seriously, there’s so much to do in the game. The main story, side missions, collectibles, different weapons with different abilities. Each character has their own perks and different play styles. While I have test played a couple of the characters out, I find myself building and focusing on decking out my main character.
Mind you, I have just recently started playing Borderlands 2… and I have dumped hours into it, and I feel I have come close to completing the game. And things that I have already done, I don’t mind doing another run by myself or with others.
NOW- the only reason why I am not giving the game play a perfect 10, is because some of the side missions can be a bit tedious. Going back n forth from point to another… much like how most MMORPGs are done. It’s not often but it does happen. Also, I felt the quest tracking could have a been a bit better or improved, instead of manually having to track and follow your quests for the regions- I feel like a log would have been much more efficient and less time consuming.
Visual/Sound 10/10-
The graphics are not realistic but rather have its own original art style which can best be compared to comic book art. It is beautiful. It is unique. It fits the game perfectly. The music is pretty dope and fits whatever seems to going on at the moment. Sounds, narration & dialogue are awesome, witty, and comical. I don’t care what anyone says, Claptrap is cool asf. Lol.
The environments are fun to explore, and with how big each free roam map is;  I often forget how detailed and active the camps and dungeons can be.
Multiplayer 10/10
One of the coolest features is being able to run with a pack in the search of loot, dungeon crawling and mission completing. The difficulty increases, and the loot (allegedly) gets better. I say allegedly, because I definitely found my rarer items on solo play through. But still its awesome to team up with a squad and mow through bandits, fight over loot, and duel to see who is the better vault hunter
----------------------------------------
The game is very fun, action packed, has absolutely no pacing problems, and I imagine will keep me entranced for a extensive time in the future.
Recommend? Y/N?
Of course, I recommend the game. Buy it full price, or buy it on sale. Buy it for yourself, or get a pack and play with friends. Just get it, and enjoy it.
Happy Vault Hunting,

This game was the most important game of my childhood it totally absorbed me in a way that I had never experienced in just about any other media. From the technical briefing manual that came with the original to the entire ambiance of the series I have been a fan since the beginning. It's funny how as soon as I booted up the game muscle memory kicked in, I had no troubles remembering how to play or what to do. the graphical update is gorgeous and I feel that surge of awe from my childhood. This is the ultimate classic to me and gives me hope that there will be a true successor to the series because of this remastered edition.
As far as some of the bug reporting I have seen in other reviews, As of yet the only bugs I have seen have been problems with the briefings breaking the game if I try to mess around too much with the camera or try to exit out of the overview too early when a briefing ends. I feel like I run a fairly healthy rig and this game certainly taxes my system pretty herd, Although I run a slightly older graphics card, so that could be it. There is also few graphical glitches in capturing units, some will change their color scheme to match your fleet and some will not.
I am (in this day and age) a pretty casual gamer and don't imagine playing this game too rigorously. However, I cannot imagine at this point in time that Gearbox has worked out all the balancing issues between the four races from two very different games.  Although since I will mostly be playing AI skirmishes, I am not very concerned at the moment. I am already engrossed in the story and trying to rack my brain with each new mission as to how I beat it 10 plus years ago.
Some wishes for future DLC's and patches:
1. Cataclysm Obviously needs to released at a future date. Although not developed by Relic, the story of the Somtaaw Kiith, the beast, and the confusion of the first years after the end of Homeworld  make it a worthy entry on story telling points alone. That game introduced some interesting mechanics that could be fun in multiplayer (or breaking).
2. Turanic raiders and Garden of Kadesh dwellers in multiplier! Balancing would be impossible for the most part, but, come on guys, everyone wants to play these factions! If anything they could make for interesting allies/opponents if played well. I Know they would require fleshing out, seeing as neither have resource collectors, but again, they are there, so why not?
3. Rigorous Multiplayer balancing of the four existing factions. Things like formations need to be worked out and the four sides need to be balanced out appropriately.
4. Mac and linux Versions! I travel with a Macbook Pro and need a fix on the go!
In the end, I can think of few games that truly deserve a remaster/reboot like Homeworld, I was happy to buy this, even with issues, for the sole purpose of carrying on this series in some way. If you love well thought out game worlds with ambiance and true engrossing originality, this is the game you should play. It is a game that builds up a mysterious, impactful science fiction universe, with excellent allusions to ancient myth and tragedy. It is a brutal, and also quiet game. It is science fiction to paint your own thoughts and character into. This is not a macho dystopian gore fest that I feel most science fiction games latch onto without developing any sort of thought of scale or epic themes that they purport to advance.

8 out of 10.  Alien Isolation is all about nostalgia.  They really did a good job of creating the 1979 movie's futuristic atmosphere.  My initial impression was that they could have done more with this and that your ability to interact with the environment around you was somewhat limited.  After getting used to these limitations, I really did enjoy the game.  There were times where it seemed playing on the 'recommended' level of difficulty was too difficult, as the Alien at some points was almost impossible to avoid and I had to replay those points over and over until finally, through sheer luck, I happened to get through it.  I also need to admit to using a walk-through a few times, because there is so little time to explore your environment for what you need (and need to know) when being stalked by the Alien and some of the more difficult other entities you encounter.  There were items in the game that you could use, such as flashbangs and such, that I really didn't use much because I could never really figure out how to throw them in such a way as to daze the Alien or anything else.  One of the main points you need to know is while you do need to fend off the Alien frequently enough, it is a game about stealth, gathering supplies, managing your health and resources, exploring, and enjoying the story.  Without creating a spoiler, I was somewhat disappointed with the ending in the game.  There were scenes in the very end that just didn't make sense and didn't fit with what we know about the Alien from the movies, as well as just being generally implausible.  If they are going to make an Alien game while trying to relate closely with the original movie, they should have come up with another ending and one that maybe was a bit more satisfying.

The Good:
The music is very fitting when it plays.  I loved walking into familiar environments like the nostromo-like ship, or the derelict.  The environments are very very detailed and some locations are down-right terrifying.  I love that they brought the original actors back to do some voices.  This game is great for nostalgia.
The Bad:
It feels like the developers went to great lengths to see how much nostaliga they could pack in (though not as badly as Aliens: Colonial Marines).  The raised cylinder/button sequence you perform at the end of the game seems very excessive for such a simple task and is almost verbatim from Alien.  It's very out of place.
Futuristic equipment sure sucks.  Flashlight batteries that drain in seconds?  Seriously?  Are they Duracells from the 20th century purchased during Walmart's going-out-of-business sale?  This isn't an uncommon gimmick but it sure can provoke ire.  It's just a way to make the game more difficult and it's completely unnecessary.  The guns sure are inaccurate.  How does a point-blank shot miss?  Also, how many times can an alien be immolated before it actually dies?  I used my flame thrower quite a bit and it just kept taking the pain.  They never hit the one in the original film with anything but the ones in Aliens just seem to fall apart when ignited.
The amazing Alien AI seems to somehow know your general whereabouts at all times, knows when you've left an area completely, and can take minutes to leave when it comes looking.  So you sit. And wait.  At its core this game is all about playing hide an seek with a computer that can cheat.  I don't recall the original Alien having a personal vendetta and tracking a single person all over the place.  It just seemed to go around killing randomly.  Why follow you acrossed the entire station?  Because you got away once?  So what!
Don't get too attached to any NPCs.
Fans of the movies will notice glaring plotholes with regards to the aliens.
This game suffers from the same issue that Outlast did.  It's tense for the first hour or two but it wears off.  When the scares grow dull you find yourself just wanting the game to end.  This one refuses that request.  It just keeps going and becomes very repetitive.  There is a reason that horror movies are only 1-3 hours long.
Many parts feel like I'm back in an MMO doing fedex quests.  One entire section of the game involves sneaking into a heavily guarded area.  You go to great lengths to get there and it turns out it was all for nothing.  I feel like I spent my time in this game all for nothing.
The subtitle for this game could be: "A Murphy's Law Story".  It feels like the developers use any excuse they can to block you from your objective.  This is one of the main reasons for the length of the game.  A great example of this is the event they throw in just before you leave the station.  It does nothing but send you back fifteen minutes just to crawl back to where you were previously.  You pretty much know when you flip a switch that something else is going to break.  You know when you finally get to the item you seek that some scripted event is going to happen to make your life more difficult.
The ending is fitting for the game.  It's completely lackluster and offers no real resolution for anyone, especially Ripley.
I'm glad I didn't pay full price for this.

The most challenging and nerve-racking first person experience yet. After finally finishing the game on the most difficult level, my body is still adjusting from the terror and the story that is Alien Isolation. The game clearly nails the feel of 1979 science fiction horror classic. Whether it is the audio, the visuals, equipment, loading screens, or the dialogue you will feel like you are trapped in the 1979 film. Supplies are critical and in low supply; how and when to use them is even more critical, and can be the difference between life and death. Every step forward feels like an achievement in itself. Narrow passages, poorly lit vent traversal, system failures, alarms, and time sensative doors, all create the perfrect environment. Data logs, recordings, corpses, and personal files all liter the surrounding areas to draw a grim and believable sense of being a sole entity aboard a doomed ship.
Upgrades, weapons, hacking equipment, and blueprints, all contribute to progress at just the right time, without feeling like they are there in abundance. Alien Isolation provides a progressive challenge, that requires patience and points of trial and error. It has no forgiveness for those who may choose to have a "run at things." A slow pace is the best pace. Every noise made can give away your location, which in turn, will leave you with very little room to hide. Even then, hiding will not always protect you.
One of the absolute best visual gaming experiences I have had. From start to finish the game looks and feels stunning. At 3840x2160 (4k), and several configuration modifications, Alien Isolation can be one of the best looking games to date. Every texture, light source, color, and asset used, makes Alien Isolation not only resemble the world of Alien, but become so visually accurate you can pinpoint things seen from the original film presentation.
Alien Isolation does so many things right, and hits on all the right nerves at just the right moment. To not own and experience this game from start to finish is a great injustice to yourself as a PC gamer. It is a masterpiece by design.

Easily one of the most well designed and unique worlds I have seen in any game, ever. Map design follows a linear story like the previous games, setting you inside a city district or fortress with a key goal. There are many different ways to reach and complete your objectives, and no shortage of side quests you can discover if you explore.
Combat can be tailored to many different playstyles, with focous on being a classic shooter, a melee masterpiece, or a stealth action game, all with lethal or nonlethal options as your actions do affect the world and story. Every single one of these playstyles is done very well, and the addition of some magic, is loads of fun.
One thing I didn't know that I really like is after you complete the story, you can start a new game with access to spells from both characters. Because of this, and the difference in story progression and playstyles, the replay value on Dishonored 2 is quite high.
Ultimately it keeps the best things about Dishonored 1, and does a good job improving upon it. Highly recommended, and  worth every penny. My only gripe is that I wish there were more DLCs because I want to keep playing it.

A neat little farm manager game, but in absolute desperate need of better inventory management options. Although it was initially fun, by the time I reached the end game content it had long since become a grinding chore that made me wonder who was really in the cage - me, or the slimes.
While at first the game offers some interesting exploration and fun farming elements, the gameplay quickly becomes extremely samey: go to the next area, find two new slimes and a food one of them likes, hybridize them, and then check back on their corral every couple minutes to feed them and sell their "plorts," the main way of getting money in the game. From a gameplay perspective, almost all the slimes are exactly the same. Very few of them need any special containment procedures that aren't solved by the time you're an hour in and buying a fully upgraded corral and a garden of their favorite food is dirt cheap.
The real downfall of Slime Rancher for me, however, was the inventory. There are only four inventory slots, and for the overwhelming majority of the game, each slot can only hold 50 items. In addition, each ranch can only hold 100 of each kind of "plort" that you have to sell manually, and there's no "quick grab" button - items are picked up and dropped one at a time.
Add this onto the fact that slimes produce plorts fairly quickly, and you get some of the worst inventory management and most boring, grindy gameplay I have ever seen in a videogame. The process for making money is this:
-Go over to two of your corrals inevitably overflowing with plorts
-Grab 50 of each kind of plort. This takes the better part of a minute of just standing in place watching plorts get sucked up, and your inventory is now full. You have probably spilled several plorts onto the ground.
-Run to the nearest market stall
-Sell your entire stock. This takes around 20 seconds of standing in place watching plorts fly into the market receptacle.
-Do the entire process again, because you can only carry 50 at a time and there are over 100 in the corral.
-Do the entire process a third time, because you probably missed a few or left some lying all over the place
-You have now emptied two of your corrals. Repeat this process for all the other ones
-You have now made a few thousand dollars. To finish the game completely, you'll need around 1.5 million.
I would pay any amount of in-game money for something that auto-sells plorts just to not have to do ten+ minutes of inventory management for every ten minutes of actual, fun gameplay.
Overall, at some point I quickly realized I had stopped having fun playing slime rancher several hours ago, so I finally decided to quit.
Oh and also the game crashed and my save was permanantly corrupted with no backup.

There should be a cute award for games like this.
This would definitely win though.
In all seriousness, this game is fun to explore after the main aspect of the game (ranching slimes and being rich) gets a bit stale. And believe me, after a few hours it will. Slime science is good to experiment in after you have lots of plorts. It's funny how the starting slime is the most important slime in Slime SCIENCE!

In my humble opinion, this is what a video game should be. Pure, quantifiable joy. you absolutely can not play this, and not smile to yourself at some point a long the way. Its been a long time since a games made me this happy.

Broforce is a game I can’t believe didn’t already exist – South African developer Free Lives has righted a mighty wrong here. Bursting at the seams with veiny biceps and draped in American flags, Broforce is a love letter to action cinema carved into lead, fired into the corpse of the nearest copy of Contra, and then brought to life via dark magic. It’s so obvious, really; a squad of Earth’s greatest heroes (and heroines)  – most of whom are only a typo away from a thick wad of cease-and-desist letters – against the worst that international terrorism, the galaxy, and the underworld itself can throw at humanity. Frankly, it’s bloody fantastic (and spectacularly bloody).
Unforgiving but (mostly) fair, frantic yet tactical, and oozing with 16-bit 2D charm, if Broforce had been released two decades ago I expect it probably would’ve been the greatest thing to happen to me since puberty. In 2015 the effect is a little less life-altering, but Broforce remains an incredibly confident, refined, unique, and content-rich run ’n gun shooter for up to four co-op players.
The objective of most levels is simple; you just need to blast and/or dart your way through several different locations and very literally get to the chopper. Some of the later levels change this up somewhat as the enemies segue from enemy soldiers to aliens, and later again to supernatural nasties, but that’s the general gist. I love how hilariously dim-witted the regular enemy mooks are but, as just one shot will kill you, you still need to play with precision. The difficulty spikes a few times across the final campaign stages, but it’s certainly in step with the sorts of games that have clearly inspired it. My only major criticism is that I noted some odd slowdown during a couple of periods where a great many alien enemies had pinned themselves in a small area on screen.
Broforce’s nearly completely destructible environments put a creativity-enabling twist on proceedings. Blast through walls to access buildings and get the drop on the baddies inside, or fire through the ground itself to tunnel beneath potential engagements. I found that particularly useful against the large, fire-spitting, worm-like bosses; you can create tunnels to get right up against the still-buried parts of their bodies and use the intact terrain above to temporarily protect you from their ranged attacks.
"The bros are quick and nimble and there’s a good level of nuance in the controls."
The sheer amount of explosive objects on screen means destruction gets pretty wild with other players involved so I’ve actually found myself preferring to play it solo, where you control the pace yourself. There’s also a dedicated deathmatch mode for those of you who’d rather work against one another than together; it’s perhaps a little too chaotic for my tastes, but it’s a laugh in short bursts. Beyond that there’s even an intimidating level editor, but if you’re too daunted to try that out you can simply browse through and quickly and easily load community-made levels. The large team of varied bros themselves are the big stars, and there are plenty of them. Rambro, Brommando, B.A. Broracus, Double Bro Seven, The Brofessional; by now you’re probably picking up on the theme. The bros are quick and nimble and there’s a good level of nuance in the controls; bros can grab walls and climb indefinitely, and automatically execute a handy flip when you’re trying to jump up and around a ledge above. They’re little more than small blobs of pixels, but the way in which each has been lovingly imagined and crafted is evident in the art that splashes on screen each time you unlock a new bro and the quaint little animated profile pics.
What’s particularly great about Broforce is that every time you die you’re forcibly swapped to a random new bro, and each of them has distinctly different weapons and abilities and require a different approach. Some are melee-focused, some have powerful, short-range weapons, some can fire longer distances, and at least one seems completely useless (yes, I’m speaking about you, Brocketeer). Some are better at using their speed to scamper past clumps of enemies, and some have the firepower to duke it out with the baddest of bad guys. Some are faster at chewing through the destructible scenery to create new paths and avoid conflicts and traps, and some have incredibly potent secondary abilities that beg to be exploited at every opportunity.
“Every time you’ll spawn as a new bro who might be better suited to the challenge ahead."
Several of my favourite bros are amongst the latter; Time Bro can slow down time to a crawl (extremely handy against bosses), Brominator has an endoskeleton form that makes him temporarily invulnerable, and Bro Heart’s “Freedom” battle cry sends enemies running (perfect if you’re being swarmed). I often wished I could swap to my preferred bro at will, especially prior to some of the tougher bosses, but I do concede that tougher bosses, but I do concede that making do with the abilities of your given bro is part of the fun. It certainly takes the edge off of repeated failures, knowing that every time you’ll spawn as a new bro who might be better suited to the challenge ahead. The fact that rescuing hostages gains you an extra life but changes your on-screen bro (and is the way you unlock new bros) also creates an interesting risk-reward dynamic; do I trade Time Bro for the extra life and a random new character, or do I stick it out?
I gleaned a great deal of joy discovering the more subtle characteristics of the bros, too. The way the Brodator’s spears stay lodged in the environment for you to jump on, or the way his body explodes if he’s defeated in battle. The way the death of one of the Boondock Bros (who come as a pair, or a trio alongside their father if you activate him) enrages the surviving brother and causes him to flash red and fire his pistols far more rapidly. The fact that the Chuck Norris-inspired Brodell Walker’s melee attack is a roundhouse kick, or that Time Bro’s is a classic JCVD split kick. Broforce is a parody done with a lot of reverence.
I also really love Broforce’s attention to the smaller details of its presentation, from the way the profile pics of each bro bounce as they run and are lit up with muzzle flashes as they fire their weapons, to the enemy kill count at the end of each level (which is usually a conga line of exploding bodies, like nuking a large group of tightly-packed Lemmings). I highly rate the sound, in particular the pitch-perfect glam rock guitar score and hilarious enemy squeals and death gurgles and its constantly screaming narrator.

The game takes place into a facility, located on an alien planet, remotely controlled by humans (through cyborgs called SynB's) to purify and use the planet's water. A short movie explains us how this facility was recently tampered by unknown forces, and our mission will be restoring it. For this purpose we'll be using some special SynB's, each of them with specific abilities, and we'll be doing it in synchronous: the most original trait of this game is indeed the ability of "moving" from a SynB's body to another's, in order to solve specifically written puzzles.
Said puzzles are the very reason for which I fell in love with this game: they're original, balanced, all different from each other (some differences also being substantials, like complete changes of background, solving them in the dark etc); some of them are harder than others, but that's why you feel immensely proud and satisfact, when you solve them!
To clear puzzles we'll use several different tools, from the most classic ones (like boxes and mirrors) to some new ones (the activator for example, a colored ray that we'll be using very often).
But the Body Changer is more than this: it's essentially a fusion between puzzles and a shooter based on old arena games. Combat mechanics are very classic (and hard in my opinion :D), but also introduce some more modern features, like the barrel roll, the abilities to attack from behind, stun, and trip enemies; the game also offers a scripted melee attack, the V-Blade attack, which is a very powerful weapon aswell.
The game's map is immense, and all zones are properly linked: progression is linear, but not trivial; intuitive, but not simple; so my congratulations to developers for hints' and doors' positions. Furthermore, every character has its own different path in the game; paths that unlock only if all of them are progressing alright, and that will cross from time to time.
Scattered through the map there are also small zones, accessible only using the correct tool, filled with collectibles called "d-Disks"; a pleasant addition to the gameplay.
I actually adored the graphic style, which has been reason of a lot of criticism; I believe it's necessary to play the game a bit to understand it.
The style is deliberately minimalist and it is obtained through a selection of geometrical motives and color matching; both elements are pleasant to the sight, light, and match perfectly with setting.
The irregular borders give to the game a touch of cartoon, and a slight distortion that, in union with the ambient sounds, instill a bit of tension on the player, making it for some horror feeling.
Game menù is minimalist too, but functional and user friendly; everything (d-Disks, maps, savegames etc) has its own big tab.
To be an indie game, The Body Changer is almost bug-free.
The only problems I had during my playthrough were related to cache; the game crashed during long session (4h+), and some of the scripts didn't reset (or saved) properly upon reloading a savegame, requiring to quit and restart the game; bullets sometimes went through my targets' head, and then there's the already known "slow run".
The fact that some mechanisms deactivate after clearing zones out (and switching to a new zone) makes some of the backtracking, necessary for gathering d-Disks at later moments, unaccessible.
The game allows only for autosaves, which is ok, but some encounters are fairly long and difficult, and in my opinion they'd require an extra checkpoint; also it was discomfort for me to switch from relaxing and stimulating puzzles to extremely long and challenging combat encounters, without an half-way between; but these are personal problems, that you may have not.
The Body Changer is a game that deserves a chance to be played and explored in all its details.
Maybe its real problem is the price being a bit high, which doesn't help a game of this genre, but during a discount, if you're up for something really unusual, it is a closed eyes purchase.
Not forgetting that the game comes with achievements and steam cards too.

I know I’ve talked about game feel before, but it keeps coming up as a key feature that games either nail down or let slip away. Your game can be as clever or beautiful or engaging as can be, but if it feels bad to play then none of that is going to matter. In the case of The Body Changer, it can’t really rely much on the former so it’s all the more damning that the latter isn’t up to par. I’m being rather hard on it here… it’s a neat idea for a game, just not one that pans out on any level.
You’re going to have to pick bits of the story out of the utilitarian opening and extremely concise terminals everywhere, but you seem to be stationed on some water facility out in space. Something has infected the precious supply and turned it blood red, and it’s up to you to get the purifiers back on line and clean everything up. “You” won’t be doing it yourself, though, because in this version of the future you have SynBs, gormless cyborgs which you can control remotely. With their help, you’ll wade through pools of goo, seal pipes, blast corrupted ‘borgs, and maybe get to the bottom of this whole mess.
The Body Changer is at least named appropriately, because most of your time is going to be spent switching between bodies with different abilities. Some are combat trained, some are shielded against the infection, and some are helpfully color-coded for the big people-sized switches they need to stand on to open doors. Opening doors is your primary concern when there aren’t monsters around, either by finding keycards, triggering switch sequences with your laser wristband thingy, or making good use of the aforementioned floor switches. Levels tend to be linear in how you progress through them to the purifiers but that’s going to include plenty of backtracking and opening side paths.
That was where I started to sour on the gameplay, actually. Your first thirty minutes with the game will acclimate you to switching bodies, grabbing items, and interacting with useless terminals. You’ll get to a room where you take control of a combat SynB and gun down some zombie ‘borgs… and then get stuck. It turns out you need to take another body all the way back to the start of the tutorial to get a keycard to proceed. You’ll need to do some similar shuffling about in later areas too, with detours through three side rooms to get to the other side of a main room or runs back to the start of the level to open something with a new colored laser.
I can see the attempt at a metroidvania-style world here but it just doesn’t work as designed. Backtracking is incredibly boring here, owing to the slow movement, extremely plain environments, and lack of compelling secrets. The environments are huge offenders here, barely reminiscent of actual, livable locations with their plain cel-shaded walls and complete lack of detail. The characters and items are not much better, looking like inflatable versions of Aeon Flux characters and moving in stiff, barely-animated strides. Items simply poof out of the air when you touch them, and ammo is represented in the world merely as 2D icons.
Every time I sat down to play The Body Changer, I got an intense urge to do literally anything else after about fifteen minutes. It feels entirely too much like a game world, full of rigid facsimiles of people and rooms that serve no purpose beyond impeding progress. Why would you even have your door controls be giant laser-activated lights ten feet off the ground? I’m sure a lot of this is by design, considering the story about synthetic servitor beings and the dichotomy of purity and infection, but it doesn’t matter as long as the game simply feels bad to play. Even the menus are plain, badly-proportioned boxes that feel like placeholders. There’s a seed of a good idea buried in The Body Changer, but it would need a better, more polished game to bring it out.

This is not your typical "guns blazing" or "shoot everything that moves" type of game. I call this a thinking man's game. Some reviews call this game monotonous, and while I can see how that could be the case, that was not the case for me. Yes, stealth is about 75% of the game, but let's be honest, much of Vietnam was either napalm airstrikes or stealth patrols, and you don't fly a plane in this game, so stealth is it. Side note: I enjoy the geographical and historical background. It really makes you understand Vietnam better (both the country and the war). As for gameplay: tough. Very tough. Press "quick save" often because each step might be your last...literally. But fortunately you can always quick load your last quick save and show those commies who's boss. Weaponry: it's a candy store for 1960's historical firearm enthusiasts. You'll get the opportunity to shoot the service rifle and pistol of the time, along with everything the enemy shoots at you. Another side note: I really like the fact that you can pick up or drop any weapon you find on the field (to include everything from AK-47's to rocket launchers and everything in between). Ballistics are also more realistic than many games I've played. For example: the 7.62 round from the AK-47 has more stopping power than a 5.56, and a .45 from your service pistol is great up close, but you can tell it slows with range and isn't as effective the farther out. Kudos to the ballistics researchers on this game. Lastly, the value for the price of this game is incredible. In closing, if you like a really hard strategic first person shooter with lots of weaponry, tactics, and simple keyboard/mouse commands, this is the one. Get it today.

The only thing missing is Cataclysm. I've gone back to these games for years and couldn't pass up the chance to see them re-done well. This is a must buy for pretty much anyone who wasn't lucky enough to play them the first time around and an easy recommendation to anyone who did.
-----------------------------------
Editors Note: This is an initial reaction review to the RM. I have only tested the original RM, and will not be playing HW2 for some time. This will be edited and updated as I play more of both. These games, and maybe the original Diablo, defined many of my early gaming memories. I've probably sunk years into them.
-----------------------------------
I like to keep these pretty short and sweet, but I'll add more if I come across something while playing.
Quick Pros/Cons
1.  IMO the original graphics were ahead of their time and aged fairly well but the overhaul is much appreciated. Looks great and there are a bunch of small visual additions/changes that make the experience better.
2.  The UI is better. Probably still could have done more here but honestly, doing so would've thrown off people who played the old games. Which ultimately might have annoyed me. They found a way to keep the feel of the original UI while making it less awkward.
3.  The formations were a huge part of the originals, and like many have said, they really do seem broken in HW1rm. Hope this gets fixed. Clearly an issue with the homeworld 2 engine not working well with the homeworld 1 mechanics. Reportedly, the formation issues are only really occuring in the original rm. So thats good I guess
4.  Ballistic weapons in the original didn't look like pea shooters. As a few others have said, this feels clunky. I'm still unsure if they are actually less effective than they used to be or whether the animations are just more puny looking.
5.  Love in-game acheivements but.. these are the lamest, just about ever. I don't care how challenging some of the missions are.
6.  I don't have as much time as I did when I was playing this 15 years ago. Some sort of time acceleration would have been nice so I didn't have to waste a real life hour resource harvesting. This is particularly annoying since it was addressed in later games. Especially with the additional resources they threw into the RM.
7. One of the more serious issues - The difficulty level of the HW1 RM is drastically lower than the original. Tons of resources and no fuel constraints. Missions that literally were soul crushing are quite manageable and probably don't require any real restarts. Half the time my issue is killing things too fast now rather than capturing them. Still, some people might see this as a good thing. It definitely doesn't require 4 play throughs to get through the tougher levels and you get the great story without alot of the frustration.
8. They kept the story, cutscenes, etc. consistent with the original. And its exactly what they needed to do. Also the music is still fantastic and the voices seem, from what I can remember, exactly the same.
-------------------------------
Conclusions
Whether you played the originals or not, these are games that just shouldn't be missed. A quality re-master is hard to come by. Get this and play it.

Coming from someone who has played both oblivion AND skyrim a LOT.
This game is good, the loot isnt as dense and you cant pick up cups and throw them around at people (no physics) yet, that only seems to encourage further exploration rather than container-scrounging every dungeon you come across like you would in previous elder scrolls games.
The only qualm I have is how easy the game seems at times...
All of the main quests, the bosses of those quests, etc. are all made so...easy...just to ensure you progress through the main story. If you complete every area and do every quest you find it's only made even more easy. I've only died from combat 3 times this game, twice from the necromancers summoning 5 daedra, one of them being a powerful variant, and once from trying to solo a world boss.
Marketplaces are gated through guilds, and probably for good reason, since everyone would just flood the market with cheap materials otherwise, and you'd have that many more people doing 1-50 maxing their tradeskill in a single day.
Combat is target/range based, because there are no physics; weapons don't actually have to hit something to hit it, like they would in skyrim or oblivion, which makes melee/ranged combat feel a bit unsatisfying...
There are no arrows for bows, and consequently no enchanted arrows. They could've been added.
Oblivion portals aren't lore-friendly; bethseda could've made them a huge nostalgia factor from oblivion, but decided to blow it off and redesign them and make them look cruddy. They're also only part of a single quest, as far as i am in the game. They looked and sounded better in oblivion ffs, and that game came out TEN YEARS AGO.
Despite all the complaints, its a solid MMO, it fails on many lore and elder-scrolls levels though. Welkynd stones, don't restore magic anymore, they're a quest item that is unusable that you never even see more than once (most likely). Sigil stones cant be used for enchantment, which wouldn't have changed the game mechanics at all considering how easy it is to enchant things, just would've been a nice nostalgic factor, hell they didn't even have to make an item for it they could've just given you a random enchantment after you did that quest and went "oh look the stone had an enchantment for you!".
They blew alot of stuff that would've made this a great game. It's sad.
At the same time, it's a good MMO, but not a great game. Will still reccomend though considering how every character in the game is fully voiced and they probably have like 500 characters throughout the game in quests with interesting stories and brutal decisions at every turn. The world is HUGE, and the content factor is huge, which is clearly what they were going for. It's worth 20-30$, lets put it that way. So are oblivion and skyrim though, considering the crazy content-adding mods they have, and how much better the combat is than this game.

I am someone who turns his back on the first sign of any horror game, but seeing how I watched Alien movie franchise when I was little and simply loved it, I couldn't say no to Alien:Isolation. I get scared easely and it haunts me for years, but Aliens are interesting to me and therefore I finished it 3 times now.
Is the game scary ? Yep. But not in jumpscares, it has only 1 in the game. It is the atmosphere of the game that makes it scary. The visuals, the amazing sound which is spot on, the details and everything else. It is a genuine Alien Survival Simulator in which you can look at the details, read the station logs and be sure that it is a part of the Alien movie franchise. Alien Isolation is considered canon afterall and I can't argue with that. The story is fantastic and I'm glad it is a part of the Alien universe now.
You're asking yourself probably, should I play the game if I am easely scared ? I can only answer with my own experience. I am easely scared and I avoid horrors completely for that reason. But Alien Isolation wasn't scary to me. Simply because I love Aliens and they're an interesting species. Everytime an Alien pops out of the celings, I can only admire the perfection they created. I really wanted to see how Ellen Ripley felt when she went toe-to-toe against an Alien and that is what this game offers. A personal relationship between you and the perfect organism.
The game will mostly be tense. Tense because of amazing visuals and the sounds of the Alien hissing and crawling around the vents, haunting your every step. It is mostly the thoughts inside the player that make it scarier, rather than the game itself. You keep on worrying constantly when and where is he going to jump out. But once he jumps out, you better find a safe place to hide or you'll be given an extra hole in your head.
The game is PERFECTION and does justice to the Alien franchise and I recommend it with all my heart. It is truly an amazing experience, it is an Alien Survival Simulator. Try it out, you won't regret it.

This is an interesting little piece of interactive fiction that takes place from 2002 to 2007, with all the narrative contained entirely in chat messages. The medium actually enhances the story, since you get to see everything your character types, whether it's actually sent or not. What you DON'T say sometimes provides more insight than what you do, which I find to be a cool addition. I also like how the various user profiles change as the years go on. Both of these features give a fair bit of life to what could otherwise have just been bland chatlog reading.
My only problem is that you're required to press keys to type out your character's messages, and it slows the game down a bit, especially when a message turns out to be much longer to type than its choice description would imply. Other than that, I find this game to be worth a play or two, especially with the multiple endings it provides. If nothing else, it's at least free, so I'd say go for it.

I recommend this game only under the condition that you never buy any of the DLC and get it at the lowest price.  It's the first CoD I've been interested in since Modern Warfare and it deserved that interest, but a lot of its value is sapped away by some critical issues.
Singleplayer campaign seems ok from what I played (though I haven't seen much of it) and the multiplayer is pretty satisfying with addition of the exosuits.  Some of the guns, throwables and scorestreaks are neat and combining them to setup unique kits allows for a nice variety of playstyles.  Despite all the great iterations on the formula, the multiplayer is choked by technical issues and business issues.
Their business model works well on consoles with the player counts they have there, but cripples the game on PC.  I've got all the DLC and pre-order bonuses, but have never once been able to play a match to make use of any of it, because you can't find matches for any of the non-standard maps or game modes.  This is compounded by issues with their networking code and also their new skill based matchmaking which even further separates the playerbase.
It reached that threshold where it was difficult enough to find a match for most things that people learned to stop trying.  They have a random gametype mode that should ideally help distribute the population through the various game modes, but it has a ridiculous name so people just funnel into team deathmatch instead.  If you want a match, you can fire up the game and get into a match quickly, but you will only ever experience a fraction of the game.
The player count has dropped low enough that there's little hope of it ever rebounding.  They needed to just provide all of the map packs for free to bring people back and improve the matchmaker, but they have little incentive to improve the sales of this when there's a new one around the corner.
The original Call of Duty, World at War and Modern Warfare were great, but at this point Activision has proven they have no interest in doing what it takes to make Call of Duty a healthy PC franchise again.  It's just routine now.
It's not a bad game.  It's a good game that's crippled.  So make sure the price you get it at is crippled too.

I can't recommend this game at full price. Because of it's broken launch, the countless amount of DLC released when the base game STILL needed so much polishing and because of the reluctance of fixing what was broken when it actually was important for early adopters. I do not think it's acceptable for a game to be this broken, even when patching fixed most of the annoying stuff a year later. There are no guarantees a developer will fix a game after release and thankfully this one did receive quite a bunch of patches.
But whatever you think about a developer releasing a broken game at first, the current game does have good gameplay value. It's mostly a cosmetic update to what the Total War series has always been, so do not expect anything super innovative here. Is this game better than the first Total War: ROME? Yes. But not by much if you can except the dated graphics from the first game. Is Total War: ROME II the best in the Total War series? Sadly no. I believe Total War: Shogun 2 is better (but features an equally dodgy AI at times). Of course, to some people the Rome theme might be more appealing than the Japanese theme. I guess that's a matter of taste.
So in short, yes I would recommend this game, preferrably at a serious discount (at least 50% off).

Broforce is a game I can’t believe didn’t already exist – South African developer Free Lives has righted a mighty wrong here. Bursting at the seams with veiny biceps and draped in American flags, Broforce is a love letter to action cinema carved into lead, fired into the corpse of the nearest copy of Contra, and then brought to life via dark magic. It’s so obvious, really; a squad of Earth’s greatest heroes (and heroines)  – most of whom are only a typo away from a thick wad of cease-and-desist letters – against the worst that international terrorism, the galaxy, and the underworld itself can throw at humanity. Frankly, it’s bloody fantastic (and spectacularly bloody).
Unforgiving but (mostly) fair, frantic yet tactical, and oozing with 16-bit 2D charm, if Broforce had been released two decades ago I expect it probably would’ve been the greatest thing to happen to me since puberty. In 2015 the effect is a little less life-altering, but Broforce remains an incredibly confident, refined, unique, and content-rich run ’n gun shooter for up to four co-op players.
The objective of most levels is simple; you just need to blast and/or dart your way through several different locations and very literally get to the chopper. Some of the later levels change this up somewhat as the enemies segue from enemy soldiers to aliens, and later again to supernatural nasties, but that’s the general gist. I love how hilariously dim-witted the regular enemy mooks are but, as just one shot will kill you, you still need to play with precision. The difficulty spikes a few times across the final campaign stages, but it’s certainly in step with the sorts of games that have clearly inspired it. My only major criticism is that I noted some odd slowdown during a couple of periods where a great many alien enemies had pinned themselves in a small area on screen.
Broforce’s nearly completely destructible environments put a creativity-enabling twist on proceedings. Blast through walls to access buildings and get the drop on the baddies inside, or fire through the ground itself to tunnel beneath potential engagements. I found that particularly useful against the large, fire-spitting, worm-like bosses; you can create tunnels to get right up against the still-buried parts of their bodies and use the intact terrain above to temporarily protect you from their ranged attacks.
"The bros are quick and nimble and there’s a good level of nuance in the controls."
The sheer amount of explosive objects on screen means destruction gets pretty wild with other players involved so I’ve actually found myself preferring to play it solo, where you control the pace yourself. There’s also a dedicated deathmatch mode for those of you who’d rather work against one another than together; it’s perhaps a little too chaotic for my tastes, but it’s a laugh in short bursts. Beyond that there’s even an intimidating level editor, but if you’re too daunted to try that out you can simply browse through and quickly and easily load community-made levels. The large team of varied bros themselves are the big stars, and there are plenty of them. Rambro, Brommando, B.A. Broracus, Double Bro Seven, The Brofessional; by now you’re probably picking up on the theme. The bros are quick and nimble and there’s a good level of nuance in the controls; bros can grab walls and climb indefinitely, and automatically execute a handy flip when you’re trying to jump up and around a ledge above. They’re little more than small blobs of pixels, but the way in which each has been lovingly imagined and crafted is evident in the art that splashes on screen each time you unlock a new bro and the quaint little animated profile pics.
What’s particularly great about Broforce is that every time you die you’re forcibly swapped to a random new bro, and each of them has distinctly different weapons and abilities and require a different approach. Some are melee-focused, some have powerful, short-range weapons, some can fire longer distances, and at least one seems completely useless (yes, I’m speaking about you, Brocketeer). Some are better at using their speed to scamper past clumps of enemies, and some have the firepower to duke it out with the baddest of bad guys. Some are faster at chewing through the destructible scenery to create new paths and avoid conflicts and traps, and some have incredibly potent secondary abilities that beg to be exploited at every opportunity.
“Every time you’ll spawn as a new bro who might be better suited to the challenge ahead."
Several of my favourite bros are amongst the latter; Time Bro can slow down time to a crawl (extremely handy against bosses), Brominator has an endoskeleton form that makes him temporarily invulnerable, and Bro Heart’s “Freedom” battle cry sends enemies running (perfect if you’re being swarmed). I often wished I could swap to my preferred bro at will, especially prior to some of the tougher bosses, but I do concede that tougher bosses, but I do concede that making do with the abilities of your given bro is part of the fun. It certainly takes the edge off of repeated failures, knowing that every time you’ll spawn as a new bro who might be better suited to the challenge ahead. The fact that rescuing hostages gains you an extra life but changes your on-screen bro (and is the way you unlock new bros) also creates an interesting risk-reward dynamic; do I trade Time Bro for the extra life and a random new character, or do I stick it out?
I gleaned a great deal of joy discovering the more subtle characteristics of the bros, too. The way the Brodator’s spears stay lodged in the environment for you to jump on, or the way his body explodes if he’s defeated in battle. The way the death of one of the Boondock Bros (who come as a pair, or a trio alongside their father if you activate him) enrages the surviving brother and causes him to flash red and fire his pistols far more rapidly. The fact that the Chuck Norris-inspired Brodell Walker’s melee attack is a roundhouse kick, or that Time Bro’s is a classic JCVD split kick. Broforce is a parody done with a lot of reverence.
I also really love Broforce’s attention to the smaller details of its presentation, from the way the profile pics of each bro bounce as they run and are lit up with muzzle flashes as they fire their weapons, to the enemy kill count at the end of each level (which is usually a conga line of exploding bodies, like nuking a large group of tightly-packed Lemmings). I highly rate the sound, in particular the pitch-perfect glam rock guitar score and hilarious enemy squeals and death gurgles and its constantly screaming narrator.
