Factorio is a Sandbox-Survival game where you play someone who crash-landed on an alien planet inhabited by a hostile race of primitive aliens that seem to, instead of going to the gym, simply breathe Carbon-Dioxide to get pumped up and angry before trying to steamroll your base.
What? Read on.
Initially, you'll have to gather resources manually in order to craft the tools you need for basic automation and basic research. You'll then start automating resource extraction, smelting, refining, production and research as you try to steer clear of the angry aliens. Eventually, you'll have automated trains loading up cargo on automated stations that's being automatically filled by automated extractors and smelteries. And as it reaches your main base, that train will be unloaded by automated cargo drones that will help you sort out your huge storage system and bring you whatever you need directly to your inventory.
And let's not forget about the construction bots that will automatically build blueprints you design. It's a simple, great feature that will make you do the "Feel Good Man" face every time you build a new Solar Array.
Of course, you're free to play, build and progress as you wish. Make your designs as compact as you can or as large as you want. Design storage and sorting systems, optimized smelting/refining/research/transport designs, or just load up your tank and troll the wildlife.
(Personally when I first started playing with trains I completely forgot about the rest of the game and simply tried to weaponize them for a few hours.)
The game features a World Generator that really lets you fine-tune your experience. You can go for a game with passive and weak enemies filled with resources, or a scarce planet filled with angry mobs. You can even make the map really narrow, only generating terrain horizontally (Linear Factorio), which is a different gamemode by itself.
The default settings are balanced and challenging enough for most people, so you can quickly jump in on a new game. And even though the game has a learning curve and can be rather complex at times, the tutorial will get you covered, for the most part.
There's also a mechanic in the game called Pollution. As I mentioned before, Pollution will make aliens (more) agressive, and they will get stronger and evolve faster as you pollute more and more. This can make you adapt, plan and upgrade your factories for lower footprint or higher production in order to progress faster before the aliens spread everywhere.
This is a really interesting feature that keeps you on your toes, and makes it so having radar stations and keeping an eye at enemies is actually useful, and sometimes necessary.
The game is already really fun as is, and features multiplayer.
Hopefully it will get further expanded and polished. If you enjoy crafting, survival, automation (especially Minecraft Tech mods), you'll definitely have a blast with Factorio!

Dark Souls 2 is a great game.
It's a bit less punishing than the last Dark Souls game, which I actually prefer.
Dark Souls 1 has a better overworld that meshes together brilliantly, but Dark Souls 2 has more of isolated stages that mesh together themselves.
Think of Dark Souls 1 as a large map, with several paths, and each path connects to another.
This sounds great, but you end up doing a lot of running around, and a lot of backtracking.
Think of Dark Souls 2 as a bit of a smaller map with fewer paths, but each path leads to more areas, even if linearly.
The ups and downs here are that you feel like you beat a level, or cleared some large obstacle, rather than just found another place. However, it makes the overworld feel less-meshed together since you do a lot of fast-traveling.
Enough about maps and layouts.
The gameplay is great. It's punishing, yet not unfair. If you die, it was because you let yourself get cought, or you made a mistake. The combat is fast and fun, yet intense.
Pvp in dark souls is some of the best I've ever had the pleasure of playing. It's really skill-based.
Pvp takes place in 2 major forms. Invasions and arenas.
Arenas take place in a few areas, and you're put into a 1v1 to the death with another player. May the best man win.
Invasions take place when another player will invade your game world, and fight you while you fight normal NPCs. This is blatantly unfair, but if you lose you don't feel inferior, BECAUSE it's unfair. You lost an unfair fight, no shame in that. Yet if you win, you feel amazing, as you just won this duel, with all of the odds stacked against you. You could be the invader, or the victim in that scenario.
Bosses in Dark Souls are intense. The first few times you fight them, they will tear you to pieces, and as you learn their attack patterns, and learn when they're vulnerable, they slowly become easier and easier. Bosses range from amazingly difficult, to becoming a cakewalk. Not because the game's difficulty changes, but because you have become better as a pleyer, and have learned how to beat them. This feeling is immensely satisfying.
I would recommend Dark Souls to anyone that loves RPGs, just know that you're in for a hell of a ride.

An excellent remake of an excellent game. The games hold up extremely well, even though the games are 16 and 12 years old. The devs reworked everything from the ground up as opposed to improving some textures like in most HD remakes. I finished the first campaign and played a few skirmish games and haven't encountered any bugs. The multiplayer is still in beta at this time since they are letting all the factions across both games play against each other, and things aren't balanced yet. There is a new UI and controls, mostly revamping the HW1 controls to make them more like HW2, and getting rid of refeuling for strikecraft in HW1. Ignore people that are complaining about this because it makes HW1 10x more playable. On the down side the formations from HW1, that were crucial to using strike craft don't work in the remastered version. Hopefully this will be fixed in a patch, but if you want a faithful HW1 experience the set includes both HW1 and 2 in their original untouched forms. Also I believe the campaign has gotten easier. I can't verify if this is because the game is simply easier or because I have played so much of it over the years.HW has a slower pace, so if you prefer 5 minute multiplayer matches HW might not be fore you. The story is very good, a rarity for a RTS, also the soundtrack and art is also amazing. The HW franchise was so ahead of its time that it is still innovative more than a decade on. No space based RTS has ever come close to besting it. The modding community has been active for the past 2 years for HW2 specifically, so you can expect a lot of mods comming out shortly. I wouldn't be surpirsed if HW: Remastered won many RTS of the year awards, like it did when it came out years ago. These games are a must play if you like RTSs or space based games.
Homeworld was unique and wonderful when released, and it still is, only slightly more so!

Easily the best 15 bucks I've spent on steam. A fun singleplayer game. You basically start a match with x number of bots, and each team has half that number. You, the player, are one of the soldiers on your side, working to capture flags and kill enemies. There are tanks, planes, helicopters, jeeps, jeeps with mounted guns on them, emplacements, you name it. If you have the "squad leader toolkit" item, you can get up to 5 bots on your side to take orders from you (attack one of the flags, enter vehicles, follow you, attack a certain point, etc etc).The matches can be fairly long, depending on what gamemode you're playing and how many bots you have in it. The more bots you have, the more it feels like you're fighting in an actual war. Without using the squad leader toolkit item, you're another soldier in the army, which is still pretty fun because you can follow other groups of bots and help them take a point. With it, though, you can lead that group of bots and strategically maneuver around the flag to take it easier. Also, custom maps integration via workshop. All around great game.

Since Enslaved was released on console I had always wanted to play it, now that I have I can say that it is a mixed bag.
My initial impression of the game from trailers and promotions was that it harked back to classic PS2 games, what it most reminded me of was Jak and Daxter, the general gameplay seemed similar and immediately I was interested. The Jak series has always been one of my favourites, anything close to that was something I would be happy to play. When I finally got the chance to purchase it on steam I had mixed feelings. The general look of the game interested me, vaguely steampunk with a scrapyard feel to it. The control scheme was close to what I expected except with more of a God of War style to it. No jump instead a roll and the combat despite being satisfying became very repetitive and was not especially free-form.
The game is split into two distinct sections, the parkour and the fighting. These sections rarely mix and when they do it is just frustrating because enemies will interrupt your forward progress at awkward times. The parkour itself is average at best. It is very constrictive and lacks any skill. Flashing handholds and bars make it a simple task of pressing the right direction. In fact the best thing I could say about the gameplay is that it is satisfying, the animations are smooth and the characters have a real sense of weight to them however this is overshadowed by the number of almost identical situations and encounters that quickly become tedious. The game has some puzzle elements, very simple but not necessarily boring.
At this point the game seems somewhat unappealing but what I mostly enjoyed about this game was the character interaction. The story is simple, not really good or bad, just enough to set the scene and move the game along. However the relationship of the two main characters, Monkey and Trip soon becomes the main focus. Trip is your captor, she placing a headband on Monkey that forces him to obey her and kills Monkey if Trip dies. This adds an interesting dynamic between the characters. Initially there is a hate for Trip and her selfishness but as the story progresses the headband stops being the reason the player looks after her. It almost becomes irrelevant. It probably sounds like the game would do little to support a strong connection between you and Trip but actually this is its most successful piece. Gameplay revolving around carrying trip through areas she can't navigate and protecting her strengthens your involvement in the relationship in a way I didn't really expect. On the other hand don't think Trip is another useless female companion for you to escort, while she cannot fight the huge mechs on her own she has many gadgets to both protect herself and aid you, so that's nice.
So should you buy it? Maybe. The main thing to consider is whether the gameplay sounds too repetitive for you. If you enjoy God of War style combat then go for it. Enslaved definitely isn't something I regret buying however it is far from being one of my favourites, it was good while it lasted.

After loads of patching, is Total War: Rome II worth it?
It's ok.
It even does things better than the original Rome.
Now, is it better than the original Rome? Not really, Rome: Total War is easily superior. But that's an insanely high bar to reach. And what Rome II does it does pretty well.
Instead of cranking out unit after unit, the requires the player to build armies around single general characters, effectively limiting your armies. This makes for both good involvement with your generals as they become characters you level up, but it also destroys a great deal of low-intensity strategy in which you could send a few units of Hastati to deal with rebels or use as scouting elements to probe regional defenses. But, at the same time, it adds needed value to your commanders instead of flooding you with loads of throwaways.
The Naval battles have some annoying inconsistencies, but marine landings are the absolutely best part of the game. It's downright cumbersome, but it's still satisfying to slam your Trireme's ram into the side of some filithy Carthaginian ship.
I REALLY love how Cavalry has been made more fragile and hoplites aren't the end all-be all of infantry. On top of that, skirmishing feels actually worthwhile, as well. This game does have superior unit balance. In addition, unit AI is more adaptable and no where near as rigid as the original when it comes to maneuver. Just because one soldier is stuck freaking out, the rest of the formation won't be affected. The politics game is nice in that attacking one faction will bring about the ire of their allies. Forcing you to consider situations carefully, at times.
The weakest comparison is the soundtrack. Rome II's soundtrack is utterly forgettable while the original had an awesome score.
Other than that, it's Total War. Grand Campaign with lots of hours to be invested in conquering the world and, unlike the first, you aren't just locked into playing Rome at first. I really like that. Though, when it advises you on the starting difficult of a faction, it's best taken with a grain of salt. Starting off with Carthage is brutal while finding most other "normal" rated factions aren't as horrible. I will give you this piece of advice: In Rome: Total War, you're charged with conquest immediately and without real consequence. Here, you really need to consider where and when you attack; There's no more early game rushes. You're better suited spending the first few turns building civil infrastructure and raising armies. In the end, however, the weakest portion of gameplay is the political meta game. And, it outright pulls lame things out of the ether to add "challenge." I was rebuilding Patavium after ceasing it and there was a revolt. This is to be expected. However, it manifested a 3,000+ man army of silver and gold chevron'd units. How did slaves become instant Ancient Operators? The art of the strategy game is lost in this day and age.
In the end, some of the strategic depth was lost, some was added.
Is it worth a buy? Only if you're a fan of Total War.

Gearbox has (re)created a beautiful-looking space strategy game that will impress those new to the series but leave oldschool Homeworld fans bitterly dissapointed. If you're looking for some fun multiplayer action you'll love this game but if you want to revisit the classic Homeworld campaign I cannot recommend it unless there's a serious effort by the devs to address the many problems in the launch version. Read below for detailed comments.
THE GOOD:
- Absolutely gorgeous graphics. Everything looks very nice and with some minor tweaking plays smoothly even on my     not-so-good laptop.
- The original artstyle in the cinematics has been faithfully recreated and, again, it all looks very nice.
- Excellent, engaging story in HW1:R, same as the 1999 classic.
- Good voice acting and music bring the experience to life.
- Multiplayer is, despite some balance issues between the HW1 and HW2 races, simply a blast to play.
THE BAD:
- The game uses a modified HW2 engine which does not seem to work very well with the HW1 campaign/units. I'm not sure how many of the problems listed below are due to engine limitations and how many can be patched in, if someone more knowlegeable about HW modding can chip in on this I'll edit the review accordingly.
- Strike craft formations/tactics simply do not work for the HW1 units. Strike craft will assume a formation when ordered to but after combat is joined they will attack seemingly random targets on their own flight paths regardless of tactics settings used, making concentrating fire to specific targets impossible and leading to a lot of losses.
- The HW1 remastered campaign in general lacks polish. Missing/bugged mission triggers, wonky AI behaviour (resource collectors in particular will randomly stop harvesting after dropping off their loads), ship engine sound effects persisting after zooming in and then out on some units, sensor manager sometimes just deciding to stop working altogether, repair corvettes apparently not working at all and simply atrocious difficulty scaling.  Expect to reload a lot to get through some missions.
- The dynamic difficulty scaling seems way out of whack for the campaign. The HW1 campaign now uses the (almost universally despised) dynamic difficulty scaling system originally introduced by HW2. In a nutshell, the enemies you'll face are generated depending on your fleet composition at the start of a mission. Some people like this idea, some don't. Regardless of how one feels about it, the system clearly has not been playtested enough as the seeming lack of hard caps on enemy numbers will lead to some unwinnable fights for players who like to build up their fleet. For example, capturing a good number of enemy corvettes in mission 2 will cause an overwhelming number of enemies to spawn in the following mission, leading to a game over before the introductory cutscenes are even finished.
CONCLUSION: I'm really torn on this but I'll have to go with a no recommendation until the flawed port of the HW1 campaign and strike craft mechanics are addressed. If you're a returning HW1 veteran definately hold off on this until the game is (hopefully) patched and/or modded to make the experience closer to the original. On the other hand those new to the series will no doubt appreciate the engaging story of the campaign. The fun multiplayer can also help a lot so consider what you want of the game and take this review as it is.

I played this game on pc and I had so much fun. The combination of stealth and magic works really well. My first playthrough was as Emily in Low Chaos and right after that I played as Corvo in High Chaos. I really like that there are a lot of options if you wanna go for low chaos. After I played low chaos and high chaos I went back to play Dishonored 1. The developers have improved the game and gameplay in Dishonored 2. And I don't get stuck if I walk too close to walls as in the first Dishonored.
What I like:
Some of the level designs are really cool and creative, I have three favorite missions and places. I like that there are many ways to deal with enemies – use powers, mines, grenades, sleep darts etc. Another good thing is the freedom in how you play: Be unseen in one mission or let guards ring how many alarms they want. Make people sleep and turn a place into a snoring town. Or go haywire on everyone. Your choice.
It was fun to escape to rooftops or use blink/far reach to get away from enemies and hide somewhere. To tease and confuse an enemy was also fun, by blinking right in front of one and then blink behind their back. Or distract enemies with a copy of yourself. Both Emily and Corvo have great powers. Upgraded Windblast made me feel like Darth Vader blasting enemies into walls. If only Fus Ro Dah would have been this powerful.
Bonecharms can be quite good. Those that aren't, just destroy them and get whalebones.
Crafting is a great addition to the game. With whalebones you can craft runes. Even though it cost me runes to learn how to craft runes, it was absolutely worth it.
The world was different in my two playthroughs. There were more bloodflies and more dead NPC: s in High Chaos where there were none in Low Chaos. People and guards comment your behavior. I like that there are some noticeable differences.
The option to have customized difficulty is nice and New Game + could be fun to try. If I play a third time someday in the future I might try these out.
What I don't like:
The loading screen when starting up the game could sometimes be very slow.  This is Denuvo's fault.
The range of some powers feels shorter than they were in the first game.
The upgraded Dark Vision was better in Dishonored 1 and in the dlc:s with Daud. It had much better range and loot was easier to see. In Dishonored 2, the loot is not highlighted enough and the colors look more or less the same. Sometimes I see loot better without using DV. It's good  that everything does not look brown and dark when using it as in the first game. But perhaps Dark Vision could be blue, like Daud´s was in the dlc:s of the first Dishonored game.
Problems I encountered:
Lag once or twice. A few times when I pressed J to go to journal, the game crashed.  Also, there were some stuttering in the beginning when I had graphics maxed out. After I lowered two of these settings, there were no more stuttering.
Dishonored 2 (in my opinion) has a much more detailed and racher story then the first Dishonored. I would 100% recommend this game if you've played the first Dishonored.

If you like base building and logic puzzle games, you will feel right at home in the world of factorio.

But puzzle games you may ask? Well, not in the traditional sense. Factorio is definitely one of the best base builders I've ever played. My estimate is that I have over 100 hours of playing Factorio before it arrived on Steam and it's still very fun and challenging. With procedurally generated maps, good mod support, adapting difficulty and constant dev updates, there's always something new to try and do in Factorio. If you're the kind of person who loves logistics management, designing functional bases or figuring out optimal designs, this is definitely a game for you.
I believe it also has a free demo so why not give it a try if you're intrigued?
So, what makes it so special? The answer is simple - it has a
. In most sandbox basebuilders the early game is the best part - you're constantly challenged by hunger, resource scarcity and enemy strength. In a few hours though, when you improve yourself, enemies become a joke and gathering resources is only a boring chore, with no end in sight.
Factorio turns this dynamic upside down by enabling you to automate almost everything. Even though you're expected to micromanage your resources and defenses in the beginning, very soon you can devise systems that do this for you while you focus on macromanagement - expanding your base, improving your supply lines, bolstering defenses. You don't have to manually dig coal or iron - you have automatic drills for that, you only need to make sure you have enough electricity so they keep working! You don't have to automatically transfer dug iron to your furnaces, you have conveyor belts and inserters that do that for you!
Basically, very soon you become the boss, the architect - your only job is to expand production, advance your tech tree and keep up with the
. The bigger your base becomes, the more pollution it creates. While this doesn't bother you, it definitely bothers the local wildlife - depending on multiple variables (like global pollution, time passed, number of destroyed nests), they become more and more aggressive and evolved. They start to migrate, their nests increase in size and new kinds of enemies start to appear that will force you to shift tactics, maybe even go on the offensive and clear out some of the dangerously close nests.
The
is very extensive and there are many moments when a new techonology completely revolutionizes your factory. For example, unlocking trains completely changes the game if you decide to use them. I've spent countless hours on building complex railroad networks with automated trains that deliver raw resources to my main base. You can make it as simple as one railroad with a 2-way train that delives a resource or you can have multiple delivery points, dozens of trains, roundabouts with signals to prevent crashes, automatic unloading mechanisms, train refueling stations, redundancies to prevent deadlocks... Your imagination is the limit.
And this is just one of the examples - when you add flying robotic drones, vehicles, power armor, automated construction, the game becomes even more interesting. In the late game you will feel like a god, building outposts with only a few clicks of your mouse, and it's always satisfying to just sit back and watch your factory work, no matter if it looks like a clockwork mechanism or like spaghetti.
There is one major thing that might turn some people away from the game - it is really a pure sandbox. Even though there's a victory condition (building a rocket), it's very arbitrary and ultimately pointless. The game is really fun when you set your own goals and work towards accomplishing them but if you're used to games guiding you by hand, telling you what are you supposed to be doing next... you're gonna be confused and bored in Factorio. There's a campaign that serves as a tutorial, and we're eventually getting custom scenarios / challenges made by devs.. but for the most part, you're left to your own ideas in the endless sandbox mode.
I also want to criticize combat. While it works well for defensive gameplay, attacking and destroying nests can be frustrating at times. In the late game your character can be killed extremely quickly so the best strategy is to just spam drones and explosives while running away from them, and loading the game if you get cornered and killed... or just build turrets close to nests and lure the horde into firing range. I believe the devs said they are going to rework combat eventually so this might not be true for long!
Factorio is a sandbox basebuilder where your base is an actual defensible, functional entity rather than something you build just for aesthetics, or out of boredom. Rather than forcing you to do all the manul chores, you're in charge of building automated systems that do all the work for you. It has good graphics (stylish 2D sprites), performs good, has stable multiplayer, excellent mod support and receives constant updates by the devs. Even though it's labeled as Early Access, it might as well be released as a finished game and I wouldn't complain - it's working great and has plenty of content, especially considering its price.
This is a fantastically challenging, puzzle solving, sandbox sort of game.

Bleed 2, how can I even BEGIN?!
This is one of my favorite games of all time, if not my favorite game ever. Sure, some may say the game is super short, but who ever said that's a bad thing? This game is AMAZING for speedrunning and replayability! It's as if the game was created for the singular purpose of speedrunning (but can also be played casually for those who would like to, of course).
Difficulty scales from pretty easy to EXTREMELY challenging (Easy, Normal, Hard, Very Hard,
). For starting out the game, I'd recommend going straight into the story mode on hard difficulty. It gives the game a fair challenge to start the game out with. When you mess up, it's almost never the game's fault. You may get hit too many times taking silly and easily avoidable hits or you're simply running/dashing into bullets, but you know you can do it if you keep going at it. Yes, sometimes RNG can screw up runs, but that's expected, since it's random, but it also adds differences to every playthrough. In some runs, you may not see all of a certain boss' possible attacks so that adds replayability, along with the unlockable characters, weapons, and abilities for tons of different play styles. For example, while some may use the bullet-time to better react to enemies' attacks, others might use it as little as possible to get a faster time. If I recall correctly, the story has some subtle and some funny changes for all of the different characters.
The bosses are the main portion of the game, as many can tell you, (though the platforming sections can be just as intense) and each one of them has a great amount of detail worked into their movement patterns, attack patterns, and designs. If you are familiar with Cuphead, then you should be familiar with bosses giving off special warnings before their attacks. Bleed 2 has the same kind of system. The difference however, is that as the difficulty is risen, boss patterns become quicker, giving you less time to react before they dish out their attacks or move across the screen. Projectiles on screen also become much more common and move faster in the higher difficulties.
The soundtrack is outstanding! All of the tracks are extremely catchy and they're fun to jam to while you play or even on the go. The art style is a perfect balance between retro and modern styles.
The controls are much more fluent, customizable, and generally better than they were in the first game. Mobility is fast, easy to get the hang of (even with a controller), and incredibly smooth. Something that I wish I had known during my second run of the game is that you can equip up to 5 different weapons at a time (some characters do not apply because of their unique weapons).
With 70 hours, and counting, I am still finding new little things to appreciate in Bleed 2, including references or throwbacks to the first game, secrets, and other Easter eggs. In order to get everything out of Bleed 2, yes, I would recommend you play through the first game, but it isn't completely necessary to understand the story. Bleed (1) can go as low as $1.24 during Steam sales, so keep an eye out for it.
I would recommend Bleed 2 without a single doubt! 10/10

Bleed 2 takes many lessons from the previous game in the series and builds up an incredible, explosive, triple-jump, slow-motion, boss-rushy journey that captivates and entertains. This 2D twin-stick shooter essentially plays like a inglorious child of Bayonetta, F.E.A.R., Gunstar Heroes and bullet-hell games. Gameplay flows and transcends the player in the game that will satisfy most demanding action junkies out there.
This game is also much more polished that its predecessor. The presentation is now improved with much cleaner graphics and very good rock music this time around. That few lines of dialogue that are considered "story" here aren't that stupid as in Bleed 1. Even the game overs flow much better and push you faster back into action, still keeping that 4th wall breaking charm. What didn't really need any improvement and still was tweaked even higher, is the quality and quantity of the bosses. Those are bigger, faster, more creative and all-throughout enjoyable no matter the level and design. Excellent work.
As I said in the beginning: The only drawback of Bleed 2 is that it literally ends after an hour of intense action. Are there higher difficulties? Yes. Unlockable characters? Yes. Additional modes? Yes. Those will make those self-improvers and S-rank chasers extremely happy, but I'm still hungry for more levels with this type of gameplay. I had a blast playing this and it's a shame that it doesn't come in the bigger package.
That being said, I believe you should help this dev out getting as much money as possible. He created a action-gameplay monster that deserves more recognition that it has right now. Buy it, play it and tell your friends. It is all around awesome title that needs to be pushed further.

After a year of support strictly for the purpose of selling us DLC that would have been included in the intial release a decade hence, Total War: Rome II is finally playable and, dare I say, enjoyable.
The Pros and Cons, because I like information to be concise:
+ On high settings, the graphics are beautiful with detailed models.
+ The game offers a great variety in units, divided amongst several core cultures and a large roster of playable factions.
+ The campaign map is huge and varied.
+ Armor and weapon models are perhaps the most historically authentic Total War has been to date.
+ Deployable defenses have been slightly expanded.
+ Diplomacy has been expanded, with a notable ability to direct allies and vassals against coordinated targets.
+ Battles between competant players on campaign who understand historical tactics are often engaging and satisyfing.
+ Multiplayer campaigns have thankfully not been removed, and in some ways even improved upon.
- The user interface is appauling, especially compared to the polish of Shogun 2.
- Naval combat is an utter joke with too many issues to list here, but was promoted as a core feature.
- Famous cities are not at all what we were promised during promotion.
- A grotesque level of homoginization exists amongst factions of similar base cultures.
- In a game centered around ancient formation warfare, formations themselves are simplistic, asinine, and limited.
- The speed of battle is far too fast, even after patching; units move too quickly, and the ratio of kills to routes is asinine.
- Roman defensive forts, promoted as a prominent feature, are simplistic, ahistorical, and shared with all factions.
- Roman tactics in general have been simply left out of the game.
- The growing emphasis upon this series as an e-sport is troubling and unnecessary.
- Capture points are senseless, placed terribly, and neuter the player's tactical choices.
- The continuation of arcadey, asinine special abilities only adds to the frustration of managing large battles.
- The AI is not at all what we were promised during promotion, with no tangible improvements.
- AI armies invariably recruit weak units and spam units of a single type beyond reason.
- Ancient tactics are severely limited; the AI cannot compartmentalize, instead charging everything in at once.
- There is no viable method of giving ground, thus rendering tactics like those seen at Cannae difficult at best.
- Family trees have been removed in favor of a weakly implemented political system.
- The new war coordination target system is limiting, and the AI takes forever to attempt set goals.
- Deployable defenses are often useless, with limited scope and range of use, and restrictions based upon general traits.
- After a year of patching, the game still cannot handle large scale siege battles optimally.
- Environmental lighting is strange, harsh on the eyes, and requires modding to fix.
- SEGA and Creative Assembly's business practices have been brazen and downright offensive surrounding this release.
I summary, Rome II subverted Empire as the disappointing child in an otherwise noble house with a high pedigree. While Creative Assembly's diligence in patching the game may seem admirable, let us not forget the reason behind the avid support. Many core features of the franchise were needlessly gutted or omitted, while many half-baked features were added that no one asked for, in the laziest fashion imaginable. I love this game, being a fan of history and warfare in particular. I cannot recommend it, because I love it despite its myriad flaws for being the single provider of large-scale ancient warfare on the market. I for one hope that one day, we see new developers take on the challenges of this genre. For CA under SEGA's direction has grown too fat for its armor, with no one to fight.

I was initially highly sceptical due to all of the reported problems it had at launch, but I bought Rome 2 at half price during the sales a couple of weeks ago, and now I play it, this game is worth its full price.
The diplomacy is much better, in my opinion than earlir games, and I like the province system. The battles are great fun, I like the feel of melee heavy armies slogging it out with suppot from ranged units.
I find the game harder than, for example, Empire. The AI, I find, is quite agressive, which is fantastic, providing an actual challenge. I have found that it is more difficult to steamroller your way though the whole map (it is, however, not impossible). I enjoy this challenge, and relish the chance to carve out my empire in the face of a relentless foe.
There are problems however, the loading times and frame rate are somehow worse for me, when they should have been improved, it is not unplayable, just frustating sometimes. But please take into account that my computer is really not great, better rigs than mine (which is to say, most computers) should be able to run it just fine).
Another irksome point is the encycopedia, it makes it more difficult to find the basic information that should more readily availiable.
But overall, I love this game, it is fun, it is a challenge and there is nothing more satisfying than crushing your enemies under the boots of the Roman legions.

Picked the game up on sale. Aside from performance issues this is amazing. I'm running this on a 4 year old mid range laptop, with a freaking GTX 480M  (pretty trash graphics card) and only 8 GB RAM and I can run this with pretty consistent 40-50. Sometimes I run out of memory and the game freezes for a few seconds but it runs fine 99% of the time, I think pretty good considering my PC specs.
Honestly I could care less about the performance stuff because if you can look past that, the game itself is really breathtaking. There's a reason why the Just Cause series has always been my favorite open world series. I think Just Cause 3 is the epitome of "Here, have some cool toys and go crazy!" When you first start out you're just regular ol' Rico Rodriguez flying from town to town waving your AK-47 and battling the dictator's army. By the end you don't fight enemies so much as you just choose how to annihiliate them. You get a great sense of progression as you unlock more stuff (especially the DLC) going from a simple rebel to a god of destruction. It's the ultimate power fantasy.
Pretty well balanced too, even the really overpowered stuff has some kind of drawback which makes using it more risky (like the nuke launcher has a huge radius making it easy to kill yourself, the jetpack wingsuit makes enemy SAM's target you, that sort of thing) and there isn't much fluff, for the most part all the vehicles and weapons fill their own role. For example, you have the ultra-fast supercar, but you might prefer to use an F1-style racecar instead which isn't quite as fast but is much less likely to flip over. Or you have a semi-automatic sniper rifle with a high rate of fire which is great for picking off gaurds with headshots compared to a slower anti-materiel rifle which is better for destroying static objects and light vehicles.
The game is pretty good from a technical standpoint. The draw distance is much better than Just Cause 2, which makes jets a lot more fun to use. The graphics are great, even when I have them turned down all the way. There is a ton of destructive terrain and objects. You can fly through a forest in a jet simply by blasting all the trees out of your way using missiles. If you don't feel like entering a military compound you can plant some C4 on a wall and make your own door. If you have the Mech Land Assault DLC you can literally pick up entire buildins and smash them into other buildings. Again the only issues from a technical standpoint is the memory issues, so I would reccomend only buying with at least 16GB of RAM unless you are fine with some occasional freezing.
Anyway enough rambling. It's a cool game. I say buy it, and if it runs poorly on your computer just get a refund.

A fantastic strategy game with a perfect combination of exciting campaign gameplay and intense and difficult real time battles.  Real strategy is required in this game to succeed not only in battle, but also as a nation.
Many options are presented to you in Rome II when it comes to your empire. Will you expand via military force and conquer all in your path? Or will you make connections, allies and trade, becoming the richest and most influential nation in the known world? The choice is yours in Rome II and it does so in great fashion.
There is always room for improvment and Rome II isn't perfect. A few things could be more fleshed out, such as general(Family Tree from TW: Attila would have been great) and I've always yerned for a more personal connection to your units within an army. A simple window for stats for that unit would be nice with # of kills and battles, total losses perhaps.
Overall Rome II is an amazing strategy game, easily one of the best. I recommend it to any RTS fan, and even newcomers. It may be overwhelming at first but it's easy to get into and has a boat load of content.

If you are a stealth game fanatic, do not miss out on this gem.

Call of duty AW, I personally feel is a step in the right direction for the franchise. The game isn't exactly the same as all the others thanks to the addition of the exosuit movement system. It feels like a breath of fresh air in what seems like a standard copy and paste job each year.
Obviously there are some pretty major flaws in the game however there are also positives to it as well.
Pros: Feels new and is a refreshment to the normal cut and paste format COD usually is made of.
Optimized very well (from my experience) I have experienced little frame drops and almost always stay above 50 fps (it usually hovers around 60 - 70) running at 1080p max settings (with the exception of AA and supersampling).
FOV slider from 65* - 90*
Cons: Horrible netcode
Dedicated servers are used but on a hybrid system of dedicated and listened servers. What is a listened server? The same damn thing we've been using this whole time. (Peer to Peer connection)
Still running on heavily modified quake engine from 1969, seriously they have to update it eventually because thats a really old engine and is far behind in terms of its graphical capabilities to something like the frostbite engine.
Gets repetitive fast, the only thing that keeps you coming back for more is the supply drop system, in which most cases you dont get what your lookinjg for anyway. (BTW has anyone noticed ASD's arn't available for pc? If they were we still shouldn't buy them cause they're a cheap and easy way to make cash)
Not a lot of people playing, according to steam there are a few thousand playing however due to cods netcode that doesn't really change anything, that or steam may have miscalculated. (They do sometimes)
Final verdict: 6/10 The game is definently good there is fun to be had here especially with the exo movement however the poor netcode and/or lack of players makes it often hard to find a match. Don't get me wrong you can still find a few but at the most its usually about 1 - 3.

Completely blows the original out of the water. Bleed 2 is extremely fast paced, incredibly fluid and unbelievably fun.
Bleed 2 is a fast paced twin stick shooter. The player character, Wryn, is remarkably mobile, being able to jump using the right trigger, and then consecitively air dash 3 more times before touching the ground. Moving the right stick causes her to slash with a katana, after which she will immediatelly begin firing an endless stream of bullets from twin pistols. You can also hold down the left trigger to enter bullet time, which consumes energy. It's very useful for when things get really hectic.
The major new mechanic added to Bleed 2 is the reflection maneuver. As mentioned above, when you initially press the right stick in any direction, Wryn will very quickly slash with her katana before firing with her guns. This katana slash is imperative, as it will send any purple colored projectiles sailing away in the direction you hit them at high speed. This single new mechanic alone adds a ton of depth and opportunities for extremely badass moments.
I can't think of any other indie game that made me smile with as much glee as Bleed 2 did, when a boss threw a car at me and I entered bullet time, air dashed through a hail of mid air projectiles, smacked the car with my sword and sent it careening right back into the boss' stupid face.
Naturally, the game will reward you for pulling off tough maneuvers like this, as not only will reflected shots deal extra damage to enemies and bosses, but skillful play will also fill the in game style meter (Think Devil May Cry) with grades ranging from D (worst) to C,B,A, and S (Best) to better contribute to your rank at the end of the stage.
The gameplay is super responsive, controls beautifully, and is just awesome to experience. The pace is very fast, the game rushes you from one awesome setpiece to another as you mow down countless mooks inbetween. Completing the game also rewards you with unlockable characters and new weapons as well as "mutators"- special little twists to the game that can be individually turned on and off (things such as showing hitboxes, eliminating all gravity, having infinite bullet time, etc.) Activating these mutators does disable achievements and saving until you relaunch the game, but they're a fun curiosity nonetheless.
The only major complaint I have for Bleed 2 is the short length. The game, even on your first playthrough can be beaten in 40 minutes to an hour, easily. However, Bleed 2's saving grace is its high skill ceiling, and the way it encourages you to always get better and to always shoot for higher ranks and scores. You WILL want to beat this game on every difficulty and unlock every character and weapon, you WILL want to S rank every stage, and you WILL want to get all the achievements. Why? Because the core gameplay is just that damn good. It makes you CARE enough to actually want to do all of those things.
I hope and pray that we get a Bleed 3 in the future, and it has a way bigger budget and more resources. There is something special here, and I hope the devs get what they need to realize their vision to its full potential.

Bleed 2 is altogether a bigger, better, more polished game than the first (much of which should be evident from the trailers).

If there's one blemish here it's that the game reuses pretty much every boss encounter from the first game, albeit with the ability to parry some of their moves back at them (making them easier than they were before), but the way the bosses are executed is simply more refined this time around.
If you liked the original Bleed there's no reason you won't love this.
For reference I completed the original Bleed twice (once on Normal and once on Very Hard), and (at time of writing) I have completed Bleed 2 once (on Hard). I plan to replay it on Very Hard, as well as try the various characters on arcade mode.

I've been playing the game from time to time since release and this is my verdict.
-Good-
Emperor Edition made the game more interesting on the campaign map.
Battles have become longer since release, which is a good point also. Inept warriors that die easily is just inaccurate and silly and made battles unsatisfying. There's no chance for strategy when a battle is over in 2 minutes. Improve on this instead by making battles more realistic and interesting, and not some angry birds copy.
-Bad-
That all factions are not playable from the start is a major minus. Paying for content that is already in the game is greedy behaviour on the creators part.
New units/content should be included in updates, not sold separately.
Game was too buggy too long, and still is buggy.
Example: Units do not continiously engage each others in combat, they stop to stare at each others after the first line has died. This problem is especially true for pike units. (This seems to have been fixed now)
Lack of atmosphere and poor music. Compare with, e.g., Medieval 2 Teutonic campaign that had excellent music and atmosphere.
Blood mod made the game look horrendously bad. It would have been better if actual wounds bled, not the entire character being drenched in gore.
Finishing moves on campaign map and in battle are just silly and makes the game look and function worse. It would have been better with "real" (historical) and absolutely shorter killing animations than hollywoodesque dancing. Most finishing moves would actually endanger the two participants for attacks from the nearest enemies, but as for now, no one standing beside can interviene in these finishing moves. It would be awesome if it actually were detremental for the reckless one by opening up for more attacks from the enemy. Best would be if the moves were just deleted.
Expansions are barely expansions at all. Compare to Medieval 2 and the Kingdoms expansions where the core settings were different. Different times, places, factions and units.

Well... As it stands right now they made HW2 okay but completely ruined HW1 in every way shape and form.
Formations in the REAL Homeworld don't work properly, they don't stay in proper formation. Capital ships can't maneuver worth beans, Destroyers are no longer the ultimate utility ship of the fleet anymore. They were designed in HW1 to keep pace with and LEAD the frigate lines. Now they're slow, lumbering beasts that just♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.
Frigates are now made of wet paper bags and fighters are slow and unmaneuverable, meaning point defenses and even heavier weapons could destroy them. Corvettes are now pointless to build. Basically you just build fighters bombers and super-capitals only and they are all that is worth building.
The GUI is NOTHING like the original Homeworld which let you have a very clean experience which didn't block anything out. If you didn't need to see the GUI at that moment, it wasn't there. One of the things that made Homeworld loveable was that it assumed you were intelligent.
Singleplayer's adaptive difficulty from HW1 is now gone from what I can tell and it is pathetically easy for an experienced HW Vet. I had little trouble in the first few missions, which was dissappointing to say the least.
Fuel consumption no longer exists for fighters which means that when I eventually reach the Garden of Kadesh I can expect to be utterly massacred by the Kadeshi. This makes the Support Frigate a useless item. Honestly, why have them anymore at all?! The whole ballance is gone by removing fuel consumption, barring the other things they've utterly mucked up.
I'm happy that they thought it worth the effort to do a remastered edition but they sacrificed the original Homeworld ENTIRELY in order to satisfy the Homeworld 2 players. The thing is... There is a LOT more Homeworld 1 fans that stayed true and bought this than there were Homeworld 2 fans (at least if my group of friends is any indication).

How love of the original game can put the bar too high for its sequel, becomes evident when one plays DH2.
The game on its own has a half decent albeit rather simplified story, I'd say two missions especially are darker and creepier then anything I played since the ol' Thief 3 Asylum mission.
But regardless of a couple of (very) nice missions this sequel ultimately feels like the underachieving handicapped little brother of the superstar the original was and still is.
Where part 1 had that cool twist near the end, here it seems they decided not to put too much energy in the story itself.
Side stories don't really exist this time around either (think slackjaw).
The last endboss fight feels way to familiar to what we have seen before, not much new stuff there.
It took me 28 hours to finish main story on a slow pace, normally you can easily finish this game under 20 hours though.
Just looking at the game on its own, I'd rate it a 7/10, not taking into account the (poor) optimization.
I recommend this game only to those who never played the (better by far) original.
DH2 is just less then DH was in nearly every way, especially story wise as well as gameplay wise, adding 2 (different) play styles does not change that fact.
Perhaps some cleverly designed DLC that takes into account ones decisions made during the main game will  save it and give it a proud place next to the original as a true classic.

This is a very solid title marred by technical problems.
The initial load times are weirdly long (roughly 90 seconds off of a SSD) although thats more of an annoyance than a legitimate issue. The real problem lies in the crashes and poor optimization - I keep a faily steady 90fps on a GTX 1080 which is smooth but fairly poor for the game's graphics. My biggest gripe is the low memory crashes. They would be understandable if one were skimping on ram, but they should not occur at 16GB. They seem to happen randomly - sometimes a few hours into playing, sometimes just a few minutes.  They also have gotten much more frequent in the later stages, and I'm unable to finish the game because of that.
Otherwise, this game is quite good. Great atmosphere, nice graphical style, incredible attention to detail (The paintings are beautiful and the ambient sounds are absolutely immersive.) Multiple playstyles are possible, allowing you to slip in and out without leaving a trace, use distractions and traps to be a cunning assassin, or just rambo your way through a pack of guards, if you desire - and every option feels smooth and satisfying.
Unfortunatley critical performance issues still exist 6 months after launch. Not everybody has these issues, but I wouldn't recommend buying unless you're confident you won't be affected.

Note: I have at least 100 hours logged on the pre-steam version.
I don't write many reviews, but I had to jump in to share my experience with Factorio. This game, in its current alpha state, is already fantastically complete and fun. Even when I bought into the alpha years ago, the game was a joyous experience. The devs are excellent  and very communicative about the progress of the game.
What's so fun about this game? Well, it's sort of a city-builder, puzzle-game, incremental game and a few other genres blended together. You start with nothing but a pickaxe and coal power, and behin harvesting your first simple resources. As things progress, you need to process those materials into more and more complicated refined products using whatever crazy layout of conveyor belts, mechanical arms, fabricators, furnaces, and other contraptions you decide are necessary. Things get complicated fast, and there's a lot of fun to be had tinkering with your factory, learning new more efficient designs, and chasing more advanced tech.
Add to that a healthy dose of combat versus alien bugs trying to defend the planet and you have a well-rounded game that will keep you occupied for hours.
And then there's the extensive mod support, which has already generated a bunch of great mods that change things up and expand the gameplay. This game is going places.
For just $20, you're going to enjoy this game.

It's really fun. Probably the only game that continues to make me laugh no matter how many times I play the story. The characters are insane with funny dialogue, although there are a few that can get annoying. The story isn't that amazing, but it kept me interested enough to finish it.
Where Borderlands 2 really shines though is the grind. It's fun to keep trying to get good gear and building a character the way you want to, although some are better than others when it comes to the hardest difficulty. The bosses are wacky and have their own gimmicks, making for interesting fights. Seeing enemies burst into items and finally getting that specific item you always wanted is always satisfying.
The comic book art style is also nice to look at and if you have a really good PC, the Physix makes it even prettier with all the blood and effects flying everywhere, Sadly the Physix is quite taxing and I can only keep it on at certain areas.
The expansion packs are fun too. There's one where it takes you to a desert and be part of a pirate treasure hunt, one where it's Nascar meets gladiator arena and wrestling, and one where you literally become part of a Dungeos and Dragons game. One of the expansions, in my opinion, was pretty dull however, which is the hunting one with Sir Hamerlock. Also the holiday ones are pretty short, only worth getting when they're on sale for a dollar. All they add is more bosses to fight.
I would say give this game a shot. If you enjoy grinding it'll be worth your while.

In a saturated market where video games are released daily you’ll see a fair share of experimental games that try to be something different and unique but fail in one way or another, but this game is the exception. One of the best aspects is that it remembers about being a game first, while being complimented by everything else. The idea is unique and something I’ve personally have not seen before, and is not pretentious about it.
The visuals are an excellent style choice and leave plenty for imagination, which makes for a unique and terrifying experience. You don’t know what is going on around you or where you are, sometimes you don’t know what is going to happen next, but that’s part of what makes this game great and tense. It’s pretty to see all those visuals slowly change in front of you by your actions, although you won’t always be able to appreciate them for too long because you’ll be in danger constantly. But they can make for pretty screenshots and wallpapers if you experiment enough.
There is no music, only small ambient sounds and the sounds made by your character and other entities. However it doesn't need any music to begin with, for it would detract from the focus, but I assure you the sound design will end up stuck in your head and you'll be remembering the sounds for quite a while. Some sounds were a little too hauting for me I must admit.
Overall is not a complicated game, in fact is not a hard game either, it can be a little frustrating at times, however I appreciate its focus on simplicity, especially because simplicity well done is a rarity. The mechanics are not hard to understand and it’s very well designed from start to finish. And really, there is not much to say; it is what it is and does a fine job, but I enjoy it for what it is and for delivering an unerving experience. It might be short, but for the small price is absolutely worth it and one of the most unique games I've seen in a while. Is even better experienced on a dark room with headphones!

Alright, let's get on with the main part of this review. Bleed 2 is a "Platform game" but I prefer to describe it as a bullet hell-like 2D side scroller, the game takes place after Bleed, Wryn is playing games when an alien ship begins to attack, she hops into action and takes down the villains with the help of her rival, pretty basic plot but this is meant to be arcade-like so I can forgive it, what really matters is the gameplay.

Loved the original Homeworld - truly a classic RTS, and one of the best space-based RTSes ever made.
This remake has MASSIVELY improved the graphics over the original - this isn't a touch-up of the game engine, the entire game seems to have been ported to an updated version of the HW2 engine, with more detailed models, beautiful visual effects and lighting (Bloom, HDR, and depth of field! DEPTH OF FIELD, in an RTS! You can tell how serious the visual style of this game is.), and a lot of mechanical similarities to HW2. The game looks very modern; it does not look like a game that was concieved and created more that 15 years ago.
However, the developers clearly worked very hard to keep the feel of the original game alive. The model detail may have shot up remarkably, but every ship looks like its original model, seen through a clearer and sharper lens. From a distance, the models are the same; close up, there are more little lights, windows, and intricate polygons. Every new ship I see is literally jaw-dropping; the amount some of the ships have improved is incredible (the Turanic ships really stand out at this early point in my playthrough). The gameplay is almost unchanged from the original - I've played HW1 so many times that most of the missions are second-nature to me, and my favorite strategies still work perfectly. There are no unpleasant surprises or head-scratching design choices; the only noticeable departures from HW1 are either immaterial (Resource collectors behave more like those from HW2, essentially docking with asteroids, but have a similar graphical effect to HW1, the big sucking beam of ionized resources), or awe-inspiring (a certain spoiler-laden cutscene in Mission 3 is all the more shocking for its terrible beauty).
The difficulty and balance seems to have been tweaked somewhat. I distinctly remember the first several missions of every HW1 playthrough being very resource-sparse; you had to maximize every RU and soon learned exactly how much you could build and when. The remastered version is more lenient, likely because (like HW2), research now costs resources as well. I have also found myself building more fighters to replace lost ships than in the original. However, some of my least favorite changes from HW2, like enforced squad sizes, were thankfully not carried over to the remake, and gameplay staples like dust clouds were brought back. Everything works the way I expect, and there are nice surprises, like the fact that capital ship explosions leave debris in a similar manner to HW2, that enhance the original gameplay. Overall, the game feels a bit easier, with the areas of difficulty being slightly different from the original and more like HW2. However, I don't think the shift will offend long-time players of the game. It's not as though the remastered version is not challenging, and I don't think most of us play the game for its difficulty curve. The strategy, story, graphics, and mechanics are more important to me than how many times I have to reload Mission 3 because a single you-know-what was vaporized.
Thus far, my only major disappointment has been that Homeworld: Cataclysm was not included in the remaster. Though I know it was not generally considered canon, and was developed by a different company with no input from Relic, it was my first Homeworld game, and I really enjoyed the storyline and some of the gameplay additions it made to the already very addictive HW formula. I think HW:C would make a great game even with all the references to the Homeworld universe removed, and I would love to see it redone in this new engine in a similar manner to HW1.

I had high hopes for this game, but sadly it continues the glitchy trend of the original.
In the first game rats could detect bodies, and sometimes guards you'd knocked out magically died.
In this one it's quite possible to be detected through walls.
NPC's will react to others going missing, but this scripting is frankly rather broken. Sometimes they act as if they've seen a body, other times it's as if you got spotted.
In clockwork mansion at one point enemies will just spawn in a hallway. (I tested this by mining the hallway in question, and the mines only trigger once you walk up to it after clearing the maze.)
The position of bodies also ins't properly saved. Resulting in most of the people I had clearly stashed outside the walls being dropped right back in patrol routes upon enter the mansion again.
There is also no shortage of graphical glitches, and making working mirrors wasn't in the cards. Something even Duke3d managed to do two decades ago.
Sound is another issue. This game was clearly not tested with surround setups in mind. Sound sources jump around, or turning causes strange cut offs.
The advertised 2 characters are just 2 tech trees, and even those overlap. I only tested the first few missions, but both unfold exactly the same way. Even story npcs say the exact same thing 90% of the time. If you were hoping to replay this with the other character for story reasons you shouldn't bother.
Apart from delivering different lines in the set pauses there is no meangingful change.
This game is probably fine if you don't care about perfect runs/technical issues, but for those of us that do it's needlessly frustrating.

I bought this game because I'm a huge fan of the Elder Scrolls series and the game was advertised as "action"-oriented. This description could not be further from the truth.
While the game may visually be quite lovely (particularly for an MMO), the quests can be engaging, and at first glance the combat does seem action-oriented, if you want a truly action-oriented MMO-style experience, you will not find it with The Elder Scrolls Online.
I recommend the game, anyway, because despite the fact that the combat really bored me to tears I somehow managed to play it for 120 hours and for the most part enjoyed myself, even though I didn't really get much of a community experience and American racist types loved to run very public slavery guilds, which I found repulsive even with the caviat that they claimed it was "lore-friendly."
That said, you'll get a better gameplay experience from single-player games. If you haven't played an Elder Scrolls game before, definitely pick up Skyrim. The Witcher and Dark Souls franchises are also quite incredible (the latter of which has great multiplayer), and are more action-oriented than Bethesda's venerable classics.
I suppose, for me, MMO's just feel so incredibly archaic, with the exception of Eve, but then that's another story altogether. Like many others on Steam, I really wish there were a neutral recommendation.

When I first played this game, it was in the early beta stages. I continued following the game until it hit its release date, and ended up not getting the game... because it totally sucked! It had poor graphics, clunky gameplay, and wasn't worth the money asked for it.
That was then.
I picked it up again recently, to have another go at it after hearing the people at Bethesda slapped the people at Zenimax on the wrist for doing a poor job, and stepping in to really fix things, and... they delivered.
As poor as it was at first release, as enjoyable it is now -- Dropping outdated DX9 for DX11 was an absolute must. The engine still doesn't measure up to Skyrim, not by a long shot, but it is "close enough" and definitely allows for the MMO aspects to still be fully used without grinding powerful systems to a halt. Kudos for that!
What it is now is a full-featured, full-bodied fantasy MMORPG, with many, many avenues to explore and as many ways to play the game. Don't expect to get bored with grinding; quests and story missions will progress you as fast as, if not faster than, grinding your fingers off with boring repeatable missions. You want to play solo? go right ahead -- you'll have a good and full experience. You like to go on raids? That's possible too. You want to team up with some friends and go dungeon diving? It's there. PvP? You bet (not my thing, though).
Although you don't have to spend more than your initial purchase, the game as it is is definitely worth getting a "plus" subscription for, too. Incredible value for your money, and if your finances change, you don't have to continue it to still have an enjoyable game to play without recurring costs.
I wouldn't recommend it when it first came out, but now? Absolutely. A definite recommendation to pick this up if you like the Elder Scrolls setting.

Factorio is one of my favorite games. It's also one of the most polished and fun alphas I've ever seen. And it even have mods that make it crazier already!
I played it a lot outside of Steam, so don't be fooled. :)
Factorio is a Sandbox-Survival game where you play someone who crash-landed on an alien planet inhabited by a hostile race of primitive aliens that seem to, instead of going to the gym, simply breathe Carbon-Dioxide to get pumped up and angry before trying to steamroll your base.
What? Read on.
Initially, you'll have to gather resources manually in order to craft the tools you need for basic automation and basic research. You'll then start automating resource extraction, smelting, refining, production and research as you try to steer clear of the angry aliens. Eventually, you'll have automated trains loading up cargo on automated stations that's being automatically filled by automated extractors and smelteries. And as it reaches your main base, that train will be unloaded by automated cargo drones that will help you sort out your huge storage system and bring you whatever you need directly to your inventory.
And let's not forget about the construction bots that will automatically build blueprints you design. It's a simple, great feature that will make you do the "Feel Good Man" face every time you build a new Solar Array.
Of course, you're free to play, build and progress as you wish. Make your designs as compact as you can or as large as you want. Design storage and sorting systems, optimized smelting/refining/research/transport designs, or just load up your tank and troll the wildlife.
(Personally when I first started playing with trains I completely forgot about the rest of the game and simply tried to weaponize them for a few hours.)
The game features a World Generator that really lets you fine-tune your experience. You can go for a game with passive and weak enemies filled with resources, or a scarce planet filled with angry mobs. You can even make the map really narrow, only generating terrain horizontally (Linear Factorio), which is a different gamemode by itself.
The default settings are balanced and challenging enough for most people, so you can quickly jump in on a new game. And even though the game has a learning curve and can be rather complex at times, the tutorial will get you covered, for the most part.
There's also a mechanic in the game called Pollution. As I mentioned before, Pollution will make aliens (more) agressive, and they will get stronger and evolve faster as you pollute more and more. This can make you adapt, plan and upgrade your factories for lower footprint or higher production in order to progress faster before the aliens spread everywhere.
This is a really interesting feature that keeps you on your toes, and makes it so having radar stations and keeping an eye at enemies is actually useful, and sometimes necessary.
The game is already really fun as is, and features multiplayer.
Hopefully it will get further expanded and polished. If you enjoy crafting, survival, automation (especially Minecraft Tech mods), you'll definitely have a blast with Factorio!

I started watching Markiplier play this game, but I quickly stopped, because it looked so cool that I wanted to experience it for myself first. I just bought it, and played for 2.5 hours straight. I love it! (And it's certainly much longer than I expected it to be — 2.5 hours and I'm not even halfway done!)
If you really think about it, Dark Echo is actually a fairly standard puzzle/escape/psychological thriller game: You navigate, you evade monsters, you avoid death traps, and sometimes you have to activate switches (represented by yellow patches). But the sound mechanic, in which you navigate by visualized sound waves, changes everything. Instead of giving you a puzzle to solve in each level, it makes navigation a puzzle in itself. And it's a puzzle that gets progressively more complicated and challenging as new elements and mechanics are introduced and combined with each other, requiring increasing amounts of cleverness to overcome.
A bonus: The fact that you are effectively walking around in pitch darkness, and often threatened by monsters and traps, makes this something of a horror game as well. Your blindness makes the experience tense and constantly charged with the threat of the unknown. And the inscrutability of your environment presents an ontological mystery: You don't know who you are, where you are, how you got there, or what the world wants from you. (I doubt any of these questions will be answered by the game, but a sense of mystery always makes horror/thriller games even more fun.)
Edit: I just played for another half an hour. When I first wrote this, I was at level 37 or 38. At Level 40, I made an important discovery, which is that the next 40 levels are a "mirror" of the first 40. Your player character finally escapes the darkness he was trapped in, stepping out into the light, where you can hear birds chirping. And then you're taken to a level select screen that's the same as the first one, except that black and white are inverted. I've played a few of these "light" levels so far, and they are largely the same as their "dark" counterparts (including their names), except that black and white are inverted, in some ways they seem to be tougher, I'm pretty sure there are more monsters, and it seems that the monsters can now move through walls. I had to stop playing only a few levels in because I was mentally drained. I'm a bit disappointed that the last half of the game seems to be just a "tougher" mirror of the first — especially since I'm not sure that it's tougher in a good way. But I haven't finished yet, and I don't know if there might be any surprises in store.

Borderlands was great because it filled a niche no other game company realized existed: cooperative shooters.
Borderlands 2 still fills that niche and surprisingly there still isn't much competition out there for this genre. Borderlands 2 does a pretty good job turning Borderland's nonstory into a relatively coherent story. The jokes range from cringeworthy to hilarious but it definitely skews towards childish humor.
As far as gameplay goes they actually took a step backwards. Sometimes in Borderlands 1 you'd get some wacky combinations, which was funny but in borderlands 2 the wackiness makes a lot of the guns you find completely useless. It turns out wacky guns are largely useless and finding too many of them becomes tiresome and just adds to the gear grind.
Another big problem is that they don't seem to know how to make enemies more difficult other than turning them into bullet sponges so at high levels fights become a huge chore. I might be in the minority but for me spending 8 minutes shooting a man in the head gets really boring. At the highest difficult even normal enemies take a bunch of hits to kill and running out ammo midfight becomes a legitimate concern early on in any area.
Not only that, but its fairly obvious that the game wasn't originally designed for the increased level caps. They didn't know what to do to add more gamplay hours so they just increased all the numbers: health, damage, and skill points. You get so many skill points now there's almost no diversity in builds. Additionally, since the enemies scale even higher fights take even longer but are in no way more interesting or fun since the mechanics are identical. One of the DLCs was literally a level cap increase.... no extra content.
A good game to play with friends but gameplay starts to suck at higher levels. The Division is a newer co-op shooter, I haven't played it but it might be better at higher levels. Otherwise, you might want to look towards traditional mmorpgs if you want a gear grind and fun endgame mechanics and fights.
Borderlands 2 is great with friends for your first playthrough. It rapidly drops off after that but maybe games shouldn't need to have a long endgame. Still, if thats the case why did they put it in if it was just going to suck?

So for those who have never heard of Smite before, it’s basically a 3D MOBA where you take the role of a mythological god of your choice and fight until death (s) in team-based arenas. With this description, you can already guess, and correctly, that this game is going to be much more focused on action than any other MOBAs you have played before. I also strongly believe that many of you who don’t particularly enjoy MOBAs that much (like me) will have more chances of enjoying this one.
What I liked most about Smite:
- The 3D view, of course. I was a bit skeptical at first, but now I can’t imagine myself getting back to the typical MOBA.
- The epic variety of gods you can chose from: Norse, Roman, Hindu, Egyptian, Greek, etc.
- Fresh but faithful to the concept of MOBA, so those who have played the genre before won’t find difficult to adapt.
- Free gems and nice daily rewards. The cash is for cosmetics and unlocking gods, definitely not P2W. Also, the Ultimate - God pack is incredibly cheap for what you get in return.
- Game-play: fast pace, full focus on action, and hella fun!
- You can forget about last hitting and focus on the team fights instead.
- The different and fun game modes: Conquest (5v5 + 3 lanes); Arena (5v5 + open); Joust (3v3 + single lane); Assault (All random, all mid); Siege (5v5 + 2 lanes); Match of the day.
- VGS – type less, play more, that’s what I always say. The Voice Guided System is awesome because it lets you send standard messages to your team. If you want, you don’t even need to type anything at all.
- The community – for now. The chat is relatively quiet, and wow, isn’t that such a relief! There’s always that random person who doesn’t make sense and prefers to type rather than playing the actual game (as mentioned above, that’s a rant for another day). Considering I am still a newbie, I have no clue if this pattern will follow through higher levels – but I am hoping so.
What I didn’t like as much:
- The map view sometimes was a bit annoying, but that might be because I am not used to it. It’s definitely easier to sneak up!
-The skins! The most awesome skin is the default one. Not that this matters much.
- UI and UX. Of course, being an UX Designer, I am going to be biased. Definitely, Smite’s interface can be improved. This has been obvious since the very beginning, when the first screen that has been shown to me was the main login screen and I had to click on ‘cancel’ to Sign Up for an account (what?)
Ok, I admit I haven’t played all game modes yet. I have been particularly drawn to Joust, because you have more control over your own character and a clear perception of how he can affect the whole game. With not as many aids, you feel like you can make a difference – for good, or for bad. (Worry not, you will still listen to the occasional ranter blaming on his ‘team’, no matter what game mode you chose). Plus, of course, the chat is cleaner when you have less people in your team. Did I just say this? I vote for a clean chat, and a non-toxic community, MOBA players deserve this. And definitely, Smite’s community is in the right direction.
As I mentioned above, the map view and whole 3D view, as awesome as it is, it is still a bit confusing for me to handle, so playing Conquest on 3 lanes definitely has its own challenges. Despite Conquest being probably the most popular mode, I admit I felt myself a bit lost at times, even a bit dumb, when unpleasantly surprised by a sneaky enemy. There’s also the fact that I’ve had enough of the standard MOBA gaming mode, so any new approach to that is very welcome.
The Match of the Day is fun, silly, and interesting.
Overall, I really like that when I play Smite, I have fun! This is and will always be the highest rating factor for me. Smite makes me not to take myself or gaming in general so seriously. It makes me enjoy the act of playing a game, it even makes me laugh about the silly rookie mistakes I make. I am still learning, and I don’t expect to be perfect, and definitely, Smite has (almost) the right community for newbies like us.
If you like the idea of MOBAs, but there were things that have put you off about them, then, I’d recommend you to give Smite a try.
