If you love the Alien franchise, this game is for you.  If you expect to hose down hordes of xenos with various weapons, this game is NOT for you.  If you hate stealth, this game is NOT for you.  If you hate backtracking, especially if you're a completionist, this game is NOT for you.
The graphics are great, the atmosphere and sounds are genius, but the game does require a hefty dosage of suspending disbelief.  The alien always sort of knows where you are, but doesn't pop down out of the vents until you screw up - I find that hard to believe.  The station is huge, and you're not the only survivor, but if things weren't done this way, there couldn't be a game.
To say nothing of the immortal and intractable alien itself. While you will uncover weapons and items that will make it go away, these measures grant only a few precious moments before he is right on your♥♥♥♥♥again.  The fact that you can't kill him is always a surprise to people who don't already know, especially after they find their first real weapon, and sometimes even for a few deaths after that.
If you can ignore those particular characteristics of your new friend, the game will be a gripping ride you will never forget.
After awhile they patched in a new hardest difficulty, and I assume they tweaked the other ones as a result.  This means if you play the game on "normal" mode the alien is slightly dumb, often-times appearing to have a baffling lack of peripheral-perception mixed in with instances of impossible awareness.  On harder modes he will hand you your♥♥♥♥♥for the slightest mistake.
People hate or love the save system.  Since you can't save just anywhere, the game becomes more intense, but there are a couple stretches in the game where more save points would have been appropriate.
The game has a learning curve and punishes the impatient.  The alien is not the only threat, or even necessarily the worst one.  You'll need to learn quickly what items and weapons to use on which enemy - and more importantly what not to use.
Since the AI is somewhat randomized within sets of parameters, you can't simply memorize the appearances of the alien and its patrol routes.  Even areas where his appearance is pre-scripted have him randomly wandering about, hunting you down, and thus also randomizing what you need to do, when and where.  Humanoid enemies represent more classic stealth with regular routes.
Have fun. ;)

It's really fun. Probably the only game that continues to make me laugh no matter how many times I play the story. The characters are insane with funny dialogue, although there are a few that can get annoying. The story isn't that amazing, but it kept me interested enough to finish it.
Where Borderlands 2 really shines though is the grind. It's fun to keep trying to get good gear and building a character the way you want to, although some are better than others when it comes to the hardest difficulty. The bosses are wacky and have their own gimmicks, making for interesting fights. Seeing enemies burst into items and finally getting that specific item you always wanted is always satisfying.
The comic book art style is also nice to look at and if you have a really good PC, the Physix makes it even prettier with all the blood and effects flying everywhere, Sadly the Physix is quite taxing and I can only keep it on at certain areas.
The expansion packs are fun too. There's one where it takes you to a desert and be part of a pirate treasure hunt, one where it's Nascar meets gladiator arena and wrestling, and one where you literally become part of a Dungeos and Dragons game. One of the expansions, in my opinion, was pretty dull however, which is the hunting one with Sir Hamerlock. Also the holiday ones are pretty short, only worth getting when they're on sale for a dollar. All they add is more bosses to fight.
I would say give this game a shot. If you enjoy grinding it'll be worth your while.

The core gameplay is a worthy successor to Bleed. It the same genre, same gameplay style you would expect from the first game without being a blatant copy/paste. If you striped the game down to textureless hitboxes, it would still work. My following criticisms don't concern the gameplay and don't detract from the overall experience nearly enough to scare me away.
The music is satisfactory, just like the first game. It complements the gameplay well but none that I found myself humming in the shower, except for both games' title screens.
The story is like Duke Nukem Forever in the way Wryn starts as a beloved hero, and suffers in a similar way. For this and the previous game the story was never a make or break factor. If you did pay attention to the story in the first game, Wryn aspiring to become a hero was a nice goal to keep you going, even though you played for the gameplay anyway. In this game you start at the top and have nowhere to go; the events kinda happen just because. Duke Nukem Forever had a litany of problems on top of the story, but you should want your game to have as many strong legs to stand on as possible. If, say, the plant newscaster guy was more skeptical of Wryn, or she had something to fight for, this wouldn't be as much of an issue.
My last critique is that some character designs, especially the Wryn close-ups, look weird. I can't put into words exactly why, just some change between how she was drawn between games makes something tick in my brain. The ending animation where she's pumping her fists in the air is especially bad. It annoys me when animation doesn't at least attempt subtle body movements such as how the chin moves when people talk. Wryn's head and arms move, but everything else is stiff.
In summary, gameplay is great and alone makes the game worth it, most other things are satisfactory but could have been much better with a few tweaks.

Lots of neat new characters, but the bosses are *absolutely not* balanced for them.
On Very Hard, there are a bunch of attacks which are unavoidable for certain characters, since many of them either have no dodge move, or only a very limited one, and no time slowing either, and little to no attack telegraphing on enemy attacks on V. Hard.
It's so bad, that some bosses are essentially unbeatable if you pick the "wrong" character, meaning that you might make it through most of a level fine (or even several whole levels) and then suddenly get stonewalled.
This is compounded by just how freakin' many bosses there are (often three or more in one level), and so you have to be able to beat *all* of those bosses with the character, or else there's no point in beating any of them since you won't be able to beat the level.
This is *even further* compounded by the fact that the health and energy upgrades from the first game are gone, meaning you have *basically no health or energy* on harder difficulties, even though Bleed 1 let you get around twice as much as you have in this game.
*And if that wasn't bad enough*, the two characters with the most unique playstyles *require* a few quiet moments of setup to be able to use their special abilities, which means you *literally cannot use those abilities* during many boss battles, because there's *no down time at all* in them.
On a different topic, the levels seem more boring than in Bleed 1. I think they're simpler and shorter, but it's been a while since I've played the original, so I can't say for sure what's different.
I love most of the new characters, and the new weapons and dodge abilities for Wryn are really neat to have, but the extra characters seem frustratingly neglected considering the various little bits of custom text for each character, as well as the few custom cutscene images added for them, and the game seems poorly paced.
Hopefully some of these things can get ironed out, because the game has a lot of potential, and a lot of good moments underneath the frustrations.

Oh my GOSH, I love this game! If you were a fan of Bleed 1 you will absolutely love this game. I'll just go through a few pros and cons and give a quick summary at the end.
PROS:
-Better Level Design
-Better Music
-Better Music
-Wryn is even cuter than last time
-Better story
-More replayability
-Gameplay is wayyy better
CONS:
-Shorter than Bleed 1
SUMMARY:
I was a huge fan of Bleed 1. I beat that game in one sitting and spent even more time trying to unlock the others weapons and characters. I honestly didn't think anything could top Bleed 1. However, Bleed 2 takes everything good and bad about the previous game and makes it about 1000x better. The music was the first thing that really popped out. The first thing you hear in the game is the original theme from Bleed, but instead on electric guitar. All of the stage music is super catchy too, I've been humming the final boss theme for a while now. The graphics are also noticabley better. Some of the characters still look a bit off, mainly Wryn and the rival, but all of the backgrounds and enemy sprites look amazing! The level design is also way better. In Bleed 1, you spent a lot of time in corridors with BS obsitcals and enemies put around every corner. In Bleed 2, all the enemies are put in spots that force you to kill them, overall bringing up your score and your cool factor B). The controls are just as good as it was in Bleed 1. One really cool new addition was the katana. In the game, you can flick the right stick (Or click the mouse) to swing a katana. This katana can deflect any purple bullets or enemies. This makes for some really interesting enemy design, making some of the bosses really fun. The levels also flow very smoothly as they all follow one quick and satisfying narrative. Unlike in Bleed 1 where all of the levels were just... there. There was really no transition between levels. The only problem I have with this game is its length. It took me about 3 hours on normal mode to beat Bleed 1. Bleed 2 took me under 2 hours on the hard difficulty. However, the game kind of makes up for it by having a ton of unlockables, however you can just get them all at once by beating the 'very hard' difficulty. Overall, Bleed 2 is a huge improvement over Bleed 1. Trust me, if you loved Bleed 1 you will love this game even more.
It's absolutly worth it. Just know it's a small game with A LOT of replayability.

Bleed 2 is a great sequel to the original Bleed, adding some interesting and fun new mechanics while retaining the core gameplay that made the first game such a good game.
the main appeal of Bleed 2 is the fast paced and frantic gameplay, which it executes very well. The controls are tight and responsive, and the levels are built to allow (and encourage) the player to keep moving at all times -  There are no unfair or cheap enemy placements.
The main portion of Bleed 2, however, is the boss fights, all of which are fun, interesting, and unique in their own way. Each of them have a different playstyle. There are very few frustrating or "Ugh, THIS ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" bosses in the game. they each have unique attack patterns to get down, which adds to the replayability of the game, which we'll get to later.
Presentation is another nail that Bleed 2 hits right on the head.The 8-bit art style has also been abandoned, which is nice because I feel it didn't suit the first game too well. each stage is vibrant and colourful, with their own unique style and colour pallette. The soundtrack is intense and metal as fxck, and the soundscape consists almost entirely of shouting, gunfire, and explosion. Long story short, the vibrant and bouncy art style and high-octane soundtrack compliment the thrilling, fst-paced gameplay perfectly.
Bleed 2 is a "short and sweet" type of game, (I finished my first playthrough (normal difficulty, not too many deaths) in just under an hour) But the multitude of unlockable characters, weapons and abilities, along with the multiple difficulty settings, and ranked arcade mode, will keep you busy for a long time. Each boss has certain weaknesses and strategies, and it feels super rewarding to master each level on higher difficulties and start climbing up the leaderboards in arcade mode.
In conclusion, If you want a fast paced, metal-as-♥♥♥♥ action platformer, You will definitely enjoy Bleed 2.

Okay, there are some issues with bugs and random crashes for many, but not all. Let's get that out of the way. Does it make the game "broken"? No, but there ARE issues to be addressed by Gearbox.
I won't go into the graphics, story etc. as many reviews have covered this. Let me instead look at the game's 'difficulty' for the new RTS gamer.
If you do not strategise and plan in 3D, which was revolutionary at the time (and still is, to my mind) you're going to have a hard time. When I played the original on release in my early thirties I DID find some of the mssions HARD, but then I wasn't used to this type of RTS. The delight was in solving the strategy for myself and finally 'getting it'!
I hadn't come across this since "X-Wing", which really was a mix of simulator anbd puzzle solving (take out X bombers to pretect Hospital Ship - if you don't in a certain order you fail).
So, it all comes down to planning and working out exactly what you need for each mission. "Tank Rushing" just will not work, and those with the biggest and baddest fleet, that takes sometimes far too much time and resources, will see you fail time and again (except in skirmish - which we didn't have back then).
This game(s) requires thought, and aside from it's beauty (the original still looks marvellous), the strategy required is compelling. You'll hit your keyboard and close the game down in frustration sometimes, but your mind will keep churning over strategies until you come back and try again (and you will).
"Brilliant and innovative" barely describes this title even today.

This is an awesome program that when paired with thier online library of free to use content is an amazing time saver in game development. That is just as simple as it gets folks.
There are free to use animations (walk, jump, idle, turn left, turn right, strafe left, strafe right) that are huge time savers for the basics. Slapping these animations to your character asset will get you play testing in no time.
Majority of thier animations you have to buy. So either pay up for a quick and generic animation package, or make your own.
Mixamo can automatically rig your character, this is another collosial time saver. It rigs and skins your character mesh which to an amature would take days, if not weeks, or you'd have to find someone to rig for you which could prove to be difficult.
Mixamo does not create animation controls for your rig. So yes, your character is rigged, but there are no controls for you to use to animate them. This means you have hours of work to trudge through before you can make custom animations. So again, either do it yourself (but don't) or get someone to make the controls for you (do this).
Fuse is easy to use and very user friendly. The UI is clean and quick to navigate. Moving the camera around your character is simple and intuitive to anyone who has used any 3D software ever, except for maybe the Creation Kit, that♥♥♥♥♥♥is crazy.
Every character will look pretty much the same. Sure, you can push and pull verts to your hearts content, but in the end when you glance back at the original mesh you'll still see remnants of that hidden in yours.
The character mesh is already UV unwrapped, as is all the clothing and hair mesh's they have available too. You can do minor texture manipulation in Fuse and then export the mesh as an OBJ with the texture files all set and plugged into a material and this can be a huge time saver as well.
The UV packing is terrible, just terrible. Sure, you can go into your 3D software and repack the UV's, and then go into your image manipulation software (*cough* photoshop) and reposition all of the textures, but that's a little bit of a convoluted process, and by the time your done with that it would have been easier to just UV unwrap the damn thing yourself and texture it yourself. So either just ignore the packing, or remake it by hand. It's not really a huge deal either way.
Don't rely on Fuse to be the end all be all for your games character creation. It'll end up lackluster in the end and your game will suffer from the age old dilema of having too many NPC's looking like not distant enough cousins. Use Fuse instead as a tool to create a base mesh with some pretty legit poly flow and then take that into Maya, 3DS Max, Blender, what have you, and make it your own. Push and pull those verts to your hearts content. Re-topologize that polyflow to make somethign unique and cool. Make that damn thing your own. In this sense, Fuse is priceless. You can then take the UV's that they already have and make your own textures and normals.
Combine this with the auto rigger Mixamo has online and you've got a pretty legit and user friendly gateway to making whatever character you want.

ALOT of people disagree with me when I say that this is one of the best Call of Duty games to date. It is different, which is what people wanted, yet they still gripe and complain about it and want a WWII CoD where they were "good". We don't need to go back to those WWII games until we nail the futuristic games, yea it makes no sense but that's what needs to happen. So quit hating on this game because it's not set in WWII and not the Black Ops series, It's leaps and bounds above those so far.
The campaign in this game is one of my favorite campaigns I've ever played. Yeah, we know who the villain was at the start, yet it was still incredibly enjoyable. The graphics are amazing, the plot is intriguing, the movement is astounding. I personally rate this a 9/10 because of how well polished and amazing this game is.
The multiplayer is also very well done. They could have done better of course, but what they went with is perfectly fine.
I've only ran into one hacker which had an aimbot on the whole match, but that's MONTHS past the release, I'm talking July 7th 2015, so it's definitely not a problem. The only problem that I had with this, and basically every multiplayer FPS is the hitmarkers don't work sometimes. For example, I was in a match with a buddy of mine, I was using the MORS - LULLABY, I know for a fact that I hit this dude in the head but no hitmarkers, so I reloaded and tried it again, hit him in the chest, no hitmarkers.... at this point I'm♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off so I pull out a ASM1, only about 5 shots hit him out of the whole clip and my sights were dead on him. He ended up killing me of course, but I got revenge by killing him a few times. However, that was rare to happen.
Finally, Exo Survival & Exo Zombies. What can I say but Bloody Good Job! (I never use that phrase, but I'll make an exception this time :D) Exo Survival is incredibly difficult if you don't know what your doing, especially on Veteran difficulty.. It will tear you to pieces. Wave after wave of some stupid AI to some what seem to be cheating AI, with breaks in between of course. During random waves, you will have to complete objectives, and if those objectives are failed, you will be penalized whether it be a loss of a hud by Hud Reboot, or something worse by Exo Reboot.
Exo Zombies.. This to me, is 6x better than what Black ops series has pushed out so far, even (as normal maps and gameplay go) World at War. It's incredibly challenging and fun to play. I'd recommend playing with a friend or several because of how hard it gets later on. Yes, it may be a spinoff of Black ops 1 & 2 and World at War, but it's a spinoff that's worth everything. The story line is very interesting and easy to follow, the zombies are well designed, and the easter eggs are hard as heck to achieve, yet pays off afterwards.
I do recommend this game to those who don't own it as well as encourage others that own it to keep playing. It's a shame for a game this well made to not have as well of a fan base as other CoDs because it's different.
I want to thank those of you who read this whole review, though, not many I would think, but I still thank you.

An excellent sequel to the original Bleed, improving almost everything from the original game and expanding it even more!
Pros:
+Moving and shooting still feel great as ever and the reflect/ parry adds a whole new depth to the action.
+A more cohesive story overall sprinkled throughout the stages.
+Arcade and Challenge modes both return and are greater than ever.
+Boss battles are excellent and are the stars of this game.
+Character Variety is much better this time around, each having their own abilities and quirks that makes them unique to play over Wryn.
+The art style is greatly improved over the first game imo, with a great sense of character and charm in everything.
+A godly soundtrack done by Jukio "Kuabee" Kallio (Also responsible for the Nuclear Throne OST)
+A steady difficulty curve that spans across all the stages and difficulties.
+Mutators that allow you to play around with adjusted settings.
Cons:
-Weapon variety is the same from the first game, Pistol + Katana is absolutely vital and you can't really make use of other weapons sometimes because of that (though you can equip more than just 2 weapons at a time now so that helps)
-Some reused bosses from Bleed 1 (which have a new move or two and are generally fun yes but still feel a little lazy)
-Stages are a bit more bland than Bleed 1's, which had things like stage hazards whereas in Bleed 2 it's mostly just enemy placement.
-Still on the short side, so unless you're into replaying on higher difficulties, and aiming for the best times/ scores then you'll maybe get 1-2 hours out of the story mode.
Overall though it's a great and worthy sequel to Bleed that improves on it in almost every conceivable way.
Only wish there was even more of it :p

Challenge mode that lets you face up to 3 bosses simultaneously and local two player co-op
However, as its predecessor suffered with, Bleed 2's story mode is very short, completing the story in under one hour...
The action never seems to stop! Bleed 2 focuses it's stages more around multiple interesting boss battles - a design choice that works really well
Whilst the story mode can be beaten in an hour, it was worth the fun and intensity. You'll also unlock new characters and weapons for completing it!
Definitely a huge and enjoyable improvement from Bleed!

Allow me to begin by stating that I consider myself somewhat a veteran of games that perform perform poorly, whether by design or due to my own circumstances. I initially spent years on computer games before upgrading to a decent machine, and during those times I was able to look past the low framerates, the stuttering, and the miserable works, in the titles I sought to enjoy.
And now, having come full circle, I find that
is among the worst performers in my entire library ... but my old ways remain, and I can ignore the filth that is poor optimization to discover and explore what truly is a fine game in all other aspects.
Gameplay-wise, this game, without a shadow of a doubt, is superior to its predecessor. Where it's not identical, it's simply better. More tools, more upgrades, more powers, more variety. You can play as either Corvo or Emily, who each have unique powers, but share a few ones as well as enhancements. What I especially appreciate are the added non-lethal manoeuvers whose absences I sorely regretted in
. Sure, you could choke easily choke someone out when undetected, but in combat, you'd have to use some finite resources to reach the same result. Say you're a chronic pacifist, but you've just been spotted. To make matters worse, you're out of sleep darts! No problem in this installment. From the front, quickly knock-out an enemy while they are off-balance, or, if you're in a hurry or just feeling sporty, perform a slide for a near-instant takedown. There are a few more options available, but I, and all others who favor gameplay with even a hint of mercy, are extremely grateful for their addition. My one and only complaint about the gameplay -- and this is extremely minor -- is the fact that you can't hide your sword while your left hand weapon/power is drawn. It could be done in the first game, but not here. So, I ask any and all modders out there: Make it happen!
As far as visuals go, I think the game delivers competently; they are certainly a step up from the original. Enjoy bustling environments in imperial Dunwall (briefly), tropical Serkonos, and even the expansive void. The settings as a whole feel full of life and activity, quite authentic. But these luxuries, coupled with an unmistakably bad engine, come with the price of widely disagreeable performance. Many, already, have turned their backs on this title due to the way it runs. I neither agree with nor scoff at them, but at times I can liken my perserverance to that of a determined amputee surrounded by impatient athletes. I say, grin, bear it, and try to make yourself comfortable! You may soon forget your troubles.
Regarding the music and sound effects, they do quite well, I think, to reinforce the overarching atmospheres of the in-game settings, and I dare say I found them a tad more enjoyable, overall, than those of the first
. However, I may be in the minority on this front, and I concede that the game's official soundtrack is disappointing, lacking what I believe to be crucial pieces from various sections of the game.
Lastly, I'll cover the story, revealing this much: It's nothing impressive on the whole, but some parts certainly stand out more than others. The beginning sequences were very obviously rushed, and the overall plot seems rather tenuous, as though the storywriters were straining to recreate the conflicts of the original game. I was not crazy about the story of the previous game either, but my personal philosophy is not to worry about plot in a game like this. Focus on the action, the processes, and there is a good chance you will find yourself deeply immersed in the world of
.
This is my first review in a good long while, and although it may not have addressed all that there is to be experienced in
, it is my hope that it may tackle the concerns of prospective players and spur at least some to give this greatly exciting and pleasant game a chance, performance be damned.

The "remastered" part is well done. Graphics, UI and all that, but I do not remember this many obvious bugs in the old Homeworld.
- My research vessel for example is completly invulnerable. I just had 30 enemy fighters and a Heavy Cruiser (!) firing at it and it just kept repairing itself at about 40% health.
- Then there is this shrieking sound that seems to come from Corvette and Frigate class ships. It stays even if you move away. Pausing and continueing the game is a workarround.
- Captured Taiidan carriers are somehow unable to build anything. Capturing them is semi-useless that way.
- Captured ships seem to play the lottery when it comes to their paintjobs. Some stay in Taiidan-yellow while others shine in Kushan-grey. (Edit: I even got one with pink stripes. YMCA-Cruiser!)
And this is just Homeworld 1 to about half the missions. None of it is totally gamebreaking, like CTDs or crashes, but it shows a rather unpolished release.
Gearbox also couldn't keep their hands off changing things. For example, Fighters don't require fuel anymore, making the Khadesh fuel ships obsolete. While the reasoning behind this is debateable (probably for HW 1&2 multiplayer compatibility), they were somehow unable to fix lacks in the user commands, for example letting Repair Corvettes guard a group of Salvage Corvettes so that they pick targets to repair automatically. This was okay 15 years ago, but today it feels really really annoying to have to micromanagement everything yourself instead of enjoying the broader strategy game in a true three-dimensional environment.
Edit: Okay, now that I played through Homeworld 1 I can only say I'm shocked. This is a typical Gearbox game. The beginning is alright and due to the story events epic, but after about half the game it becomes a static "move there and jump". Its like the enemy AI is turned off. At the end I had 7 Heavy Cruisers, not of them built, and also 12 Destroyers. And guess what, the Taiidan rebels gifted me two more, like it wasn't easy enough yet.
It was said the enemy fleet scales with what the player has, so I was hoping for an epic battle at the end. What I got was 3 enemy Heavy Cruisers. You can guess how epic that was.
Another AI shutdown happend at the giant hyperspace inhibitor 2 missions before the finale. There are three jumpgates which you are supposed to destroy, because they'd send reinforcements otherwise. Thing is, there are no reinforcements, EXCEPT when you go for the gates. But then you are already there to destroy whatever comes through. If you leave the gates in peace, you can do your thing without the AI trying to stop you.
This was the easiest RTS I've ever played in 20 years since Dune 2, simply because the AI does absolutly nothing. Combined with the goddamn annoying sound bug, Homeworld Remastered 1 is a complete waste of time!

If you are looking for remastered HW1 do not buy this game in its current state.  If you are looking for remastered HW2 you will enjoy it.  The remaster is HW1 ported into a tweaked HW2 engine.  The HW2 engine has limitations that break or substantially change core mechanics for HW1.
The Good:
-Looks fantastic.  Manages to update ship models and graphics while keeping the feel and asthetics of the orginal
-Its pretty
-It really does look nice
The Bad:
-Formations (one of the best and most important mechanics in the game) are flat out  broken in HW1  (HW2 limitation)
-No bullet ballistics, hits are determined by RNG (HW2 limitation)
-No Evasive mode for units
-No fuel for fighters (Probably a HW2 limitation)
-Good number of crash bugs, sound bugs, and gameplay bugs of varying seriousness
Hopefully formations will be patched but the cause is a HW2 engine limitation so dont hold your breath.

On release Rome TW 2 (Or Total war: Rome 2 I guess) left much to be desired. It was not rare to face armies consisting of nothing but slingers. As if that wasn't enough the load times were horrific and the balance on some structures just made no sense.
Now however, a year later, The Creative Assembly has really put their backs into it and turned this game into what it is supposed to be. For a new comer to the Total War Series, you are better off going for one of the older titles. Rome 2 is one of those cases where it's 1 step forward and 2 steps back. While there are many nifty features, and takes place during ancient times, set backs such as a clunkier user interface, lack of personal family tree, and the removal of several co-op multiplayer features such as changing the settings to your co-op save file before the game starts, being able to build and recruit units during your partners turn, etc... Some civilizations feel like copies of the other, and some other civilizations don't have enough unit diversity and development to make the game interesting in the long run. Regardless, this is a cautious buy, unless you love warfare in Mediterranean/Western/Eastern Europe theatre.

As most people know, the release of Total War: Rome 2 far exceeded disappointment. With multiple bugs, glitches and it was simply impossible to run with a better framerate than 10 fps. So, with the release of Atilla coming very soon, how did this game turn out in the end?
The patches have seen the Rome 2 become the polished game we expected at release. It is a good game and very enjoyable, I myself have clocked almost 500 hours on this game. The recent emperor edition release has further enhanced the game, with better unit balancing, and an overhaul of the game's combat engine and mechanics. However, even though the game has become the enjoyable Total war game which we play today, it still ultimately comes out as a dissappointment. It lost many of the great features which currently reside in Shogun 2. The fact still remains that they have stripped many unique features from the game, like customizable multiplayer generals. It is also evident that the game still doesn't look as good as a video released of so called "pre-alpha footage" (if you know what I'm talking about). All in all, at the end of its days Rome 2 is ultimately a game worth buying at its current price, but still serves as a disappointment to the series and the hype that it recieved. It is clear that Total War: Atilla will be the game that Rome 2 was supposed to be.

Where do I begin? The excellent Campaign which had everything you could want: the Best graphics, incredible story, amazing actors and just was incredible to play. The Exo Zombies was huge fun I have to say, such as: Finally varied zombies and not generic boring ones e.g. Exploding zombies, charging zombies, emp zombies, (those were dochbags to say the least.) Infection zombies and undead dogs to name a few. I absolutely though exo zombies was a blast, cool zombie weapons as well that were incredible and equipment.
As well as quite well designed maps that were a good size apart from the first one. My only complaint was that because this was Sledgehammer's game there was no Pack A Punch, instead there were MK levels which you had to be strategic about for ammo purposes and strength wise.
Lastly there is the golden syrup AKA, Multiplayer was fun and very very different like: for starters there's the Exo Suit which has abilities, exo slide, (improved a lot upon from Ghosts) exo jumping which was super fun, then there's the new way you throw grenades which was different. Next is the grenade and equipment options there is SO MUCH, you have emp grenades, threat grenades, spike grenades, which you could throw at someone and then pull it back and other stuff.
Scorestreaks are very different now that you customise them, adding 3 layers of options to them such as being able to add extra guns to your air scorestreaks and changing the gun on your turret to a laser instead. Finally there is the last few things I could think of: You can completly change the look of your soldier now with all the clothing and gear options which I though was great, then there's the weapon variants, hate them or love them your choice but I think their great basically you can get Enlisted, Professional, Elite and Legendary variants. I just wish you could buy Advance Supply Drops on PC like you can on console it just helps if you really want that loadout piece or helmet now and not spend hours of game time to try and get it. The weapons themselves were amazing with options of 3 round burst to 5 round burst guns, then you have the fully automatic's and the shotguns were quite nice actually for once and I have to say there was really no weapon I didn't use or enjoy.
The dedicated servers aren't really there but that really isn't Sledgehammer's fault people blame Activision for that screwjob. The PC options are great for graphics and other options (shading, aliasing to name a couple), I can honestly say this is the BEST Call Of Duty game in years: it has so much more options for customization and the sound and map design are truely exceptional, that paired with the weapon selection and exo suit put this game in my Top 3 Call Of Duty Games. Call Of Duty Advanced Warfare NO.1 Call of Duty Black Ops 1 NO.2 and Call Of Duty Modern Warfare 1 NO.3. I hope at least some of you understand my review and liked it. Smite is a third-person online MOBA game, developed by Hi-Rez Studios releasing on PC, Xbox One and due to be released on PS4. You play as the visage of a god from mythological lore and take part in different game modes against other opponents.
The major difference with Smite over other MOBAs is that you play from a third person perspective, and plays with the same sort of controls as other third person action games. The game is very arcade like in that the majority of your abilities are skillshot based rather than selecting a target and having your character auto aim for you. The game has over 70 different gods to play as, each having their own unique play style, abilities and characteristics.  There are at least seven different game modes to play in, Conquest, Arena, Joust, Assault, Siege, Clash, and Match of the Day. My favourite mode out of them all has to be arena. The matches take no longer than 20 minutes, and the players that take part in them are genuinely really nice to be around. Being a fairly novice player at Smite compared to a lot of people, I felt that Conquest, which is considered the main game mode, had a much more hostile community vibe to it with more abuse and flaming coming out of chat than any other mode I played in.  As with most MOBA type games, your characters equipment plays a key part in how well you perform, and Smite is no different. There is a wide variety of different gear to choose from, allowing you to play your character however you choose.
Smite is built using the unreal engine 3.0 technology, which provides graphics full of detail and presenting a higher graphic level than most MOBA games. The character models are all high in detail and really well animated using rag doll effects. The game’s sound effects are OK, you have to pay extra for your characters voice pack, but you still get a little bit of flavour speech here and there.
The tutorial system at the start of the game does a very good job of explaining the games main mechanics and explaining the main game mode, and I felt it got me to a sufficient skill level in order to jump into the main online game. I have been playing for about ten hours so far, and I am at that point where I can quite often find myself at the top of the kills score board, and having the least amount of deaths too. I am not saying I am absolutely amazing all of the time, but I don’t feel as if I am being carried by my team anymore and doing more good than not. This is the sort of game where practice makes all the difference – the more you play the better you’ll get.
I can honestly say I am completely hooked on Smite, and have been playing it for the past week every night after work. The matches are a perfect length before they start to drag on, and the accessibility of any of the game modes makes it really quick to find a match online. The game would be even more enjoyable if you play with friends on coms, but even from a solo perspective, I can see myself playing Smite for hours and hours.
I did have a fairly annoying technical issue which I was unable to resolve, and that is really rapid frame rate drops and freezes. I started playing the game on 4k, with all of the settings maxed out; obviously I noticed the freezing – although it only happens when you open a menu, or a kill is announced on screen. So I dropped the resolution down to 1440p, although the same happened, reducing the resolution even more to 1080p only to find it still occurred. More so, even reducing the graphics settings did not cause the issue to disappear either, so it makes no odds whether I was playing on 4k max settings, or 1080p with low settings; the freezing happened regardless. Looking online the issue appears to be with the servers, so hopefully this can be resolved in a future patch.
Smite is one of the first MOBA games I have played for a length of time longer than 2 hours. I tend to normally stay away from this genre of game because I know how much of a time hog they can be, and I am the sort of person who will just find myself going down a rabbit hole with it, with that said, I do intend to keep on playing Smite, at least a few times a week due to how easy and quick the games are to get into. MOBA fans and even third person action skill based game fans will want to be checking this game out. The free to play model is done really well, with buying extra heroes rather than using the weekly rotation selection, and cosmetic items being the only things you can purchase.  You can pay £20, 99 to unlock every single hero in the game presently as well as any future gods as well. Personally I wouldn’t purchase this as I was perfectly happy using the weekly selection of gods, but if you intend to get really stuck into the game; it may be worth picking up this pack to unlock all of the heroes.

My play experience with Black Mesa was nothing short of amazing. The level design gets a little confusing at times, but once you figure out what you're supposed to do it is very rewarding. Weapons are all very fun. In addition, I feel like the team for Black Mesa knew exactly how to limit the player's ammunition so that certain things like tau cannon energy or satchel charges are actually exciting to find. Puzzles and exploration are interconnected by challenging stretches of combat that might actually have you begging for some suit energy or health in the next room. The wild story makes for interesting enemies and combat. I love seeing milita engage aliens and actually find themselves struggling; it's believable.
I mentioned exploration, and boy there is a lot. If you haven't played this game you should just to see how the team pulls together certain areas and captures the character of a location so perfectly. The Black Mesa testing facility is the ideal place to introduce unique environments: labs, frozen areas, radioactive silos, alien habitats, cliffsides, and a lot more. Some areas seem a little drawn out (there's one where you have to hop between conveyors and swim through sewage for just a little too long...), but on the whole I was always pleased with design choices.
This game is a little old at this point, but the dev team has a lot in store with a completed last chapter taking place in Xen set to drop this December. A new dynamic lighting system is also in the works which will do away with the static light in favor of real time light depending on where the source is. I am awaiting the last chapter with the highest hopes. The dev team has released screenshots taken straight from the game, and they look great. Pick up this game if you haven't; it is a true tribute to the original Half-Life that brings a lot to the table.

Short, but sweet and offers a challenge. no boss overstays it's welcome with repeats (edit: there is one but she only appears twice and the second time is sort of the "final boss"... sort of.), and the ones that do are technically returns from the first game given a bit of updating and new attacks to keep them fresh and more importantly, keeps them from feeling like they are actually rehashes.
side notes
-shorter than the first game, but only because it gets straight to the point: most stages are divided into two sections or quickly swap between two types of play: a platformy section with cannon fodder to mow down, and the Bosses. there is no in between.
-the Guns/Katana combo is advised: most of the game is built around this hybrid setup where the first input doubles as a short ranged slash with a more important use: the ability to reflect attacks. it's followed up by rapid gunfire, making it the de-facto DPS and damage option until you get good at dodging to be able to get away with not using them.
-expect to die. not as much as, say Dark Souls or Furi, but you will die. the true challenge is being able to get SSS rank, where you get Time (go fast to win S), Damage (See also Bayonetta's golden rule, don't get hit for S), and Style (same, but it's built up by doing damage to enemies and bosses so you can't just speedrun, taking damage reduces this and DYING kinda makes it impossible to get more than a C or D). do not expect to get all of them first run.
-some weapons are Situational but extremely useful in said situations. for example: one of the bosses gets stunlocked by the unlockable Rocket Launcher. another that is a pain to take down thanks to reflecting your attacks allows for a patient player to wreck face with proper usage of it's piercing charged shot. almost as if they took a megaman approach with the unlockable weapons.
Main Complaint:
not very long but it's better to deliver rock solid gameplay and tough but fair bosses than to be overly reliant on story.
don't pick this up if you want a long game. do pick this up if you want to kick asses in style and have fun doing so or are seeking a challenge.
General verdict: you see that yes, do you not? short, sweet, and straight to the point action. old school challenge distilled into a pure bullet hell platformer hybrid.
also if you truly seek a challenge, start on Hard. do not do Very Hard until you know you can take Hard with minimal damage.

I've owned this game since June of 2014 and played for at least 80-100 hours before it was released on Steam.
There's a free demo available on the website (and on Steam, theres a button on the right hand side) that you can check out to see how it suits you. A few minutes into it, I already knew I'd want to get this game:
You're building conveyor belts, robot arms, mining drills and other things in various ways to produce items and manage your resources.
And you can put a lot of thought into figuring out the best layout for your production lines, or just build it the way it's looking the most beautiful to you. Either way, you're constantly learning about new aspects to consider when expanding.
The devs are a shining example of how Early Access has to be done. There are weekly blogposts from the team ("Factorio Friday Facts") in which they explain what they've been up to, talk about programming problems they solved and are very transparent about their plans.
Whenever the community had a mixed opinion on a something the team was working on, they would revise their plans, taking into account what feedback they had received. Generally, you'll find the devs are trying to get feedback to most things they do, and you can find them replying on the forums regularly. They seem willing (and personally so) to make the game the best it can be.
It may take a while between big updates for the game to release, even a few months. After a major update, there are usually weekly updates with fixes and small additions. Possibly, the update schedule will be different after the Steam release though. Thanks to this cycle, the game is pretty stable.
I plan to play it some more when it comes out of Early Access, but as I mentioned, you can easily spend tens of hours in the game without having done everything that's possible. Many have played for hundreds or possibly thousands of hours.
Get it now if you want to play it already - it's content rich and mostly very polished - or if you just feel you want to support these devs.
Edit: I've nominated the game for the "I Thought This Game Was Cool Before It Won An Award" Award during the 2016 Autumn Sale. And again in 2017 for a Custom award.
Because honestly, it just as much deserves the "Just 5 More Minutes" and custom "Early Acces that's actually playable and fun" Awards. Too bad you seemingly can't nominate the same game multiple times.

Firstly, let me start by saying that as a rule, i am not a huge snooker playing person - although on occasion i do visit my local snooker centre from time to time for the past 30 yrs.
Snooker games have always been a 'niche' market and thus explains why there are very few and far between...
However, since re-visiting those old games developed by Blade Interactive, my interest has somewhat been revitalised!
Blade Interactive had developed quite some great snooker games over the latter years during the 'noughties', with officially licensed venues/players/rules etc - however, due to the current standards in computing capabilities, they are looking/feeling very dated.
As soon as i was aware of the Snooker Nation 'simulation' i was quite happy and bought the game on sale at £1.99 (which isn't bad by any means)...HOWEVER...this pricing unfortunately explains why it's such at a low price! :(
The game isn't bad - The graphics, steady framerate and physics are all very well done and polished. The control system is also catered to those seeking either a 'pick up and play method' or the no assists way.
The game stumbles with the A.I., which in all fairness, is completely pointless...
No matter what method or difficulty you're playing with, the A.I. has no skills whatsoever and at best can only manage very minimal breaks (the highest i've witnessed is 37!)
There's also some amount of 'bugs' i've experienced and although they've not been 'game breaking' in some sense, it just adds to the complete lack of re-playability this game has.
I could go on for hours providing every minute detail and issues this game has, but i see no point in doing so when the developers are most likely not bothered to develope this title any further....and it is a real shame...this had some real potential i think.
Is it worth the £1.99 i paid...? - Yes if you want a quick knock around...
However, because of the flaws this game presents (mainly the A.I.), i'd have to say i wouldn't waste the small amount of money on this...
Put it towards a game that you'll truly want, because looks aren't everything!

The term "HD Remake" is thrown around a lot these days and conveys almost the same amount of infamy as "Early Access". Homeworld Remastered, however, is an absolute exception. Gearbox seemed to have made it their goal to stay as true to the original as possible, while still carrying it over to 2015. Very successfully so, I might add!
Quick overview:
Homeworld's core game mechanics have been entirely preserved for Homeworld Remastered, down the smallest detail. It is delightful to see how extremely well Homeworld's rather unique approach to 3D real time strategy has aged.
Graphics have been revamped while absolutely keeping in line with the game's distinctive art style. It's beyond anything I expected.
NB: The original Homeworld 1 user interface has been forfeited in favour of Homeworld 2's much leaner and less cluttered UI. Smart move, really.
Sound and music, both in terms of recording quality and ingame sound engine, had major overhauls. Very noticeable. After all, they got none other than Paul Ruskay himself, who scored Homeworld's original soundtrack.
This "remastered" version was clearly done by people who appreciated the original game for what it represented back in 1999 (and many years to follow). They gave it a loving, respectful, much desired and much needed facelift to bring it to modern systems.
The result is nothing short of stunning. Players new to the series are absolutely recommended to take a closer look at the revival of an RTS cult classic; Homeworld veterans will immediately feel at home and - as in my case - nostalgic as hell.
10/10, easily.

While brilliant in many ways, from it's incredible and authentic atmosphere, Alien: Isolation soon wears out its welcome. The first 5 hours of this game were some of the best I'd experienced in a game, but after 25 hours, I was ready to quit.
Everything about the game looks and sounds amazing, making the player feel as though they are really there.
The alien that hunts you is not fully scripted, but AI controlled and unpredictable. Players must hide or use makeshift implements to distract it.  While this is sometimes great, it becomes frustrating when you die over and over.  The first death is shocking and scary.  The tenth is just tedious.  A lot of it comes down to poor level design.  The Nostromo DLC missions, and some places in the main game, like the escape pod sequence, are outstanding.  Too many other places are way too cramped or lack the ability to maneuver effectively.
Many sequences in the game involve these very creepy and uncanny androids that have turned hostile.  Despite the great visual design, encounters with these things often turned into a Benny Hill sequence of running around a table a dozen times as they chased me.
There's a thin line between a horror experience being tense and being frustrating, and this game frequently breaks it.  The presence of constant save stations broke the immersion, and are a sign that the designers intended players to die frequently, which as I've said saps games of tension.  Amnesia: The Dark Descent handled things much better, through the use of checkpoints to ease players dieing too often.
The game needed more quiet moments, perhaps filled in with some puzzle elements (Ripley is supposed to be an engineer, so an organic way to implement this could be her fixing various parts of the station).  The game is also way too long.  There felt like there were 2 or even three moments when the game was going to end, but it kept going, long after the gameplay had shown all it had to offer.
The worst offender, though, was that we simply encounter the alien way, way too much.  After a certain point, the player is so accustomed to the creature, and has had the time to figure out all the gamey ways to get around it, that it's no longer scary.  That's why the most effective horror movies or games show the monster only sparingly, so that the player is not familiar with it.
I do look forward to a sequel to this game, and I think with a few tweaks, like a more intricate level design and a more sparing use of the alien, it could be a remarkable experience.

Black Mesa is the gold standard for remaking an older game. Most remakes tend to be ports to newer consoles with higher frames per second or slightly-better graphics, but Black Mesa goes above and beyond the minimal effort that companies put into their re-releases. It shows that, sometimes, a fan project can surpass AAA games of the same genre.
If you've played Half-Life, you already know the story of Black Mesa. An experiment gone awry results in an alien invasion at a New Mexico research facility, leaving you to escape the disaster area and figure out how to set things right. Not much has changed in terms of pacing, but some improvements over Half-Life's level design have been implemented. Annoying sections like On a Rail's maze or We've Got Hostiles' vent tunnels have been heavily cut down. The mod has a better overall "flow" to it than Half-Life, though a couple levels like Apprehension still drag on.
The graphics are stunning. Crowbar Collective has pushed the Source Engine to its limits, and it shows. Everything in the facility feels vibrant and real. The game has pretty good optimization as well, meaning that lower-tier computers should be able to play it smoothly with reduced settings.
Black Mesa's gameplay feels fluid. Quality of life changes, like sprinting and infinite flashlight battery life, make navigating the levels less of a chore and more of an adventure. All of the classic weapons return looking sharp and mostly unchanged. Enemies from the original game are less sluggish and far more deadly than before. Don't underestimate anything, as even the simple Headcrab Zombie poses a far greater threat than you'd think.
The Steam version of the game has some features that the 2012 mod lacks. There is a multiplayer mode and support for Steam Workshop. Weapons look and animate better. Most of all, the HECU Grunts no longer have their cheesy Solid Snake voices like they did in the mod! Now they sound like soldiers caught up in an unpredictable conflict, not canned voices from an action movie.
Joel Nielsen did a great job with the game's soundtrack. I would recommend checking out his website after you've beaten the game. My personal favorites from the album are "Questionable Ethics 1" and "Forget about Freeman."
All in all, Black Mesa is a solid first-person shooter that harkens back to the old days of save scumming and exploration. I would recommend buying it if you're a fan of the Half-Life series. Even at full price, it's worth every penny.

Dishonored 2 is boring.
One paper, it might seem like a slam dunk. In terms of gameplay, level design, setting, it delivers exactly the same experience as the first one, and that's good news. The problem is that the content itself is mind numbingly boring, so enjoying the game is impossible.
The biggest problem is the writing. Let's go over its many issues:
- The story borrows the main idea of the original game's story (someone takes control of the empire using force, now you are wanted, and need to reclaim it with the help of a bunch of outcast supporting character). That's already kind of disappointing, but whatever, the writing itself can theoretically deliver despite the unoriginal concept. Except that:
- The story progresses in a way that feels like a series of standalone missions, not like a continuously expanding narrative. It's a strange feeling since there is a literary arc to the whole game, and you do discover things about your adversary along the way, but each conclusion of a mission feels like a major plot device is crossed off the story, so instead of an evolving story, we get a story that shrinks as you play on. For example, Paolo, the leader of the Howlers, makes a brief appearance in the 4th mission, is absent in the 5th, and is dealt with in the 6th. That's quite a waste of an interesting character. A lot of plot points in the game feel like this. They are presented, and then they're gone, sometimes in the same mission.
- The characters are very boring. The cast of supporting rebel NPCs was one of the good things about the original game. In Dishonored 2, you get 3 NPCs, and most of them only join you in the middle or the late part of the game, so it's very empty in the seafaring rebel headquarters. The characters themselves aren't really worth talking to outside of mendatory briefings. That Void dude is still here, interrupting your game to mentally jack off about how mysterious he is.
The game has a few interesting story points, like when you discover the identity of the crown killer, or there's a level in which you get to travel back and forth in time, which is not only an interesting mechanic, but also creates a mystery that is fun to uncover. But these occurances are rare. I was really bored playing Dishonored 2, and I'm not looking forward to replaying it.
I can't really call this a bad game though. It's a case of good game, crappy game for the series, but I can't really recommend it to anyone without a fair warning, and this is therefore a thumbs down for me.

Dark Echo has a great novel concept and a nice art style. Unfortunately, it does not fulfill its promise. I liked the beginning a lot, but becomes boring and tedious later on. I played the dark levels on Android and some of the white levels on PC, so I can compare both versions.
There are 3 main mechanics in the game (tapping, sneaking, throwing rocks). They are interesting early on, but no other concept is introduced later on, and there are no new mechanics introduced in the later levels (maybe except moving objects). The game seems to be a half-finished, with so many interested things that could have been introduced in the game, but weren't.
The number of levels is low. There are 40 dark levels, which you can finished in a couple of hours, and 40 white levels, which are the same levels with many more (and bigger and faster) enemies, and a very uncomfortable full-white background. There's not much motivation to play the white levels. Also, one wonders why there aren't more unique levels than 40. Given that designing new levels seems extremely easy, their current number feels more like a demo than a regular game.
The controls are unfortunately very poorly implemented. On touch devices, it's very hard to sneak, and sometimes you perform a regular step instead of sneaking, which means instadeath in later (white) levels. Imprecise controls on touch devices was a reason why I switched to PC version for later levels. On the other hand, on touch devices you can very easily throw rocks into arbitrary direction, and it's very easy to precisely position your enemy. Mind-bogglingly, you can't do that on PC. Even though it would be very obvious to use mouse cursor to throw rocks, you can't, and you can only throw to 8 basic directions using the keyboard. Also, you always need to face the direction you're throwing into, so you can't distract an enemy by throwing a rock to the side when running away, as it would be natural. With gamepad, you can throw to arbitrary directions, but as is usual with a gamepad stick, aiming is hard. So while PC version makes it easier to move, it makes it harder to aim compared to touch devices. In none of the versions you can control your character
. Controls were my number 1 frustration when playing later levels. The ideal controls seem so obvious - left mouse click to walk, shift to sneak, space to tap, right mouse click to throw to the exact direction. Yet it is not there.

Dark Echo is a minimalistic exploration game. You are shrouded in darkness (or, for the second half of the game, in blinding light), and the only way for you to navigate through the levels is the echos of your footsteps (represented by colored lines which radiate out from where you’re standing). You have the ability to stomp your foot (making louder echoes), walk silently (to avoid alerting enemies to your presence), and throw stones (to make echoes in a remote location to lure enemies away).
The game is very simple; there are only a handful of mechanics. There are red enemies who move towards the last sound they were in range of earing, there are pits of water which slow you down and which make a lot of sound to move through, there are red areas that killed you if you moved into them, there were walls that would collapse when you made a loud sound (opening an area but also attracting enemies), and there were moving blocks which pushed you around.
Mostly, the game worked fairly decently; you are introduced to all the games’ mechanics gradually over the first half of the game, and navigate through a series of increasingly-difficult levels which force you to combine the mechanics in increasingly interesting ways.
While the game was mostly fairly solid, the moving blocks mechanic was probably the most frustrating; while it only appears in a handful of levels, the fact that the pushes are so difficult to see ahead of time is kind of frustrating. Eventually you figure out how they work (for a while, I just thought they were sloped areas that I was skidding down), but at times it felt like the game broke its own rules, such as one level where you had to navigate up little ramps that felt like they actually were sloped areas on the sides of the room.
Mostly, though, the game played very fairly, and even the frustrating levels were mostly quite short. After beating the game, you could hunt back through for treasures, or play through the “light” versions of the levels, where additional enemies were added in to make you play more carefully (as well as the layouts of some of the levels being changed to make them more difficult).
That said, the game is nothing super special; the gameplay isn’t really amazing, but it is decent enough. Ultimately, this is a sort of time-waster game – the sort of thing you’d play while chatting to someone or doing something else, sporadically playing it. It was originally a mobile game, and I suspect it is better suited to that platform simply because of its “play in short bursts” nature.
Still, it is okay, and if you’re looking for something to do between doing other things, it isn’t a bad choice, and goes to show that just because you don’t spend a whole lot on graphics doesn’t mean you can’t make a visually striking game. Just dont' expect it to be anything more than a distraction.

Dark Echo is a mobile game with unique minimal graphics, which some people view artistically. In actuality, the game is a top-down casual adventure game with sound built into the graphics. Yes, it's unique, but the game quickly runs out of material and becomes irritating to finish. The low price helps, but it's not a game I'll likely remember.
The core gameplay is to reach the exit, avoiding red traps and pushing yellow plates to open walls. Detecting objects requires sounds, so most of the time you will be sending out foot pings to map out rooms. The real gameplay opens up when enemies are introduced, and sounds become a risk of detection. In the best moments, Dark Echo is about outmaneuvering enemies and feeling smart about your moves.
In the worst moments, Dark Echo is about trial & error memorization of traps and enemies, since the optimal playstyle is to make no noise. Issues come up when the game throws in more enemies and more water, forcing you to drag groups further out of the way so you'll have more time to move. Enemy detection also shows issues, as detection is dependent on sound lines hitting enemies. Sound lines may be pretty consistent, but it would make more sense to be doppler waves for consistency. Rock tosses will generally miss at medium range, unless the rock hits a wall to amplify. Too much time is spent spamming rocks to move enemies just right, and waiting on the slow death animation.
Although the game has 80 levels, half of them are repeats with added difficulty. The survival horror concepts are lost with the flood of identical enemies and repeated deaths. The puzzle elements are minimal switches, and no real mental challenge outside memorization. The lack of tension and challenges leave the game feeling like a grind to finish, despite being short. It would take closer to 5+ hours to complete, and I left the game idle overnight. I suppose the game isn't too expensive, but I wasn't impressed or pleased by the second half. Sadly it's another artsy game that says nothing and puts style over substance.

Compared to the first Bleed this game is an improvement in many ways. The controls feel a lot smoother and precise which makes dodging attacks a lot easier. Unlocking everything was quite fun as well, though the highest difficulty was a bit frustrating in some fights. Compared to the first game however, Bleed 2 is a bit easier on the highest setting.
The reappearance of the bosses of the first game is nice and anticlimatic at the same time. Battling them with the overhauled mechanics is fun, but it also feels a bit like filling in for the lack of ideas.
Its biggest downside is the way too short campaign, the game really needs a few more levels to feel long enough. Even with the replay value you are through after a few hours.
Altogether its a nice and fun game only lacking some more levels.

I got C's and D's on most levels.  I made it through the game like this on hard mode in 91 minutes, which feels a little short. Wow, this has to be one of the most innovative minimalist games I've played in a long time.  Most indie games these days seem to try to take an existing game as an archetype, strip out all the fluff, and leave the core mechanic, whatever that may be.  By and large, this makes for a great game, because it's hard to invent something truly new, but slightly easier to see a AAA game fail, read the reviews, and then re-hash it taking all the negative comments into consideration.
Dark Echo, on the other hand, creates a whole new mechanic, and makes a wonderful game out of it.
In a funny way (and bear with me here), Dark Echo's "special sauce" (that genre-holotype-defining quality of the first game in a string of variants) reminds me a little of Amnesia, Dark Descent... The main mechanic of that game was that if you can see the monster, it can see you, so you have to tiptoe about and hide away in corners, turning your back to monsters so they can't see you.  If you loved that juxaposition, you'll love Dark Echo.   In this game, rather than light (sight), it's sound that allows you to see the monsters, but as soon as you 'see' them via your echoes, they 'see' you too!  So it's a constant game of making just enough noise to 'see' by, but not too much!   A lovely little balancing act that can take a few deaths to get right!
In another funny way, it reminds me a little of Ico (again, bear with me).  After all, I hear you say "Whereas Ico was a visual extravaganza, this is a minimalist line drawing!".   I'm referring to the atmosphere, really.  The wonderful sounds, the echoes, the vastness of some of the 'spaces', the lack of explanations, the constantly running away from stuff.  It's got a great little mythos going for it.  I wouldn't be surprised if someone didn't write a little fan fiction for it...
So, what is it?  In it's essence, it's a puzzler where you have to navigate a top-down 'level' full of tricks, traps and 'monsters', to reach the 'safe zone'.   So far, so simple.  The hard part is the aforementioned visibility mechanic and managing it so that you can navigate around without being caught.
The game comes in two flavours: Dark and Light.  The light levels are (by and large) the same as the dark levels, but with a few added monsters and/or water.   In a funny way, the light levels feel like the 'completion' of the dark levels, or possibly that the dark levels were a 'trial run' of the light levels.   Often water is placed at critical places to slow you down, and make lots of splashes for the bad guys to hear...  Sometimes the level's structure is adjusted ever-so-slightly to make you change your tactic on the second run-through.   Some of the levels are identical, but with a monster or two thrown in.  For most of the second half of the game, I felt that things were new-enough to merit finishing the game.
So, as someone who doesn't have a lot of time any more to play games, I'm happy to say that Dark Echo ticked all my boxes: It's new, it's amusing, it's inventive, it's minimalist, and doesn't break its own rules all the time.  Everything's well laid out, sounds fantastic, and yes, wear headphones! It creeped me the heck out! :)

This review is very positive toward the game. This game is worthy of at least one play through. The developers got it right. The game has the atmosphere, sounds, and visuals of the original Alien movie. And that's the point. This game is a survival game that depends a lot on patience, not run and gun gameplay nor a rush-to-the-end experience. The game could be described as a sneak and hide game with a scifi twist. There are collectibles (ID tags and written/audio logs) that are a definite part of the experience. And since the game saves your missions, the player can replay parts of the the game to get every collectible. When the credits finally role, you will have a since of accomplishment.

I noticed that I've been far too kind to a lot of free-to-play artsy games recently, and I made a private promise that I'd go on a negative streak. I started with "You Have to Win the Game", and I suppose I might as well continue with Dark Echo.
Now, I'm not recommending Dark Echo because I think it's a bad game. Dark Echo is an incredibly unique game with a stealth system all-it's-own. I just personally don't like it. But if you think the points I bring up won't bother you, then by all means buy this game.
Dark Echo is a stealth/horror game built around the idea that you're blind and have to rely on sound to guide your way through what I think is a castle with a ton of enigmatic monsters living inside it. The mechanics are very unique. If you choose to move quietly to not disturb the monsters, you won't be able to see far ahead and predict incoming obstacles. However, if you choose to be loud and find out what's ahead, you might attract monsters who will eat you. But all this challenge and fright is pretty much diminished by the rocks. Once you get those all the levels that follow are an absolute piece of cake.
Dark Echo is certainly a horror game. It plays well with what you see as well as what you don't see, and uses sound to amp up the atmosphere and tension. But without a story, context, or building challenge to the monsters I didn't find myself sweating with terror at the end. I felt relieved, sure, but I know if the game put a little more oomph! into it, Dark Echo could be so much better, and so much scarier.
Again, if this sounds appealing to you, go nuts. Dark Echo is still an incredibly unique experience. But beyond the sometimes blandly simple levels and lack of story to really put things into context (and the added on padding where you simply play through all 40 levels again, but in the light), it just wasn't a game for me. But it might be the perfect game for someone else.

I found no performance issues on PC. I'm running an Intel i7 4720Q Haswell Refresh and Nvidia 980M (4GB dedicated) with 16GB RAM on a SanDisk SSD with Windows 10 1703 and the game was smooth as, even on the highest graphics quality mode. Their recent addition of the demo was really useful in knowing how the game would play before buying. The loading times are slightly longer than the first game but it's still great considering it's very new. I did however get 3 game crashes (whole window just closes instantly with no warnings or errors displayed), usually after doing several subsequent load-recent-saves, but I save regularly so didn't lose much. I'm impressed based on comparison videos on YouTube that graphics quality is identical on all 3 platforms.
I've only played as Emily so far but it's been a great game, usually spend about 3-4 hours per mission and there are 10 missions - same as the first game. A major bug from the first game is fixed as well where bodies would disappear or show as kills even though you used non-lethal. Also the new ability to see stats during-mission helps a lot for doing a low chaos playthrough. The mission objectives can sometimes look broken (even though objectives have been acheived) and are missing options sometimes when you do get clues e.g. from the seemingly same homeless guy which would have been nice to have in order to get a complete picture.
The best thing about the game is the level design, especially in the levels The Clockwork Mansion, A Crack In The Slab, and The Grand Palace. Each of these have been excellently designed and you just want to keep tinkering and exploring these mansions. There is some new functionality in the mansion in 'Crack in the Slab' which permits time-travel in order to avoid obstacles. I would have loved to seen this used more in the game but I think it's good it wasn't overused because it would likely make the game a bit daunting. Zero Punctuation does raise a good point that it's a cool gameplay mechnic that does disappear like you never had it.
I felt a bit underwhelmed with the ending on low chaos (but I mainly did a no-powers low chaos playthrough so I'm sure there is more there when I replay) and wanted to see the clockwork soliders used much more as they were my favourite part of the game. There is just enough challenge given in stealth and obstacle avoiding, stealth difficulty is up a bit more compared to the previous, enough amount of puzzles to keep you guessing, and so many ways to complete a level. I will replay as Corvo with a lethal run next time to see the other side. I would love to see some DLC or some kind of follow-up.

I've been playing this game for more than a year now and have hundreds of hours spent in it.
Factorio is a game where you have to build a rocket on an alien planet and launch it into space. To do so you need to research technologies and build factories that do the work for you. Everything in this game can be automated.
You start small by mining resources by hand but gradually unlock new technologies and buildings. You can build huge train networks, a logistics system with robots that fly around delivering items to other chests and yourself and a lot of different kinds of weapons, like a flamethrower, missiles, tanks, 3 kinds of combat robots and laser turrets which you will need, as the natives (called biters and spitters) on this planet will try to destroy your base if it creates too much pollution.
What I like most about this game is that you can rebuild it anytime without the need to invest resources again, as removing a building just places it in your inventory and it can be placed someplace else instantly.
As soon as you have construction robots, you can duplicate parts of your factory or your whole factory by blueprinting with a selection box and place it somewhere else, which makes it easy to expand your factory without manually having to place things down.
The map is procedurally generated and infinite in every direction, also giving you the option to change ore/oil/enemy size, frequency and richness as well as starting area (how far away the nearest biters spawn) among other settings.
There is also peaceful mode, when activated the aliens will not attack you unless you attack them first.
There is an active modding community that has made a lot of useful mods like trains that automatically lay rail tracks, remote train control, mods that show you the remaining ore in your ore fields and complete overview over the logistics network. There are also several big mods that add faster and improved machines, new intermediate products so you need to rethink your factory and new technologies.
The devs are very transparent with the development of their game, they are posting some insight about the game and upcoming features every friday on their blog (Factorio Friday Facts) for over 2 years now.
They also listen to the players. When they announced a new entity (the Circuit Network Connector) required to connect a building to that network a few weeks ago, most of the players were against that change so the devs revised that idea.
If you're even a little bit interested, the devs have a demo on their website:

Original Review:
As it stands today (Jun 2 2015), Fuse is being sold on steam at a price of $100. Yesterday Mixamo was bought by Adobe, and it was announced that Fuse will be free. So no, I definitely do not recommend buying Fuse at this point. Mixamo has said that Fuse and autorigging will be available for 6 mo, beyond that is anyone's guess.
