As a fan of the Total War series since the original Rome installment, i would grade the overall game as a 9.5 on a scale of 1- 10.  If you are new to the total war series, the game will be frustrating initially until you grasp concepts of faction traits, upkeep, public order, and specialized settlement construction.  For those who have play a Total War game before, you will have a lot of fun with the tweaks that have been made to provide greater detail and allow for greater flexibility in achieving your aims however you see fit (military, through agents, etc.).  The grand campaign is great, especially if you have all free and dlc factions.  The additional campaigns (caesar/gaul, hannibal/gates, imperator augustus) are entertaining and challenging, but subsequent playthroughs were broadly similar.  One contribution that I would like to make for anyone considering the purchase of the Wrath of Sparta campaign is to not be swayed by the negative reviews.  Aside from the grand campaign, I have found the Wrath of Sparta to be very enjoyable with elements from the first game such as unit conscription across multiple turns.  I went and added steam funds to my wallet before reading the reviews and after redeeming the funds, decided not to purchase the Wrath of Sparta because of the poor feedback i saw from the community.  A friend of mine sent me the dlc anyway, and I have played it constantly since.  For anyone who likes real time strategy games, previous games in the Total War series, or is a fan of history or a specific time period covered by an installment - I would highly recommend any of the Total War games.  This game would have been rated a 10 for me had the initial tweaks required by numerous patches been addressed/resolved prior to release AND while I am aware that there are 100s of different units in the game - I would like to have seen more diversity within each type of culture.  For instance - pretty much every Hellenic faction (excluding Successor Kingdoms, some Black Sea Colonies) has 2 or 3 high quality melee/spear units (generally being named some variation of 'hoplite'), has 4 cavalry units which are weak comparatively, and has solid but basic archery units.  The ships are essentially the same for all factions.
Overall, you cant go wrong.  At the very least, I can guarantee anyone who buys this game that they will definitely get their moneys worth.

Dark Souls 2 may be one of the most engaging, captivating, and engrossing RPGS I've ever played. At the same time, it's not without its problems, and though the positive outweighs the negative, its flaws need to be considered when considering whether or not it's worth your (significant) time.
When it comes to presentation, there's a lot to love. Though it's not cutting-edge and sometimes muddy up close, the game looks great from a distance, with towering, dreary castles and vast lakes of lava making some striking impressions. The enemies are all varied from a visual standpoint, and most fit in with the varied and distinct themes of their areas.
The bosses are just as well-designed from a visual standpoint, though a few too many seem to be some variation of "two is better than one";
.
This can be forgiven, however, when you consider that all of their battle themes fit perfectly and set the tone of the fights very well. It almost makes up for the fact that with the exception of the starting areas, no zone has an ambient theme, which is an unfortunate omission.
The story is smartly delivered through item descriptions and keen environmental observation, which help sell the thick atmosphere of traversing through a condemned prison or foggy, mazelike woods. The NPCS have some interesting stories to tell accompanied by solid voice acting, but the main plot is far more cryptic than necessary and feels like it's trying too hard to make you piece things together yourself.
"Showing, not telling" only works when you are shown enough tidbits to fit the picture on your own. Exposition isn't always a good thing, but it's oftentimes a key factor in understand what the hell is going on. That being said, the side-stories are wonderful, perfectly delivered, and oftentimes leave you with a real emotional reaction (even if some rely on finding NPCS in random areas).
The gameplay is a more thoughtful, tactical version found in typical action-rpgs. A stamina meter governs actions, and exhausting it is a very bad idea. Thus, unless you're far more powerful than your enemy, battles require patience, precision, and prediction as you read your opponent's attacks.
Going back to the bosses, their quality is a little scattershot; some, like
offer fair difficulty, cool design, and memorable fights. Others, such as
are too easy or are eyesores. Even worse are the few fights that go in the other direction and feature unfair mechanics that throw skill out the window and force you to exploit AI.
. Regardless, a few too many have grab attacks with iffy hitboxes and take reduced damage when they're readying or recovering from a failed grab.
At the end of the day, though, more bosses are fun and challenging than are pushovers or unfair tests of glitch hunting, and I enjoyed fighting most of them. The ecstasy felt upon their defeat is incredibly rewarding.
Leveling up is done via spending souls, which can be acquired from enemies, selling items (which only becomes available distressingly late in the game) and consuming findable items. Souls are also your primary currency, which would normally be a bad thing, but the game is balanced so that at a certain point, the leftover souls you have after leveling up can be used to purchase supplies. Early on, balancing your need to grow stronger with your desire for more items or ammunition requires a great deal of thought.
Though almost all the areas are visual marvels, and a few stand out for being perfectly balanced in terms of length and difficult, others last far too long or have annoying mechanics that drag the experience down.
.
Still, like with the bosses, the majority of these areas are fun, and all of them look quite cool and are deeply atmospheric, with self-contained stories and oftentimes disturbing history.
In terms of online, the game falters a bit more. The community is awful, but in terms of what the game can control, it still falls behind with rampant lagstabs (backstabs even when you're clearly in front of the enemy) and a few balance issues, especially with regards to magic. Still, cooperating with people is fun, and not being able to communicate creates an interesting system dependent on trust. Some of the covenants are also fun-I got a kick out of serving a (literally) animal king.
Overall, Dark Souls 2 offers far more good experiences than it does awful ones. The death penalties can feel like artificial ways to block experimentation, the community is toxic, and the quality of areas and bosses is hit-and-miss, but I don't regret my time with Dark Souls 2. The atmosphere, side-stories, upgrades, solo and cooperative gameplay have given me more than enough reasons to dump an unhealthy amount of time into this game.

[ I will keep this short and sweet because I am a fellow developer and friend of the creator(s) of Bleed and Bleed 2. The play time available on Steam does not accurately depict the number of hours that I have spent with this game. ]
Bleed 2 is a large step up from the original. It is fast, and it is fun. Bleed 2 is what an action-platformer should FEEL like. The player has a high speed and level of mobility. It really sets you up to feel powerful and intelligent while continuously throwing new challenges at you. Several difficulty modes allow the game to be a blast across almost any level of player which keeps the game rewarding, but accessible. I cannot say that I am a hardcore gamer, so I am unsure if it speaks to the top 10% of ultra-experienced platformer veterans, but I had an absolute blast with this game. The music and sound design are also very notable. One of the only games in recent memory that I tend to crank the volume while I am playing. Bleed 2 is not incredibly lengthy, but the multiple difficulty levels which affect enemy/boss speed, power, and reaction time, several unlockable characters, and the option for couch co-op allow the game to remain substantial.
For what it's worth, the developers of this series are incredible people and I would highly suggest supporting them. Whether it be Bleed 3 or something completely new, I am confident that the team will continue to impress. They certainly haven't let me down.

The only real problem with the game is that some attacks come so fast that even with the tell it's impossible to dodge until after you've seen it once before.  That being said, infinite lives in the story mode makes it largely insignificant of a problem.

TL;DR: Bleed 2 is an amazing, fast-paced side-scrolling action shooter with dozens of fun bosses, incredibly fitting music, and epic proportions of polish all making up for its somewhat short campaign.
I was a fan of the original Bleed, and upon hearing of a sequel being released I picked it up to give myself a few hours worth of a new experience. Boy what a few hours those were, turning into at least 10 hours within the first couple days. 10 hours doesn't seem like much to an outsider's perspective, but when you consider the game can be beaten in around 30 minutes, then it must be doing something right. Hidden among that shorth length are some of the most memorable blazing fast encounters I've experienced from games in quite some time. I wasn't a big fan of side-scrolling shooters in the past, but I think this game has sparked my appeal to the genre.
In this game, you play as Wryn, the "Greatest Hero of All Time" triple-jumping back into action to stop an invasion from a powerful being named Valentine. Each level lets you shoot, slide, slash, and slow time to better your odds against several returning and unique new enemies. You'll face robots, rivals, and revenge-seeking loyalists while running from explosions, rising on missles, and ricocheting around space ships too! The variety is incredible. Despite this, the story follows a more linear route as opposed to the hit-list from the last game, and yet manages to have many more unique and fun bosses to fight (with some from the previous Bleed game returning)
The biggest thing that jumped out at me though were the minor differences from its predecesor. For starters, Your default weapons are the pistols AND katana, which allows you to both shoot reflect certain colored projectiles back at enemies, or even reflect the baddies themselves! This creates a great new gameplay dynamic were shooting is no longer the only method to thining the number. The plethora of cosmetic changes (better sprites, better bullets, and better sound effects) only adds to the presentation. On top of all that, the change in soundtrack was a big step in the right direction. Rock 'n' roll action tunes seem to fit the pace and setting better than Bleed's chiptunes.
My only real complaint is its short length, which can be forgivable given its tight focus on mechanics and replayability. I find the difficulty settings on the whole to be a touch easier than the last game, but much more fair, a similar sentiment I share with the arcade mode, where you play through the whole game on a single life bar. I admire the small features like replay recordings and challenge modes, all which simply serve to enhance the original game. Even now I feel like going back this second to shoot more robots and reflect missiles.
I've seen a few people complain about the games pacing. On the contrary, the pacing seems even better in this game than the last, since its very fast-paced and action packed. As of time of writing, I have yet to try the multiplayer mode, a situation I plan to aliviate soon. I doubt it will disappoint, as the rest of the game has passed will flying, pink/purple colors! I highly recommend it!

A fun, fast, satisfying sequel. I'll note right away that this is a very score focused game, much like the original. No RPG mechanics, barebones story, no fluff - my first run through story mode took about an hour on Hard.
However, what is here is absolutely nailed - so far I'm enjoy this just as much if not more than the original. The stages are fairly short but each boss is satisfying to fight and none overstay their welcome. The unlockable characters in particular (and weapons, to a lesser extent) are excellent for adding a bit of variety to each run, as each offer unique abilities - and every character feels well equipped to deal with each stage. There is noticeable consideration taken towards making sure the game is still challenging and fun with all of them.
Pretty much the only downside I can note at the moment is how there's very little feedback when you take damage. Sometimes amidst the chaos it's hard to tell when I get hit, and paying attention to your HP bar is equally difficult. While it may get easier to notice with practice, it makes learning how to avoid certain attacks early on pretty rough.
Despite that minor gripe, this is an easy recommendation to anyone who enjoyed the original, and if you haven't played that, I recommend both if you enjoy fast paced score attack type games.

Note: I have at least 100 hours logged on the pre-steam version.
I don't write many reviews, but I had to jump in to share my experience with Factorio. This game, in its current alpha state, is already fantastically complete and fun. Even when I bought into the alpha years ago, the game was a joyous experience. The devs are excellent  and very communicative about the progress of the game.
What's so fun about this game? Well, it's sort of a city-builder, puzzle-game, incremental game and a few other genres blended together. You start with nothing but a pickaxe and coal power, and behin harvesting your first simple resources. As things progress, you need to process those materials into more and more complicated refined products using whatever crazy layout of conveyor belts, mechanical arms, fabricators, furnaces, and other contraptions you decide are necessary. Things get complicated fast, and there's a lot of fun to be had tinkering with your factory, learning new more efficient designs, and chasing more advanced tech.
Add to that a healthy dose of combat versus alien bugs trying to defend the planet and you have a well-rounded game that will keep you occupied for hours.
And then there's the extensive mod support, which has already generated a bunch of great mods that change things up and expand the gameplay. This game is going places.
For just $20, you're going to enjoy this game.

Well... this is a pretty tough call. I absolutely love snooker, and any snooker fan will probably love this game too, and considering the price, there's no reason not to buy it if you're into the game. However, I'd struggle to justify the purchase if you're not a fanatic.
The physics are great. A game that finally accurately depicts side, yay! I've always loved my masse shots so it's pretty fun to do them on here too. They're very tricky though; no matter what power I set it to, the side kicks in earlier than the guideline shows.. perhaps that needs to be attended to?
The AI is good, but needs a little more balance. This is one of the few things that were fixed in the like, two updates this game has gotten, but you still see really low level AI get perfect safety shots when they can't pot a black off its spot. Honestly. I do feel like its priority needs to be looked at to - you'll sometimes see them go for a baulk colour when they can still force something on the blue. Positional play is probably the biggest issue, and I'm sure this is something way harder to fix, and is why the hard AI is REALLY hard. They consistently play like they've already won and are playing exhibition shots. It's ridiculous. If you could improve their positional play, watch a few games, see how snooker pros make their decisions, rework the AI based around that; nigh impossible cut shots are awful to play against when you play a good safety and they get out 9 times out of 10.
There have been a couple of bugs, which is fine as the game is in Early Access, but as noted earlier, barely any updates! Not good. Partly unfortunate timing due to the VR hype train and other games and whatnot, so of course this game would get sidelined as it's a bloody snooker game for crying out loud, but a little more love would make this game far more approachable. Valve haven't ditched TF2 after 8-9 years or whatever, and they're still making money off that through constant updates - show some love to the game that needs it most is what I'm saying, really. Back to the bugs though, sometimes pots wouldn't register if they almost don't go in, like it just skips to the next player's turn... sometimes the AI just plows straight into a colour off the break if you've snookered them (like literally, straight into the colour in front of them)... I found a weird one today where I loaded up an old tournament I was still in qualifying for and I was apparently losing 0 frames to 3 when it was a 1 frame game (I don't recall playing these out) and I won a frame and won the game. Pretty funny, but weird.
Well, you do kinda get what Cherry Pop say... a full tournament. There really do need to be other, shorter options to make it less of a boring, monstrous challenge. Would be nice to see shorter championships, like the Masters, or the other UK / Europe ones, perhaps. Again, with lack of updates, planned features haven't made it into the game. Rest usage would be very neat, but would only really happen with a realistic shot update, which again, no bueno there. Multiplayer is there, but barely anyone is ever on, and it's pretty much the same system as Pool Nation, which is fine, but ughhhhhh.
Overall, Snooker Nation Championship is a decent snooker game. Its main strength is the accurate physics and simply the fact that there's no better game around. A LOT of work needs to be done to bring it out of Early Access, which I don't see Cherry Pop doing as that effort may not be worth it for such a niche game in their eyes. But, and this is more directly to the devs, there is simply no other rival. You hold all the cards. Don't just throw them away, do something; the building blocks are there for an amazing snooker game, work on making it more user-friendly, more unique.
Get it if you love snooker, you seriously will not regret. New to snooker? Only if you have the money to burn and can accept the loss of a few dollars.

The Homeworld series is the prime example of a (space) RTS done right. Everything from level of detail on ships, to gameplay, to mod support, and optimization are excellent.
Now, I have a terrible gaming setup, a ATI Radeon 4350 graphics card with a AMD Phenom x4 910 processor. For those of you who don't speak computer hardware, this is a low end PC from back in like 2008. A piece of junk. Homeworld 2 ran great on it, and much to my surprise, so does the remastered edition. I have yet to see any serious frame issues despite playing it on a PC that is almost worth more as scrap metal than as a trade in. Granted, this is with most of the graphical settings turned low or off, but this just goes to show that you don't even need a decent computer to run the game.
But for those of you who haven't played Homeworld, here’s a little about the remastered edition of the game:
Its space RTS involving 4 races with up to 8 players. Each faction gets 4 different classes of units: Fighters, Corvettes, Frigates and Capital Ships with quite a few other utility class units. There are 2 Races from Homeworld 2, and 2 from the original Homeworld. There are significant differences between both generations, which is kind of interesting, especially when you consider the fact that both games are so fundamentally different, that they basically are incompatible with each other without serious modifications. Because of this, the devs, being so considerate of the loyal fan base, even decided to throw in the original "untouched" versions of both Homeworld 1 AND Homeworld 2, which is absolutely amazing when you consider the fact that Homeworld 1 is so old that you can't even run it on most systems.
All in all, if you are a Homeworld fan, this buy is a no brainer. If you aren't a Homeworld fan, you're getting 2 fully retextured, rebalanced, beautiful and tactical RTS games with their original untouched (and now playable on your PC) versions. This game is a true classic, and I can't wait to see what mods make it to the Steam Workshop!

Before I start I just want to mention that I’m structuring this review for three key groups: people who are looking at Homeworld for the first time, the Homeworld 1 veterans, and the Homworld 2 veterans. Overall, this Remaster does get my thumbs up BUT in its current state there are still PLENTY of problems that need to be addressed (and therefore mentioned). I would also ask that you ignore my “play time” because sadly on my older laptop I have not been able to get Homeworld working properly, but my brother has (for the entire night in a span of about 10 hours) generously let me play on his account.
Now, let’s begin…
The Homeworld Experience for the new:
Homeworld is a 3D RTS type game that is done in real time and on xyz grids that allow full 3D gameplay (in comparison to 2D xy grid games such as Starcraft or Command and Conquer). If you are a fan of RTS games, be it the two games I have mentioned or Sins of a Solar Empire, you should definitely try this game. In this game, you start off with your “mother ship” and resource collectors, and your goal is to mine resources and research new ship types, and then build those ships to make fleets and then blow up your opponent. During this process, your enemy(s) will be doing the same thing, and there are even possible side objectives or challenges that can be undertaken to gain more resources to help further your cause. In the original games, there were already hundreds of different strategies utilized in multiplayer, but with these new side objectives and challenges it allows for even further diversity.
Factions are also extremely interesting to note: you have the factions from both original games, Homeworld 1 and 2, merged together in the same multiplayer experience. They are, to my surprise, actually quite balanced in gameplay. The game has really brought out the “rock paper scissors” aspect of what this game was originally about, but now with all 4 of the factions present there is a lot to take in and know what counters what, it can be a bit of a learning curve to memorize it all. This, in turn, adds to the diversity of strategy and player style you will see done by the AI and (especially) other human players.
And let’s not forget the campaigns. Two 16 mission journeys that put you through breath taking scenarios, all about a race of Humanoids that must make the journey back to their ancient home (Homeworld 1) and then defend it (Homeworld 2). Each campaign mission isn’t your standard “here you are, go blow up that person” and offer varieties of gameplay, such as in Homeworld 1 there is a mission where you can only use strike craft to complete your objective, or you have three minutes to destroy a massive ship that will ram right into your mothership if it is not taken out. Homeworld 2 offers the same mission diversity, and even gives you unique ships to fight and use throughout the campaign.  On top of that, the research method through both campaigns makes ships limited to specific types as you unlock more and more by progressing through the campaign, which allows players to get used to every single ship type and see their strengths and weaknesses, making the campaign not only fun and interesting, but all in all can be boiled down to a giant tutorial of how every single thing in Homeworld works.
On a final note, if you ever get bored with the remastered game, I highly recommend playing Homeworld 1 Classic, it features the original UI and game mechanics such as no unit cap in games that can be very fun to experiment with.
Seriously, if you Love RTS or space games and have not picked this title up yet, I seriously recommend you do so. It isn’t perfect, but I assure you that you are not only getting what your money ‘s worth but also are going to really enjoy it!
From the eyes of a Homeworld 1 Vet:
This section of the review focuses on the negative aspects and what has “survived” from the homeworld 1 game.
I think the biggest thing that irks me about the remastered Homeworld 1 is that they moved it to the Homeworld 2 user interface and model. In doing so they had to can a lot of Homeworld 1’s key features that made it stand out from its 2nd game, and now everyone I have talked to who preferred 1 over 2 has agreed with me that Homeworld 1 remastered just seems to be a decently gone mod for Homeworld 2.
The following is a list of features that are not in the remastered from Homeworld 1:
-Refueling: your strike craft can go anywhere infinitely without being tethered to anything, allowing them to operate in the game independently and much more of a threat to areas such as your resource operation.
-Harvesting:  in the first game, your harvesters flew around the asteroid and made them shrink as they collected resources (as well as dust clouds could be harvested). Here in remastered, they must dock with the asteroid to extract resources because of HW2’s
-Repair: ships have to dock with other ships to repair them. While this isn’t a change for strike craft, frigates, capital ships, and resource collectors could be repaired at a range in Homeworld 1
-The unit cap can’t be turned off in Multiplayer. This takes out a big chunk of what made some of the craziest HW battles that crazy (we’re talking hundreds of strike craft per person duking it out for superiority in a 6 person game)
Also, formations are a little annoying, and if you don’t believe me, I want you to go onto Homeworld 1 classic, build 9 ships, and put them into wall formation. You’ll get a nice 3x3 2d wall of the ships in a nice and orderly fashion. Do the same in HW1 remastered and you’ll get this weird cross thing with random gaps, and adding more ships to it just seems to make the cross bigger. Tactics are also screwed up with formations, and ships in specific tactics won’t always behave the same in formations the same ways that you might remember it from the Classic game. There is a new learning curve here (or bugs) that do need some attention whether you like it or not. Ships also have a tendency to partially break formation while moving (especially sphere), and on a small side note, sphere formationing ships and telling them to guard something won’t automatically make them form a sphere around the guarded ship. Again, this creates a small learning curve for the vets.
And we will complain about it, but it’s Homeworld, and we will still play it and eventually get used to it.

This game is just absolutely incredible. To begin, though, it's worth pointing out that this isn't a game for everyone: in particular, if you have no interest in narrative-focused games then don't bother playing Enslaved. The gameplay is enjoyable, sure; clambering around the gorgeous environments is fun, and the combat is solid (if a bit repetitive). The focus for Enslaved, however, is definitely, without a doubt, on the story it tells, the feelings it provokes, and the experience that it leaves with the player.
It would be easy to say that the game isn't breaking any new ground here, since it's an adaption of Journey to the West, but the writers took the building blocks of that familiar story, placed them in a completely different setting, and created something both fun and compelling. Aside from the very end, there are no surprises in the plot as everything is clearly foreshadowed; if anything, though, this just increased the impact of certain scenes, as the game builds up feelings of excitement, anticipation, or dread.
To me, this is the key to Enslaved's success: every aspect of the game is crafted almost perfectly to evoke these strong emotional responses, from the music to the writing to the visuals (especially the excellent mo-cap for facial expressions, which adds a whole lot to the delivery of each character's lines). By the time the game ended, it really, truly felt like a long journey, and to me that's the most satisfying emotion after completing a game--even with its disjointed environments and simple, text-based transitions (a la "two weeks later", etc), it still conveyed all the feelings one would expect with a subtitle like "Odyssey to the West."
While the gameplay isn't the focus for Enslaved, though, it's still very much enjoyable. The combat felt a bit simple, and there were a few too many fights that were a little bit too long, but fighting has a really satisfying, visceral feel to it. The boss battles perfectly encapsulate both the positives and the negatives of combat: they're exciting and well-crafted, but they take a bit too long to beat and a couple fights are recurring and get a bit boring. About two-thirds of the way through the game, I was starting to get sick of the regular encounters with enemies, but it obviously wasn't enough to dissuade me from the game entirely. The platforming, while a bit simplistic in nature, never got old to me; the puzzles are solid if not spectacular, and the collectibles are a nice diversion without taking away too much of the focus from the rest of the game (Alan Wake really suffered from this).
It bears repeating, however, that Enslaved is first and foremost a narrative-focused game. It's a fantastic choice for those who enjoy video games as a storytelling medium, as it provides an incredible experience to the player. It's not as fully realized as something like Spec Ops: The Line--where every single aspect of the game contributed to its narrative--but Enslaved does an excellent job of combining a great story and fun gameplay into a single package.
Also, if you played and enjoyed it on a console, it is absolutely worth picking up on PC; it looks and runs very well, and it deserves to be seen at 1080p+/60FPS.

As a fan of the Total War series since the original Rome installment, i would grade the overall game as a 9.5 on a scale of 1- 10.  If you are new to the total war series, the game will be frustrating initially until you grasp concepts of faction traits, upkeep, public order, and specialized settlement construction.  For those who have play a Total War game before, you will have a lot of fun with the tweaks that have been made to provide greater detail and allow for greater flexibility in achieving your aims however you see fit (military, through agents, etc.).  The grand campaign is great, especially if you have all free and dlc factions.  The additional campaigns (caesar/gaul, hannibal/gates, imperator augustus) are entertaining and challenging, but subsequent playthroughs were broadly similar.  One contribution that I would like to make for anyone considering the purchase of the Wrath of Sparta campaign is to not be swayed by the negative reviews.  Aside from the grand campaign, I have found the Wrath of Sparta to be very enjoyable with elements from the first game such as unit conscription across multiple turns.  I went and added steam funds to my wallet before reading the reviews and after redeeming the funds, decided not to purchase the Wrath of Sparta because of the poor feedback i saw from the community.  A friend of mine sent me the dlc anyway, and I have played it constantly since.  For anyone who likes real time strategy games, previous games in the Total War series, or is a fan of history or a specific time period covered by an installment - I would highly recommend any of the Total War games.  This game would have been rated a 10 for me had the initial tweaks required by numerous patches been addressed/resolved prior to release AND while I am aware that there are 100s of different units in the game - I would like to have seen more diversity within each type of culture.  For instance - pretty much every Hellenic faction (excluding Successor Kingdoms, some Black Sea Colonies) has 2 or 3 high quality melee/spear units (generally being named some variation of 'hoplite'), has 4 cavalry units which are weak comparatively, and has solid but basic archery units.  The ships are essentially the same for all factions.
Overall, you cant go wrong.  At the very least, I can guarantee anyone who buys this game that they will definitely get their moneys worth.

ESO isn't your typical MMO. It has a great depth with classes and races and allows for you to not be controlled to be one cerain play-style. You arn't really restricted to what armor or weapons you can equip for your class and arn't restricted to how you play for your class. You could be a templar and be a tank a healer or a DPS. Though some classes are better for certain things there isn't much retriction. There is a huge gathering sytem and crafting system in the game which allows for some exciting playtime. It feels nice to create yourself a full suit of armor upgrading it, then enchanting it. You get to feel a real sense of power. The lower level armor sets don't look the best, but the higher tier armor sets can look awesome. The aesthetics of the spells can be exciting and the looks of some of the effects can be great. The world alone is full of detail and some mobs can look dull while others can be menacing. The PVP in this game is challenging and competitive which requires teamwork and skill. The PVE is exciting, difficult, and rewarding. ESO is also NOT pay to win. The in game shop only has cosmetics costumes, mounts, and pets. However you can use ESO plus which grants you in game perks for 15$ every month, but overall in regards to money the game is buy to play with and optional in game subscription which grants perks and an cosmetic in game shop.
Overall ESO is a great MMO, I would definately put it up there in regards to the top MMOs.

I've been exploring FUSE a lot as a source for characters for a UE4 game I'm trying to develop. I had a  month of the "indie pack" (not on steam, but through their subscription) and successfully got a FUSE character moving around in the UE4 environment.
FUSE is unique in that it's essentially middleware that's trying to do the jobs of 5 people in a team that usually consists of 10, so it won't be able to do everything, and doesn't claim to. It'll be able to make awesome looking characters that are rigged for very cheap, and on their site, there are animations you can buy. Or, because the characters are rigged, you can animate them on their own.
Will FUSE characters be able to immediately drop into (name of program)? Probably not. They might need some coaxing. You might have to get really into (said program) and learn what it is that makes it work... but this is a good thing.
For UE4, a hang up was on the skeleton and the material quality. For months, I was going on their forums and freaking out about how a UE4 skeleton download option would be great, or how sometimes the materials didn't come through looking the best - because UE4 didn't naturally know how to handle some of the FUSE character's files. Well, after months of awesome awesome customer support on thier forums -  they came through with that skeleton. Plus, not that it's their job to fix things in a totally different program for me, but they're planning an update for the UE4 materials.
I'm a believer. These guys are keeping pace with the bigger game engines and are inching closer and closer to that "dream product" you want it to be. They've bitten off a lot, but they're delivering, and i'm very excited to see where this goes - and to use it in my game.This is a tool, and an awesome one, but just don't expect it to go ahead and make your game for you!  That's your job!

This game is an absolute masterpiece.
It's not that often when an arcade action game comes out that just feels so perfect.
I would write a long review but if you even remotely like arcade games/action games/shoot em ups/bullet hell style games then you will VERY LIKELY enjoy this game greatly.
And of course, if you enjoyed the first Bleed (which is on sale for 2 dollars at the moment, just buy it if you haven't played the first one yet) you will certainly enjoy Bleed 2.
The quote from Hardcore Gamer pretty much describes my feelings of the game accurately in a few words: "Side scrolling action perfected.”

After playing Bleed to completion nearly once a year, I knew that I had to pick up Bleed 2 at release. And I can proudly say that the sequel was worth the wait.
First off, the combat. Although it doesnt have quite as many weapons as the original Bleed, it makes up for it due to the versatility of the weapons themselves. The default Blade+Pistol combo allows for the action to focus a lot more on reflecting attacks, a feature that I personally thought was underdeveloped in the original. Also, now that you can have more than 2 weapons on your equip wheel, you'll be able to get to your favorite weapons faster than going into the menu, going to weapons, and swapping out one of the slots for it like you had to do in the original bleed.
Next, the level design. The levels in Bleed 2 are more of a segway towards your next miniboss/boss, compared to the majority of the experience like in the original. Although it allows for most of the time to be spent fighting bosses and understanding new patterns, I think that the stages could have had more obstacles. For example, one of my favorite non-boss moments from the original Bleed was the beginning of the Dragon stage, where you had to quickly dash through mini platforming-puzzles before it moved down to the next area. Meanwhile, in Bleed 2, none of the stage hazards were nearly as challenging as the Dragon one. Also, I miss the occasional foreshadowing of what each boss would be (Gibby and Stu hopping around in the background, etc.)
Now, for the most prevalent aspect of the game, the boss fights. Due to them being the new focus of the game instead of the levels, I was able to enjoy the new mechanics used by the bosses. Compared to the original Bleed, the boss fights are much more interactive, as there are many more options on how you can dodge/conter attacks.
Lastly, the replayability. Although the game is very short (1 hour, 1:10 first playthrough), the post game unlocks will keep you coming back until you've gotten them all, as they allow for new playstyles and challenges compared to the base experience.
Overall, I would reccomend that you play Bleed 2. Even though the levels aren't as challenging, the boss fights and the refined mechanics make the experience more focused and unique. :wrynhappy:

I played entirely too much of the original Bleed when it came out on the Xbox Live Indie Market.  I suspect I will be playing entirely too much of Bleed 2 as well.
For those that aren't familiar, Bleed 2 is a run and gun action game, not so dissimilar from old arcade titles from the 16/32-bit days of video games.  You play as Wryn, a woman with the ability to dash multiple times in mid-air, deflect projectiles with a katana, shoot a never ending stream of bullets, and slow down time.
Bleed 2's story mode is a direct continuation of the original.  It's a stage based campaign with very focused, linear levels. While it lacks the humorous twist of the original, and has less input from our heroine, it's still a fun and humorous trip that goes for roughly an hour.  This game removes the ability to spend points to level Wryn up, but does give you new weapons and types of dashes to use whenever you beat one of the difficulty levels.  Personally, I like this decision as it removes the incentive to repeat stages for the express purpose of grinding, and can instead be designed around a specific amount of HP and "slow down time" meter.
The overall presentation is drastically improved over the original.  The colors are bold and make it easy to pick out what's a threat to you and what isn't, the animation looks very good, and the music is pretty solid.  The set pieces and environments are well done too.  I would also like to mention a couple of very helpful visual cues added to this game.  One is that any projectile/object you can deflect glows Wryn's color.  So if the object is purple you can deflect it, which takes all of the guess work out of defending with the katana.  Another nice addition is that when you've used up all of your airdashes, Wryn's boots leave a puff of smoke instead of the usual trail, making it easier to keep tabs on when you need to touch the ground again.
If you played the original you'll see some familiar faces, sections of levels, and enemy patterns, but it's not so much that it feels like a rehash.  Each encounter has enough content added onto it that they still feel fresh.  There were even a few moments where I found myself getting hit by attacks simply because I assumed that they would follow the same pattern as the original.  There's definitely plenty of new stuff to warrant a revisit from fans of the original, even if it does sometimes feel a bit too familiar.
Much like the original, increasing the difficulty expands what the enemies can do.  This is something I'm pretty happy about as many games simply crank up enemy HP and the amount of damage you take.  Going from Normal to Hard still gives you good reasons to stay on your toes and keep an eye out for new attacks which help keep things interesting.
Arcade mode also returns, allowing you to take a straight shot through the entire game in one go cut scenes and continues excluded.  One new addition to Arcade mode are health pickups.  In the original, you had the one health bar for all of Arcade mode so it's nice to be able to refuel between stages.  What is especially smart about this addition is that the extra health is usually slightly out of the way, thus adding to your time, and it resets your Style meter.  So the more casual player can get a breather, and those aiming for the fastest times and highest scores still have some risk/reward to contend with.
The incredibly silly Challenge mode is back as well.  This mode lets you hop into an enclosed arena and fight up to three bosses... all at the same time.  Is it reasonable? Not at all, but it's a fun "what if" style mode that's definitely worth trying.
Bleed 2 is a fantastic little game.  It may be short, but it also never over stays its welcome or feels like it has any filler.  It looks good, sounds good, plays great, and has plenty of replay value for those that enjoy what it has to offer.  If you're a fan of old-timey run and gun 2D shooters, I highly recommend it.
- Update:
So it's been a couple of months and I haven't played it as much as I thought I would, but I stand by my recommendation.

Best multiplayer horror survival experience I've ever had!
The game doesn't go easy on you, not at all, and that's something really impressive. I won't make a description of the game like the one you see on the store page.
In either of the two game modes, survival and objective, your success lays in your skills, resource management, and, more or less, in your team's cooperation.
No More Room in Hell has a perfectly realistic approach on survival, and not the traditional horror survival, where you can only hide and run from monsters and try to find a way out of the surrounding madness. Well, sure, in the objective mode, you can try to complete all the objectives, call for help and get to the extraction point, but, in most of the maps, you can't do that without friends who can carve a way through the hordes of zombies, and even then, if you run blindly to the objective and leave everyone behind, you'll just end up surrounded, and all the zombies that you've passed by will come to bite you. You'll end up being a nuisance if you (somehow manage to get past the hordes of zombies following you and) go back to the rest and ask them for pills to slow down the infection and for bandages to stop the bleeding. You can't just stand there and kill zombies mindlessly, either; after you use up all of you ammor, they'll spawn faster than you can kill them with a melee. It's always best to stay with your fellow survivors and progress smoothly, know when you have to slay zombies and how many of them, so that none of your team -INCLUDING YOURSELF- will get caught by them. This applies when you're the only one standing, too.
The game is not all about skill and teamwork. If you get hit or bitten, you won't die, unless you're out of health. Unless you let yourself carried by the others as if you were a little crybaby or RNG God blesses you with good weapons, ammo and fortunate zombie spawns (little to no runners), which is very unlikely to happen, you'll find yourself worrying about your health. If you get hit by a zombie, you won't necessarily die, but you HP will certainly go down, and you might get an injury or an infection. When your HP is dangerously low and you become less and less able to distinguish colors, you'd better find yourself an HP crate, or a first aid kit, and be ready for a lengthy surgery. Injuries will slowly drain you HP untill you either die or bandage yourself up to stop the bleeding(You can stop it with a first aid kit as well). Infections are the nastiest ones. When you get infected your sight quickly starts to blur out, and when everything turns black, you're one of them. The worst part is that 99% of the time you won't be able to stop the infection unless you die and respawn. You can, however, to use Phalanx pills to slow down the infection. Once you use them, you get your sight back and you can breathe freely for a couple of minutes. The only way to actually cure an infection is by using the super rare Gene Therapy. This gene therapy is a one-time vaccine that can cure the infection. The problem is, it's so rare that most of the time it won't even appear in the map that you're playing. Only some maps have this syringe and it normally spawns once in the whole map. It can also drop from supply crates in Survival mode, with a very low chance. If you lay your hands on this piece of gold, it can be you ace in the hole. Most team mates would feel the urge to kill you if they noticed a syringe in you hand, though.
So yeah, No More Room in Hell is a tough game, where you constantly have to prove your skills in order to kill more than a couple of zombies and not die at the hand of a mere walker, manage your gun's ammo, which can't really be found around every corner and finally, have a team that can -more or less- make up for each individual's mistakes or lack of skill, so that -more or less- at least some of you can make it to the extraction point, and hell, by "team", I mean real people, and not everyone is reliable and cooperating, provided that they can even understand what you're saying. It's not just the zombies and RNG that put you in all kinds of situations, it's also the playerbase. Whether you believe that you have to help your team or carry by yourself in a group where the others are either dead or for himself, you have to adapt to the requirements in order to be called a survivor. And this is a game, so you can retry if u fail; you're human, and you'll ultimately adapt to game, the map, the mission and your team, and from a newb with 10/2 you will become a veteran who can score 200/0 and have some of those achievements that less than 1% of the players have obtained.

After playing a few hours I would say there is a fun game here, but...
Aiming sucks, you may get stuck on a helicopter jumping out of it before it explodes almost every time. The stutter is extremely frustrating. The game may play well for a while and then goes into fits. I said there was lots of content, well... The towns are mostly empty with a few pointless npc's walking around aimlessly. You are limited in what you can do, other than blow stuff up, but it really leaves out a lot of options to cause a ruckus in different ways. You can't crouch or use cover and you move slow. Very underwhelming. There are TONS of posts in the Just Cause forums covering great ideas for what they could of done. Hopefully in the next game.
I was kind of having fun but I cannot recommend this game as it just doesn't feel finished, tested or properly optimized. Mad Max was in a wasteland so I understand the lack of content, but was still impressed with how much you could find. Just Cause is not a wasteland and should be a full environment where you can do more than float around and blow stuff up. I realize that is the premise but it gets redundant. With the devs lack of response to players performance complaints from day one (with all types of systems) and, from what I have seen, no input in the forums or implementation to fix performance, even having some fun sometimes and getting hours of play out it, I can't say I support this kind of development. What a game! (When it works...) I have to say I'm surprised by EIDOS (don't know the developer very well). When you compare this game's stability to either of the two Tomb Raiders (2013, 2016) there is a laughable void between them. The bugs I am finding are really bizarre: Occassionally, my XBOX ONE controller just disconnects from the receiver (I found out that the receiver itself was disconnected by the game I can only assume); When the controller doesn't disconnect The video driver will freeze. This is not a driver issue but some weird bug involving all three (game, GFX driver, XBOX driver); and of course, the infamous memory bleed bug.
Having said all that, let's look at the possitives:
Massive open world to play with. Great missions and a great fun concept (it's like GTA if your characters had a sling shot attached to their arm and a parachute that opens and close by itself). Massive improvement over the last game (though that is far more stable). The rendoring is beautiful and the gameplay is easy to get used to. The side missions are extensive and the rewards are worth one doing them (for once in a game).
Bottom line. If this game was stable I would recommend it and then some. Unfortunately the bugs, for the moment, cast a huge shadow over the game itself. Fingers crossed that they will have a good working patch soon. Then I will change my recommendation.

I cannot recommend buying into this game as it currently stands in its unfinished form. Here's why...
I bought Pool Nation FX in its early stages of development because of the addition of a "Snooker" game. The developers (Cherry Pop Games) were very keen to turn this into a serious, well-made snooker game and progress was originally good with lots of support from people wanting a great snooker game. CPG decided to take all the suggestions from the PC players and put them into a "new" paid-for version of the game called "Snooker Nation Championship" which I bought into with hope and excitement. The graphics were great but the old bugs, issues and problems from PNFX were still present along with some new seriously bad sound issues __ so basically a cut and paste job from PNFX to SNC.
However since promises of updates the develpment of this game has stalled completely with no feedback from CPG leaving the game unfinished and unplayable.
In the meantime CPG have realeased a new virtual pool game, which seems to be successful and are working on a virtual hockey game now too. To add insult to injury they have relased an "update" of SNC on the X-box while we, the PC punters are still waiting...
So for many months now I have bought into a belief that this snooker game is going to be great while all along playing a half-hearted botched, unenjoyable, bugged game with no real improvent on the PC to date.
Cherry Pop Games, to date, simply cannot be trusted.

I am really glad I got this during the winter sale, it's a pretty expansive game and more then worth the $10 I paid but not the $60 regular price.  I have a few specific complaints but I think together they make the game feel a bit shallow compared to shogun 2 and the non tw games I play.
The most dissapointing things to me;
The biggest thing is the agents, they all basically do the same things (which really bothers me for some reason, they all have unique aspects but it's not big) and if you try to fight a handful of factions an agent-apocalypse is possible, where they just swarm you and disrupt your armies and cities, while your own agents fail to stop them and usually end up dying so now you have unleveled agents trying to stop a horde of level 5+ agents....
The army system, it's more strategic but annoying, since you can't just recruit levies to take care of unrest, gotta have a general there for some reason, and with 1 tpy this eats up up to half your generals life (usually not that much but still at least 10 years for any big conquerors).  This also leads to the generals not really gaining any meaning before they die.
The province system; great idea bad implementation, makes things more strategic and the recruiting system is better but it really doesn't extend past that and feels really shallow, especially when some regions are group seemingly at random and people are upset that the city 400+ miles away now has a fishing dock.
The political system is still a bit borked in EE, for example in my roman game, I see I have a chance for civil war, so I adopt every general I can, promote everyone to their max rank, and spread rumors about the un-adoptable generals.   SO now im both consuls, the only provincial governor, and have at least 1 person at every rank, basically in charge of the roman government, as well as controlling 90% of the army, except I net lost influence so people are no longer threatened by me and theres 0 chance of a civil war.
However, this is a huge game with lots of potential to have fun, it runs well and I haven't noticed any real bugs.  The things above can be annoying but they don't destroy the game.

Do you remember the first time when you played
? And while you were running through a prolonged and almost infinite hill, pushing the jump button you realized that now Mario could fly. And then, you were amazed with this magic sense of discovery while you explore a vastness sea of pixelated clouds. Creating the magic illusion of exploring a new world in which every single element is full of novelty, an explosion of the senses.
Our gaming memories are full of this accomplished moments of realization. Like the first enemy that you glitch in
. The first kiss you give in Yoshirou Kimura’s cult classic
. Or when you rewinded the time in
to reach an unattainable floating plattform for the first time.
has one of these memorable and most captivating single moments experienced in recent videogames. In the form of the first time that you keep pushed the action button, and releasing it you can see how an explosion of visible and corporeal sound waves helps to materialize a previously occult and cryptic hidden dimension. With a plethora of abstract and evocative geometrical forms dazzling our eyes with pure joy. An intense array of emotions are concentrated in this mere act of pushing a single button. As an expression of why the videogames are considered art.
In its first hours, this magic sense of realization never ceases. An absorbing sensation that creates an oppressive feeling in the player, while he’s surrounded by invisible menaces laying in the shadows. An universe where the most feared ghosts plaguing our subconscious are waiting for us surrounded by darkness. Waiting to become corporeal with the mere stimulus of a sound.
We can only figure the world that lies beneath
via the materialization of sounds, this fragmented instant of time when a a wave elongates making tangible a mysterious and almost cryptic alternative reality that lives isolated in a corner of our memories, close to our childhood traumas. Playing
is like doing a unconscious journey through our fears and hopes, only using our imagination in a synesthetic way, associating sounds and its geometrical effects with inner terrors. And all of these sound elements are augmented by one of the most cohesive artistic designs seen in a videogame, clearly influenced by the paintings of Rothko in its constant use of the black and red colors.
Its level structure is not so distant of a stealth game, where we need to generate geometrical forms thorough sounds to confuse our captors. With a perfect difficulty curve that adds new elements and functions at a very slow pace. The 20 first levels serves as a tutorial, and from 20 onwards, you should prepare to die a lot. It’s like an even more minimalist approach to the VR missions seen in the first
. Also,
shows its smart design nature by using the name of each level as an evocative clue to resolve its main obstacle. A demonstration of the love and care that its creators have put in the development process.
Maybe
can be seen as a small game. But it’s a game in which every single element has been created with an ambitious and creative approach. A short but extremely polished experience that tries to not saturate the player with irrelevant content. Over the years and with the consequent saturation of the gaming market, I appreciate games that really try to be small but memorable journeys. Significative creations in gaming history that we will never forget.
Note that
isn’t the first experiment created in the videogame medium to recreate the experience of being a blind person. Previously, the japanese punk videogame designer idol Kenji Eno created
for Sega Saturn. A game that was designed with blind people in mind, using only sounds and with not a single image. In his next game, Kenji Eno will use the sound as a design fundamental again, with the release of
. A survival horror with invisible enemies, that only can be detected by using a sound radar.
Sadly, Kenji Eno passed away in 2013. But I’m sure that if he lived today, he would become fascinated with
.

text:
This experience will stay with you forever.
As the blurb suggests, Dark Echo sees you utilising sound to enable you to visualise your surroundings. The sounds you create ricochet around you in the form of coloured lines. You goal, naturally, is to escape the darkness, and escape whatever the hell is in it with you.
I found the gameplay enjoyable overall. The difficulty curve is just right - with a bit of persistence and some careful planning, navigating the darkness can be fun, sometimes scary, but achieveable for everyone. Controls consist of basic movement, throwing stones for decoys, clapping your hands (with various degrees of strength, depending how long you hold the button down for), and stealth. And you'll probably be using stealth quite a bit.
You have your white, regular soundwaves for normal surfaces, yellow for switches. But the real fun starts with blue and red soundwaves. Blue is for water, which is something you'll want to avoid on account of it being so noisy, and red you'll also want to avoid, on account of it being able to kill you at a touch.
And oh my god, if you die. The first time I died I almost leapt a full metre out of my chair. The death scream is perfect. In fact, most all the sounds are done to perfection. From your echoing footsteps to the sound your hands clapping together, it is very well done.
Dark Echo really is a worthy addition to any gamer's library. While it lacks a story of any sort, it does do everything else right, giving us a new take on fear, exploration and stealth. Even if it doesn't sound like fun to you (I don't imagine how this could be) get this game and give it a try. Price alone is reason enough.

I went in wanting to enjoy a story, and I came out with more than I expected. I grew attached to the characters, the world, and was left with a memory of the experience and a bit of an open future to ponder on for the characters and the world they were in. The main things that shine through for me were the acting, characters, and storytelling elements, they are what I was looking for. The combat and traveling elements within the game were entertaining, watching Monkey climb around and do a great deal of acrobatic moves was cool, but if you are expecting the ability to miss a ledge or not make a jump based on your skill as a game player you should look elsewhere. Most of the action elements are there to help allow time for dialog between the two main characters, allow you to invest a bit of time and thought in them to grow attached to them in a sense, and as a way to get from point A to point B while drawing connections to the actual storyline. All of this adds up to an ending where you are attached to the main characters and are supposed to care about their story and survival. It doesn't seem to be getting a sequal due to low sales by the developers standpoint, but that doesn't matter because the story is complete in it's own rite.
I played through the main story and will play through the Pigsy DLC, but may or may not come back to it to play through the story an additional time. I know I would enjoy it again, much like rereading a good book, but since there are other books on my shelf I will probably move on...who's to say though that I may not come back to it again one day, as I feel invested in the characters, and may want to relive the experience again.

I've owned this game since June of 2014 and played for at least 80-100 hours before it was released on Steam.
There's a free demo available on the website (and on Steam, theres a button on the right hand side) that you can check out to see how it suits you. A few minutes into it, I already knew I'd want to get this game:
You're building conveyor belts, robot arms, mining drills and other things in various ways to produce items and manage your resources.
And you can put a lot of thought into figuring out the best layout for your production lines, or just build it the way it's looking the most beautiful to you. Either way, you're constantly learning about new aspects to consider when expanding.
The devs are a shining example of how Early Access has to be done. There are weekly blogposts from the team ("Factorio Friday Facts") in which they explain what they've been up to, talk about programming problems they solved and are very transparent about their plans.
Whenever the community had a mixed opinion on a something the team was working on, they would revise their plans, taking into account what feedback they had received. Generally, you'll find the devs are trying to get feedback to most things they do, and you can find them replying on the forums regularly. They seem willing (and personally so) to make the game the best it can be.
It may take a while between big updates for the game to release, even a few months. After a major update, there are usually weekly updates with fixes and small additions. Possibly, the update schedule will be different after the Steam release though. Thanks to this cycle, the game is pretty stable.
I plan to play it some more when it comes out of Early Access, but as I mentioned, you can easily spend tens of hours in the game without having done everything that's possible. Many have played for hundreds or possibly thousands of hours.
Get it now if you want to play it already - it's content rich and mostly very polished - or if you just feel you want to support these devs.
Edit: I've nominated the game for the "I Thought This Game Was Cool Before It Won An Award" Award during the 2016 Autumn Sale. And again in 2017 for a Custom award.
Because honestly, it just as much deserves the "Just 5 More Minutes" and custom "Early Acces that's actually playable and fun" Awards. Too bad you seemingly can't nominate the same game multiple times.

I downvote this game not because it's BAD; but because there are some severe problems that take this game from enjoyable to horribly frustrating over the course of its needlessly long run time. It's decently creepy, but suffers from a lack of narrative focus, bland environment, and it runs out of steam about 2/3 of the way through, the last 1/3 coming off as heavy padding.
GAMEPLAY: standard FPS control scheme. You wander around the ship seeking various objectives, with the alien, android, or other humans serving as obstacles. Ripley has very low health, and the alien will insta kill if you're caught in its grasp. In other games this might be an issue, but here it works, given that the focus is avoiding enemies via stealth. Noise attracts enemies, so you will primarily be sneaking around and hiding. To aid with your task, you have a motion sensor, which is pretty fun and intuitive to use. It doesn't tell you exactly where the enemy is in relation to the map, only if it's in the direction you're facing, how close, and if it's above/below you (based on the size of the dot and its location on the screen).
Your other big item is your tuner, used to bypass security systems. It's reminiscent of Bioshock's hacking system, but is much less interesting; it essentially amounts to "match the pictures with a timer", which is not only easy, but jars a bit, as it seems like a pretty weak security system, unbefitting of a futuristic spacecraft. There are other such puzzles, including "match the numbers" and "press E stop the moving icon within a specified area", to the same effect.
Furthermore, there's a crafting system to create weapons and distraction tools (like molotov cocktails and noisemakers). These can be upgraded with blueprints, but I only found a few of the tools useful; furthermore, the crafting feels a little half-baked, as you will find many more components than you'll need. There isn't really a sense of urgency in inventory management as there is in other horror titles, something this game could have used a bit more of.
Other items include blow torches (for opening metal panels), a maintenance jack (for operating machinery and opening doors), and a flashlight.
Perhaps the biggest issue with the gameplay - or lack thereof - are the non-interactive moments. Almost every action has a short, non-interactive section. Press E to watch Ripley type something into a computer. Press E to watch Ripley open a door, etc. It comes across as an attempt at being cinematic, but ends up being frustrating due to just how often control is taken away. In one instance, I ran into a room past a stunned enemy to retrieve an item. As Ripley stood and admired it for a few seconds, said enemy came up from behind and started attacking her, while I had no recourse, waiting for my control to resume. Now, lack of control in horror is an important thing; but this is completely the wrong way to go about it. It's tedious at best, outright bad design in some instances.
VISUALS: The game looks great. Character models are especially good; they're well-detailed with bags under their eyes, visible pores, etc. The rest is equally good; early in the game, I actually recoiled at a fireball that spews from a broken fuel pipe.
Unfortunately, the great visuals are let down by the setting. I'm not sure why the ship has to consist of 85% bland metal corridors with piping and wiring along the ceiling, but it doesn't make for exciting atmosphere - especially when the environments are so dark. Darkness is good in horror games; but with the limited light we have, we should have something to look at besides graffiti and trash on the floor. When I think of this game, I recall a samey, grey-green colour scheme that makes all of the areas blend together.
AUDIO: Excellent as well - the highlight of this game. The voice acting is great, with Ripley in particular having an excellent performance. Her voice trembles as she whispers in the presence of the alien, and screams in breathless rage after having been nearly killed. The supporting cast and audio files are similarly well acted, as are the enemies. The alien's screech upon seeing Ripley quickly becomes something to fear, as with the calm, English-accented admonishments of the androids. Music isn't overly relied upon, but nothing overly noteworthy when it appears. Aside from being a nice aesthetic touch, the audio is quite an important aspect of the game - you will quickly learn to hear the beeping of the motion sensor to identify the presence of enemies, and the direction of the thumps in the vents that the alien is climbing in.
HORROR: Running and hiding from the alien and the andrioids is very tense and creepy, given that you are virtually defenceless...for the first portion of the game. It can sometimes give way to tediousness, but for the most part, planning your route around the enemies is quite engrossing. Unfortunately, the player isn't given much respite from the enemies, almost always evading either the alien or the androids. This game could have greatly benefited from the odd chapter with few to no enemies, perhaps with human enemies as an obstacle (as they aren't encountered much), or some more challenging puzzles. Give the player time to miss the primary fear factors - let them become accustomed to running unmolested, collecting items, feeling in control of things - before ripping the rug out from under them.
The horror is especially reduced around the 1/2 to 2/3 mark, where the player is given a flamethrower. On the one hand, it feels like they've earned it - but on the other, it makes scaring off the alien far too easy. And once the fear factor of the alien is reduced, the rest of the game quickly becomes tedious.
STORY/PACING: The story is present, but let down by the game's biggest problem: the pacing. The player is introduced to Ripley's character and motivations for exploring the ship, and then sent off to perform miscelanous tasks. Go to talk to  this person. But the elevator's out! Find another way around. But the power's out! Turn it back on. And once you get there, all you get is another upgrade to use in a bland, sparesely decorated area you've already visited. When the few important plot points occur, it feels like they're added to further pad the game. Similar titles get by with little story - Amnesia: The Dark Descent comes to mind - but that game is much shorter. This game has 18 chapters; by chapter 12, I was ready to wrap it up. But the game continues on, having you visit the same areas, performing the same tasks, stalked by the same creature. At one point, a character sacrificed themselves to aid Ripley, but the drama fell completely flat because I had no memory of who this character was. There is little reminder of what's keeping the character going, aside from "escape the ship". More immersive games have a central, driving goal the the player is reminded of. Silent Hill, for example, reminds the player in various ways that the end goal is to find Harry's daughter in the midst of other secondary objectives. This game has Ripley running errands on a spaceship, from which we can assume she'll escape eventually.
Would I recommend this game? It's hard to say. On the one hand, I enjoyed the tension, pacing and scares of the first half of the game. On the other, it wears out its welcome, becoming tedious towards the end, and doesn't do much to innovate. I would recommend a game like Amnesia: The Dark Descent or Outlast before Alien: Isolation. Perhaps if those haven't satisfied your itch, give this one a try.

First of all - almost all the negative reviews I see here are wildly misinformed! You should know what you're getting with this software (unlimited free character models with textures - and 2 free rigs a week) - and it is an ENORMOUS time and money saver for those who need custom character models on a budget.
Let me clear a couple things up:
1. You can ABSOLUTELY export your characters as OBJ files and load them in anywhere
2. If you want to rig/skin your characters for animation you upload them to Mixamo - and get 2 free per week.
3. Mixamo also has free animation packs that can be downloaded to get you character up and running in-engine
All claims to the contrary are just wrong. So where are there additional charges:
1. If you need MORE than 2 rigs a week
2. If you want to purchase their custom animations
Now here's one thing to bear in mind: if all you do is export one unrigged character mesh (with textures) as an OBJ file - you've paid for the cost of this software EASILY. Any decent character modeller will charge many times that for just the model. If you add in a rig/skin and free animations you could pay for this software 30 times with one character.
The Fuse models in general look very good - nice topology and high-res textures. Pretty nice editing tools as well. Easy to work in the app, and updates have been consistently high quality. Mixamo also listens very closely to their userbase and is extremely gracious about feedback.
Now is Fuse perfect - no... it's still in development. The major weaknesses are in variation and editing. Specifically, it still needs  ton of additional content: clothing, hair, accessories, etc. In addition, there are some un-editable meshes (like hair) that would allow for a lot more diversity if they were editable. I also wish it was easier to get started with a basic variation of gender/age/build/ethnicity... like some macro controls before digging in and customizing. Or even better would be automatic randomization within those broader categories.
I still find it a bit difficult to get nicely-middle-aged characters (especially women). They either get too wrinkly or too pristine.
The randomization features are helpful as well, but I wish I could clamp them within a range of non-cartoonish values sometimes.
I'd also like to see native substance export - or at least more export options to match various pipelines (like various PBR).
Finally, I think Fuse is starting to suffer from prosumer-focus. Namely, you have a million nicely named sliders for adjusting parameters, but it is getting cumbersome to navigate the options. Some power-user tools (key commands and modifiers for the mouse) may need to come along soon.
Overall, this is extremely impressive software that can save you a small fortune. I can go from idea to a lip-synched and animated character in Unity within an hour.

I played the original Homeworld for days on end and hoped by the infos released, it would be a remarkable bundle of glorious HD childhood remembrance. I was wrong.
One of the main reasons I didn't really play and / or like Homeworld 2 was related to fleets. Yes, one of the main things elevating this game from other RTS was bothering me. Why? The AI didn't have a fixed fleet (size) like in HW1, but instead was composed of units perfectly cancelling out your whole fleet. You captured Frigates, Destroyers, Cruisers only to get them destroyed by counter-units spawned exactly for this ship.
In HW1 you had a unique fleet consisting of Kadeshi, Turanic and Taiidan ships mixed with your run-off-the-mill standard units. It was simply put beautiful. They kept their original paint job and most of them performed extraordinarily. You cared deeply for your units because you couldn't build new ones to replace them, because they were unique. If you built units, it was mostly supporters and / or special ships. Why? Because resources were scarce and had to be consolidated around the necessities. You used what you had carefully and many a time you had to reload a game because you lost one too many ship or one dear to you.
Then, in HW2, you had this urge to capture cool Vaygr craft like missile frigates. Boy was I proud to finally have captured a few of those. Then I harvested resources the old fashioned way and prepared a fleet to be able to counter everything I thought could be thrown at me. In the next mission I was always surprised to find the enemy being able to kill every last one of my ships at will, because his fleet strength was measured exactly by mine. This made me realize that capturing and keeping special or even more useful ships than mine was futile. I had to scrap every single one of them just to not be overrun and lose them in the next mission. After one or two missions I came to the conclusion that I had to scrap all ships excluding ship production vessels if i didn't want a mass extinction to happen. My fleet at the end and start of each mission basically was a Chinese sweat shop.
This moved me farther and farther away from caring just the tiniest bit for my fleet - because why would I? Everything was interchangeable or could be rebuilt. It was always the same. Scrap and rebuild. Scrap and rebuild. At some point I just produced ships to counter the enemy, not to have an effective fleet. The ones built faster were in higher numbers than the rest, because who gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥ right? They will be scrapped either way. I realized that this was not the type of game I was expecting a HW game to be and abandoned HW2 for good.
Now they made this gorgeous looking game and based it on the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI fleet mechanism that HW2 had. I feel betrayed because the previews don't talk about that and just blow sugar up its♥♥♥♥♥ They removed many functions like the support frigates' repair beam or group capture with salvettes. It's a nightmare of micro management wrapped in gorgeous HD graphics. I will NOT play the campaigns of either of them because it just pisses on my childhood memories of HW1. Too many things are wrong with the game and I will wait until they address it. The forums are aflame because of the same reasons.
I even bought the CE because I was so sure it would live up to the original. At the moment it's nothing more than a HW1 mod for HW2 with better graphics. The formations are broken, the launch manager is a mess, research costs money, the "z"-with-selection-rectangle functions are missing altogether, the AI fleets are dynamically generated based on your fleet.
I liked the serenity of the old HW1. You had your objective, completed it and collected resources while getting your fleet ready for the next mission. You built ships, organized groups or just watched your harvesters do their work. The new games focus more on massive battles - which are literally pre-programmed - and watch all you built up explode and scatter just to win by  a hair.
If you liked the "Transformers" movies, this one is for you. If you liked the original HW game, you should wait.

All in all, you get the gist of the original, and twice the content for fittingly twice the price, though it's nice to have the "fresh take" on old bosses be refreshed, and not brand new.
If you've played the original, Bleed 2's narrative is a touch more coherent, the graphics and audio have a nice level polish to them, the mechanics are smoother, the upgrade shop and platforming segments (essentially fluff and padding, in my opinion) have been cut and streamlined respectively, leaving you with a fast-paced and bullet-dense experience. A boon to late-game arcade mode play.
It also incentivizes co-op and parrying far more than the original with its color-coded parrying system, on top of condensing parry and fire into one action.
10/10 would recommend, with a friend.
