Bleed 2 is a game that's hard to quantify.  At its core,  it's a very solid experience.  The systems are excellently designed, the new additions (such as sword swipes occuring with trigger pulls and reflecting certain attacks) are brilliantly thought out.  I can't stress enough how well the game's control and interaction was thought out.... but it feels like, after this was perfected, the developer realized he needed a game to use it on and kinda just filled up the levels with mostly forgetable minibosses and extremely lackluster platforming.
Length & Value:  Bleed 2 is a very short game.  Very short.   It's an arcade styled title at its heart so it clocks in at around... 40 to fifty minutes for your first time (including quite a few deaths), if that?  Unless this is a game you see yourself playing repeatedly, you should wait for a sale.
Difficulty:  Honestly, Bleed 2 is a lot easier than the first game.   I wouldn't even rate it as very hard as far as the genre goes.  The minibosses in particular are painfully simple at times and they become the bulk of the gameplay (more on this later).  Big bosses however are really special and interesting to fight, it's a polished experience, but they feel like they take too much damage.  It's a fairly short affair.
Pacing: This is where Bleed 2 falls apart, at least in my eyes.  It has a massive issue with its overall pacing compared to the first game.  In Bleed 1, you would platform and shoot through a short-ish level. During this time, the boss you'd soon fight would sometimes act as a distraction or an enviromental hazard.  This lead-up really allows you to feel the Protagonist's power level as she zips around the traps, projectiles, and enemies.  The experience of the levels was a liberating one, and allowed the player to savor the (often claustrophic) duels with bosses far more.
Bleed 2, does not have this.  Instead you will have miniboss after miniboss with short, FF13-esque corridors between them.  We're talking, thorugh the first level, it's only a handful of seconds between each of the bosses and really destroys the flow of the platforming.    The level sections are also very lackluster.  Usually it's just a few floating platforms to hop between with enemies (seemingly quite a few recycled from the first game).  And then you get to the minibosses, who are pretty spongy, and lock you into a small room for a duel and stop your forward progress for a while.
It's baffling that the platforming wasn't more fully realized, especially when the game is very short as it stands.
Boss quality:   The game's Furi-esque focus on bossfights wouldn't be an issue if they were fun. They aren't.  After twenty minutes I had to take a break because of how boring it got. It's  largely just one bulet-sponge boss after another, eadch with their own little gimmick, but not a very trying one.  There's a few exceptions with stage end-bosses but even then it doesn't really offset the lesser encounter.   It would've helped if there were interesting interaciton with the enviroment, or lots of boss-stages, or transfomrations- something to increase the interactivity.  But there's not much.
All in all, the experience left me lethargic rather than empowered.  It wasn't what I had hoped out of such a long awaited sequel.  That's not to say the game is terrible, it's just... not one I'd really recommend.  Your mileage may vary.
And first negative review for the title, huh?  Comments section isn't gonna be pretty.
EDIT:  One thing I forgot to add is how weapon unlocks work.  Remember in Bleed 1 how you could buy weapons throughout your first playthrough? Not anymore. Now it's done by beating the game on (whichever) difficulty level.
So you better enjoy the dual handguns+Katana, because it's all you get for your first playthrough.

Best multiplayer horror survival experience I've ever had!
The game doesn't go easy on you, not at all, and that's something really impressive. I won't make a description of the game like the one you see on the store page.
In either of the two game modes, survival and objective, your success lays in your skills, resource management, and, more or less, in your team's cooperation.
No More Room in Hell has a perfectly realistic approach on survival, and not the traditional horror survival, where you can only hide and run from monsters and try to find a way out of the surrounding madness. Well, sure, in the objective mode, you can try to complete all the objectives, call for help and get to the extraction point, but, in most of the maps, you can't do that without friends who can carve a way through the hordes of zombies, and even then, if you run blindly to the objective and leave everyone behind, you'll just end up surrounded, and all the zombies that you've passed by will come to bite you. You'll end up being a nuisance if you (somehow manage to get past the hordes of zombies following you and) go back to the rest and ask them for pills to slow down the infection and for bandages to stop the bleeding. You can't just stand there and kill zombies mindlessly, either; after you use up all of you ammor, they'll spawn faster than you can kill them with a melee. It's always best to stay with your fellow survivors and progress smoothly, know when you have to slay zombies and how many of them, so that none of your team -INCLUDING YOURSELF- will get caught by them. This applies when you're the only one standing, too.
The game is not all about skill and teamwork. If you get hit or bitten, you won't die, unless you're out of health. Unless you let yourself carried by the others as if you were a little crybaby or RNG God blesses you with good weapons, ammo and fortunate zombie spawns (little to no runners), which is very unlikely to happen, you'll find yourself worrying about your health. If you get hit by a zombie, you won't necessarily die, but you HP will certainly go down, and you might get an injury or an infection. When your HP is dangerously low and you become less and less able to distinguish colors, you'd better find yourself an HP crate, or a first aid kit, and be ready for a lengthy surgery. Injuries will slowly drain you HP untill you either die or bandage yourself up to stop the bleeding(You can stop it with a first aid kit as well). Infections are the nastiest ones. When you get infected your sight quickly starts to blur out, and when everything turns black, you're one of them. The worst part is that 99% of the time you won't be able to stop the infection unless you die and respawn. You can, however, to use Phalanx pills to slow down the infection. Once you use them, you get your sight back and you can breathe freely for a couple of minutes. The only way to actually cure an infection is by using the super rare Gene Therapy. This gene therapy is a one-time vaccine that can cure the infection. The problem is, it's so rare that most of the time it won't even appear in the map that you're playing. Only some maps have this syringe and it normally spawns once in the whole map. It can also drop from supply crates in Survival mode, with a very low chance. If you lay your hands on this piece of gold, it can be you ace in the hole. Most team mates would feel the urge to kill you if they noticed a syringe in you hand, though.
So yeah, No More Room in Hell is a tough game, where you constantly have to prove your skills in order to kill more than a couple of zombies and not die at the hand of a mere walker, manage your gun's ammo, which can't really be found around every corner and finally, have a team that can -more or less- make up for each individual's mistakes or lack of skill, so that -more or less- at least some of you can make it to the extraction point, and hell, by "team", I mean real people, and not everyone is reliable and cooperating, provided that they can even understand what you're saying. It's not just the zombies and RNG that put you in all kinds of situations, it's also the playerbase. Whether you believe that you have to help your team or carry by yourself in a group where the others are either dead or for himself, you have to adapt to the requirements in order to be called a survivor. And this is a game, so you can retry if u fail; you're human, and you'll ultimately adapt to game, the map, the mission and your team, and from a newb with 10/2 you will become a veteran who can score 200/0 and have some of those achievements that less than 1% of the players have obtained.
Great fun, challenging, but not impossible.

I'm going to start by saying, if you haven't played any of the Dark Souls games before, DON'T.
GO FOR A WALK.  MEET A PERSON.  GET MARRIED.  HAVE CHILDREN.  GO TO SCHOOL.  GO TO WORK,  TAKE UP TENNIS.  HELL, TAKE UP SMOKING.  DO ANYTHING ELSE BEFORE YOU WASTE YOUR EXISTANCE ON THIS SERIES.
Now that that's out of the way I can say, this is one of the GREATEST AND MOST SIGNIFICENT GAMES OF THIS GENERATION.  The mix of action, and stratagy is a marriage unlike anything I've seen.  The combat gameplay is tight, the story is perfect for a videogame, in that it doesn't get in the way, and you savor every morsol of it you can get,  like I really can't compare this to anything else.  It's nuts.

I never got into dark souls, mostly because the frame rete issues were a detriment, but really the game just didn't grip me.  DS2 fixes that, with great pacing, early on.  Where it matters.  Like that very first hit of crack pipe...
But what's wrong with it?
I spent about 100 hours playing the game,  having beaten standard mode, played a bit of sunken king, and really taking my time with it, (IE dying a lot, and wasting souls on mid tier weapons) you would think that to not be a huge number of hours for one RPG, that you really enjoyed.  Heck, any final fantasy takes around 70 to finish, so what's the big deal?
Well the hours I spent playing dark souls were not like the hours I've spent playing other games.  The hours I've spent other games have been relaxing, calming experiances, whereafter I've left feeling refreshed, rested even, as though I've done something enjoyable.

I didn't find school, collage, highschool, etc to be that difficult, just a little uninteresting.  When it was difficult, it was only because I had made it so.

Well, I'm a bit stuck on level 29 right now, and given as how there are 80 levels to this game, I highly doubt I will be finishing it. However, conceptually, it is pretty cool, and in practice, the game mechanics work well.
Basically, it is pitch black with the only light coming from sound, which bounces off the walls and objects, thus illuminating your path briefly. Also, your footprints leave a trail. Sadly, the sound also serves to attract an all consuming evil, in the form of red lights. Normal sound is represented by white light, doors (and I guess treaure although I'm not exactly certain how that works) is represented by yellow, and water (the bane of your existence in this game, lol) is blue. Somewhere around level 20, you find rocks which you can throw to distract the all consuming evil, which is especially handy when you also have to cross water (which also slows your movement). Each level basically ends by finding the exit "doorway" which explodes with white light when you step into it.  Oh...and you can also move with stealth, which reduces your sound radius and helps you to sneak through that pesky all consuming evil.
There are some other nuances so far, such as needing to use rocks to break through walls, and certain levels where you cant hide from the all consuming evil and simply have to run for it. The level I am on currently, you have to cross waterways which actually push you into the awaiting evil (I guess this is the waters current).
The game does have full controller support, which is how I play it.
Anyway, I actually think this is a stellar game, and minimalistic perfection in what is essentially a unique puzzle game.
I give this game 8 muffled footsteps out of 10 with the remaining 2 betraying you to the all consuming evil, which I will simply dub as Shoggoth.

I'm gonna do something a little off. I'm gonna recommend a game I didn't personally like. How can I possibly do that? Because Alien: Isolation is designed well and doesn't do a lot of things wrong but has one major flaw that, for me at least, did end up ruining the experience. But I don't think it's fair to completely condemn a game for only one problem. I may be harsh but I'm fair.
To start off, it is a good game. The level design is a little repetitive, but since it's a moderate sized space station, that's somewhat expected and is at least realistic. The atmosphere is dreadful through out the entire length of game time, adding to many tense moments and, this is gonna sound cheesy, heart pounding sequences. The game mechanics are varied enough to keep you learning new things. The crafting system is rather token and doesn't do anything new and exciting but never feels pointless. The items are all useful except for the smoke bomb which I never personally used once. The graphics look amazing, though the facial animations look kind of...strange. The characters in cut scenes some times look like puppets when they speak. And the enemy encounters, especially with the Alien, are very tense. The game does pull some pretty cheap little tricks on you but it never feels like it's trying to completely cheat you.
Now, on to what kinda screwed this game for me. It's too long. To be more specific, it lasts longer than it needed to. To explain better, I'm gonna use my personal favorite survival horror game, Fatal Frame, as a comparison. Fatal Frame was also very tense and dreadful but it knew when to end (being only about 4 or 5 hours long), making the experience more satisfying when it's over because you feel accomplished making it through. Alien: Isolation on the other hand continues on and on and on until I just got sick of it. See, if there's one game genre that really benefits from moderation, it's survival horror. This game does a great job of building atmosphere and having scary moments, and I admire it for that. But when I'm 15 hours into a horror game that I really feel like it should've been done and over with at least 7 hours prior, I don't feel accomplished anymore. Xenomorph (THE Alien) is an invincible hunter that will one-hit kill you in most situations.  That fact alone makes him one of the most terrifying enemies in videogame I've ever faced, and is pretty much the star of this game.  The AI is very well done as pretty much any clues to your location like flashlight, stepping sounds, and releasing breath can give you away.  Xenomorphs also rip open locker doors and crawl through vents, so you are never safe anywhere.   Stealth is really well done: as long as you don't give away your location, and you look for traps and tells, the only thing that will kill you are your own mistakes and carelessness.  Unfortunately, there's a long lull in the 2nd half, and it kind of takes away from the core strength of the game.
The Good:
- The gameplay: This is a survival horror game, and it does a fantastic job showing that you are the powerless being that is being hunted.  If you are discovered, you are dead.  Thankfully, the game gives you plenty of places to hide, and remembering where the hiding locations are is crucial.
- Art direction and art assets: This game looks like a period piece from 1979 Alien movie.  It takes how the future was envisioned in the 1979, and it's recreated here, including lighting and shadow.  I also enjoyed the 70s/80s motifs like cassets tapes, clicky keyboards, and green on black screens that is reminescent of BBS/modem days.
- The sound: every step that Xenomorph takes is loud and intimidating whether he's on the floor or in the vents.  In fact, just hearing him run along in the vents is very terrifying.  Also, almost all enemies in the game have audible tells, so it contributes a lot to gameplay.
- Xenomorph AI: This guy is always hunting and looking for something.  Make any noise, he'll come into the room searching for you.
The Bad:
- Pacing: The first half of the game is absolutely terrifying.  So terrifying that I could only play it in about hour or two hour chunks.  Then the game pretty much turns into a walking simulator for about the third of the game.  Last bit of the game felt just as great as the first half.
- The tools: The half the tools and weapons felt useless throughout the game.
Overall:
9/10 - One of the best survival horror games I've ever played.
Gorgeous and brilliantly optimized. Perfect atmosphere. Terrifying.

I'll likely update this review with more information as I dive further into the game, but as it stands, Factorio feels a whole lot like a really in-depth mod for Minecraft, but top-down. It's kind of like your standard survival-crafting style game that's so popular at the moment, but instead of base building being your priority, automation is.
You start from the bottom with absolutely no form of automation, and your goal is to gather resources manually, so you can eventually build an elaborate series of machines including auto-miners, conveyors, chests, electrical wiring, electricity generators, etc... To gather your standard resources as efficiently as possible. On top of all that, you have to also build up your defenses, including weapons and armor for yourself, and automated turrets for the portions of your factory that you're not currently at, in order to defend from randomly appearing waves of enemies that vary in difficulty.
Better yet, the game isn't even remotely difficult to get a grasp of. The single-player campaign is basically a series of easy-to-understand tutorials, and whenever you feel you understand enough of the game, you can quickly start up a fully customizable sandbox-style game.
The community for this game has existed for quite some time prior to its release on Steam today, so there's plenty of massive mods you can download and mess around with whenever you're finished with the 100s of hours worth of content the vanilla game promises to offer up.

I love this game! I bought it off their website, so it doesn't show my hours played on Steam.
You'll build a huge factory with a major issue being getting resources from the output of one part of the factory to another. There are many different types of manufacturing pieces. And all of it needs to run on power.
It becomes a perfect example of what spaghetti code looks like, and organizing and thinking through more elegant designs is a major theme.
Carbon footprint is also an issue, as burning more coal eventually generates enough pollution to attract the local wildlife, which will tend to want to eat you and your lovely factory!
Driving the whole progression is the technology tree.  The goal is to build a rocket to get off the planet.  But the technologies take exponentially more resources to research, and building the resources creates an exponential complexity of your factory.  It will twist your brain into a pretzel!
-------
Update after many more hours:
I walked away from this game for many months, as the amount of content was overwhelming, and the game felt a little burdensome.  So I quit.
Maybe games like this feel like they are just too much to fathom.  But then recently I tried nosing around in it again.  So I will try to explain the progression.
First Few Games:
Learn to deal with biters and the basic mechanics.  Build really bad factories and be bombarded by continuous biter pressure.
Several Games In:
Try out a bus architecture (or be doomed to eternal spaghetti).  This is the game I'm currently in.  I'm finding the blue and green technologies work up to this point of creating an initial factory.
There are videos of people speed building with biters turned off.  They build gigantic sprawling factories.  But I don't care.  Biters are the initial games, so I try to design with no steam engines pure solar to reduce pollution, and a giant wall surrounding the whole structure.  I still haven't used trains.  Will I ever beat the game?  Who cares?  It's fun right now with this little thing I'm trying to work out.
Okay so back to the bus architecture:
There's more to say about busses, but... you'll have to find out for yourself.
Blueprints:
Blueprints are wonderful PROVIDED you carry modular armor and have a personal roboport.  See?  It's an overwhelming review by now isn't it?
Conclusion:
I can't explain everything in this game because even at almost 60 hours in, I've only attained maybe 70% of the content.  What is beautiful is that upon understanding the content that's just the first step.  Going back in and finding the right arrangement is what makes Factorio beautiful.

-It's kinda short. The levels are very short and serve as transitions to the real meat of the game that are the boss fights.

It really depends what you want.  If you just want quick and simple models, and aren't fussed about detail in their form, this is good.  If you want to really get into the detail of the character and model the anatomy to exactly how you envision it, this is not for you.  It's basically the equivalent of a "model wizard".  Choose head, next, choose torso, next, etc...  Morphing is extrememly limited compared to Daz3D, for example, which is free.  Any rigging involves uploading to their site, after creating an account, and using your 1 free montly rig or subscribing.  Subscribing opens up more options, but it seems pointless when there are better free tools, and better subscription based software (Autodesk), or the hotkey driven free Blender software (create, rig and animate...but you have to remember a lot of keys).
In the end, I would not recommend this for any serious modeller.  If you're a game creator and don't want to spend ages modelling extras for your game, choose this...but on sale.

In the past I've heard a bit about how cool Homeworld was, and I have to say I am thoroughly impressed. Being a big fan of the RTS genre, when I heard about this game I immediately wanted to try it out, but alas, it was unavailable. So when I saw "Homeworld Remastered" on Steam's front page a few weeks ago it went straight to my wishlist, and I ended up buying it the day before release.
I was concerned that I might have impulsively spent $30 on something that wasn't really worth it, but now I have no idea why.
Having played around 4 hours of this game over the two days since release, I've only gotten more endeared to the game and how epic it feels. Building a huge fleet of frigates, destroyers, and battlecruisers and then proceeding to wipe out some poor AI... Awesome.
Some Quick Pros and Cons
PROS:
-- Phenomenal feel, moving ships around in 3D space doesn't feel confusing or difficult. While I have yet to employ it significantly, I'm sure it will make things quite interesting.
-- AI is, for the most part, pretty smart. While it makes some dumb moves from time to time it doesn't give up unless all is lost.
-- Oh my word, the visuals are incredible! Next time you have a large group of fighters engaging the enemy, select one of them, focus and zoom in. Large-scale, small-scale, everything looks beautiful, even on my puny GT 630.
CONS:
-- There's some minor bugs, like when moving ships I'll occasionally lose my mouse cursor for a second or two. Every so often the sound skips and repeats 1-2 second snippets of a clip.
NEUTRAL:
-- Gameplay moves a bit slower. It requires patience to build up a sizable attack force and deploy it to wipe out the enemy, but once that combat starts you really grasp the benefit of taking the time to work.
I may expand on this review as I spend more time playing the game, but if you're still doubting whether you want to buy this, let me eliminate any doubt. The Homeworld Remastered Collection is an awesome piece of work. For $35, you get an incredible RTS, its sequel, and the remastered versions of both. Hopefully Gearbox will provide a demo at some point, but if you're a fan of the RTS genre, purchasing this shouldn't be a question.

I think they did a good job on this re-master. I have all of these games and the missing cataclysm game. I bought this off the shelf originally before it became GOTY in 1999. I played this until the game disk broke in a move 5 years ago. It’s my all-time favorite game.  I have been a fan since the first time I played the single player campaign.
What makes this special? Why should I buy this RTS? If you like RTS games, and enjoy a challenge this is the game for you.
This stands alone in the RTS world for many reasons. The 3D combat is truly 3D unlike other 3d perspective RTS games.  Persistence of units in the single player campaign is another major change to other RTS games that I have never seen. If you lose a unit in one mission it is gone forever. If you build a new ship of any kind it will follow you to the next mission as long as you can keep it alive. I have never seen this in any other RTS game like this. The economy side is a little simplistic but I personally don’t think it detracts from the game.  This is a 16 year old and 11 year old game, but it’s one of the best games I’ve ever played. Well worth the cost.
The atmosphere is second to none in the original. I enjoy the story in both, but the story is a little weak in the second game. The re-master is beautiful. I have not had anything bad to say so far.
I wish I could give it two thumbs up.

Only just getting back into these great remasters, but without doubt the amount of effort expended here far surpasses most other "HD remasters".
The Good:
-The textures and cinematics have been updated and have improved in quality to a staggering degree,
-The Audio, both music and dialogue, are excellent and crystal clear,
-The gameplay is just as fun and immersive as I remember.
-A plethora of new built-in skirmish features such as king of the hill style elements and of course the cross-race battles, all optional, and all great additions that keep the gameplay more current.
-Also retains its predecessors' knack for displaying beautiful graphics with very light load on the system, even older computers should make it look very fancy indeed.
Any downsides? Well:
-One or two tech hiccups, in particular a CTD graphics bug which, for me at least, was solved by turning off shadows, not a huge sacrifice, especially in space, but a little annoying.
-I have heard of other bugs, though have experienced none of them myself, but so far my game time is limited to the campaign and skirmish.
-You also have to create a third-party account for multiplayer - painless and quick, but you have been warned.
Conclusion? All in all 100% solid gold angel-moon cheese! A certain buy for any long term fan of the series, and VERY highly recommended for any fan of RTSs in general wanting a breath of old (but ironically, very fresh) air! Get it now!

Now, I don't want to spend the next few paragraphs constantly drawing comparisons between this and Dishonoured 1. But I'm afraid that, that is where it will be going, so apologies in advance.
Dishonoured 2 is awesome ! And it should be, because the first game was. And why should that be ? Because it's pretty much nearly EXACTLY the exact same game. See ? The two are so similar and near indistinguishable from each other, I had to use the word "exact"
. Fair enough, it's a new generation and the graphics might be a bit flashier (Perhaps not the right phrase to use but we'll roll with it and get to that more in a minute), and it's a brand new story (if somewhat drab here and there). But
have played it excessively safe here, with little to no thought on innovation. D2 is to the first game, what Batman : Arkham Knight is to Arkham City. The scale might be larger, (map wise anyway), but there's not really enough here to set the two games apart. And despite this size and scale, D2 has a feel very much akin to that of a DLC expansion. One that just simply adds more. More, more and more of the same.
As I waffle this out, I am currently close to the endgame and it is only just starting to faulter a little when weighed against it's predecessor. Which as you may remember got steadily more awesome as it went along. D2 doesn't seem to be following that pattern at all. Preferring to maintain a steady pace throughout. So steady infact that if you could view D2s progression on an oscilloscope. I'd make a safe bet that you would be treated to little more than a steady flatline throughout.
So far for missions one through eight, the bar hasn't been raised one single iota. That's not to say that the game hasn't had it's moments and does on occasion show a style of design that is simply wonderful. The Mansion of the inventor
being particularly noteworthy. I won't ruin any suprises but my goodness, from a level design perspective it's just pure art. It's bloody lovely to experience. Even if it does come with the downfall of the wooden clockwork robots. A feature which has been lauded around to much fanfare by adverts and "professional reviews". But for me I was sorely disappointed, seeing as they can see in every direction, are tough as nails (with other nails knocked into them), and are seemingly impossible to stealth kill. Which ultimately made what could have been a genius legendary level, to rival and surpass any level on any game ever; By turning it into a mindless (but sadly necessary), open war destructathon. Which would be fine if this wasn't supposed to be a
game.
A couple of levels later comes the home of a guy named
, Which also has a fun and beautifully designed level involving.. Well, again, "spoilers". Which I am most hesitant to do, but take my word, it is wonderful, has to be experienced and is equally as inventive as the Jindosh Mansion.
Had read quite a few articles on the run up to release about all the innovations Arkane had made to this sequel. One from Rolling Stone springing to mind. But when you're in the thick of it traversing the environment, they are barely noticable.
Plotwise, yeah it's OK and is more directly linked to D1s DLC rather than it's main campaign. Though the whole alternative plague business is so very naff. Just like Dunwall in the previous game, the city of Karnaca has been slowly turned into a massive disease ridden cesspit. Though instead of hordes of wandering rats; This time it's
that are the source of the cities troubles. These nesting insects are sort of like mosquitos, except they act like they've been snowballing PCP whilst chugging down steroid & vodka chasers all day. Which just seems like a cheap and convenient way to bridge similarity between D1 & 2 and give an excuse as to why Karnaca (just like Dunwall before), has been reduced to a sprawling slumpit. Only it doesn't quite feel right on this occasion tbh. And it sticks out like a man in a mucky mack at a nudist beach, throughout the entire game. And unlike the first Dishonoured, they are pretty much the only creatures that you will encounter throughout. You won't spend enough time near the water to be bothered by the nibbling fish. And the barnacles have been written right out.
Graphics are good (Stunning even), when there are lighting effects about. But in the shaded areas the textures appear harsh and ugly. Also gone for this second outing, is the beautiful art style. It is similar, but the unique way that the last game was portrayed, with having the painted textures and noticable brushstrokes on every surface. All that is done away with and it feels like Dishonoured has lost its face somewhat. Like if the next Borderlands came about without it's comicbook style artwork. It is completely to its detrement.
My biggest bone of contention for this sequel is "Blink". Yes, that most basic of basic skills that you aquire at the start of the game in order to get around the environments quickly and unseen. Except this time, this skill is absolutley horrible to use. Blink now comes with a downward curve on its aim. And you are going to flabberghasted at the weird angles you're going to have to point the camera in order to aim for certain platforms. It's just well... STUPID. With that bloody pointer sticking to ANY surface... Apart from the one that you want to actually aim for. There are also occasions when you can't seem to jump 2 foot in front of you, for being "out of range". Yet other occasions you can leap half way across the map. Not sure what Arkane did to this most basic of basic abilities.. But I wish they hadn't.
Also done away with is the stealth / shadow icon... WHY ? I don't get it.
So that's Dishonoured 2. Great in some places, astounding in a few, way worse in others and on the whole is a much more plodding affair than Dishonoured was. Featuring some gorgeous settings, yet somewhere along the road, Arkane seem to have struggled in filling and fleshing out their world this time around. If you played the first game, you will more than likely enjoy this one. If you haven't played the first game, then go do that. As it is a far more solid, functional, rounded, unique and enjoyable experience than this sequel can ever hope to be. And from a game mechanics perspective; It almost feels like D2 should have really been the first game. As it feels like more of a step backwards, rather than an evolution.
Nevermind. Perhaps if or when this ip eventually becomes a trilogy. A third game might readdress this balance somewhat.
***EDIT*** Ok so actually in the long run, I had to quit playing to avoid falling into a permenant Dishonoured 2 induced coma of terminal boredom. You may find it interesting so I will keep the blue thumb up. But tbh It ended up being rather mind numbing all in all (Like so many releases that are being fetched forth from AAA land this generation). A bland chore that just didn't hold my interest long enough to be bothering with in getting through to the final mission...

I'm gonna do something a little off. I'm gonna recommend a game I didn't personally like. How can I possibly do that? Because Alien: Isolation is designed well and doesn't do a lot of things wrong but has one major flaw that, for me at least, did end up ruining the experience. But I don't think it's fair to completely condemn a game for only one problem. I may be harsh but I'm fair.
To start off, it is a good game. The level design is a little repetitive, but since it's a moderate sized space station, that's somewhat expected and is at least realistic. The atmosphere is dreadful through out the entire length of game time, adding to many tense moments and, this is gonna sound cheesy, heart pounding sequences. The game mechanics are varied enough to keep you learning new things. The crafting system is rather token and doesn't do anything new and exciting but never feels pointless. The items are all useful except for the smoke bomb which I never personally used once. The graphics look amazing, though the facial animations look kind of...strange. The characters in cut scenes some times look like puppets when they speak. And the enemy encounters, especially with the Alien, are very tense. The game does pull some pretty cheap little tricks on you but it never feels like it's trying to completely cheat you.
Now, on to what kinda screwed this game for me. It's too long. To be more specific, it lasts longer than it needed to. To explain better, I'm gonna use my personal favorite survival horror game, Fatal Frame, as a comparison. Fatal Frame was also very tense and dreadful but it knew when to end (being only about 4 or 5 hours long), making the experience more satisfying when it's over because you feel accomplished making it through. Alien: Isolation on the other hand continues on and on and on until I just got sick of it. See, if there's one game genre that really benefits from moderation, it's survival horror. This game does a great job of building atmosphere and having scary moments, and I admire it for that. But when I'm 15 hours into a horror game that I really feel like it should've been done and over with at least 7 hours prior, I don't feel accomplished anymore. I'm not gonna give any major spoilers, but it pulls a lot of BS to extend the game length further. Here's a fun idea: take a shot every time the main character tries to do anything and it fails, and then try not to die of alcohol poisoning. Dead Space did the exact same thing. I suppose it's to add to the feeling of dread. But all it really does is drag out the game, probably because many consumers now complain that they don't get their money's worth if they finish any game in less than 60 billion hours. I get what they were trying to do. They wanted this in depth world with backstory and such. But this game could've been about the length of Fatal Frame and I would've thought it was way more effective. Instead it just got tiresome and predictable.
But, again, I am recommending it. It drags like a dog with an itchy butt. But I'd be lying if I said it didn't have enough decent moments to play it.

What this had done was essentially that it created a sort of genre that had previously not existed and it did this very well.
Bleed 2 did not disappoint at all. With the tight controls that platformers deserve and new working concepts that the players deserve, this game is truly something special. On top of the unique quad air dash and bullet time from the first game, a Katana was added to bring a whole new aspect to the gameplay. The katana provides a very organic way of deflecting projectiles that works so very well. This game's scoring system like many older arcade games has unlimited replayability.
With added customization, localization, and play modes- this game has it all. It captures the old nostalgia of arcade games with an indie game that is worth more than it costs (in my opinion as a fan of the series), Bleed 2 is a must-own title for anyone who enjoys: Platformers, Action Games, Twin Stick Shooters, Arcade Games, Bullet Time, Boss Fights, Story/Campaign Play, Couch Co-Op OR Bullet Hell games. I use the work OR instead of AND because this game can appeal to a massive variety of gamers for a large variety of reasons.
Finally, this game has the feel of Megaman X as you start the game and proceed through the first level. The music, the style and the action successfully re-create the general feel of excitement and anticipation that Megaman X made me feel as a child. The game starts strong and the gameplay remains strong throughout the entire game. With adjustable difficulty, this game is for anyone who likes video games and I highly recommend it to everyone. Definitely a gem of 2017.
One last mention... this is the only game I have (besides Bleed) that controls equally well with the Mouse and Keyboard, PS4 or Xbox One Controller AND the Steam Controller (which is my personal favorite way to play this game). The developer was nice enough to create a Steam controller binding for Bleed 2 that handles the game perfectly.

Enslaved feels like several of my older favorites wrapped up into one fresh game.
Okay, let me tell you first what this game is like. Regular gameplay mostly consists of light to medium challenge level platforming with controls and puzzles that send me straight back to the first Jak and Daxter. Combat is very fast paced and all about balancing blocking and combo attacks, so in the heat of all of it you end up somewhere between God of War and Dynasty Warriors. Boss battles each have a different trick to beating them that lies somewhere in your arsenal of attacks and abilites, much like Ocarina of Time boss battles. Inbetween all of this, you've got pockets of well-placed and well-paced storytelling set in a harmless-looking world that can trip you up if you're not careful; this is what makes this game feel so nostalgic despite being relatively new.
So when you put all of this together, you're left with this unshakeable feeling the whole time you play; You're having FUN. Not stupid, mindless fun. Not epic, over-the-top fun. Just good, plain FUN that hearkens back to a lot of good classic titles.
Now, this game is of course not without fault but I truly can only complain about two things. Unlike many games, Enslaved is actually too easy at points, particularly when it comes to the platforming. There are a few real challenges, but many times you are left wondering if you did something right or if it really was just that easy. Secondly, you can really feel the engine behind this game. Unreal has had many good games across all of its iterations, but unfortunately I have found that most titles that use it end up being fairly archetypal in presentation; Enslaved does not break the mold.
In the end, I still give Enslaved a solid 8/10; It's a unique, satisfying game with an old soul.

But, as stated, the game is in EA so that's perfectly understandable.
As for the mechanics, the game takes probably about half an hour to get the hang of. If you already know the rules of snooker very well and watch the sport regularly it will be even quicker probably. The design of the game is good and the graphics quality are great. The controls are actually really well thought out, and the user interface is handy - particularly the aim assist, which goes red if you're aiming at a ball which isn't on, for example. Definitely a game to unwind to with a beer after work, or something light hearted to play if you're a bit stressed out.

When you get that tricky shot on the cushion just right, and the side on the cue ball perfect, the ball pots, the white comes away from the cushion perfect for the black - it's just satisfying for any snooker fan. If you don't know snooker very well, but enjoy playing other table sports, you may also find this game really interesting. Definitely well worth the few pounds paid for.

I discovered this game around half a year ago. I first tried out the demo. I liked it. I loved it. In under 15 minutes, I was convinced to buy the full game. So I'm going to make two reviews: One for the people who don't like reading a lot and those who like reading a lot.
1. Get iron.
2. Get copper.
3. Get coal.
4. Make machines.
5. Get more iron and copper.
6. Realize that green circuits are too little. Make more machines.
7. Make train tracks.
8. Make a robot logistic network.
9. Sit back and relax as you watch your magnificent factory.
10. Realize that you have been, all this time, been in the middle of train tracks.
11. Train comes.
12. Train hits you.
13. You die.
11/10 would get hit by a train again.
Factorio is a game about surviving in a foreign planet with nothing but a few scrap metal from your destroyed spaceship. With these ingridients, you will make your first—wait for it—pickaxe. You're probably going to be like: "Oh **** another Minecraft/Survival/Crafting game. Not worth my time or my money." Guess again. Factorio is on a different league. It creates it's own niche. Like I've said two times now, Factorio is a game about making
. "Factories?" you say. "Why the hell would I want to make factories? Is this some brand new **** that's like roller coaster tycoon?"
No, my friend. This game is about building factories, organizing infrastructure, creating efficient setups and watching your own creation make a replica of itself (eventually). Yes, you craft...for like the first 15 minutes. But then you'll have machines crafting things for you. You'll have to start small. A few miners. A few furnaces. But before you know it, you're staring at a monolithic structure of belts, machines and inserters which you could happily call "Your baby factory." And like your own baby, you have to
it.
So far, there are only a few handful of "native" aliens in the land. Your machines that pollute their ecosystem will eventually trigger them to launch an full-on assult. But of course, you will have defenses ready: turrets, lasers, robots, a tank and even your trains (your trains are op. They gotta nerf that ****). You defeat the first wave. But don't go celebrating yet. They'll be back stronger, faster and more tankier.
As you up your defenses and keep building new infrastructure to your factory, you will eventually have enough firepower to—guess what?—run over their houses and collect their eggs (it will say "Alien Artifact" in the game, but it's obviously alien eggs) which will be useful for crafting end-game items and for finally getting a rocket off the planet.
I've spent around 100 hours each into my saves. I only have 3 saves for now, where in two of them I have already launched the end-game rocket. It's
fun.
Anyways:
1. Content-rich Game (way polished that 90% of the Early Access games here in Steam)
2. Active developers.
3. FFs. (It's sort of a newsletter that the devs writer every friday to let everyone know what they've been up to. Basically so we know they're not just slacking around.)
4. Can be played casually or seriously.
5. Loads of replay value.
6. Has a big modding scene (although not in Steam Workshops...yet).
1. End-game content is a bit lacking...but then again this is in Early Access so that is expected.
2. WE DO NOT HAVE ENOUGH GREEN CIRCUITS HOLY ****
3. Train Deaths (The amount of train deaths is 10x more than the average Biter-Alien deaths).
Not yet convinced? Try the demo. You'll thank us later.
Extremely fun and addicting. I spent 2 hours on the tutorials because of how addicting it was to keep making more factories.

Solid foundation for a game. As it stands, Ravenfield is a FPS that requires no huge investment of time to learn the ropes or use the guns and vehicles you want to use. The AI can be challenging at times, but never so much that you feel like you're out of your league against them. Allies and enemies will be confused at night and may not always see you. Maps have dynamic control points that help direct battles. I'll compare this game to Running With Rifles- it's a sandbox war that lets you play as you wish, letting you experience the game in your own way. Having mods can be a plus, but the base game itself is interesting enough for a few hours of play time. I think it's worth the investment.
I think the game would be better with the option of a 3rd person POV, perhaps an immersive storyline that makes you feel invested in the cause. Without it, Ravenfield is very much a "enter the map and play for basically forever" because even when you win a battle, the battle doesn't stop. I see that AI commanding is coming soon, this is good. Right now, I don't know if you can drive a vehicle and order npcs to man the guns, for example. Having the option to tackle the enemy with a friend or two could be nice, but I know I wouldn't play the game for PvP even if there was an option.
Overall good game. Could use some extra facets to really seal the deal.

Now, I don't want to spend the next few paragraphs constantly drawing comparisons between this and Dishonoured 1. But I'm afraid that, that is where it will be going, so apologies in advance.
Dishonoured 2 is awesome ! And it should be, because the first game was. And why should that be ? Because it's pretty much nearly EXACTLY the exact same game. See ? The two are so similar and near indistinguishable from each other, I had to use the word "exact"
. Fair enough, it's a new generation and the graphics might be a bit flashier (Perhaps not the right phrase to use but we'll roll with it and get to that more in a minute), and it's a brand new story (if somewhat drab here and there). But
have played it excessively safe here, with little to no thought on innovation. D2 is to the first game, what Batman : Arkham Knight is to Arkham City. The scale might be larger, (map wise anyway), but there's not really enough here to set the two games apart. And despite this size and scale, D2 has a feel very much akin to that of a DLC expansion. One that just simply adds more. More, more and more of the same.
As I waffle this out, I am currently close to the endgame and it is only just starting to faulter a little when weighed against it's predecessor. Which as you may remember got steadily more awesome as it went along. D2 doesn't seem to be following that pattern at all. Preferring to maintain a steady pace throughout. So steady infact that if you could view D2s progression on an oscilloscope. I'd make a safe bet that you would be treated to little more than a steady flatline throughout.
So far for missions one through eight, the bar hasn't been raised one single iota. That's not to say that the game hasn't had it's moments and does on occasion show a style of design that is simply wonderful. The Mansion of the inventor
being particularly noteworthy. I won't ruin any suprises but my goodness, from a level design perspective it's just pure art. It's bloody lovely to experience. Even if it does come with the downfall of the wooden clockwork robots. A feature which has been lauded around to much fanfare by adverts and "professional reviews". But for me I was sorely disappointed, seeing as they can see in every direction, are tough as nails (with other nails knocked into them), and are seemingly impossible to stealth kill. Which ultimately made what could have been a genius legendary level, to rival and surpass any level on any game ever; By turning it into a mindless (but sadly necessary), open war destructathon. Which would be fine if this wasn't supposed to be a
game.
A couple of levels later comes the home of a guy named
, Which also has a fun and beautifully designed level involving.. Well, again, "spoilers". Which I am most hesitant to do, but take my word, it is wonderful, has to be experienced and is equally as inventive as the Jindosh Mansion.
Had read quite a few articles on the run up to release about all the innovations Arkane had made to this sequel. One from Rolling Stone springing to mind. But when you're in the thick of it traversing the environment, they are barely noticable.
Plotwise, yeah it's OK and is more directly linked to D1s DLC rather than it's main campaign. Though the whole alternative plague business is so very naff. Just like Dunwall in the previous game, the city of Karnaca has been slowly turned into a massive disease ridden cesspit. Though instead of hordes of wandering rats; This time it's
that are the source of the cities troubles. These nesting insects are sort of like mosquitos, except they act like they've been snowballing PCP whilst chugging down steroid & vodka chasers all day. Which just seems like a cheap and convenient way to bridge similarity between D1 & 2 and give an excuse as to why Karnaca (just like Dunwall before), has been reduced to a sprawling slumpit. Only it doesn't quite feel right on this occasion tbh. And it sticks out like a man in a mucky mack at a nudist beach, throughout the entire game. And unlike the first Dishonoured, they are pretty much the only creatures that you will encounter throughout. You won't spend enough time near the water to be bothered by the nibbling fish. And the barnacles have been written right out.
Graphics are good (Stunning even), when there are lighting effects about. But in the shaded areas the textures appear harsh and ugly. Also gone for this second outing, is the beautiful art style. It is similar, but the unique way that the last game was portrayed, with having the painted textures and noticable brushstrokes on every surface. All that is done away with and it feels like Dishonoured has lost its face somewhat. Like if the next Borderlands came about without it's comicbook style artwork. It is completely to its detrement.
My biggest bone of contention for this sequel is "Blink". Yes, that most basic of basic skills that you aquire at the start of the game in order to get around the environments quickly and unseen. Except this time, this skill is absolutley horrible to use. Blink now comes with a downward curve on its aim. And you are going to flabberghasted at the weird angles you're going to have to point the camera in order to aim for certain platforms. It's just well... STUPID. With that bloody pointer sticking to ANY surface... Apart from the one that you want to actually aim for. There are also occasions when you can't seem to jump 2 foot in front of you, for being "out of range". Yet other occasions you can leap half way across the map. Not sure what Arkane did to this most basic of basic abilities.. But I wish they hadn't.
Also done away with is the stealth / shadow icon... WHY ? I don't get it.
So that's Dishonoured 2. Great in some places, astounding in a few, way worse in others and on the whole is a much more plodding affair than Dishonoured was. Featuring some gorgeous settings, yet somewhere along the road, Arkane seem to have struggled in filling and fleshing out their world this time around. If you played the first game, you will more than likely enjoy this one. If you haven't played the first game, then go do that. As it is a far more solid, functional, rounded, unique and enjoyable experience than this sequel can ever hope to be. And from a game mechanics perspective; It almost feels like D2 should have really been the first game. As it feels like more of a step backwards, rather than an evolution.
Nevermind. Perhaps if or when this ip eventually becomes a trilogy. A third game might readdress this balance somewhat.
***EDIT*** Ok so actually in the long run, I had to quit playing to avoid falling into a permenant Dishonoured 2 induced coma of terminal boredom. You may find it interesting so I will keep the blue thumb up. But tbh It ended up being rather mind numbing all in all (Like so many releases that are being fetched forth from AAA land this generation). A bland chore that just didn't hold my interest long enough to be bothering with in getting through to the final mission...

Changing the difficulty vastly changes the game, and I will be re-playing the heck out of it, honing my skills each time, and trying to unlock all the things. Stylish action games, be it high quality shmups, beat-em-ups, or character action games are hard to find these days. When one comes out, the entire community jumps on the chance to play them because it's likely there won't be many more throughout the year. Bleed 2 caters to that audience with flying colors. It takes the first game's refined gameplay and improves it even more, all while not wasting your time. Many games like this pad out the experience with minigames and/or long walks to the next piece of action, but Bleed 2 is basically an arcade game; fast, short, to the point, and almost no downtime. I played through it in one sitting (about 45 minutes on Normal with a few deaths) and felt immersed the whole way through. The new bullet reflect mechanic adds an interesting dynamic to the core gameplay from the first title and also keeps things fresh.
Much like an arcade game, most of the replay value will come from self-imposed challenges along with the healthy amount of unlockables. This game won't satisfy anyone looking for a meaty 6-8 hour experience, but is a great fit for any other action game fan. With the refined gameplay and lack of rough spots in the campaign, it will offer many hours of fun to anyone willing to unlock everything and attempt to go for high scores.

So at the time of this review I’ve sunk 24 hours into this game, and there are a few things to say;
So at 24 hours, I’ve done a fair amount of the story, not because the story is long, but because I’ve put off doing most of the missions, they really are not that interesting, most of the time it is protect this, blow up that, so if you're looking for your next story game to get immersed in, look elsewhere...
Let’s get right to it, the wingsuit, by far this games more redeeming feature, it is A JOY to use, whether it is flying through tunnels or over large (what I presume are) vineyards it is always fun and lovely to control.
The gunplay is fairly similar to Just Cause 2, fairly standard to use, my only minor complaint is the crosshair, but regardless of that it is fairly enjoyable for the most part.
Driving/ Flying is again similar to Just Cause 2, Easy to use, feels good to control, it just really isn't as much fun as when you wingsuit...
A thing worth mentioning is the infinite C4, this is a nice addition and makes blowing things up that little bit nicer and easier.
Now the upgrade system in this works of "Gear Mods" which you get for completing challenges, so doing a wingsuit challenge unlocks some gear mods for the wingsuit, and so on. I don't like this system, it makes the game very grindy, and can take a while to get some of the better ones. In-fact I’d probably say this is my least favorite feature.
There is a huge amount of stuff to do in Just Cause 3, the map is divided into provinces and areas, and within that are bases and settlements to take over, you also unlock challenges from when you "Liberate" an area.
HOWEVER, as we all know Quantity does not equal Quality, this task gets repetitive really quick, as much fun as it is, it is essentially the same ... every time.
CPU: Intel Xeon 1240 v2 3.4GHz
GPU: GTX 970
RAM: 8GB DDR3
Now.
This is where it starts to fall apart a little. As the specs above show, my machine is pretty powerful, However, I suffer from some performance issues that irritate me. I try to maintain at least 60 FPS on all my games, but this will drop very occasionally but when it drops it is noticeable, which is the more irritating thing.
Another thing I seem to be suffering from is a strange occurrence when the game will make itself Windowed (I'm normally running Full screen), and then sometimes minimize itself as well, this happens REGUARLY and gets very annoying while playing, it might be my setup, but I have never had this problem on another game.
One thing of note. If this game did NOT have the wingsuit, in it, I’d probably recommended leaving this game and go pick up Just Cause 2 for a good price. But the wingsuit is so VERY nice to use, and the game can be very satisfying at times.
Quick Points;

Dark Echo doesn't just rely on soundwaves to build it's world, it uses the imagination of the player themselves to fill in the details of this deep, dank and deadly cave. Drawing you in with atmospheric sound design the world around you begins to take shape, from a drop of water rhythmically falling from the ceiling to the deadly monsters lurking around every corner. The controls feel very tight, every single foot step has a weight to it. As the levels go on the game remains fresh, introducing new concepts and challenges at a fair and even pace. If I had one complaint it's that the elements of horror don't feel frantic enough, running away from monsters feels more like a jog through the mall than a life or death situation. Perhaps this is because the game wishes to be more of a puzzler than survival horror. Still loved that loud DEATH SCREAM though! There really is nothing else like Dark Echo, highly recommended!
PROS
-strong atmosphere
-smooth difficulty curve
-extremely unique mechanics
CONS
-monster encounters could be more intense

Before I give my review/opinion I wanna admit that I have never reviewed a game before and I was and still am a huge fan of mmo shooter games, especially 3rd person shooters .One day I decided to play a game that was very popular on social media, youtube and also among some of my friends..........DOTA. I downloaded the game and started playing it and in the 1st match itself I was very uncomfortable with the controls which was the total opposite of what the controls in shooter games are like. The concept of using mouse to click on the map to move and that locked auto attack aim thing was something I was very unfamiliar with, I thought that I might get used to it and played for a couple of hours but it was really hard to adapt, I was merely a feeder in game and I was getting killed as soon as I was in the sight of an enemy player and my teammates were more interested in bullying me rather than trying to win the game. Athough I hated the controls I really loved the concept of mobas and I wished if it had some real action with shooter like controls, seems like my wish became a reality and SMITE was released, I heard a lot about smite and how differnt it was from your conventional mobas. I started playing smite after it was released on steam, I had some problems with the game crashing quite often so I removed it from steam and downloaded it from the official hi-rez website and it really solved the crashing issue. My 1st experience playing smite was awesome, right from the 1st match itself I felt at home and the main reason for it being the controls and the 3rd person view, I felt like I was playing a 3rd person shooter when i was playing a hunter god. The perspective, contols and the skill shots made the game much more involving and fun to play, I liked the whole fight among gods theme, character designs and their abilities. Although the controls are like a shooter game the whole gameplay is based on mobas which consists of leveling up, using the gold that u earn to buy the right items and taking down objectives like towers, phoenix and enemy titan. So smite combines the best elements from third person shooter games and mobas to give an awesome experience to its players.
Although I have played smite for a lot of hours I dont have a huge playtime on steam because I removed it from steam and downloaded it from the officical hi-rez website .So I think that I have enough experience to share some points.
Some positive and negative aspects of SMITE as follows:
+easy to learn but hard to master.
+third person view and contols are like shooter games.
+good character/map design and abilities are a delight to watch, especially the ultimates.
+no pay to win elements which is not the case in most of the shooter games, real money can only be used to buy god skins and some other things that dont give u any sort of upper hand in the game.
+competitive like DOTA and LOL. Smite supports competitive esports and the prize pool of WC is quite big aswell.
-unbalanced match making is one of the biggest flaws of smite, they are trying to deal with it but I dont see much progress even after some of the major updates, I think that teams must be balanced according to kill/death/assist ratio of the most played gods of individual players.
-imbalanced gods and items, smite is working really hard to balance gods and items by nerfing of buffing them in every patch and they have achieved success to certain point but they are still not close enough to achieving equilibrium and I know that its a very tough task. That reminds me of a god I have been playing a lot lately ....[Cabrakan]....smite please show him some love.
-the community when I started playing smite was good or maybe thats what I thought but over the course of time I came acccross some really toxic players who harrass u even after the match sometimes by messaging u, the only think u can do is report them of block them. But we cannot expect everyone to be polite to us right ? If there is heaven there will be hell and if there is good there will be bad. I would recommend u to buy a gaming headphone for using voice chat, make some good friends on smite and make a party to play against others, thats the best way to excel at this game because u need a lot of co-ordination and communication to make the best out of ur team to win matches.

Story:
The story of Alien Isolation is interesting, you are Amanda Ripley looking for your mother Ellen who is lost on the ship Nostromo, the game is mainly about Amanda's emotional journey and her time on the Sevastopal station. Although the story's delivery isn't strong due to mediocre voice acting and lot's of padding it's still intriguing as this story never actually happened in the films.
Presentation:
Creative Assembly have gone all out in terms of presentation for Alien Isolation, the detail of this atmospheric world is outstanding, from the jaw dropping lighting system to the whisps of smoke coming from vents you will honestly feel like you are in Ridley Scotts retro futuristic world.
Gameplay:
The gameplay of Alien Isolation is what makes it different from other survival horror games, for example in most survival horrors the paths of enemies become pretty predicatable after you've died a few times, the twist with Isolation is that you never know when the Alien is coming, you could be walking through a corridor and it will just drop at any time, this is affected by player actions for example if you are running or perhaps shooting another enemy this will change the aliens behaviour accordingly.
Soundtrack:
CA have nailed the soundtrack of Alien Isolation, whilst staying true to the original score they have added some of their own ideas which pays off very well creating some real tension during chases.
Verdict:
Creative Assembly have categorically created one of the finest survial horror games to date, not only have they captured the atmosphere of 1979's Ridley Scott's Alien but they have fundamentally delivered a scary and unpredictable experience. If you are an Alien fan or just enjoy a true survival horror this is for you.

At this stage, this is the game it was meant to be. The Rome 2 we deserved. A whole year after it was released.
The battles are satisfying, tactical, and well paced. Fight animations and movements are superb, as if watching a battle from a blockbuster movie. Blobbing is non-existent (except for difficult pathfinding areas as expected). The arcade feel of the battles have been toned down significantly, with battles also lasting to the 20 minute mark at least, typically longer, on large battles.
The campaign is however still too easy even on hardest difficulties for the moderate player. A few hours in and you will be knocking over empire after empire. City development is interesting and lets you tailor each city economically and militarily to what would benefit you the most in relation to its surroundings and bonuses.
Graphics are just amazing. Optimization is no worse than any AAA title, however you will need a beefy PC to run decent frames on the max settings. Lower settings will work fine but you will miss out on a lot of exclusive animations and graphical features. Trust me, the difference between low and high are staggering. You will think you are playing a different game on each setting.
Glitches are few and rare. Co-op/online is stable.
There is no reason to skip over this game if you love huge, stunning, dynamic battles with a large variety of units and factions. Any lover of Total War will feel this is a good step in the right direction (at least on most features).
Don't worry about buying any DLCs though. They are a waste of money,

I discovered this game around half a year ago. I first tried out the demo. I liked it. I loved it. In under 15 minutes, I was convinced to buy the full game. So I'm going to make two reviews: One for the people who don't like reading a lot and those who like reading a lot.
1. Get iron.
2. Get copper.
3. Get coal.
4. Make machines.
5. Get more iron and copper.
6. Realize that green circuits are too little. Make more machines.
7. Make train tracks.
8. Make a robot logistic network.
9. Sit back and relax as you watch your magnificent factory.
10. Realize that you have been, all this time, been in the middle of train tracks.
11. Train comes.
12. Train hits you.
13. You die.
11/10 would get hit by a train again.
Factorio is a game about surviving in a foreign planet with nothing but a few scrap metal from your destroyed spaceship. With these ingridients, you will make your first—wait for it—pickaxe. You're probably going to be like: "Oh **** another Minecraft/Survival/Crafting game. Not worth my time or my money." Guess again. Factorio is on a different league. It creates it's own niche. Like I've said two times now, Factorio is a game about making
. "Factories?" you say. "Why the hell would I want to make factories? Is this some brand new **** that's like roller coaster tycoon?"
No, my friend. This game is about building factories, organizing infrastructure, creating efficient setups and watching your own creation make a replica of itself (eventually). Yes, you craft...for like the first 15 minutes. But then you'll have machines crafting things for you. You'll have to start small. A few miners. A few furnaces. But before you know it, you're staring at a monolithic structure of belts, machines and inserters which you could happily call "Your baby factory." And like your own baby, you have to
it.
So far, there are only a few handful of "native" aliens in the land. Your machines that pollute their ecosystem will eventually trigger them to launch an full-on assult. But of course, you will have defenses ready: turrets, lasers, robots, a tank and even your trains (your trains are op. They gotta nerf that ****). You defeat the first wave. But don't go celebrating yet. They'll be back stronger, faster and more tankier.
As you up your defenses and keep building new infrastructure to your factory, you will eventually have enough firepower to—guess what?—run over their houses and collect their eggs (it will say "Alien Artifact" in the game, but it's obviously alien eggs) which will be useful for crafting end-game items and for finally getting a rocket off the planet.
I've spent around 100 hours each into my saves. I only have 3 saves for now, where in two of them I have already launched the end-game rocket. It's
fun.
Anyways:
1. Content-rich Game (way polished that 90% of the Early Access games here in Steam)
2. Active developers.
3. FFs. (It's sort of a newsletter that the devs writer every friday to let everyone know what they've been up to. Basically so we know they're not just slacking around.)
4. Can be played casually or seriously.
5. Loads of replay value.
6. Has a big modding scene (although not in Steam Workshops...yet).
1. End-game content is a bit lacking...but then again this is in Early Access so that is expected.
2. WE DO NOT HAVE ENOUGH GREEN CIRCUITS HOLY ****
3. Train Deaths (The amount of train deaths is 10x more than the average Biter-Alien deaths).
Not yet convinced? Try the demo. You'll thank us later.

Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is an absolutely fantastic journey that serves as a re-imagining of the classic Chinese novel of the 16th century, Journey to the West (translated into Monkey and abridged for english speakers). The novel is an extended account of a Buddhist Monk named Xuanzang (also known as Tripitaka), as he journeys to the west, fraught with danger and trials - travelling with the protection of three sinners seeking atonement. These three protectors (Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing), each make an appearance in the video game, in one form or another. Enslaved is a creative take on the subject, so expect many unique and interesting variations on the story.
Enslaved: Odyssey to the West's main draw is it's absolutely gorgeous visuals, which are bright, detailed and compelling for such a sombre post-apocalyptic atmosphere. The soundtrack is an ambient masterpiece, full of wistful tones and quirky beats. It meshes into the stories journey almost seamlessly, which really attributes to the games total atmospheric effect. Ambient sound effects bring life (or the sense of abandonment), to the game as well - from birds chirping in the distance, to the sound of the wind rushing through the foliage. The motion capture techniques used are excellent, especially the facial animations. Characters show genuine emotion (and thanks to the absolutely fantastic actor performances), manage to sound genuine as well! Andy Serkis and Lindsey Marie Shaw deserve much praise for their performances!
With that being said, the mechanics of the game are a fair step down in quality. Gameplay IS entertaining, but lacking in anything new. Combat is enjoyable, although there are not many variations on how to tackle an enemy. Stun shots, power swings, light hits and heavy hits. Shields, wide attacks, counters, etc. It's generic, but secondary in regards to the visuals and story. Platforming in the game is efficient and fast. You essentially spam jump + direction to get to your destination. You can't jump in the wrong direction, nor can you actually fall... so don't expect a platforming experience similiar to Uncharted or Tomb Raider. You don't have to watch where you're going or what you're pressing. The greatest issue as far as I'm concerned, unfortunately, is the poor use of the camera system (especially for the PC). When in combat, or while running around, the camera tends to zoom into a wall here, a ledge there, or a piece of sky over yonder! This game is NOT optimized for keyboard and mouse. Neither are the graphical settings. In order to change any of the settings, you would need to access the actual files for the game to represent any changes in graphics and controls. Nothing can be changed ingame.
Now, while this title has it's fair share of flaws (from it's gameplay mechanics to it being an abysmal port), it still boasts stunning visuals, a fantastic soundtrack, and an excellent story with memorable characters and scenes. I would recommend this game to any fan of the genre, as it's worth the money and the time spent!

I loved every moment of this game. This game has near perfect nVidia 3D Vision support with the use of Helix mod and between the excellent motion capture and lush post-apocalyptic setting it's just so damn beautiful. I took many 3D screenshots, but I'll have to import them into Steam to upload any of them ;-) Heck - even the menu screen is at least a thousand times more awesome in 3D as it is in lamo 2D!
Since this is a third person game I played it with an Xbox 360 controller with no problems, but I hear that it doesn't fare so well with keyboard+mouse, so if you don't have a controller you might want to stay away.
I enjoyed the story, though I have a feeling this might be a bit of a hit or miss affair for different people. It is very much focussed on the journey the characters endure and how it affects them - the motion capture really adds a lot here as they perfectly nailed the characters facial expressions and body language, which really says a lot more about themselves and their journey than the words they use.
The character's backstory is a bit light and I would have appreciated a bit more detail, particularly on Monkey (the main character). Plot wise it might be a little light / simplistic for some, but I didn't mind because the focus was really on the personal journey of the characters. I'd love to talk about the ending a bit, but that would be spoilers so I'll just say it made me think and reflect on a few events from the story.
This game offered me a rare chance to discuss my hobby with my fiance, as the game is adapted from the classic Chinese story Journey to the West and it was interesting to talk a bit about the similarities and differences between this and the original story. Obviously the futuristic post-apocalyptic setting of the game is quite different to the original and a lot of elements have been changed to fit the setting and work in the context of a video game, but there are plenty of similarities - the character's names, Monkey's slave headband, the fact that Monkey rides on a cloud (of different sorts), PIgsy's advances and even Monkey's fighting stick (which packs away when not in use so he can hide it on his arm / in his ear).
Gameplay wise it's a fairly standard spectacle fighter & third person platformer with a couple of *very* basic puzzles every so often. The combat hit a pretty good balance for me - button mashing works some of the time, but there's a few different enemy types that need different strategies to deal with effectively. Cover is important to avoid weapons fire and/or remain hidden - plus there is a distraction mechanic which can be used to safely move from cover to cover. Certain enemies can be used against others if you do a finishing move on them first so there is a bit of strategy involved, but nothing particularly difficult. It did seem like using ranged attacks was a bit OP, but I tend to prefer melee when I have a choice so that didn't bother me, though it took me most of the game to work out the timing to pull off a counter attack.
Without giving too much away I must give it bonus points for the final boss fight as well - the fight feels very epic, but they didn't make the mistake that so many games do of changing up the gameplay - you're just using the exact same platforming and fighting as you have been through the rest of the game, but this time it's all part of a rather awesome showdown.
Finally, this edition comes with the Pigsy's Perfect 10 DLC. Pigsy's character provided some comic relief in the main game, so naturally it follows that this DLC is more humerous and light hearted than the quite serious main game. I'm not sure whether to call Pigsy a side character or a main character you only meet halfway through the main game, but whatever the case this DLC is a completely separate campaign following Pigsy's quest to quite literally make a new friend. This really felt like DLC done right - Pigsy plays quite differently to Monkey as he does not have any melee weapons and uses a combination of gadgets and his gun instead. I was pretty happy with the length of this DLC - it perhaps could have been a little longer, but I don't think it was too short.
I score it a "You should play this" / 10

This game is beautiful, but very simplistic.
The NPC companion will literally nag you to do everything, even obvious things like flip switches. The game UI also assumes you constantly forget what button to press to interact with things, or won't know what direction to go without big glowy signs. Sure, jumping and climbing through the environment looks cool, but it's all button mashing and it's virtually impossible to fall off ledges or fail in any way (you need to push a button to drop off a ledge even if you want to -- and you can't actually jump very high unless there is a pre-set acrobatic handhold already there for you to look fancy using).
Interacting with your NPC companion has a couple interesting ideas (like being able to distract enemies and direct them to cover in firefights) but she's mostly just hysterical baggage with plot-important hacking skills. Combat also has more options / upgrades than it actually needs, since it's mostly button mashing since enemy AI is fairly dumb. No point in a game trying to have special attacks or tactics if the gameplay itself doesn't require them.
This is the typical AAA mash-button-get-cutscene video game -- lots of style and narrative but weak on actualy gameplay substance. It can be an enjoyable timekiller / interactive movie, since the setting and story are interesting, but as a game it's fairly mediocre.
