Better game than the first in all respects: better graphics, more varied gameplay, two playable characters instead of just one, larger levels, and I wouldn't say the story is better, but it's definitely equal to the first.  It does maintain the original's major flaw of the lack of a light/dark based stealth system (ala the original "Thief") making stealth encounters play somewhat flatter than they otherwise might have, but you have so many different ways of approaching objectives that it's an easy flaw to live with.  Minor flaws aside, Dishonored’s appeal has always been its world building and universe, more so than its plot, and the sequel doesn’t disappoint in that regard.  The best part of the series is just wandering around the world, spying on the private lives of the colorful characters you encounter, and taking in the game’s unique “what if magic existed in the late 19th century?” aesthetic.
That said, many seem to have had performance issues.  I hate to be the awful person who says, "It's running fine on my machine" when lots of people are having issues, but it does run fine on my machine.  Now that there is a demo, though, you no longer need to pay to take a risk to try it.  Download the demo and see how it runs for yourself.  Just be sure to play it until the 3rd mission, which is the first city hub that you will encounter.  The city hub levels are the most graphically demanding, but it's worth noting that there are only 3 of them.  So even if your performance takes a hit during them, they are a relatively small part of the game and basically just function to connect key areas of missions where most of the actual gameplay takes place.
Anyhow, I've read that this has sold less than the first.  It's a shame that technical issues have marred the success of what is otherwise one of the best AAA games I've played in a long time.  So definitely give it a try now that they've fixed most of the bugs.  I'd like to see more games like this in the future!

Dishonored 2 is much like Deus Ex: Mankind Divided. It tries to do what its predecessor did, which doesn't feel fresh or cool anymore, it doesn't fix the predecessor's mistakes and it adds new ones.
The short story is, this game is BORING.
* PLOT *
It fails. Nothing makes me care about any of the characters on the screen. Most of them don't even have a character, only costume design. The game will throw names and documents at you, and you will just shrug them off. Of course, if you're a fan, you can MAKE yourself be interested, but the game itself doesn't do anything to achieve that. There isn't a sinlge memorable scene (except maybe the beginning), or a dialogue, or a character.
* GAMEPLAY *
First, doing a pacifist/stealth run will be just as mind-numbingly mundane as it was in the first game, so don't even bother. If you want good stealth gameplay, get MGS5 or HITMAN. Dishonored 2 fails to make it interesting. Stealth/pacisit run will take away about 60% of in-game abilities and items without providing anything in return: there are many abilities designed _only_ for lethal runs, there isn't a single one designed specifically for a non-lethal approach. The game's attempts at "chastice" you for being lethal look just as silly as before and only make you wonder why it'd dangle those cool lethal opportunities for you only to later tell you that killing is frowned upon. Mind you, doing a pacifist run will not feel rewarding at all; a lethal approach at least provides some cool fatalities.
The lethal approach isn't exceedingly fun either, though. It CAN be, but only if you want to make it fun yourself, and that's what's most youtube videos on Dishonored are about: the authors come up with clever combinations of powers to execute them in an interesting way. However, the standard game doesn't require anything spectacular from you, regular fights don't involve anything special and get old pretty fast, and you can't just easily weave all of your cool abilities into the fight; you'll either need to plan ahead (which isn't as fun as planning perfect Hitman kills), or you'll end up doing some standard fencing and shooting your pistol, with an occasional grenade or a drop assassination.
If the authors stopped flirting with forcing two different approaches into the game and focused on one of them instead, the gameplay could've been deeper and more engaging. Take a note from Batman: Arkham or even Assassin's Creed.
By the way, in 2016 the guards are as stupid as they were in 2012. They can kill you in a crowd, some shoot guns, but that's where their strengths end. Not only they're stupid, they're also deaf: a group of guards inside a building can stay oblivious to a sword-and-gun fight between half a dozen people outside. Circling around them is boring as there are no deep stealth opportunities, while killing them requires no challenge because they're weak and mostly all the same.
* DESIGN *
While the game looks great, the recognizable style and atmosphere are there, and each level has a touch of unique color palette, ultimately every chapter is the same. You walk down some streets, kills a few small packs of guards, then enter some sort of a posh/derelict building, wander around floors looking for hidden runes/bonecharms, and then come across a boss which can be either boringly killed (not a single memorable fight) or incapacitated via some kind of a 'deus ex machina' method which is blatantly shoved into your face. Rinse and repeat. Just like the plot, the design just doesn't make you care. Basically every level is a series of puzzles, involving doors, windows, Walls of Light, guard posts, etc., and those puzzles just aren't very interesting or hard.
* VERDICT *
Like the first game, it feels like a lot of wasted potential. The problem is, there was much more potential here and it is wasted almost completely, which just makes me sad. Unless you really, really try to MAKE the game fun for you, it'll never be fun by itself.

It really is the game Alien fans have been waiting for, even if there are a few minor niggles here and there.
The Alien itself is terrifying, and the design and animations of the creature as exactly as Giger would have wanted - it is a fitting tribute to the artist, and equally scary and frightening.
The setting, Sevastopol, is fantastic. Combined with the fantastic visuals and audio design, there is a real immersive sense of dread and horror when the station is slowly falling apart. Pipes burst, dust and grime falls from the ceiling, and areas are dark and dim without being too low-key or desaturated.
It's an indie game with the budget of a triple A game, and it works wonderfully. Although the game can be frustration with its save system occasionally, in retrospect it is fitting for the challenge of the game. Even if it is a little bit over-long towards the end of the game, the tension and atmosphere created by Alien: Isolation is worth the price tag alone - especially on sale.
9/10
P.S: The 'Last Survivor' and 'Crew Expendable' DLC are basically role-plays of the second act of the original 'Alien' film, and are incredible experiences for fans of the series!

It's exactly my type of game. I support it. I have played more of the free version, but this seems like a much more polished version even if it is early access. It's a fun singleplayer FPS with pretty seamless AI. You've got multiple weapons, and even a wartime weapon called the 'swift', of which I find way too quiet. All in all I really like it but I have a few suggestions.
Suggestion #1 : Shooting Range. I think a shooting range would be a fun way to see all the weapons once you're done updating the game. You can't really see them on the field, because of the pew-pew and all that happening that can kill you. Something like WarMode's safehouse would be nice.
Suggestion #2 : Improve everything aesthetic about the weapons. The weapons sound awful, and in the case of the semi auto pistol look awful. The pistol just looks like 2 boxes. The only good sounding weapon is the Shotgun.
Suggestion #3 : Add a system for unlocking weapons. For example, you can get new weapons by killing people, getting achievements, and climbing the ranks in campaign. A system similar to WarMode, except you start out with a few weapons already. Just give us multiple ways to unlock them.
Suggestion #3.5 : Add customization options. For example you get to unlock suppressors, sights, mounted grenade launchers, etc by killing people, getting achievements and climbing the ranks in campaign mode. A system similar to Battlefield or WarMode. Just give us multiple ways to unlock them.

I love this game! I bought it off their website, so it doesn't show my hours played on Steam.
You'll build a huge factory with a major issue being getting resources from the output of one part of the factory to another. There are many different types of manufacturing pieces. And all of it needs to run on power.
It becomes a perfect example of what spaghetti code looks like, and organizing and thinking through more elegant designs is a major theme.
Carbon footprint is also an issue, as burning more coal eventually generates enough pollution to attract the local wildlife, which will tend to want to eat you and your lovely factory!
Driving the whole progression is the technology tree.  The goal is to build a rocket to get off the planet.  But the technologies take exponentially more resources to research, and building the resources creates an exponential complexity of your factory.  It will twist your brain into a pretzel!
-------
Update after many more hours:
I walked away from this game for many months, as the amount of content was overwhelming, and the game felt a little burdensome.  So I quit.
Maybe games like this feel like they are just too much to fathom.  But then recently I tried nosing around in it again.  So I will try to explain the progression.
First Few Games:
Learn to deal with biters and the basic mechanics.  Build really bad factories and be bombarded by continuous biter pressure.
Several Games In:
Try out a bus architecture (or be doomed to eternal spaghetti).  This is the game I'm currently in.  I'm finding the blue and green technologies work up to this point of creating an initial factory.
There are videos of people speed building with biters turned off.  They build gigantic sprawling factories.  But I don't care.  Biters are the initial games, so I try to design with no steam engines pure solar to reduce pollution, and a giant wall surrounding the whole structure.  I still haven't used trains.  Will I ever beat the game?  Who cares?  It's fun right now with this little thing I'm trying to work out.
Okay so back to the bus architecture:
There's more to say about busses, but... you'll have to find out for yourself.
Blueprints:
Blueprints are wonderful PROVIDED you carry modular armor and have a personal roboport.  See?  It's an overwhelming review by now isn't it?
Conclusion:
I can't explain everything in this game because even at almost 60 hours in, I've only attained maybe 70% of the content.  What is beautiful is that upon understanding the content that's just the first step.  Going back in and finding the right arrangement is what makes Factorio beautiful.

Better game than the first in all respects: better graphics, more varied gameplay, two playable characters instead of just one, larger levels, and I wouldn't say the story is better, but it's definitely equal to the first.  It does maintain the original's major flaw of the lack of a light/dark based stealth system (ala the original "Thief") making stealth encounters play somewhat flatter than they otherwise might have, but you have so many different ways of approaching objectives that it's an easy flaw to live with.  Minor flaws aside, Dishonored’s appeal has always been its world building and universe, more so than its plot, and the sequel doesn’t disappoint in that regard.  The best part of the series is just wandering around the world, spying on the private lives of the colorful characters you encounter, and taking in the game’s unique “what if magic existed in the late 19th century?” aesthetic.
That said, many seem to have had performance issues.  I hate to be the awful person who says, "It's running fine on my machine" when lots of people are having issues, but it does run fine on my machine.  Now that there is a demo, though, you no longer need to pay to take a risk to try it.  Download the demo and see how it runs for yourself.  Just be sure to play it until the 3rd mission, which is the first city hub that you will encounter.  The city hub levels are the most graphically demanding, but it's worth noting that there are only 3 of them.  So even if your performance takes a hit during them, they are a relatively small part of the game and basically just function to connect key areas of missions where most of the actual gameplay takes place.
Anyhow, I've read that this has sold less than the first.  It's a shame that technical issues have marred the success of what is otherwise one of the best AAA games I've played in a long time.  So definitely give it a try now that they've fixed most of the bugs.  I'd like to see more games like this in the future!

Dishonored 2 is much like Deus Ex: Mankind Divided. It tries to do what its predecessor did, which doesn't feel fresh or cool anymore, it doesn't fix the predecessor's mistakes and it adds new ones.
The short story is, this game is BORING.
* PLOT *
It fails. Nothing makes me care about any of the characters on the screen. Most of them don't even have a character, only costume design. The game will throw names and documents at you, and you will just shrug them off. Of course, if you're a fan, you can MAKE yourself be interested, but the game itself doesn't do anything to achieve that. There isn't a sinlge memorable scene (except maybe the beginning), or a dialogue, or a character.
* GAMEPLAY *
First, doing a pacifist/stealth run will be just as mind-numbingly mundane as it was in the first game, so don't even bother. If you want good stealth gameplay, get MGS5 or HITMAN. Dishonored 2 fails to make it interesting. Stealth/pacisit run will take away about 60% of in-game abilities and items without providing anything in return: there are many abilities designed _only_ for lethal runs, there isn't a single one designed specifically for a non-lethal approach. The game's attempts at "chastice" you for being lethal look just as silly as before and only make you wonder why it'd dangle those cool lethal opportunities for you only to later tell you that killing is frowned upon. Mind you, doing a pacifist run will not feel rewarding at all; a lethal approach at least provides some cool fatalities.
The lethal approach isn't exceedingly fun either, though. It CAN be, but only if you want to make it fun yourself, and that's what's most youtube videos on Dishonored are about: the authors come up with clever combinations of powers to execute them in an interesting way. However, the standard game doesn't require anything spectacular from you, regular fights don't involve anything special and get old pretty fast, and you can't just easily weave all of your cool abilities into the fight; you'll either need to plan ahead (which isn't as fun as planning perfect Hitman kills), or you'll end up doing some standard fencing and shooting your pistol, with an occasional grenade or a drop assassination.
If the authors stopped flirting with forcing two different approaches into the game and focused on one of them instead, the gameplay could've been deeper and more engaging. Take a note from Batman: Arkham or even Assassin's Creed.
By the way, in 2016 the guards are as stupid as they were in 2012. They can kill you in a crowd, some shoot guns, but that's where their strengths end. Not only they're stupid, they're also deaf: a group of guards inside a building can stay oblivious to a sword-and-gun fight between half a dozen people outside. Circling around them is boring as there are no deep stealth opportunities, while killing them requires no challenge because they're weak and mostly all the same.
* DESIGN *
While the game looks great, the recognizable style and atmosphere are there, and each level has a touch of unique color palette, ultimately every chapter is the same. You walk down some streets, kills a few small packs of guards, then enter some sort of a posh/derelict building, wander around floors looking for hidden runes/bonecharms, and then come across a boss which can be either boringly killed (not a single memorable fight) or incapacitated via some kind of a 'deus ex machina' method which is blatantly shoved into your face. Rinse and repeat. Just like the plot, the design just doesn't make you care. Basically every level is a series of puzzles, involving doors, windows, Walls of Light, guard posts, etc., and those puzzles just aren't very interesting or hard.
* VERDICT *
Like the first game, it feels like a lot of wasted potential. The problem is, there was much more potential here and it is wasted almost completely, which just makes me sad. Unless you really, really try to MAKE the game fun for you, it'll never be fun by itself.

I think this game is more fun than its predecessor. However, that's just when the framerate is normal...
This game has some serious memory problems. I've got a pretty decent computer, so normally the game can render 60 fps. However, it frequently drops or freezes as soon as the game spawns new actors or geometry or something else happens. I did stomp the settings to almost lowest possible and it helped a little (probably mostly because of texture size), but I still get jerky FPS.
For extra irritation, you can't properly customize your keybindings in the game. If you do, the game adds two entries in the keymap file that the game isn't able to read. This leads to the game defaulting the controls every time you start the game. Also, there are multiple entries that can be changed in the config file that doesn't appear in the custom key binding screens, which means that the keys you happen to bind on those keys may get interrupted. Like (hold) Detonate Explosives on F (you can only rebind (tap) Detonate Explosives), and Look At on R.
There is a workaround for this, by editing an unmodified kepmap.txt (not a typo), but it shouldn't be needed. I can't see how the config thing can be that hard to fix that it isn't sorted out a half year after release.
Until these things are fixed, I would not recommend anyone getting this game. If they do fix these issues, I would happily recommend the game, because it is really fun (to me at least) when I don't experience those frustration elements.

Bleed was one of my all time favourite video games. I thought it would be impossible to improve upon yet somehow Bleed 2 managed to be even better than the first with better graphics, a killer sound track, excellent game play and much more.

Bleed 2 is an arcade style, side scrolling shooter that is meant to give you a challenge. Taking place after the events of the first game, Bleed 2 has you control Wryn again to deal with an alien invasion.
Story wise there really isn't much to say, Bleed was never really known for its story but gameplay wise I think Bleed 2 makes many great changes that improve the game's overall appeal of fast-paced action and tough boss fights that keep you trying over and over again, especially on harder difficulties.
Some of the bosses are new, some come from the original Bleed but most of them are tough because of the low margin of error in their attack patterns and the speed at which they output moves. It's not always possible for you to tell what attack is coming before it's already making it's way to you, which is where the ability to slow down time comes in handy. This is a game that tests the reflexes for the hardcore player looking for a challenge but its lower difficulties also accommodates the more casual players with an abundance of health and checkpoints in all the maps.
The progression element was taken out in Bleed 2, instead now you only unlock items once you've beat the game on a certain difficulty but since the double pistol and katana combo would only be less ideal to use than other weapons in select few circumstances, the lack of a progression system isn't as bad as one would think.
I don't know if I'd recommend this game for someone looking for a casual time, but if you want a challenging 1-2 hours, give Bleed 2 a try on very hard difficulty. The mechanics here are solid and the tight controls ensure that every death you face is a fair one and that every victory comes with a good deal of satisfaction.

It really is the game Alien fans have been waiting for, even if there are a few minor niggles here and there.
The Alien itself is terrifying, and the design and animations of the creature as exactly as Giger would have wanted - it is a fitting tribute to the artist, and equally scary and frightening.
The setting, Sevastopol, is fantastic. Combined with the fantastic visuals and audio design, there is a real immersive sense of dread and horror when the station is slowly falling apart. Pipes burst, dust and grime falls from the ceiling, and areas are dark and dim without being too low-key or desaturated.
It's an indie game with the budget of a triple A game, and it works wonderfully. Although the game can be frustration with its save system occasionally, in retrospect it is fitting for the challenge of the game. Even if it is a little bit over-long towards the end of the game, the tension and atmosphere created by Alien: Isolation is worth the price tag alone - especially on sale.
9/10
P.S: The 'Last Survivor' and 'Crew Expendable' DLC are basically role-plays of the second act of the original 'Alien' film, and are incredible experiences for fans of the series!

Before I give my review/opinion I wanna admit that I have never reviewed a game before and I was and still am a huge fan of mmo shooter games, especially 3rd person shooters .One day I decided to play a game that was very popular on social media, youtube and also among some of my friends..........DOTA. I downloaded the game and started playing it and in the 1st match itself I was very uncomfortable with the controls which was the total opposite of what the controls in shooter games are like. The concept of using mouse to click on the map to move and that locked auto attack aim thing was something I was very unfamiliar with, I thought that I might get used to it and played for a couple of hours but it was really hard to adapt, I was merely a feeder in game and I was getting killed as soon as I was in the sight of an enemy player and my teammates were more interested in bullying me rather than trying to win the game. Athough I hated the controls I really loved the concept of mobas and I wished if it had some real action with shooter like controls, seems like my wish became a reality and SMITE was released, I heard a lot about smite and how differnt it was from your conventional mobas. I started playing smite after it was released on steam, I had some problems with the game crashing quite often so I removed it from steam and downloaded it from the official hi-rez website and it really solved the crashing issue. My 1st experience playing smite was awesome, right from the 1st match itself I felt at home and the main reason for it being the controls and the 3rd person view, I felt like I was playing a 3rd person shooter when i was playing a hunter god. The perspective, contols and the skill shots made the game much more involving and fun to play, I liked the whole fight among gods theme, character designs and their abilities. Although the controls are like a shooter game the whole gameplay is based on mobas which consists of leveling up, using the gold that u earn to buy the right items and taking down objectives like towers, phoenix and enemy titan. So smite combines the best elements from third person shooter games and mobas to give an awesome experience to its players.
Although I have played smite for a lot of hours I dont have a huge playtime on steam because I removed it from steam and downloaded it from the officical hi-rez website .So I think that I have enough experience to share some points.
Some positive and negative aspects of SMITE as follows:
+easy to learn but hard to master.
+third person view and contols are like shooter games.
+good character/map design and abilities are a delight to watch, especially the ultimates.
+no pay to win elements which is not the case in most of the shooter games, real money can only be used to buy god skins and some other things that dont give u any sort of upper hand in the game.
+competitive like DOTA and LOL. Smite supports competitive esports and the prize pool of WC is quite big aswell.
-unbalanced match making is one of the biggest flaws of smite, they are trying to deal with it but I dont see much progress even after some of the major updates, I think that teams must be balanced according to kill/death/assist ratio of the most played gods of individual players.
-imbalanced gods and items, smite is working really hard to balance gods and items by nerfing of buffing them in every patch and they have achieved success to certain point but they are still not close enough to achieving equilibrium and I know that its a very tough task. That reminds me of a god I have been playing a lot lately ....[Cabrakan]....smite please show him some love.
-the community when I started playing smite was good or maybe thats what I thought but over the course of time I came acccross some really toxic players who harrass u even after the match sometimes by messaging u, the only think u can do is report them of block them. But we cannot expect everyone to be polite to us right ? If there is heaven there will be hell and if there is good there will be bad. I would recommend u to buy a gaming headphone for using voice chat, make some good friends on smite and make a party to play against others, thats the best way to excel at this game because u need a lot of co-ordination and communication to make the best out of ur team to win matches.

Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is a game with nice production values and better than average storytelling. It's also one of the most boring games I've ever played. I see it in my Steam queue and I end up wanting to do the dishes instead.
The combat is cliched borderline button-mash with the pre-requisite unnecessary RPG experience system tied in. So if you want the regeneration perk that breaks the game right off the bat and makes health packs almost unnecessary, start running around for those red-colored experience points! You'll be able to grab it after you collect about 60 of them.
Platforming is constant, and it's the kind of platforming designed by a really fussy nanny that doesn't tolerate failure. It's almost impossible to fall to your death, and the game only lets you change positions only if you go towards the shiny handhold things. The puzzles are in the style of Quake II, that is that they are actually not puzzles but busywork. Like doing the dishes, then having to take the mashed robots out to the recycling bin.
Even the narrative that the game loves so much isn't great. The fundamentals are fine, except for the part where there's no clear antagonist and the game doesn't go into detail about what's going on. It's still better than usual, but the drive of the game disappears about halfway in when the developers decide it's time to kill the big bad man introduced only really introduced near the end of the game! Woo hoo, I like it when my villains are pop-up targets to shoot in the face! Like Pop Tarts! Pop Tarts shaped like Hitler!
It's eighty minutes of movie stretched to five hours. And because something's gotta be done with the other three hours and forty minutes, there's undisciplined game design, busywork masquerading as puzzles, and robots that are evil because there's evil robots, evil robots with guns, and sometimes there's evil robots who enslave people. Pbbbbthhhhhhhhppppppp. Watch it on Youtube instead.

I think that the Total War Series was right to Choose Rome 2 as the next Total War Game, I've been an enthusiastic Total War fan since Medieval Total War 1.  I Loved Rome 1 Total War, and Have played over 1,000 hours. I played the rest of the Total War games and really enjoyed them, especially Medieval 2, and Shogun 2.
That being said, I tried to like Rome 2 Total War... I tried so hard, and couldn't. The Game is terribly broken. I pray that someday it is fixed and fun to play. To be fair I haven't played Rome 2 after the first few months it was released, and many (but not all) little glitches have been fixed since then, but the things that ruined the game for me have not, to my knowledge been, nor will be, fixed. I have only played 12 hours at this point, and I am know that the game has improved since I played it.
First of all The Army/General system is dumb!  No longer can you send some units to hold a bridge, or split your forces to accomplish multiple goals. You can't lure enemy forces out of fortresses, nor can you deplete the armies to that their cities are weakly defended. YOU CAN ONLY MARCH A FEW ARMIES AT A TIME,!!!!

Construction in cities is so dumb I don't have time to talk about it. Instead let me role play,  "Ahhh I have my great city, with tens of thousands of people, time to choose what to build, oh look I get a hand full of options to choose between, hmmmm dock, or stable or inn   hmmmmmm.    WHY CAN"T A CITY HAVE ALL OF THEM? what real city says, oh I'm sorry you've filled all six-eight building slots, we can't build any more. The building and city management seems so dumbed down it is not only uninteresting, but frustratingly limiting. Also I shouldn't have to choose between two buildings to decide what defense is SPAWNED to protect the city! To see an intelligent model for comparison observe the way it is done in Rome 1.
Also Why can't you build city walls? how is it a siege without walls? baahhh
My review is that I love that creative studios made this game, I just wish they had made it well. I dreampt about this game for years. When it was released this game dashed my faith in Total War and the direction it is taking. I've gone back to Rome 1 and medieval 2 because they are much better games. I also really enjoy Shogun, because even though they had started to mess up building management, the game still contained soo much genius, art and strategy that it was a blast.
I plan to Check in on Rome 2 every year or so, hoping that either through patches, mods, or a combination of the two, this game can become a worthy sequel to Rome 1.

This game is perfect. I don't know why people keep ♥♥♥♥♥ing about it. But I don't see any problem with this game, as of the moment of this report. The animations are sick, especially when you combine it with some battle mod, this can be come one of the most epic and bloodiest battle games.

The Elder Scrolls Online: A truly amazing MMO
Pros:
- Beautiful graphics
- Little to no lag
- Fun quests

Cons:
- Confusing to new players. It took me about 2 hours to fully understand how races and classes worked together, and still don't understand the alliances and the differences between them.

- Skill points are hard to come by. Sky stones are very rare and requiring 3 for a skill point seems kind of unfair. I'd lower it to 2 so it's not insanely easy to get skill points but not incredibly difficult either.

Much awaited title!
Played until completion from the release.
Although the game is better in several points compared to its first version (DkS: Prepare to Die), I found a few lacking.
The improvements:
- Playability is definitely better. This enhances mainly the PvP experience, imo. DkS 2 is better for PvP in every way you can imagine.
- Spells are there. not just shoot blue fat arrow, but a few utility spells as well, as AoE and a ultra cool magic sword slash.
- Graphics are better, but this is to be expected... The main improvement on it was the decent port to PC. FROM actually took the time to develop the game into a PC envirorement, leading to this beautiful game.
- Character builds are now more complex. A few stat changes made this possible, in a way you have to sacrifice something good to get something good (on DkS attunement and resistance were simply too easy to sacrifice).
- Global Death Count!
For the shortcomings:
- Lore. Yeap. Dark Souls 2 is lacking in lore compared to its first. ***SPOILER ALERT*** You're basically in a kingdom in which its king fought a war against giants and stole something. from my perspective it looks like a few stories at the same time, without links between them.
- BGM is, aside from the last boss fight, not as immersive as I expected.
The game is worth its price and it is a wonderful addition to its series!

I played the original Bleed and I absolutely loved it. As a matter of fact, I still haven't beaten the Arcade Mode in it...and with Bleed 2, that's going to have to wait.
First of all, Bleed 2 is a single-player game. Many look at this and say "Is it gonna be worth it? There's not much to do, right?" But I argue against that. Bleed 2 is a game where its main goal is not just to beat the Story once and to get all the achievements, it's to really master the game itself so that you can beat it with ease. If you've played Devil May Cry, Bayonetta, Metal Gear Rising, or...well, Bleed 1, you're gonna like this.
A quick run on Hard (that's assuming if you're good; please keep in mind I played the original, which probably helped me out a lot) got me some unlockable characters, weapons, AND different abilities for Wryn, so once you master the game with the standard moveset, you can find ways to break it with all of the new characters and abilities you've got. The original Bleed had a shop system where you bought items as you gained more points; this has been removed in favor of (I'm assuming) beating the story on its various difficulties and completing Arcade Mode (one life only).
The atmosphere of this game is also really great. Despite the name, it's not as dark as it seems. Wryn is an incredibly cheerful protaganist in a world filled with cats shooting her with rockets, a cowgirl blasting projectiles everywhere, and a flower guy reporting her actions on the news as she marches on to defeat the villains of this colorful universe.
Also, the music is astounding. While the first had chiptune based music, this one has a full-on soundtrack, filled with guitars and some electronic undertones mixing. It's done by the same musician who did the Nuclear Throne soundtrack, so if you liked his work on that, this soundtrack is even better (they don't sound the same though, not by a longshot, and that's a good thing).
While I haven't even scratched the surface of Bleed 2, I just wanted to take a moment and say how great this game is thus far. If you want an indie game that's ACTUALLY a game, one that clearly is about having fun over trying to give you a life lesson or being some crummy Kickstarter scam, Bleed 2 is the place to b(l)e(ed).

The pink-haired hero is back, the world renown bad♥♥♥♥♥and beloved hero now going for a promotion to Greatest Hero of the World. Wryn returns with her slick, stylish acrobatics and her rapidfire dispensers of justice, and brings some flashy new reflecting mechanics to the table in the sequel to Bleed. The surprise sleeper-hit Xbox indie title has come a seriously long way since its debut five years ago with even tighter and more refined dash controls, a way sharper visual style with much more fluid animations but the same great retro feel, and an even wilder journey into the very cosmos itself.
What was once energetic and fast-paced gameplay is now full-on hyperactive chaos due to the addition of the color oriented bullet-reflecting mechanic. The same satisfying three-stage air dodging is here but the addition of a quick-slicing sword that attacks at the quick tap of an attack adds an entirely new layer of depth to the already face-melting combat of Bleed. The adorably and diabolically designed enemies populate your screen with each transition and unleash a hail of bullet-hell patterns
The bosses are what really seal the deal in Bleed 2. Like some kind of Treasure inspired Alien Soldier boss battle onslaught they seem to come endlessly between frenetic sections of platforming that whip by you in a flash. Each ridiculously imaginative boss and their intuitive attack pattern tops the last in terms of sheer genius. Intense chases on the tops of missile-launching trucks, careful parkour through the skies across streaming rockets, and careening mechs that are gargantuan in size and chase you through crumbling city streets are only some of the backdrops for these incredible showdowns.
Beautiful bright and poppy compositions from the fantastic and legendary Jukio Kallio grace each stage, with a bit of seriously ferocious energy when needed. Some serious guitar riffage for the hectic chases through city scenes and some serenely kosmiche synth sounds for the more introspective ventures into otherworldly scenery. Songs that sound like they'd be fitting in some kind of a bad♥♥♥♥♥90's anime epic, there couldn't be a more fitting soundtrack for the cartoonish yet tough and stylish world of Bleed 2.
I'm blown away by what has been accomplished with Bleed 2 since its predecessor. My expectations have been more than surpassed, I've already spent a good 10hrs replaying the different modes and I'm still not totally confident with my parrying and dodging skills. It's also incredible what a world of difference Jukio Kallio's soundtrack makes, I'm completely infatuated with it as I have been with his past soundtracks (particularly with doseone for Gun Godz). Bleed 2 easily ranks in my top sidescrolling action games of all time, holding a spot right between various Treasure classics. (I definitely get a Dynamite Headdy vibe from some of the almost theatrical set-ups for boss fights)
Bleed 2 comes packed with some great extras and unlockables. There's multiple extra modes to tackle before or after the story, including an Arcade mode with multiple playtstyles to chase you score through the whole campaign in one go and an insane Challenge mode that pits you against multiple bosses at a time. With a whole arsenal of new and unique weapons to tear through stages with and some familiar faces that appear as playable characters to unlock and even bring with you into some co-ordinated co-op.
With so many new ways to play, such a fresh and sharp new look, and an incredible soundtrack that brings the series even more to life than ever before Bleed 2 beats out its already legendary-status predecessor ten-fold.

Bleed 2 is an absolutely phenomenal Action/Run&Gun game full of intense combat and delightfully frequent and inventive boss battles. If you're a fan of old Treasure games such as Gunstar Heroes and Alien Soldier, don't sleep on this.
While playing the original Bleed is recommended, it is not required.
Fans of the original Bleed will be happy to know that its successor is improved in nearly every way. There's a lot more attention to detail, visuals and audio have improved considerably, the new color-coded parry mechanic adds another layer of strategy and the difficulty settings, particularly Very Hard, feel much better.
The game is not without its shortcomings, though. The weapon variety in Bleed 2 feels smaller and less relevant than it did in Bleed, due in part to the necessity of keeping your katana close at hand at all times. The variety also doesn't quite feel as fun as it did in Bleed; unlockable weapons largely just feel like visual twists on the existing "projectile" and "melee" weapons. Apart from the default weapon (combo), the only weapon I really used beyond experimentation was White. Granted, the default weapon combo of Katana/Pistols felt so good that everything else felt more like a gimmick.
The story, while cute in its own right, didn't have the memorable twist of the first, either. It's told in a much more engaging way, but the story itself is more straightforward with fewer surprises.
There's also no "shop" in Bleed 2 for better or for worse; you unlock characters, weapons and abilities by fulfilling objectives (eg beating the game on such-and-such difficulty) so those who enjoyed replaying levels for currency to upgrade Health/Energy no longer have that option.
In terms of length, Bleed 2 feels more or less the same length as Bleed, but each second of gameplay is far more action-packed than its predecessor, and has more than double the number of bosses. Triple? I don't know. There's a lot more bosses.
In terms of polish - while Bleed was an excellent game, Bleed 2 is a much more polished, and much higher quality experience.
It's a tight, action-packed experience that I wholeheartedly recommend. If you're a fan of action games at all, you definitely owe it to yourself to give it a try.

Bleed was a revolutionary step forward in sidescrolling action games, and Bleed 2 is the further evolution of its amazing mechanics. The dual analog movement/shoot setup and dodge mechanics still feel unique. The fast-paced combat is satisfying, feeling almost like a puzzle to solve during each encounter. The new deflection move adds a lot of depth to fights, and the boss battles are as memorable as they are numerous. Bootdisk has really stepped up their work on the visuals and the soundtrack is killer.
This is the total package! Do not sleep on this one!

Disclaimer: I got the key for free. But I’m going to buy a copy and send it to a friend, just because I think the game is amazing.
Bleed 2 is an action game by Ian Campbell. The game features air-dodging, bullet-reflecting and tons of bosses. What makes the game so amazing is how dynamic it is. The feeling of unstoppable movement forward will capture you at the start of the game and won’t be releasing you until you finish it. If any game can be described as “action packed”, this is the one.
•	Constant movement, amazingly dynamic gameplay: crazy tripple jumps that make up for a fast playstyle
•	LOTS of Interesting Bosses: be it a truck that keeps jumping on the road, the rotating particle emitter that affects the physics of all enemy objects of the screen or the cowboy on the flying board.
•	Cool pixel-art style that has a great old-school feel to it.
•	From easy to incredibly hard: there’s a difficulty for everyone. Changing them remarkably affects the feel from the gameplay. When I picked normal, it felt like walk in a park / play through just to see what happens next. When I picked “hard” – the game became a real challenge, it was really hard to survive without using slow-motion.
•	Good replayability (new characters / loadouts / mutators)
•	Controls on gamepad take some time to get used to, were not really convenient for me
•	Dying does not feel punishing at all: I died mostly during the boss fights, and then I would respawn with full hp, making it much easier. (Counter argument: there are different difficulty levels which make the game more challenging, but respawning still remains the same)
•	One playthrough is extremely short (might be an advantage for some)
•	If Joystick is connected, it will be shaking (even if you are playing from keyboard)
I personally suggest playing the game with mouse + keyboard, but apart from the gamepad controls and dying, there’s not much else. Other than that – the game is awesome. I absolutely love the game and really recommend grabbing it right away. I’m serious. Never have I been as positive about suggesting a game as this time. Hell, my girlfriend liked the game and she normally avoids arcades with lots of shooting like plague.

Disclaimer: Do not buy this game if you do not own a gamepad.  The mouse support is about as bad as it gets.  I use kb/m whenever possible in third person games and I had to use a gamepad for this one.
Enslaved is a well-written and satisfying-but-simple spectacle fighter with a heavy story emphasis and some minor puzzles.  It is a post-apocalyptic adaptation of a classic Chinese novel "Journey to the West."  There are several nods to the original story, such as the names of the main characters which may interest those who have read the book.
The writing is excellent for the most part and acted very well.  The game manages to be both serious and humorous while telling the story and rarely feels out of place.  My one issue is the way that the two main characters Monkey and Trip meet.  The meeting should be the biggest source of conflict in the entire story, yet it is glossed over and forgotten within a minute.  It reminds me a lot of the criticism aimed at Tomb Raider 2013 and Far Cry 3 for how quickly those main characters got used to killing people after leading normal, peaceful lives up to that point.
Gameplay is pretty simple and definitely nothing groundbreaking.  The game is a simple yet satisfying spectacle fighter with simple one-button traversal mechanics.  You also need to solve a few basic puzzles to make it through some levels.  It is quite easy even on hard difficulty.  Unfortunately the game makes use of seemingly randomly-placed fixed camera angles that can easily confuse the player and will sometimes make your character immediately walk back through a doorway after entering a room.  The other big issue with the camera is during combat itself.  It likes to jerk the camera around randomly every time you attack and zoom way in so it's impossible to keep track of enemies other than the one you're attacking.  It may also cause motion sickness.  It's a stupid design decision chosen just to make the combat more flashy, as seems to be a common problem with spectacle fighters.
The game has a nice art style, but average last-gen console-quality graphics.  I find that this is enough to hamper the art style in what should be a very beautiful game, which is very unfortunate.  It still has its moments, but it would be an absolutely gorgeous game if the developers had put any effort into the PC port.
Speaking of the port, it's just about as lazy as it gets.  The mouse is treated like a joystick and is given a deadzone when you go into aim mode, just like Dead Space.  It's basically useless and I found it unplayable.  Graphical quality is limited to low/medium/high though it thankfully has a separate toggle for motion blur which looks even more fake and ugly than most games.  There are no graphical enhancements for the PC version.  Button prompts always show controller buttons even if you don't have one plugged in.  The game has a custom mouse cursor, yet the mouse doesn't work in menus.  The one good thing about the port is that the game uses Unreal Engine 3 so it runs very smoothly and will handle 120/144 Hz flawlessly with only a minor config tweak.
So while it's far from a perfect game, mostly due to poor and outdated design decisions and a lazy port, it's quite fun and a great story experience.
The Premium Edition on PC also includes the Pigsy's Perfect 10 DLC.  It turns the game from a simple-but-satisfying story-focused spectacle fighter into a sub-par stealth/cover shooter starring a fat, disgusting, misogynist pig on his quest to build a robot girlfriend.  Seriously what were they thinking?  Thankfully it was short.

Enslaved: Odyssey to the West was a game that I had always heard was good, but I had never known anyone who had played it. When it went on sale recently, I decided to snag it. Boy am I glad I did!
The story of the game is quite interesting, as you play a Prince-of-Persia-esque character named Monkey who is enslaved by a girl named Trip to escort her home through the American wastelands. The two have an interesting relationship with one another, and the cutscenes/in-game sequences make playing through Enslaved worthwhile alone.
The graphics looks great, I played everything on maxed out quality at 1080p without a hitch. The voicework was amazing, and was surprised to find that the great Andy Serkis lent his voice to the main character. Gameplay mechanics, while function spledidly, can become somewhat repititious, especially during combat. Upgrades and a few special moves help keep things fresh, but towards the six hour mark of my eight hour playthrough, I was looking forward to the platforming sequences and not the combat.
I would recommend this game to anyone, whether or not it was on sale, but if you can find it on sale, pick it up now! You won't regret it!

Even after 16 years Homeworld remains the king of the RTS genre. Tactically complex, beautifully imagined, and now lovingly restored for modern systems, it has lost none of its charm or fire. The new textures, sounds, and effects are stunning and the gameplay holds up as if it was new this year. If you're a fan of games like Starcraft, Dawn of War, or Supreme Commander you owe it to yourself to play Homeworld. If you're a fan of Homeworld than the only reason you should be reading this is because you're waiting for the download to finish.

An epic score, three dimensional RTS mechanics that remain unmatched, a superb hard science fiction plot, a great art style, and now with the visuals to match.  It's as good as you remember it being... and that's certainly good enough.

It's Homeworld 1 and 2 with allot of new paint (especially the former) so I will just state the good bits and bad (mostly linked to HW1).
Good bits:
Salvage vettes work just as well as they always have... possibly a bit too well(I nicked every single corvette the Turanic Raiders threw at me... if the Standard Corvettes could salvage, neither they nor the missile vettes can use their special abilities, I'd be set for life but as is I gotta keep a 12-16 strong wing of "nice ship you have there...shame if someone were to.... enlighten you of it".
Even on medium settings the game looks magnificent, both cutscenes and regular play, and the gameplay of Homeworld 1 is fully intact.
Not much else to say, it does everything right almost.
Nitpicks:
1. My biggest problem with Remastered is that in Homeworld 1 you can no longer choose to play as either Kushan or Taiidani nor can you alter the paint scheme. The former can be excused, with ample applications of salvette, but the latter is a bit aggravating as a veteran of the original.
2. The cutscenes, both between missions and in-game, in Homeworld 1 seem a bit faster than the original versions... it's nitpicky but it kind of feels off to me slightly.
3. The streamlining of Homeworld 1 in terms of screens (no more separate build or research screeen from the normal one) though welcomed in certain regards also makes it a bit painful to macromanage everything. In the original the gameplay would pause when you were in the other two screens ergo it is a bit missed somewhat.

Rose tinted glasses is a risk with the 'golden oldies'. Homeworld was a fantastic game back in the day, and to get that out of the way immediately: It still is.
So, I recommend the game. But it is worth knowing ahead of buying that it is not a perfect game. It looks like a 2015 game. The game doesn't play like it, though. The campaign has a great story, but it has an unforgiving side and as your fleet stays with you throughout the game, it can be punishing or require loading. In that regard it's quite 'oldschool'. That is not necessarily bad - or good - but is something you should be aware of.
As for the multiplayer, there's some region limiting that can be worked around, but you don't get more epic space battles than multiplayer Homeworld. Nothing even compares.
I note that a lot mention bugs. I haven't run into any, for what it's worth.

This is a great tool, hjowever, it is a tool whose intent is usually misunderstood by the people who try/buy it.
This is a tool for 3D artists, not regular schmucks. It has a very small starting pool of assets that is there not to actually use them (although you can) but to familiarise yourself with the system.
The actual purpose of this tool is to give 3D modelers and artists a quick way to reuse assets by making everything modular.
Why bother making 6 different models with the same uniform? why bother going in there and editing the models individually every time? Just export the uniform and import it in Fuse, then you can apply it on pretty much anything, change materials, change shapes and so on.
It relies on your own abilities, and needs you to be able to create your own assets, which to people like me is an immediate showstopper, but can be great for someone with the right skills.
Bottom line: This is a great product for ARTISTS. If you think this is going to be "I am a strong and independent programmer who don't need no artist", you are sorely mistaken.
Still, it'll allow you to make some passable proof of concept models for a prototype or even some passable models for games where you don't look to closely at the characters, like an RTS or a top down game of any kind.
Must buy for small teams, in my opinion, adopting it now will save you hours of work down the line.

I'll likely update this review with more information as I dive further into the game, but as it stands, Factorio feels a whole lot like a really in-depth mod for Minecraft, but top-down. It's kind of like your standard survival-crafting style game that's so popular at the moment, but instead of base building being your priority, automation is.
You start from the bottom with absolutely no form of automation, and your goal is to gather resources manually, so you can eventually build an elaborate series of machines including auto-miners, conveyors, chests, electrical wiring, electricity generators, etc... To gather your standard resources as efficiently as possible. On top of all that, you have to also build up your defenses, including weapons and armor for yourself, and automated turrets for the portions of your factory that you're not currently at, in order to defend from randomly appearing waves of enemies that vary in difficulty.
Better yet, the game isn't even remotely difficult to get a grasp of. The single-player campaign is basically a series of easy-to-understand tutorials, and whenever you feel you understand enough of the game, you can quickly start up a fully customizable sandbox-style game.
The community for this game has existed for quite some time prior to its release on Steam today, so there's plenty of massive mods you can download and mess around with whenever you're finished with the 100s of hours worth of content the vanilla game promises to offer up.

Just a brief history. Dark Echo is a brilliant mobile game that managed it's way to Steam. The game is minimalistic at best and was created in a short 48 hours for Ludum Dare's Minimalism Contest eventually placing second place. Out of 1600 entries. This is a much more refined and improved version.
This game creates horror and suspense, being one of the most creepy games I've played so far, all while retaining it's simplicity.
The game starts  out by placing you in the footsteps of a blind person alone in the dark. It doesn't give you a clue where you are, what do you encounter and who are you. It is all up to your imagination.
See those red lines chasing you? You don't know who they are. Could be a monster, a zombie or maybe even a serial killer. It is all up to your imagination to find out.
The only clue left is the game's engaging soundtrack - dripping water, doors, creaking bridges, the growling of monsters - it all provides an engaging experience and feel to the game when you play it with headphones, which is recommended by the developers.

and has a farly unique feature to it: Slow-motion!
You can literaly toggle slow-mo for the match and get time to think, aim, or whatever, by pressing a button.
The weapon-designs, and the generell selection are good:
The weapons are detailed, but fit the look of the soldiers. You can select from 9+ primary, and 3+ secondary weapons.
You also have 3 slots for grenades, support packages and rocket launchers (which take up 2 slots).
The Maps are well-designed, and you can add workshop-maps, so you basicly have a LOAD of ground to cover (literaly).
The four modes, Point Match; Batallions; and Spec Ops, Haunted, have good concepts, although spec ops needs a workover.
Now that the community can make their own weapons and maps, you have so much more to do and discover.
Evreything in all the game is great (at least to me) and worth the money!

ADHD Version: Don't buy Ravenfield unless it's $10 or under in its current state. There isn't enough content in the game to justify it being $15, however it is fun for what it is (just not $15 worth of fun). It shows potential, that's it. Wait until there's more content, or wait until the price drops to a more reasonable level.
Full Version:
This game shows promise for what it may be able to achieve by the time this game is no longer considered 'Early Access'.
It runs really well, which is to be expected with these graphics, and that's really great for gameplay purposes since I can have hundreds of Computer players without framerate drops. Speaking of graphics, they are very unique and adds to the charm of the game. There's a wide selection of weapons to be used as well as vehicles (that take a bit of time to learn how to control it right) and land weapons like cannons. There's a lot of potential for modding capabilities as well. However, that marks the end of all the good I can say about this game.
There's not enough going on in this game to justify it being $15 on Steam here, in other words you're paying for more than there actually is in-game. It didn't even go on sale during the Steam Summer sale which is rather annoying. In its current state, Ravenfield is just a promise of a lot of great things to come. Maybe give it a year and it will be worth $15, possibly more.
So in conclusion, wait until it's on sale, costs less in general, or has more content to justify this kind of price. Other than that, Ravenfield is awesome.

Just finished the game, and I've got to say, it was fantastic.  I was worried coming into it, because I read a lot of reviews and forum comments that said this was a game "on rails", completely linear and therefore, terrible.
Well that's just wrong. Sure, it is a linear game, but I thought there was still enough exploring of the areas you went though that it was open enough. Just because a game isn't an open world/sandbox game, doesn't mean it's bad. As for the game being on rails? I read a review that said the game babied you, showed you exactly where to go and what do the whole time, but in my case at least, that wasn't true. There was a few times in the game I was stuck, and not because of a bug in the game, but because I was stumped. And when I figured out to do, it was a slap to the ol' forehead, but that type of puzzle platforming is good to me.
Now on to combat: There is some criticism to be made, because outside of "boss" battles, there are like 3 or 4 different types of enemies you will fight throughout the game. Once you learn the best way to take each one down, combat becomes easier, but I still died my fair share of times in the game, trying to figure out the right strategy for the certain environment/enamies I was dealing with.
The combat system is not cut and dry though, even though there are limited combos you can learn in the game. But the different combos come with the upgrade system, as well as many other "perks" that you sometimes find in games like these. Somewhat similar to the Batman Arkham games "perk" system (Only other recently played game that has something like that, so it came to mind).
Last word for combat: It's freaking awesome feeling and looking to finish off a group of mechs, they've got some great animations for the final kill. And that's not to mention the cinematics of the boss fights/finishes.
Now where the game is really great, is the story. That's what got me to buy the game regardless of the negative reviews/comments. I saw a lot of good reviews/comments saying that the story made the game worth it. I honestly didn't think the rest of the game was as bad as people make it out to be, but I will agree that the story is fantasic. It really isn't the best story ever, but it's pretty damm good, and what makes it even better is the feeling you will develop for the characters in the game. I can't even get into that part of it because of spoilers, but if you like a good story with engaging characters that you develop bonds with, then this game is probably one that you will enjoy.

With only a couple of hours of this game under my belt at the time of this writing, I whole-heartedly recommend playing it. For a game I've never heard of prior to its release on Steam, I've enjoyed my time with it more than most major titles I've purchased here.
I'm unsure of how to phrase this without comparing to other well-known series, but as far as gameplay goes, the movement and combat feels a step up from Assassin's Creed(a game which obviously had a bit of influence on this)'s repetetive combat and oftimes cumbersome parkour aspect. Combat here feels fluid and unpredictable, but more importantly, makes you as the player, feel powerful.
As far as characters go, Monkey (that's you) and Trip (the redhead) are one hell of a dynamic duo with a great story pushing them forwards. Once again drawing comparisons to other popular games, Trip is Monkey's Elizabeth (ala Bioshock Infinite), with the added bonus that your life is almost literally tied to hers. Upon their meeting in the prologue, Trip enlists Monkey out of desperation using a headband that wires directly into his brain. Along the way, it has its bonuses such as providing him with a HeadsUp Display and forcing him to obey her commands under threat of death.Slowly, but surely the two bond in their journey to return her to her home. Their dynamic is only buffed by the spectacular voice acting for both characters and flawless animations bringing them to life. Elizabeth was a great companion, but if you want a friend you can really grow to care about in your games, play Enslaved.
Also, the game is ♥♥♥♥ing gorgeous. Beautiful scenery and character design.

Let me say that the blue thumbs up here is more of an "acceptable vs. the competition" than a "10 out of 10 must buy!".  On the contrary this is niche software that I would only recommend to people looking to quickly make unique characters in bulk.
Before we get to pros and cons let me elaborate on my previous statements.  ACCEPTABLE VS. THE COMPETITION:  honestly there's not much competition in the standalone 3D character creation market, the most notable being DAZ3D and MakeHuman.  DAZ produces very high quality characters but the costs and licensing are a huge turn off.  MakeHuman is free and open source, but making more than a basic model requires a fair amount of research and experience.  I have found Fuse to be the most user friendly option, with ideal quality levels for realtime use, and a decent range of content, at a reasonable price.
RECOMMEND TO PEOPLE LOOKING TO QUICKLY MAKE UNIQUE CHARACTERS IN BULK:  If you only want to make a few detailed characters with unique features and apparel, you might become frustrated with Fuse's selection and limitations.   However Fuse is great for making groups of characters with enough variety that each will look unique.  I suppose a good example would be a party with 20 guests, nobody wants to hand sculpt 20 models, but you also don't want to reuse the same generic background character 20 times. 20 unique characters can quickly be made with Fuse, and the party wont look like a clone convention.
PROS:
Ease of use, the UI is simple and clean, pick parts with the click of your mouse, customize with sliders, easy.
Balance of quality, the meshes are game optimized while maintaining enough detail to be used for close ups.
CONS:
Exports static objects, this is my main gripe with Fuse, your purchase allows you to customize T-posed models only.  I'm sure just about everyone reading this is intending to pose and/or animate their characters, which requires skinning and rigging.  You can do this yourself in a 3D modeling program like Blender, however the process is tedious and sort of defeats the purpose of using a separate character creation program.  The creators of Fuse conveniently offer an auto-rigging service for the price of $50 per model.  Admittedly you get 2 free auto-rigs per month with the purchase of Fuse, the above 20 party guests example would either cost $900 or 10 months to complete, and suddenly DAZ3D's pricing seems less absurd.
Limited selection, you can make humans and zombies, and you can clothe them in modern business/casual attire, Fuse also has a few torn bloodied clothes and a handful of medieval outfits.  If you wish to use something like sci-fi or military clothing you'll need to create the models yourself in a 3D modeling program and import them into Fuse.  There is a fair selection of substances, however there is no support for importing texture images (.png, .bmp, etc.) so to get custom textures in you'll need to use Substance Utilities (Google it).  However the skin substance is non-replaceable, you can make the skin any color you wish and adjust settings like age and freckles, but it will always have a fleshy texture.  If you want to make a model with lizard-scales, or metallic skin, or such, there is no way to do that in Fuse.
In short, Fuse is great for producing T-posed characters in modern civilian, medieval or undead fashion, everything else will require further investments of time and/or money.

This game is definitly not perfect but is a definite step up from the original launch. There are still some bugs such as ships traveling through land and siege engines being stuck in the open. The AI can sometimes keep moving it's units back and forth until you attack but i have noticed that with all the total war titles.
The AI is much better on the campaign map and will hide its units for an ambush or fortify defensible areas against attack. It is very aggresive and will show no mercy against newly captured and unguarded cities. ALWAYS destroy all enemy armies before advancing. The AI on the battlefield is not as bright as on the campaign map but will always hammer your archers with a cavalry charge from the back even if it means scuicide. It will also attempt to surround you and try to outflank you instead of a head-on assault.
The graphics are very well done with a couple of odd textures. The units move smoothly and are visibly tired and will run much slower if tired. Siege battles are well done with one walled city to a province and 1-3 unwalled towns within the province. It provides a good balanced between sieges and assaults; although most of the major battles will take place in the major cities.
Units are varied very well between each faction but wiht the same style of units per culture or related factions. Each unit types has major advantages and disadvantages: the spartan hopolites and pikeman for example, are superb against cavalry and frontal assaults, but are tightly packed and vulnerable from flanking, archers, or siege weapons.
the tech system is completely different from any other total war and is not the best. It splits into two parts: civil, and military. The trees are poorly done and are not deep at all. there are usually only 2 braches per section. If you like the family systems and ruler systems you had in previous total war games, you will be disappointed. There are no families or even rulers, it is all about holding political power among your faction. Having your balance of power too low or too high will result in a civil war and many army stacks appearing at your capital. You have gravitas and gerontens. It is pretty confusing at the start but once you get the feel for it it becomes easier.
Overview: Rome 2 is a huge step up from the original launch and has a very well done AI. There is a great balance between walled cities and small villages and unit types are very well done with weaknesses and strengths. The political are tech systems need a total makeover but could work in the future.

Broforce is that special kind of games that combines one’s love for classic 8-bit run & gun adventures with 80’s action films then adds a small dose of all things ‘Merican.
While titles like  Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon pay homage to the cheesy sci-fi B-movies of the 80's, Broforce pays its respect to the action films that defined the early blockbuster era of cinema. The story follows evil terrorists, aliens and demons as threaten the peace of the world, so America dispatches Broforce to Americanize them.
The gameplay is simple; a Bro is dispatched to a country and tasked with liberating it. This is achieved by killing the terrorist in each stage and the devil boss followed by raising the American flag. Players must also rescue a Bro who has been captured by the enemy — this unlocks new playable characters while adding an extra life. To overcome the challenges of each stage, players have to use the Bro’s special ability to their advantage. The destructive levels along with the many opportunities to set traps allow players to embrace their strategic imagination.
Overall this is an example of why indie games have become so popular in the last few years. It’s a reminder that all it takes to make a good game is a unique imagination along with a some nostalgia.

As "pretty" as Black Mesa looks, it's core changes make it a less fun more boring and repetitive game.
Let's be honest, it's impossible for Black Mesa to be better than Half-Life. It's got it's flaws, but when you have a masterpiece being compared to the remake...
Visually, it's dull. Ton of dark greys, lots of blue, coloring problems here n there, and it's on the Source Engine, which has neither the early technology charm of Half Life 1, or modern day acceptable graphics.
When I put "pretty" in quotes, it's because while yes, the game had a graphical update, it's artistic value is some of the most dull I've seen. I put some blame on the Source Engine. It's impressive what this lil engine can do, but it's gotta go, we need an update. 2004 is when HL2 came out, every game on that same 13 year old engine, has the polygonal "Ews" and texture quality "meh"
Artistically, the game appears to not care about color schemes or layouts. I can remember many sections of Half-Life because of the artistry involved. They did everything they could to immerse you without taking you out of the experience. Every action had an immediete response. It was fast paced, snappy, fluid, and responsive. It kept the player within the game at all times by not making them wait, or if they do, then they have something within it in the mean time.
Black-Mesa, takes it's time for "cinematic" purposes. This is one change behind the mentalities of the game. On one hand, you have a game with a story apart of it, and tight memorable level designs and situations, and gameplay. On the other, you have a bunch of fans trying to make a dream game, without fully understanding the game's original perspectives, even if they were to try their own thing, it's not as good as the original because of the obnixious "new-age" outlook on the game. It's going to happen with fans obviously.
Oh boy, while they got a few guns well updated, most look less interesting. I think it has to do with trying to make the gun models look like those boring "high quality cool" guns you see in Half-Life gun mods. They have no real soul in them, they're just high quality for high qualities sake.
Artistically, Half-Life's guns are immediete, you can decipher them easily at any point just by the model and texures.
In BM they're all black and boring, besides the revolver, which they did well, that and the glock.
Half-Life, did have guns that weren't incredibly accurate, but were still just point and shoot. Black Mesa is aswell, and the gunplay between the two comes down to preference. I still feel like Half-Life's is better, but I'm calling my bias on this. I prefer shooting at someone and the bullets spread, but still hit him. Like a shotgun I suppose not good at explaining it, and in BM it's just not as satisfying to gun down enemies, but they
the crowbar, never had a problem with it, tho at one point it felt like the range was too short, either got used to it or was some odd glitch.
While I understand the changes to level designs, the new designs show off the core differences in developer mentalities between OriginalValve (pre-HL2) and the BM team. Meaning oh boy comparisons!
The level design is less free flow, and doesn't try to improve from the original in layout, so much as emulate it, whilst wanting to change it. It's not an easy line to walk, but most people just choose either or. Or else, you get a mixed bag, unless you really know what you're doing, and everyone's on board.
Personally, I'd prefer that if they were to change the level design, that they make changes using hindsight of the original's flaws and strengths. And to be fair, there are some great moments, but there's alot of downgrades from the original. You gotta do longer or less fun things to progress, and within the first levels, you can just feel the missing elements of Half-Life.
If you're not going all the way, then you should adapt the game's charm, feel, atmosphere, theme, life, mechanics. and layout.
This doesn't mean copy the game point for point, but update the themes and life of the game. Tho do note, that I'm not saying they're "bad" just not as good.
Black Mesa feels like a mixed bag, because on one hand, I see a team that might actually be pretty competant, but held back by Engines, design mentalities, team not on the same flow, and indecisiveness, I also see those compromises pretty much everywhere, there's an artist behind these changes, that's not completely on board, at least that's my perspective. Not putting them down, but I feel like ma and pa are arguing again when playing this.
The changes don't change alot, but they affect game feel.
Now follow me here, you know how in Half-Life you could beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of corpses and they'd explode?
Shooting enemies feels emptier in this game than the Half-Life, not sure what it is tbh. At face value Half-Life's gunplay should feel more empty, but Black Mesa just makes enemies react less, physically and FX wise.
The Gunplay is different, enough to notice and feel.
The level design is different, enough to notice and feel.
The models and lighting are different.
The voices are different.
It's nice to have change, but they never expand or improve via hindsight. Remember, every part of a game is important. And it feels like some stuff is still fuzzy in that department.
Models looks weird and offputting. Design removes and changes without improving.
7/10, I see great potential behind this, but as of now, I cannot write much more, I am tired and may update this to be more cohesive. At any rate, it's not a bad game or buy, but it felt amateur and misguided. I believe the team should go through and make changes for the better, instead of trying to stick as close to the game's layout as possible. Adapt and improve, not change and remove. blah blah.

This game is ultimately one of the best games I have ever played, considering that this was a remake of 1998 Half-Life and that the team at Crowbar Collective added more to the base with their own creative vision and freedom. This is what Half-life is supposed to feel like. Horrific and dreadful with a terrifying atmosphere, you play once again as Gordon Freeman and you come across hordes of zombies, unsuspecting alien attacks and the relentless HECU marines all in an attempt to stop you in your tracks, as you witness the aftermath and death of several innocent scientists and security guards that were caught in the crossfire of hostiles that come their way.
This game, the Half Life games in particular, probably a few even more is not like any other mainstream shooters. It doesn't hold your hand and you have to figure out things the way you are supposed to be as a scientist. Minimalistic hud, no dumb texts or messages floating around your screen telling you how to play the damn game and pointers telling you to pick this up, pick that up, press that button, pull that lever, go here, go there go the f*ck where the game wants you to,
. This game is gonna make you scratch your head as you figure out a puzzle, and you are meant to get stuck at levels and it is only up to you to figure out how to achieve such an objective. It's brilliant. It's no CoD. There are no cutscenes, and there are no QTE's to ruin the flow of your game. It's all up to you as a player, to play the game as you want. Of course, the game is linear, but the best part is this game makes you feel like as if you're exploring a huge world, and it is designed that way. You have to look for clues, look for ways here and there on how to reach or get to a particular spot. And I tell you, this is what makes a true game. It's all by yourself to figure things out. Perfect.
It's about time that I've let go some of these mainstream shooters. Of course, I still love some of these particular games, they're probably designed to be causal and all for fun, but this game is one hell of a beautiful experience. Thank you Valve for making such great games in the past, and thank you Crowbar Collective for making their formula even better.

Much better than I anticipated.  I love smashing things up with Monkey.  Controls are slightly clunky from the animations, but that doesn't stop the fun!  And, this game has one of the most awww moments in gaming history when Monkey carries Trip on his back.

The Good:
* nice looking locations
* great color palette
* interesting characters
* good facial animation on Monkey and Piggy
* interesting story setup with the PC getting enslaved by the companion
The Bad:
* shoddy PC port, random 5sec hangs, glitches that require Alt-F4, audio in cut scenes can get out of sync
* bad looking facial animation on Trip when it gets emotional
* platforming is 100% linear with no sense of exploration
* some actions and dialog bits get overused a lot
* a story that doesn't know what is wants to be about and changes tone completely numerous times
* extremely low number of NPCs, so you never get much world building
* the game never really develops the enslavement theme, it's there in the beginning, then completely forgotten, then returns in a WTF twist ending
* frustrating checkpoints
* restrictive camera makes it often impossible to look around
Despite numerous frustrations with the PC port quality and some bad game design choices, the overall game still leaves a pleasant impression. When it flows it's a lot of fun, the world is nice to look at and the banter between characters is interesting. But one can't help to see this as a missed opportunity, as the story never really develops properly, instead it just jumps around and big issues from the beginning are kind of forgotten soon after or they pop up again in ways that completely contradict the earlier setup. It would also have been nice to have more freedom exploring, as all the platforming is just jumping from one glowing ledge to the next, fall death is impossible, so you can do it basically blind.
The included DLC "Piggy's Perfect 10" turns out better then the core game, as the new player character comes with numerous new abilities that allow much more variety when it comes to defeating enemies. It's story doesn't really go anywhere, but is told in a consistently funny style.
