Enslaved: Odyssey to the West hit consoles in 2010 and while many critics praised it, few bought it. Those that did sang its priases but the game ended up being a huge commerical flop. This was a game with some notable names involved from a studio which had disappointed many with their sophomore release, the PS3-exclusive Heavenly Sword. Alex Garland, who had previously written Heavenly Sword and was also has a varied film career writing the likes of Dredd and 28 Days Later, was joined by Andy Serkis who was coming off his amazing mo-cap performances as Gollum in the Lord of the Rings trilogy.
Based on the legendary Chinese novel Journey to the West we play as Monkey, a grizzled but powerful man with a shadowy past but with tremendous agility and combat ability. He awakes on-board a slave ship where prisoners are being taken to a mysterious place known as The Pyramid where they are placed under the control of ancient machines that had rendered Earth a desert wasteland. The ship crashes however, allowing Monkey to escape along with a young women named Trip. Fearful of what this man might be capable of but still needing his help Trip fits Monkey with one of the devices that the slaves on-board the ship had so that she can prevent him from hurting her and force him to help her get home.
What follows is a lot of Prince of Persia/Uncharted-esque platforming with puzzles, a lot of hand to hand combat and the occasional bit of third person perspective shooting. While these styles of play were already well-worn in video games and some might find the gameplay a tad repetitive this game has some truly special things going for it.
First off, the story is excellent. Monkey and Trip both grow as characters, warming to each other and becoming friends. Their odyssey is an interesting one which while not featuring many other characters always keeps the player aware of the stakes, helped enormously by great voice acting from Serkis and Lindsey Shaw.
Graphically, this game still looks great four years later. I am not too sure just how much upgrading was done for the PC version but it looks great in no small part due to the excellent art design. The main characters are realistic and every aspect of this game has been tuned to perfection. I took more screenshots of my PC playthrough than I have any other game I've bought on Steam and that's because this game is GORGEOUS to look at. A four year old game with great art will always beat a 2014 game that's the same dingy browns and greys that many "blockbuster" titles serve up today. To further assist the great story is the cut scenes feature absolutely superb facial expressions and reactions. Quantic Dream may brag about how realistic their characters look but Enslaved features scenes where such grief is communicated just by looks and expressions between characters, it's heart rending and amazingly impressive.
Between the fantastic performances, a compelling story and a beautifully crafted look and feel to the game, I can't recommend this highly enough. Not to mention the inclusion of an active and non-annoying companion character show Enslaved was truly ahead of its time especially after the praise that Bioshock Infintie and The Last of Us would be praised for doing similar in 2013. It is funny to see features that other developers would tout years later that Ninja Theory acheived here. This might truly be the most overlooked game of the last console generation and even though Namco nixed a sequel after poor sales the game lives on with the fans. Playing Ninja Theory's Devil May Cry suggests that they have not forgotten either as little visual touches, not to mention a painstaking attention to detail, reminded me of Enslaved as I played through DmC.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anybody looking for a good story, strong voice acting, and a sense of style and artistic creativity you just don't see very often in mainstream games these days.

Good game but rather short. Count on about 10-12h to finish it.
The story is quite classical but the end is very reminiscent of old SciFi movies. Gameplay is console-type, with combat from a gamepad, with possible combos/chains. Character development is nil aside from upgrading your attacks.
You actually only get to play Monkey and you have a limited control, only occasionally over Trip.
There is no real choice and no sotry branching. The rare decision you have to make is "do I try to sneak those mech or do I rush and fight them ? ... considering sneaking them will likely fail and I will end fighting them anyway ?"
Special mention to the crashes during chapter transition. It happened to me four times. Fortunately, it crashes *after* saving your chapter completion. But it's still annoying.
So why did I like it ? The visual are real nice. The post-apo world has its own identity, the feeling of having survivors tracked by relentless mechs, slavers. I actually enjoyed the two main characters. They are cute on their own, strange way.
The game is built like you would watch an action movie. The story unfolds, you are going through it. Objectives on timer are probably the most entertaining because you have to do it fast. Combat against bosses is also entertaining because you never have to simply bash through a bag of hitpoints (you actually can't defeat them that way), there is always something to defeat them, strengthening the "action movie" aspect.
The story is finally well summarized by the title : a journey to the west. Which is a promise to find answer, or to get revenge, to give sense to all of this.
It's good entertainment while not stellar. If you can grab it at a low price, on sale, it's worthy.

I love this game! I bought it off their website, so it doesn't show my hours played on Steam.
You'll build a huge factory with a major issue being getting resources from the output of one part of the factory to another. There are many different types of manufacturing pieces. And all of it needs to run on power.
It becomes a perfect example of what spaghetti code looks like, and organizing and thinking through more elegant designs is a major theme.
Carbon footprint is also an issue, as burning more coal eventually generates enough pollution to attract the local wildlife, which will tend to want to eat you and your lovely factory!
Driving the whole progression is the technology tree.  The goal is to build a rocket to get off the planet.  But the technologies take exponentially more resources to research, and building the resources creates an exponential complexity of your factory.  It will twist your brain into a pretzel!
-------
Update after many more hours:
I walked away from this game for many months, as the amount of content was overwhelming, and the game felt a little burdensome.  So I quit.
Maybe games like this feel like they are just too much to fathom.  But then recently I tried nosing around in it again.  So I will try to explain the progression.
First Few Games:
Learn to deal with biters and the basic mechanics.  Build really bad factories and be bombarded by continuous biter pressure.
Several Games In:
Try out a bus architecture (or be doomed to eternal spaghetti).  This is the game I'm currently in.  I'm finding the blue and green technologies work up to this point of creating an initial factory.
There are videos of people speed building with biters turned off.  They build gigantic sprawling factories.  But I don't care.  Biters are the initial games, so I try to design with no steam engines pure solar to reduce pollution, and a giant wall surrounding the whole structure.  I still haven't used trains.  Will I ever beat the game?  Who cares?  It's fun right now with this little thing I'm trying to work out.
Okay so back to the bus architecture:
There's more to say about busses, but... you'll have to find out for yourself.
Blueprints:
Blueprints are wonderful PROVIDED you carry modular armor and have a personal roboport.  See?  It's an overwhelming review by now isn't it?
Conclusion:
I can't explain everything in this game because even at almost 60 hours in, I've only attained maybe 70% of the content.  What is beautiful is that upon understanding the content that's just the first step.  Going back in and finding the right arrangement is what makes Factorio beautiful.

Note: I got this game months after it came out and had patches and ran it at around 55ish FPS at moderate or so settings, 1600x900p resolution.
As someone who loves stealth game, and enjoyed Dishonored despite some occasional clunkiness, this was a great followup. The plot is very solid- not perfect but fleshed out as much as it needs to be.
The ability to play as either Corvo or Emily, a decision you make before Mission 1 and lasts with you for the entire run of the game, affords different skills unlockable for each character, supporting different playstyles. Emily has abilities more conducive to a non-lethal &/or low-chaos run, while Corvo has more stabby-stabby, alarms-going-off, crossing-swords style.
Audio is pretty fine; voice-acting is non-cheesy most of the time and the graphics are really great if you've got the components to back them up.
Gameplay is enjoyable and combat is FAR less clunky than before. The new powers feel generally pretty sleek, strategically-open and flatout fun. The amount of routes and options available to handle different scenarios of travel, managing enemies present, and dealing with your final targets generally make you feel like you have a lot of choice, and I rarely if ever felt limited in my autonomy over any given situation.
The different playstyles (and the additional challenge of doing a no-powers run) add to replay value and, while it didn't exist until a patch added it in, I started playing post-patch and could enjoy New Game Plus, which is a feature that allowed for a ton of replay value for me personally. After beating the game and having a game-beaten save, you can use the NG+ setup to start over, select either Corvo or Emily, and now you have all the abilities of both characters available for unlocking, so your playstyle is unrestricted by character choice and is more broad/flexible by having the full-range of abilities at your disposal. You also start off with all of the runes you've spent on powers in the prior playthrough and are free to continually accumulate more through plays, meaning you could theoretically eventually start a run with all of Emily & Corvo's powers together. You also retain knowledge of any disenchanted / dissolved bonecharm you destroyed to learn the power of for later crafting. NG+ seriously amps the replay value here.

Dishonored 2 is an amazing game. The PC port is bad, but if you're willing to reduce your settings, it should work fine.
I found the world to be quite enthralling, and some levels, like the clockwork mansion, were brilliant. I don't get why people hate on the game, I really liked it, and I've played the first Dishonored at least 4-5 times over.
If you have doubts about whether or not your setup will run this, download the demo, and if you complete the second mission without a hitch, you should be good to go.

Play the free demo with the first 3 missions and you'll see if the game works on your system: I was a bit scared by some reviews saying it doesn't run smoothly on a GTX 1080, but I finished the game in high chaos and had abolutely no technical issues whatsoever. Stable 60 FPS, no slowdown or crashes to desktop.
If you liked the first one this is a must have: it took everything that was good in the first game and manage to improve on it. The level design is even better and combined with the spells offers a lot of replayability.  The universe is dense and immersive, packed with a lot of little details that gives life to it: notes, diaries telling the stories of characters you'll encounter during the missions. The way you play and your actions will influence what's happening in the world and how people react: the dialogues will change, and sometimes even the actions of NPC.
The only minor complaint I have is that some new weapons or gadgets would have been welcome. There are new options for the crossbow and the pistol (new types of ammo and weapon extensions), but other than that it's the same stuff that was in the first Dishonored. Also it would have been nice to know a little bit more about some of the main characters.

Short version:
I liked it. Despite what some people think, it isn't a clone of anything. Expect 3 to 6h to complete. Direct improvement of first ReThink game.
Long version:
For starters, I'll say I'm used to First Person Puzzle games, I like this genre. I completed Portal, Talos Principle, Magnetic Cage Closed, QUBE, Antichamber, and others, including ReThink (the previous game).
Now, the review:
ReThink | Evolved is, basically, a direct improvement of ReThink, as the name suggested it.
Core mechanic: you place various cubes freely (instead of on a grid-like structure for the previous game) to redirect colored lasers from their source to colored end points. Several types of cubes are there, from the basic "straight that way" to "split the colors", "source cubes" and a few others. In later tests, "shieldbridges" (toggleable bridges) will add some difficulty. Later again, you'll have to think the puzzles in 3D.
If you didn't like the floor-tiles puzzles from the first game, there are still a few in this one, but waaaaay less.
About the plot, "you have to do puzzles for some reason". Don't expect more than that. Not a problem, this game doesn't pretend to do more.
Now, pros and cons (at the time I'm writing this):
Pros:
- Solid core mechanic with various elements, keeps it interesting to the end.
- Annoying mechanics from the previous game are either removed or improved.
- quite long game, and sometimes you have to choose your path (two different sets of puzzles, happens 3 times). Expect 3 to 6 hours to complete it the first time, based on your experience with FPP games.
- Smooth difficulty curve.
- A working fidget spinner. Because reasons.
- Beautiful graphics.
- Beautiful non intrusive ambient music and sounds.
- Several options, especially for an indie game. Amongst others: FOV slider, detailed performance settings, rebindable keys.
- Currently available in 4 languages, only through texts (English, German, French and Swedish).
- Active developper, will fix small bugs within hours at most.
Cons:
- The fidget spinner falls on the ground when you take a cube, so you might lose it if you're not careful.
- No real plot, but that's not a real problem.
Now, is this game a clone of [other game]? (I remind you I know those games very well.)
- Compared to Portal:
- White walls: as any overly clean building, like labs, hospitals, some companies... Basic design.
- Lasers and cubes: Portal only has one type of cube with one color. There are more here, it's a direct improvement of Portal.
- Jumping pads: basic gameplay elements since the dawn of FPS games.
- Emancipation grids: basic gameplay element in many FPP games.
- Light bridges: agreed, for the concept. But it was either that or bring back the annoying cubes from the first game. Would be a shame.
- No-gravity areas: Portal funnels and the areas in this game are completely different.
- Portals: there isn't any here.
- Compared to Talos Principle:
- Blue and red lasers: in Talos, lasers collide. They. Collide. If you still think this game is a clone, I feel sorry for you.
Random rant:
- Your opinion is irrelevant, the dev is in your friend list!
Because I asked for rebindable keys in the first ReThink game, testing was easier with a direct conversation. Why would I delete friendly and helpful people from my friend list?
My opinion of this game isn't biased. I bought the game, played it blindly, and genuinely liked it.
Now, it's up to you. Want to buy it? Go ahead! Don't want to? Then don't. Have fun anyway. :D

Reviewer's note: I got this game through the Humble Bundle.
In the FPS world back in the 90s, everyone was trying to create the game that would take Doom's crown. Well, Half Life might have been it. This fan remake is using an engine that hasn't particularly aged well, and it's missing the Xen levels (although they're supposed to be coming soon, but who knows if we'll get those for free), but I would say that for any fan of old-school FPS games - or for people who are tired of modern, super-budget games which take only 4 hours to beat - Black Mesa is a mandatory purchase.
This isn't your typical run-and-gun shooter. If I described it as a "thinking man's Doom", I'm not doing it justice. This is an intelligently told story which escalates into a war between worlds. There are jumping puzzles, there are things to see and do. The enemies are typically terrifying. Importantly, in many places the environment represents a serious threat and you'll have your heart in your mouth while negotiating them. Unfortunately the game goes mental with such puzzles towards the end, but in the first half of the game they will inspire your dread.
Maybe this opinion won't be too popular, but I've always hated the weapons in this game. For an otherwise highly intelligent game, the gun selection doesn't seem to have been thought through very well. When you finally get your hands on alien tech, you get a glove which shoots hornets and you can throw little bugs which DON'T attack other aliens and will instead come back to you and wreck your day. Yep, you get a weapon that won't hurt most enemies but will happily kill you. There's even an achievement for killing bad guys with it. Even the Black Mesa team knew this weapon was bad.
Your best human military weapon for most of the game is a crossbow. Let's just think about this: a cerebral sci-fi game's best weapon is a CROSSBOW. This should explain why you'll come to dread the engagements which take place in the game's later chapters, where you will face gargantuan super-aliens and fully operational battle tanks (the game dispenses tons of ammunition and health packs around such engagements as compensation).
You will constantly feel under-powered. I think that's supposed to be the point. You're just a scientist wearing what amounts to Space Marine power armour.
Well, in spite of the weapon selection, which is by far the worst I've seen in a game, and the prevalance of annoying jumping puzzles in the late-game (save often!), this is a cornerstone of FPS gaming and you need it now. The good hugely outweighs the bad.
This game is a gem. Please strongly consider making a physical release. I want to add this to my collection!

They've added two new types of attacks, as well: Hyper attacks and Special attacks. You also get to play as two characters (almost) at once.

ENSLAVED™: Odyssey to the West™ Premium Edition on the PC is an infuriating experience (played on normal difficulty)
The game is only worth playing for the story, which is interesting, well told and the character animation is very well done.
Now the controls is where this game hits the floor, the camera goes bonkers during combat and the controls are not very responsiv. The aiming... , thank god the aiming reticule goes red when I am on target, because otherwise I would be lining every shot up for 20 minutes.
The most memorable part of the game was the first chase scene, because I died a lot - A LOT! and I did not even know you could skip the long cutscene that immideatly follows the previous checkpoint. Apparently they never felt the need to tell us you can skip cutscenes. BACKSPACE is the key that allows you to SKIP CUTSCENES folks. That combined with some bad decisions in the upgrade tree from my part (went everything into armor thinking it would keep me alive longer) made combat a nightmare made me curse out loud I closed the game because it made me angry and filled me with regret for buying this game, so I can't really reccomend this to other people.
Don't buy it - unless you like console ports and have massochistic tendencies - if you do buy it - play on the easiest difficult and upgrade your stun capabilities.

This game is pretty good. It's not the greatest thing I've ever played, but if i didn't own it anymore and needed to buy it again, i would. It doesnt bring anything new to the table, theres nothing i havent seen or done before in this game but its still fun and feels familiar. It's EXTREMELY good for the price i got it for during the Summer Sale, and would still not be a disappointing purchase if i were to pay full price.
The thing that stands out the most to me in the game is the level design, it's absolutely beautiful. The city of New York in a post-apocalyptic state overgrown with trees, vines and bushes. The texturing could REALLY use some work though. It all looks great from afar but once up close things arent quite as good looking, although that takes nothing from the game IMO. Gameplay > graphics no matter how you look at it.
Theres a LOT of environmental puzzles in a Prince of Persia type of way. Lots of climbing and jumping around on destroyed buildings and other things in the environment. That' one of my favorite aspects of the game, I've always loved that sort of thing. Prince of Persia is one of my favorite game series ever.
The storyline in the game is GREAT. I'm really enjoying it. I'm not going to talk about the story though, as i don't want to be the guy dropping spoilers in the reviews, that's always gotten on my nerves when people do that. The writers for this deserve a lot of credit for making this game what it is, because if the story wasnt enjoyable i think i would have already moved on to another game. There is a lot of games with the same style of game mechanics as this one, so a solid story is important in this genre to me.
The combat is pretty fulfilling, you have a decent variety of moves and such although it could use a little more. It reminds me a lot of God of Wars combat the way you fight in this game. The combat IS repetitive, though it hasn't felt like it was so far. You have this laser staff type thing, you can use it for melee combat and also to shoot energy projectiles at enemies. So far I've come across two different ammo types, a normal energy charge and then a stun charge but there may be more throughout the game I'm not sure. There is quick time events, but they're not very often and they're usually just a single button to press to finish off an enemy. Speaking of enemies, that's one thing this game could've use, more variety of enemies. You fight the same mechs over and over and over.
You collect red orbs which are used to upgrade your health, your shield, your combat abilities and your staff. To me that's always been kind of a generic way to fill in the spaces to give a game more content and another purpose of playing, but the game does not rely too heavily on this so it does not bother me. They are found just layting around in random places and they are dropped by enemies after you defeat them.
You have a female character with you at all times that is an integral part of the story, and you have to make use of her abilities to get through some parts of the game. You put her on your back an dcarry her through mine fields, she can create a decoy that attracts gunfire so you can get to places that have turrets watching, you can toss her up to palces you cannot reach for her to help you get where you need to go. Theres also other things you can do with her, but i'll leave that for you to discover.
Theres whole seperate campaigns in the bonus content section, i thought that was pretty cool. You can assume the role of other characters in the game and play through their stories. A nice addition to an already satisfying game. Would be great if other games did this also.
If i had to describe this game through comparisons to other games, i would say this is the lovechild of God of War, Prince of Persia and Assassin's Creed. The game is good enough to be placed next to any of those 3 and stand strong in competition with them, even though this is nowhere near as well known or liked.
I havent completely finished the game yet, but i feel I've played enough to give an honest, fair review and right now on a scale of 1 through 10 i would give this game 8.5/10
If you are a fan of any of three series mentioned above, you shouldnt hesitate to give this one a try.

Dishonored 2 is an amazing game. The PC port is bad, but if you're willing to reduce your settings, it should work fine.
I found the world to be quite enthralling, and some levels, like the clockwork mansion, were brilliant. I don't get why people hate on the game, I really liked it, and I've played the first Dishonored at least 4-5 times over.
If you have doubts about whether or not your setup will run this, download the demo, and if you complete the second mission without a hitch, you should be good to go.

Play the free demo with the first 3 missions and you'll see if the game works on your system: I was a bit scared by some reviews saying it doesn't run smoothly on a GTX 1080, but I finished the game in high chaos and had abolutely no technical issues whatsoever. Stable 60 FPS, no slowdown or crashes to desktop.
If you liked the first one this is a must have: it took everything that was good in the first game and manage to improve on it. The level design is even better and combined with the spells offers a lot of replayability.  The universe is dense and immersive, packed with a lot of little details that gives life to it: notes, diaries telling the stories of characters you'll encounter during the missions. The way you play and your actions will influence what's happening in the world and how people react: the dialogues will change, and sometimes even the actions of NPC.
The only minor complaint I have is that some new weapons or gadgets would have been welcome. There are new options for the crossbow and the pistol (new types of ammo and weapon extensions), but other than that it's the same stuff that was in the first Dishonored. Also it would have been nice to know a little bit more about some of the main characters.

The following are a few nitpickings:
1) As a stealth game, it doesn't utilize shadow like the Thief series does.
2) It restricts you from carrying more than three stun mines, though you can carry other stuff which you may never use.
3) The ending is disappointing in that you don't spend much time conferring with Corvo. It would have been nice if this father-daughter video sequence was a little more elaborated on. You just saved your empire and your dad, getting Corvo's reaction to that would have been cool.
Those are just nitpickings, Dishonored 2 is a fine sequel to Dishonored.

Now onto my problems with this game, there are two MAJOR problems that can be easily seen.
The company that issues this game seems to act like they do not care much for it or put in much time thinking when releasing game-changing updates. There are many gods that are just SO much better than other ones it is insane. Hi-Rez seriously needs to have a balance patch before they continue to add a god every month. If I had seen this game for the first time I would instantly think that is still in beta because of how poorly balanced some of the items and gods are.
Now the other major issue.
This is completely out of Hi-Rez's power, but it still needs to be said. The community for this game is just plain atrocious. The people are awful. I've seen first hand when someone didn't do so hot in a game, a teamate will try to convince other people to report them for INTENTIONAL feeding of the other team, when it is obviously unintentional. This is even worse in the ranked gamemode because the second someone dies on your team, 9 times out of 10 a person will go "You rock!" in a painfully sarcastic way.
Hi-Rez can easily improve this issue by implementing a dedicated voice chat in game, instead of having to download an external program that crashed on most computers.
I'd have to give it a 7/10.
I encourage you to play this game with friends so you don't need to deal with the community.

This is a lovely looking game with great character design and animations. The backdrops and scenery are wonderful and breathtaking. Unfortunately, the gameplay is nothing special nor is the story. You are shuffled along a plot that does not make very much sense and eventually doesn't even pay off.

This game isn't very complicated. It has no difficult puzzles or branching ways to accomplish your objective. You can either bypass killing mechs in a sort of sneak mode, or go all out into a berserk mess (my preference).
Where this game does shine, however, is in character development. We follow two characters throughout the game. Trip, a tech-savy teenage girl who is looking to get back home, and Monkey, a beefed up tank that ends up getting caught --against his will, no less!-- in Trip's journey.
While I was playing, I wasn't sure whether I would recommend the game or not. The graphics were good, imo, but I don't have too high standards if the story is worth it. As it happened, the plot of the story (in regards to the world's situation) didn't progress until almost at the end. The story of Trip getting home and the subsequent decisions she takes from there, however, were the main focus of the story.
As the chapters ended and started, you got a sense of the characters. The picture of their pasts gets painted little by little as they interact with one another. The relationship between Monkey and Trip starts rocky at best, then very slowly and very naturally, it starts to shift into respect, then friendship, then a sort of co-dependance that gives way to love.
So, in short, if you like character development and do not mind some romance in a story, you will enjoy the game.

Rome II is the remake of rome total war. It was released in an awfull and unfinished state back in september 2013 as happened with Empire Total War. But fortunately, the developers continued working on fixing the game, something that didn't happen with Empire. So, my review is based on the Emperor edition not the version of the game as it was on it's release day. It would be a totally negative review.
Pros:
*Great graphics ,detailed models and variety of the soldiers characteristics.
*It has some historical accuracy. (For history buffs like me it's not enough).
*The system which combines small battle animations in order to make impressive choreographies.
*The use of both naval and land units combined in battles.
*The ambush battles are Improved, the units aren't visible until they attack.
*There are already 14 playable factions in the base game.
*Two campaigns (Grand campaign and Augustus)
*New political system and civil war.
*Multi core support at last.
*Over 100 factions which act independently Instead of one rebel faction.
*The soldiers look less like mindless and emotionless robots. Especially when you hear them talking in the battlefield.
*The provinces system with the edicts that can be enabled in every controlled province.
Cons:
*There are still bugs.
*Most of the factions that belong to the same culture are more or less identical, they have just different colors instead of being unique in their own way.
*Some factions have a lacking unit roster which may cause trouble if you want to expand your empire.
*No family tree. It would be really awesome if the new political system coul be combined with the old family tree system.
*The transport ships system makes fleets loose a big part of their reason of their existence.
*The soundtrack is too generic and dull. I know, It's a minor problem for the majority.
*The AI is not the best of the series, but it still offers chalenge and fun.
*The agents are not really specialized on specific actions. They shoud be designed tso they would be useful in different situations.
*The naval battles are not really enjoiable as they used to be in shogun2.
*You can't build walls to protect your cities.
*The grand campaign map needs more cities and towns, it feels empty. Pelloponese for exmple has only one city on the map, Sparta, which means that if you control sparta you control the whole Pelloponese.
*The battles are too fast and there is no time for maneuvers.
More than a year has passed since Rome II's release and 16 patches have been released also, and the game now is in a great state but still it's not worth of paying 50 Euros, I believe it's price should be 35-40 Euros. I reccomend it to every total war fan. Also there are many mods that can satisfy every unsatisfied gamer.

After a fair few updates and fixes, and a few price reductions too, i finally decided to give this a go.
I can't say i'm really impressed based on my experience of the older total war games. Although the graphics have been updated a fair bit, they still look ugly beyond all belief, i know the graphics in rome 1 are primitive, when you look back, but at the time, they were impressive, and even now look acceptable. Whereas, playing rome 2, i just find the visuals extremely lacking, and this is even without considering the horrible zombie faces, which essentially effect anyone who doesn't have a high end computer. Soldiers turn into strange, gangly skeletons with ps1 level graphics, that look attrocious, and far worse than rome 1.
And this to me is the only 'strong suit' this game has going for it. It looks better. And in gaming, visuals are not top of the list, gameplay is:
And the gameplay of Rome 2 is no where near as satisfying as the previous titles. Enemy AI is still pants, unit cards still look all the same, choice of factions is pathetic, as most are now DLC, which to me is insane, as the core game costs less than some of the DLC right now, while the sale is on. I find that the teams are no where near as balanced either, in the first rome, it was possible to win with any faction, they were all viable choices. But in Rome 2, i cannot sincerely say the same thing.
Tid-bits: The music isn't as good, which is sad, as the first game had top-tier music, some of my favourite strategy music too, most strategy games for me have fairly forgettable soundtracks, but rome 1's was amazing, as was medi 2. But rome 2 has lost that, and just has generic bland battle music.
Voice acting is abysmal. I felt alot more invested in the first game thanks to that badass barbarian commander, and the battle narration. In this one, they all sound similar, and just have voices that sound like i did them, y'know when you get a friend and play 'voice actor' for a laugh, that's what this sounds like, not professional. In fact, alot of the soldier's battle cries were performed by the game's creators, who last i checked, aren't actors.
I can't reccomend this to anyone, if you're a fan of the old ones, avoid it, even in the sale, it's just not worth the bother.
And if you're new, go buy shogun 2, rome 1, or medi 2. They're a much better introduction to the series.

The Alien movies have spawned many games over the years yet none have duplicated the original film’s suspense, thrill and terror.  Until now.  Alien Isolation is a exquisite homage to the original Ridley Scott masterpiece.
The most striking aspect of Alien Isolation is the atmosphere.  Not only is the player filled with a constant sense of trepidation and terror, but the developers have created a setting that truly makes the player feel like he or she is on the original movie set.  Everything from computers, to space suits to the design of the ship and station is an outstanding recreation of the 1979 film.  The game oozes nostalgia and instantly connects to any fan of the original.
The graphics are really great and the game is Oculus compatible although I did notice some aliasing issues.
The story is fairly good however the length of the game can tax the players resolve.
All in all a great game I rate it an 8.5/10.  If you choose to buy it I also recommend the secondary purchase of an extra pack of drawers as you will need it.  I recommend Fruit of the Loom 100% cotton undies as they gave me the least rash every time I sh!t myself.

I must say that I love a good horror game dearly and I dont mean action games wearing the skin of a horror game
( Resident Evil 5/6, Dead Space 2/3, or Silent Hill Downpour and Homecoming)
Now it has been along time since a triple A, Big name game company made a proper survival horror that really put the fear into me and scared the♥♥♥♥♥♥right out. If we look at the history of video games based on any of the Alien movies we realize very quickly that the majority of them are absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥with nearly no redeeming features and more importantly none are scary. Believe or not the one company who's had the most attemps in recent years at making an Alien game is SEGA,
I really dont know how they still had the rights to work with the franchise after the awful Aliens: Colonial Marines game. Since all it seemed like they were doing was hiring people who grew up eating paint chips to design the games while♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥the master works of Ridley Scott and James Cameron. All that aside someone over at SEGA corporation must have stopped their decade long binge of heavy drinking and cocaine ingestion long enough to realize "you know what, why do we keep handing off Alien to developers that code their games by beating thier hydrocephalic heads against the keyboard and instead lets hand it off to some competent people to make a new Alien game!"
Enter a wonderful group of people known as The Creative Assembly best known for the Total War series of real time strategy which I am a fan of. When this first announced I was a bit perplexed by the idea that these guys would try to make a survival horror...well I sure am glad they did!
Breaking out of the mold of pervious concepts for a game based on Alien, The Creative Assembly made the bold chioce to ditch the "action pack" designs that came along with the world of Alien's (thats the second movie) and decided to focus on the Ridley Scotts Sci-Fi horror masterpiece...Alien. The idea of being alone and helpless in a confined space with nowhere to run or hide except for an empty cupboard and at any moment something may just snatch the life out of you. This is the feeling and thoughts I get when I think of Alien and not a bunch of meat head marines shooting off thier pulse rifles in vain screaming "game over man, game over!!"
So now that we have gone back to genesis things have become more interesting. 15 years after the event on the Nostromo, Amanda Ripley has spent most of her life trying to find out what has happened to her mother. One day an evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ from Weyland-Yutani shows up and says the flight recorder from her mothers ship has been found and they would like her to head off to a decommissioned deep space station and pick it up. That may sound like a pretty weak starting point in the story for some people but I say "♥♥♥♥ off and choke on a copy of Colonial Marines!" that piece of crap was just one long bad story so shut up!
Now then where was I....Ah yes so once we have made it to our deep space paradise we find ourselves in a very hostile  environment and the only thing you find to be remotely welcoming are scores of empty cupbroads for you to climb into, cowering in fear, thumb in mouth, praying to god that you dont sneeze at the wrong moment. If your lucky enough to pass the in-a-dark-closet-dont-sneezing test then you get to freely explore the ruins of Sevastopol Station by means of crawling along dark corridors on your belly picking up pieces of scrap so you can craft a noise maker out of a pair of busted speakers, duct tape and some copper wire...sounds like what I do in my personal time but anyways lets move on...
Now thank god the game isn't just centered around the Alien itself or else things mite get a little stale, there are plenty more to worry about. The andriods on the Station seem to have turned on the people living on the station due to a quarantine protocol  issued by the computer core known as APOLLO and have begun bashing in the skulls of anything with skin and a pulse ( boy this sound familiar) and I personally think they are more of a hazard than the alien. You will also get to meet the last surviving inhabitants of space station  and  boy are they sure glad to see a new face. So glad they greet you using the traditional paranoid-guy-with-a-gun method of trying to put one between your eyes.
God damn this place sure has alot of problems but all these factors add up to one hell of a true to life "I don't want to be here!! make it stop mommy" horror experience that I just can't get enough of, but be ready to commit alot of time to get through this game. Unlike other horror games where running is a very viable option Alien Isolation rarely gives you such opportunities and if you think for a moment that getting off your hands and knees and spriting towards the nearest exit is a good idea then I'll say your gonna end up prodded to death by a silver colored mini mouth 90% of the time.
Take your time, lisent to  the lovely sounds of foot steps by the stalking death coming for you and above all try to enjoy yourself!
Look I know I'm being silly here but honestly I LOVE THIS GAME!! the story,atmosphere,characters, game play mechanics are outstanding and most importantly the ALIEN. You can feel that it's alive and is living for the sole purpose of snuggeling up right to you and giving you the kiss of death.

Having played the original HW games, I can honestly say that Gearbox did an excellent job in modernizing the GREATEST space rts game of all time.

Homeworld Remastered, is a good example of how a remaster should be.  This game consist of all the homeworld games to date (except for deserts of kharak).  If you're an RTS fan, this is a big must-have to any space fans and RTS fans out there.  Full 3D control, no constricted to the usual 2d plain that some space rts games have.  A long, challenging single player with lots of ways to finish them.  If you plan on playing the campaign, good luck, the difficulty in this game can go from easy to insane in a short time, mainly depends on how large your fleet is on later missions.
Homeworld 1 Remake.  It has issues.  The biggest offended is the fact its just or feels more like a Homeworld 2 mod, but I guess its understandable, especially since they want all the races to be playable in skirmish or multiplayer, so they gotta keep them in the same engine.  The problem, a lot of HW1 features a missing.  So far they fixed some of them, mainly repair beams and I believe the harvesting.  All they need now is to brick back real time ballistics instead of an RNG chance system that homeworld 2 uses.  The other thing they need to fix is formations, luckily they're on the work for that, and the patch looks very promising.
Homeworld 2 remake.  Since the remaster is using the HW2 engine, anyone who played the classic version already know how the gameplay is.  To the newcomers, homeworld 2 is the result when a developer is rushed to release a product, before release, the story was  to be much more larger (look up Homeworld 2: Dust Wars) however despite this, Homeworld 2 has one of the biggest or dedicated modding community out ther, check the workshop or the HW2 MODDB if you wanna see.
The things Homeworld 2 improved upon is the gameplay and obviously graphics (look at the classic HW1 and HW2, the difference in graphics is big) and the remaster just makes HW2 (and 1) a lot more beautiful.
Gameplay is good, its one of the best an RTS game offers, especially with its full 3D movement.  In a multiplayer match, you can send your units downwards (or upwards) towards the opposing fleet, and they'll never know whats coming to them (especially since we're so used to the usual 2D plain in RTS games)  The story is simple in the game yet emotional, especially since the Race you play as is almost extinct (spoilers)  Multiplayer is great too, even if you go against AI, its still a blast, because of the gameplay, you may find yourself too distracted looking at whatever your units are doing.
tl;dr  Its a Must-have RTS game, buy it.

So an update to my review earlier.  So... it is Elder Scrolls and the story and questing is pretty decent.  I like the lore and all of that.  They also tend to have events for special days of the year.  Is the game worth a try?  Sure, especially if you are an Elder Scrolls fan.  Anyway I will list some of the good and the bad...
The Good
1. Not too grindy for leveling compared to most other MMOs.
2. Skill system is pretty decent.  Each class can use  magika or stamina based setups so one class can play like two or there different styles.
3. The music is nice.
4. The art looks pretty decent.  I like that it isn't that cartoony or anime-style junk.
5. The lore is pretty decent and at times hilarious.
6. The quests are like Elder Scrolls quests, not the... go kill 100 goblins and come here or...  run across the map to deliver a stupid note and then run back.
7. The subscription gives you a bag that allows you to have infinite space for crafting items and access to all DLC.
The Bad
1. Glitchy - They will release a patch or an event and it will break other things in the game.  A quest may not be able to be completed, it may break the dungeon queue system completely, you may lose items from your bank or inventory, etc.  They also seem to take a while to be able to figure out the issue and fix it... only to break the same thing again days or weeks later.
2. No "auction house."  This can be good or bad depending how you want to look at it.  There is no central store, instead guilds pay millions of gold to rent NPCs that you bid for every week that sell your items for you.
3. The game feels unfinished.  They allow players to make "add-ons" which is a nice thing, however, it feels like they did this to lessen THEIR work-load.  For example, the each feature at a trade guild's NPC is horrible.  You can't just search for the item by name and the filters really suck IMO.  You also don't have buff/debuff timers that you can see without bringing up a menu that takes up a large chunk of your screen and goes away when you move.  Unless you can time things yourself, you have to guess when you need to refresh a buff or debuff.
4. Balancing - Yes, it is an issue in every game to an extent.  However, these guys will let something sit at the top for 3-6 months if not longer before they over-nurf it.  If you don't run certain things you will have a much harder time or just be unable to do things.
5. Trait system - Great idea, except... most of them are completely worthless.  I feel they could have done a better job with these and making more of them viable.
6. Crafting - Making potions or food is alright, but making gear is a waste of time.  Currently, only one crafted set is any good for "end-game" content.  The rest involve grinding out map content or dungeons to acquire.  It takes a long time to be able to max crafting and research the traits and IMO its not worth it at all currently.
7. Animation canceling and insta-death - So you can use light attacks to cancel animations for skills to up your DPS because of how they designed the game.  No, I don’t think this was their intention but they have no way of fixing it.  There are also not really any "cooldowns" so you can sit there and spam most skills.  Sure, its cool for PVE content, but once you take it into PVP.  You can get skills off pretty fast.  Some glitches with their system, allow you to kill a player before the see you even hit them on their side.  No, it  isn't due to connection lag, it is a feature of their combat system.
8. My Issues with PVP
a. Doesn't seem like they care a lot about it.
b. It is a 3-for all instead of a1v1 or 4-for-all This leads to one faction or the other being "ganged" more often than not and even with good players you aren't going to be able to fight off two full armies so you pretty much quit and come back later once they took your stuff and start taking it back.
c. Insta-deaths and animation canceling in PVP as I listed above.
d. Balance issues as I listed above.
e. Lag in PVP is horrendous at times (sometimes in dungeons and the overworld as well.)  Your ping will sit at 90-120 and jump to 400+ randomly for no reason.  This is something anyone can observe sitting somewhere.  Also in PVP certain skills cause loads of lag and you can use them to kill groups of enemies.  While they are locked up you can run them over pretty much.
Anyway, those are my thoughts on the game.  Do I think it is the best game ever?  Heck no!  Do I think it is the worst?  Nah...  IMO probably and unfortunately, the best MMO out there at the moment and will probably continue to be because of all the crappy ones being released the past couple years.  ThePVEe content is pretty nice in ESO and the PVP is between alright and meh.  If they fixed their game up a bit it would knock everything else out of the park entirely.  I have put my fair share of hours into it.  I will continue to play it most likely until something better comes out (whenever that might be.)  Hope you find this information helpful.  If it is on sale give it a try.  Don't pay full price though.

Ok. So most positive reviews about this game are just jokes. This review is intended for those who want some actual info on the game. Broforce is a pixel-art shooter indie game that's main feature is the ability to play as a famous action movie hero. Each bro has a unique play style. Some of their weapons are similar, but still defer from one another. Their special abilities, which have a certaint amount of uses, are all unique and have varying effects. You fight terrorist, robots, aliens, zombies, and satan himself. The levels are well designed, and it's likely you'll get stuck on a few of them as the difficulty ramps up. Combat comes down to either an all out fire fight if you choose to charge in head on, or you can play stealthily and slowly work your way through the levels. Which technique you use heavily depends of the current bro you have. Extra lives are given when you rescue P.O.W.s and change to a new random bro. after so many rescues a new bro is unlocked. The gameplay is fast and chaotic and may be considered a con by some. Overall, and excellent idea with excellent execution.

It was quite good news to us that we were able to play co-op for the story mode and both players get to clear the story mode at the same time. However, this game has one serious bug in its co-op mode, which randomly freezes the guest player. The bug is killing almost all of our passion to keep playing the game because apparently this bug has been known since 2015 and it's still not fixed in August 2017! Something we found which seems to make the bug less likely to appear was that we suspect the bug was due to the map generation when both players are quite far away. We tried to keep our characters close to each other which seemed produced long lasting gaming experience. But anyone who plays this game in co-op mode knows that it's pretty much impossible to be sticking together throughout the gameplay, since several objectives require you to split and complete them seperately. It seems that Koei has kind of given up on patching this game, which is why I choose to give a negative review.
Despite my negative review on its online co-op mode, the single player experience is very solid. I have played Dynasty Warriors 8 previously and I'd say this game has its unique elements compared to DW8. The custom character seems quite fun and the survival mode is good place to easily try out wepons (a little spoiler or tips, you can simply switch weapons on your custom characters for farming weapons since your custom characters will maintain its levels depite having different wepons). There is still one thing I really hate about the single player, which is its controller support, in particular steam controller. Apparently just setting controller to xbox360 mode will not work so your controller needs to be mapped to keyboard in order to function properly.
Overall, it's a decent single player game, but a terrible multiplayer game. Shame on Koei for abandoning the support on bug fix for this game.

Enslaved is a mostly overlooked game by the developer Ninja Theory, the same guys who later went on to make the controversial reimagining of the Devil May Cry franchice "DmC".
It takes its inspiration from a classic Chinese novel, but places it in a post apocalyptic American setting. The premise is certainly intriguing, but the game is in my opinion held back by its weird gameplay decisions and annoying AI characters.
The gameplay is a mix between Gears of War style cover based shooting and Prince of Persia style platforming sections. It also has some melee combat for good measure. Enslaved pretty much mixes and matches different elements from different inspirations, but these elements really lack dept. Combat boils down to tapping a few different attack buttons and rolling away, while the platforming sections work with a context sensitive "platforming" button. You can complete pretty much 90% of all the platforming by just pressing up on the analog stick and mashing the platforming button. Probably the most refined thing is the cover based shooter mechanic, but it is also the one that feels the most out of place for this type of game.
The game is also totally relient on your AI partner characters, and the experience is very much on rails. You always have a partner character yelling instructions at you. This really makes the game feel like you are just a dumb monkey following instructions rather than figuring out stuff for yourself, which is ironic, because in the story you actually are ENSLAVED (get it!?!) by another person and have to follow his orders.
A lot of the game areas are decayed versions of actual American landmarks, and that might be memorable if you are American and patriotic or just generally like cool looking video game levels, but I kind of just breezed through all that not giving it much thought. The visuals of the game are very good and especially the character animations during combat look impactful. It looks like a decent PS3/XB360 era game. I had some minor problems with the shadows, but they might have been caused by some graphics card driver incompatibility rather than the game itself.
In the end I would probably not recommend Enslaved. It's an interesting game, but more so in a bad way. It has some bizzare gameplay elements that really don't work together and the AI character nagging and the blatant linearity of the game is annoying in an interesting fashion. If you really want to see Prince of Persia and Gears of War come together in an interesting game setting you might want to give this a shot, but the probability of anyone wanting that is quite low.

I find that the teams are no where near as balanced either, in the first rome, it was possible to win with any faction, they were all viable choices. In fact, alot of the soldier's battle cries were performed by the game's creators, who last i checked, aren't actors.
I can't reccomend this to anyone, if you're a fan of the old ones, avoid it, even in the sale, it's just not worth the bother.

I was cautious before buying Fuse given previous bad luck some Mixamo products many moons ago.  But Fuse is a good offering from Mixamo.  The bare bones:
Pros:
Easy To Use - I can't think of a 3D human generation program that's easier to use (even easier than MakeHuman).
Output - I can export to exaclty what I need to make the model work in Unity or Source.
Animation Variety - I'm not a fan of how Mixamo does animation, so I have many other animations I use with Unity's mecanim system.  The free model rigs are mecanim compatible with some settings changes.
Free Rigging - This is a huge deal for me because I am slow at rigging (can take me a day for one model), and Fuse does it in 2 minutes online.  This greatly improves my workflow, and you get two free per week.
Substances, Shaders, Colors - This is a great feature.  If you couldn't change the colors and substances of clothing, I wouldn't recommend the program.  This allows for variety with some tweaking.  This means you can have models wearing the same outfit, but it will look different because you can change the coloring/patterns.
Import Own Assets - I haven't figured out how to do this yet.  You can't just drag and drop (bummer).  You have to tweak your models and textures, and I just don't have time to play with it at the moment.  But I can imagine this being a huge deal later.
Free Animations - There are some free Mixamo animations online, and plenty of paid ones.  I think you can also request certain animations.  I don't use Mixamo animations, so this is kinda meh for me.
Cons:
Clothing Limitations: There's not much variety included.  There are only so many parts to choose from for body parts and clothing.  If you want a soldier, you have cammo tops and bottoms, but no helmet.  If you want chainmail and plate armor, I hope you brought your own to the fight, because you can't get it here.  I really hope they fix this, and start including more clothing options.  Otherwise, this program is going to become useless fast.
Overlapping Meshes - I know it's hard to get clothing meshes to not overlap, but I really expected more compatibility especially given the lack of clothing options.  For example, jeans and boots overlap each other, and the worst part is you don't have a lot of choice in the matter because you can't change the meshes of the clothing.  I think the program should allow users to change the clothing meshes slightly to avoid this problem.
Aging - Fuse has a rather humorous wrinkle overlay, and that is how you make age differences.  You can make your standard 20-30 something adult just fine, but you can't have realistic elders over 40, and no kids / teens in your world.  This needs to be fixed.
Mesh Limitations - If I want an Orc I shouldn't have to take the model into another program to alter it enough to look like an Orc, then bring it back into Fuse to rig it.  Nor should I have to take time to reformat my own model to bring it into Fuse, just to have it auto rigged.  This is my biggest negative about Fuse.  The whole point of having a bipedal humanoid model maker, is to include all these options inside the program.  If you can have pointy ears, then you should be able to have pointy teeth, droopy cheeks, knobby knees and elbows, etc.  There are sliders for almost every part of the body, but they are incredibly limited.
Overall, this ia a good program with A LOT of potential.  The list price as of the date I'm writing this is $99, but it's on sale for $49.  I really feel like $49 is what it's worth with all these cons I have.  So I don't feel cheated, and I would recommend this program for the indie modeler as long as it stays at $49.  If more clothing content is added, and the bulk of the cons are fixed, then it might be worth $99.  Especially considering that MakeHuman is free, and includes no clothing, substances, or free rigging.  So really, that's what you are paying for.

Youtube Review:
I've played this in alpha off Steam for quite a few hours and decided to review it here as well as it's actually a really original and very entertaining sandbox crafting game.
In essence, Factorio is an assembly line simulator, where you, as the only survivor of a crashed space ship, has to construct an entire factory-full of mining aparatuses, forges, smelters and so on in order to build a tremendous array of tools. As the trailer demonstrates, you can eventually create advanced weaponry, vehicles, trains and huge self running factories whose main goal is to support your industrial hunger.
I wasn't sure if I was happy about the 2D sprite graphics at first, but to be honest, it makes so much more sense to make this game in 2D rather than complex 3D as it makes it so much more charming and gives it this old-school Starcraft feel as well, especially since you'll get zerged by aliens a lot.
So here's a thing, there are a native species on the planet that don't really mind you as much until you start polluting the planet. As soon as the smoke chimneys go up and trees start dying, that's when you can expect to get your alien friends to come for a visit. Which is why you're given quite an arsenal of various guns and turrets that can be automated as well.
But in all honesty, this game is not for the weak of heart or mind. All of the resources are limited and you only get one life. If you die, the game is over and you will have to either reload an old save or start from scratch, depending on the difficulty mode.
Other than that, this game also includes an extensive research tree, a campaign mode with storyline and a very detailed tutorial, a puzzle mode where you are given limited resources or space to solve various problems and there's even multiplayer!
All in all, for the price, I think this game is definitely worth it.
In summary:
PRO:
original crafting dynamics
tons of tools
vehicles
goal driven, but also sandboxy
puzzle modes
multiplayer
good music
mod friendly
huge educational potential
CON:
graphics may be disappointing for some
combat is very simplified
challenging...actually this could be a PRO
no respawns (permadeath)

Let me frontload the message here: I highly recommend you buy this game! It's ridiculously fun.
Now, on to the details:
Factorio is a sandboxy logistics/resource management game, where you automate
the things. I honestly can't recommend this game enough; I've sunk several hundred hours into it already prior to steam release, and I'm sure there are a couple hundred more hours of gameplay to come.
The premises are simple, but they make for deceptively deep gameplay. Gather resources, create a factory with conveyor belts and assembling machines to automate processes.
If you're a min/maxing type of person, you can definitely get your fix on OCD'ing layouts and optimising for throughput. If you're an unorganised guy, you can spaghetti-conveyor-belt your factory to your heart's content. If you want to get your geek on, you can do all sorts of wacky logic builds with combinators, similar to Redstone in Minecraft.
The game is incredibly stable and well-optimised for an early access release. The developers have excellent interaction with their community on their forums, the subreddit, in Twitch streams, and with their blogs.
Factorio has great modding support. If you're burned out on the vanilla game, you can extend it's lifetime with overhaul mods like Bob's Mods and Dytech. And some “vanilla+” mods like FARL (Fully Automated Rail Layer) and RSO (Resource Spawner Overhaul) are absolute must-haves once you’ve settled into the game.
All in all it's a solid 95/100, which is incredible considering the game is still in early access. I warmly recommend it to everyone.

Fuse is a truly fantastic bit of software and a real time saver for anyone wishing to create a game, animated film / machinima or image which needs a convincing humanoid character.
If you were not convinced by the earlier versions you definitely need to give 1.2 a go. I did and was completely blown away.
The improvements are immense and the sheer variety of characters you can create with Fuse is now mind blowing.
Even a professional character designer will find this package useful, especially with the ability to import your own models for use as hair, clothing, accessories or even complete base character replacements. Fuse has become a one stop character workshop and inspiration tool.
The topology of the mesh is great, the UV Map is well laid out and perfect for painting on in an external app (3D Coat / Zbrush) with ready made high res, diffuse, normal and spec maps. The export settings can also be set to occlude hidden polys so you get a really efficient mesh if you have loaded your guy / girl / zombie up with loads of accessories. ( providing you don't want them to get naked in game - ugh what kind of game are you making freak! )
If you are not an artist or struggle with skin textures; the detail settings on the skin in Fuse are now ridiculously good. Good enough to be completely usable in a game or application without any further modification in an external app. Sun exposure, beauty spots, freckles, wrinkles, make-up... Everything you could possibly need!
Why start from scratch when you are pressed for time?
If you are an aspiring game developer wanting to create an open world / sandbox game like GTA which needs a load of background characters or a fighter like Mortal Kombat / Street fighter : You need Fuse! It will literally save you thousands of pounds and give you a much better chance of achieving your dream.
Pro's: Even if you do not plan on using the output (and you would be crazy not to), Fuse serves as a fantastic concept tool. How many times have you wasted hours of your life creating a character in other software packages only to fall out of love with it, change direction and bin it? Fuse is also great for fast idea generation, concept images and mock ups. I normally always start with a pencil sketch or a starter mesh in Zbrush or 3D Coat. Even the fastest sculptor will never be able to get to this level of quality in such a short amount of time.
The Algorithmic Substances in Fuse are gorgeous and they have done some amazing work on the skin shader.
Just buy it!
Over and out.

As a huge fan of Bethesda's, Elder Scrolls and Fallout games, I waited off buying Elder Scrolls Online as I read it was a completely different experience from the single player games I was used to (also thee subscription was also a big no-no).
As games like Skyrim are so well know, I will try to compare this to that, as a lot of people like myself might be confused at how this game will play when compared to it. I have never played many MMO's except for Runescape when I was younger, and so I cannot say whether this is better for you than other MMO's.
The feel of the game is very much the same as the rest of the Elder Scrolls games, and the world is exactly what I would have wanted as you can now explore many different parts of Tamreil than before, seeing the home of the different races, and therefore getting more backstory and feel for the differences between races.
I feel the biggest difference this game had from Skyrim was the combat system, which in skyrim was very 1v1 and had a more difficult feel when groups of enemies appear. Its almost as if the scale of the combat has been changed, as now you can fight hoards of enemies and much more interesting 'bosses'. This I suppose is more like what MMO's usually do, but the skyrim combat allowed for more interesting tactics like stealth, whereas ESO has less of that.
Another big change is the crafting system, which in ESO has a huge assortment of different options. For weapons and armour you now chose the material, quantity of material, style and trait. This allows for many more combinations of weapons and armour, but is a steep learning curve go through until you fully understand what you are doing. But this allows you to make armour in any material which is styled to your race (or any other race if you'd prefer). I remember in Skyrim and Oblivion, making dwarvern or elven armour which looked good, but looked aweful on some races and roles, whereas this new crafting system allows you to make a bigger variety of styles to suit your needs.
As well as weapon and armour crafting you also have provisioning for food (which is actually useful for once) which gives you 30 minute boosts in health, magic or stamina. There are literally hundreds of ingredients which you can use in hundreds of recipes, and for a while you struggle to find the right ingredients, and fill your inventory with useless ones. Gradually as you find or buy more recipes you will get this under control and will reduce the amount of crap you feel you have to carry; around as someday, 200 berries might be useful!
The alchemy is very much the same, however uses an additional item to decide on whether you make a potion or poison, and what level they will be.
The enchanting is a bit weird, and seemingly complicated as you have to chose three runestones for each enchanting glyph which you then add to weapon/armour/jewelry.
These three runes decided on first the level and strength of the enchantment, the effect of the enchantment, and then the quality. So you will end up being confused by the weirdly named runestones, but once you use them it tells you what they do and you will have enchanting figured out.
The multiplayer aspect of the game is a weird one, at some points quests say they are solo only, and some are just quests you and friends can decide to do at the same time, however some require a group of 4 to play, as the dungeon areas will be leveled to a group of 4, so on your own you might struggle a little (a lot). Luckily there is also a feature to do these dungeons with randomers in a group finder, so you can still play ESO completely even if you are the only person you know who has the game.
The subscription (ESO+); which I don't and have never had, seems to only add in features to make things a little easier. You will get a small boost in xp and gold gained, and will get some other handy features like an unlimited crafting bag, so you can carry around hundreds of berries without worrying about a full inventory. The main benefit is being able to play all the DLC whilst you have ESO+ and also you get some crowns every month which you can spend on purchasing anything you want, either the DLC you want to have forever, or and other things like pets, mounts, apparels.
It is worth me saying that I dont feel I NEED to get the subscription to enjoy the game, I rarely ever consider it, other than when I fill my inventory (which happens regularly), as there is so much in the game that the extra quest lines aren't needed for a veeerry long time.
In summary, the combat is on a bigger scale, the world is gigantic and gorgeous, the quests are what you are used to in Skyrim, and the crafting is complicated, but allows a huge amount of possibilities if you want that. I definitely recommend the game to anyone who loves and other Elder Scrolls game, as long as you are not looking for a sequel, as this is definitely NOT the same as Skyrim, but takes Skyrim, and blows it up into an MMO, which adds in a bunch of good things, but also takes away a lot of the simplicities. The only complaints I have are the sometimes very unreliable framerates, and the annoyingly easy to fill inventory, but these are minor problems in an overall great game.
Too me most epic start for a ES. It still has some work to do but I believe Skyrim can be this game I would love it more. Keep the updates coming we need ESO:Skyrim dlc

When I first tried Elder Scrolls Online, I wanted to cry. The beta and launch should have by all rights been complete disasters, and they were for the average Elder Scrolls fan. It was a terrible experience without any hint of fun. Needless to say, I never thought I'd visit it again, even after certain factions like the Dark Brotherhood or the Thieves Guild were added, cause I didn't believe they could have fixed the game.
Later down the line, they provided a free week to try out the game and everything they had changed. I was kinda impressed, but there was still one thing that really bothered me and that was the progression curve and structure of areas. You were not able to explore at all, ever. You would find monsters too powerful for you if you tried to freely roam, even if you were "technically" prepared. Despite my momentary enjoyment I still thought the game was not worth the time and effort.
Then came the big E3 announcement. "One Tamriel". It basically said that. if you want to explore, do it! Only your gear stops you now! Needless to say, I got excited. I see no way something like that could fail (except if you hire a bunch of monkeys on typewriters to code for you, but surely they wouldn't do that), and with the new price drop and Gold Edition, it seemed like the right time to get in the game.
What I never realised is that the DLC areas already used a system similar to the upcoming "One Tamriel". Once I went to said areas, I was able to for the first time geniually have fun in Elder Scrolls Online. Who knew that making a good and unique game that caters to your fans instead of copying unrelated others would work, right?
Long story short, I'm having fun playing it, slowly going through what it has to offer. And if the upcoming update is even remotely close to how the current scaling works, I'd say you'd be missing an amazing experience if you didn't give it a try.
The only "serious" downside to it are the microtransactions. They are a bit too much in your face with an in-game store. Though credit to the art and UI design teams, cause it doesn't really feel like it's taking the immersion out of it, for me personally.

Enslaved is a fairly traditional third person advanture game.
It claims to be an homage to the Chinese novel -Journy to the West. I must admit my research was minimal but I found that the homage is mainly the three main characters. Their personalities and visual design. The plot doesn't seem to be emulating the novel, other then being a journey in the western direction.
The visuals are where the game shines. The post=appocalitic world it depicts is beautifull even it it's utter devestation. Toppled buildings are sprinkled with lush greenery, invading the ruins of man's fallen empire. Billboards, while whetherd with age, still display their colorful messages brightly. And the animation of running, loping, jumping and swinging is just perfectly executed.
The plot is the standard post appocalyptic sci-fi. Monkey and Trip escape the clutches of a mysterious hostile empire, which uses the technology of the old world to conquer the new. There's a bit more under the surface, but not much.
The relationship between Monkey and Trip is relativly interesting. She controls him through a metal headband that compells him to obey her (the same technology used by the antagonists to enslave humanity), echoing the magical thightning crown of the Chinese epic. But slowly they develop genuine friendship and affection. Although there's a bit of a twist there as well.
I liked the game. The gameplay and plot are solid even if they are not particularly inventive and the visual style is trully marvalous.

Aside form some wonky controls and a camera that can get on your nerves sometimes this game is an underrated game. Trip is smart and real and Monkey is just cool. The story is awesome and if you haven't played it do it.

The combat is in the same vein as God of War and Devil May Cry, but it is very simplified and has limited combo options. However, the combat is still entertaining and is not what this game is about. This is a very cinematic experience with many cut-scenes and progressing through the narrative adventure is what really keeps you going.
Aside from the the monkeyman that you play as (aptly named "Monkey"), I felt that the characters were designed very well, and again the voice acting is great across the board. Animations are smooth and satisfying, and the environments are beautiful and detailed.
The writing is pretty good, except for a few small things (e.g. "EMP pulse" is redundant) but if you are able to look past the minor flaws in this game, I think it is definitely worth your time.

This console port doesn't bring anything new to the table that would make it a great video game.  So, without game mechanics, you've got to fall back on characters, locations, and story, which is another name for 'a movie'. That's what this game is: a movie interspersed here and there with the usual action-game features. There's a rail-shooter, there's cover mechanics, there's blessedly few quicktime events. There's a few puzzles and quite a bit of platforming, and a few races. The controls are good, but you might end up fighting the cinematic camera more than you'd like. There's also a frustrating lack of affordances in the world -- although wall-grabs are easy to identify, it is impossible to tell which ledge is the one you're supposed to jump off of.  Your character will spend a fair amount of time balking at obvious jumps.
Combat, when it happens, will mostly devolve into button mashing. There's nothing too complex or new, here, and you won't become frustrated because you can't get the 16-button long sequence of button pushes to get the one move that works.
Instead, this game is remarkably forgiving, and lets you play along with the story and with the characters. And that's where this otherwise standard game shines.
Andy Sirkis voices and acts the main character with the unfortunate name. He lends his character a gravitas that sometimes seems missing from games. There's real character growth going on, here.  When you mix that with a world that is beautifully realized, it all pretty much works.  If you are a fan of the old LucasArts adventure games, like The Dig, but want a little more action to go with your story and characters... if you want some better visuals, then this might be the game for you.
Saving happen at save-points, and while there are a few with terrible placement, they're generally pretty good. There's about 10 hours of play in here, but Piggy's add-on is worth another few hours of play and might actually be more fun than the main game.  I think I paid $20 for this, and I feel no regrets at that price, although I can't help thinking it would be a better weekend rental than a purchase.  Also, like most console ports, this is probably best played with an Xbox controller.
