I really wanted to love Dark Souls 2 and I feel that I've given it more of a chance simply because it is a Dark Souls game and let me just say that it isn't a bad game at all.
Control wise I don't really have any major issues with the game, it seems to want you to roll a lot more than using a shield but thats about it really.
Graphically the game still looks nice, animations are improved and there are more small effects this time around, the issues as mainly with the art design and attention to detail which seems lower this time around, its a shame as this was what give Dark Souls its look and set it apart from Demon Souls.
Challenge is where the sequel really let me down, the original was such a fine tuned instrument that its easily broken and DS2  does seem to be broken in this regard, but only just. There is too much of everything in this game, items, enemies, bonfires, secrets and bosses that the game would need hundreds of hours to get a basic handle on most things, the original asked you to spend time but it never demanded this much, also enemies seem to hit a lot softer this time around, they telegraph their moves a lot more and constantly track you until the final swing making them dumb homing missiles which only really allows for one or two techniques, most enemies also seem to share move sets so your going to get very used to certain types of enemies, they have tried to add a few surprise moves to enemies maybe to balance the issue but all this does is seem to annoy and feel like cheep shotting you. Even early tough monsters like the ogres have an odd sit down attack that once you see it makes killing them childsplay where as before that they could grab you even if they had clearly missed their attack.
I recently went back to play DS1 just to see what the difference was and its like night and day, enemies hit harder and faster, telegraph a lot less and only track on the wind up which makes fighting very satisfying, I got a little scared fighting a dark night again early game and he nearly killed me because I tried to wait him out DS2 style and he literality went to town on me and I had to remember to be evasive and aggressive again.
NPCs seemed boring to me in DS2 they really did seem bored to be in the world themselves and the only character I remotely liked so far was Gavlan, who obviously wheels and deals!
Level design isn't as bad as a lot of people say its just that the original was nearly flawless almost all the way through, and this time around its just OK there are a few issues here and there but its the difference between the two which makes it pale.
Covenants seem less exciting this time around even though I wasn't really into them much in DS1 they did seem to add a little something to do after end game and had some interesting rewards, this time around it seems as though they tried to intergrate them more but they seem even less rewarding than in the original.
I'm not a huge fan of the stat system that runs through both games and feel a more streamlines system would have helped the game immensely, that could be just me though but I found leveling in both a bit dull and avoided it if I could, that said DS2 seems to encourage it a bit more in this game and I do feel it has been slightly improved over the original.
Multiplayer has improved for co op while the pvp aspect seems worse, its a lot easier to get help to fight all the various bosses, I would say its been a bit too easy to do so making bosses a cake walk if you wanted them to be, I don't know how playing with friends has been as I don't seem to have any :-( sob, but the game feels more friendly now. Pvp doesn't seem to exist properly and when it does seems really unfair one way or the other with the bell tower and blue guardians being examples, I don't see why From doesn't just let all enemies be hostile or non hostile to give pvp some balance and introduce some small arena areas into levels, pvp didn't work well in the original and now its worse I think. I know that Soul Memory annoys a lot of people and I do agree thats its unnecessarily complex now, DS1 let you go heavily equipped against new players as long as you kept your level low, I have done it, it is funny doing it to other players ie lvl 15 chaos fireball, it isn't fair but it would be easy to just make an equation which works as level vs equipment and be done with it.
I think I rate the original DS1 8/10 with a unique recommendation to play over some 9/10 games.
I rate DS2 for me as 6/10
For me DS2 has turned into a dungeon crawler packed full of items and content where you fight monsters, collect treasure and then rinse and repeat for hours and hours and hours, this game could have been made into a MMORPG. Its slightly more frustrating than it is challenging and it doesn't improve on the original enough to justify using the Dark Souls brand.
It seems the game designers went for quantity over quality and it shows in lots of little ways, some people may prefer this Dark Souls and I'm sure they will appreciate the vast amounts of content and the challenge in their own way, however it doesn't make it a better game at heart and even if I preferred this version I would still be rating it the same way.
I think we will be waiting a while for a true successor to the Challenging Fantasy Action game throne. CFA for short!

Dark Souls 2 is what I would call a spiritual rehash of Dark Souls minus the amazing atmosphere and vivid game world. I originally recommended this game as something worth playing, but after the release of Scholar of the First Sin I can no longer do so. I think a more appropriate name for that version of DS2 would be "Dark Souls 2: The Game We Promised You Last Year, This Year.
Pros
+ Smoother combat.
+ Prettier graphics and cloth physics.
+ Improvements to humanity, equipment durability, and weapon upgrades.
+ Excellent DLC experiences.
Cons
- Comparatively bland game world.
- While gameplay is smoother, enemy attack tracking is blatant and unapologetic.
- There are a ridiculous number of gang-up bosses, and a notable shortage of memorable fights.
- The best experiences are limited to paid DLC.
- Soul Memory PVP matchmaking, where the number of souls you have accumulated throughout the game (whether spent or lost) is used to determine who can get matched with you.
The improvements to Humanity are the most notable upgrade over Dark Souls. I spent most of the first game hollow because there were no apparent benefits to being human, I was immune to a sizable population of griefers with noob-crushing PVP builds, and I didn't need to use 10 points of humanity to be considered "fully human."
Dark Souls 2 has reversed the system, and adjusted it so that there are only benefits to being human. You can be invaded by PVP attackers whether you are human or hollow, and while there are multiple stages of hollowing (which further decrease your maximum health,) there is only one stage of humanity. Being human means you get access to co-op summons, an increased item drop chance, no health penalties, and you're less ugly.
The worst part of the experience was how many of the bosses were groups of enemies rather than a single, formidable enemy. The Bell Gargoyles and Ornstein and Smough from the first game were memorable because they fell outside of the norm. In Dark Souls 2 many of the bosses are otherwise-bland enemies that appear as standard mooks later in the game, and most of their challenge comes from trying to keep them all on-screen at the same time. This makes for some very boring and tedious fights, and only emphasizes the lack of imaginative boss characters that really make a lasting impression.
Lastly, the DLC is bittersweet in its entirety. It has some great boss fights and interesting areas to explore, but it reeks of a Prepare to Die Edition clone. Sinh, the Slumbering Dragon? Hello, Kalameet. Sir Alonne? Hello, Artorias. This doesn't go to say that the fights are exact copies of one another, but there are enough similarities in the movesets to irk me. I just think is says something that the most enjoyable parts of Dark Souls 2 are the parts that are the closest to mimicing Dark Souls.

Imagine your walking through a prison, water up to your knees, you kill three hulking behemoths. you feeling good, full health, suddenly a crazy zombie throws himself at your feet as you try to stab him in the face with your sword, but your sword... doesn't have the right hit boxes to hit something on the floor. Now your dead because he exploded. Your like well imma take a break before i go and recover all my souls. Now your dead again, killed by the spawn killing crossbow ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s at the bonfire you spawned at because you forgot about them. Now your souls are gone, but with a vengence you come back and make it just a little bit farther. This is dark souls 2... at times. I've played both dark souls and demon souls and loved em both, this new addition to the series improves on somethings and takes a step back in others. Combat now adds a duel weilding stance that is intresting/cool. It adds more variation/immersion to combat and can be very effective. Lances are one of the new additions to the weapon list and they're great for PvE. I love the game but below i discuss some of the things that aren't so great (updates might eventually fix some of them though).
PvP some say is better but i think the PvP was better in dark souls. It's more accessible and easier to get into, which is better but the pvp itself I think is worse. Why? Well a lot of things aren't viable. I almost never see someone using a katana or regular sword, instead lots of cheap tricks are used- ranging from super deadly dark magic to the machine gun like crossbow, both of which can one shot you. On top of that the hit boxes are messed up. Magic that looks like it completely missed will hit at times. You'll also miss things that are right in front of you when you swing your sword or even hit them from a metre away like magic. People stagger a second after you hit them, which when your using a dex build that relies on speed can really mess you up. When their greatsword smacks you in the face despite the fact that you've cleaved through their body you'll feel the BS that is stagger delay. There's also some pretty bad ganking (having to fight multiple people which for all intents and purposes results in an unfair fight) like the other souls games but it can be fun and it feels great when you put those kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s down.
PvE has taken some steps forward but you can still cheat your way out of almost every situation (a lot of the times with range attacks) which gets very tempting when you're getting killed over and over and over... anyway if you play legit and find the right people in pvp this game is great. If you play this game be prepared to fall off cliffs and die in some pretty $hitty ways (you will be punished if you're not careful at all times). No way can i say this is a bad game, it has some faults, but i can overlook them for all for the great content, good combat, and lots of customization this game has to offer. Thanks for listening and i hope you take the time to enjoy this game as it's one of the best rpgs out there.

Total War Rome II is a decent game mind you, but not a good one.
I never really played the previous Total War games so I do not come from that perspective, I come from have playing mostly Paradox games from the overall campaign overlook and just various other RTSes for the battle perspective. I felt as if in this game a lot of my actions aside from actual militaristic movements were useless and even militaristic movements feeling often times just "Gotta change the buildings and then move onto the next city." Coming from a person that played Paradox games before this game seemed to lack consequence to the actions you take.  In EU4 if you annex a province in the HRE, you just get every single member trying to destroy your very being. In Total War Rome, I annexed the entirety of North Africa and nobody cared.
Aside from just that though, there is so much else that feels like it means nothing. My connections to generals literally means nothing, I can just go for the guy with the biggest stats and lock him in, nothing past that. Basically speaking, you can play the entire game without looking at the political screen of your nation. As a huge fan of CK2 it feels that interpersonal relationships and dynasties mean nothing in this game, and that is because for the most part it does mean nothing. Or what about those missions you occasionally get but you probably just complete because it was a part of your plans anyways, or that mission that you just don't do because you don't care about it, because there is no reason to care about it.
Then once you're ahead by enough, you can easily reach the point when you doing battles is literally pointless outside of personally want, in my eyes why fight a battle when you will win it without wasting the extra time? The whole game feels like it is unpolished and not done, because it is not. This game as I simply put is not a bad one, it is just definitely not a great one and mostly certainly not worth putting 60$ into. It's a stretch to say that this game is even worth it when it is 75% off. Though this game, like many Paradox titles suffers from the fact that a lot of DLC that should be in the game is just set at a price on steam. Though by no means do I like paradox for those actions, I do feel like the DLC that is bought on those games actually is an addition to the game, not just another factor within what the game should already be.
So in summary the game lacks meaning nearly every action you take in the game, and the goals the game sets for you are equally meaningless. You can get much better games that display far more mechanics and usually more in-depth as well.  It is also not worth anywhere near 60$, it's not a polished game. For a game to justify that much money it has to be something that was actually cared for and this was not.

Yep, I'm reviewing this. Yep, I love it. Yep, I hate it even more than I love it. Fuse is an ingenius software for creating characters, the only problem is, how the hell am I supposed to use that? The characters are uploaded to their site, then you can download them into blender, and voila. You have a model. But you can't use it, unless you're used to making models all the time, because the process of making the character usable in games, are terrible and makes you wanna kill yourself. So. Yeah. Great software, no use for it.

My background: I'm a 3D generalist with several years of experience working primarily with Maya and secondarily with 3DS Max and Cinema 4D. I also draw comics. I was interested in Fuse as a tool that could speed up character modeling for both animation and comics references.
It's a great tool for quickly roughing in your characters, and there's a pretty great spectrum of body types that you can create. Personally I'm not into purely heroic-type characters, although you can certainly easily create them with Fuse. For me, the real test is how well it can create "average" and "imperfect" people. It does a fine job. It's particularly useful for me, because I also have the skillset to further tweak and adjust the models in the 3D software of my choice.
Some reviewers seem to be frustrated that Fuse cannot do everything perfectly for them, without having to have any skills as a 3D modeler. To me, that seems a little unfair. In a matter of several minutes I can create a character that's pretty close to what I have in mind. That cuts out hours, if not days, of my previous workflow. Having a couple of automatically generated rigs free each week is a reasonable value as well. If I need more than that, I can either pay for the autorigging or I can rig them myself. Like I said, it is pretty reasonable if you have some skills established working in 3D. I was also happy to see that there is a free custom script available for rig controls for Maya.
One feature that I'd like to see included in the future is a facial rig of some sort, whether that be by including bones for the face or generating a set of blend shapes. I understand Mixamo has a face tracking package that works with your webcam, and they provide a guide to the blend shapes that it looks for. It would be really cool if Fuse could generate those automatically. The interface in Fuse does include a few sliders for adjusting facial expressions, but doesn't include a basic set of phonemes for mouth animations, for example.
Overall, it's a nice value and I would highly recommend it for other people like me who already have some proficiency with working in 3D.

As a huge fan of Bethesda's, Elder Scrolls and Fallout games, I waited off buying Elder Scrolls Online as I read it was a completely different experience from the single player games I was used to (also thee subscription was also a big no-no).
As games like Skyrim are so well know, I will try to compare this to that, as a lot of people like myself might be confused at how this game will play when compared to it. I have never played many MMO's except for Runescape when I was younger, and so I cannot say whether this is better for you than other MMO's.
The feel of the game is very much the same as the rest of the Elder Scrolls games, and the world is exactly what I would have wanted as you can now explore many different parts of Tamreil than before, seeing the home of the different races, and therefore getting more backstory and feel for the differences between races.
I feel the biggest difference this game had from Skyrim was the combat system, which in skyrim was very 1v1 and had a more difficult feel when groups of enemies appear. Its almost as if the scale of the combat has been changed, as now you can fight hoards of enemies and much more interesting 'bosses'. This I suppose is more like what MMO's usually do, but the skyrim combat allowed for more interesting tactics like stealth, whereas ESO has less of that.
Another big change is the crafting system, which in ESO has a huge assortment of different options. For weapons and armour you now chose the material, quantity of material, style and trait. This allows for many more combinations of weapons and armour, but is a steep learning curve go through until you fully understand what you are doing. But this allows you to make armour in any material which is styled to your race (or any other race if you'd prefer). I remember in Skyrim and Oblivion, making dwarvern or elven armour which looked good, but looked aweful on some races and roles, whereas this new crafting system allows you to make a bigger variety of styles to suit your needs.
As well as weapon and armour crafting you also have provisioning for food (which is actually useful for once) which gives you 30 minute boosts in health, magic or stamina. There are literally hundreds of ingredients which you can use in hundreds of recipes, and for a while you struggle to find the right ingredients, and fill your inventory with useless ones. Gradually as you find or buy more recipes you will get this under control and will reduce the amount of crap you feel you have to carry; around as someday, 200 berries might be useful!
The alchemy is very much the same, however uses an additional item to decide on whether you make a potion or poison, and what level they will be.
The enchanting is a bit weird, and seemingly complicated as you have to chose three runestones for each enchanting glyph which you then add to weapon/armour/jewelry.
These three runes decided on first the level and strength of the enchantment, the effect of the enchantment, and then the quality. So you will end up being confused by the weirdly named runestones, but once you use them it tells you what they do and you will have enchanting figured out.
The multiplayer aspect of the game is a weird one, at some points quests say they are solo only, and some are just quests you and friends can decide to do at the same time, however some require a group of 4 to play, as the dungeon areas will be leveled to a group of 4, so on your own you might struggle a little (a lot). Luckily there is also a feature to do these dungeons with randomers in a group finder, so you can still play ESO completely even if you are the only person you know who has the game.
The subscription (ESO+); which I don't and have never had, seems to only add in features to make things a little easier. You will get a small boost in xp and gold gained, and will get some other handy features like an unlimited crafting bag, so you can carry around hundreds of berries without worrying about a full inventory. The main benefit is being able to play all the DLC whilst you have ESO+ and also you get some crowns every month which you can spend on purchasing anything you want, either the DLC you want to have forever, or and other things like pets, mounts, apparels.
It is worth me saying that I dont feel I NEED to get the subscription to enjoy the game, I rarely ever consider it, other than when I fill my inventory (which happens regularly), as there is so much in the game that the extra quest lines aren't needed for a veeerry long time.
In summary, the combat is on a bigger scale, the world is gigantic and gorgeous, the quests are what you are used to in Skyrim, and the crafting is complicated, but allows a huge amount of possibilities if you want that. I definitely recommend the game to anyone who loves and other Elder Scrolls game, as long as you are not looking for a sequel, as this is definitely NOT the same as Skyrim, but takes Skyrim, and blows it up into an MMO, which adds in a bunch of good things, but also takes away a lot of the simplicities. The only complaints I have are the sometimes very unreliable framerates, and the annoyingly easy to fill inventory, but these are minor problems in an overall great game.
Too me most epic start for a ES. It still has some work to do but I believe Skyrim can be this game I would love it more. Keep the updates coming we need ESO:Skyrim dlc

When I first tried Elder Scrolls Online, I wanted to cry. The beta and launch should have by all rights been complete disasters, and they were for the average Elder Scrolls fan. It was a terrible experience without any hint of fun. Needless to say, I never thought I'd visit it again, even after certain factions like the Dark Brotherhood or the Thieves Guild were added, cause I didn't believe they could have fixed the game.
Later down the line, they provided a free week to try out the game and everything they had changed. I was kinda impressed, but there was still one thing that really bothered me and that was the progression curve and structure of areas. You were not able to explore at all, ever. You would find monsters too powerful for you if you tried to freely roam, even if you were "technically" prepared. Despite my momentary enjoyment I still thought the game was not worth the time and effort.
Then came the big E3 announcement. "One Tamriel". It basically said that. if you want to explore, do it! Only your gear stops you now! Needless to say, I got excited. I see no way something like that could fail (except if you hire a bunch of monkeys on typewriters to code for you, but surely they wouldn't do that), and with the new price drop and Gold Edition, it seemed like the right time to get in the game.
What I never realised is that the DLC areas already used a system similar to the upcoming "One Tamriel". Once I went to said areas, I was able to for the first time geniually have fun in Elder Scrolls Online. Who knew that making a good and unique game that caters to your fans instead of copying unrelated others would work, right?
Long story short, I'm having fun playing it, slowly going through what it has to offer. And if the upcoming update is even remotely close to how the current scaling works, I'd say you'd be missing an amazing experience if you didn't give it a try.
The only "serious" downside to it are the microtransactions. They are a bit too much in your face with an in-game store. Though credit to the art and UI design teams, cause it doesn't really feel like it's taking the immersion out of it, for me personally.

Easy to pick up, difficult to master, Factorio is a sort of base-building/tower defense/puzzle game all wrapped into one coherent concept. You explore, you build, you acquire new resources, you develop new technologies, and you protect your shiny belongings from the ever-present horde of bad things that want to destroy it.
No specific thing in Factorio is really complicated, it's the interacton between structures and the scale that really make it shine. Factorio lets you do a whole lot of creative stuff using simple building blocks and logic tools. The graphics aren't amazing, but they are effective at displaying what they need to in a game that could easily get cluttered with too much information.
It's also moddable, if you start to get bored with the vanilla game you are still just scratching the surface of what you can do with Factorio.
The steam integration isn't perfect, but it's still early access and being steadily developed.
If you like base building and tech games with epic scale, you will probably enjoy Factorio.

I'd had this game in mind for a while, and finally picked it up because it went on sale - absolutely worth it.  I thoroughly enjoyed the story (always one of the top selling points for a game with me); it had great pacing and the spectacularly voiced characters were wrapped up in a sci-fi setting that doesn't get bogged down with exposition, sprinkled over with just the right measure of philosophical inquiry.
Gameplay-wise, I'd have to say the experience reminded me of Star Wars: The Force Unleashed - sans the excessively annoying boss QTEs and exhaustively long list of combo attack chains.  Monkey's climbing sequences are scripted to oblivion, but I still found them fun.  Trip manages to be a mostly competent tagalong, except for a thankfully small number of times when she must be thrown across a gap (good rule of thumb: always jump after her and mash the heck out of your "interact" key).  One personal irritation I had was the occasional limitation and snapping of the camera, which made orientation a bit of a headache.  Replay value is not especially high, but I plan on playing it again!
Overall, I'm a happy gamer.  Definitely worth the sale price - and I would've gladly paid the regular price for it had I known I'd be this pleased.

Overall, Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is a great game. The story in engaging and the voice acting lends an incredible sense of immersion. At times, it hard to tell they aren't real people. Even the combat system, which borrows heavily from God of War, is well put together.
Where it really starts of come off the rails is the platforming elements. The game was developed first for consoles and clumsily ported to the PC. It doesn't play well without a controller since you frequently need to move or interact in a direction between the 8 cardinals. For time-sensitive parts, this causes no end of frustration as you'll be doing the right thing but not QUITE in the right direction and then plunge to your doom or get eaten. Even the instructions on how to use certain abilities reference controller buttons.
When the game doesn't lock the camera to a fixed angle, the game is very playable with a mouse and keyboard. Even the bits it borrows from Prince of Persia and Uncharted are incrementally improved. Handholds are rarely difficult to find after a little searching, and paths through the game are usually fairly clear. Even the puzzles are the right mix of difficulty and rewards.
Overall, Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is a solid game that could have used more love during the port.

Total War Rome II is a decent game mind you, but not a good one.
I never really played the previous Total War games so I do not come from that perspective, I come from have playing mostly Paradox games from the overall campaign overlook and just various other RTSes for the battle perspective. I felt as if in this game a lot of my actions aside from actual militaristic movements were useless and even militaristic movements feeling often times just "Gotta change the buildings and then move onto the next city." Coming from a person that played Paradox games before this game seemed to lack consequence to the actions you take.  In EU4 if you annex a province in the HRE, you just get every single member trying to destroy your very being. In Total War Rome, I annexed the entirety of North Africa and nobody cared.
Aside from just that though, there is so much else that feels like it means nothing. My connections to generals literally means nothing, I can just go for the guy with the biggest stats and lock him in, nothing past that. Basically speaking, you can play the entire game without looking at the political screen of your nation. As a huge fan of CK2 it feels that interpersonal relationships and dynasties mean nothing in this game, and that is because for the most part it does mean nothing. Or what about those missions you occasionally get but you probably just complete because it was a part of your plans anyways, or that mission that you just don't do because you don't care about it, because there is no reason to care about it.
Then once you're ahead by enough, you can easily reach the point when you doing battles is literally pointless outside of personally want, in my eyes why fight a battle when you will win it without wasting the extra time? The whole game feels like it is unpolished and not done, because it is not. This game as I simply put is not a bad one, it is just definitely not a great one and mostly certainly not worth putting 60$ into. It's a stretch to say that this game is even worth it when it is 75% off. Though this game, like many Paradox titles suffers from the fact that a lot of DLC that should be in the game is just set at a price on steam. Though by no means do I like paradox for those actions, I do feel like the DLC that is bought on those games actually is an addition to the game, not just another factor within what the game should already be.
So in summary the game lacks meaning nearly every action you take in the game, and the goals the game sets for you are equally meaningless. You can get much better games that display far more mechanics and usually more in-depth as well.  It is also not worth anywhere near 60$, it's not a polished game. For a game to justify that much money it has to be something that was actually cared for and this was not.

A fantastic re-imagining of the original Half-Life, Black Mesa masterfully utilizes graphical themes and atmospheric tones to firmly establish a new, yet similar world of the Half-Life of 1998.
Black Mesa is a community-made remake of the original Half-Life, built by Crowbar Collective using elements of the Source Engine. Both new and old elements will come into play in Black Mesa, with the former having an exceptionally important role in establishing the world as beng a new place yet being the same old Black Mesa compound from the original game.
What makes BM stand out as a title is what it does with the Source Engine, and what signature props, objects, and ambient lighting techniques it uses to convey to the player the difference between the HL Black Mesa and the BM Black Mesa. The opening car ride does, in the same vein that the original did, properly convey a sense of awe as the player enters the world. The usage of new elements gives BM a feel that's unique, it's neither fully Half-Life 1 or Half-Life 2, it's fully Black Mesa, a re-imagining of the original Half-Life, and it expounds on this with grace and integrity.
As a re-imagining, several elements of the original game are modified in simple yet interesting ways, I won't give any particular spoilers, but near the start of the game, there's some major difference in progressing through the game, an element that is injected perfectly through properly established precedents and learning curves. Several elements throughout the game are different than the original Half-Life, keeping the player both on edge throughout, while also establishing the world as being similar, yet ultimately different from the original title.
While the game is currently without a Xen chapter, in my opinion, the game remains a fantastic title due to its starkly unique re-imagining of the original Half-Life, standing unique in its position as a game that's neither a verbatim remake nor a totally independent idea of itself. It's a wonderful blend of both those concepts, and for that reason I must recommend it as both an excellent re-imagining and as an excellent independent title.

Having finished the included HW1 campaign so far I feel I can put in a good review of this remaster effort.
First up getting it out of the way, we all know it but it must be said. The updated visuals are great! Not much more to be said there, the franchise has aged well visually, and now it looks even better.
Sound is good, though in some zoomed in situations it can get buggy. I suspect docked fighters may be emitting engine sounds currently, causing quite a racket. Other than that I don't recall any issues.
Gameplay is much improved with the HW2 style UI placed into the HW1 campaign. Sometimes the campaign difficulty can be brutal, but at least you won’t find yourself needlessly losing so many ships due to fighting against the interface and AI behavior.
The addition of HW2 style end mission resource collection is also going to save you hours of work and fill your pockets between missions. Rather than having to seek out every pocket of resources on a map manually long after your objectives are complete, you can now simply hyperspace jump out and watch all remaining resources auto-deposit into your stores. This combined with smart battle management means you won’t be so dangerously broke all the time.
Bugs I've observed in a 9 hour playthrough of the remastered HW1 campaign:
-At least 3 times a keypress ('esc' did it one time) has caused my game space to go black. Fixed by saving, then re-loading that save.
-Occasionally small objects will confuse AI navigation, either bumping into them, or treating them as large invisible walls. On the last level I had to fly high over a sparse asteroid belt that I don't recall being an obstacle in the original.
- I had ONE full game crash that happened at random. not too bad for 9 hours of play on day one.
I highly recommend this game to those looking to replay a classic, and those trying it for the first time. The campaigns will throw a lot of curve balls at you, and having to restart a mission, or even loading up from an earlier mission will be necessary at times, but at the core level I think this is an easy RTS to pick up, not to mention the great story.

If you had a tear blinking in your eye when you heard the theme music after 16 years, welcome friend, this remaster will give everything you need to bring back old memories, in HD!
Homeworld had redefined the RTS games 16 years ago with its unique 3D space view where you could command your fleet not only horizontally but vertically. Since there is no terrain here, strategies are diverse, entrapping the enemy fleet in a crescent shaped formation was never more satisfactory.
Combining the original beautiful story with immense graphics after 16 years, Homeworld Remastered Collection is definitely a must buy for both the old gamers who will re-enjoy everyhing in a more eye-appeasing manner but also for the people who have never heard of it, for this is the game coming from the best times of PC strategy gaming, where story and gameplay elements were put forward than hollow graphics. Good point is, now you can have both!
Only downside of this collection is that it does not contain another classic; Homeworld Cataclysm. I would really like to go through the story of mere miners of Kuun-Lan against the vile Beast, but seems like the source code of the game was lost when Barking Dog Studios hit the dust.

This is one of the best COOP games I've ever played, heck even playing it Solo is fun enough (though, it can be tedious during some main quests). Released in 2012 and yet I'm still playing it in 2016: still have a lot to explore, achieve (you thought that getting all Steam achievements can be your end game, huh? How about in-game achievements, too?), level up (still having 1-2 characters to level up to max level and then getting all characters on the top of Overpowered level) and, of course, I still need to get MORE SHINY GUNS.
:
+ Catching story line, and then -- BAM -- you get the DLCs for more! + more Side-quests!
+ NPCs, their intros and VAs (seriously, just listen to Mr. Torgue). There's even the weapon manufactures commercials (check it out on YT)!
+ Jokes, references, memes, Easter Eggs! Lots of them!
+ Characters and their backstory.
+ COOP, up to 4 players.
+ Replayability: you have Normal + TVHM + UVHM modes to do and then, once you got Lv.72, you unlock OP1-8 levels +  Badass Tokens + [for hardcore perfectionists] you have in-game achievements in additional to Steam ones!
+ Loot: a single item can get different levels, rarity, stats, weapon parts (that actually affect the weapon's stats!), mechanics etc.
+ Explosions -- these are beautiful.
+ Guns. Glorius guns. (while it's not the bazillion we've been teased about, there's still lots of them)
+ OST -- varying from ambient to boss themes -- it's still eargasmic. Too bad that some of awesome tracks aren't listed in OST.
+ Enemies. Ohhh I'm sure your most hated ones will be Juggernauts, Fire Threshers and Rabid Skags/Stalkers. Prepare to die & rage.
+ Interesting mechanics: grenades that fire bullets?! A shotgun that fires swords that explode?! A shield that turns you into One-Punch Man?! GO GET IT. + with DLCs and updates you get more stuff, Pearlescent and Seraph with their own features.
(sadly, there are):
- You can't start on higher difficulty if you already unlocked it. For every character you got you have to unlock and play through every Difficulty mode (Normal -> TVHM -> UVHM). Can be tedious and burning out if you don't speedrun through or not using save edit.
- The game is about getting a better gear with each level you get. The grind. While I find it pretty OK-ish, some players may not like it.
- The game isn't perfectly optimized, so you can experience FPS drops even on high-end PCs, but it's still worth it.
- Easy to mod stats. You can encounter players with modded weapons or stats -- they can not only kill things by just looking at them but also drop some of their shinies ruining the fun for you (if you pick up the drops, it's all up to you).
- Can be rough for Solo players (everytime you die the boss/enemies get their HP restored back to 100%)

Good platformer. It has some obvious influences from Super Meatboy and Metal Slug. In terms of difficulty it is more casual and forgiving. You will die many many times though. There are tons of different bros each with their own unique attack and unique special ability. Each different bro changes how the game is played and adds both variety and difficulty as your playstyle must be constantly slightly adjusted. For example there is a sniper bro with a slow rate of fire but can headshot accross the screen. There is a demolition bro that can rapidly lob packs of TNT. Rocket launchers, lasers, machine guns, time warping, homing missles, rocket packs, controllable mechs, and melee weapons. Your bro changes frequently throughout each level with deaths and extra lives which are both plentiful. This is my opinion is what makes broforce have the most appeal. Every level can be won without the special abilities, but they add big variety.
Graphics are pixel art. Sound is a heavy metal track that fades into the backround of bomb blasts and bullet spray which are all well done.
There are some obvious cliche's and all of the bro's have funny tribute abilities. If you play with friends: dying and team killing in hillarious ways are common place in every game. Each level has check points, and a clear ending that can usually be reached in 30 minutes with exception of later levels that ramp up in difficulty.
As other reviewers have noted most default attacks cannot be aimed but rather fire in a straight line ahead. Most enemies are built with this restriction in mind. Enemies can also have longer range, higher rates of fire, etc, which makes your own timing of jumps and fires the skill factor. Each enemy's fire patterns can be predicted, but there are lots of different enemy types, and explosives. Everything in the environment is destructable, and most enemies can be destroyed by leveling the map under them, of wich most levels provide plenty of explosive resources to do so!

Let me frontload the message here: I highly recommend you buy this game! It's ridiculously fun.
Now, on to the details:
Factorio is a sandboxy logistics/resource management game, where you automate
the things. I honestly can't recommend this game enough; I've sunk several hundred hours into it already prior to steam release, and I'm sure there are a couple hundred more hours of gameplay to come.
The premises are simple, but they make for deceptively deep gameplay. Gather resources, create a factory with conveyor belts and assembling machines to automate processes.
If you're a min/maxing type of person, you can definitely get your fix on OCD'ing layouts and optimising for throughput. If you're an unorganised guy, you can spaghetti-conveyor-belt your factory to your heart's content. If you want to get your geek on, you can do all sorts of wacky logic builds with combinators, similar to Redstone in Minecraft.
The game is incredibly stable and well-optimised for an early access release. The developers have excellent interaction with their community on their forums, the subreddit, in Twitch streams, and with their blogs.
Factorio has great modding support. If you're burned out on the vanilla game, you can extend it's lifetime with overhaul mods like Bob's Mods and Dytech. And some “vanilla+” mods like FARL (Fully Automated Rail Layer) and RSO (Resource Spawner Overhaul) are absolute must-haves once you’ve settled into the game.
All in all it's a solid 95/100, which is incredible considering the game is still in early access. I warmly recommend it to everyone.

Easy to pick up, difficult to master, Factorio is a sort of base-building/tower defense/puzzle game all wrapped into one coherent concept. You explore, you build, you acquire new resources, you develop new technologies, and you protect your shiny belongings from the ever-present horde of bad things that want to destroy it.
No specific thing in Factorio is really complicated, it's the interacton between structures and the scale that really make it shine. Factorio lets you do a whole lot of creative stuff using simple building blocks and logic tools. The graphics aren't amazing, but they are effective at displaying what they need to in a game that could easily get cluttered with too much information.
It's also moddable, if you start to get bored with the vanilla game you are still just scratching the surface of what you can do with Factorio.
The steam integration isn't perfect, but it's still early access and being steadily developed.
If you like base building and tech games with epic scale, you will probably enjoy Factorio.

This software is laughably bad. :( The Fuse program itself is just a front-end for their model-selling website. The best output you can hope for from Fuse directly (free) is an un-textured OBJ file and some separate textures for you to manually skin everything. If you want a rigged FBX model, you have to pay on their site (you get 2 free rigs per week) - and the prices are just insane. A single character with some animations will set you back hundreds of dollars. If you want - there's a yearly subscription plan with a very hefty price point (>1000$ per year). Even funnier, if you edit your character and want to regenerate the rig for some reason - it's a new character and you have to pay again.
If you're a small developer and are looking for an easy way of making rigged characters for a game - stay away from this program. The models aren't even all that good - they often have some mesh problems with vertices in weird places and overlaping surfaces that may cause flickering problems. If I payed the full price and not the 18EUR, I would be really annoyed now... This is the moment, when one wishes Steam had a refund policy.

Samurai Warriors 4-II isn't a bad game; a sideways thumb would be most appropriate if the option was available. The game does leave to be desired though.
The base combat is some of the best in the Musou games, and Naomasa may be one of the most fun characters Omega Force has created. That's really where the praise ends though.
The game has MUCH less content than other recent Warriors games (I finished all of the major content in about 35 hours. It took me almost 90 to do the same in DW8). There isn't enough new content to warrant a second "Samurai Warriors 4", and what has been added/changed is not really all that good or interesting. A survival mode has been added (this time with no Lu Bu), as well as a revamp of the story mode (which may be the worst/most dull story/musou mode I've experienced in one of these games).
The game also feels like a sloppy port. PS4 models were used but otherwise the game is using PS3 graphical options. While online mode is included, good luck finding anyone to play with in-game unless you coordinate with someone beforehand. And while I haven't noticed anyone else say anything about it, there's a very strange issue in-game where horses seems to have zero AI whatsoever when called (They zig zag all over the place and take forever to actually line up with you). This shouldn't be anything close to a problem, especially since DW8 had no issue whatsoever.
Overall, the base gameplay in SW4-II is very enjoyable, but that's where the positives end. The PC version is sloppy, and frankly SW4-II itself just isn't a game that should have been made. A SW4XL would've given a much better increase in content and would have been much preferred over this. Play it if you like Samurai Warriors/Musou games a lot. Otherwise, pass on this for one of the other installments in the Musou series.

To be fair, Borderlands 2 boasts a lot of content.
But the problem lies in that that content comprises shooting, shooting, and more shooting (and looting, looting, and more looting). Problem: other games have done shooting (think Bulletstorm) and looting (think every Bethesda RPG) better. Borderlands' content seems calibrated to appeal to the MMORPG crowd, whose chief stimulation lies in grinding through samey levels and samey enemies just to increase their XP bars and watch slightly higher numbers fly out of enemies when hit.
Gearbox's marketing department would also like you to think that there's a wacky setting and story to add depth to the basic, uninspired gameplay. That setting is, however, just window-dressing, Handsome Jack has some great lines, but that's all they are - lines, utterances to generate the illusion of wackiness. Bosses get splash-pause intros, then you kill them. Bye-bye, interest and narrative compulsion.
Just buy Tales from the Borderlands instead.

This game was magical. I'm not sure how else to put it. Maybe I was just in need of a good story but I'm not sure I care. I enjoyed every bit of Enslaved. The story was simple but well thought out and, for me, really felt alive. As far as games go there were some minor "issues" that should be mentioned: Some choppy screen rates, awkward lighting, blocky animations, but they were few and far between and didn't really take anything away from the experience. The puzzles were simplistic but still had a nice rhythm to them and the overall flow of the game just felt right. Combat was also rather simplistic but still left your options wide open. With no set combos you were really just free to go crazy with it but in doing so it didn't feel like you were just mashing buttons.
Notable parts to mention for me included:
1.Great voice acting as well as an interesting script that felt realistic at every moment. Nothing felt too cliché or over done and It was really easy to relate to the characters and their emotions from sad to funny and angry to carefree.
2. Story. It's a story about a journey and questions that may not have answers. Very relatable and has a strong impact for better or worse. For me something like that is timeless and deserves many replays.

3. I'm kind of a sucker for the unreal engine
Enslaved doesn't feel like it's trying to be some ground breaking adventure game that has new twists and is trying to force some special mechanic. It just feels like a solid, down to earth, absorbing story that really carries you along, is easy to relate to and keeps you interested.

Plain Sight is quite disorienting to play. It's movement system is similar to Super Mario Galaxy mixed with some M.C. Escher inspired level design. It's very difficult to manoeuvre in a deliberate fashion towards your opponent. I guess this is why the lock-on system was implemented, it helps a lot but also lowers the skill ceiling as it's easy to lock-on to an opponent from across the map in order to travel towards them.
The options menu is severely lacking. The graphical quality options are only a toggle between either high or low, they can not be customised. Some anti-aliasing would have helped as Plain Sight really needs it. There is also an issue where the game appears to be locked to a maximum of 48 frames per second. There are no sound level options, only on or off. Slightly annoying as I like to watch/listen to other media whilst playing video games, so I have to alter this through the Windows volume mixer.
Plain Sight seems like it could be a fun game, unfortunately there is absolutely no one playing this as of writing. I can only rely on bots. Achievements also seem to be bugged or are restricted unless you're playing against human opponents. Its current abandoned state means I can not recommend this game, even if I did enjoy the gameplay (sort of).

A very well polished mod in at least the single player portion. Areas and NPCs are great, giving off a familiar look to Valve's 1998 work but also extends some more practical and "realistic" extras as well. Gore also stays true to Half Life. Though it's no Brutal Doom or DOOM 2016, the entrails and limbs flying about still fit the bill. All in all, the visuals and spectacles are very well done while the gameplay is no slouch either. The multiplayer, though looking promising, seems mostly dead which is a shame.
Go ahead and buy the game during a sale if you're at all interested in the Half Life series. You'll feel right at home with what Crowbar Collective has brought us.

A fantastic re-imagining of the original Half-Life, Black Mesa masterfully utilizes graphical themes and atmospheric tones to firmly establish a new, yet similar world of the Half-Life of 1998.
Black Mesa is a community-made remake of the original Half-Life, built by Crowbar Collective using elements of the Source Engine. Both new and old elements will come into play in Black Mesa, with the former having an exceptionally important role in establishing the world as beng a new place yet being the same old Black Mesa compound from the original game.
What makes BM stand out as a title is what it does with the Source Engine, and what signature props, objects, and ambient lighting techniques it uses to convey to the player the difference between the HL Black Mesa and the BM Black Mesa. The opening car ride does, in the same vein that the original did, properly convey a sense of awe as the player enters the world. The usage of new elements gives BM a feel that's unique, it's neither fully Half-Life 1 or Half-Life 2, it's fully Black Mesa, a re-imagining of the original Half-Life, and it expounds on this with grace and integrity.
As a re-imagining, several elements of the original game are modified in simple yet interesting ways, I won't give any particular spoilers, but near the start of the game, there's some major difference in progressing through the game, an element that is injected perfectly through properly established precedents and learning curves. Several elements throughout the game are different than the original Half-Life, keeping the player both on edge throughout, while also establishing the world as being similar, yet ultimately different from the original title.
While the game is currently without a Xen chapter, in my opinion, the game remains a fantastic title due to its starkly unique re-imagining of the original Half-Life, standing unique in its position as a game that's neither a verbatim remake nor a totally independent idea of itself. It's a wonderful blend of both those concepts, and for that reason I must recommend it as both an excellent re-imagining and as an excellent independent title.

Oh the gliteches, crashes, and horrible horrible UI. This is by far one of the WORST games I've ever played when it comes to setup, and user interface. With all that said, it is still extremely fun to play after you're able to set things up, if you're a fan of the series (XXXXX Warriros) then by all means pick it up (perhaps when it's on sale), otherwise the shortcomings may be a bit too much.
Pros
-Not that many, but the game is what you'd expect from the Warriors series, hours of mindless button smashing killings with pretty and flashy lights.
-Custom character creation - create your own character and level them up.
Cons
(List is fairly big on this one, but don't let that discourage you, most of these are annoying rather than game breaking)
-Stuttering - I'm running a i7 4790k, 32gb Ram (work not gaming related), and a GTX1080 (gaming not work related this time), and the game still stutters at random moments.
-Crashes - I've completed 8/14ish campaings so far and this happened on 2 levels of 1 of the campaigns, after searching formuns, it seems to be a fairly common problem and the only solution was to save your game after every battle so you could resume if it did crash
-UI - horrible for online multi-player. You're only able to play 1 map with a friend, and at the end you get disconnected. This would've been fine back in 1995, but we're in 2017 (ok 2015 when the game was released) online multiplayer is not a new concept.
-UI pt 2 - the Store, it is only avaialble during character selection. minor annoyance but it would be nice to be able to go to the store from the menu, or from the battle preperation screen (screen right before starting the game).
-UI pt 3 - Calling your horse - This has been a theme throughout the games (i recall having similar issues with DW4) where the horse will keep running around
-Controls - This one is the hardest to get by and almost made me return the game after 10 minutes of play. Being a console port you would expect the controller scheme to be good, but then you'd be wrong. The right stick is useless, Camera is controlled by the left trigger and right trigger (wtf?!!?) leaving the other buttons to be configureable. Which leaves you with 6 (a,b,x,y, left bumper, right bumper) while you need 10 or more (currently switch characters, call horse, use ability, switch ability are all bound to keys) and you have no vertical control of the camera. I thought this may have been the case becausae i have a logitech controller, but my friend with a genuine 360 controller was having the same issues.
-Cinematics - Sometimes I like to follow the story, other times i just want to get to the killing. If i'm playing a new story for the first time there is no way to skip the cinematics.
Again, this may seem like a lot of cons, but i'm still enjoying the hell out of this game. If nothing else, this is a great hack and slash where you end up slaying over 1000 enemies or more per map. The amount of selectable characters and different weapon/play styles means the replay value is huge (also a nightmare for completionists). After all is said and done, I'd still buy the game, but definitely wait until it went on sale.

I want to be able to emphatically recommend this game.  I was excited to explore Japanese history with the typical embellishments of the Dynasty Warriors franchise, and Dynasty Warriors 8 seemed like a strong-ish enough port for me to give this a try as well.  I'm sad to say that this requires much more effort to be playable (and I still haven't managed to get the camera controls to work properly).
The game itself is quite worthwhile.  The two-button-plus-specials combat is the same as ever.  Leveling and character progression is interesting with the inclusion of "strategy tomes" that allow unlocking of new abilities.  Custom characters are welcome, though choices are a bit limited (especially in color selection).  Individual stories are a lot shorter than I've seen in the Dynasty Warriors games, but this actually allows the game to feel less stale as you move from one storyline to the next fairly quickly.  I also like being able to switch between two different characters on the fly, but you'll occasionally be saddled with choices that don't exactly suit whatever your playstyle prefers.  The objectives are a bit less obtuse in this game as well, so you won't be stuck trying to figure out what some optional objectives require, but a few of them stay hidden until you wander into a specifc location or event to unlock them, which is quite annoying.
Unfortunately, the gameplay is absolutely hamstrung by horrific controller support.  The most egregious is the inability to select inputs for movement and camera controls.  Mind you, these *are* customizable when using the keyboard.  I have no idea why I can't select what I want to use with a controller.  There is no mouse support either, so camera controls are still abysmal when using WASD.  Button prompts do not reflect any controller, but this is less problematic once you figure out what the different symbols used instead actually mean.  Even so, combat is bouncy, and the inability to effectively control the camera is a source of great frustration.
I'm also not a fan of the general menu interface.  Getting to your gear to modify weapons and mounts is annoying and it just isn't very pretty overall.  It looks more like a fan project than anything professional.  Additionally, there are some textures that look horrific next to others and the game crashes every time I try to bump the resolution higher than the default setting.
All in all, if the adaptation to PC was better implemented, this would be a welcome addition to my library.  As it stands, I'm frustrated in combat because of incomplete controller support.

I'd probably shoot myself before spending one hundred dollars on this. It looks great on the store page, sure, seeing the nice looking Spy being edited, animated, and put right into SFM. That's how they getcha.
First of all, most of the animations you have to pay for on their website. UPDATED FOR 1.3 version
====================
First thing first: I have purchased this software on sale; but my review is based on the full price, to be honest and fair.
What this software does? It allow you to create from scratch, a character that can be either animated by you, by someone else, or from Mixamo itself. Their pipeline is well established, and they offer quite a good service, if you look at the point of view of the indie studio. Now indie doesn't mean "the lonely guy in the basement, with 100 bucks in his pocket"; Indie nowadays means a group of people with some cash to start with; that has a plan or a kickstarter, so the prices of course are adjusted for that audience (their cost per credit is quite high; animations cost between 10 and 50 dollars, and their all acess is a good deal if you have at least a thousands to invest).
But back to the product; I mentioned Mixamo services, since the software is very tied to their service, altho it is a standalone, you may want to consider the fact that they planned this software to be complemented by their service.
How does it work as stand alone character creation? Well, not so good.
The first limitation is due the nature of the application itself: if you offer cookie cut templates, there is only so much that you can achieve. The new version offer somehow a customization array of parameters, but mostly they don't really work as you would imagine. Take any character creation in your favorite MMORPG game, and try to see how many different characters you may get (including the random feature or just tweaking the parameters by hand), and forget about it in Fuse.
You can achieve few different characters (face wise), even modifying the ton of various blendshape added to the mesh; I am not sure how you can achieve characters like the ones that they show in their promo pictures, because most of the time, they all look the same (unless you go for deformed/stylized characters, where the shape of the head and face may be more important).
You have the capability to import your characters and clothes (which require to be fitiing specific requirements described on their site, to be fully compatible), but then you end up with a sort of lego where you mix your content, with alternate fortune.
But not all of it is bad; the software is solid in creating the generic guy/girl, and has a decent amount of variations for clothes and hair (hopefully there will be more soon). The substance implementation is quite the deal, to swap quickly clothes and give variety; altho this works if you need generic characters to populate a background. I believe that what Fuse does best is to be a crowd generator, more than a character generator (altho MakeHuman doesn't get any better, but at least is free).
The app is stable so far; had no crash or issues with exporting and importing, except few times where the textures were disabled, and I had to go back and forth between the various texture areas to get them working again. The output files are clean and import fine in Unity, with or without the auto rig offered by Mixamo.
Overall, I would recommend this software, but barely. If you find it on sale, get it, because is a good deal, but at full price, I would rather use MakeHuman. To me this is a 3 out of 5.
It is a really valid software, that cover one aspect of game character development, but it fall short to deliver the full experience, and it is sad, because it has a lot of potential and is really nicely done. I hope the future version will get closer to give the user a one stop solution to make either crowd characters or main characters.
If I need to make a cast of characters for a Final Fantasy game; I would like to say "let me grab Fuse, it does all that I need"; import my custom clothes, generate unique characters and export them.
Suggestions:
1) the random button should create characters variation, not just scramble the sliders with random values; I can put my 4 years old doing that; while would be more useful to actually have a function that create heuristically, characters that are usable (you can add flags to specify if the character has to be human, alien, cartoonish and so on, to make things easier on your side).
2) More variety with the morphs, instead of quantity; they often are exagerations of normal human features; while in a face, you can see that the differences are much subtle. On this, MakeHuman create more realistic characters, even without the plethora of textures that Fuse has.
FIXED, THANKS!!!!!!!!
3) Make possible to save as template, the characters that you make. For example; I may want to make a character and save just the head as template, and make different bodies, instead than start all over from the default and change all the values. You can also re-import the figure and filter just the head, but it is cumbersome and not really user friendly....the character is there, ready, why close and import it again, instead of just save it as template?
=================
4) Clothes import: would be interesting to have something like DAZ does, with their conforming clothes that adapt to any figure; or like Poser Pro that is able to adapt a piece of clothes for any figure. A system like this would add a lot to Fuse; allowing users to import clothes geometry from anywhere, and just adapt it to the model, without having to modify them.
While in 1.3, there are improvements; it is still a ton of work to import obj and adapt them to the Fuse character. IF I need to spend more time to adapt something; then the advantage of Fuse fade away.

Campaign starts strong but with crashes, performance issues, and bugs.  Finishes awful, making you feel like each minute you waste on it is being robbed from you, an ugly bait and switch compared to the earlier, more enjoyable levels.
A great performance by Kevin Spacey and incredible graphics are wasted on this game.  You can't enjoy his performance while watching it stutter along at what feels like 3 frames a second.  You can't enjoy the graphics while the game is crashing.  You can't enjoy the game at all past roughly the halfway point of the campaign.
Even assuming there was some miracle patch that fixed all the framerate bugs, texture bugs, and crashes, the game design simply gets worse as the campaign goes on.  Early missions are made to keep you on the edge of your seat, later are nothing but filler, including a level where you basically walk through a long cutscene.  The various CoD devs clearly have not learned much from the community's constant hatred of quicktime events and "real time cutscene" crap that keeps you from having any actual control while you are "playing" the game.  By the end, I felt like they should have been paying me to play it.
The multiplayer is basically broken, balance issues so unfixable that nobody bothers to play, making finding matches impossible.  At least that saves you from having to suffer through the multiplayer problems, including a moronic design decision that makes one gun do more damager the higher your current framerate is.
I would avoid this game unless you have the incredible patience to deal with the constant crashes in singleplayer, had no interest whatsoever in multiplayer, and it went to under $10.  Even then it would not be a strong recommendation, but mainly to see the potential future of video games having leading actors in them.  That concept is pretty cool, it is a shame this pile of crap is the representative for the idea.

This game had a novel way of fighting, but the player base dwindled due to a lack of fufilling depth in the gameplay. The player jumps around gravity fields while locking on to targets to ram them. The exhilerating mechanic eventually falls flat. This fall could be due to needing gameplay adjustments such as altering character speed, time to kill, field of view, and similar design decisions that can be done with telemetry.
The game impliments overall level ups (like COD and other games do), temporary round purchases (similar to Counter Strike), and other such features. Unlike those games these features do not seem integral to the game feel and instead come off as layered on top to add complexity. A further in depth exploration of the root mechanics through a sequel or update might result in a more lasting community. The game could make the similar jump Rocket League made from its prequel. While it was worth a purchase originally, its currently hard to recommend an empty multiplayer game even though this one comes with bot support.

AS for the game, it's a third-person suicidal robot simulator. You go around slicing up other robots with your sword and then when you want your kills to COUNT, you have to self-distruct yourself.
Sounds simple, right? Well, it would be if it weren't for the facts that:
1) If any other player (or AI) kills you BEFORE you can self-destruct, then you lose all the points you had stored up
2) you can run on walls, ceilings, etc. Basically any surface on the map you automagically cling to it. The 'bound/unbound' mechanic takes a little bit to get used to
Plain Sight is a game that has unique rules and a unique style/aesthetic & it's one I recommend at least TRYING once in your life.

I had heard of this a few years back when it was still fresh on the shelves, but I was talked out of getting it because the store clerk said it had some pretty bad reviews. Since it was cheap with the Steam Summer Sale, I figured I wouldn't really lose much if it really
. The fact is, I really, really enjoyed this game.
The number one reason why I really enoyed it? It's based on the same story that Dragonball is, and the nostalgia factor alone made this game awesome for me. You've got your Goku, complete with a Power Pole and Flying Nimbus; you've got your Bulma and all her hacky, science-y ways; and you've got your Oolong, lecherous and...well, a pig. Throw all this together, add some high-octaine violence, neat mechs, and a gorgeous environment and you've got yourself a fun game!
The environments are beautifully crafted and it's tempting to just stand around and oggle them for hours. The story is pretty decent too, and the voice acting and motion cap is as to be expected with Andy Serkis on board. The combat is a bit lacking; it's just your typical hack and slash, reminiscent of God of War with the special moves when enemies are weakened. You can basically beat the entire game by spamming left click and the odd "E" in combat. There's also an upgrade feature that I pretty much didn't use beyond extending my sheild abilities (seriously, who bothers to upgrade the staff?). And, to extend the gameplay, there's your token hidden trophy collection element.
All in all, very good game in this gal's opinion!

So... Everything I said just changed with 3.0 which just came out...
The 3.0 UI - user interface - communicates much better after whatever simple tweaks the programmers did.  Much better.
The 3.0 performance actually performs on Windows well, unlike the 2.x versions that were kind of like an anvil tied to their leg while their linux counterparts were flying by in their 3rd Generation Pontiac Grand Ams.
Animation Frame imports and Macro love.  PD Howler owns AF imports, while OpenCanvas owns the Actions recording because of their portalgraphics forum.
That is, these are the areas, the UI, performance on Windows, and the animation frame editing that I saw the most need from the 2.x series.  And they worked on all of them.  Are you kidding?  The greatest need I see now is a worldwide forum
.  If they do that, and do it right, Krita will be a heavyweight on Steam.  (I have no expectations though.  Everyone will have different priorities.  From the standpoint of growing the community and making Krita more popular, this forum idea would be the best investment of time they could make.  Most especially with the recent loss of didlr, the Krita team could not ask for better timing.)
The only thing that is less than stellar is their lack of package options for Linux.  I know we all want to simplify package systems... but I don't think we really are there yet on Linux.

Having used both the free version and recently having bought the steam version, I have to save that the free version has quite a few things that gemini lacks, and it's kind of frustrating to switch to gemini when it just feels inferior. but I love Krita and want to support them, so I guess I'll shoulder the burden.
I would definitely say to download the free version and find another way to support them though.

I generally don't write reviews, but this game in particular has sparked an interest. Early access, $15, singleplayer only, is it worth it?
I found myself playing this game for almost an entire day when my ISP had an outtage in my area, but outside of that here is my list of pros & cons:
:
- The amount of bots are only limited by what your PC can handle
- The AI on your team split themselves into squads of 4, pushing areas together and waiting for each other on vehicles, and seemingly have a leader as you will notice a common hand signal being given by some bots when they are with their group (this is very helpful if you're driving a vehicle like a transport boat with bots in them, as they tend to not exit the boat even when you reach land unless you're in the area the bots intended to go)
- The AI has really good control of aircraft (their ground vehicle control on the other hand can be up and down)
- At the start of rounds bots do a pretty good job of balancing the amount of troops that go in each direction so 1 direction isn't entirely stacked
- Overall, the game is a great way to kill time
:
- The developers have very much expressed they won't be adding multiplayer, which is a shame considering even having co-op with 1-3 friends or so would be a great selling point
- The AI just like any other game have some sketchy behaviours, sometimes they cheat in very minor ways
- Even on hard the bots aren't that difficult to kill, your deaths are generally just being caught off-guard or by vehicle and a majority of your losses if any will just be because the enemy's bots bested yours
- You yourself don't seem to be on any squad as I mentioned above regarding bots, so good luck getting bots in your vehicle unless you join a vehicle already occupied by a bot(s)
- There's no way to kick bots out of vehicles or trade spots with them without killing them
- If you reach land with a transport boat and you were driving it, bots won't get out unless it was the area they intended to go if it was driven by AI (read pros above about kind of understanding where they want to go)
- There's no way to interact with your AI, meaning they are doing their own thing all the time while you are doing yours
- The game modes have no natural ending, meaning all there is is a GUI popping up saying which team won for a few seconds, then it goes away and the game continues so you have to end the game yourself which is just very awkward
- All modes except Spec Ops (WIP so the mode isn't really worth playing in its current state) don't allow you to change the win condition numbers, and it doesn't scale based on the amount of bots either so the more bots there are the faster the games "end"
- The bot pathing with water vehicles is pretty linear so it's not uncommon to see them ramming into each other every now and then, this sometimes applies with the rest of the vehicles
- Vehicles seem pretty hard to use considering how easy it is to take them down (aiming in a vehicle doesn't compensate for the vehicle turning, so it becomes difficult to aim in it) as almost every bot has an RPG or something to deal with helicopters and such, and shooting enemies out of a vehicle isn't very hard either
- Bots tend to walk in a lot of moments they could be sprinting
- There's a really annoying mechanic where most of the time with almost any weapon (I heard headshots tend to negate this), when you kill an enemy, they're not really dead, instead you just knocked them down into a ragdoll effect like they would if they died but they get back up in a second or two and you have to finish them off (killing them the 2nd time should make them die for sure) - I like this mechanic but it happens way too often; I don't think it should be happening if you get shot in the chest or so by a sniper
: If you are fine with the singleplayer experience and you look forward to the promising updates the developers have proposed, this is worth the $15. The modding community is already pumping out some custom maps, so you shouldn't be too quick to get bored of the maps. However, this game is merely just a way to kill time or hop on for a couple of games (as of now anyways with the small amount of content it has), not something you would dedicated hours daily to (in my opinion),

Factorio is an absolutely awesome game. Even though they call it "alpha" and it's now in early access, this game is more polished than many "finished" games. This isn't early access done right, this is early access done *perfectly*! If they went home tomorrow and called this "released", I'd be disappointed, sure. If if you didn't know this was in early access a day before, you'd think this is a stellar release!
I've clocked several hundred hours into this game, playing alone and multiplayer, modded and vanilla. The gameplay has already been discussed at length in other reviews, so let me instead focus on other qualities that make this game stand out:
Community & Development
+ active development with lots of intormation about what is going on (e.g. Factorio Friday Facts)
+ active community
+ developers listen to community
+ still more features to come!
Quality of Life & Settings
+ excellent UI and consistent keybindings for almost everything you could want, "the devs thought of everything"
+ *everything* is rebindable (over 50 independently bindable actions, shift, ctrl, alt, whatever you fancy, and yes, that is a good thing!)
+ very good options menu, monitor selection, ui scaling, vsync, 6! different sound levels for different effects
Performance
+ great performance (thousands upon thousands of resources move through your factorio at the same time)
+ great performance on multiplayer
Modding & Multiplayer
+ stable multiplayer (had a disconnect a few updates ago, but no real problems to speak of, played over 100 hours of it)
+ active modding community
+ mods work on multiplayer
+ everything is moddable (need some UI stuff? need a different inventory? need different enemies? different tech tree? terraforming? new enemy AI? new resources? difference balancing? *everything* is moddable!)
+ I mentioned that that stuff works in multiplayer, too, right?
+ can be launched as dedicated server
Custom Worlds
+ infinite, procedurally generated worlds
+ want one huge continent? want more lakes? do you smaller iron ore fields? do you want more crude oil? do you want larger enemy bases? Do you want copper ore fields and make each of them alrger? Do you want less enemies? Do you want your iron ore to yield more resources?
+ can toggle enemies to "peaceful mode" so they won't attack you unless you attack
+ did you find a great map? Share it easily with others, or use it yourself to start afresh on the very same map
+ don't want an infinite map? sure, just enter the dimensions you want
Yes, I have some issues with the game as well:
- multiplayer needs port forwarding
- you will obsess over optimal factories
- might feel a bit overwhelming at the beginning, there is a tutorial though, and the tips and tricks are *actually* useful! (that's a +)
- some minor quality of life additions would be amazing! (Factorio already sets a *very* high bar on this, I can't think of any game where I've been more often impressed at the little details the developers have paid attention to)
- car handling is a bit wonky, it's fun, though! (oh, did I mention there's mods to change that?)
- more detailed statistics in the vanilla game would be nice!
- mod management needs to be improved
All things considered, besides captivating gameplay, both vanilla and modded, this game puts most other games to shame with its polish, performance and moddability. And still, they call it early access. They have a vision and they will not consider releasing their game before it's "perfect".
tl;dr: If you're into base building, this is the game to get! If you're not into base building, you should try the demo to get a feel for the game. If someone deserves your money for a game, it's these devs with their phenomenal game!
