Dishonored 2 takes place several years after the events of the first game, and continues the story of the two main characters. Emily Kaldwen now rules Dunwall as its Empress, with her father and bodyguard Corvo Attano by her side. But a new threat has emerged, sending them on a new quest.
Like the first game, this is a stealth focused adventure which is played from a first person perspective, and this time around you can play as either Emily or Corvo.
The good
•	Enjoyable stealth mechanics. If the player is seen, there’s no instant mission failure. You’re allowed the chance to recover from the mistake, either by fighting or escaping.
•	Emily and Corvo have access to different magical abilities, meaning their playing styles should feel different. I’ve only played as Emily so far but her abilities really suit a stealthy playing style. She can see enemy locations, and their vision cones, through walls, which is useful for avoiding detection. She can teleport to reach high ledges, escape danger, and quickly get behind enemies to perform a silent takedown. She can link 2 to 4 enemies or civilians together so that whatever action you perform against one (kill, takedown, etc) will affect them all instantly.
Emily can transform into a shadow creature which actually seemed to be less stealthy than her Human form, but it does allow you to pass through small rat holes. She can also create a doppelganger (a copy of herself), to distract enemies or even fight alongside her, but I acquired this power towards the end of the game and I didn’t get chance to use it.
•	Wide range of available weapons and gadgets including sword, pistol, crossbow (with 4 types of bolts including fire and sleep), stun and shrapnel mines, normal and sticky grenades.
•	Fantastic level design. Every level has multiple paths leading to your objective, and most of them have lots of verticality. You’re encouraged to explore to find runes which allow you to upgrade abilities, bone charms which grant passive buffs, and coins/valuable loot which you can use to buy equipment upgrades at black market shops. Two standout missions take place in a clockwork mansion which has a changing layout due to moving walls/floors, and an old ruined mansion where you can switch between the past and present to solve puzzles and avoid/takedown guards.
•	Story is fairly simple but is well written, and has some interesting characters.
•	Great voice acting including 2 Daredevil actors (Vincent D’Onofrio and Rosario Dawson) in supporting roles.
•	You can influence the story by your actions. Each mission has a main target who you can choose to either kill or defeat non-lethally. Crucially, the non-lethal options aren’t just a case of “I’ll leave you alive because killing is wrong and I am morally superior, please don’t attack me again later when I least expect it”, which always annoys me when it happens in a game or a TV show because its just stupid. Dishonored 2’s non-lethal options remove any future threat in clever ways, which made me actually want to pick those options.
•	It took me 17 hours to finish the game, which is significantly longer than the first game, and also represents good value for money.
•	Controls are fully rebindable and work great with mouse and keyboard
•	I managed to get a consistent framerate of 60 FPS for 99% of the time without spending much time tweaking settings.
The bad
•	Combat against enemies who are aware of your presence isn’t particularly enjoyable. I felt very weak, and the rare occasions when I found myself fighting against more than one enemy led to me dying very quickly. (Again: I played as Emily. Perhaps Corvo is stronger ... although I remember feeling the same way about the first game).
•	Your right hand is always holding your sword and left hand is for everything else. No option to equip pistol and crossbow together, or crossbow and a spell, or whatever combination might seem useful. (Skyrim’s system would work great here).
•	I suffered five crashes to desktop (no error message). Four happened when opening the journal, one while just moving around. While this didn’t ruin my experience, it was still annoying. During the last couple of hours I was a bit paranoid, forcing myself to hit quicksave every few minutes to avoid losing progress. One of the reasons that I wait a few weeks/months before playing a game is to allow the developers time to fix major bugs. Dishonored 2 is the most unstable game I’ve played for a long time.
The recommendation
My complaints are relatively minor issues (no game is perfect). Dishonored 2 is a really enjoyable game and it should be placed very high on your wishlist, assuming you’re happy to take a slower, stealthy approach. From a story point of view, I don’t think its essential to have played the first game, to enjoy this one.

It's a time warp back into the past. One of my favorite RTS games makes a return with remastered enhancements that bring new life back to the Homeworld universe. Gearbox and Blackbird Interactive did a good job with the enhancement and I hope this success will continue to drive forward as they expand on the series. I haven't played any multiplayer yet as I'm focusing on the campaign and skirmishes. This is one of those games you want to bath in the full treatment and not rush any one particular feature. There's plenty to do and much value to absorb.
Graphics
+ Plenty of in-game options to enhance graphical quality.
+ Models and textures are pretty sharp and detailed.
+ Nice explosion effects.
+ Lots of tiny details like ship damage decals, resource extraction effects, lens flares, sun rays, etc.
+ Space environments are beautiful.
- Shadows are a bit "noisy" around the edges. Not as high calibre like other games.
- UI is a bit dated looking and could have been enhanced better.
Audio
+ Music suits the gameplay and the environments well. Quality is very crisp.
+ Sound quality is pretty good and feels crisp as well.
+ Explosions and cannons have a good punch on my sub.
- Game lacks 3D positional audio, which would have enhanced the immersion as your camera rotates around ships and battles.
Gameplay
+ AI gives a good challenge. It keeps the pressure on as you foucs on survival.
+ Good balance of combat & time investment. Skirmishes are not to long and not to short. You're always on the move.
+ Classic RTS that sticks to the tried and true formula. Research, build, and tactics all within a space theme.
- Little awkward there's no easy way to pan around quickly, or that the camera has a limit on the zoom-in/out range. In most modern RTS games, you move around quickly. Given the 3D positions in Homeworld, it can be awkward to get your camera in the right position without first orienting it on an object nearby, then moving over to where you want to go.
Campaign / Single Player
+ Just like the original, only better with the new HD visuals and audio.
+ Challenging missions and interesting story with a sense of adventure.
Quality
+ Haven't run into any breaking issues so far.
- ESC key doesn't bring up the menu like you would expect in most PC games.
- PrintScreen is not the default screenshot key. ScrollLock is (like what?). Can't seem to bind it to PrintScreen either.
Overall
+ Would recommend this game. Homeworld is fun RTS, now with better visuals and audio. Combined with modding support, the possibilities are open for the community to introduce new scenery, new game modes, total conversions, etc. Add on 2 games + the originals, plenty of campaign missions, adventerous story, good music, AI skirmishes, and multiplayer. There's a lot of value here and if you haven't tried the Homeworld series before, consider checking this little gem out.

Hacking and slashing your way through thousands of enemies without a second thought has never looked so good.
I grew up playing way too much Samurai Warriors on PlayStation 2.  It was a fantastic, if mindless, way to blow a night.  Samurai Warriors 4-II follows the same recipe of kill a ton of enemies until you get to the "Big Baddie", then kill him, too.  Still, it isn't a perfect game.
Personally, I'm not a fan of subtitled games.  The Samura Warriors that I grew up playing was dubbed over, and it made the games much more enjoyable.  I don't want to make sure I read every single text box warning that appears when I'm hacking my way through another 1,000 enemies.
The power-up system of using scrolls to gain new abilities seems new and interesting until you realize every character gets the same tree in slightly different shapes.  The only difference is a "special ability" that, once unlocked, can be used by every character.
Leveling up weapons is also a bit frustrating.  I think it works well enough if you want to focus on a character or two, but if you're interested in playing all of the characters it becomes more of a chore than engaging gameplay mechanics.
Finally, the DLC prices are just obnoxious for what are just skins.
Still, Samurai Warriors 4-II is a fantastic game.  Fighting is flashy, smooth, and easy to learn.  There's just enough strategy and thought needed to keep it intersting.
If you love to imagine yourself in an era of mass destruction, then this is your hack-and-slash game!

I finally figured out why I love Smite so much.
I just got into Smite this week and I love it. I’ve played LoL and Dota 2 before. I preferred LoL’s gameplay over Dota’s (in my opinion) slower pace, plus Dota 2 seemed more complicated. That said, I stuck with Dota because all the Heroes were free, and my brother-in-law played it. But neither ever clicked with me to the point where I really LOVED the game. LoL and Dota were more like “Everyone loves these games. I’ll keep playing until I figure out what’s so great.” With Smite, I never had to TRY to get into it. I just really enjoy playing it.
Here’s what I love about Smite:
1. You have direct control of the character. In the other Mobas, you have to click to where you want them to go, so in my opinion, there’s always a slight delay. I never felt in complete control. It's very much like an RTS.
2. I don’t need to fight with moving my camera. I always struggled with moving my camera in LoL/Dota. Trying to see what the other players were doing, when I got the the edge of the screen I needed to scroll it further. In Smite I don’t even need to think about it.
3. I like playing a simpler version of the standard three lane mode. I have trouble with map awareness and all the different rules for where roles play and which area has what. Smite has Joust and Arena, which are just the right speed for me.
My love for Smite doesn’t mean LoL and Dota 2 are BAD games, it’s just that Smite fits my preferences better.
Okay, time for ONE more game! Really! THEN I’ll got to bed.

NOTE: This is the same review for the other two games in the original Deponia trillogy aswell. I thought that as they are a continuation of the same story that they should stay together.
The
trillogy is a classic point and click game on a wold filled with garbage. In the trillogy, you assist the, at first forgettable/dislikeable, protagonist Rufus try to reach the floating paradise of Elysium. Over time, the originally forgettable Rufus uses his witty dialog to slowly get you on his side rooting for him on his quest.
+Amazing story
The story, although only really played out during cut scenes to new areas, is deep in detail. It pulls you in, really pulling you into the world.
+Funny
Not many games have blaitently funny dialog, but these games definatly do. Rufus has funny responses to other characters, his own acvtions, and stuff you try to have him do.
+Characters
All the characters seem fleshed out quite well. Each has a uniques personallity, displayes different emotions, and just act different. The variety is also pretty good.
+Enviroments
Most enviroments are well detailed with other people and objects to bring the scene alive. In some cases, youll get people who are from other games showing up in the envirments aswell.
+Music
The music worked well with each area you would be exploring. Although mostly being simmilar themed, it all was different and interesting.
-Animations/Movement
The walking animation on Rufus, for me was a bit weird. He didnt really face where he was going and took odd paths to where he needed to go.
-Duration
Some areas seemed too short, while others were too long. It was an odd thing and may have just been the way I solved the puzzles in each area, but it struck me as odd how I could clear one area in ~30 min and another in 2+ hours.
The
trillogy is an amazing set of games that brought back tthe nastolga of point and the point and click style. The quirky dialog was fun to hear and laugh at resonces. The story makes the narcissistic Rufus someone whos actions have you rooting
for the duration of his adventure. If you have some time free I can highly reccomend all the games in the
trillogy and

Now, I will make a note right now, I am a diehard Homeworld Fanboy. I played Homeworld 2 just a few months ago at the most recent. I also played Cataclysm fairly recently. However, Homeworld 1 eluded me after my childhood. You see, when I was 8, we got Homeworld 1 and I enjoyed it... that is, up until the asteroid mission where I could never get past it and never truely knew how the game evolved or even the ending.
In fact, this, was the first time I have ever seen the ending of the original Homeworld.
I loved it.
It wasn't without its faults, but I couldn't really expect them to take a 15 year old game, ship it into a new engine, and fully remaster it without some issues being present. If you expected it to be perfect, you are a fool.
They kept a lot of the basic gameplay elements that I remember while improving the bad things I forgot about. Here is a quick list of pros, cons, and bugs that I experienced.
Bugs:
Mission 3 broke for me on the first playthrough. I killed the frigates, but never got the objective to salvage the trays. Luckily it was a short mission and it was the only time I had to restart a mission. Might be worth checking out though.
Pathing/AI seems to be extremely poor. The biggest issue I saw with this has an obvious answer too. Its the Homeworld 2 engine and that engine was not designed for single ships put into a chosen formation by the player. This causes OBVIOUS issues when you try to do it. Ships will immediatly drop out of their formations when combat starts and make no attempts to have any sembelence of sanity until the battle ends. Of course, this causes Homeworld 1 fighters to be damn near useless and you are way better off just running all frigates and capital class ships because they are useful past being cannon fodder... In most situations. On the Asteroid mission I got stuck on as a kid, I lost like 8 frigates to really terrible pathing which seemed to be caused by buggy asteroids.
Pros:

This game is a classic in the RTS genre.
If you enjoy RTS games, and want an experience without some of the super deep multi-resource management that some games give, this one might just be for you.  Resources are but a single type in this game, which works just fine in my opinion.  It doesn't really need multiple types of resources.  People looking to manage tons of different resources might just be disappointed.
When it comes to the story, these games are very good.  Cut scenes are a bit old-school with their graphics, but the remastered version is definitely remastered and even better looking.  Don't expect super realistic graphics, but do expect to have your mind go "woah" when you experience twist after twist in the great stories.
When it comes to the challenge and game play, these games are pretty good.  You can't adjust the difficulty (that I can find) but you definitely are going to be challenged.  Thinking in 3d (heck yeah!) can help quite a bit because you do additional damage if you attack the sides of an enemy ship (anything other than front = more damage).  Surprising the enemy AI isn't likely, but that's alright.  If you find the game too easy, setup your own challenges.  You have the ability in this game to "capture" enemy ships.  When I first played it, I set myself the challenge to build the biggest fleet possible capturing as many enemy ships as possible while making sure that mine don't die.  That was VERY difficult.  Find that makes it too easy later because your fleet is too big?  (yeah your fleet and resources are persistent) then perhaps challenge yourself to NOT capture any ships, see how you fair.  Plenty of ways to challenge yourself here in other words.
Graphics got a good leg-up with this HD remaster.  Definitely much better looking textures, though the models themselves might feel a bit dated if you zoom way in (fewer polygons than you might expect).   Audio also had a great job done on it's remastering.  Everything sounds excellent so far.
Now I'm not going to say the game is without flaws.  Sure, almost every game has some.  In the last 5 hours that I've played, the game crashed to desktop twice.  Annoying sure, but I got in the habit long ago to make lots of saves so I don't every really loose much time.  Multiple saves across multiple missions is also a good idea, as you might think you beat one mission "well enough" only to find yourself low on resources and ships later on.
I've also experienced some of the same bugs that were in the game back when it first came out.  Sometimes the pathing for the ships isn't the best and a few will all get hung-up together.  Simply find the one messing them up and then tell it to move and the others will begin moving again.  I've also seen several instances where the capture ships will latch onto an enemy ship but not move it towards your mothership.  No problems, undock them and recapture the ship and you are going to be fine.  Little things like this DO show up in the game, so don't expect it to be perfect.
Still, the experience that is Homeworld and Homeworld 2 is beyond a doubt one worth visiting.  If you played them and really enjoyed them in the past, you will DEFINITELY enjoy them again.  It has been long enough that many won't remember all the details or story as well.  If you haven't experienced these games before, they are still worth thinking about taking a look at.  Remember, you are getting TWO complete games here for $35 so that isn't too bad!  If you still don't like that, just wait for a sale and then you must pick it up.  If you didn't like Homeworld before, you probably won't like it now.  Duh!
Anyways, two thumbs up for this HD remaster and two excellent games.  Here's wishing that they'd make a Homeworld 3 with today's technology and game design powering it!

This is hands down one of the best games I have ever purcahsed and played. It ranks among the top 3-4 games in my personal 'favorites' list. If we are looking strictly at money for play time value, then Factorio is probably one of the best if your into this type of game. I mean 500+ hours (many people have quite a lot more), for $20? It's just one of those games that you can't get enough of. I have done I think 3-4 playthroughs casually on my own, and I'm on I believe my 8th Let's Play series on my YT channel. The possibilities are pretty much endless.
Now for the pros and cons.
Pros:

I have several hundred hours played in this game from prior to its steam release.  Although as of this writing this game is listed as 'early access,' it is largely feature-complete, stable, and deserving of your purchase on the basis of what it *is*, not what it *could be*.
What this game *is* is something akin to a "3X" game -- the player eXplores the randomly-generated map, eXpands his or her base, and eXploits the map's natural resources to go ever bigger, currently culminating in one (or more) rocket launches, using resources at a scale that would be unfathomable at the game's humble beginnings.
The core theme of this game is automation, where processes that were once difficult and resource-intensive become simpler and easier as the player's factory (and skillset) expands.  This carries through with each main aspect of a base:
*) With mining, the player begins the game with a single, small mining drill and smelting furnace, but the game ends with huge fields of large electric mining drills, mininghundreds to thousands of ore per second.
*) With crafting, the player intially hand-crafts everything "in their pocket" (which is to say manually); quickly the player will place automatic assembly machines to craft "science packs" (the game's core progression mechanic), structural pieces of the factory (such as transport belts and power lines), and finally advanced items such as efficiency or productivity modules.
*) With logistics, the player transitions to hand-moving resources from miners/smelters to their destinations, to laying out simple transport belt paths, to laying out long "bus" prudction lines for high-volume production, to (depending upon map setting) creating entire train networks to bring raw resources from outlying areas to the main production areas.
*) With construction, the player transitions from small, built-to-purpose layouts, to larger, expanding layouts to finally automated construction from (player-designed) blueprints with the aid of flying construction robots.
Whereas the Civilization series is famous for its "one more turn" feeling, this game has an equivalent "must go deeper" feeling -- clearing up one bottleneck or expanding one production area provides a glorious feeling of progress where everything laid out so far works like a well-oiled clockwork machine, before the backlog is sorted through and the next challenge becomes apparent.
This game will not appeal to those seeking action-oriented gameplay (the combat system is there but somewhat rudimentary -- it exists mostly to keep players "honest" with defenses rather than to provide a true strategic challenge, under most map settings), but it will appeal to those who enjoy "base-building" games such as Prison Architect.
I recommend the game wholeheartedly.

When Just Cause 3 was first released, it was plagued by bugs and problems, however I jumped in any way, remorseful of the fact I missed the pre-order bonuses.
And to be honest, I'm glad I did. Even though it does occasionally stutter a small bit during large explosions, my experience with Just Cause 3 is seamless.
The main campaign is okay - I have played more enjoyable ones, but it's still pretty good. Once the campaign is over, there are still a multitude of collectables to find and challenges to complete, and even then the gamecertainly does not feel exhausted at all.
The map is phenomenal, with masses and masses of land to be explored, driven around, flown over, and so on.
As for the DLCs:
Sky Fortress was, mediocre. It certainly wasn't bad, and the bavarium wing suit introduced in it is an absolute godsend.
However, the more recent DLC, Land-Mech Assault, was at least in my opinion fantastic. I absolutely love backstories, so the whole backstory surrounding life on Insula Lacrima for the eDen corporation, its employees and its technology was fascinating, and all the rusted, disused buildings and stations just added to that sense of 'I wonder what it must have been like?'. The mechs are also fantastic, and the power core is a fun EMP-esque weapon to mess around with.
All-in-all, I have to give Just Cause 3 a 10 out of 10. A phenomenal game in pretty much every respect.

This game reminded me of Bioshock, Half-Life and Thief series, but with more freedom and choices in playstyle and story.
By saying freedom and choices in playstyle and story, I mean you can do whatever you want with the story, approach it with whatever mindset or roleplay or morality you want to have. You can play as purely evil or purely good, neutral, or a mix of those things, You can play as very stealthly, a shadow that cannot be seen, a stealthy assassin, a very brutal mindless killer, an artistic killer, a skillful swordfighter, an uncatchable freerunner, or anything really, the game caters to all kinds of playstyles. and your choices will affect the story and the outcome in the end
The story is short but memorable and worth it. First of all, there's a single campaign, but two characters to choose from (Father and daughter) at the start, and those two characters will have different dialogues, reactions, and perspective in the story of the game, kinda similar to the Leon and Claire scenarios of Resident Evil 2, but in a lighter way. So replayability is basically doubled for the campaign, and there are lots of different endings, depending on your character selected and your choices and approach in playing the game, and it's a big plus to replayability(or you can just watch the different endings on youtube) also, the lore is pretty interesting and I would definitely like to see more of it. The game can also stand on it's own, and you don't need to play the first one in order to relate to this game, so that should clear things up with franchise newcomers.
The graphics are simple, similar to the original Dishonored, it has it's distinct artstyle that's not aiming for photorealism but not aiming for cartoonish as well. While the game runs decently, it could do a lot better, but it's playable and enjoyable, given my specs.
Level design is one of the best, the story and levels are linear, but there's a ton of ways you could go around a level, so it's not really purely linear. there's a certain mission that I liked the most, one of the best levels that I've seen in a game ~ a thing I would like to see in more games, but I wouldn't spoil it here. The NPCs are surprising as well, their reaction, behaviour, and AI are very well made, they took their time in creating the dialogue for many of the scenarios that could happen in a certain playthrough, not just the generic NPCs, but also the story characters as well.
Overall I enjoyed the game, A beautifully designed story rich game with lots of freedom, choices and replayability.

I feel like now, after around 25 hours and 2 playthroughs, I've seen enough of the content to be able to write a review of it. This review wont be summarising or explaining the game at all, however more of an extented pros and cons list.
If (like me) you were a fan of the first Dishonered game, then you are going to love this. It genuinely feels and plays much like the first game which I thought would be difficult for Bethesda to achieve. Now we have 2 playable characters (Corvo & Emily) with their own individual powers aswell as a whole new place to explore also.
My first playthrough consisted of Very Hard difficulty, no supernatural powers, low chaos and no times being spotted. Each mission presented a great enough challenge so that getting passed each section left me feeling satisfied, rather than it being overly easy. In the same playthough I also tried to find as many of the collectables as possible which, as I didnt have the various supernatural abilities took me a long time to do, but is worth going for due to the different smaller jumping puzzles and searching required to get them.
My second playthrough was with all of the powers, trying to build up my 'chaos level' as high as I could killing everyone in my path, on again the highest difficulty. This still felt like enough of a challenge because of the amount of enemies, and again left me feeling satisfied enough when clearing a level or finishing the game.
Another place where this game shines is the level design. Each level gives you something new to play around with making them each unique, presenting their own challenges to encounter. This ranges from whiches, to the clockwork solidiers and so on. In addition to which, it honestly feels like there are countless ways to tackle each level. Playing through the second time I made sure to see as many ways possible to be able to reach the objective, and either do it lethally, or non-lethally. Sure enough, there was more than plenty of ways to do it, and definately earns another playthough just to try do them all.
However, when pulling the game apart to look at the details, the main problems are simple. On lowered difficulties the enemy ai are ridiculously stupid, meaning they're virtually sitting ducks half of the time, but on hard, or very-hard they are more intelligent.
Secondly, if you are one of the lucky enough people to own a NASA computer, this game is
however, to the rest of us this game is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to run, even after the patches it seems most people are running the game on lowered settings. It's worth notable mention that if you are unsure whether or not this game will run on your machine, there is a demo where you can play the first 3 missions or so. Seems as though alot of people missed this.
Overall for me this game earns a spot up next to the original Dishonered game for me, i felt it to be just as much fun, and challenging as the first game and I will sure as hell be playing this a hell of alot more to come. It shines in so many different aspects that any fan of a stealth based game OR a fan of just running around killing people like its WW3 are going to love this game. Would very highly reccomend to most players.

Dark Souls will always be my favourite Souls game out of the three considering I played it first, however Dark Souls II improves upon the original in almost every aspect.
First off, visually the game is a big improvement. The lighting may not be quite up to what was originally shown at E3, but lets just forget about that. The game looks pretty damn amazing in some areas, particularly Majula (the starting/hub area). The aging engine has been vastly upgraded, the lighting and animation looks great.
Gameplay wise, there are some changes however the game stays mostly true to Dark Souls as you would expect. The changes that are put in place are mostly for convinience and are a welcome addition.
You can expect the same brutal difficulty when you enter a new area, until you figure out the best plan of action, just like the other Souls games. If learning from mistakes in gameplay isnt for you, you may want to think again before buying Dark Souls II. However the rewarding feeling you get from clearing a difficult area or huge boss is worth it.
I'm biased, but overally I'd definitely recommend Dark Souls II. Its a completely fresh gameplay experience that deters from the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ hand holding AAA ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t titles we're used to nowadays, and I'm hoping due to the popularity of the series now that other developers follow suite.

Short story, play Dark Souls one first.
Long story, this game could have been great, but there are many problems that cause it to fall into the trap of being EXTREMELY aggravating. Keep in mind this is all coming from someone who has played through the game three and a half times and has played through Dark Souls one Twice.
Pros:
The combat through most of the game is superb. It is slow paced but lethal. Every single melee weapon in the game feels like it has a lot of weight behind it. Furthermore, just about every weapon in the game has a unique move set.
The graphics are fairly good in my opinion.
The story is pretty good, though it is nowhere near the level that dark souls one was at.
Some people claim that the beginning of the game is badly designed because the woman who allows the player to level up is “hidden”, but frankly one cannot blame the developer for expecting players to see the blindingly obvious bonfire when they enter the hub area and then notice the first NPC since the old fire keepers standing over a cliff wearing a green cloak that contrasts with the dark blue ocean behind her surrounded by messages telling the player to talk to her.
Cons:
Basically every problem in the game likely stems from the lead developer being absent from the development.
The first problem everyone will likely come up against is the incredibly slow recovery item usage animations. The developer decided to tie recovery item usage animation speed to a stat called agility. This must have seemed like a good idea at first, but unfortunately it means at the start of the game the player character is basically like “OH NOES, I AM BEING ATTACKED BY A LEGION OF ZOMBIES AND IF I DON’T DRINK THIS POTION FAST I WILL DIE *slowly brings flask out of pocket and brings the top up to mouth, gently licks top before taking a single sip of potion, gargling it, and swallowing it, and then slowly bringing the flask back down and putting it back in pocket, all the while standing completely still like a chump*”. It is easily one of the worst decisions they could have made while making the game.
The second major problem with the game is that almost all of the bosses are either gimmicky or bland. The developers, not having their lead dev on the team at the time, must have not been able to create that many bosses that had any real substance to them. One of the bosses is literally just a swarm of rats. That’s it. A bunch of rats is a boss in this game. Because obviously the lock on system in the game is more than good enough to handle fighting a metric crap ton of relatively small, scurrying enemies in an attempt to find the one who the player needs to kill to end the fight. Another boss is a giant two headed spider that shoots lasers out of its mouths. This may sound cool, until you realize that the boss’s only weak points are its heads and that dozens of infinitely spawning smaller spiders chase you around the whole fight. There are a few interesting bosses like the Looking Glass Knight and the Guardian Dragon, but nothing to the level of Smough and Ornstein or Manus in Dark Souls one.
The third major problem with the game happens to be an entire area known as Belfry Luna *SPOILERS*. It is a very small area compared to the other areas, but holy crap is it terrible. There is a covenant that specializes in having players invade other players in the area. Problem, the covenant has so many members invading non-stop that if you take more than a two or three minutes to get to the boss, you are guaranteed to be invaded, and then while dealing with the first invasion, you are guaranteed to be invaded again and be in a 1v2, and then you are guaranteed to die. Another problem with the area are the little shadow dwarves defending it. Alone they are not a problem, but in the area the player needs to be in to open the door to the boss there are literally six or seven of them, half of which chase the player around endlessly and the other half of which shoot the player with bows and arrows with pinpoint accuracy. The boss of the area is the recycled gargoyles from Dark Souls one. The catch is that when one gargoyle gets to about half health, another one spawns. This adds needless difficulty especially for melee characters who have to get up close to the damaged gargoyles and inevitably get surrounded.
Overall, it is somewhat better than most rpgs out there, but its flaws make up for a game that is vastly inferior to the original.
PS, I do not really want to comment on the PvP because I have not really played it much.

- a sandbox game, set in an alien world, where main theme is building an automated factory.
If you love automating things and coming up with efficient desings, and engineering large functioning systems, and just an idea of building a huge factory appeals to you... then this game might become your new favourite.
There is a Demo available on the game's website to let you have a feel on how it works.
In Factorio you start out small, gathering resources manually... and slowly amass them to, eventually, automate the production.
From miners that dig ores and furnaces that smelt them ... to assembly lines and oil extractors... to setting up train lines to traverse alien world and even launching a rocket to space... Many things are possible to create in Factorio.
I will say in advance... Conveyor belts are bread and butter of many factories.
A technology tree, a very handy tool, will aid you on your path to greatness in factory-building. It will unlock better machines and more ways to tackle various challenges the game presents you with.
If something doesn't work... then experimenting with various tools to create something that does work is a sure way to go. Or just expanding that Electricity network might do as well...
Even though Factorio is all about automation, combat is also part of a gameplay.
One thing to keep in mind... Keeping pollution of a factory under control is key to your survival.
It is vital to find ways to protect yourself and your evergrowing factory from local population of an alien world, and keeping atmosphere clean might just buy enough time to develop defenses against irritated locals, who are also known as biters.
Factorio has built-in Campaign mode, which works as tutorial and presents basics to a player. More advanced gameplay happens through Freeplay... which also has various settings that can change difficulty of the game.
There are Scenarios present in Factorio, which act like challenges to test your knowledge of the game.
Factorio supports modding too, so it is possible to change your gaming experience entirely.
There is also a Level Editor present in Factorio... Not feeling like building a factory? Design a map, or a challenge, for others to experience.
Of course... can't forget about Multi-player. It is even more fun building a factory with a friend or a company.
For past few years developers have been working hard on this game. It went through many iterations and changes and is still being updated fairly frequently. There is no sign of them stopping working on Factorio. My favourites are "Friday facts" posts from the devs, where they talk about the progress they made on the game and their future plans.
You can build a factory however big and complex you want... your creativity is the limit. With what tools are present in Factorio, you are ultimate designer of an automated system in your world.

Factorio is a game which starts on a alien planet where you must try to build a highly efficient factory however you see fit. Beware though, there are natives alien species who aren't to fond of your poluting endeavours. Be sure to defend your factory with turrets and ship ample amounts of ammo to them in order to keep the aliens from destroying everything. The more you polute the more the aliens will develop and start to build new bases which will result in more frequent attacks and in some cases will result in evolved alien species!
The game starts of simple with simple non-electric furnaces and ore drilling machines which mainly require coal and ore to function. Most of the tasks in early game are trying to kickstart your factory into a steamrolling Skynet-like machine which is hungry for more resources. Later in the game you will need to build complex infrastructure (belts/rails/robotics networks) in order to fullfill the need of your hungry factory. You will also want to be constantly researching for new technologies which will help you in your quest for global domination of the planetary resources.
If you like building large factories and managing them while also blowing up alien insects, this game is for you. Trust me this game is really really cool once you get going. There might be some times you are facing some hard challenges getting some research done or building a complex factory but the community in this game is amazingly helpful. So if you have any questions you will probably find help on the official forums, reddit or on the steam community.
The graphics in my opinion are awesome, they really caught the late 90's era of PC games with their art style. The soundtrack is also really good and I recommend buying it too.
There is also multiplayer included in this game, although I have never tried it (lack of friends liking this type of game) I'm sure it's an even more fun experience building a factory together...or two seperate rival factories!
Last but not least, this game is still in early access. Which could be a reason for you not to buy it. On the other hand the developers have made sure the game is 99% stable before they went on Steam early access so this is one of the most stable early access games you will ever see.
It's hard to describe this game further without spoiling everything you need to see/play it to understand, it's simply awesome. Buy it, you WONT regret it.

I've now played JC3 for well over 400 hours, and 100% completed the vanilla game and all three main DLCs, as well as gotten every achievement (vanilla + DLC) and acquired quadruple the chaos score of every other friend who owns this.
I like me some 'splosions.
Just Cause 3 is a slightly half-arsed AAA game about moving ridiculously fast, blowing things up and messing around with a massive open world. You play as Rico Rodriguez, a former secret agent who has dropped into his mother's mediterranian island homeland of Medici to annihilate the regime of General Di Ravello.
Biggest selling point for JC3 is moving around in it. Movement is insane in this game. Your arm-mounted grappling hook can hoist you up a mountain in moments, your (infinite) parachute might as well be an airborne sniper tower because you can use any weapon with it, and your unrealistic wingsuit essentially makes you a fighter jet Transformer. You can combine these three to move ludicrously fast, such as grappling the ground and slingshotting yourself while using the wingsuit. It's not just efficient and satisfying, it's damn fun.
The gunplay is pretty basic. Shoot the dudes, grenade the dudes, shoot their heads and they die quicker. However, you can deal with enemies in many more ways than just bulletspam: You can grapple them to perform a turbocharged dropkick (PHYSICS!), or plant one of your limitless supply of C4 explosives on their face. The grappling hook also has a tether function that lets you connect two things via a wire and pull them towards each other; Soldier vs. car / soldier vs. concrete wall / soldier slingshot off a cliff / car vs. fuel tank / tank vs. fuel tank, etc. Your movement ensemble lets you attack from any angle, and grapple to any vehicle to hijack it, including airborne fighter jets and helicopters, so while there isn't much enemy variety, fighting them remains fun.
Your objective is to break things. There's a lot of things to break, and they all explode in extravagant and very pretty ways. Fuel tanks, football pitch-sized satellite dishes, excavators, bridges - the lot can be torn down, and all of them are subject to the physics engine. Very nice.
Helicopter and plane controls are very good. Boat and car controls are alright. Motorcycle controls are horrendous. They all take some getting used to, but once you do, you should have no problems. Apart from every vehicle you bail out of becoming a bomb. Remember Soldier vs. car?
Game cares not for the laws of physics. Drag a train car via one tiny rope up a cliff, it doesn't care. Creative license in the name of fun and entertainment. I approve.
Side challenges unlock gear upgrades, and they're pretty nice, but I wish you could unlock them by other means. Some of the challenges are a bit irrelevent to what the unlock, like the grappling hook upgrades being tied to a game about dragging ore into a big pit via a car-mounted magnet. Apart from that, there's destruction time trials, car bomb races, and wingsuit courses, so I give it a pass.
Difficulty: Eh. You're an unstoppable murder engine by the end, but the late-game bases can still be quite challenging.
Medici's beautiful. The explosions are also beautiful. The game looks damn nice, just look at the pictures. They're not shopped, that's pretty much in-game footage.
The devs cut a lot of corners to get this out on launch date. Missing textures on certain out-of-the-way things, slightly shaky LODs, debris disappearing in front of you, that sort of thing. Nothing major.
The soundtrack's pretty good throughout, the heat level music's one of my favourites. The dynamic battle themes in military bases sometimes feel a bit... "un-dynamic" if you know what I mean.
Sound effects mostly alright. A lot of good explosion sounds. A lot of recycled car noises, though.
Cutscene quality top notch. Voice acting and comedic timing is brillaint. Dimah, Mario, Sheldon and the others are nice to watch and listen to.
Rico delivers one-liners a lot. They get a bit grating after 429 hours, and a patch added some new ones which were slightly ♥♥♥♥♥ier. NPC dialogue's good voice acting, but somewhat limited number of lines - you'll hear the same ones a lot.
Surprisingly rich. Not *RICH*, but a nice backstory.. A series of collectible audio diaries let you find out exactly how Di Ravello came to power, and conversation snippets around towns and in cutscenes reveal just a hint of explanation about the mayhem going on around you.
As for the plot: There's this thing called Bavarium in Medici that everyone wants, because you can make forcefields and nukes with it. You get to pilot forcefield tanks and use handheld warheads that can level bases in moments. GOOD ENOUGH FOR ME
JC3 can lag immensely if you don't have a high-end graphics card (I have a £115 AMD one, runs at max settings no problem). Game has a confirmed and chronically unpatched memory leak, perhaps for all eternity. More than 8GB of RAM is
reccomended.
♥♥♥♥♥on of bugs. No game-breaking ones, but minor annoyances sprinkled throughout. Cars flipping out into the sky, corpses calling for backup, Rico's animations going a bit weird, cutscene audio/video desync, towers fizzing out of existence mid-collapse. I can bear it, but you might not, so be warned.
No save slots? Really? I have to perform a surgical file transplant every time I want to start a new game so I don't erase my 100% save.
SQUARE ENIX SERVERS. Online leaderboard for little challenges. It has an offline mode, but it will try to exit it the moment it gets internet. Minor annoyance.

This is a flawed game, let me state that up front.
In light of that, the fact that it is still incredible speaks to how astoundingly well it accomplished what it set out to do. This is perhaps the most tense and terrifying game I have ever played in my life. If you enjoyed the original Alien film, and also having the wits scared out of you by survival horror games played at night in the dark with a quality set of headphones at high volume, you will not be disappointed in the slightest.
The fact that this game is also on sale for 12.49 USD right now is really a steal for such a high quality experience. You won't see it again for such a great price for a while, I imagine.
Let me get the few cons out of the way first.
The animation on some of the humanoids, particularly the faces, is not very believable at times and a lot of the characters are difficult to get attached to due to a lack of character development and sense of humanity. I think some improvements in this regard could have improved the experience. This is not true for them all, but a majority of the time I found myself not caring as much as I wanted to about their well being. Some of the human AI behavior is downright comical, particularly in comparison to the Alien.
The crafting system is a good idea but a bit clunky. I honestly recommend playing this game on Nightmare difficulty because even on Hard you will have a ton of crafting materials thrown at you. I had a difficult time keeping myself stocked enough to deal with every situation on Nightmare though. That heightened the terror for me knowing I might not be able to build another noisemaker for a while as I chucked it desperately across a room in order to escape a bad situation. So my advice, play on Nightmare if you want the true horror experience.
The infamous save stations. I see what they were trying to do, to build tension while you save not knowing if you will be safe in the process. But in the end it just becomes repetitive, immersion breaking and tedious. I think I would have preferred an unintrusive standard autosave system, perhaps without any manual saving to preserve the sense of peril in getting through an objective. Some people really don't like this feature but I only found it a minor annoyance.
The pacing at times felt a bit off and while I actually enjoyed the game's extensive length, some people feel it is too drawn out. I don't agree but I can see where they are coming from.
The various computer terminals around the station as well as the recordings are a little bit of a cop out in terms of exposition but the voice acting is quality enough that it's not THAT bad. A bit too much of the story is told through walls of text that are hard to read given that you are constantly trying not to die.
Now for the good, essentially everything else!
The atmosphere is extremely well executed. It is very faithful to that of the 1979 Alien film, so if you were a fan of that you will really enjoy this aspect. From sound design to lighting and the situations that you are put into, the atmosphere succeeds at terrifying you as much if not more than the Alien itself. This is a sign of masterful horror, and is part of what makes the first film so effective. You rarely see the creature but it still feels omnipresent. Truly well done on all fronts.
The way you use your equipment against the Alien is handled pretty well. In the words of Ash when asked how they can kill it, "You can't." The best you can do is temporarily fend it off in a number of ways and then hope your plan of escape works out. Again I emphasize playing on Nightmare as the rarity of your equipment will heighten this effect immensely. The glitchy motion tracker you get on Nightmare also adds an element of uncertainty.
Finally there's the titular creature. The Alien. The AI, animation, sound design, visual artistry and sheer terror this virtual creature invokes is all absolutely incredible. The feeling of being hunted is palpable and if you play by yourself in the dark with the sound cranked up, you will get a truly visceral experience. You will likely be physically uncomfortable as you listen to its heavy footfalls over metal gratings from inside the questionable safety of a locker or an air vent. There is essentially no situation where you are 100% safe and if you don't find a way to keep moving, eventual death at the hands of the creature is basically inevitable.
I would say the two main reasons this game is worth the money are the atmosphere and the Alien itself. If you are a fan of terrifying and tense experiences such as Dead Space, Amnesia, Slenderman and its spiritual imitators, or even Doom 3, this game will knock your socks off. Or soil your undergarments. Either way you won't be disappointed.

Samurai Warriors 4-II is the 2nd SW game to come out on PC since SW2 in 2006. The PC port for that was basically ripped from the PS2 version which is kind of weird seeing how the 360 version came out a year before the PC version. Samurai Warriors 4-II is supposed to be a "complete" version of SW4... meaning KOEI just put 1 more character, removed Chronicle Mode and replaced it with Survival Mode from SW1 and 2 and removed all the Legend stories.
Gameplay: The gameplay has changed a lot from its predecessors and it feels more like you can crush everyone in your path easily without having to run around slowly looking for enemies and wasting time on them just for KOs. It's pretty easy to get 1000KOs in a battle now and its easier to kill enemies. This is probably because of the new Hyper attack they added which replaces the useless charge attack from SW1, 2 and 3. It's OP on weaker enemies but any enemies with shields or main officers can't be killed with them unless their defences are weakened. So I guess that's okay. You can now control 2 officers at once which makes it easier to plan out attacks, unlike in the previous games where you did all the work, you can now order the secondary officer to move to this place or attack that guy while you do the main thing.
Story Mode: The story of Samurai Warriors is the same as the other ones, but this time instead of playing the same levels as each character and basically getting bored, you play stories from a clan/group's perspective. Also you can choose who your secondary officer will be from a list so you can choose who's perspective you want it to be personally.
Survival Mode: I never really enjoyed playing this back in Samurai Warriors 2 and tbh it's pretty boring here too.
Creating a character: It's the same as SW2 and 3 but now you can upload your own images onto your character so their clan symbol could be anything you like.
Graphics: The textures are taken from the PS3 version but the models are from PS4. It's annoying that KOEI never decide to enhance the graphics for PC version. Luckily there's a graphics mod that makes the textures look better, the colours more like the PS4 version and just stuff like DoF or lens flares. The map still fades from a close distance though which is annoying. The game runs at 60fps easily at full settings.
Basically, if you enjoy the Warriors series, whether it's Hyrule Warriors, Dynasty Warriors, Warriors Orochi or even the past Samurai Warriors games... you'll enjoy this game. The only thing you need to worry about is changing the graphics, but that's only if you're picky like me lmao

This game kinda spoiled Dynasty Warriors for me.
If you already played a "Musou/Warriors" title, then you know the drill: choose one of many(in this case 50+) characters, and then slash your way through
thousands of enemies. Anyway, if you played Dynasty Warriors, then you might be pleasantly surprised by some of the things that SW does.
SW4-II comes with three game modes:
and
.
features twelve stories with five missions each. Every story focuses on a different group of characters or a different clan, while each story still follows the same general plot that leads to the battle of Sekigahara in 1600. At first only a couple of stories are available with more being unlocked as you finish them. A nice detail is that depending on which second "buddy" character you take along, you see different movies/conversations before the battle.
is the same as the story mode, with the difference that you can replay the story mode stages with any characters you like, instead of being restriced by the characters taking part in the story.
comes with two sub modes: Endless Castle and Challenge mode. Challenge maps are five maps, each with a certain objective. Results can be uploaded to online leaderboards. Its not a game mode most people are interested in, but its worth playing once to unlock the characters after each stage.
The castle is a 100 floor survival marathon with random objectives on each floor, except for milestone floors(10,20,30 etc.) which have set objectives and come with unlockable rewards and bonuses for the castle.
This is where I go back to Dynasty Warriors. While DW8 features are relatively stationary gameplay, SW's gameplay has a bigger emphasis on fluidity with a strong forward drive. Compared to SW, DW seems slow and almost clunky.
There are four character types in Samurai Warriors4-II:
and
Each type sets how the character will evolve upon level ups. A normal character for example will eventually be able to chain normal attacks into a long combo, while a power character has more individual power combos to follow up with, and so on. All characters have basic attacks of all the types though. So starting a combo with a power attack, will always propel a character forward into enemies, no matter which type he is. The type merely sets how they evolve beyond that.
Every character has its own skill grid, on which you can buy skills to use and upgrade attributes. There are no EX skills in SW, but every character has its own unique special "epiphany" skill. One character for example can become invisible, with attacks out of invisibility doing more dmg; another one can lay mines, another can set up a magic barrier etc. Every character's unique skill can be unlocked on the skill grid at lvl30 for the other characters to use. So you can equip a character with various skills from other characters if you want, making for interesting combinations.
In this game you take two characters into battle as opposed to one in DW. You can freely switch between the characters anytime, and give commands to the character you're not using; like moving to a certain area or attack a certain commander. Characters that share a friendship can even unleash their musou attacks together(shown by an emoji in the character selection.)
The mission structure itself seems like a step up from DW8's. In general its the same (mostly) linear mission design, but packed into multiple clearly distinguished objectives and bonus objectives(some of which unlock at random, or based on your actions.) The mini map has also gotten a bump in that regard. Be it paths, objectives, or commanders and events, everything is much better represented and easier to spot than on DW8's map. Its also smaller than DW8's and doesn't hang in the "middle" of the screen like DW8's did.
One thing I personally found a bit disappointing, is the amount of "bystander" characters. Meaning characters who have no major or minor part in the story, and just there for you to use in
If you include characters, who are available as buddies in one or maybe two missions in
, then that number is relatively high.
As DW8XL, this is a PS3 port with PS4 character models.
the quality of textures and the visual quality in general are noticeably better in this game, so while being ported the same way, there's still a clear difference in quality between these two. A lot of which comes from the updated engine. Visually the whole game seems more refined; and with all the effects on the screen and the PS4 character models, the nature of the port doesn't weigh as much, or isn't as visible as its the case with DW8XL(which can look quite "ehh" sometimes.)
Also, this game runs better than DW8XL(which came out before) for me when maxed out, even though its looking a lot better. DW8 had quite a few dips and microstutters but none of this is happening here. Maybe a sign that Koei is slowly getting it together when it comes to ports.
I only played the game with Xbox360 controller, so I can't say anything about mouse+kb controls. However, the game uses PC key prompts when using the Xbox controller.
One more personal thing regarding the design at the end. I'm a big fan of the
games by Koei. If you ever played them, you know that there's a clear difference in design between the more historical design of characters in Rotk, and the over the top, fictionalized version in DW. Some of the designs in DW have always turned me off quite a bit, to a point where I didn't really wanna play some characters solely due to their design.
This clash between designs is still happening here with SW and the designs in
(the Japanese counterpart to Rotk.) But I can stomach the fictional designs in SW a lot better for some reason. It's a personal thing of course, but I wanted to mention it anyway.
This is my very first Samurai Warriors title ever. I've been playing Dynasty Warriors and Romance of the three Kingdoms since PS2 times and I'm a big fan of the setting. So it feels kinda weird to say, but after playing this, I don't think that I'll revisit DW too often. In a franchise which's gameplay consists entirely of cutting through countless enemies, the game with the better flow when doing so, definitely gets my favor.

I'm quite fond of Musou-type games and Samurai Warriors 4-II is no exception. There is a dearth of games like this on PC and this is a fairly competent port technically, though it suffers from a total lack of mouse control similar to Devil May Cry 4.
Coming from Sengoku Basara: Samurai Heroes on the PS3, the action and characterizations of the various warlords here are considerably less over the top, though still pretty silly in their own right. If you have no previous experience with either series, imagine Japan's warring states period reimagined as a shonen-esque martial arts anime. Characters wear flamboyant garb, yell their attack names out and have inexplicble magic-like abilities. One of the characters is even a straight-up sorceress.
Like other Mosou games and games with similar elements of many, many levels and collectible items like the Naval Ops series on PS2, the Choro-Q games, or Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker and Phantom Pain, SW 4-II is an incredibly dense experience. There are multiple five-level story campaigns, a range of difficulties, weapons and horses to collect, dozens of characters, a free mode where you can use any character in any story level, support for custom characters with the ability to import images from your hard drive to use as symbols, and a survival mode with no less then a hundred floors, and associated one-off challenge levels. If you enjoy the core gameplay enough, you will find many, many hours to spend here. If not, you will likely find it bland and repetitive, as there are certainly games out there with more variety.
I only wish someone would make a Musou-style game set in either Warhammer universe, or something.

When I first played Dishonored 1 (on the Xbox), I fell in love with it, the story was compelling, the powers and abilities were stunning, allowing me to do things I never imagined. And giving me amazing plot twists, even after memorizing every single route, combo, weapon, etc. I was still compelled by it. And in my opinion, I believe that Dishonored 2 has excelled as a succesor to its predecessor.
1. Adding and Improving
-Dishonored 2 has added brand new weapons, abilities, and powers all of which can be used in various ways, the powers and abilites can also be built upon by going down different branches, but of course, being a completionist such as myself, I tried my best to tap into all abilites and fully upgrading them. The powers and abilities differ between the game's selectable protaganists:
Corvo: The righteous badass who saved Dunwall from the devastating Rat Plague and saving Emily (hopefully) from the clutches of his former allies.
Emily: That's right, that little fragile girl you rescued from the first? Well guess what, she has become a new (and quite sexy ;) ) brand of badass.
Both characters offer completely different perspectives of the storyline, such as the death of Empress Jessamine, each other, past and current allies, and more. (Didn't I mention that they also have different abilites?) Both characters will wind you in, making you feel as if you are in those royal shoes of theirs. Hell, either character might just make you think differently at the situation at hand, possibly develop or lose morals. Anyways, with two different perspectives that give you different insights, emotions, and thoughts on situations, and new powers and weapons that either allow you to sneak by silently or ABSOLOUTELY DEMOLISH AND MURDER YOUR ENEMIES IN AN EITHER VIOLENT, METHODIC, OR STRAIGHT-UP BRUTAL STYLE OF DESTRUCTION OF SOULS!
....sorry about that, kinda got carried away there. :D (F*ck you, Howler Gang.)
Another improvement Arkane has made, is the level design. The graphics (in my case) were serious upgrades from the previous game's visuals. Giving you a more relaxed, serious, or even post-apoctalyptic atmosphere in the game. Nothing like beheading your enemies on the sunny beaches of Karnaca, am I right or am I right? Arkane have also done an exemplary job at expanding the levels, adding several routes to follow by, more events to experience (or more like eavesdrop upon), and generally more time for exploration.
2. Story
-The main story of Dishonored 2 is quite riveting, although kinda rushed in some cases. The story is affected by the events and characters of Dishonored 1, so every once and a while you might find a few small references. (BTW to truly understand some of the shock the story gives you, play the DLCs of Dishonored 1) The story also somewhat immerses you in the political atmosphere of the game, such as the tense pressure there was upon Emily beforehand, as well as the corruption that led to her being overthrown. It may even cause you to develop some hate or love for some of the characters in the game. The story too, has some of its own plot-twists like the first game had. And if you take some time to look into your target's history, as well as alternative ways to deal with them, it may actually cause you to use that grey matter up north to think about how the rest of the story will be affected and how the Empire overall will be impacted in the aftermath.
3. No Golden Cat
No Golden Cat :(
But it would be very bias and I would be forming an echo-chamber for others if I acted like a complete Bethesda/Arkan fanboy about the game, it does have some of its own problems, the major one being the optimization issues. The Void Engine that Arkane used for the game may grant you a great framerate/graphical experience or hell on Earth, no matter how God-like or potato-like your computer is. I had a rather good time, so luckily my composition of parts fitted well with the engine. I will post my specs below if anybody would like to see them.
Overall, the game is something that I am glad to deem the "Amazing Successor" Award and the "Greatest Improvements" Award, which are becoming quite rare to hand out now due to developers treating us like♥♥♥♥♥♥and giving us half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥content. Arkane was close to the edge of delivering us that, completely due to the optimization issues. Overall, Arkane just needs to work upon the optimization issues of the game, so whether you play upon a rig hand-crafted by God himself, or if you play upon a half-eaten potato, everyone can enjoy the game.

I finally figured out why I love Smite so much.
I just got into Smite this week and I love it. I’ve played LoL and Dota 2 before. I preferred LoL’s gameplay over Dota’s (in my opinion) slower pace, plus Dota 2 seemed more complicated. That said, I stuck with Dota because all the Heroes were free, and my brother-in-law played it. But neither ever clicked with me to the point where I really LOVED the game. LoL and Dota were more like “Everyone loves these games. I’ll keep playing until I figure out what’s so great.” With Smite, I never had to TRY to get into it. I just really enjoy playing it.
Here’s what I love about Smite:
1. You have direct control of the character. In the other Mobas, you have to click to where you want them to go, so in my opinion, there’s always a slight delay. I never felt in complete control. It's very much like an RTS.
2. I don’t need to fight with moving my camera. I always struggled with moving my camera in LoL/Dota. Trying to see what the other players were doing, when I got the the edge of the screen I needed to scroll it further. In Smite I don’t even need to think about it.
3. I like playing a simpler version of the standard three lane mode. I have trouble with map awareness and all the different rules for where roles play and which area has what. Smite has Joust and Arena, which are just the right speed for me.
My love for Smite doesn’t mean LoL and Dota 2 are BAD games, it’s just that Smite fits my preferences better.
Okay, time for ONE more game! Really! THEN I’ll got to bed.

The Rating System: Good refers to the obvious positive qualities, the Bad is reserved for nitpicks and gripes that don't necessarily ruin the experience, the Ugly is for the worst parts of the game, meant for serious consideration before purchase.
The Good:
Broforce is a game, like Hotline Miami, that banks on its cool factor to draw you in. You play as recognizable pop culture icons, each having wildly varying abilities, such as the Terminator, John Rambo, and Neo from The Matrix. If crossovers are something you like, this game has it in spades, with numerous references everywhere. You can tell the developers had a blast making the game, and love their chosen subject matter just as much as their audience. A game BY action movie fans, FOR action movie fans. Gameplay is built around very simple to understand, intuitive mechanics: You've got a basic attack, a special ability and a punch button. You start with a random character, your only goal is to reach the end and kill a non-threatening demon or tough boss, and terrain can be broken by shooting or punching it. However, the true meat of this experience comes from how unpredictable the game is. Sometimes you're forced to tunnel under the enemy for a surprise attack. Sometimes you have to shape the terrain into a set of stairs or platforms to pass an area because an explosion happened that you weren't expecting. The biggest element of randomness comes from the characters themselves. You spawn with a randomly selected character, and since you never know who you're going to get, you're constantly forced to radically alter playstyle and re-evaluate the level on a moment to moment basis every time you die. You may be given a character with a massively powerful weapon that knocks you back when you use it, you might be given a super fast character that's tricky to control, you might be given one with no ranged attack at all and relies entirely on traps, melee or grenade throws. Despite how that sounds, it's challenging, but never overwhelming and certainly never complicated. This mechanic makes the game stay fresh even when you've beaten it time and time again, as no two playthroughs are exactly the same.
BroForce is random by design, intending to give you the most gut busting "what the crap was that?!" moments it can, and the mere fact that you're playing as action movie stars in such a cartoonishly over the top world with such easily accessable pick-up-and-play simplicity make it a hilarious burst of fun for an hour or two.
The Bad
The screen is zoomed out just a little too much, making it difficult to tell who's who when you're playing with a friend. There's a couple of characters that have flaws that make certain parts of the game unfinishable until you can get a different one. For example, Highlander is extremely slow, which means that if you're stuck with him on a part that requires you to move quickly - such as if an unkillable boss monster is chasing you - then you must simply die and hope for a faster character to be chosen when you respawn. The game has plenty of levels, the level design is fine, but the game itself has long strings of levels where there are few completely new enemies or hazards to play with, and because of the inherant simplicity, that can make the game boring for some people. While it doesn't bother this author in the slightest, the constant overuse of the phrase "bro", may irritate some players after a while, and its constant ridiculousness could wear you out. It really isn't a game that's meant to be played for very long.
The Ugly:
The bugs are its biggest downfall. On the final boss in particular, I had actually succeeded against him several times, but for whatever reason the.. for the purpose of avoiding spoilers, "cutscene" wouldn't happen, making the camera freeze until I paused and restarted the entire level over. On semi-rare occasions, the level wouldn't load properly and entire sections of the map would be missing, making it unplayable until I closed the program and restarted it. Another major failing is a lack of tutorial. If you aren't familiar with the characters you're playing as, then their abilities will likely be completely foreign to you, and you'll be wondering what the hell you're supposed to be doing with them or why they're behaving so differently. Take Leon the Professional for example. His punch button isn't a punch at all. It teleports you in any direction, even through single block walls, and he's the only character who's like that. His special ability is to mark enemies for an off screen sniper to kill, the only one that does that too. I've never seen the movie this character is from, and as such, was left very frustrated at first when I lept down to try and punch an enemy only to appear down below the floor and into a bottomless pit, or tried to use their special ability infront of a super enemy and end up getting killed as the sniper wasn't able to finish them off fast enough. You can easily adapt and learn each character's abilities, but as I said, this could be easily remedied with a light tutorial when introducing the character.
Finally, it all boils down to this: Its greatest strength, its ease of play and simplicity, can also be its biggest failing for certain people. This is an arcade game at its heart, if you're looking for a fulfilling experience that'll allow you to dump hours upon hours into it (ex: Fallout), or some in-depth strategic gameplay (ex: Team Fortress 2), you should know that this may not be your game. If you just want to blow up some bad guys using satisfying methods that're almost entirely up to your own imagination, laughing at the constant movie references while high fiving your friends, then give it a try.
Final Verdict: 7/10
The occasional bugs are often enough to take a couple points off and the flaws in some of the characters bring it down an additional point, but were these issues patched and balanced out in future updates, I'd have nothing at all against the game. As my Mark of the Ninja review implies, I love games that offer you a simple goal, gives you the tools you need and leaves how you complete that goal almost entirely up to you. That's a big part of why I like this game so much, but it's the ridiculous dialed-up-to-eleven charm and hilarious unpredictability that make the game well worth the already cheap price in my opinion.
I also adore its theme song.  \m/-

They were blissfully unaware of their captivity, smiling away their endless days, happily living as cogs in this churning machine of industry.

9/10, would go re-evaluate my perspective on industry again.

For those that have not yet played Factorio, do not let the number of hours played fool you, due to the fact I have been playing the non-Steam version for a long time, and have easily played hundreds of hours. If you already have Factorio, it is likely you are not even reading this, or forgotten that most early backers probably have a Steam Key Available.
The basic principle of the game is simple, you just have to build a bunch of assembly lines to get back into space. There's just one small detail, and by small I mean relentless creatures that do not take too kindly to your existence. You will find yourself mining ore, stone, wood, and drilling for oil to supply an ever increasing complex production chain of goods. All while researching new methods in which to build, new materials to create, and defend yourself from the "locals".
Now, if this sounds like your average builder game, you are wrong. Not only do the creatures try to kill you, but the bigger your base gets, the more pollution you create, and the more pollution you make, the bigger and badder the creatures get. So, consider the hostility of the planet to be simbiotic to your success in growing your base, which keeps the game nicely scaled to your progress. Normally, you get to a certain point where you are doing so well that nothing can stop you, except in Factorio that just throws down the gauntlet to the creatures that will wreck your day if you let them. Make a car, they get tougher. Make a tank, and well you get the idea.
Add in multiplayer, infinite map, random map generation that has LOTS of options (including a peaceful mode), and you have a very replayable game.
Pros
Cons
In short, I honestly think it is easily one of my top 20 games I would recommend to someone. Be it playing with friends, or playing the game solo, there is something for everyone.

Factorio is a fiendishly seductive simulation game. I bought it in 2014 when it was still an alpha, but you wouldn't have known it by playing it then. Of all the games I've seen that have tried to build off the Minecraft experience with an individual twist (and Steam has pushed a lot of them at me) , Factorio has easily had the strongest individual concept; it breaks away from slavish 3D block world-based imitators to make something definitely inspired by Minecraft and its many technology-themed mods, but only using them as a springboard to colonise some fresh gameplay space for itself.
Factorio is a line production optimisation simulator. You might not think a game whose most basic element is a device that picks things up from behind it and places them in front of itself could go anywhere interesting, but you would be very wrong. The game's genius begins to shine through when you assemble a basic ore refining line, automating the transport of raw ores to furnaces, then to storage. Then you extend the output line, adding a factory that converts iron plates into gears. Then another that turns gears and plates into transport belts. You don't have to make them yourself anymore! Then you build some turrets to defend your nascent industrial complex from the sedan-sized bugs that come to attack it (and you) every now and then. You add another factory that makes ammo so you can dump a stack into each turret and focus on building other things... pretty soon, it's 3am and you've declared war on the xenos threat that's continually trying to stymie your mining and production operations by attacking everything in sight. Congratulations, you're Weyland-Yutani and you're not going to be run off by some damn natives. Pack a thermos and top up the flame throwers, it's bughunting time.
Factorio is a remarkably well-executed indie game. It isn't perfect, and has areas that are still very 'beta' at the time of the Steam EA release, but its core mechanics are rock-solid. The multiplayer experience is very stable for a game with such complex systems. It's already inspired at least three imitators of its own (Big Pharma, Infinifactory and Farlight Explorers) and a whole raft of LPs, construction guides and Youtube content. The developers are committed to making a game with the best production values their resources allow - they listen to the community, incorporate the best ideas from the ingenious modding community into the main game, and have just been excellent all round.
Factorio is a game that, if you've read this far, you should buy.
