With Alien: Isolation currently being discounted by the Summer Sale I find it necassary to write this review as the game may not justify a full retail price, but most certainly when discounted.
Alien: Isolation does almost everything right in regards to horror as a genre, and this is coming from someone who typically avoids horror games as I frighten easily. It does not rely on jump-scares to induce fear but rather the constant reminder that you are the prey and rarely are you at any type of advantage. At times I found myself almost holding my breath between save-points but the satisfaction of progress makes it all worthwhile. The only only type of leverage you have over the enemies aboard the station is your wit's, ability to analyze your surroundings, and the few tools you have to distract or slow your attackers.
The level design, gameplay, graphics, sound effects and music work together so fluidly that it won't take long before you're immersed in this beautiful and unforgiving game. In regards to the slightly controversial AI and the arguements that at times you feel cheated or that your death is not justified, I believe that in a way it adds to the fear. While this may not exactly be fair, it's still a rare occurence that only inches you one step closer to the edge of your seat.
I'm sure there are many like me that passed this game up because of it's few mediocre reviews/ratings but it's large amount of pros outweigh what little cons you could find. I can't recommend this game enough and for a discounted price I truely believe it will cater to more than just those with an interest in horror and sci-fi. Lastly I 'strongly' recommend wearing a headset while playing as it will without a doubt increase the tension and let you fully experience the game the way it was meant to be played, terrified.

I  don't recommend this game for one reason, and it's a very serious flaw IMHO.  Here is an example, I'm trying to get from point A to point B to retrieve an item to progress, the tension is high and the fear is strong so I'm moving as slowly as I can while keeping an eye on my radar.  My enemy is all around me running down hallways, climbing through the vents, and his direction can change at any second.  I spend the next hour making my way through the mission seeking cover under hospital beds and hiding in closets.  A lot of time hiding in closets....but finally, my goal is close and right before I reach my destination a loan refugee shoots me in the face.  Dead.  Now guess what?  I have to start completly over from my last save.  The last hour of my life?  Completly wasted.  And there lies the problem.  With a game this tense and it's focus on stealth and hiding, only being able to save at save stations is completly stupid.  As you can see I have 13.3 hours on record and I'm not even that far into the game.  I have tried and tried to look past this flaw but at this point I can't do it anymore.  Don't get me wrong, I actually REALLY like this game.  The fear and tension here is something that most games just can not pull off, but when you spend multiple hours sneaking around and hiding (trust me there is a LOT of hiding) it takes all the immersion out when you die and have to turn around and do it ALL OVER AGAIN.  Now if you don't mind replaying long and sometimes tedious sections to get to the end game then by all means go play this game, but if not don't bother.  If they would just offer an alternate method of saving complete with automatic checkpoints this would be one of the best games of it's kind.  As it stands now, it's just a extreme pain in the♥♥♥♥♥

I decided to write a review for this game even though it is essentially at the end of it's life cycle.  Basically, if you haven't picked up this iteration of Call of Duty, then I don't think you'll need to.  If you are running some less-than-stellar hardware or a GPU that isn't that great I'd just recommend straight away not to pick this up as the PC port is still not fixed.  With my specs, I do run the game without any isseus at all, but I originally played this game with an ASUS R9 270 and it was a horrifying experience due to only have 2GB of VRAM.
The single player story?  Typical and uninteresting.  I never finished it.
The multiplayer is extremely fast paced and unusual.  It can be disorienting at first because you'll need to keep an eye out for enemies everywhere.  If you like standard and consistant gaming where a team takes map control and holds it down, then AW is not for you.  The exo movement system renders this type of gaming basically void as anybody can now jump across or move across the map with incredible speed.  Many times in Domination, I'll take the A flag and by the time I'm on my way to B or C, there will already be enemies on it.
Many multiplayer games will pretty much be consistant with the phrase, "Bal of Duty: ASM1 Warfare."  These two weapons are essentially all you need as their engagement ranges literally make everything else obsolete.  There are other great weapons such as the HBRa3, but you'll always put yourself in a statistical disadvantage by not using the ASM1 or the Bal-27.
A particular aspect of the Exo suit that I enjoyed was when it game to dodging and evading.  It was nice to quickly get out of a bad situation.
I got the game as a marriage present from my friend just after Christmas in 2014, a month after initial release.  At the time, the game was pumping and servers were full. Around April of 2015, severs were emptying out.  At this point in time, AW functions like an old 90's game where there is a very small core group of players that are only online around a certain time of the day.  The only game modes you'll really be able to find constantly are TDM and Domination.  (Mostly TDM.)
Ultimately, I'd recommend not to pick up this game because it is more or less already dead.  The playerbase is highly anticipating Black Ops 3, and have gone back to play Black Ops 2 and other CoD games.  Advanced Warfare was an interesting idea and I wouldn't be against Sledgehammer making an Advanced Warefare 2 - I just hope the second time around they'd make a significantly better PC port and take weapon balance a bit more seriously.

The larger maps are rewarding - with lots of lore tucked away in notes and books and plenty of loot if you're a fan of lining your pockets with everything that isn't nailed down. Emily's powers are a fun challenge to navigate and the inclusion of an actual no powers mode with its own effects on the world is a bonus.
If you're a fan of the first game and your PC can handle it, definitely grab it while it's on sale. It's definitely worth it. If you're not keen on the first game or can't really see yourself enjoying a different setting in the universe, you might want to pass it up (tho I at least suggest trying the demo since it lets you try the first few levels).

I hope the dev continues updating this game. And a few things that I believe could make this game even more fun:
-Getting downed? Having to crawl with a pistol? It could be a fun mechanic. (Maybe able to toggle on or off)
-More weapons, obviously. But that can be easily offset with workshop support.
-Same with maps
-More modes? Like maybe a sandbox where everyone congolmorates and fights over one point? Temple is fun because of the crazy warzone over that bridge. Might be cool to have something like that with two sides.
-Fall damage? Maybe play into the "going down" mechanic if you fall off a cliff. Again, maybe toggleable.
-Maybe more gadgets, and fine tune the vehicle mechanics. They are definitely servicable, but could use some tuning. :D
All in all, I like that this is singleplayer. I wish the option for multiplayer was there, but I appreciate that I can just mess around for myself. This game is worth the money, and is quite polished for an early access game. (Also, maybe allow us to turn off that "blown out sound effects" thing when you get hit by explosions? After playing the first instalment of Deponia, I had quite a few criticisms, mostly about the characters and storyline. However, despite these flaws, I did enjoy the game and so I couldn't resist continuing on to the next chapter. I much preferred the puzzles in this chapter, although I'm not sure if it's because I was now used to the way the game "thinks" and thus found it easier.
I liked many of the game mechanics and was able to play most of the game without any walkthrough. Again, however, some of the puzzles were quite obscure, or just out of reach so that when I did look up the solution, I either thought "What? How was I supposed to figure that out?" or "Argh, I basically did that!". Still, I appreciated a lot of the scenes and in particular the different places to explore.
The humour is still great, and some of the new characters added some depth to familiar scenarios. As with the first instalment, I still think there was too much dialogue in some places. I also still have major issues with the representation of the female characters in this game, in particular the way Goal is objectified not just by Rufus's creepy possessive pursuit of her as a prize or trophy, but also in the game mechanics. There are also a couple of cutscenes that were just unnecessarily vulgar and borderline predatory. Goal is a great character, and I love the additional dynamism her character got in this chapter, which made it even more of a shame to see her remain as an object to be ogled and played with. Blech.
Overall, it's still a good game, though I wouldn't pay full price for it. I got both Deponia and Chaos on Deponia in the sale and I'm very happy about that. I wouldn't pay more than €10/$10 for either chapter. If you can get the whole lot on sale, even better.

Great game so far! Love this game, it has really good cartoony type graphics, some really nice animations. The story is amazing. Let me just give a quick summary:
The game takes place in Silentia, a dream fantasy world of a young, sad circus clown named Sadwick. The story starts as he wakes up in his travelling circus trailer after having experienced a recurring nightmare, where he sees the world falling apart.
Sadwick wanders off to a nearby forest and meets Bobby, a Chaski, messenger of the King. Bobby is heading to Corona, the royal floating castle, to deliver a powerful artefact, the Whispering Stone, to the king. He claims the end of the world is near and that the land is already breaking apart and the Asgil, a hideous horde of underground creatures, are surrounding Corona. He tells Sadwick he has been unsuccessfully seeking an oracle named Shana who may have advice on shortening his trip, and asks Sadwick to help find her. Sadwick believes she could interpret his nightmares and convinces Bobby to give him the Whispering Stone to activate a secret passage that could lead him to Shana. Shortly after Bobby gets scared away and disappears in what Sadwick believes was an Asgil attack. Sadwick manages to locate Shana and finds out that his destiny is to destroy the world.
Shana directs Sadwick to a nearby island to find mysterious Kalida who eventually takes him near Corona. There Sadwick manages to listen in to the plans of Asgil leader Loucaux but gets captured and thrown in a jail cell. After successfully escaping, he manages to board a flying train to Corona, where he meets Bobby again who tells him that he is too late and the king has locked himself in his quarters. After exploring the castle, Sadwick finds a model of a planetary system linked to the flow of space-and-time itself. He meets the royal astronomer who tells him that the Whispering Stone represents the planet Silentia in the model of 5 planets and that he must repair the system to restore the balance and activate the fountain of the Water of Life to wake the king who has fallen ill.
Upon repairing the mechanism, a blue sphere from Sadwick's nightmares appears saying that Sadwick is inevitably ending the world. Trying to prevent that, Sadwick jams the planetary system's mechanism stopping time itself and breaking all of the world into pieces. The Asgil occupy what is left of the castle, but Sadwick manages to trick Loucaux and reactivates the planetary mechanism again, restoring the cadence of time. He escapes and arrives at the king's quarters, where he instead finds familiar settings and a large mirror. Upon looking into the mirror, another boy drags him into a room with two opposite mirrors. The boy explains that in reality Sadwick is this boy lying in a coma in a hospital while the blue sphere is his father reading him stories. Sadwick then breaks the mirror he came from and wakes up in the real world.

OVERALL RATING: 8/10
Graphics: 10/10
- Should be mentioned that it isn't the most optimised but with a few tweaks you can get it to run
just fine.
Gameplay: 9/10 - Actions feel mostly fluid, there will be some moments though when you
grapple to something you didn't mean to. The balance in enemies isn't the best either.
the soldier 'grunts' take very few hits to kill and take far too long to kill you, while the armored enemies would take over a clip to kill.
-  there are extremely cheap ways to die in this game that are rage-inducing.
-  It is clear and evident that they tried to add other events and try to mix things up to avoid
repetition and the game getting stale but it still does get boring fast.
Story: 7/10 - The devellopers tried to make us feel more attached to the story by adding meaning and value to the characters but it becomes too predictable when a character is going to die in the story and how the entire story plays like a cliche film.
Replayability: 6/10 - it's the same action, same enemy reactions, same turn out of events. It can get boring so fast that you (Like myself) wont finish the campaign for a while.
I wouldn't regret my purchase, but I do still believe the price is too high for the experience you are getting.

With Alien: Isolation currently being discounted by the Summer Sale I find it necassary to write this review as the game may not justify a full retail price, but most certainly when discounted.
Alien: Isolation does almost everything right in regards to horror as a genre, and this is coming from someone who typically avoids horror games as I frighten easily. It does not rely on jump-scares to induce fear but rather the constant reminder that you are the prey and rarely are you at any type of advantage. At times I found myself almost holding my breath between save-points but the satisfaction of progress makes it all worthwhile. The only only type of leverage you have over the enemies aboard the station is your wit's, ability to analyze your surroundings, and the few tools you have to distract or slow your attackers.
The level design, gameplay, graphics, sound effects and music work together so fluidly that it won't take long before you're immersed in this beautiful and unforgiving game. In regards to the slightly controversial AI and the arguements that at times you feel cheated or that your death is not justified, I believe that in a way it adds to the fear. While this may not exactly be fair, it's still a rare occurence that only inches you one step closer to the edge of your seat.
I'm sure there are many like me that passed this game up because of it's few mediocre reviews/ratings but it's large amount of pros outweigh what little cons you could find. I can't recommend this game enough and for a discounted price I truely believe it will cater to more than just those with an interest in horror and sci-fi. Lastly I 'strongly' recommend wearing a headset while playing as it will without a doubt increase the tension and let you fully experience the game the way it was meant to be played, terrified.

I  don't recommend this game for one reason, and it's a very serious flaw IMHO.  Here is an example, I'm trying to get from point A to point B to retrieve an item to progress, the tension is high and the fear is strong so I'm moving as slowly as I can while keeping an eye on my radar.  My enemy is all around me running down hallways, climbing through the vents, and his direction can change at any second.  I spend the next hour making my way through the mission seeking cover under hospital beds and hiding in closets.  A lot of time hiding in closets....but finally, my goal is close and right before I reach my destination a loan refugee shoots me in the face.  Dead.  Now guess what?  I have to start completly over from my last save.  The last hour of my life?  Completly wasted.  And there lies the problem.  With a game this tense and it's focus on stealth and hiding, only being able to save at save stations is completly stupid.  As you can see I have 13.3 hours on record and I'm not even that far into the game.  I have tried and tried to look past this flaw but at this point I can't do it anymore.  Don't get me wrong, I actually REALLY like this game.  The fear and tension here is something that most games just can not pull off, but when you spend multiple hours sneaking around and hiding (trust me there is a LOT of hiding) it takes all the immersion out when you die and have to turn around and do it ALL OVER AGAIN.  Now if you don't mind replaying long and sometimes tedious sections to get to the end game then by all means go play this game, but if not don't bother.  If they would just offer an alternate method of saving complete with automatic checkpoints this would be one of the best games of it's kind.  As it stands now, it's just a extreme pain in the♥♥♥♥♥

I personally feel that this is probably the best Warriors game available for PC outside of Dyansty Warriors 4.
For fans of the series (Dynasty or Samurai), you will find that this game uses many of the mechanics from the originals and doesn't try to change too much. The big changes in mechanics include the ability to use skills during the match which you can only use in increments. Also, you have to select two characters (in single-player only), and you must keep both of them alive. This is probably my only issue with the game. This system changes the dynamic of the game, because sometimes in certain cases it will be only yourself and your other selected partner going against a boss. You might be doing really well against the boss, but then all of a sudden you get shot by an arrow then your partner gets mousoued by the boss and he dies instantly. This breaks the game basically because he is now not performing the function you desired and making your game unnecessarily difficult.
Survival Mode is absolutely fantastic. Using human elements mixed in with the dramatic elements of the scene allow for a really interesting dynamic. Players choose whether to ascend higher into the castle for a higher prize and risk it all, or just give up and keep what they have. Free Mode is basic and unfortunately only inherits from story levels, so sometimes the conflicts don't make as much sense. Story mode is just like you remember from the older ones. Corny as hell. Some of the storylines are actually pretty good though and provide some legitimate humor; they make Magoichi Saika look like such a tool though.
In comparison to other Warriors' games, there is great diversity between characters. While the amount of characters is not huge, there is much diversity in play-style. You can play two different characters and have drastically different experiences with the game. With the ability to play about 10-15 character centric campaigns, you have the ability to experience almost every character in the game.
Unfortunately, another issue I have with this game is that if you play co-op you are required to play the main character with no other option. Simultaneously, the connection shuts off with the other player after each match, and since there is no lobby, you have to restart a match after every single map. Co-op is not allowed for survival mode either which hinders the experience because survival mode is fantastic and there could be a really interesting difficulty curve presented in survival co-op with tweaked rewards.
Lastly, the PC port definitely works a lot better than older titles. Controller support out of the gate, actual keyboard prompts, etc. Definitely not perfect but I believe it's the only Warriors game on Steam that actually supports 60 fps so they're getting there. If a concern was regarding the port quality this is the best one. However, there are a few things missing, and the keybindings can be a bit confusing. I recommend using controller for sure, but even then it doesn't translate the keyboard prompts to controller prompts. It's still fairly obvious though, as the standard mapping is pretty self explanatory.
Overall, Samurai Warriors 4-II has a few issues in regards to its' co-op and addition of new mechanics, but ultimately it's probably the best Warriors game you could get on Steam. I recommend it on sale if you're new to the series, but if you are an old fan like me, full price should be fine.

A hugely under-rated hit that sadly never really took off due to being a singleplayer only experience... but oh, what an experience.
An apocalyptic remake of Monkey Magic, you play Monkey, freed from robot-slavers by Trip, an engineering genius. She sees Monkey's savage power and enslaves him using a headband while he's knocked out, and when he wakes she tells him that if she dies, he dies and that he needs to take her home.
It's the growing relationship between these two that really makes it all happen.. from the startingly realistic facial expressions to the excellent voice acting to the superlative writing, a lot of what makes their relationship blossom goes unsaid; a nice change from the simplicity of most story-telling these days.
Throw in her Uncle Pigsy later in the game and a whole bunch of simple but entertaining platforming and combat sequences, this game will charm you right up until the stunning epilogue... an epilogue might I add that most reviewers seem to have missed the point of; not every 'boss' needs to be a combat-behemoth.
Highly recommend at its current price, or take a stab when it goes on sales. This is one of the most enjoyable singleplayer experiences that I have played.

Enslaved has all the wrappings of a decent action game. The particle effects and art direction are pretty good, and overall cinematic kind of feel. This is a *story* game, first and foremost. The game part could have used a little more work.
The main gripe is that the platforming is extreeeemely straight forward. All you do is pick a direction and a button. These controls are simply not interesting enough, compared to typical platforming aspects, even in this new-age market...
The exact same criticism can be used on the combat, in which the auto targeting is extremely annoying. The boss fights I've encountered tend to pretty much ignore that you just dodged out of the way, the AI has zero turn radius time, and will auto-target you anyway. Of course, this can be countered by being farther away so the attack uses time to reach you. However, you need to be close up to attack effectively, so it's a toss up.
I've encountered numerous glitches where the boss AI will run at a wall indefinitely, or even stand completely still for no apparent reason. It's immersion breaking, to be sure.
Finally, it's completely frustrating how the beginning of some huge sequence has an unskippable cut-scene, often between 10-20 seconds in length.
The only save option is auto-save, which is a very very annoying aspect to include in a game full of collectibles.
I broke the game early on by investing a SINGLE POINT into health regeneration. The game went from absolutely relying on the game giving you health packs, to not caring at all.
Micro managing an extra unit has some interesting interactions - giving the game one of those common puzzle-platformer vibes. However, in combination with the action and "platforming" sequences, it definitely feels as though the developers had too many ideas and not enough time to get it all just perfect. If these gamey parts were developed a bit more, I'd be enjoying myself too much to write a review.
All the whining aside, the characters have highly talented voice actors. Monkey and Trip are cool characters. Monkey was most definitely inspired by Sun Wukong. Trip is a female technophile, she makes what could be interesting puzzle situations into a stall-for-time situation. Further, it's easy to tell the animators were the most skilled people on the team. If you look past the faults of Enslaved, which I've named pretty much all of them... you can enjoy a decent interactive story and a tolerable gameplay. Just take breaks, ignore your inner voice asking for more trial and error, and I'm sure any gamer can find something of value (fun).

EDIT: (Having played a bit through the HW1 Campaign on Remastered)
By all means, Homeworld set the bar on what it really meant to have a space RTS. The original was ground-breaking, and the particularly leisurely pace of the missions as well the ability to keep your fleet between missions reinforced the desire to use tactics, and made each loss of a destroyer a tear-jerker. Needless to say, the game was memorable.
Homeworld 2 was another great game, but I wasn't as much a fan of the strict Rock-Paper-Scissors, and completely transient nature of my fleets. I felt like I was rebuilding from scratch every mission, as if my ships were made out of paper. Some of the grander tactics were substituted with spamming the proper counter, making ground, rinse and repeat. I didn't feel as connected to it, but regardless, Some people prefer its interface and overall playablity.
In the Remastered Edition, Homeworld 1 is basically Homeworld 2, with a story and ships from the first game. Now, on the surface (and for the first few missions), this works fine. The ability to use Evasive or Aggressive tactics (which increases evasion or accuracy respectively) are gone in favor of
general 'behavior'.
A few missions later, and I realized that even my strike craft were not staying in formation. If one has played the first game, one may understand the importance of this, as I'm sure many of the other reviews have noted. Now, I can take this loss in Homeworld 2; the game was different. But there is a problem in Homeworld 1.
Homeworld 1 fleets and missions were not built with the intention of using the Homeworld 2 engine (duh). First of all, a lack of fuel (for both your units as well as the AI's) is okay... until you reach the Garden of Kadesh, and the main element of the Kadeshi forces is their constant need to refuel. Without fuel, this mission has completely changed in nature.
A couple missions later, one is fighting the ghost ship... and the mission has completely changed (due in part to the changes to the ships), one is forced to use Corvettes and Fighters against Anti-fighter and Anti-corvette  frigates (an entire fleet mind you!) without squadron tactics or formations... see the dilemmia?
Now, this may seem like I'm ragging on this game pretty hard, but I don't want to come off too hard. This is NOT a bad game, this is still a great game. But, this is not the same game that came out in 1999. It looks like it, (and damn is it beautiful), but it's not the same at the core... not ultimately.

Game Grade: A-
Shorthand Review:  Fight against an army of the undead as you battle to be extracted.  Teamwork is key in any hope for survival.  Yet again, selfishness is another alternative.
Detailed Review:
The wait is finally over for anyone who has been searching for a free zombie fps game!  This game has just about every aspect of a normal zombie inspired game, but is free (unlike most).  Even though its free, the graphics don't suffer.  Also, there are different game modes you can play which allows for great replay value.  A downside to the game involves the community which will be addressed later on.  This game sure makes up for the install time.
As many of us know, free games can be... kind of... crappy.  From the graphics to the rough game play, free to play games can make you cringe.  This one, however, is not like those awful let downs.  No More Room In Hell offers average graphics and smooth game play for free.  You cannot say that about a lot of games now, even games that cost an arm and a leg.  If you are familiar to Garry's Mod, then those are the graphics you can expect (many props can be found in GMod).  As long as your internet is half decent, this game will run smoothly.  This is coming from me with 150 KB/s internet speed.  Loading is quick and downloads take a few minutes.
There is a surprising amount of replay value in this game.  Normally, free to play games don't offer a lot of playtime.  With No More Room In Hell, there are many game modes involved.  You can either survive several hordes of zombies or battle to be extracted by the military.  Another bonus to this game is the amount of achievements it has.  For anyone who is like me and loves getting achievements, this game is great for you.  You can get almost 100 achievements which will have you coming back to get more.  You can expect to find yourself playing countless hours on this game.
The only downside I see in this game is the player base.  By this I mean the people playing the game (obviously).  These people that you are playing with are supposed to be there to help you fight off the brain dead flesh eaters.  Instead, you can find yourself screaming your head off as your teammate becomes one of those brain dead morons.  This is not very common, but should be expected.  This game is best played with friends, as many zombie games are.  However, you really should expect those “trolls” in all games.  Do not feed the trolls and move on.  Chances are they will just crawl back under the bridges from which they came.
All things considered, this game is really fun.  It is a real time killer that you will actually enjoy.  For anyone out there will poor internet or a bad computer, you can more than likely play this game with ease.  I hope this review helped you get an idea of the game.  It is a lot to read for a free game but at least you won't need to worry about wasted download time.

Imagine if Super Meat Boy and Metal Slug had a kid it'd be something like this.
BroForce is a retro-looking, fast-paced shoot-em-up with destructable environments and a lot of unique gameplay aspects.  You play as one of many "Bros" (spoofed movie characters like Mr. Anderbro from The Matrix, Bro Hard, BroboCop, etc.) and each time you save a Bro in a level, you get an extra life, but the interesting thing about that is that you also BECOME the Bro you just saved, so you're constantly changing characters, each with their own special abilities and fighting styles. On top of that, the action is fast and often challenging (but never unfair) and there are even some simple environmental puzzels that will take you a moment to figure out (how do I get across that impossibly wide chasm? How do I make it across this bridge that's exploding before I have time to run across it?).
If you like action games, pick this up.

Deponia franchise games despite having a story as a backdrop. The real focus has always been the comic side, usually using sarcastic answers as a way to pass the mood. Since the offenses despite the way it is interpreted by the situation itself, end up becoming something funny that also serves as a way to take the possible tension of the situation. Chaos on Deponia game is a point and click adventure genre mixed with humor and a moderate dose of puzzles, created and distributed by Daedalic Entertainment.
Its main objective is to save Deponia ( "Deponie" means "landfill" in German), known as the planet trash that which Rufus, the main character, wants much to see far and try numerous times to escape, until one of those times Rufus eventually you find goal and is exactly at this point that that his personal goal ends up becoming a much bigger goal. What Rufus ever wanted was to leave this place and go to Elysium (This is the word, by the way, used to designate a paradise by the ancient Greeks), and this time the situation comes fully expected, perhaps more than usual to be precise, and gets involved in an accident which ends up passed out across Goal. As I had said what was particular goal has grown and developed in a way that soon Rufus was seeing on a mission to save Deponia from total destruction.
In the first version of the game it happened in the small town of Kuvaq and its development is now happening in the Black Market Floating Red Sea Rust, with more characters to interact and more local exploitable.
About Goal, she barely had a share in the previous game however this time the game almost revolves around her and their personalities, which were fragmented by a new drop caused by Rufus. Thus by means of a remote control can change between 3 figures, each with unique situations and dialogue:
- Lady Goal, intelligent, educated and snobbish.
- Spunky Goal, aggressive and rude.
- Baby Goal, naive and childish.
The visual cartoonized the game is really lovely however the colors are less vivid than the first, it serves to pass the climate change. The game has a more tense atmosphere, the beautiful Kuvaq garbage mountains now give way to scenarios that much convey the feeling of decadence in which the planet is but the beginning seemed to be denied or perhaps a lack of acceptance of truth.
Things that caught my attention in particular:
- Visual landscape quality and the level of detail
- Each character has unique personalities and are well explored, both by their attitudes as the dialogues.
- The moments "musical" excel the songs of the game.
To conclude, I believe that this is a great acquisition, but obviously I do not mean only this title after all this is a continuity and a real experience is required to play from Deponia to Goodbye Deponia. The entire assembly has just finally forming a work that has an incredible brightness.

Let me get this straight, you want me to tell you a review about this game? Whoever you are, you might as well go to the curators, because if you've come for a review on this game, you've come to the wrong place. However, if you have come for an outstanding chocolate chip cookie recipe, you've come to the right place.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

Enslaved: Odyssey to the West Review:
In our short lives we are greeted with a few games that really strike at our emotions and leave a mix of lingering feelings. For me Enslaved: Odyssey to the West happens to be one of those games. This is one of the few games where my first girlfriend and I spent time playing/watching one another on this journey. She barely played many games and I can't even re-call what made her pick this one out. She wanted to watch me play it but I convinced her to play and I do the watching for once. We really bonded even more over this game as story began to lay itself out before us.
Anywho now to the actual review. While the PC port had a few much needed tweaks in it's ini file to make the visuals look better and run at 60+FPS; The game still holds true to what I remember enjoying on it's console debut. That being said I was very surprised this cult classic made it's way to PC as it barely got any recognition on the console front years ago.
Once tweaked the game looks even more gorgeous than I remembered. The combat is still simplistic but it has enough variety to where you don't get too overly bored with it. There's also 4 skill trees to upgrade Monkey varying from, health, shields, blocking, combat moves, long range shooting moves and more. If you collect as much tech orbs as possible as you play the game upgrading becomes easy but you may miss a few along the way. The platforming is some of the best as it meshes well with enviroments but it doesn't have some of the fine-tuning of critically acclaimed platformers but it gets the job done.
The story however and the relationship between Trip and Monkey is where this game shines. The story is a re-imagining of the novel Journey to the West written by Wu Cheng'en. Unlike the original story that was set in a fantastical version of ancient China, the game is set 150 years in a future post-apocalyptic world following a global war, with only remnants of humanity left, along with the still active war machines left over from the conflict. We begin with Monkey being imprisioned on a Slaver ship as well as Trip. Trip soon escapes and Monkey follows after as she just sabotaged this Slaver ship. Both had similar goals get to the escape pods. Soon after a very ungraceful landing; Monkey wakes to find a Slave headband attached to his head and the girl Trip claiming she fit on to him. Monkey attempts to threaten Trip to remove or else to which she gives a command which causes him a great deal of pain unless he obeys the command she issued. She reveals that she had modified the headband to work with only her voice commands and that if she dies or her heart stops for whatever reason the headband would send out a lethal charge and kill Monkey. Realizing this puts some hesistation in Monkey's demeanor;  She demands Monkey to bring her back home to her village and there she will remove the headband and free him. With no options of being free from Trip; Monkey agrees reluctantly.  As the story flows Monkey and Trip begin to bond and start forming a endearing friendship as their feelings about one another change through the story. No longer will it feel like Monkey is just a disgruntled slave to Trip but a caring guardian. Trip also goes through some pretty interesting changes herself but I can't reveal what without spoiling anything.
From there we are greeted with Enslaved's world which is a post-apocalyptic world based on our own. The game never directly tells us how the world ended up in such a poor state of ruins but the enviroments in fact do. Glimpses of a war, a revolution, remamnants of war-like mechs, and much more. As you play the game you can connect these pieces of what the world was like before this in the form of "glitches"/masks that are pretty well hidden. While optional these end up being rather important to a key part of the story but no spoilers on that will be in this review.
Enslaved is definitely one of the few games that I hope many get to experience from last genration as it is a wonderful story that just about everyone should at least experience with one playthrough. Overall it takes about 8 hours to complete the main story, but they've also bundled the dlc in this edition under the extras section which I have yet to start. So what are you waiting for? Give this game a go and tell everyone just what you think of it.

For those that have not yet played Factorio, do not let the number of hours played fool you, due to the fact I have been playing the non-Steam version for a long time, and have easily played hundreds of hours. If you already have Factorio, it is likely you are not even reading this, or forgotten that most early backers probably have a Steam Key Available.
The basic principle of the game is simple, you just have to build a bunch of assembly lines to get back into space. There's just one small detail, and by small I mean relentless creatures that do not take too kindly to your existence. You will find yourself mining ore, stone, wood, and drilling for oil to supply an ever increasing complex production chain of goods. All while researching new methods in which to build, new materials to create, and defend yourself from the "locals".
Now, if this sounds like your average builder game, you are wrong. Not only do the creatures try to kill you, but the bigger your base gets, the more pollution you create, and the more pollution you make, the bigger and badder the creatures get. So, consider the hostility of the planet to be simbiotic to your success in growing your base, which keeps the game nicely scaled to your progress. Normally, you get to a certain point where you are doing so well that nothing can stop you, except in Factorio that just throws down the gauntlet to the creatures that will wreck your day if you let them. Make a car, they get tougher. Make a tank, and well you get the idea.
Add in multiplayer, infinite map, random map generation that has LOTS of options (including a peaceful mode), and you have a very replayable game.
Pros
Cons
In short, I honestly think it is easily one of my top 20 games I would recommend to someone. Be it playing with friends, or playing the game solo, there is something for everyone.

Dishonored 2 is a worthy succesor of its predecessor.  It looks (and since recently, runs) amazing, and builds really well on the story that you finished in the first part. Factorio is a fiendishly seductive simulation game. I bought it in 2014 when it was still an alpha, but you wouldn't have known it by playing it then. Of all the games I've seen that have tried to build off the Minecraft experience with an individual twist (and Steam has pushed a lot of them at me) , Factorio has easily had the strongest individual concept; it breaks away from slavish 3D block world-based imitators to make something definitely inspired by Minecraft and its many technology-themed mods, but only using them as a springboard to colonise some fresh gameplay space for itself.
Factorio is a line production optimisation simulator. You might not think a game whose most basic element is a device that picks things up from behind it and places them in front of itself could go anywhere interesting, but you would be very wrong. The game's genius begins to shine through when you assemble a basic ore refining line, automating the transport of raw ores to furnaces, then to storage. Then you extend the output line, adding a factory that converts iron plates into gears. Then another that turns gears and plates into transport belts. You don't have to make them yourself anymore! Then you build some turrets to defend your nascent industrial complex from the sedan-sized bugs that come to attack it (and you) every now and then. You add another factory that makes ammo so you can dump a stack into each turret and focus on building other things... pretty soon, it's 3am and you've declared war on the xenos threat that's continually trying to stymie your mining and production operations by attacking everything in sight. Congratulations, you're Weyland-Yutani and you're not going to be run off by some damn natives. Pack a thermos and top up the flame throwers, it's bughunting time.
Factorio is a remarkably well-executed indie game. It isn't perfect, and has areas that are still very 'beta' at the time of the Steam EA release, but its core mechanics are rock-solid. The multiplayer experience is very stable for a game with such complex systems. It's already inspired at least three imitators of its own (Big Pharma, Infinifactory and Farlight Explorers) and a whole raft of LPs, construction guides and Youtube content. The developers are committed to making a game with the best production values their resources allow - they listen to the community, incorporate the best ideas from the ingenious modding community into the main game, and have just been excellent all round.
Factorio is a game that, if you've read this far, you should buy.

I was really skeptical of this game prior to purchasing it. I'm a huge fan of the Elder Scroll series and was really put off by reviews claiming that this was a vanilla MMO with an "Elder Scrolls Skin." After playing this for ~150 hours, I have to say I wholly disagree.
First of all, the best MMO ever was Asherons Call. That is the bar by which I measure this game and all MMO's. I played WoW when it first came out, but I found it boring quickly (before hitting level max). I find that most MMO's, especially those that try to emulate WoW, have a quest system that makes you feel like you're doing chores. "Do this, fetch this, please save my daughter." Rinse and repeat. The excitement to level progression, loot, and crafting just wasn't enough to keep me playing.
The biggest selling point to this game is Content, hands-down. If you liked Skyrim and Oblivion because you felt immersed in the world, this game has the same feel. If you loved Skyrim and am looking for the next one, this will definitely satisfy. This has all of the excitement of a single-player MMO, but you share the world with other players. You can group or go solo. You can wander the world and take any quest, just like the single player series (Thanks to the One Tamriel update). Frankly, this should be the new bar by which all MMO's are measured, usurping WoW. This is exactly what you'd want an RPG in a large, shared world should play like. The quests feel unique and interesting. The world is absolutely beautiful and immersive.
There's a lot to talk about with respect to this game. The battle system limits you to 5 abilities and an "ultimate." No more action bars with 324802 options. This means that while you have a wide variety in how you build a character, how you play him in a group is a strategic decision. I love this. There are over 500 skill points to spend, but you never feel overwhelmed by what to choose next. It's quite possibly the best skill tree ever created. I remember being impressed with "Path of Exile" because of the skill tree, but it was overwhelming.
Crafting is great. PvP is great. Questing is great. Battle system is great. PvE is great. World is great. Everything seems really well balanced. Ultimately there's so much content with the DLC's that I'm not sure you'll ever run out of things to do.
I highly recommend getting the ESO subscription, and treating the non-subscription version as a demo. Yes, it's $15/mo. But the devs have committed to 1 DLC / quarter, which is ~$40/DLC, which is worth it. Each DLC adds quite a lot of content. The subscription also gives you coins (premium currency), and more than enough to never feel like you're missing out.
If you like RPG's, really immersive RPGs, you will absolutely love this game. It's exactly what you'd expect an Elder Scrolls MMO to be. It's everything that made Elder Scrolls great and everything that makes MMO's great wrapped into one, with the ONLY caveat being the subscription (which IMO isn't really a cavat, considering the massive content updates they provide).

Chaos on Deponia is a good point-and-click adventure.  The puzzles are challenging and the narration is comedy gold.  I still can't understand what the narrator is singing between Acts, but I think that might be part of the joke.
Some of the puzzle clues are obtuse and frustrating initially, but the solutions always seem so obvious in retrospect.  I like a game that forces me to think about things in new ways.

"Chaos on Deponia" is the second point-and-click game in Deponia series. It features a goofy protagonist, Rufus. He still lives on a garbage filled planet Deponia, from which he always plans to escape. Rufus is a walking disaster. You can expect water to catch fire when Rufus is around. There is something about smart mouthed Rufus that reminds us of Guybrush Threepwood, classic point-and-click hero.
PROS:
- Pretty and colorful cartoon graphics.
- Humour: edgy, sarcastic, sometimes dark.
- Good voice acting.
- Decent story: with love, deception, mystery and revolution.
- Balanced difficulty.
- Cool locations.
- Interesting characters (Bozo, Toni, Goal, The Revolutionists).
- Classic point-and-click feel.
MEH:
- You get to visit some locations quite often, which makes background music somewhat annoying.
- Some animations are sort of lazy. But that's to be expected from an Indie game with limited budget.
CONS:
- Some puzzles are not so intuitive, you may require walkthrough (I had to use it about 4 times).
If you enjoy classic adventure games, "Chaos on Deponia" is just for you. It's not a masterpiece, but is good and you won't regret spending 10 hours to complete it.
GAMEPLAY 8/10
GRAPHICS 8/10
AUDIO 8/10
STORY 8/10

This game is GOTY 2014 for me.
The brilliant recomposition of the atmosphere, the overwhelming pressure that hits you when you feel that death is around the corner - and oh boy what a terrific monster is hunting you, the Alien, aka Xeno. 'A survivor', 'perfect' as the words of Ash.
The graphics are literally some of the most beautiful I've ever got to see in a game, and with some mods on PC, the game looks even greater!
But visuals are even better because the devs used all of the art in the Alien movie to deliver us an environment as the one in the movie.
Details....details everywhere. From the sound of the 'futuristic' computer as thought in the late 70s to the keycards, this game could be a sequel of the first movie.
Aside from the visual immersion, every single dialogue, every mission, every time you press a button, run, crouch, there's an insolent - yet magistrally created and kept - fatal faith suspended on your head.
Amanda Ripley is alone, and the adventure keeps on drawing you to a pessimistic looking end.
Ridley Scott soul was all around in this mov...I mean game.
Now onto the gameplay.
You said survival? Well guess what, you won't have a single second where you'll feel safe...Amanda saves her progress on some kind of composting machine, and it takes 3 seconds or so for the machine to process and actually save.
But within those 3 seconds, the game is still alive, anything can happen, death also. How genius is that?
Same goes for the crafting system, no pause, menu and here goes my magic potion. Na-a.
The Xeno AI is the best thing to happen to video games. You pretty much can't predict it. Beside a few scripted entrances to scare the player in the best way, the alien will stalk you, hunt you wherever you possibly are.
And for me this is where the game succeeds and truely means the horror-survival words.

NOTE: This is a review more centered on the PvP aspect of Dark Souls II.
Dark Souls II is an intense dark-fantasy action RPG, sequel to FromSoftware’s critically acclaimed Dark Souls, and spiritual successor to Demon’s Souls.
One step forward, one step back. That seems to be the pattern of Dark Souls II. For every improvement that FromSoftware made, it was countered by some sort of flaw. However, on top of failing to respond to many of the issues present in both the original Dark Souls and the first game in the series, Demon’s Souls, new problems have also been added to the spectrum. That being said, let’s start off with some the game’s enhanced features.
Pros:
•A fantastic PC port. Unlike in the original Dark Souls, it runs at a consistent 60FPS and there is no need for a mod to make the game run well, even on lower-end machines. This, of course, effects both single and multiplayer interactions positively as lag is much less of an issue.
•Better connectivity to other players. In Dark Souls, I remember struggling endlessly to find a summon to help me with a difficult boss or to invade some poor, unsuspecting traveler as they trudged their way through their own grueling world. Summoning and invasion items almost always work properly and instantaneously when connecting you to another player.
•Overall better mechanics. Controls seem much more responsive and polished. Thanks to the new Adaptability stat, players can add more variety to their builds when considering their playstyle: whether you are going to use a big, heavy shield or are relying solely on your mobility. Raising adaptability adds invincibility frames to your rolls, so fast-moving characters will find this very useful. However, it also effects how quickly you raise your shield or drink estus, so it is still worth investing in on heavier builds that deem these actions important.
•More engaging covenants. Most covenants in Dark Souls II serve a purpose, but are usually PvP specific (there are a few exceptions, such as Heirs to the Sun). They dramatically improve upon the subpar covenant system of the original Dark Souls and carry much more significance. Will you be a Blue Sentinel, sworn to protect the meek Apostles of Blue, or will you be a dark servant of Nahr Alma in the Brotherhood of Blood, a merciless god who demands sacrifice and works through you? The dueling mechanic introduced in Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition is also much smoother and worthwhile as you can PvP to your heart’s content whilst also gaining ranks in your covenant (if you win, of course).
Cons:
•Soul memory. It’s a love it or hate it kind of deal, and unfortunately, I despise it. As you gain soul memory tiers, PvP becomes progressively more unbalanced as you are pitted with players hundreds of levels higher than you. In the highest tier, you can be connected to anybody between 15 million to 999 million soul memory.
•Netcode. This has been one of the largest disappointments for myself and the many Souls players who engage in PvP regularly. We were promised dedicated servers from FromSoftware, but instead received “dedicated summon signs/invasions,” which, don’t get me wrong; I enjoy the instantaneous connection, but laggy multiplayer interactions have consistently plagued the Souls series since Demon’s Souls and I was hoping for something more this time around.
•Balance flaws. FromSoftware seemed to brush the PvP community aside in the midst of creating Dark Souls II. Their design decisions reflect their desire for players to continue going into successive new game plusses and to endlessly level their character to counteract the increasing difficulty of the game. Due to the soul memory mechanic, players wishing to engage in a PvP “meta” like the previous Souls games are often versed against extremely high level characters with the best armor, spells, weapons. This creates a lack of purpose in creating a “build.”
•Invasions are almost completely absent until NG+ or beyond. There is a striking lack of availability to invasion items in NG. This is due to FromSoftware’s attempt to counteract the act of “twinking” present in previous Souls games, which to anybody unaware, was when a player would acquire end-game level equipment and invade in areas designed for low-level characters. This often connected them to brand new accounts/players and that were easy pickings when versed against their over-geared foes.
With all of this being said, if you asked me “Is this game worth buying?” I would immediately tell you yes. Though the game is flawed, it is still a much better experience than the generic, rehashed, and hand-holding games that are currently flooding the market. Also keep in mind that despite the game’s shortcomings, it is still very early on in its life and I expect many things to be reconsidered and revised in the future.

Remember, the following is simply my opinion. Feel free to disagree if you find a point unfair.
Hmmm, Dark Souls 2. Would I recommend it to people? Well to be honest it would depend on the person. Obviously this isn't going to be a game that appeals to everyone but if you're reading this review chances are that you haven't bought the game yet or are scouring Steam to find the popular opinion for your own review to march to. So I'll be as straight-forward as I can. XD
Is the game good? It's ok.
Does it compare to the original Dark Souls? No.
It might seem a little unfair to compare the sequel to the original but honestly, there's really no way not to do that.
Now I haven't completed the game yet and quite possibly never will. But am I ragequitting? Is it too hard for poor little me? Not at all. I played through the original DS as well as other hard games like Super Meat Boy and Faster than Light. It's not the difficulty that gets to me in DS 2. It's the grind.
See, one of the key differences in DS 2 is that the souls are finite. Enemies will stop respawning after ~15 killings and don't come back. Thus, anytime you fail to retrieve your souls after dying you lose souls to spend permanently. It is theorectically possible to kill everything and lose all of the souls availible in the game. Leaving you with no possibilities but to start over again with a new character.
Also, because I haven't completed the game, I'm not going to talk about the story, NPC's, and other similar topics because i have no right to talk about them.
This had a very negative effect on me. My style in the original DS was to explore, find all the items, and eventually face the boss. Dying was a common occurence but while I lost time and souls I never lost OPPURTUNITY. I could just try again and nothing was truly lost. But because DS 2 has finite resources, dying and failing to retrieve them means losing those resources with no pleasant way to get them back. As such my gameplay turned into farming. I'd go through a level, killing enemies until I was in danger of dying then I'd head back to the bonfire, heal up, and repeat until the area was devoid of enemies. This is GRINDING. It's not a fun way of playing it's a chore. Eventually though, I would clear out part of a level, and being able to more freely explore is satisfying. However, it seems, that in an effort to make the game less susceptible to farming and grinding, it brought out all of that within me. (If you play the game and don't do what I did. You may find the game a lot more enjoyable. Playstyles do vary from person to person.)
Another problematic gameplay mechanic was the loss of max health each time you died. Now I understand that this was a mechanic in Demon Souls of which the DS games are spiritual successors to, and on it's own I wouldn't mind this mechanic. It's certainly not as horrible as some others claim it to be. But because it's paired with the limited respawns of the enemies, this makes dying both more common and more punishing. There are ways to reverse this or lessen the effect but those are again finite resources that you will eventually lose the oppurtunity to use.
Healing is also a little different. There's a new item called the soul gem which is a consumable to restore health. But there's nothing wrong with. Instead it's the staple of Dark Souls healing, the Estus Flasks that bother me. In the original Dark Souls the number of Estus Flasks you had was based on the amount of kindling the bonfire you were resting at recieved, the lowest amount you could get was 5 (max:20) However, in DS 2 you have to find Estus Shards to get more Estus Flasks, which are your only reliable healing method. If you miss them, you don't have Estus Flasks and the game is that much harder for you.
This is a small extra point but according to my friend who made it to the end of the game, the enemies aren't diverse and their placement leads to some very dissapointing moments. A key example would be those ordinary hollow soldiers. They are the standard enemies in DS 2 and you meet them in most of the begining areas. But what occupies the final level? Those ordinary soldiers. Nobody special. (I haven't seen the final level, but I trust my friend and he's more a fan of the series than I.) Imagine if you went on an epic RPG quest and the final bosses castle was filled with slimes, the most basic of all enemies. This is what my friend saw, and you could probably guess how he felt. He also mentioned that a lot of bosses were susceptible to backstabs which are (for those who don't know) the strongest out of all the possible attacks you can do which almost every weapon can do.
This one is not so much of a bad thing as a different thing, but unlike the original Dark Souls, where the map weaves and interlocks with itself in very interesting fashion, DS 2 spreads out from the center, which is Majula. The paths don't intersect or weave together in any way. So it's much more linear and you can teleport right from the get go so moving between the paths is easy. However, because Majula is the hub where everything is, you'll be visiting it a lot. Want to level up? Majula. Want to upgrade your armor? Majula. In fact, if you want to do anything, you'll probably have to visit Majula. This isn't a big problem for the game, but when you compare it to the first DS, where you could do a lot of those things at a single bonfire, it could be seen as a step in the wrong direction.
Now by this point you might be thinking to yourself "Dark Souls 2 sounds horrible! Is there anything good about it?" The short answer is "yes". A slightly longer answer is "Yes, but really nothing (aside from updated graphics) that the original DS didn't do."  Dark Souls 2 is not a bad game. Let me repeat that.
Dark Souls 2 is not a bad game.
There are some refinements that it does have. Magic has been nerfed to be not as overpowered in the single-player experience. Backstabs are harder to do in the sequel as well. Certain enemies react to light. And a lot of other small stuff.
But all of these small refinements don't compensate really for what was lost in the gameplay changes. Simply put, it's just not as good (in my opinion) as the original Dark Souls.
And that is why I clicked the "Don't Recommend" option. If there was a middle ground option I would have chosen that one. Or I would give the game a C+ or something. Again, it's not a bad game. It just doesn't live up to the hype that it generated, and while killing the bosses and clearing levels are rewarding as ever, the road to get there is more painful than they needed to be.
I'm sure that FromSoftware did their best when they made this game. But I feel that they missed the point of dying in the DS universe. Dying isn't fun. Being punished and weakened for dying isn't fun. Being able to learn from the deaths, trying again, and again, trying new tactics, getting stronger despite all the times you died, and finally overcoming the obstacles to stand on top. That is where the fun is.
I wish the best for FromSofteware on their future projects and thank the team for their efforts on the Dark Souls games.
(If you didn't find this review helpful, state why in the comment section. I'm always seeking constructive criticism to better my reviews.)

However, if you have come for an outstanding chocolate chip cookie recipe, you've come to the right place.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

Particularly something like Mercenaries 1+2, where the gunplay was better, the destruction was more fun, and the gameplay loop was much tighter and more rewarding. Even the story was more compelling with factions that mattered with branching paths for story and multiple endings.

Let me get this out of the way now; I love the Warriors franchise and I think Koei and Omega Force make good games, but they really need get some of their act together.
This is not a good PC port. It has many problems. Oh so many problems so let me begin.
Terrible keyboard controls and no Xbox One controller support: If you do not have a controller, do not buy this game. Keyboard controls are awful and make it impossible to move the camera around. If you have an Xbox One controller, don't use that either. Your camera will forever spin the the right and none of the buttons will work properly in game. I had to download two programs so I could get a PS3 controller working on my PC before I was able to play the game.
There is no English voice acting: It should just be a rule of anything at this point in video games that if you intend to release a game in the West, you should dub that game in English. Koei decided not to here, and that's a big problem. Trying to fight the enemies in front of you while trying to read that tiny dialouge box at the bottom of the screen is unbelievably annoying. It's gotten me game overs at least 3 times now.
Last gen textures: They used PS3 textures for the ground and sky but they used the PS4's character models. I don't get that. Why wouldn't you just use all PS4 textures? Why is that so hard? You already did it with character models so why not go all in with it?
Things I liked so you know I'm not just salty: Character creator is nice.
When you do play with a controller the game feels good and responsive.
Hanbei Takenada is the best character.
There. Just don't buy this game. Get a Wii and play Samurai Warriors 3. Sure the graphics suck but at least you get English voice acting. And you'll get a much better story in that one than you will here.

I'm so happy! It's like my youth has been given back to me only better! Everything that was great about Homeworld and Homeworld 2 is still great, and now the visuals are appealing again too!
The ships in this game sparked my imagination and forever influenced my perspective on science fiction engineering and now they look better than ever. The models are essentially the same but the textures are amazing and far more detailed than I ever would have expected.
Properly normaled and bump-mapped, the Higaaran mothership finally looks like a giant industrial work. All of the fleet of both Higaaran and Vaygr ships are lovingly brought up to speed with modern machine capabilities. Even the HUD overlays are sharper and more clearly defined. The backdrops are gorgeous as ever and buffed to a fine polish with better lighting effects. In fact, all the graphical effects are much improved, from hyperspace windows to Kharaak burning from orbit, the game looks amazing now and the gameplay holds up after all this time.
The cut-scenes are still impressively animated and mostly unchanged, although if my memory serves me the images are sharper and there are a few additional elements I don't remember, but the masterful voicework on both the narrated cuts as well as the idle radio chatter from your units still sucks me right back into the struggle to return the last of my people to my Homeworld.

Overall this remaster is great and definitely worth buying if you like RTS games.  I rank it my 2nd favorite RTS of all time behind the original Starcraft and its expansion.  Heres my review of it:
The good:
The art is amazing.  The remastered textures, sounds, music, and models are all more than I had hoped for.  The new visual effects make the game as impressive today as it was when it was first released (the HW1 graphics were amazing for when it came out in 99).  Playing through the story is as fun and enjoyable as I remember it being.  I'll be spending a lot more time playing this for the next few weeks.  I like how my capital ships stay grouped up and in formation after hyperspacing from one mission to the next, that saves a lot of time setting them up.
I haven't gotten around to Homeworld 2's campaign yet, but I doubt I'll be disappointed there.  That game is still easy to pick up and play today as it was 10 years ago.  So the graphical update to it will do little but make everything better.
The Bad:
While the remaster is great there are many changes from HW1->HWRM.  There are a lot of core changes to gameplay when the game was translated over to the new engine, many of which affected the strength of support craft, fighters, and corvettes in negative ways.  Such as:
* Fighter/corvette formations having no effect on their behavior in a fight.  Corvettes don't face their targets when circling, meaning certain types of corvettes only use half of their guns in a fight.  This hurts Kushan the most because of the way their guns are laid out.
* Guard works completely differently making it impossible to form defensive corvette walls and fighter balls.
* Support craft healing abilities require them to be right next to the craft they are healing, as opposed to a comfortable distance away.  Making them both slower to heal because they have to maneuver into position and less effective because they cannot respond as quickly.  It also means two support frigates cannot heal each other.  They just circle around each other trying to sniff each others butts, like a pair of dogs.
* Ships have wierd accuracy issues.  Many times their shots are no where near their targets, even when their target is stationary.
* You can only build 2 units at a time.  In the original you could build 2-3 of each unit type simultaneously for a total 10+ units being built at one time (3 fighters, and 2 of each of the other types).  And that isn't even counting a carrier.
* Research now costs RU and having multiple research vessels does not let you research multiple technologies at once.  Previously research was free and you could designate either a single or multiple research vessels to either research multiple things at once or one or two things very quickly.
* Resource collectors will sometimes completely ignore patches of resources and claim that the map is dry.
* Everything is less reponsive.  I think this is due to the engine, but I every click and command was crisp and responsive from the original.  In the new engine everything just feels more floaty.  Kinda like Starcraft 1 -> Starcraft 2 responsiveness.  I don't know why this is so hard to achieve in newer games but its something I've noticed.
Because of that, the game plays about 60-70% accurate to the original.
The Ugly:
Of the new remastered graphics I'm very impressed with the missile effects ... when zoomed in.  When zoomed out they aren't there, and you can barely tell where the missiles are by the small missile pods.  In the original you could clearly see missile trails even when fully zoomed out.  And the ending credits are missing the music from Yes, but I heard that was due to a licensing issue.  If you want to see the original credits in their glory just visit youtube.  I have crashed once, and when getting back in game it completely screwed up my hotkeys in a mission where I really needed them to work from the start.  And finally, you need a "Shift" account to play multiplayer.  Its completely pointless to make one because they then force you to link it to your steam account before you can play.  Why couldn't you just use my steam account to begin with?
I definitely recommend this game, but if you don't mind old graphics for HW1 you will find the original actually plays much better than the remaster.  As for HW2 its probably a direct upgrade, since this is just a modified HW2 engine the game is running on.

Looking forward to several more years of this game!

I'm a veteran of the PS2-era days with DW3/4 and SW1. I haven't played any of the Musou games since because I fell off the world of console gaming, and Dynasty Warriors never clicked on the same level as Samurai Warriors did.
Samurai Warriors 4-II is a full-on SW game. I'm happy to see how far the series has progressed. The gameplay is still solid, the controls are still tight, the missions are still sometimes overwhelming and aggravating, the sense of progression and personal achievement is still there, and they've smoothed out the most aggravating portions of the series. This was done through the new sweeping attack systems which let you clear out large amounts of weak enemies in very satisfying ways, while keeping power/normal attacks for officers. It also has character switching, so you don't have to run back and forth all the time, instead you can set your secondary character to go off and have some fun on the opposite side of the map, and when things need to get done, you switch over instantly and get them done. You lose far fewer battles due to time constraints, but that also means that objectives come faster and require you to make tactical decisions whether or not to actually do them.
In short, it's a classic Musou game, and it's a classic Samurai Warriors game. Koei delivered a surprisingly good port for the PC, and I'm happy to give them dosh if making good ports to PC is going to be a common occurrence. I had no issues getting my old Logitech Rumblepad 2 set up and working, even though it's DirectInput. Not a lot of games nowadays support DirectInput, even though they should, seeing as how XInput is a lesser variety of satan.
One thing to keep in mind is that the DLC is extremely overpriced for what it is. I wouldn't mind paying for them at $1-3 price points, but $8+ or even $25+ for costumes is insane. They never go on sale either. Keep in mind that Koei is still a Japanese company used to Japanese business practices. Japan is a place where a full DVD/BD set of an anime series can run up to $200 for a single season, so simply put, we in the west are not the target audience so we don't get treated as anything other than a nice little market where they can get some extra cash.
Oh, and Koei saw fit to spare us from horrendous English-language voice acting, and instead kept the original Japanese audio. That's very nice, and the translations are alright. Sometimes there are moments where you go "Wait, that's not what that means, not even close" but those are mostly moments where they at least tried to localize some sort of phrase or mannerism or joke that you wouldn't get without a cursory understanding of the language.

Dishonored 2 is great sequel to it's first installment.  The levels are well set up for you to perform creative kills on enemies with your abilities.  Both characters are very fun and have their own cool style; Corvo's abilities are a lot more stealth centered for taking things slow, while Emily's abilities are a little more fast paced.  Emily is the better character if you are looking to do crazy things like flying through the air all the while catapulting enemies below you up into the air.  Corvo is good if you played Dishonored 1 and want the classic abilities, and if you want to take time with your kills.
It's a great game with a lot of room to master each ability and pull off sick combos.  I love games like that.  The game has a lot of replayability in my opinion, so it should keep you busy.  Have fun, and high chaos for the win.

A good game although perhaps not quite as good as the original Dishonored.  Sleep darts are in short supply, and you can only carry five.  Therefore, I emphasized the use of stun mines that can take out multiple enemies with the proper upgrades. Pistol bullets are readily available, but I never use the pistol.  There are still a ridiculus number of guards, and they are extremely perceptive even in Shadow mode.
I liked the fact that in these games you are rewarded for not killing and penalized for killing.  That is a refreshing difference between the Dishonored series and most other games.

Absolutely spectacular remake of the beloved HW franchise.  The graphics are amazing, and the changes they made to both HW1 and HW2 are much needed (for example, getting rid of the fuel requirement in HW1). These games are STILL the best RTS ever made, and they really shine here.  If you've never played Homeworld, you've never experienced the best the RTS genre has to offer.  Homeworld has been my all time favorite game since its release, so I am very critical of anything Gearbox is doing with this franchise.  I'm happy to say that the remastering was done with a TON of care and love, and the bugs I've seen are very few and far between-a relief in this day of publishers releasing so many unfinished games.  It can only get better from here.  Way to go Gearbox, you've successfully brought back Homeworld!  Now make Homeworld 3 so all my dreams can come true!

This one is a classic and well worth getting. A lot of reviews say that the game aged well and that Homeworld never really needed the remastering treatment it got. And yet. And yet the work Gearbox did in concert with the original development team, the original voice actors, the concept artists, and the original game's modders shows a loving respect for a series that should never have gone fallow since Homeworld 2 came out. The remastered version is gorgeous and the gameplay hasn't aged a bit. I still tear up hearing the choir singing Barber's Agnus Dei.
This is a great game and a work of art well worth having in your collection. I look forward to seeing what Gearbox's enthusiasm will bring to the series in the future.
