I gave the first game a recommend, and I'm not really sure why--I suppose because it was the first Daedalic title I ever played. Especially after playing The Night of the Rabbit, though, I felt particularly put off by Rufus's character more than anything else. It feels like so much "bumbling idiot nevertheless gets the hot chick" trope, except Rufus is if Guybrush Threepwood had a LOT more misogyny... not to mention the (otherwise interesting) core gimmick of //nonconsensually// remote-controlling Goal (which seems like a flagrant "Woman as Trophy" name there). I'd feel better if it turns out she's fully a robot/cyborg vs. a woman with a brain implant for what reason, but I haven't looked up spoilers to find out without playing part 3. What Goal sees in Rufus despite her awareness of how terrible a person he is doesn't make sense--sort of caring about Deponia not getting exploded + wanting all of her back together vs. splintered doesn't = great relationship material worth forgiving the physical violence he's brought upon her (ESPECIALLY when he totally meant to do it).

I really like it in an overall point of view, but lack in some other categories.
PROS.
-Great Soundtrack.
-Nice character design.
-THANKS for the japanese voices and subs.
-Two character at the same time, this is nice because you can at least sense a little more of "strategy and control" over the battlefield.

CONS.
-Expensive and really not useful DLC's
-BAD BAD BAD button mapping while using a controller, this games are intended to be played with a controller, playing this with a keyboard/mouse is TERRIBLE. I recommend using a gamepad but you need to learn the buttons yourself, and sometimes the counterattacks and special attacks are hard because you need to remember which button do each thing.
-Short story mode :(
-Weak fighting system, I know it is a hack & slash game but KOEI needs to make a change in this, not adding more powers or giving the enemies a harder punch, I would like to see a little more of strategy and control from the player over the field and one on one battles. I feel sorry to see the lame cavalry only charging toward nothing specific or archers units being killed without remorse without doing anything special, just standing there. The minor soldiers don't have a purpose, and the bannermen are useless, you only kill them as soon as possible and say goodbye to the challenge, another weak unit are the barrack captains, these guys don't feel to have any important role more than morale it would be good to see these guys having an impact in numbers and reinforcements...
-I don't like the weapon system on these Samurai Warrior, it's hard to understand and a little complicated, we only want to have the best weapons possible as soon as possible and destroy everything with amazing powers. In older Dynasty Warriors games KOEI used a Level Weapon system, where you started with an odd looking weapons in level 1, but while you complete missions and kill units your character level up an you weapon do it also, changing in stats and appearance I REALLY LIKED this kind of system...easier and the changing look in the weapons was like an achievements. (Obviously you needed to to something special in certain map to get the ultimate weapon)
Personally I like this game, it could be better but is fun to play.

This game is a great sequel, and changes / improves many features from the last game.
Performance:
I am running a average i5, GTX 1060 build and the game runs on high, about 55-60 fps indoors and 50-60 in the town area, runs perfectly smooth with very few lag spikes, and never crashed once during my playthrough.
Gameplay:
I love the fact that there are now new and improves abilities within the game. Corvo comes with his regular loadout from the previous game, with slight upgrades to make playing as him much more smooth. Emily's new abilites give me a reason to want to collect runes and spend the time choosing what I want to invest into, they allow very different playstyles and can be used in all the different scenarios you get yourself into. Although many abilites were enchanced for Corvo, I felt that the game should have implemented some more non-lethal playstyle abilities for both the characters to use, as in order to get a 'good' and 'non-chaotic' ending you have to spend more time in being careful that you dont kill some random dudes, I feel like the game should support the non-lethal route more, making it easier for first time players of the dishonored franchise, as lethal seems to be much easier playstyle to go with. The new bonecharm system is cool, but only a few bonecharms I found were useful to be honest, I specced into crafting bonecharms with Corvo and I felt it was a bit of a waste of time and runes really. The new powers/abilites spec tree is quite interesting, and I feel that most of the buffs obtained with runes are the same if not better than some of the bonecharm powers. The new black market feature is probably one of my favourite things about Dishonored 2. The fact that you can hunt down and rob the markets, or stock up on supplies while in a mission is great. The biggest change that I have seen is new mission styles, not only can you delve into and explore a clockwork house with changing walls and floors, escape and break into a palace, assasinate somebody at his own party, travel through time and play pretty much two levels at the same time and break into a witch infested mansion. I feel that the game has more variation than the last, and some of the non-lethal options have been well thought of, instead of rendering every key figure unconcious, you have to
Also, one last thing. I feel that the overall feel of the game and the difficulty consideration has increased, the game seems so enchanced story wise, and the enemies can prove troubling at time, causing the need to come up with new tactics to beat them. But with the new difficulty setting, with over 20 options for certain aspects of the game, even veterans can still feel intrigued to play again and again. Oh and the fact that Corvo is voiced is literally a reason to buy this game. If you're having doubts, do what I did and get the demo to check performance and if you like the game. 10/10 recommend, looking foward to any possible DLC.

With the original
, Arkane set themselves apart as much more than a small studio that made a couple of good RPGs (Arx Fatalis in particular). It was a landmark stealth game with a beautiful and intricate fictional universe that took the torch from the Deus Ex franchise and held it ever higher. It was a custom-made immersive sim that plundered the fire of the titans among immersive first-person games (Deus Ex, Thief, Half-Life, BioShock) and forged a whole new experience in gameplay and worldbuilding.
With Dishonored 2 they attempted to repeat the formula and surpass the excellence of the original, and they both succeeded and failed at the same time. They succeeded because the level design is just as good and in some cases better than the original; because the gameplay is just as fluid and slightly more complex, introducing several new powers and abilities that expand the reach and grasp of the players, allowing them to move unfettered in their paths of violence or pacifism. It looks visually stunning and includes several fascinating details in the environment. As a game, it manages to overcome its own conventionalities to reinvent itself beautifully.
However, it can fail as a product because it was developed with the newly-engineered in-house Void Engine, which is poorly optimised to deal with the diversity of CPU-GPU combos in the current market. I can't say I experienced major issues, but then I waited about three months before delving into it, having waited for the patches and optimisations, and yet still encountered quite a bit of unstable framerates, particularly in NPC-heavy areas. On the other hand, I've read several reviews and comments saying that it is
. So it's a bit of a lottery: some say they've had no issues whatsoever, and others experienced heavily impaired framerates that make gameplay very frustrating.
On top of that there's Denuvo in the form of a loading screen when you start the game, showing the split faces of Emily and Corvo, and a loading bar that sometimes takes but a few seconds, and sometimes over a minute. Denuvo is very intrusive as DRM goes. It requires weekly-or-so online verification, and if you're stuck offline for some time you won't be able to run the game (this happened to me in particular at some point). I've also read a couple of reviews where the buyers complained that they upgraded their hardware after buying it and then had to go through some Denuvo red-tape hoops before they could run the game: apparently it monitors your hardware as a way of ensuring that you have the same hardware as you did when you bought the game, which is preposterous for a PC gamer. Hopefully Bethsoft will have Denuvo removed at some point in the future, as they removed it from DOOM, but I wouldn't hold my breath.
As ambivalent as this review may seem, I do recommend it with all these caveats out of the way. I'm currently in the middle of my third playthrough, with Emily, having done a Flesh and Steel/Pacifist/Ghost run at first and then a High Chaos run, both with Corvo. Emily's powers are much more interesting and fun, however, and I kind of wish I had tried them on my first or second playthrough when the game was fresh on my mind and eyes. But everything that made Dishonored great also makes Dishonored 2 great: not just the finely tuned stealth gameplay; or the coherent, immersive worldbuilding; or the iconic dystopian art direction; or the myriad possibilities of reactivity to the player's choices and gameplay approaches... It's all of these things combined and more: all the little things you notice as you play it for the nth time. Buried under the mess of the Void Engine and Denuvo there is a truly great game, rich in replay value.

Don't mind what steam says. I played this for over 30 hours. This is one of the most complex games I have played lately. You start very simply, on a planet, in middle of nowhere. Your objective is to build a rocket sillo and launch a satelite into orbit. So you start mining iron ore. But you need iron plate so you have to melt it. You need furnace for that. But that needs to be fueled so you start mining coal. You better make it automated, or you'll get frustrated. Awesome! Now do it for copper too.
Congratulations! You have 2 most used basic resources that you will need. We forgot about one thing. Those things polute and that will attract alien life form. You better have enough bullets for them. Prepare for zerg rush!
And this is only first 20 minutes or so of the game. "Soon" you'll be making engine, rockets, fuel and off to the alien base to kill them. Why you might ask? Well, here comes on of the most important resources for the end game. Alien artifact. You will need A LOT of them.

The first time I saw the Factorio trailer, I was already hooked.  I bought the game years ago and it's still great.  The difficulty is highly configurable, and there's some truly massive mods as well, so it will stay interesting for years to come.
At it's core, Factorio is game about automation and logistics.  The challenge is creating an increasingly large production and logistics system with a clear final goal of launching a rocket.  Factorio has an amazing sense of scale and the 2D nature of the game works extremely well for this genre.
I highly recommend Factorio to anyone who enjoys logistics puzzles, resource management, and the casual, automated slaughter of monstrous alien bugs.

This Review shows my personal opinion about the game. NOTE: English isn't my mothertongue, so please excuse any language errors I make in this review.
I'm playing this game now for about 2 years and so far I haven't encountered any gamebreaking bugs (at least not in the experimental/unstable channel). This game is about creating your own Factory using Mines, Furnaces, Transport Belts, Inserters (little cranes that put items from the ground/containers/belts to other ground/containers/belts), Assemblers, later Trains and even later in the game: Drones (like inserters, but not bound to the location).
You're having very slow start with a coal drill (drills ores using coal) some iron plates and a furnace: Barely enough to get started. You gather resources to create more furnaces and drills, so you don't need to gather all the resources by hand. Now you have to walk between your 2 - 3 mining sites to get your stone, iron and copper and to put new coal into the drills and furnaces. You start building a centralized storage and refueling system for your drills furnaces and resources. You still need to craft everything by hand.
Time for some research!
You build your first Steam Dynamos to get electricity and replace your coal drills with electrical drills. Now you build a research facility and research Automation I! You get assemblers! Assemblers craft items for you. e.g. 2 iron plates to 1 iron gear and with another assembler 1 iron gear + 1 copper plate => 1 research pack. Now you have automated your basic research! Yippie!
Up to this time you may still have encountered the first enemies which you had fight of with a simple pistol! Let's research turrets, automate ammunition production, research walls and create a defense line. Now you're pretty save from those biters ... at least for a while. But as time goes by your resources are all used in your factory; You need to find new ore deposits, then transport the resources to your base and hope no biters attack your new outposts.
Later on you get the trains (which can be automated ... what a surprise) with these you have access to even more ore deposits. you know have resources, 90% of your crafting automated and no more space. you'll need to clear of those Biter Bases. Once done you can finallly research the technologies to build a space rocket ... Now you *just* need to build a rocket ... Tada you've finished the game ... if you're fast in about 5to 9 hours. if not in about 100 hours.
In my singleplayer world I have a small factory and about 30% automized of what i wanted to automized ... after about 50 hours of playtime (on this world)

Black Mesa, for the uninitiated, is a full fan remaster and reimagining of the original Half-Life but within the source engine. In that it is an older school first person shooter that pits the player as Gordon Freeman in his debut adventure showcasing where the myth surrounding the character came from.
Talking about the original Half-Life 20 years later is borderline redundant: Half-Life changed almost the entire industry and changed the way people treat FPS games. I initially stated it was "older school" as opposed to actually being old school due to the fact older games were less believable in their settings and environs. Half-Life felt like a believable world as opposed to a bunch of abstract arenas with a rough theme running through them such as Doom or, to a degree, Quake. Structurally buildings made sense and your route, even if it was utterly linier, felt like you were feeling your way through a maze of office blocks, abandoned missile silos, open desert and test labs. Despite that it still retained the old magical pockets of being able to carry a small arsenal in your pockets and the fact Gordon seemed to be an Olympian in his movement capabilities and would only ever go anywhere running like Sonic the Hedgehog.
Jump forward to Black Mesa and while there have been some subtle changes, it does show a nice counter between older, late 90s / early 2000s game design and more modern sensibilities that made the original a classic. The most blatant change is the huge leap in fidelity in both sound and the visuals. Where there was a slight degree of abstraction in the original due to technological reasons, Black Mesa pushed the creaky old Source engine a good degree to look leagues better than Half-Life 2. There were never any moments where I spent a moment or two trying to decipher what an object was and almost everything has a place or reason. If anything the shear attention to detail for a mod team gone commercial is staggering, making many fully fledged products backed by big publishers look utterly weak in comparison. No it is not an effect laden Unreal 4 challenger with skin textures that rival reality, but for the meagre engine it runs on the fact almost every character you meet has a unique face is incredible! Not only that but in the department of the sound design the original Half-Life clearly cut corners in places either due to budget or the fact the technology did not hold up, meanwhile Black Mesa has almost every person you meet (enemies excluded) having some form of unique dialogue and, in many ways, unique circumstances, fleshing out an already brimming game world more. Before if a guard meets you in a hallway maybe he would say something running to a script, then again he may just look at you, say "hello" and you be on your way. Now he will likely give a comment on the situation in the surrounding area and even be fully animated, with head motions and facial expressions and full hand gestures, including some situations where they interact with the environment (using computers, punching something etc...) giving the game a much richer feel to it.
While the game does expand on the way things looked and felt it does "fix" things in some ways. In that context it flat out changes a lot of sections around a lot. Some sections such as 'On a Rail' and 'Surface tension' have been shortened while the areas of 'Unforeseen Consequences' just passed the initial labs have been fleshed out a little. Not only that but the way you gain items and weapons has been changed up slightly as has their use. The initial weapons such as the crowbar and the Glock have had their positions changed to appear later on as well as the Revolver replacing the Shotgun early on, Shotgun actually appearing just before the silo doors for 'Blast Pit'. Also some weapons have changed such as the afore mentioned Magnum having an ADS alt fire, which is needed considering how much tougher some enemies are.
It is hard to comment on if these changes are good or bad. Some will welcome these changes as they may indeed fix issues with the original e.g. I personally thought 'On a Rail' was too long originally. However a purist will no-doubt be maddened at the changes brought in and simple things like changing the Shotgun and Magnum will make their blood boil, but its down to if you can tolerate these changes.
Like the recent HD remaster of the original Resident Evil you may or may not like it. Sure its more palatable to modern audiences, but some people play for "JILL SANDWICH" moments. Thankfully, there is nothing that radical in Black Mesa.
So would I advise Black Mesa? At the moment, I veer more towards no unless you are really hungry for some Half-Life. It has that rather ugly distinction of being an Early Access game and, at the time of reviewing, lacks an ending. As I've hopefully made clear what is there is an incredible game thus far and it will certainly be well worth buying but  it currently lacks the entire Xen section. Yes Xen was hated by many in the past, but the redesigns of some of the levels here are so well done I anticipate to see what they do with this final section and maybe even we may see it elevated to the standards of the rest of the game.
Also worth noting is that some sections are not fully baked in yet. Surface Tension is still undergoing some tweaks and there is a relatively finished version on the Steam Workshop, it is still a little off both in its pacing and also it contains the worst parts performance wise of the whole game.
On the plus side the actual progression done in the Early Access period looks to be really good. I played the mod when it first hit in 2013 and, while I generally enjoyed it, there were some spots where it was certainly lacking. Initially the shooting in game felt wrong, weapons having the wrong recoil, sound and animations. Now everything feels far more weighty and has an appropriately chunky feel to them. The new MP5 feels great and the little touches like bolting weapons when fully empty just adds to the meatiness of it all.
In many ways Black Mesa is the Half-Life 3 we did not get, further expanding on the detail to the world continued with Half-Life 2 and expanding on the mechanical and situational world rather than reinventing the wheel. As mentioned it reflects the HD remake of Resident Evil in that it reminds us of how a game can feel if a designer stepped back and tried to make something with a 90s centric design philosophy, and in the decade of nostalgia, maybe that is what we need from games. If Half-Life 3 were to ever happen, this is a nice stepping stone while we wait.
When it is fully done, a must buy at full price or not! If it is on a discount sale during Early Access, maybe give it a shot.

Alrighty, been a while since a games impressed me enough for me to want to leave a review...
So I must say I've only recently gotten into stealth games as well as horror games, and this game most definitely did not disappoint. The games graphics are phenomenal! Never had any problems with any of the AI, occasionally the Xenomorphs model would clip through lockers I was hiding in but that never effected gameplay.
The different enemy types require different methods/strategies to deal with (I won't go into any detail as not to spoil anything) and gave a good sense of variety. My biggest complaint probably is I thought the human AI was a little dumb in the way they reacted to threats/you. The aliens AI seemed pretty awesome for the most part, and while I read that it can learn to react better to your distraction tactics and such I obviously never used them enough to get to that point.
I thought the pacing was pretty good as well, though some people might finish the game faster than I did as I play super paranoid (constantly checking motion tracker and waiting to watch for any patterns in the AI's current movement)
The game is definitely challenging and if you can't sit still to wait for the right time to make your move and can't stand crawling around at a slow pace while you sneak around this game probably isn't for you. I mean maybe on lower difficulties you can run around like an idiot more and be sort of safe? I dunno what the lower difficulties are like, I dived right into hard and finished the game in about 21 hours I think? (According to my gameplay time and taking an hour off for like loading screens/menus/being afk)
I wasn't a big fan of the ending but I also wasn't surprised by it, but I suppose you'll have to play through to decide whether you like it for yourself. I feel proud to know though that according to steam achievements only like 5% of steam players have finished this game on hard and I can count myself as one of them... Not sure if I have the guts to take on nightmare mode though...
Overall really awesome game! Highly recommend it!

I'm recommending this game very cautiously...
I will first mention that this is an excellent horror game. The Alien flavour is definitely there; it's a definite treat for Alien fans, the art direction is gorgeous, the atmosphere and gameplay are genuinely nervewracking, and the titular Alien that stalks you throughout the entire game is so unpredictable you'll be on the edge of your seat, praying it does not find you as you hold your breath and lean back in that locker you're hiding in.
However, two things have annoyed me to the point of frustration about this game:
-The Alien
Yes, I know I just mentioned the Alien being terrifying (which it is!), but I think that because it is so unpredictable, it will kill you many, many, many times; this wouldn't be so bad if it weren't for the fact that the game starts to become very repetitive after a while of getting mauled so many times. Add to that a harsh difficulty regarding the Alien (it seems to be able to figure out where you are after silently crawling away from it, only for it to reappear three seconds later where you are (and likely kill you)) and a no-checkpoint save system that's extremely unforgiving, and you're looking at many instances of you traversing through the same areas again and again and again, trying to accomplish your objective, only to be killed once more. It's at this point it becomes less terrifying and more frustrating.
-Bugs
No, I'm not talking about the Facehuggers (though they are in this game - and they're dangerous!) This game seems to have a lot of gamebreaking bugs that have not been fixed as of this writing. There have been many instances of the game not following the expected narrative, and it would load into some totally random area that has no bearing on the current objective. As a result, the game will not update your objective and you'll be forced to wander aimlessly, forcing you to either restart from your last save, or worse, from the beginning of the mission. I've repeated a mission three times to no avail in getting past it simply because it won't let me go to the next place it's supposed to let me go to. This has frustrated me to no end and I cannot finish this game simply because the game won't let me.
To sum up, Alien: Isolation is a very good horror game that will keep your eyes glued to the screen in terror, but be aware of how unforgiving this game can get, and perhaps wait until Creative Assembly can patch all the gamebreaking bugs this game has.

I generally enjoyed the first Deponia (I propose to rename the series "Disapponia") game, but the horrible pacing of the ending made me wary of getting this one.  It was on sale for $3 so I decided to go for it.  If the most favorable outcome were true, this game would have made up for the faults of the previous installment with better writing and a larger world.  Unfortunately, that is not what happened.  While the world may indeed be larger, my desire to explore it has been completely destroyed.
In the hour that I played, every single line of dialogue was about how much of a fool Rufus is.  All realism has been thrown out and Rufus no longer behaves like a human.  The humor is predictable and the actual game seems less important on the developer's priorities than the bad jokes about the protagonist.
I simply couldn't continue playing after the scene with the robotic dog because the writing was that bad.  The same voice recordings were recycled too many times throughout the dialogue and the puzzle was severly disappointing.  My favorite parts of the first game were the unconventional and devious puzzle solutions that weren't immediately obvious and helped me to relate to the character of Rufus.  This scene alone destroyed that as the solution to the puzzle was yet another joke about his inhuman stupidity.  Rufus went from a likable trickster to a complete clown who cannot hope to be passed off as a realistic character.
This is very disappointing, as the world in which Deponia is set has the potential for a great experience and I was genuinely interested in where the story would go in this game.  Now I have no motivation to play any further because I just don't want to see whether the writing could possibly get any worse.
In addition to the poor writing, this game also seems to have worse voice acting than the first and the animation just feels lazy.  The latter of these complaints was also a problem in the first Deponia game, but I was willing to overlook that for a well-made game overall with good art and effort put into other places.  Since this game obviously doesn't have the second part, the lack of believable animations only adds to my disappointment.  It's unfortunate that I will not be able to enjoy Deponia's wonderful art because of the horrible design of the game.
I really have to wonder what this game's target audience is.  The humor is too banal and predictable to be enjoyed by an adult but the puzzles are too difficult to be figured out by a child.  I was under the impression that the first game was targeted to adults but I have trouble beleiving that could be true considering how immature this one is.
My advice is that you do not invest in the Deponia series, as this really isn't worth anyone's time.  If you don't believe me, you should be able to come to an agreement quickly enough to still be eligible for a refund.  While the first game was a good experience for a $2 game on sale, this is overpriced even at its current $3.

This game started off rough and even after these years it still doesn't seem to be the polished game I was hoping for. I was not one of those crying war when it first released and was littered with bugs as well all know. I could go file my taxes in the time it took to complete one turn. I still enjoyed the game, perhaps I was misty eyed at reliving my first experiences with the original Rome Total War.
For me the number one postive thing about this is game is the modding community. Without them Rome would still be a mess. I've installed everything from enhanced graphics to troop rosters. Having a larger selection of soldier types from the vanilla offerings is perhaps my favorite feature. On top of that people have taken it upon themselves to create entire campiagns rework general and agent perks and create new nations.
I still have problems with this game however, agents are perhaps the most annoying feature though am sure a lot of people like them. Create a spy spam coercion and watch your spy ranks grow to infinite proportions, at least I was able to do that, bypassing the agent limit. One can wipe out an army rather quickly with 8 spys posioning their supplies.
The AI is still rather dumb even after the latest patch, a year or so late to fix. Assault a town with a few artillery and watch them wipe out an entire army that refuses to leave the cap area. This has changed somewhat as the enemy will now rush you blindly instead and die. Though my last few games I've noticed them staying onto their cap again. I rarely play hard mode so perhaps its different but even the AI trying a simple tactic like flank rarely works unless its one or two cavalry units.
Diplomacy I've found to be a mess as well and its a feature I'd like to work the most. My latest game had myself fighting Armenia. I crushed 5-6 of their armies killings just as many generals, and took 3-4 towns and cities from them. Did they want peace, nope. My power rating compared to them was laughable and yet when I offered peace to recover my armies they rejected it. Common sense is gone, even bringing a nation to its last town on the verge of defeat offer peace and I've been rejected. Heck even make them a vassal and its no, though lets not forget having a vassal is a waste as well since they are dumb as bricks.
With my 500+ hours I clearly don't hate the game, it has its quirks like anything. I love the modders out there and I still enjoy the combat and history that Rome brings. I think am just dissapointed in the noise dive the series took, the response from Creative during its release was sad in the way they treated their community. The latest DLC is a joke from what I've been hearing, thank you reviewers for allowing me to dodge that bullet.
Would I still recommend this game?
Yes in using the mind set Rome II is a foundation for all the great mods out there. Make Rome II into the game you want it to be and it will be a fun ride, the sad thing being it took a loving community to make the game into what it should be.

I've played almost every MOBA in the book (DotA, League, Infinite Crisis, DotA 2, Strife, HotS, etc etc) and Smite is by far my favourite both conceptually and mechanically. However, Smite is one of the few MOBAs I picked up very late... most of the above titles I played in Beta or just after release. Smite's marketing isn't the best, and if you watch videos and read around, it looks clunky / silly / weird... well, it is. But it's also extremely fun.
---
Pros:
Reliable servers around the globe and cross-server play. This is great for me as I live in the UK but have many friends in North America and elsewhere overseas.
Flexible build paths which actually work (you don't have to lock into the meta to contribute).
Variety of maps, all with reasonably short queues, and a "map of the day" mode featuring modes suggested by the community.
HUGE quantity of data ingame. If you've played x many MOBAs where you've felt "oh, if only I could check check my..." to evaluate your performance (as I have), well, Smite gives you everything you could want with data points both ingame and after. However, for new or younger players, this gratuitous quantity of maths could be a con.
Built-in replays, match history, and voicechat (Curse Voice partnership).
Mature and dedicated playerbase; I find it a bit more friendly than on League or DotA as well.
Reasonably priced added content and NO pay-to-win features. You can even buy all Gods (read: heroes/champions) present and future for one set price, so you don't have to grind or spent loads of money collecting them.
Inuki (just google this guy, he's awesome).
---
Cons:
The art style feels older than League or DotA 2, even though it's a newer game. Partly this is due to the 3rd person camera being less kind to the graphics, but I suspect it's mainly due to a lack of attention. Graphic designers cost money and Smite doesn't run on a League or DotA budget (unfortunately).
Funky camera and mechanics take some getting used to, and feel a bit less fluid than on other major-title MOBAs.
Not for new MOBA players. The very things that make Smite awesome can make it very frustrating for newbies. If you're new to MOBAs, you might want to try honing your skills on a more accessible MOBA first before coming to Smite. BUT the playerbase I have found to be pretty friendly (as MOBAs go) so they will give you polite advice on build paths etc.
Even with cross-server play, the playerbase isn't as large as League, DotA 2, or HotS. So you will find some matches feature players with extremely disparate skill levels if you queue up outside of peak times. And unlike on League, the matchmaking will always err on the side of getting you into a game quickly, even if it's not very balanced.

This game is pretty swank. It's at least twice as big as Dark Souls 1, and has significantly more content than the previous entry. The story ties back into the original, but I can't say how without potentially spoiling things.
The gameplay feels a bit less solid than the original initially, but that's primarily because they changed the way the stats work and how everything scales, and the enemies you fight feel considerably less 'original' than DS1's. Dark Souls 2 has a much more human aesthetic for a lot of it's enemies, and most of what you'll be fighting is humanoids with weapons or weird mutations.
Despite my complaints, the combat feels fairly responsive, and it's a nice change of pace from popular action RPGs that have flashy attacks that don't seem to do much damage, and combat that boils down to lots of button mashing. Encounters in Dark Souls typically only last a few seconds, but they're considerably more tense and thoughtful than most other games, with both you and your enemies able to end eachothers' life with only a few well selected actions, or tragic mistakes.
For the most part, I enjoyed it, and I recommend it to fans of Dark Souls 1, or people wanting a more challenging game that isn't challenging because of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t traps or impossible difficulty, but challenging because it respects you as an adult and doesn't hold your hand.

Alright, I originally had a negative review for this game, but I realize it was for the wrong reaons, I will explain. For the record, the concept of the game is fantastic, play as several different gods from different panthens such as greek, roman, hindu, chinese, japanese ect. However there are a few things that irritate me.
When playing the game, you will notice serveral things. The first, is that some gods are unbelievably broken, especially on initial release.
Another thing you will notice is that, unless you are playing in ranked(which you have to be level 30 to do) and even then, a lot of the random people you play with are either rude or silent. SMITE is a team based MOBA. If one person doesnt carry their weight, it can spell destruction for an entire game. If the tank doesnt take damage from enemies or toweres, the ADC gets killed. If the assassin doesn't gank, you lose your lane. However I find that most people just do whatever the hell the want. They are either totally silent, or complain that you didnt do something. An example of this would be if you were a mage and just survived a gank, you have 10 health left. You give the command VVB(Be right back) and start to teleport away. As soon as you get back to base, a teammate complains that he just died because you didnt stay, even though you said you were going back to base and that he shouldnt have gone in.
This may seem like a very minor issue, people will just say ignore it, however I have seen that it does effect games, players will fued with each other, saying that one person is garbage as an assassin or tank or support, instead of focusing on the game and giving constructive criticism. Also there are only so many times you can see a person just jump into a 1v5 fight and complain to everybody else that it was our fault he died, before you just throw your hands up and just saw WTF.
It all boils down to communication, a coordinated team that communicates through skype or curse is going to win 99% of the time. If a team is fighting amongst themselves more than the enemy team, you might as well just surrender and save yourself 30 minutes.
However, if you do have communications you are more likely to win. This is why I give this game a thumps up, If you have friends or people who arent likely to trash you just for a simple mistake, this game is fantastic, especially considering its free. There are a few other things that irritate me though, like the season 3 joust map, I just find it a bit bland and watered down considering this new map only has 2 mana buffs and an attack buff. As well as bull demon that if killed, gives health and mana regen as well as disabling the enemy tower for a minute or so. It wouldnt be so bad if the bull demon had as much health and did as much damage as the fire giant in conquest. Instead a level 8 hunter with even a little bit of lifesteal and/or crit can take it down in under 30 seconds solo.
Like I said the game has issues, but if you have friends you can communicate with, you can overcome these problems with ease.

I’ve been a Koei fan since before they merged with Tecmo. To start off, Samurai warriors 4 II runs decently on my pc and considering I don’t have the best rig around that means at the very least the game was optimized decently and has probably gotten patches since it first went up on the steam store. Below is a break down of things you need to know before deciding to buy.
-Samurai Warriors 4 II has less characters than the most recent Dynasty warriors entry. However, each of the 50 something characters feel very unique and there don’t seem to be any cloned move sets. There are just enough characters everyone will be able to pick out a few favorites!
Additionally there’s a pretty nice create a character mode. It seems minimalist on the surface but in fact you can go into greater detail and even make a character who has mismatched colored eyes. I found overall there were enough choices to make me content. It isn’t as good as the character creator in Saints Row 4 but you’ll still be able to have fun with it!
-The chronicle mode has been replaced by a sort of “castle of doom” mode where you enter Nobunaga’s haunted manor and face steeper challenges the higher up you go. The “challenge portion” has you complete specific challenges to get rewards whereas the “raid mode” version of the castle merely has you fighting increasingly tougher foes.
-The gem system has been replaced by a tome system in which you collect different colored books from fallen officers to unlock the skills and buffs for each character on a hexagonal grid. It’s very similar to the leveling up system in Ninja Gaiden 3 Razor’s Edge.
-There’s no English voice acting but the written translations of what’s going on seems good enough.
-Even on “easy mode” the game can be pretty challenging on certain maps and enemies seem more prone to block or counter you. The artificial intelligence here seems just a bit more “aware” then it has been in past musou titles.
-The story mode is more character driven here than it was in the original vanilla version of SW4. Believe it or not there are some rather touching moments but when you’re not reaching for a handkerchief you’re having to endure some of the cheesiest camp ever cooked up in the land of the rising sun! However, most musou fans are accustomed to this as these games are very “romanticized” and take their liberties with history. SW4 II is a lot like “Game of thrones” only it doesn’t take itself quite so seriously! Sure, people die and hearts are broken but there’s a distinct lack of blood, gore, incest, and♥♥♥♥♥♥ Then again, depending on who you are that might be a good thing! Grim-dark realism isn’t always “better”.
-Weapons are now upgraded in shops by fusing them together. Fusing weapons of a similar type is the best way to get results but it’s not necessary. Those of you familiar with the Orochi series will adapt to this type of upgrading right away. It’s pretty much the exact same system.
-Combat in SW4 II is distinctly “faster” than in other musou titles. You can literally dash around at lightning speeds while knocking enemies together into the air as if they are a demented Katamari ball of human meat! “Team combos” make a return too as when you’re close to your partner you can combine your might for some screen filling spectacles. Of course every character has their own signature attacks as well.
-There are at least a few memorable emotion inducing soundtracks that really stand out and the music overall fits the theme of the game nicely.
-On the battle field you can now switch between two characters with the mere press of a button. Believe me, this comes in handy!
-Controller support included!
Overall I “do” recommend SW4 II BUT I have a few caveats. One is that none of the characters gradually get new alternative outfits as they are leveled up. (Like in Warriors Orichi 2-3) Sure, you can get a “bathing towel” for two female characters but that’s it. Prey your pockets are steep cuz it’s time to make way for DLC! Want extra levels? Want some sexy eye candy? Want some nice audio tracks from previous games? You can certainly have it but you’re gonna have to sell your organs or newborn child to be able to afford it all.
It was nice how in past musou games there were more unlockables but it feels as if SW4 II was a bit “gutted” to string us along with multiple paid transactions.
You mad? Yeah, I don’t blame you and I even understand why people might sit out on this title because of the dlc shenanigans. Sure, musou games have had dlc for awhile now but the prices seem to be getting higher and the amount of “in game content” to unlock is shrinking. SW 4 II makes that more painfully obvious than any warriors title before it.
I love Koei/Tecmo but it’s my humble opinion they should treat their fans better. When the bulk of dlc content equates to over $100.00 (More than the game itself) it’s time to reprioritize the current business model!

The time has finally come for me to write this properly. Impressions not so fresh by now, but general idea and opinion on the game has been formed by now. I played through this game 1.5 times, with first playthrough being non-lethal, find-as-much-as-you-can-letionist, took my sweet time exploring with Corvo on normal difficulty - this resulting in missions taking around 4-5 hours since I wanted to see every nook and cranny; the other half of the playthrough was with Emily, also non-lethal, on hardest difficulty, ghosthrough. Additionally, I played around with combat a bit to test it out. I think I have a fairly decent idea on different aspects of the game.
I have been and still am a huge fan of the original game. It was the title that actually got me into gaming and made me love stealth games. I was really looking forward to another entry in the series, seeing how good of a job they did building the world around and it would seem like a waste of a great material - when DH2 was announced, I was hyped. I couldn't wait to dive back into this world and explore more. That actually happened - we get a glimpse of Dunwall and spend the majority of the game in beatiful city of Karnaca. The mission areas are bigger, there are a lot more secrets and places to see and no matter if you agree to take powers or not, game gives you ways to traverse the city. That is right - you can actually do proper flesh & steel playthrough and tell the outsider you're better off without his 'influence'.
Powers. For Corvo, they are the same ones used in the original title - what makes it different are the upgrade trees. You can spend runes to upgrade blink to a time-stoppind-Daud's-blink, you can even make it a kick-blink for combat purposes. There are many more that probably float on the internet already so I won't list them here - options to spice up gameplay are there, are fun and could even alter one's playstyle this way. Emily's powers are interesting, pretty much all of them are designed to be available to a stealth and a combat focused player, with example of Domino allowing to kill or knock out linked targets or Shadow Walk allowing to pass an area unnoticed or stealthily murder/knock out people. My personal favourite was combo of Mesmerize and Domino, to get an extended reach on people that would otherwise be unaffected by the former and then knock everyone out. If, for whatever reason, one wouldn't want to play with Emily/Corvo and still wanted to try out different powers New Game+ is in the game, runes are carried over and all of the fancy magic is available to either you choose to play with - unless flesh & steel route is chosen, then runes get converted to coins.
The story here is a very weird thing. It is simple, yet cluttered. Pacing is all over the place. Best description I could give of it would be that it is there. It does give you some reason to move forward but it's a secondary objective, I'd say. With the original I felt some sort of urgency, maybe not to the point of always rushing to objective because 'there is no time for exploring' but the job had to be done, the reason was solid, the drive was strong. It wasn't all that present in the second; I could partially blame this on bigger areas that could result in forgetting why are we actually in here in the first place. The newly introduced Bloodfly infestation was rather underwhelming. It doesn't fall under 'another Rat Plague' category as it seemed to be advertised as, but is just a minor inconvenience at most. They made a good job making Nest Keepers, they certainly are damn creepy and seem more scary than Weepers. The antagonists were either not memorable, undeveloped or amusing. Some of them didn't get enough exposure to give you the 'ah, he/she does this, has influence and power, has to be stopped for sure for being a shitebag!' and pretty much become the 'oh, that was this oh-so-powerful person? welp, not anymore!'. Allies are alright. Not much better, just alright. They pretty much serve as shelter providers and purpose/reason givers. Outsider has changed from his initial iteration, not only in VA but also attitude. Many people seemed to hate that decision, but personally I think it fits the narrative better. Instead of being a passive observer he always was, he now has the reason and right to show something more than indifference.
Dialogue. It was ranging from atrocious to alright-ish. I understand that they wanted to change their direction but it didn't work out all that well; lines sound like forced poetry and sometimes come off as more shallow than deep - that is very apparent in very first visit in the void where player obtains the Heart. With that, another problem emerged and it being overexposure. What players of the original first speculated about that could then later be confirmed or denied by devs through questions on social media, now was blatantly shown. Part of the fun were those speculations and subtle hints, the general mistery surrounding them - now a bit killed with obviousness.
So, what could possibly keep me playing? The actual gameplay! This is a completely different story and I could probably compliment on everything they've done with it. First DH's gameplay was highly praised and got a few complaints here and there from the community - to which the devs listened and improved everything that could be improved. Now available to you in nearby stores: air knockout, combat choke, all new types of darts for your crossbow including stinging bolts making enemies flee, new mines and more! Non-lethal playthroughs have definitely been made more interesting, seeing how many tools they added to improve it. Not to say anything about combat. Perfect parries are actually doing something now and help to get things done.
The AI has been vastly improved, with normal being hard as it is - I wouldn't recommend doing first playthrough on ghost, as for many it could prove a frustrating experience because of that. Enemies are incredibly perceptive, they pay attention to doors that were previously closed or opened, missing patrol companions, can also notice you peeking through the corner, and other disturbances. They also search more thoroughly, checking dumpsters, under the tables. Makes for a tense and fun experience if you don't find yourself a good sneak. In combat though they might not shine as much - they are a bit harder, definitely much more brutal but still don't pose much of a challange for many. That doesn't take away from the fact that slaughtering people is just as fun - if not more fun - as it was in the first game. An interesting observation was also that when you overwhelm guards by murdering their friends, the lower ranked ones might terrified try running away. Oh, and they can trip on stairs. Or generally trip. They definitely trip on stairs.
Graphics are amazing. Art direction has changed from the original, differences are visible and it is just as good in it's own way. Many times it was pointed out that they wished to make it all look like a 'painting in motion' which, in my opinion, they nailed. Colour scheme makes it all just nice to look at. NPCs still have their iconic, kinda comic-like features like bigger hands, long, weirdly formed faces, smaller heads. Civilians varied and made the urban areas feel alive.
That is my take on the game. Would I recommend it? Yeah, I would. The story might not be best and fall flat but gameplay is definitely worth it. They improved on everything that was in the original title, added new, interesting ways to do whatever one wishes to do and reward for being creative and finding alternative solutions. If you liked the original, it's a buy. Same if you like stealth. And there's a demo now. So hey, just try it. It's fun.

I will first mention that this is an excellent horror game. The Alien flavour is definitely there; it's a definite treat for Alien fans, the art direction is gorgeous, the atmosphere and gameplay are genuinely nervewracking, and the titular Alien that stalks you throughout the entire game is so unpredictable you'll be on the edge of your seat, praying it does not find you as you hold your breath and lean back in that locker you're hiding in.
However, two things have annoyed me to the point of frustration about this game:
-The Alien
Yes, I know I just mentioned the Alien being terrifying (which it is!), but I think that because it is so unpredictable, it will kill you many, many, many times; this wouldn't be so bad if it weren't for the fact that the game starts to become very repetitive after a while of getting mauled so many times. Add to that a harsh difficulty regarding the Alien (it seems to be able to figure out where you are after silently crawling away from it, only for it to reappear three seconds later where you are (and likely kill you)) and a no-checkpoint save system that's extremely unforgiving, and you're looking at many instances of you traversing through the same areas again and again and again, trying to accomplish your objective, only to be killed once more. It's at this point it becomes less terrifying and more frustrating.
-Bugs
No, I'm not talking about the Facehuggers (though they are in this game - and they're dangerous!) This game seems to have a lot of gamebreaking bugs that have not been fixed as of this writing. There have been many instances of the game not following the expected narrative, and it would load into some totally random area that has no bearing on the current objective. As a result, the game will not update your objective and you'll be forced to wander aimlessly, forcing you to either restart from your last save, or worse, from the beginning of the mission. I've repeated a mission three times to no avail in getting past it simply because it won't let me go to the next place it's supposed to let me go to. This has frustrated me to no end and I cannot finish this game simply because the game won't let me.
To sum up, Alien: Isolation is a very good horror game that will keep your eyes glued to the screen in terror, but be aware of how unforgiving this game can get, and perhaps wait until Creative Assembly can patch all the gamebreaking bugs this game has.

Chaos on Deponia is the second entry in Daedalic Entertainment's Deponia point and click trilogy. The title was initially released a mere 10 months after the original, showing that Daedalic had already made plans to further the series before they even knew whether or not it would be a success. This review has been written with the idea that you, the potential buyer, have already finished and/or know the basic story of the original Deponia; spoilers for the first game ensue.
The sequel picks up what seems like only a few hours where the original had ended, bringing Goal and Cletus back into the picture almost immediately. The storyline sticks to the same basic plot, where Rufus attempts to escape the junkyard of his home planet by finding a way to Elysium. Further plot points are unveiled, including new information on the Organon, and the exact reason as to why they want to blow up Deponia, and what they stand to gain if they do. Wenzel is missing from this installment, but a plethora of new characters are introduced; although most of them do not stand out anywhere near as well as the original cast does. Still, most of them are enjoyable additions to the crew, and characters that were introduced later in the first Deponia see their backgrounds flourish.
As anyone who has played the original Deponia knows, these games are tough point and click adventures. Chaos on Deponia is even harder than the original, and much more confusing at times. Instead of just one Goal, now Rufus must focus on three different Goal personalities; Lady, Baby, and Spunky, all of whom must be interacted with using certain dialogue points, at specific times, to trigger events that will further the progress of the game. On top of that, there are more obscure solvents to puzzles, like putting a straightened banana into a drain, and turning down the in-game music volume at a determined point; just very bizarre, cryptic solutions which seem to plague the entire game. Likewise, there are also some rather frustrating mini-games, most notably the dolphin/submarine battleship simulator. This, again, is not a game for those who do not enjoy a hefty challenge, or who do not wish to use a walkthrough.
The charm of the humor and wit within Chaos on Deponia seems to have worn thin from its predecessor, as a good chunk of it is just more of the same. As the story wears on, Rufus becomes progressively more irritating rather than humorous, and it gets tiresome hearing Goal and the rest of the crew putting him down and rejecting him constantly. Sure, he's the main hero and he's also an idiot, we as the audience understand that; it really doesn't need to be pointed out during every single snippet of dialogue interaction between Rufus and the others. On a brighter note, the voice acting is still superb and the communication between characters is well written. Daedalic have also kept in the Chorus Guys, which are an absolute fan favorite from the first Deponia.
As far as the graphics go, they're even better this time around than in the original title. The colors are more lively and vibrant; where Deponia mostly stuck to rustic browns, reds, and oranges under a bright blue sky, Chaos on Deponia steps out with lavish purples, greens, and blues, all the while keeping the grimy hues and undertones of a world encapsulated by, and built out of, junk. To convey the feeling of visual depth and activity in the scenes, there are a variety of things that move in both the foreground and background now; the water is one that I really noticed the most. As well, the soundtrack has even gotten an upgrade, which I didn't think was possible; yes, it's even better in Chaos on Deponia than it was the original game... so good that I wonder why they haven't made it available for sale.
While Chaos on Deponia is a decent follow-up to the highly acclaimed Deponia, the title just doesn't stand up to the classic; even though they were released such a short time apart. This sequel does last longer, however, especially if you're not using any sort of walkthrough to assist you; otherwise, you're looking at 8-9 hours of playtime. If you really dug the original Deponia, go ahead and grab this to further the story. However, if you're thinking of getting in to the Deponia series, just grab the classic instead; even though this game does give the backstory at the beginning. I wouldn't call Chaos on Deponia disappointing, but rather just not as charming as its predecessor.

Lets get this out of the way, ESO is not not Skyrim Online.
Moving on, The Elder Scrolls Online didn't start off that well, with a lot of people quitting at launch, which is understandable, subscription was required and it was in a bit of weird state. However, over the course of the past few years the game has gone through a pretty great transformation.
Subscription is now optional, and basically acts as a Season Pass with a some benefits. There's new content every couple of months that almost always adds something new and fun, or something that was missing from the base game (Dark Brotherhood, and Thieves Guild).
The graphics and sound are also pretty good, combat is okay, PVE can be fun with groups, and PVP is an absolute blast. But the story is probably hands down the best aspect of the game. That and the community is also great, people are always looking for things to do in game, and it's pretty easy to gather people into a party to do a dungeon or delve.
Overall this game is pretty great, and definitely worth it if you're an Elder Scrolls fan.

It has some serious issues such as amazing amount of bugs. There's  some weird mini-stuttering going on and I have no idea why, because no matter what graphics settings are on it's still there from time to time and it seems to be completely random. Probably it's some issue of game-engine itself. Luckily, it's nothing game-breaking and I was able to enjoy this game in many ways most of the time.
It's better than previous installment in this series, there are improvements in everything gameplay-wise. For example, controlling vehicles is good now (still not perfect, but definitely better) which makes especially land and sea races enjoyable and replay worthy. It is actually worth to do all the collectibles just to see the beauty of this massive game-world in a lot of details.
Story is more interesting than in JC2, but storytelling itself is handled very badly again. Although there are 25 story missions, only several of them are truly memorable. Overall I'd give it like 7,5/10 and recommend to buy it for discounted price. It's just sad that it could have been one of the best games ever made if only it had better story missions and storytelling, better optimization and multiplayer with tons of activities.
In the end I hope that Avalanche will make another Mad Max game rather than another Just Cause. I think we had enough of fun with Rico already.

+ Melee which is the main element of gameplay feels very satisfying , don't except variety like in dmc, but still it's done right.
+ Fluid controls ,also remappable, runs smoothly.
+/- Highly scripted and very linear.
-  Platforming and puzzle elements are functional, but both lack any imagination and act as little more than a distraction from the combat zones
- Some camera problems when platforming
- The combat is initially frantic and exciting, but soon it becomes clear it lacks any sort of depth.

Where to begin on this one?
Over the years I've played all the Total War games from the first Medieval to this one and I have to say that they always seem to improve on the game mechanics and playing structure every time.
The graphics and attention to detail in this game is massive in scale and truth be told you can only take it to the max with a serious gaming pc. However that being said, even on lower level pc's the details are still brilliant and a real wonder in gaming technology. The shadow and lighting effects in particular couple well with the attention to detail on every soldier, building and terrian you will see. Right down to the links and badges on armours and scuffs on buildings from a landing fire shot. You won't be disappointed with the partical effects either, such as fires from burning seige towers and units.
The gameplay aspect of this game also gives the player a good sense of reward and feedback in both campaigns and quick battles. For the quick battles, the AI I find is responsive and on the higher level of difficulties, will respond to your strategies very quickly and is unforgiving when you make a mistake. You can recover and counter with the variety of special abilities you have from your general and units though as with the other games. Rome II gives you more to work with in this area, depending on what kind of general you have, the abilities vary. This sinks in with the campaign and can be very decisive in any battle.
The campaign itself again has been overhauled, the political system gives you a chance to compete with other families and opponents within your faction, always ensuring your dominance. If you fail to play the correct political games or fall from grace, you'll hit the civil war feature. Your faction splits, at least from my experience, and you'll end up fighting against each other until there is a winner. Allowing enemies to gain the advantage over you, definitely something to avoid. It features a wonderful economic system to compliment this, always keep an eye on the treasury while building armies, you'd be surprised how fast you can run out of money. The research function can help increase funds and military aspect so check that out definitely.
To sum it up, this is one of the best RTS games of our game and if you're a fan of the series I seriously suggest you buy it. Looking forward to Total War Atila very much. :)

The Samurai Warriors series is the "Japanese" version of Dynasty Warriors, meaning instead of having hacky slashy combat in ancient China, you're doing it in 1500s Japan. Like any Warriors, they play pretty much the same: Kill (or rather K.O.) a bunch of people, defeat a few dozen Officers, and defeat the big boss or achieve win conditions.
The big difference, though, is this PC port. DW 8: Extreme Legends was a direct port with nothing really added and no online features. This port of Samura Warriors 4-II, however, includes local and online multiplayer. This is a big, big win for fans of the series.
There are some downsides to this port, though. The controls are buggy to set up and 100% of the prompts; like press Y, X, etc; are all in the PC icons. Meaning, it's a cross with a line going over it, rather than the X button. It's confusing and hard to figure out at first. The second problem is that the entire game has Japanese VOs. Sure, the English dubs were always horrible, but for those of us who are used to voice overs, having to look directly at the small text to see what a character is saying during battle is annoying. If there was a HUD custimization, this problem could be fixed immediately, but, as it stands, you gotta just get used to it.
I'm hoping some mods crop up for this game soon to make it better, since it already pretty good. I'd highly recommend it to anyone who is a Warriors series fan.

tl;dr at the bottom (spoiler: buy it!)
Update: Still (Nov 17) going strong and still awesome as in the beginning!
I bought this game late 2014 and have been playing it on and off for more hours than I am willing to admit. While the game principles are seamingly simple with only six or seven raw ressources in the game, the complexity involved in creating massive scale factories is amazing. You start off small, but within minutes you go for your first automation, evolving to the point where you just tell your robot army to construct any building you want.
However all this technology comes at a prize. You need to expand further and further away from your relatively safe starting point. While you expand your cloud of pollution will as well, until you meet the natives. While Factorio is not a war game in itself, this war of industry versus nature will be a big part. You can choose whether you go for the exterminator approach and just wipe out all native hives close enough to threaten you or you can go into turtle mode and hide behind your automatically repaired wall of turrets. There is also the option to disable the attacks of the natives, so they will only ever attack if you hit them first.
But all of these are just the basics. It is entirely possible to finish the game without delving deeper into the concepts, but if you want a whole new world of complexity awaits you. You can setup complicated logical networks, regulating your factory so you will never have too much or not enough of anything. Or you can even build full computers within the game using just the basic logic given to you. There is always room for improvement, some small optimisation here, a faster belt there, a new train station, .... and I am nearly out of something, so lets wipe some aliens off the map so I can get more.
Speaking of trains, in my opinion building giant train networks is one of the most fun aspects of Facotrio. If you are familiar with OpenTTD, the train mechanics are similar to it. If you are not, it follows simple rules that allow for trains to go where you want, when you want, transporting what you want, all without your intervention once the rail network is setup. Later in the game, trains will be your primary way of transporting raw ressources to your factory, because you will need to cover ever growing distances to satisfy your hunger for more of just about anything.
The map generation is entirely random and based on a seed you can supply to play the same map again. During creation you can specify some parameters, like ressource distribution and enemy strength and density, afterwards there are no limits to your expansion. You will run into natural obstacles, both removable (rocks, trees, enemies) and permanent (lakes) and will need to adapt your factory to these conditions.
At some point you will have hundreds or thousands of machines, inserters and belts everywhere, but Factorio was build for this massive scale, While it is entirely possible to overload your computer with gigantic factories, this will take days of non-stop expansion. Most players will never get to this point, if they are not aiming for it. The performance of this game is great. It is very stable and even with big factories it runs smoothly. The graphics fit the theme perfectly. While they are not on the same level of recent triple A RTS games, they look really good and bring the point across. Everything is easy to identify even on higher zoom levels, which you will love for maintaining at least some level of understanding of your factory.
And if this still is not enough complexity, you are free to mod this game into oblivion. Even in alpha there are so many mods out, you can not try them all. Apart from the smaller "single purpose" mods there are giant mods that add more ressources, more processing, more items, more guns, more vehicles, more of everything and most importantly more complexity. Also there are some that remove some tedious work, like rail laying or gathering wood. The amazing thing is that most mods will work together without too much of a hassle. There are some incompatibilities here and there, but for the most part you can mix and match to your liking. Also there are some mod packs which not only ensure all mods are working together nicely, also sometimes include some fixes to make everything fit together even better. And if you want to mod yourself, the same principle applies as for the base game. You get a basic LUA API from which you can build your gigantic mods with as much content as you want. Another great aspect of choosing LUA as the modding language is that you can freely look through the source code of mods and learn how things are done or adjust some aspects more to your liking.
So if this was not clear enough yet, I highly recommend this game. To top if off there is a demo available on the website, so feel free to try before you buy.
tl;dr:
If you are into basic, easy to understand concepts, that allow for extremly complex constructs and enjoy a chance to challenge yourself, give this game a try. Even if you are looking for more of a relaxing game, Facotrio can be that as well, just do not underestimate the natives.

The time has finally come for me to write this properly. Impressions not so fresh by now, but general idea and opinion on the game has been formed by now. I played through this game 1.5 times, with first playthrough being non-lethal, find-as-much-as-you-can-letionist, took my sweet time exploring with Corvo on normal difficulty - this resulting in missions taking around 4-5 hours since I wanted to see every nook and cranny; the other half of the playthrough was with Emily, also non-lethal, on hardest difficulty, ghosthrough. Additionally, I played around with combat a bit to test it out. I think I have a fairly decent idea on different aspects of the game.
I have been and still am a huge fan of the original game. It was the title that actually got me into gaming and made me love stealth games. I was really looking forward to another entry in the series, seeing how good of a job they did building the world around and it would seem like a waste of a great material - when DH2 was announced, I was hyped. I couldn't wait to dive back into this world and explore more. That actually happened - we get a glimpse of Dunwall and spend the majority of the game in beatiful city of Karnaca. The mission areas are bigger, there are a lot more secrets and places to see and no matter if you agree to take powers or not, game gives you ways to traverse the city. That is right - you can actually do proper flesh & steel playthrough and tell the outsider you're better off without his 'influence'.
Powers. For Corvo, they are the same ones used in the original title - what makes it different are the upgrade trees. You can spend runes to upgrade blink to a time-stoppind-Daud's-blink, you can even make it a kick-blink for combat purposes. There are many more that probably float on the internet already so I won't list them here - options to spice up gameplay are there, are fun and could even alter one's playstyle this way. Emily's powers are interesting, pretty much all of them are designed to be available to a stealth and a combat focused player, with example of Domino allowing to kill or knock out linked targets or Shadow Walk allowing to pass an area unnoticed or stealthily murder/knock out people. My personal favourite was combo of Mesmerize and Domino, to get an extended reach on people that would otherwise be unaffected by the former and then knock everyone out. If, for whatever reason, one wouldn't want to play with Emily/Corvo and still wanted to try out different powers New Game+ is in the game, runes are carried over and all of the fancy magic is available to either you choose to play with - unless flesh & steel route is chosen, then runes get converted to coins.
The story here is a very weird thing. It is simple, yet cluttered. Pacing is all over the place. Best description I could give of it would be that it is there. It does give you some reason to move forward but it's a secondary objective, I'd say. With the original I felt some sort of urgency, maybe not to the point of always rushing to objective because 'there is no time for exploring' but the job had to be done, the reason was solid, the drive was strong. It wasn't all that present in the second; I could partially blame this on bigger areas that could result in forgetting why are we actually in here in the first place. The newly introduced Bloodfly infestation was rather underwhelming. It doesn't fall under 'another Rat Plague' category as it seemed to be advertised as, but is just a minor inconvenience at most. They made a good job making Nest Keepers, they certainly are damn creepy and seem more scary than Weepers. The antagonists were either not memorable, undeveloped or amusing. Some of them didn't get enough exposure to give you the 'ah, he/she does this, has influence and power, has to be stopped for sure for being a shitebag!' and pretty much become the 'oh, that was this oh-so-powerful person? welp, not anymore!'. Allies are alright. Not much better, just alright. They pretty much serve as shelter providers and purpose/reason givers. Outsider has changed from his initial iteration, not only in VA but also attitude. Many people seemed to hate that decision, but personally I think it fits the narrative better. Instead of being a passive observer he always was, he now has the reason and right to show something more than indifference.
Dialogue. It was ranging from atrocious to alright-ish. I understand that they wanted to change their direction but it didn't work out all that well; lines sound like forced poetry and sometimes come off as more shallow than deep - that is very apparent in very first visit in the void where player obtains the Heart. With that, another problem emerged and it being overexposure. What players of the original first speculated about that could then later be confirmed or denied by devs through questions on social media, now was blatantly shown. Part of the fun were those speculations and subtle hints, the general mistery surrounding them - now a bit killed with obviousness.
So, what could possibly keep me playing? The actual gameplay! This is a completely different story and I could probably compliment on everything they've done with it. First DH's gameplay was highly praised and got a few complaints here and there from the community - to which the devs listened and improved everything that could be improved. Now available to you in nearby stores: air knockout, combat choke, all new types of darts for your crossbow including stinging bolts making enemies flee, new mines and more! Non-lethal playthroughs have definitely been made more interesting, seeing how many tools they added to improve it. Not to say anything about combat. Perfect parries are actually doing something now and help to get things done.
The AI has been vastly improved, with normal being hard as it is - I wouldn't recommend doing first playthrough on ghost, as for many it could prove a frustrating experience because of that. Enemies are incredibly perceptive, they pay attention to doors that were previously closed or opened, missing patrol companions, can also notice you peeking through the corner, and other disturbances. They also search more thoroughly, checking dumpsters, under the tables. Makes for a tense and fun experience if you don't find yourself a good sneak. In combat though they might not shine as much - they are a bit harder, definitely much more brutal but still don't pose much of a challange for many. That doesn't take away from the fact that slaughtering people is just as fun - if not more fun - as it was in the first game. An interesting observation was also that when you overwhelm guards by murdering their friends, the lower ranked ones might terrified try running away. Oh, and they can trip on stairs. Or generally trip. They definitely trip on stairs.
Graphics are amazing. Art direction has changed from the original, differences are visible and it is just as good in it's own way. Many times it was pointed out that they wished to make it all look like a 'painting in motion' which, in my opinion, they nailed. Colour scheme makes it all just nice to look at. NPCs still have their iconic, kinda comic-like features like bigger hands, long, weirdly formed faces, smaller heads. Civilians varied and made the urban areas feel alive.
That is my take on the game. Would I recommend it? Yeah, I would. The story might not be best and fall flat but gameplay is definitely worth it. They improved on everything that was in the original title, added new, interesting ways to do whatever one wishes to do and reward for being creative and finding alternative solutions. If you liked the original, it's a buy. Same if you like stealth. And there's a demo now. So hey, just try it. It's fun.
