Black Mess--no, that isn't a typo. Although this game may have a lot to offer, it suffers from some very significant flaws that I believe result in a bit of a mess.
It's important to understand that Black Mesa is an old-style first-person shooter that's very similar to the other Half-Life games. It seems to bridge the gap between Half-Life and Half-Life 2 offering elements of both games. It has puzzles that are very similar to the puzzles in Half-Life, and it has some of the characters and graphics-features from Half-Life 2. On the positive side, it is a very engaging game that makes you want to continue playing.
Unfortunately in many places I was prevented from continuing to play. I either got stuck as a result of game-play issues or the game made my computer crash or both. Not one to give up easily, I found some good walkthroughs on YouTube that helped me find that hidden passage in some dark corner or whatever else was stopping me. Finally, however, I was presented with a jumping puzzle that I just couldn't get by. End of game!
So if you're anything like I am, you'll be less than thrilled with Black Mesa. I suppose I'll be playing Grand Theft Auto V or Dishonored 2 which are much more professionally designed than Black Mesa and more fun.

Everybody knows the plot, thus I'm going to focus just on my personal experience.
This game is excellent from beginning to end. I don't only mean graphics, that are excellent too, but the hole game. The mechanics are very familiar and fun, there's loads of action and you'll always feel a little bit nervous for what's in the next corner.
Soundtracks in this game are amazing, sometimes it made me feel desolation and guilty and other times it made me feel the danger of the situation and get adrenaline.
Action, puzzles, a little bit of stealth and bosses. This game knows in a smart way when to slow down the gameplay and when to unleash lots of action. You're not going to feel alone, there's fellows all around Black Mesa. And most importantly, they have PERSONALITY as opposed to HL1. Some fellow scientists are too afraid to follow you to the escape, some of them betrayed fellows to survive during the resonance cascade incident, and some of them wants to help you in any possible way. When the moment to leave scientists and guards comes, they just don't AFK and idle, they'll just find a sit to wait or talk to each other.
When you feel too nervous and need to relax just wander around but don't continue and when you're ready for action you just continue and you'll get action almost instantly.
Guns are goddam rad. Personally I love the crowbar, I used it a lot to quickly kill headcrabs and to break things. The assault shotgun is kick♥♥♥♥♥ the Gluon gun is excellent and oh dear, how I love the TAU cannon! By the way, snarks are so cute in this game :)
Some things that I dislike are NPC animations, they are not good and sometimes they are stupid. The Linux port crashes sometimes (if you use Windows don't worry). The ladders can be really annoying. And I think that's all.
There's still lots of things that I missed and loved. Take a moment to buy this game and revisit Black Mesa from a new perspective.

:  It's a good point and click adventure.  I absolutely recommend if it's on sale.  Whether you want to pay full price is up to how much of a point and click enthusiast you are.

The second of a three part series where Daedalic takes on Monkey Island and should be looked at as part of the series.  This is the weakest episode in the series.  If you played and enjoyed the first game, you will enjoy this one.  If not, you can stop here and not bother continuing.  If you are starting the series fresh you should pick up the first one.
As a part of Daedalic's Monkey Island-like humor series, the jokes are in there, and they are numerous.  Again, I can't say anything here is any better than the other two games.  Translation problems factor in and some of the humor will leave you confused, as it did in the other two games.  Some of the humor is unintentional because of the aforesaid translation.  Some of them, a few of the less funny sexist jokes, the Scandinavian guy, that part where you ----- -- baby dolphins ---- ----, did not leave me insulted so much as wondering how the writers could have believed I would think that funny.  Perhaps this is just me not entirely getting the German sense of humor or me just calling out tasteless as I see it.
The pace of the story has slowed down a lot.  A large chunk of the game involves character development for Goal.  Rufus changes little from the first game and any hopes  you may have that he is really a decent person are taken outside and shot several times.  Any character development he receives follows the direction of writer's butt monkey and someone the player wishes something bad would happen to.  Fortunately, you do become attached to the colorful cast of side characters and part of the enjoyment of playing the game involves seeing who's life Rufus will ruin next.
The gameplay shows Daedalic's polish to the adventure gaming genre which leave you wondering why nobody else tried some of the changes they made.  As an example, the inventory can be brought up and down with a hotkey on your mouse wheel.  Details are well drawn and animated, with your attention going to things you should pay attention to so you don't have to do the mouse search across a background for that one object.  There are keyboard shortcuts and a highlight button to show all the intractable objects.  Things like this keep me playing Daedalic's games even through parts I don't enjoy.
The puzzles are more complicated than they were in the first game.  If you don't like being in an area with a large bloated zone with several puzzles dropped in your lap at the same time, working on all of them at the same time, that is the entire first - and largest - part of the game.  Nothing drove me to frustration and any problems could be solved by thinking about them for a while, but there is a large area to cover and a lot of things to tinker with in order to figure out what you need to do.
There are a few stand out moments, the first puzzle you solve, teaching you how to apply several gameplay basics, after you go through the basic tutorial was hilarious.  Hilarious enough for me to restart and replay it a few times.  The second moment was when I had to go and change the game's options to solve a puzzle.
Your mileage may vary for a lot of this game but I'd still call it the weakest episode in the series where Daedalic tries to correct some of the problems made in Deponia and end up creating new mistakes.  If you are not into Daedalic's adventure games or adventure gaming in general this is one you can skip.  If you are into the Deponia series and really enjoyed the first game enough to continue the story then, by all means, pick this one up.

So as with any MMO, this game needs to get compared to its older ivy league school PhD brother, Dr. World of Warcraft. This game is NOT what would be described as a "WoW Clone". While this game can have a grindy style of gameplay at times, it doesnt have to and it certainly doesnt make it similar to WoW. But we will continue to compare the game to WoW and why its different.
So WoW has many more classes to choose from. ESO has 4 (or 5 with Morrowind). The difference here that people dont realize is that with the 4 (5) classes that ESO has you can (for the most part) recreate all the WoW classes. This is because Classes dont limit you to your crafting/weapon/armor abilities. "Sorcerer" doesnt mean you are limited to light armor and staff weapons. You can go the traditional route, but you can choose a medium armor and dual weild skill line/armor if you wanted. This is what sets it apart. You really get that full "build" experience.
Now as an Elder Scrolls game, lets compare it to skyrim. You get that same Lore experience, you get the sam races, you get that vibe. And like everyone else says, this is NOT Skyrim online. Its an MMO, it goes to all other parts of Tamriel (which let me add is HUGE).
Leveling feels slow in the beggining, but hang in there. Its worth it.
The game is pretty. I reccomend looking at Addons (esspecially a minimap addon) and visual enhanching programs like Hook 64 just to make the game a tad better.
If youre looking for a non-traditional MMO and enjoy TES lore, this is a great game to check out.

Alliance quests: Basically, when you start off, you technically have access to 4-5 regions (based on your alliance). You are supposed to complete them one after each other, fairly linearly. That's fine. The reason is: 1. The levels increase 2. The story progresses as you traverse the region
In addition to your alliance quest: each region has multitude of quests unrelated. Every city/village has 1 or more quests to complete. Do them!~ They are great
In addition, several dungeons exist with their own quests. Every region has ONE dungeon that requires a team to complete. Unnecessary storywise, but it unlocks: skills, items, a new quest. it's worth it but if you never make enough friends to do it, you miss nothing major.
Skills: Great! All unique and useful. But not necessary.
As I said, every alliance is unique. Every alliance has AMAZING characters and GREAT storylines. I owned the game without the steam browser so you can't see how much I actually played. It has to be 200+ hours. And I beat all alliances at least twice.
BUY IT. As for expansions: Ignore Imperial City, but Orsinium is great. Haven't tried the rest.

Playtime is very short but...
It's got both the Homeworld 1 an 2 you've known and loved kept in their original forms.
And you get bonus, completely graphically remastered versions of both as a bonus. Graphic job is really awesome. Seeing the HW1 ships, all of them really, modernized is just awesome.
Not only that, but the multiplayer beta actually allows you to launch the HW1 races against the HW2 ones if you want. There's nothing like taking those olde salvettes(salvage corvettes for the uninitiated) to yoink those vaygr missile frigates to bring back to your mothership for capture. Races of both games literally kept the majority of their ways of doing thing(except perhaps for strikecraft fuel) from their respective games... yet both of them meeting in combat in the same multiplayer skirmish somehow works very nicely. Stuff like HW1 races still using research ships(instead of carrier or mothership modules) for tech, or salvage corvettes instead of marines frigates.
In fact in the later's cases the way players capture ships has been kept intact for the players of both teams with HW1 races using their salvage corvettes to physically latch onto enemy ships to drag them back to the mothership for captures(being able to capture down to strikecrafts if so wished) whereas HW2 races still uses marines frigates that physically board enemy capital ships to capture them on the spot but are unable to capture strikecraft as well as having a hard time to maneuver around other frigates which HW1 salvettes can easily latch to.
Similarly, races of both games still handle strikecrafts respectively the way that they used to with HW1 races building and deploying them as individual units while HW2 races seems to still build and deploys theirs as squadrons. Encounters between the two have, so far, seemingly remained balanced(I've had some fun taking a group of HW1 Heavy and multigun corvettes against a bunch of Vaygr strikecrafts, or later deploying a HW1 strikecrafts-locking gravwell to immobilizes a rush of enemy strikecrafts from that same player).
There's also some new gameplay options such as capturable relics on the map able to give you various advantages during a multiplayer game, over which you can see some scuffle between players for the control of, amongst a couple of other things.
And, hey, the game just got released and already there's Steam Workshop support with mods for HW1&2 Classic already being released.

This game really has me confused. On the one hand I think that they have masterfully caught the atmosphere and feeling of the first Alien movie completely and just walking around and feeling that you actually are in that world is amazing to say the least. The environments are gorgeous late 70's sci-fi with analog computers and claustrophobic hallways. I absolutely loved it. But on the other hand, the gameplay gets really tedious really fast and I easily spent the last 6 hours of the game being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at it not ending. To say that it overstays its welcome is a massive understatement and it ended up being almost 3 times as long as I feel it should have been. I completed the game in little over 17 hours and of those 17 hours I thoroughly enjoyed the first 3. Then the Alien showed up.
I know it's kinda weird to say this but the Alien actually ruined the game experience for me. When it first shows up it's fricking amazing, awful, horrible all those things you want to feel when playing a horror game, but that quickly took a turn for the worse when the damn thing won't ever leave you alone again. After it is first introduced, you can't take two steps without the damn thing jumping out of a vent between you and where you need to go fetch something to open a door somewhere and quite frankly, that's not scary. It's tedious, dull and serves no other purpose than to make you sit in a damn locker for 10 minutes while it circles the table infront of it. Being pretty much completely unable to progress due to it blocking your path at every single turn sucked the joy and fear right out of the game and left some kind of boring as hell hide and seek game. And once I pained myself through all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t because I wanted to see how the story would unfold, I did enjoy that part, and finally got to what I thought was the end after 7-8 hours and thought to myself that okay, it wasn't THAT bad, the game promptly slapped me in the face and pointed to the remaining HALF of the damn thing. Seriously. It. Never. Ends. And that is not a good thing.
At the halfway mark, you're pretty much space Rambo with the entire arsenal you've managed to scrape together which completely strips away any notion of vulnerability you might have had earlier and you can just go and blast your way through any and all things that stand between you and your current objective, and correct me if I'm wrong, but that is not how a horror game should behave.
In the end I spent the final 4 hours of the game being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at it for not ending when it had so many opportunities to do so. It just wasn't any fun. But I'm unfortunately a completionist and I was going to see the ending, despite how bad the actual game was at that point.
So finally, do I recommend the game? Both yes and no. If you like the Alien movies and want to experience that great atmosphere in a game then yes, you should check this out and play the first 4 hours. But if you want an actually good game then no, you should not play this because the gameplay behind the awesome setting is boring, uninspired and downright tedious. As an overall experience I cannot recommend this.

Alien: Isolation isn't without its problems. The story is a little bloated, and doesn't always flow well; it sometimes relys a little too much on aping the first Alien film; the lack of a jump button and the prevalence of chest high obstructions that you can't climb over is often hilarious; because of what happens during the game, it doesn't really sit well within the mythos of the films. Despite these things though, I cannot recommend this game enough. It's an incredible achievement, in atmospherics, lighting, sound design and artificial intelligence. Sevastopol and its inhabitants have huge amounts of character, and the replication of the 70's future from the first film is impeccable. I would argue that Amanda Ripley is one of the best female leads in games (though that's not exactly hard) and an example to anyone that broey dudes do not have to always be protagonists. The game scales well on lower tier systems, but I would recommend playing it on as high settings as you can manage, to get the most out of the wonderful lighting effects on show throughout.
Highly recommended for fans of horror games and of the Alien franchise, probably the first game of that franchise not to blow the big one since Aliens Vs. Predator.

Alien Isolation...oh boy...where do I begin.  First off, think of this as more of an interactive movie (and it's the 20 hour director's cut version of that movie) than a game.  You play a supporting role.  You will act in the scenes of this "movie" and will be forced to do many retakes of those scenes in which you don't play your role perfectly.  It's really hit or miss during each take as none of the other actors will play their roles exactly the same.  Yes, you will be doing a whole lot of trial and error.
The "game" has a certain Dead Space vibe throughout in which you'll perform more tasks than you can count and stll feel like you aren't accomplishing anything.  You'll travel through many locales over and over, starting at point "A" and ending up and point "B" only to find out that you'll be heading back to point "A" again.
The game looks great and is fun at times, but I think the frustration outweighs the fun more often than not and that's a shame.  They were really close with this one, but unfortunately fell short.  I'd give it a 4 out of 10.

The port WAS atrocious (mostly because the controller support was garbage), but this fixes literally every issue the game has:
I am having the time of my life with this game. I have played it on PS4 as well, and despite the PS4 version using higher quality assets (slightly higher resolution textures, more vegetation, slightly higher quality vegetation, higher resolution volumetric lighting and more vivid lighting), it suffers from nearly continuous framerate drops into the 50 FPS making the game feel much less consistent, and it drops even further than that when attacking large masses of enemies due to the particle effects. It also suffers from lower quality post-process antialiasing and a complete lack of anisotropic filtering. Depth of field was removed in the cutscenes as well.
On PC, by forcing high quality antialiasing and anisotropic filtering, as well as a completely locked 60 FPS at all times, the gameplay experience is far more consistent and the image quality much cleaner. In my opinion, it looks better as a whole. Especially due to the frame rate, this is the version to play, IMO, but that doesn't excuse the fact that the higher quality assets should have been available on PC as well.
During local co-op play, both the PS4 and PC versions are locked at 30 FPS, but the PS4 version commonly drops even lower than that, still making the PC the preferable experience gameplay-wise. However, seeing as Dynasty Warriors 8 Xtreme Legends is 60 FPS with no issues on PC during local-coop, I don't understand why they removed that from this game's PC version. Still, this is the better game gameplay-wise, by far.
Overall, an extremely addicting game that is a blast to play in co-op. The best Warriors game made at the date of this review, and a highly recommended purchase.

Inspired by but very loosely based on the ancient Chinese tale,
, ENSLAVED: Odyssey to the West is one of the best 3D action games I have played. With a script written by Alex Garland as well as voice acting and mocapping by Andy Serkis, the story is one of the best I have experienced in a video game. Set in a post-apocalyptic USA, art design is splendid and it looks like the art team took their inspiration from the documentary
, which isn't a bad thing. Setpieces are amazing, from beginning to end.
Gameplay however is merely adequate. Yes, it gets the job done. Yes. platforming segments are fun, especially if you love Uncharted-style platforming. But puzzles are super-easy and combat is just... perfunctory. It's not deep and it just seems to be there for the sake of being there.
The PC port isn't perfect either. I had input problems occasionally (usually after cutscenes). And while I have a fast PC (Core i7-3770, AMD Radeon HD7870XT), most times the game didn't feel like it was running at 60fps even though I had it vsynced. I didn't check but it also seemed that anti-aliasing didn't really work even though I had it switched on in the settings. I'm also left wondering whether the game was even running at 1080p.
But even with those slight hiccups, I enjoyed my time with it. I wholly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good action-platformer. It truly is an underrated gem.

For a game released in 2010, all I can say is DAMN! those graphics hold up well even in 2014.  Of course I had to go through the steam forums and tweak those configuration files manually to get the graphical settings configured but the results were well worth it.  The game itself was great and I can see why they got all those 9/10 reviews back when it was originally released.  I'm glad that a PC release was made and as with most games that originated on the consoles, an XBOX 360 controller or equivalent is highly recommended.  Good gameplay and a decent story to boot! :-D

Well... It's a solid autoplatformer. Nothing groundbreaking, but if you're not averse to games like Prince of Persia 2008 or Uncharted, you might find the game to your liking as well. Funnily enough, the platforming segments are even less interactive than widely panned PoP2008 (single button+stick for directional input).
The environments, especially in the opening chapters were simply beautiful. Great use of color, lush vegetation, decayed civilization. Personally, out of all UE3 games I've played so far, I believe only Spec Ops: The Line could top this game graphic/design-wise. It gets minus points for some rather questionable texture work (at times you would think UE3 glitched out and stopped loading mip-maps of the texture after the first one) and the later levels, especially the junkyard ones, which simply didn't look as nice as the opening segments.
Story was... there, I guess. Doesn't make much sense if you try to piece it together, but oh well. It's an action video game, if I wanted a story that wouldn't insult my intelligence I'd read a novel. Characters were all right, mocap work very impressive.
Unfortunately, where Spec Ops was a really solid, (un)pleasant experience, I can't say Enslaved was as stress free. There is a well known bug with the game, which results in it freezing randomly once in a while. I'm not sure if you can call it stuttering when the freeze can last up to 30 seconds, and can be almost immediately followed by another one lasting as long. Also, shadows during cutscenes were beyond broken for me.
As you can imagine, this completely kills immersion, and is downright infuriating if you're hit with this during a fight or a timed platforming section. I hope my neighbors won't think badly of me now, with the amount of swearwords I uttered while playing (or rather waiting to play) the game.
DLC was a completely separate thing, both story and gameplay-wise. And I do mean separate, where the main game had mostly QTE, platforming, fights and bits of shooting, DLC is pretty much a cover-based forced-stealth puzzle game. Reminded me more of an Oddworld game, truth be told. Later sections devolved into shooting galleries, which is a bummer.
Overall, both the main scenario and DLC are a good way to spend a few hours. Your enjoyment of it will be largely dependent on how much the bug I mentioned will affect you, and, well, how much you like interactive movies.
Price I'd pay for the game and wouldn't feel ripped off? $3.75 tops.

This Review shows my personal opinion about the game. NOTE: English isn't my mothertongue, so please excuse any language errors I make in this review.
I'm playing this game now for about 2 years and so far I haven't encountered any gamebreaking bugs (at least not in the experimental/unstable channel). This game is about creating your own Factory using Mines, Furnaces, Transport Belts, Inserters (little cranes that put items from the ground/containers/belts to other ground/containers/belts), Assemblers, later Trains and even later in the game: Drones (like inserters, but not bound to the location).
You're having very slow start with a coal drill (drills ores using coal) some iron plates and a furnace: Barely enough to get started. You gather resources to create more furnaces and drills, so you don't need to gather all the resources by hand. Now you have to walk between your 2 - 3 mining sites to get your stone, iron and copper and to put new coal into the drills and furnaces. You start building a centralized storage and refueling system for your drills furnaces and resources. You still need to craft everything by hand.
Time for some research!
You build your first Steam Dynamos to get electricity and replace your coal drills with electrical drills. Now you build a research facility and research Automation I! You get assemblers! Assemblers craft items for you. e.g. 2 iron plates to 1 iron gear and with another assembler 1 iron gear + 1 copper plate => 1 research pack. Now you have automated your basic research! Yippie!
Up to this time you may still have encountered the first enemies which you had fight of with a simple pistol! Let's research turrets, automate ammunition production, research walls and create a defense line. Now you're pretty save from those biters ... at least for a while. But as time goes by your resources are all used in your factory; You need to find new ore deposits, then transport the resources to your base and hope no biters attack your new outposts.
Later on you get the trains (which can be automated ... what a surprise) with these you have access to even more ore deposits. you know have resources, 90% of your crafting automated and no more space. you'll need to clear of those Biter Bases. Once done you can finallly research the technologies to build a space rocket ... Now you *just* need to build a rocket ... Tada you've finished the game ... if you're fast in about 5to 9 hours. if not in about 100 hours.
In my singleplayer world I have a small factory and about 30% automized of what i wanted to automized ... after about 50 hours of playtime (on this world)

I've played this game for over 2 years now, during which time, the developers have shown a high degree of responsibility and accountability. I would heartily recommend this game to anyone who enjoys some good base building or is enthralled by the idea of designing a factory.

Basically a massive, complex, and awesome game of risk, in which you can choose to resolve battles yourself on the battlefield. It is somewhat complicated, with a steep learning curve, as the game requires military and civil management, building and upgrading cities, managing politics within your own faction, plus diplomacy with other nations, But, it does capture the feeling of building and maintaining an empire. If you're all about the battles, this game is not for you. But if you like battles on the battlefield, plus managing a long-term campaign of world domination (which, while mostly military, also contains civic and economical goals) then I highly recommend this game.
If you're a fan of the Total War series, or have played Rome: Total War, you should get this game. It has it's quirks, but there are mods etc that help you build the ultimate strategy game.

This is a fan-made recreation of the original Half-Life - the seminal FPS which eschewed classic "hunt down x number of keys in order to progress" in favour of a more story-driven narrative based approach to game design. The puzzles while still "old-school" feel more organic than most older FPS games, and therefore make it infinitely more replayable.
So why not just buy and play the original Half-Life? Well, in 2017, the graphics and animations of the original can be very janky, and after playing any modern title, or indeed Valve's own Half-Life 2, Half-Life 1 can become a bit of a chore. The
Crowbar Collective, Black Mesa's development team have the answer. Half-Life, lovingly recrafted in the Source Engine, the tech powering Half-Life 2, and the Portal franchise, and rebranded "Black Mesa" is a love-letter to every kid who first trudged through the titular facility, wondering just what the hell was going on and how it could all possibly end well for the protagonist, the ever-suffering physicist, Gordon Freeman.
And that is really the biggest problem with Black Mesa. It is not yet finished, the final levels of the original game are notorious for horrific jumping puzzles and a mundane final boss and so the developers, The Crowbar Collective, have elected to exclude it from the current game and release it as a free patch when it is complete. This is disheartening as I first played a fully functioning version of this mod back in 2015 or so (for free I hasten to add). It wouldn't be such a terrible move if there was adequate payoff, but ending where it does, Black Mesa feels incomplete.
Having said this, the shooting mechanics are great, the music is top-notch, rivalling some of Valve's best efforts in some key setpiece scenes, and it is also one of the most atmospheric first person shooters ever created, with a true sense of dread in every strobe-lit hallway. The effect of this cannot be understated. Valve Software, the original developers of Half-Life and its sequel/s has always excelled at creating player urgency and agency, pacing the narrative experience to justify the run and gun gameplay at its core while making the player feel smart as they evade traps, solve situational puzzles and generally survive the waves of enemies.
I have deliberately avoided story spoilers, as Half-Life was made around that time when games did not hold the player's hand, they had to think for themselves, uninterrupted by cutscenes, a design decision that carries into this reimagining. Half-Life (and therefore, Black Mesa) is an example of what video games as a medium can achieve, without simply emulating "movie moments". Discovery through gameplay is a key part of a Half-Life experience, and Black Mesa delivers this in spades. The most fun in a story driven FPS and an atmosphere that rivals Metro, Black Mesa is (very nearly) the epitome of "full package".
I consider Black Mesa and Half-Life to be the same game. I know this is an unpopular view, as many of the original designs have been tweaked or even completely removed in favour of new work by the Crowbar Collective, and I do not want to diminish the achievement of the developers which is in short, astounding, but I have to implore anyone who bothers to read this (why do I write these?) to skip out on the original, or Valve's own ludicrous "Half-Life: Source" in favour of Black Mesa which is simultaneously a more ambitious, and more tightly woven experience from beginning to "end". Black Mesa is well worth 20 dollars, and I can't think of many more games that give you such value for money despite its lack of a solid conclusion.

It's got both the Homeworld 1 an 2 you've known and loved kept in their original forms.
And you get bonus, completely graphically remastered versions of both as a bonus. Graphic job is really awesome. Seeing the HW1 ships, all of them really, modernized is just awesome.
Not only that, but the multiplayer beta actually allows you to launch the HW1 races against the HW2 ones if you want. There's nothing like taking those olde salvettes(salvage corvettes for the uninitiated) to yoink those vaygr missile frigates to bring back to your mothership for capture. Races of both games literally kept the majority of their ways of doing thing(except perhaps for strikecraft fuel) from their respective games... yet both of them meeting in combat in the same multiplayer skirmish somehow works very nicely. Stuff like HW1 races still using research ships(instead of carrier or mothership modules) for tech, or salvage corvettes instead of marines frigates.
In fact in the later's cases the way players capture ships has been kept intact for the players of both teams with HW1 races using their salvage corvettes to physically latch onto enemy ships to drag them back to the mothership for captures(being able to capture down to strikecrafts if so wished) whereas HW2 races still uses marines frigates that physically board enemy capital ships to capture them on the spot but are unable to capture strikecraft as well as having a hard time to maneuver around other frigates which HW1 salvettes can easily latch to.
Similarly, races of both games still handle strikecrafts respectively the way that they used to with HW1 races building and deploying them as individual units while HW2 races seems to still build and deploys theirs as squadrons. Encounters between the two have, so far, seemingly remained balanced(I've had some fun taking a group of HW1 Heavy and multigun corvettes against a bunch of Vaygr strikecrafts, or later deploying a HW1 strikecrafts-locking gravwell to immobilizes a rush of enemy strikecrafts from that same player).
There's also some new gameplay options such as capturable relics on the map able to give you various advantages during a multiplayer game, over which you can see some scuffle between players for the control of, amongst a couple of other things.
And, hey, the game just got released and already there's Steam Workshop support with mods for HW1&2 Classic already being released.

I'm a diehard Homeworld fan, but this "Remastered" collection is very disappointing so far in playing my first several hours.  It is riddled with bugs, even more than the original (which is saying something).  Even with Gearbox saying they rewrote the engine, I see some extremely similar issues to the old game.  I can deal with minor change such as ship costs (and apparently Fuel is no longer a resource for Strike craft), and I'm still a fan of the plodding pace and solitary atmosphere, but the issues I'm going to talk about make the price tag of this remake painful to have forked over.  It's amazing this was released in this state and I'm having a hard time believing that much work really went into it.
Here is my current laundry list after playing for about 7 hours today (release day):
Hotkeys and information.  Some ships have "special attacks"; good luck finding out what those are or whether they exist, until you find the hotkey for it and try it.  There are no more detailed info panes for ships now, at least that I can find, so you have very limited info on anything's capabilities.  Also, this game causes some kind of interference with system hotkeys... including preventing my ability to use in-game Shadowplay, which is what I use for videos and streaming.  UI for units currently selected is very small, slow and klutzy.
Queueing up multiple Research ship pieces will result in only one being built.
Capturing and Salvaging problems.  Salvage Corvettes will fight over the same pieces, following each other around.  You cannot tell a group of them to capture a group of enemies either; you must pick them one at a time.  Friendly units will happily open fire on any unit you have in tow, even though it is on its way to the mothership to be assimilated and poses no threat.  Harvesters will also fight with them over carried salvage.  Salvage Corvettes or Harvesters carrying salvage will clump up and prevent each other from delivering anything to a Carrier or Mothership.  Likewise as above, you cannot target groups of salvage to gather with a group of ships; it must be one at a time, or waiting for Harvesters to try and do it on their own.  Finally, a personal gripe; why do they make it hard to distinguish what ships you own after capturing them?  At least they could have changed the color of the exhaust trails or something to make it easier to know what's happening in a battle.
Pathfinding.  There are clipping issues and other bits of forgiveable things, but sometimes ships of any kind will lose their minds and do a dance in place until you figure out what direction they need to get free.  When you need groups of ships to engage combat quickly, sometimes they will spend 5-15 seconds trying to recover their formation before they'll engage.  Also, as with the original game, rarely (but comically, at least if you're not playing) a ship you ordered to move (whether part of a group or not) will decide to go off in some completely random direction and will not stop.  Ever.
Asteroids.  Oh god, these are horrible... This was always a frustrating level, but now when destroying asteroids, they fade away for a moment, and then slowly create a few dangerous new ones that can't be shot at right away.  The biggest problem there is that you can't select these new ones to attack half the time; if you try, sometimes your idiot ships will just start driving straight into them.  Ships will do no defensive or proactive fire whatsoever against the asteroids.  To boot, when you start the mission, if your carrier ships are on Auto-launch, all your little brittle ships will line up in perfect parade order to get themselves killed.  Finally, when you lose the first dodge-the-asteroid mission, the screen fades to black, but the rest of the game keeps running.  No end screen or anything like that, and you can hear your actions on the keyboard still having effects.
Drones.  These little morons will kamikaze into your own ships whenever you activate or deactivate them.  Oh by the way, how do you activate them, you say?  Must be a button or something convenient, right?  Nope:  It's Ctrl-Shift-D.  And you'd never know unless you went through the game options for the key bindings.  I also had issues getting a group of Drone Frigates to respond to this command when deactivating; I often had to do it for each one individually.
Repairing.  Pathfinding issues aside, it doesn't appear any Repair Corvettes or Frigates will repair some corvettes that you've captured from the enemy, at least some of the time.  Groups of repair ships will also have the same arguing issues between themselves as Salvage Corvette/Harvesters when trying to patch up the same ship.
I'm going to keep playing it to get my money's worth, but I'm afraid I can't recommend this remake at all, as compared to just going out there and getting free or almost-free copies of the original games.  The graphics are much prettier but they aren't mind-blowing for 15 years of progress, and certainly not worth this price.  I'll probably find more issues as I go along, but I'll try to stay optimistic.

Well after playing this game for ~90 horus and achieving lvl 228, I have to say its quite good, but not as good as the first Dark Souls. I always had a feeling that something is missing.
The things that I liked:
- Dark Souls feeling; by that I mean the whole fighting and movement mechanics.
- Overall graphics and art, allthough the real time lighting was subpar and not that creative, like the tomb of giants in ds1.

The things that I didn't like:
- Geography and the sense of place is totally misleading, how come when I rise in the elevator from the poisonous tower, I get to Iron Keep which is surrounded by the lava landscape. There are more such examples in the game, like when you go underground below the Tower of Flame and see a huge cave with an opening (which is actually under the see leve). Also you had to fight 4 hard bosses, because you character can't get over a pair of boulders???!!!!(near the shrine of winter)
- Some places and bonfires made no sense like the third bonfire in Forest of Giants (whats the point of this area?). A lot of places are really small for their function, like Undead Crypt or Grave of Saints.

I finished off Enslaved:Odyssey to the West yesterday.  Overall I found it marginally enjoyable!  After thoroughly enjoying Ninja Theory's work on the DmC reboot, I was excited to come into this, but it's a very different game, and doesn't sport anything close to the highly technical, challenging combat system of DmC.  In fact, to be quite critical for a moment, most of it's gameplay systems felt pretty shallow.  The combat is fairly simple, and the platforming is context-sensitive.  It also does this annoying thing where it litters collectable items in nooks and crannies, items that you want because they'll provide currency to upgrade your character.  This is usually fine, but devolves into the stupid when they're still present during moments of high drama or time pressure in the storyline.  Your NPC companion yelling for help, and you're rooting around in a trash bin in an alley for upgrade currency.
I'm also torn two ways on the context-sensitive jumping.  On the one hand, I'm not sure the gameplay would have been enhanced at all with the ability to fall to your death and then having to restart sections of the game.  On the other hand, as you go through yet another sequence of holding directions and tapping 'A', you sort of find yourself wondering what the payoff is.  Certainly it allows you to have more confidence in trying things, because you flat out aren't allowed to if it would mean your death, but it kind of neutralizes any sense of satisfaction about the successfully traversing the level.
However its atypical plot, colourful, post-apocalyptic U.S. setting, and service-ably written/acted characters bring it up a bit.  Also it clocks in at a perfect six hours.  Surprisingly, the game was co-directed by Andy Serkis who provides both the voice and mo-cap for the main character, with excellent results.
If you want a character action game that's a bit different from the rest, I recommend checking it out.

Probably the biggest surprise in Enslaved: Odyssey to the West was how engaging the story was. The vibrant post-apocalyptic setting serves as the backdrop for an entertaining narrative that is driven by quality dialogue and voice acting. The game also features some really nice facial animation technology which helps capture emotions and bring even more life and believability to the characters. As for the gameplay side of things, combat is a bit simple but the speed, fluidity and flair of it makes it very satisfying nonetheless. It feels Darksiders-esque and I found it improved over time as upgrades and new moves were unlocked to add a little more depth. I enjoyed the hoverboard-style segments that were scattered about to mix things up from time to time, and the boss fights were fun as well (the final boss in particular was a blast).
On the downside, while the combat is mostly enjoyable, the gameplay as a whole has a tendency to become repetitive. There's a distinct lack of enemy variety and the platforming was a bit too automatic for my liking (a poor man's Prince of Persia, so to speak). The camera work is inconsistent during platforming sections which leads to the occasional uncomfortable camera angle, while the movement controls felt a little too touchy and over-sensitive. I also wasn't very fond of the unskippable cutscenes when replaying through specific sections, although thankfully they aren't all that long or numerous to begin with.
As for the quality of the port, it's well-optmized and should run fine on even below average hardware while looking sharp and maintaining a high FPS. Unfortuantely, settings like AA and AF aren't adjustable in-game and are instead tucked away in a config file.
Overall, I found Enslaved: Odyssey to the West to be a flawed yet captivating and stylish platformer/brawler where the whole is better than the sum of its parts. Definitely worth playing.

Disclaimer: I've been playing Factorio for not quite a year, from the later .11 releases all the way through the recent updates.
tl;dr I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys strategic base planning and building.
Factorio is a game about building a factory to automate your resource collection and item manufacturing, and researching more efficient ways to do the same. Then automating your automation. Then going up another few automation levels. You'll start by hand-mining resources, hand-assembling items, and running around to get things where they need to be. But that just starts the power curve.
Want a bunch of robot minions to automatically construct a new manufacturing area for other robots to automatically deliver materials to and take products from? Want to ship large quantities of items from distributed bases? Want that amazing feeling of accomplishment when your base is just right and moving you along to your final goal?
Well you won't get that last one, because it always feels like there's something more to do! Short on iron? Better go find another deposit to mine. Not enough circuit production? Add in some new assemblers and route the results where you need them. Base doesn't look right/efficient? There are plenty of opportunities to tweak your infrastructure. Just researched a new tech/tool? Better automate that ASAP.
And by the way, the indigenous life doesn't like all this pollution you're spreading, so you'd better put up a good defense. Or maybe you'd better take the fight to them!
Cons:
Takes a bit of time and effort to learn. Initial 20 minutes of a new world is relatively the same each time.
Pros:
I have gotten more value/fun from this game than anything else I've bought in years. It scratches so many itches in just the right way, from planning to building to researching to base defense, it does so very much right. I've spent 40+ hours on multiple bases, and they've all been a blast.
I highly recommend this game, especially to fans of strategic base planning and building.

For someone that's played through all of the Half-Life games previously, Black-Mesa lives up to the hype. The devs took upon a mountainous goal in trying to remaster and in some ways recreate one of the most influential fps games of all time. Fortunately, they nailed it. If you've never played any of the Half-Life games, this is a great way to get introduced to the franchise. If you have played them, particularly HL1, in the past, then this will be both an enjoyable and a nostalgic trip down memory lane.
There were many things that I found to be great about this game. The first and most obvious is the graphics. They nailed a modern look of Black Mesa, and seeing the classic levels of HL1 now looking extremely realistic was a treat. Second, the gunplay. If the gunplay didn't live up to the superb feeling of HL1's guns, and the juicy satisfaction of getting kills, then this game would be in the gutter quickly. Fortunately, the devs did a tremendous job on the guns, with added attention to detail on some of them. For example, you can now aim down sights with the magnum, which is a nice modern touch (that I'm sure would frustrate a few retro fans :)).Third, the game is functional! If you've played Half Life: Source, then you know about the various bugs that people encounter when playing that game. I've played it myself, and the biggest drawback from it is those bugs, they make it almost unplayable at times. Fortunately yet again, this game had no major errors for me, and felt well polished. I hope the Xen levels are just like this!
Despite how much I enjoyed Black Mesa, I do want to mention a few of the negatives I noticed, so that this review doesn't make it out to be a perfect game. One, the AI. Living up to HL1's revolutionary AI is a tall order, indeed, but the AI in this game could definitely use some improvement. From what I played, it seemed mediocre at best, and either make the game far too hard, or far too easy. Consistency was lacking with the AI, and if they can improve upon that, then the game will become much more enjoyable. Two, I'm personally not a huge fan of the lighting. I know, this might seem a bit nitpicky, but HL1 was not a game that forced use of the flashlight often. You could traverse through most of the game's puzzles and corridors being able to see just fine. Conversely, Black Mesa is the exact opposite. I found myself having the flashlight on for the vast majority of the game, to the point where it felt excessive/annoying. If they brightened the game up a bit, that would make it much more enjoyable.
In conclusion, I can now definitively say that Black Mesa is my favorite remake/remaster of any videogame that I have currently played. There are few games I've really wanted to love as much as Just Cause 3, and even fewer that are as hard to love.
Just Cause 3 is one of those kind of games in which the developer has absolutely no idea as to why the original game was popular, similar to Saints Row 3 for instance. What it leads to is a lot of changes no one wants that somehow makes it a massively worse game overall. Avalanche handing the game off to their New York based studio as opposed to doing it themselves is likely playing no small part in that.
The game immediately starts off with a scripted sequence in which you stand around on a plane doing... A whole lot of nothing. This in itself sets the tone for all of the missions ahead pretty well. They can all be amounted to one of two tasks; you either have to protect something/someone, or you have to destroy something. It gets incredibly stale incredibly fast, and with them adding a lot of scripted elements into the mix for these too; it also becomes really unfun.
Now if you thought just the game part of the missions was bad enough, you thought wrong, because there's still the atrociously bad story to take into account too. All the writing is just plain not funny or engaging in the slightest, and I think Mario might be one of the most obnoxiously written characters I've yet to encounter in a video game. He is the closest I've seen a video game come to making it's very own Jar-Jar Binks. Constantly in your face since the developers were oh so certain you would love him, and constantly incredibly unfunny. Thankfully, at least the developers themselves must have realized how awful their writing is, because they did have the decency to make it incredibly easy to just skip all cutscenes.
That's enough for just the missions, as for the rest of the game and more specifically the gameplay it's something of a mixed but mostly bad bag. I will begin by saying that I really enjoy using the wingsuit to move around, it was a needed addition that does the game well. If the wingsuit itself was the welcome addition to the game, then the gear mod upgrade system is most definitely the unwelcome one. In an attempt to copy a lot of other modern games, they added a system for upgrading your tools to get a lot of basic abilities. All it leads to is removing the sense of freedom that Just Cause 2 had, in which you were always capable of doing everything at any given point.  Rico himself feels like he controls a bit more heavily, and the camera tends to be just a lot too zoomed in, too. All in all, the gameplay just completely lacks the freedom which Just Cause 2 had. Which is, again, an example of the developers completely failing to understand anything about what made it good.
On first glance, the map and the activities around it seem a lot more interesting, but soon you realize there's not actually a whole lot to them. They are all pretty same-y and quickly stop being fun. Activities almost all amount to you needing to fly/drive through rings or destroy some stuff. Probably the only creative ones are the ones for upgrading the tether, in which you use the tether to attach a ball to your car then drive it around collecting rocks. Yet the gear mod system I mentioned earlier is directly tied to them and how you do in them, so you have no choice but to continue doing them in order to get the most out of your various gadgets. These activities are also how they try to compensate for the much, much smaller map than that of Just Cause 2, but with how monotone they quickly get it just does not work at all. The settlements themselves are a bit more fleshed out than those of Just Cause 2, but the amount of fleshing out does in no way compensate for just how much less content there is.
Oh and on a quick footnote, the PC port itself is absolutely horrendous as well. Terrible performance on systems that should run it just fine, and memory leak issues causing frequent crashes. It's an absolute joke of a PC port and it makes me sick that it's been out this long without them having done much to fix it.
In conclusion, or a tl;dr for those not interested in this wall of text. Just Cause 3 is an incredibly disappointing game both as a sequel to Just Cause 2 and as a game of its own. It does very little right, and very much wrong. I can't possibly recommend it to anyone at all, even less at the price they are currently asking for it. It's just not even remotely worth it.

TES Online got a lot of mixed reception when it came out. Fortunitely, the developers have been doing a decent job of listening to the community and making changes. They've come a long way since their launch.
The gameplay and mechanics are pretty easy to pick up. You also have freedom when it comes to roles you want to play. If you can have a role as a tank, but  if you want you can also train to be a healer as well. In this regard it's somewhat similar to the TES games. You have the ability to try different types of gameplay. The only steadfast attributes are some of the perks of your race. Some races will have perks that make them a bit better in some roles than others. The Imperials, for example, lend themselves to sword and shield combat.
There are some people who don't really like these mechanics. Generally the critisism (from what I've seen) is that there aren't well defined roles and each character is too much like the others. I guess it's a matter of preference.
When they made the subscription optional there was concern that it would go the way of F2P. or "pay to win". Fortunitely that hasn't bene the case. You pay for the game, DLC, and some other mostly cosmetic things. The closest thing to pay-to-win would be getting the monthly subscription, as you get a bit of a bonus to xp gained. The subscription also gets you access to all the DLC while you have it. There's also the Imperial pack that give you the ability to play as an Imperial character, plus some extras like a mount (horse). Otherwise everything is obtainable in the game. You can buy the base game and play that for a long time before diving into DLC content.
ESO has some characteristics that are common for MMOs. There are some uninteresting quests and the ocasional grinding. To help with that you can go anywhere in the world, even if you're a low level character and the area is meant for people thirty levels higher. You have the freedom to make your own way without having to do a lot of useless stuff just to move on to the next area. The story is pretty interesting if you are interested in the lore of TES. You could ignore most of it if you really wanted.
TES draws on the lore established in the other games. If you're someone who likes learning about the TES world and what history and secrets it has to hide you'll very much like what TES has to offer. On the same token, if you're not familiar with TES lore or don't care that much then you don't have to follow TES lore to play the game.
The graphics and controls are pretty good. It's among one of the nicer looking MMOs, and as long as you have a dedicated GPU you should be able to play it. TES Online can scale depending on your hardware. The controls are pretty similar to the other TES games, like Skyrim or Oblivion. On the audio side, it's solid. There is a lot of voice-over lines, which is welcomed and helps with immersion.
While TES Online is similar in gameplay to the other TES games, it is different. If you are expecting 'Skyrim Online' you probably will not get what you expect. If you feel it doesn't meet your expectations in that way I recommend playing a few hours so you can get a feel for the game.
Edit: Some people have noted the large disk usage. This, unfortunitely, is true. This is especially true if you haven't updated in a long time. Even with a fast connection it can take a long time to download then apply 13 GB. Fortunitely, updates this large aren't all that common. From what I recall it's mostly when major additions to the game are released, like one of the DLCs.
TLDR: It is an overall good MMO with good lore, gameplay, audio, and visuals that TES fans will especially like. If you are new to TES lore it's still an easy game to pick up. You do have to pay to get it and the DLC, but there is no subscription fee. It is also not pay to win game, like some F2P MMOs are.

In This Version: A heartfelt review.
What a HUGE HUGE HUGE HUGE disappointment. This travesty uses the 1000% garbage HW2 interface. 10000 times my heart broke within the first few seconds of playing. Homeworld 1 is the legendary game that everyone loved, and homeworld 2 is just a junk sequel with 1/100th the fun because they crammed in a terrible interface and bogged it down with a few layers of pointless micromanagement on top of each boring ship. Homeworld 2 and subsequently Homeworld Remastered are LESSER gaming experiences compared to the original homeworld. What a waste of everyone's time. In the original HW, you simply build a ship, and from there it requires nothing more than a direction and a target. Fighters and corvettes could be docked and launched easily because they were stored in class-based groups. In this version, they are stored as useless individual units and you have to shift-click each little turd in order to launch them. In the original HW, you could have a research thread for each research ship you had. In this version? Single file, please. In the original, movement was only handled by pressing the 'M' key, in this version, just right click on empty space with a unit selected! Too bad thats the same command that controls the camera movement though, so count on accidentally moving your units all the time or at least bringing up the movement arrow and having to cancel. What else? In the original skirmish vs cpu and multiplayer, you could play with nearly infinite resources (without harvesting), and with UNLIMITED unit caps. My glorious fleets would crush all comers, including my framerate. I'm talking thousands of ships here. In this neutered version? No chance, the max resource injection is a baby-soft 3000RUs. In this version you can no longer control the probability of the AI attacking you in skirmish mode. The 'building' interface is probably the worst part. In the original, all ships that could be built were listed on ONE screen, and the text was small enough that you didn't need to scroll. Units under production were displayed over the text, simple and as wholesome as apple pie. In this version you have to click on the category of ship you want to build first, and then select the ship class to build. You cant miss it because it takes up damn near a 1/4 of the screen. For your convienience it has a 2d picture beside the name. In the original? 3D model WITH ACTUAL stats including armor and firepower ratings. Building in this version sends the ship into a horrible little pukepile called the queue. You shouldn't pay much attention to it because it is tucked away in the very far corner of the screen and you usually have to scroll down to see it all. To recap at this point: everything relating to researching, building, and controlling ships is rancid catpoop compared to the original. The actual 3d 'health bars' are also insanely 10x bigger in this version than the original, like they actually block the entire scene with only a handful of ships selected. Speaking of ship selection, the original let you select certain types of ships out of a larger group by giving you a text list. In this version you are given an array of icons to choose from, and lo and behold if it is the one part of the UI that doesn't fill the whole screen, but keeping with the theme of SUCKASS the icons are blurry and all look the same so at a glance you can't tell them apart. Don't fret though, if you hold the cursor over the picture FOR A FEW SECONDS the alt text pops up. The number of selected ships is also a blurry secret, shhh! In this version there are ugly unneccessary lines that show where ships are moving to or what they are targeting. Perfect for people who have never played Homeworld and have ADD or severe brain damage. Okay, there you have it, play by play every piece of the game has been a bucket of rotting fish up to this point. On to the ships now! Oh boy they changed all the stats on the original ships why not. Costs are different just because. Missiles aren't as effective because THEY WERE USEFUL. The sensor array apparently does NOTHING now. Ion frigates are made of baby powder. View distance seems to be different, lets assume it is just because it would ruin the original gameplay. If you can't see a small enemy, don't worry! The nice game will put a nice red triangle around it so you don't have to think or pay attention.
Graphics were okay for sure. They did well to preserve the original designs. Explosions were cool and I had solid FPS
The sound was meh, the mothership is putting out a horrendously annoying drone at any distance. A bug?
To sum up my feels? This isn't Homeworld. This is a mod of the sequel to Homeworld that no one liked. You can't play this and say, "I played Homeworld!". No, this is just Homeworld 2, which I TRUELY AND GENUINELY HATE. By hate I mean I wish it was dead or was never made. Anyone responsible for the HW2 UI, or deciding to base the HW1 Remastered version on Homeworld 2, is NOT A 100% COOL PERSON, and can never achieve that rank in life. They at least had the decency to include the original version.
I only recommend this for the original version. Just play that, Okay?
Edit after playing some more:
Max unit cap is a joke! 29 capital and 39 frigates? Homeworld 1 lets you build thousands!
The capital ships are a lot slower, weaker and less manuverable than HW original. Heavy Cruiser is useless without Hyperjump
The missile destroyer's missiles can't hit anything, they literally warp through the enemy ship. Bug?
HW1's awesome formations are TRASHED. Sphere formation used to be so cool.

Pros: Characters are quite well written (especially Trip and Pigsy), some interractions are really funny. The story is interesting and engaging. Visually beautiful game.
Cons: Although presented as "action" game, I'd say it's much more a 3d platformer than anything else (with some easy puzzles thrown in). The game is linear - the only choices you get are in the "chasing mechs sequences" where you can take 1 out of the 2 paths (no effect on story). Everything else in the game is linear - there is only one way to progress through the level. There are some questionable mechanics - the controls are always camera based (pressing A makes Monkey run left in relation to the camera, not the actual left of the character). This wouldn't be a problem, except the game sometimes "takes over" the camera by locking it somewhere in the corner of a room etc. It's a little annoying, but not game breaking. The controls in menu or upgrade menu are not very good, if you're using a mouse and keyboard.
Conclusions: I still recommend the game, but I would recommend using a controller with this one. You can play with mouse and keyboard - the controller experience is much better. I'd rate it 8/10 (or 7/10 if playing without controller).

I remember playing this game on a console when it first came out and never finishing it, due to some pretty solid, but uninspired gameplay, but fast forward a few years, and I find myself playing this game again.  My issue with the game play remains unchanged, but I've come to appreciate the asthetics and presentation.
Andy Serkis (famous for his role of Gollum from Peter Jackson's LOTR trilogy) doubles as the dramatic lead and voice director, while working with a script by Alex Garland (28 Days Later). I remember playing Enslaved on the PS3 and that I was unimpressed by it. I have no idea why, because I absolutely love it after having played the PC version. It managed to pull me in right from the start and it has that fine mix of solving puzzles, platforming and combat that only few games have these days. The combat starts off shallow, but once you get access to the shooting part of your staff it becomes immensely satisfying. Hitting robots feels heavy and right, and looks great in motion.
Platforming is pretty much the same as the later Prince Of Persia and Assassin's Creed games, You can swiftly move horizontally and vertically without being afraid to fall to your death, which is always a bonus if you ask me.
The puzzles are of the platforming kind and usually require pressing (and holding) a button. It's not all that exciting and that's why there aren't a lot of them in this game. Which is good. It's just enough to keep it from being boring or frustrating.
The graphics are awesome (except for a few shadow glitches) and there are lots of colors used for the environments. It's truly beautifully made. The same goes for the characters. They are very well animated and the faces - usually a bit flawed in many, many games - are great, making it not awkward to look at whenever a cutscene starts playing. The voice acting is done extremely well, and by well known people; one of them being the great Andy Serkis. That guy just has a great voice and his motion capture performances are through the roof. Just awesome.
The story is deep and makes you think, and the game is just long enough before it becomes a chore. It lasts around 8-10 hours. If you want to find all of the orbs it could take you several hours longer. But no more, because it's a linear game and there just aren't any collectibles to be found here. Which is great for me, a guy who just wants to play through the story, but not for those collectors out there.
Enslaved is a wonderul experience and I sincerely hope more people will give it a try. It deserves another chance, people. This is it.

This Review shows my personal opinion about the game. NOTE: English isn't my mothertongue, so please excuse any language errors I make in this review.
I'm playing this game now for about 2 years and so far I haven't encountered any gamebreaking bugs (at least not in the experimental/unstable channel). This game is about creating your own Factory using Mines, Furnaces, Transport Belts, Inserters (little cranes that put items from the ground/containers/belts to other ground/containers/belts), Assemblers, later Trains and even later in the game: Drones (like inserters, but not bound to the location).
You're having very slow start with a coal drill (drills ores using coal) some iron plates and a furnace: Barely enough to get started. You gather resources to create more furnaces and drills, so you don't need to gather all the resources by hand. Now you have to walk between your 2 - 3 mining sites to get your stone, iron and copper and to put new coal into the drills and furnaces. You start building a centralized storage and refueling system for your drills furnaces and resources. You still need to craft everything by hand.
Time for some research!
You build your first Steam Dynamos to get electricity and replace your coal drills with electrical drills. Now you build a research facility and research Automation I! You get assemblers! Assemblers craft items for you. e.g. 2 iron plates to 1 iron gear and with another assembler 1 iron gear + 1 copper plate => 1 research pack. Now you have automated your basic research! Yippie!
Up to this time you may still have encountered the first enemies which you had fight of with a simple pistol! Let's research turrets, automate ammunition production, research walls and create a defense line. Now you're pretty save from those biters ... at least for a while. But as time goes by your resources are all used in your factory; You need to find new ore deposits, then transport the resources to your base and hope no biters attack your new outposts.
Later on you get the trains (which can be automated ... what a surprise) with these you have access to even more ore deposits. you know have resources, 90% of your crafting automated and no more space. you'll need to clear of those Biter Bases. Once done you can finallly research the technologies to build a space rocket ... Now you *just* need to build a rocket ... Tada you've finished the game ... if you're fast in about 5to 9 hours. if not in about 100 hours.
In my singleplayer world I have a small factory and about 30% automized of what i wanted to automized ... after about 50 hours of playtime (on this world)

I was doubtful about the game when I first heard of it. Where is the fun in building factories? We already have a handful of those crafting/survival games out there, what sets this apart? One day, just for the heck of it I went to their site and I tried their demos. On paper the idea of building a factory didn't appeal to me but I fell in love with the game the moment I started playing it. Once you start you cannot stop. This game has to be experienced in order to appreciate and see its real beauty.

I've picked up the game in the Early Access in December 2014, i've ended up playing it straight for 1.5 months while I was on hiatus at that time, so I've put like 300 hours into it in first 1.5 months. After that I had huge factories, crazy multiplayer, modded games, and so on.
I would estimate I have sunk about 700 to 800 hours into it since then and still going strong, diving more into mods.
This game just knows how to scratch your OCD and it's money for value ratio is over 9000.

The devs summarized the game pretty well on the store page, so I recommend reading that.
You manage a factory that you build up by yourself, the emphasis is on automatization rather than manual labor like in other gathery-crafty games, although you have to do some of it at the beginning. The options for buildings and technologies are pretty deep as they are. It is pretty fun and challenging to optimize and to keep your factory running. Expanding a production lines, merging them with new ones, building train lines to supply your factories with basic resources and keeping the technologies rolling gets difficult to handle.
On top of the whole factory thing there’s a nice mechanic, where the alien native lifeforms get angry if you pollute too much. Meaning they'll get harder to kill and be more aggressive as you continually pollute, so you have to defend yourself and your base while you work your way to build yourself off the planet.
I played around 50 to 60 hours with the game in a short amount of time a couple of months back and stopped playing entirely after I researched/built everything I could. Like other crafty-buildy games the end goal is pretty weak, you have to make a building and fill it with lots of resources and you'll get a message that you've won. The game was very fun at first for me, but there isn’t much else if you get bored from the basic concept (although I guess I got burnt out from playing it too much, which speaks about how good this game is). There's more content in the scenario pack to challenge yourself, the game has plenty options to set up a newly generated world and there’s good mod support too, so there are things to try out.
The devs updated the game steadily in the past and I didn’t have a single technical problem with the game yet. I played a bit of the multiplayer too a couple of months ago, it worked okay then and based on the blog post I read, they improved it a lot since.
The game has a nicely detailed and animated isometric look to it too, kind of like in Cossacks or Commandos, which I like very much. The UI is barebones, but it gets the job done. The controls of handling the inventory and the items work nicely too, it’s well thought out and the different actions can be rebinded.
There’s a demo on
, which I assume is outdated, but it’s free if you want to try out how the game plays.

I was intrigued about this game when it was released but was skeptical that the gameplay could keep me satisfied enough for a $50-60 game when it was released. I ended up buying it for about $12 when it went on sale and I was surprisingly impressed by what I found.
Environment
The game does an amazing job at replicating the look and feel of the original Alien movie, integrating the 70's view of futuristic into many aspects of the game. The fine details really make you feel like you are on an actual space station with living quarters, kitchens and medical bays. There are a wide variety of unique looking areas that your character travels to but a lot of the areas in between look the same and can get repetitive.
Gameplay
The gameplay was my biggest concern going in as I thought hiding from an invincible alien would get tiring quick but there is so much more to this game than that. Other threats such as humans and androids exist. These enemies enable you to change up your strategy and go in guns blazing if you would like, which is a nice change of pace. The Androids are downright terrifying as they have glowing red eyes and are much harder to kill than humans.
The Alien itself is also terrifying as you have no way to defend yourself in the early part of the game. It is an amazing enemy that truly evolves before your eyes. The creature will learn to track you by noting open doors and containers. I was shocked the first time it ripped open a locker where I thought I was safe from all threats. You will find that the flame thrower will become less effective as time goes by too.
One of the most important elements of the game is using your various items available as effectively as possible. Some items are meant to be merely a distraction(noise maker) while others like the pipe bomb can kill a room full of humans. Enemies get stronger and smarter as you progress through the game and require you to change up your tactics and use every resource available. Using rewires are crucial as turning of lights and air purification systems help you sneak past threats too dangerous to take head on. The game also scatters in a lot of mini games that are mostly designed to increase the amount of time to access a console or open a door so an enemy can sneak behind you. They do a great job at adding layers to the experience.
Music
The music truly makes this game complete. I almost always played this game in a dark room with the volume up. The volume is very helpful at indicating when the Alien is in the room or when it has left. The game can be pretty intense when you are hiding behind a desk and the music is getting louder and is at its peak as the alien stands just on the other side waiting to either strike or move on. Not know whether it has sensed you or not is quite a thrill.
Story
The story didn't strike me as anything amazing. The main character is Ellen Ripley's daughter who is striving to find her lost mother. We find out in Aliens that Ripley was in cryogenic sleep for so long that she outlives her daughter. There are a few clues of Ripley's presence throughout the game but I thought the tie-in was a little weak. The rest of the story is enough to make the gameplay more interesting as it fuels your characters actions and gives you hope for survival. There are a few good twists but mostly the story just involves♥♥♥♥♥♥going wrong and the next objective is to move onto plan D cause plan C didn't work.
Overall
I was very satisfied with this game. The gameplay was very engaging and challenging. Some reviews complained that save stations where too far apart and constant death meant replaying areas over and over. I only had one instance when I had to replay an area several times but I just had to change my strategy and be a little more careful. Having an enemy that can kill instantly on site and cause you redo a small area is part of the what makes this game so terrifying. I feel that save stations have adequate spacing.
I definitely recommend to anyone who is on the fence as I was in the same boat and ending up loving the experience.

This game is probably the weakest of the trilogy - but that's not to say it isn't good. It's still hilarious, still fun and it still has a good story. There were two problems, in my opinion:
1. The puzzles were sometimes too obscure. While this game certainly improved on some aspects of the first game (most of the time I actually had some idea of what I was doing, and some sense of progress, whereas in the first one I tended to get stuck much more often) - it still suffers a bit from being a little
hard in places. I'm not saying that I want it to be easy - no thanks - but this game is so big and sprawling that it sometimes got very confusing as to where I needed to go next. (on the other hand, it did improve quite a lot on the first game. Some new mechanics were pretty good).
2. Parts of it do feel a bit like filler. The actual story part of the game is extremely stretched out (
). It was fun, but it was slow going. It set up a lot of important stuff for the third game, obviously, but not a lot happened in this one compared to the others.
But, still, it was a good game, like the others. I love this universe, the characters, the humour. In this game, it was especially the humour, being a bit more lacking in story and character development than the others.
Overall, it was fun, and important as a setup for the third one, which I think is easily the best. Obviously, if you're playing the trilogy, you
miss this one - you probably won't even be reading the reviews for the second game if you've played the first - even so, I'm going to give it an 8/10 for anyone who might be reading.
