I bought this game in Feb 2015 and have literally played it hundreds of hours. The game is a bit brutal to newcomers in the beginning as the tutorial teaches you how to play, but not what everything does. For me that is/was half the fun in figuring out what things do without looking them up on a wiki.
Factorio is amazing in that you are controlling a guy that has crashed on a planet and needs to collect local resources in order to build a ship to get back home. In order to do that you'll be building factories to move things, combine things, etc.
The first 3-4 play throughs you're going to realize that you could have done something different to make things more optimized. The more optimized the factory is the better things flow. You will make mistakes and learn from those mistakes and the crazy thing is you'll keep coming back for more.
There is A LOT of content in the current state of the game. It is listed as an alpha, but wow, you can play for a good 20-30 hours on a single save before you even start to run out of things to do. If you play with the settings and make resources more scarce or the alien biters more abundant you can make the game harder as you bet better.
Currently the end game is where the game is lacking. Once you research everything in the technology tree there is little left to do and you'll usually end up creating a new save and going again.
Multiplayer is a lot of fun. It's still in its infancy, but there are a few dedicated servers available if you look in the forums and a server browser should be coming in a later version.
Overall I can't recommend this game enough. It's worth every penny and I'm so excited for Factorio to come to steam and find a wider audience.

I've been playing factorio with a handful of friends for quite some time now, and it has been a hell of a ride seeing what competent devs can do with some time and effort. The graphics, UI, optimization, damn near everything has been updated multiple times in ways that are noticeable to the player.
The game typically starts you off (you can customize the pants off the world gen) with some trees, iron, coal, copper, oil, rock and water nearby. At the time of this writing you get a furnace and a drill, both powered by coal. Slap that drill onto the iron and place the furnace on the output, feed them with coal (which is easily mined by hand) and you have begun what will undoubtedly be hours and hours of planning and building.
You can grab some of that iron, mine some stone, and beef up production first by making more drills and furnaces. You can start making grabbers and conveyor belts to move things around, perhaps drilling coal that will be transported to your furnaces and fed to them automatically. Regardless, things will expand at a rate you likely didn't think yourself capable of, and before long you need to worry about defendin your pollutant-ridden factory from the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ off wildlife.
A lot of the game's progress is tied to research, which is done in a lab with special craftable items. Before long you'll be making automatic crafting stations and turning raw materials into science packs without lifting a finger.
Once you get automation going, simply watching what you've built is a constant source of pride and almost zen-like calm (until the warning sirens are going off again and you have to ventilate some aliens). This is where the game's optimization really shines. I'm not typically one to compare to other games, but I played a lot of Tekkit and other related Minecraft mods where bulding a factory has a lot of parallels to Factorio. My experience making factories in Minecraft was always riddled with poor performance as soon as I got some things moving along nicely. This is not the case with factorio, you can watch as your belts are moving around dozens of items smoothly, then it becomes hundreds of items being moved along belts, grabbers, and trains. This keeps on increasing but the game still runs great. LAN multiplayer works great, the occasional bug here and there but nothing game breaking that I've run into while playing the last few versions.
Multiplayer is great, too, cooperating to make a large factory or even friendly competition to see who can make a better factory (while sharing the same research)
I reccomend this game heartily, and even this lengthy review doesn't do it justice, IMO.

Chaos on Deponia is an excellent point ‘n’ click adventure with exceptional dialogues and character portrayal, but the puzzles sometimes reach old LucasArts levels.
If Deponia’s role was to introduce players to a fun little point ‘n’ click series, Chaos on Deponia’s role is to throw everyone into the deep water. This game doesn’t kid around. The tone is more serious, and in some regards, darker: you are required to commit murder and animal abuse, just to name two of the morally questionable mandatory actions.
The story puts a larger emphasis on Rufus and his interaction with Goal (or Goals, since she is three people now) and the other characters. This not only portrays his selfish personality, but also evolves it in a quite realistic way. The dialogues are, without doubt, the greatest strength of the game.
The plot… not that much. The central issue of the planet’s destruction is shoved into the background to lead you in some wild goose chases. And when the story arc finally remembers it should lead somewhere, it suddenly abandons several smaller threads without explanation.
Progressing can sometimes be a gargantuan task with intricate, several-step, whole gameworld-spanning puzzles based on typical adventure game logic. (How do you win at rock-paper-scissors? By destroying a pair of sunglasses to gain entrance to a submarine, of course!) The minigames are more forgiving, thankfully.
Despite these setbacks, Chaos on Deponia is the highlight of the trilogy, and one of the best Daedalic games– worthy to be in the library of any point ’n’ click fan.

The game can be seperated into two catagories. You have your typical PvE which consists of most of the game. But you also have PvP which is a side note to the main game that can add an entirely new layer to the gameplay.
The open ended character building and leveling is a nice feature where you can specalize you character in the format that you want to become more attuned to certain play styles.

All in all I have to say this game for any fault it may or may not have is a really good play and it is worth the cost.

It was a lifechanging experience and I remember how I couldn't sleep at nights and curled tightly in my bed. Since then I watched all the movies many times and played all major games about the alien. Now I thought nothing about this creature could scare me. I've seen too much of it, too often and games usually don't scare me anymore. This time I was terribly wrong. The Alien: Isolation is different. I was in fear again and literally my hands were cold-sweating all the time. I had to put on something because I was simply cold. This game is really scary especially first few hours after you encounter the alien first time.
Ok, it's supposed to be a review-comment sort of thing. The first thing you notice after you run this game is graphics quality. It's simply outstanding. Lighting is perfect and makes everything looking very realistic. The models are perfected in any way and have that specific retro style like in the movie. They have great textures and are very detailed. I have played only a few games in my life with such great graphics. At the same time the performance of this game is very good too. It works on maxed settings for me and my graphics card don't sweat as much as with Ghost Recon: Future soldier, which is much older, burns my graphics card and looks kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ even on maxed settings. Next thing is sound... the sound effects are realistic and diverse, music is partially based on the Alien movie. Sometimes you can hear chunks well known from the movie. The xenomorph acts as if it was really intelligent and moves creepily. Sometimes it checks the lockers you hide in, sometimes checks under the table. Finally the game is long and diverse. You have slower moments and more tense ones so you don't get bored easily. Sometimes you have to go out into the space. I didn't feel that specific monotony present in so many games.
To sum up, I would rate this game 9/10 and only because of two things... First - the alien can't walk on walls, Second -the ending is a bit underwhelming. Anyway I strongly recommend this game but you'll need plenty of time, nerves of steel and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of patience to finish it. I also recommend playing on the hard level. It's easy enough to finish the game without major problems and hard enough to create enough tension. I think lower levels could be too easy... but I haven't tried them, perhaps they don't differ that much? I don't know :).

I wasn't too impressed initially. Shogun 2 was my first TW game, and I simply love the Japanese feudal era and their unit types more.
Compared to Shogun 2, Rome 2 has some improvements though:
+ Rome 2's campaign map is gigantic (EU + Middle East + Northern Africa)
+ Political system is more varied
+ Generals and Special characters die off more frequently due to the time span -- you won't be using the same generals you started with, this makes your armies feel less static
+ Armies are named, have their own traditions (customization separate from the general) and the army name can be revived if they are obliterated
+ Diversity among factions, Romans have completely different units than the barbarian factions for example
+ Towns are tied together in provinces, sharing building effects and happiness/dissent
~ Armies can only be raised by generals, instead of in towns and from generals

Rome 2 may not have as cool of units as Shogun 2, but I can see I will have many more campaign playthroughs  simply due to the size of Rome 2's map. Shogun 2's map was the relatively small island map of Japan in which you mainly conquered either from North to South or vice versa, feeling somewhat linear after awhile.
If you haven't played a Total War game, but love strategy and 4x games, this game or Shogun 2 is definitely worth checking out. Additionally, the TW games are infused with history.
I picked up Rome 2: Emperor Edition in December and have yet to have any issues that may have plagued the game originally at its launch.

My first MMO that I've ever played! I've got some mixed expectations but at the end The Elder Scrolls® Online: Tamriel Unlimited™ turned out to be a pretty decent game.
The only other Elder Scrolls game I've played so far was Skyrim thus let's check out what makes ESO different from what Skyrim did.
1. The Story: While Skyrim was kind of slow in developing it's story, ESO has a quicker pace on how it presents it's storyline to you.
After you did the intro mission that introduces you to what you can expect to come later, you'll be released to the world. The amount of missions and other content is IMMENSE. I've been playing for more then 100 hours now and still have barely experienced 50% of all the available PvE story content.
2. The Meta Game: When you're not focusing the main story line there's plenty of other stuff to do. Sidequests, Crafting and Dungeons wait to be explored and everything with other people running around.
Especially the other "travellers" make the game feel much more vivid than Skyrim.
There's plenty of NPC's inside towns talking to eachother and doing other miscallenous stuff, while in Skyrim every Town felt more or less as dead and empty like a cemetery.
3. The Gameplay: Not going to lie here, the MMO elements are undeniably strong. Levelling takes alot of time to do and crafting ingredients are partly incredibly difficult to find. While in Skyrim it was rather easy to become an Overpowered Demi-God that One-Punched Alduin the Worldeater into Oblivion, it'll mostly never happen in ESO since you're more or less always on par with other players on a similar level to prevent you from curbstomping every other player in PvP.
After all I can very much recommend this game to get when it's on sale again. The graphics and overall presentation of the game is pretty decent regarding its MMO nature.

I've been playing ESO since Beta (tack on about 3.5k more hours onto my Steam hours for ESO if that sort of thing matters to you). For the most part, ESO has been an above-average action-combat MMORPG (once ZoS fixed all the release hiccups). The combat was rewarding and satisfying. The customization is rather extensive. Post-1.6, ESO has been on a decline, due to the dev team's incompetence and greed. Bugs that have been around for months, if not years, continue to exist and ZoS's excuse is "We cannot replicate it". Churning out DLC and Crown Store items takes precedence over releasing working content and/or bug fixes. If something is broken in PvP, expect it not to get fixed until the next big update. The CP system has wholly gutted any semblance of balance ESO once had, and it doesn't seem like correcting the CP imbalance is anywhere on ZoS's radar.
If you enjoy near-endless resource regen,clunky combat, and hackers(who got caught and recorded) having their permabans rescinded days later, then ESO is for you. And One Tamriel has fixed nothing and has only broken more elements of the game, and if that isn't enough to deter you, ZoS has also made it impossible to play on multiple accounts via the Steam client.
If you have a modicum of respect for yourself and your money, you'll avoid ESO and anything else ZoS is ever involved with.

As someone who's played DW2-8E, WO1-3 and SW1-2XL (Never owned a Wii, so I missed 3 sadly) and now SW4-2 (Essentially XL), I'd rate this addition to the franchise as one of the better ones overall.
Pros:
Combat is much, much better than it's Dynasty counterparts. It's far more in-depth and engaging and the addition of Hyper attacks makes combat seem far more enjoyable when you're cleaving your way through thousands of peons.
Another staple of the Samurai Warrior series is the inclusion of in-game objectives which greatly affect the flow of battle. Completing or failing the objectives as you come across them can have major impacts for both armies. If you're a completionist, there are usually 2-3 objectives per level that will likely require you to replay the level using a different set of characters.
60 FPS. I can't stress how much smoother this plays in comparison to DW8XLCE and 8E.
If you're into anime, the storytelling and art direction will be right up your alley.
Cons:
It's in Japanese. There isn't an English dub available and at this point I doubt there will be. Because of the anime-styled characters, some parts of the game just weren't enjoyable for me. Absurd characters like Masanori Fukushima threating to "Punch you in your big head" just ended up making me glad there wasn't one at times.
It's a grindfest unless you buy the DLC Mounts and arguably the DLC weapons. You can access a tier of unique weapons for each character by completing a certain set of objectives on a given level, just as it's always been in the Warriors series, but by the time you reach that point you're probably just playing to 100% everything.
I've had the game crash a few times while using the Store between levels, usually after buying out all of the times. I've not had the game crash while playing, mind, but it's something toconsider. I've also  had significant frame drops with large amounts of enemies or in very fire-heavy missions (Such as Takatora Tōdō's first level).
No SW4 Clan stories. I don't know if they'll ever add them as a DLC or if they eventually plan to release a SW4-2CE like they did with DW8, but all of the main stories are focused around a single character as a primary character with a selection of secondary characters based on the level.
Conclusion:
If you enjoy the Warriors games for game play then buy this. If you're not an anime fan like me, try to bear with the story and in the worst case turn off voices then check the map more often. I'd rate it a solid 4/5, I'd give it a 4.5 if the dialogue wasn't some awful anime imitation. If you had to choose between buying this and DW8E then I'd get this.
Beat em up. What more do you want? Get it.

It's easy to understand why Alien: Isolation gets such disparate opinions, since gameplay consists of pretty basic and mundane tasks for most of the time, with just a little combat (which can be avoided, though a few times it's pretty hard to do so). While you do those things, however, there's an alien that kills you instantly so you have to be very careful and silent, which coupled with the incredible atmosphere, made possible by the art direction and sound design (play with headphones!), makes for an extremely immersive game. Even in moments when you are doing nothing, you think something can happen anytime which keeps you on your toes.
Some people say the game is too long (took me around 20 hours) but for a stealth and exploration game I think it's a good length. And I thought they balanced well the amount of time facing the alien and time facing other threats; too much alien might have been overkill.
Negatives for me were the story and characters (merely serviceable, though Amanda is a somewhat likable protagonist), and the ending was extremely abrupt. The save system was a problem for me at first (I dislike stealth games with no quicksave) but I got used to it and thought the save stations were very well spaced throughout the station.
All in all, while not everyone's cup of tea, those who enjoy stealth, survival horror and immersive experiences ought to give this one a chance. And if you're a fan of the original Alien, then what are you waiting for?

Chaos on Deponia is an excellent point ‘n’ click adventure with exceptional dialogues and character portrayal, but the puzzles sometimes reach old LucasArts levels.
If Deponia’s role was to introduce players to a fun little point ‘n’ click series, Chaos on Deponia’s role is to throw everyone into the deep water. This game doesn’t kid around. The tone is more serious, and in some regards, darker: you are required to commit murder and animal abuse, just to name two of the morally questionable mandatory actions.
The story puts a larger emphasis on Rufus and his interaction with Goal (or Goals, since she is three people now) and the other characters. This not only portrays his selfish personality, but also evolves it in a quite realistic way. The dialogues are, without doubt, the greatest strength of the game.
The plot… not that much. The central issue of the planet’s destruction is shoved into the background to lead you in some wild goose chases. And when the story arc finally remembers it should lead somewhere, it suddenly abandons several smaller threads without explanation.
Progressing can sometimes be a gargantuan task with intricate, several-step, whole gameworld-spanning puzzles based on typical adventure game logic. (How do you win at rock-paper-scissors? By destroying a pair of sunglasses to gain entrance to a submarine, of course!) The minigames are more forgiving, thankfully.
Despite these setbacks, Chaos on Deponia is the highlight of the trilogy, and one of the best Daedalic games– worthy to be in the library of any point ’n’ click fan.

It's a great addition to the Deponia game trilogy. If you enjoyed the first game, then pick this up! You're missing out! I would recommend playing the games in order. If this one looks interesting, but you haven't played the original Deponia title, then pick it up first.

What can i say that could sum up Factorio in a few words? Dedication, developer commitment, player involvement regarding development of the game, huge replayability, countless addons, the list goes on and on...
This game basically is every neurotic and OCD gamers wet dream. You want something overly complicated? check. You want endless possibilities in how you make your factory every time you start a new game? check. You want addons which can make things even more complicated up to the point where you will need a PhD in Mathematics and Construction Engineering just to get to the damn thing to work? check and check!
The graphics are not on the same level as for example Far Cry Primal, or XCOM 2, this game is not a mindless game where all is required to point at zombies/terrorist/nazis or whatever and shoot, if that is something that is most important to you than this game might not be for you.
Honestly, in my opinion there are only a few games that come close to this beautiful piece of artwork that we have the honor of calling a videogame. Kerbal Space Program, Portal and Minecraft are quite possibly the only games in my opinion have the same kind of gameplay, replayability and playability as Factorio has.
I have no doubt in my mind that Factorio has the potential to become a huge hit on Steam. All the required ingredients are already in the game to make this a huge hit. But don't take my word for it, go buy it and see for yourself! This game and the developers who worked on it day and night really deserve it.

Factorio is a game about automation and making a factory.
You start off alone with a bare handful of resources. You must begin small - creating a mining station and some basic furnaces. Then begin to build power infrastructure - coal fired steam engines and such. Use this to power electric miners and automate the production of things. Iron becomes gears, iron plates and gears can make conveyor belts. Conveyor belts  allow for you to move things around, and then the logistics challenge begins - creating a fully automated factory to produce science packs that can be used to discover new technologies. Bring in trains, logistical robots, construction robots, solar power, laser turrets and powered armour. Work your way up to a rocket, which is where it currently ends, although it is intended to go further, in the future.
All the while the native biters are being agitated by the pollution you produce, I hope you can defend what you have made.
I love the devs, I funded this back in the original indiegogo and have seen this develop so much. The devs have always been awesome, they have kept a blog going with a post every Friday for the best part of (if not more than) 2 years.
Please give it a try, there is a demo available. It has lasted me for hundreds of hours.

Factorio scratches so many itches for people with OCD , or who like building , or survival, or incremental games. Truly fantastic destroyer of time. The gameplay and building aspects of this game are so tight and fun. If you like Any of the above sort of games you're going to love this one.

Warning: Factorio is extremely addictive. The more you know, the more you want to know. The more you play, well... you get the idea.
This game is for people who want to settle in for the long haul - no such thing as a quick game, but make no mistake, every day, hour, minute and second will be filled with something to do. And then redo, when you figure out a better way of doing it.
So what is Factorio? Essentially, you just need to launch a rocket with a satellite after landing on an alien planet. But you don't have a rocket, and you don't know how to build one. So you have to build research labs, and provide materials for research, but you have to gather those materials. To gather those materials you need mining, smelting, and other equipment. To make those? Well, you start with a pick-axe and work your way up.
Simple, right? Well, no. This isn't your planet. In fact *you* are the alien, and all those factories you're setting up are causing pollution, which the native inhabitants don't very much appreciate. So much so that they will seek you out, hunt you down, and put and end to your day and your factories. So you need to defend, to attack, to improve your military capabilities. You need to decide what's most important to research, and where to expand into, what to build, when to upgrade, and how to move the resources around. And there's limitless ways of doing it.
Need a hand? Bring a friend! Factorio has multiplayer. While it's still being improved, it's very playable (providing you have a good solid connection). Work together (or against each other) to build the best factories, learn new techniques, and show everyone what you're made of.
Factorio has elements of Minecraft/IndustrialCraft, and for players of RimWorld, and Prison Architect, it's a must have.
The devs are keenly responsive and deeply care about the community, the forums are active, the game sees weekly progress reports, and frequent updates to fix bugs. There's a plethora of mods, and modding support is fantastic (even the base game is a mod). DyTech and Bobsmods alone will extend the playing life of the game by a huge factor.
Since the game is in early access, and at this time hasn't been released, it's unfair of me to post criticism.
If you buy the game, know that you are getting a very solid game right now which is completely playable and will give you many more hours than AAA titles. You will also be supporting an already solid development team, and more and more improved updates will come more and more frequently (as has been demonstrated by the hiring they've done).

I bought Factorio a very long time ago. Even back then it was a fresh and unique idea to build your own factory. The first few moments I've played I knew I will love this game. It's probably best described as kind of a puzzle adventure action strategy simulation.
There is so much content, I'm sure it will take a many days of your precious life until you discover and build everything Factorio has to offer. The game is about managing your transport belts, so you can get everything where you want to have it. The game is about creating a network of materials and advanced products, e. g. the third generation of science packs is incredibly complicated if you don't have any clue about everything works as the game is also about the joy of figuring out how to accomplish certain things. I remember being very happy when I've finally figured out how to let drones place your solar panels automatically with a blueprint.
Although admittedly the game can be a little scary at first considering the amount of content included, Factorio is ten (or even a hundred times) more satisfying and rewarding. There are no obvious bugs to be found since the devs put so much effort in bugfixing it's almost unbelievable. As far as I remember every major version has been being checked for even the tiniest and nastiest bug for weeks - or rather months. All machines, trains, resources, transport belts, trees - everything - look just beautiful. If you can't see the love put into this game here then you are probably a lost cause. lol
Seriously, if you have a soft spot for either puzzlers, adventure, action, strategy or simulation games I can highly recommend this gem. You will get so much content for its money, Factorio certainly doesn't need to hide behind the one or other AAA game.
Oh, did I mention it even has multiplayer?

The beautiful thing about Homeworld is that the original game, before being remastered, aged extremely well.  I played through it (the unremastered version) earlier this year actually and it was very hard to believe that the game was 15 years old.  So given that it now looks absolutely stunning, it feels very, very modern.  In terms of quality, this game (in my opinion) would easily worth a lot more than it's current price tag if it was a new game releasing for the first time.
So if you haven't played Homeworld before and are wondering if it's still worth playing now,  I'd highly recommend you go ahead and pick this up because this is a game that has survived the test of time and plays just as well today as it did back when it first released.  It is not one of those remastered releases where the gameplay mechanics aged badly despite some pretty new textures.
For those of you who are already fans of the original Homeworld and are just reading these reviews to find out if this remastered version is worth picking up, the answer is yes.  You can rest easy knowing they didn't break the game or try to change it or somehow ruin it doing something stupid, it  feels, and plays exactly like the original game, and visually, it maintains the original look and feel so well that despite having far more advanced visuals than the original, in a sense it looks exactly how our nostalgic brains probably think we "remember" the first looking, back when it's visuals blew us away oh so long ago.

Pros:
1) There IS a game. There are quests, Items, Weapons, and Things to do in the game.
2) PvP is regulated. A level ten can beat a Veteran Rank 14 Player. The only thing stopping him is if the VR14 player's gear is better than his, and it usually is.
Cons:
1) The quests are boring, and tend to be very similiar to eachother.
2) The sixty dollar price tag is incredibly expensive due to the fact that, one, the game is no longer new, and two, if you want to have any fun with your game, you are going to have to spend at least $30 bucks in microtransactions to aquire the items neccesary to progress through the game.

I prefer Samurai Warriors on PS2. Compared with other Warrior's titles today, SW4-II feels really dated. Most of the moves are imported from SW1 and despite some great innovations made for DW8's combat system, they weren't carried over.
SW1 felt really immersive. Especially for me; for the most part it understood it was a period-piece and it was easy for a Japanese history-buff to feel like they were participating in the battles of the Sengoku Jidai. SW4-II feels more like an anime. The character designs are flamboyant, awkward and uninspired. The music, however, is really good and I've enjoyed this game's soundtrack long before it was released outside Japan. That said, even the music feels watered down compared to SW1.
This port is plagued with quite a few technical issues. I'm sure everyone's experience will vary, but...
I had to run the game in windowed mode otherwise, the game would get jittery. There's tons of framerate issues, that I ironically fixed by setting all settings to high and turning of dynamic shadows (I think that's what it was called). The textures are taken from the PS3's versions and not the PS4's-- lame, but not exactly a deal breaker on its own. When I begin to add all these issues together, I'm shocked to see that this is the first time I'm not enjoying a Warriors game.
I've played thousands of hours between DW1-DW8 and SW1. Sadly, I don't want to add another single hour into SW4-II.
I actually still want to recommend this game. My issues (aside from the technical, which can be worked around) are mainly subjective and based on my tastes. However, because the port does feel sloppy, and I feel Koei didn't put much effort into this title (especially considering this is a remake) I won't.
This game is still pretty cool, but get it on sale. I paid $35 for it, but still think that's too expensive for this experience. I'd rate this game at $20 max. If you have a PS4, I'd also suggest buying that version over this.

If there's one thing I can say about this game is: WORDS CANNOT DO IT JUSTICE. However I wil try.
Visually STUNNING, with a storyline that while not too unpredictable works VERY well, beautiful character development and two brilliant protagonists, Enslaved is a game that will have you laughing at its lightheartedness (or at least chuckling), weeping at its dramatic/heartwrenching stuff (or at least feeling quite sad), hating characters, then loving them, then hating them again. This game's story is a rollercoaster, wonderfully woven together, possibly due to it being loosely based on the brilliant "Journey to the West".
As for the gameplay itself, where to start. The climbing and navigating through the levels is very smooth, with the lovable protagonist feeling truly as nimble as a monkey and strong as a gorilla, even though he's very much human.
The sections with The Cloud are just an absolute treat, and serve very well to break the otherwise limited navigatability (is that even a word?) of the world. The first time I used it I just ran around for 5 mins doing nothing but enjoying it.
As for combat, I found myself wishing for more and more with every encounter. Combat has a very powerful element to it, as getting to whack the enemies to bits with the main character's weapon is immensely satisfying, and always left me feeling the adrenaline rush at the end of each group fight. My advice, if you enjoy action games, play it on Hard, I just couldn't get enough of whacking these enemies around and I think on Normal they would've died much quicker.
TLDR: This game is BEAUTIFUL, has a truly great story, loveable and memorable characters, and fluid and smooth gameplay. Definitely one of the best games I've played this year (although it's older on console)

Monkey, a strong, brutish loner and fellow prisoner also gets free by virtue of his raw power and brawn. Trip quickly realizes that Monkey is her ticket to freedom and is her only hope to survive her perilous journey back home. She hacks a slave headband and fits it on Monkey, linking them together. Dishonored 2 is a stealth-action game made by Arkane Studios. Set in the fictional Empire of the Isles, more especifically in the cities of Dunwall and Karnaca, you play as returning protagonist Corvo Attano, or the now-Empress Emily Kaldwin, 15 years after the first game. Most of it is set on the second city Karnaca, a really beautiful sunny mediterranean-inspired city, with sometimes even modern architecture in some newer buildings, and guards wearing lighter clothing.
Let's get the bad stuff out of here first: the game runs pretty bad for what it is. Made in the brand-new idTech5-upgraded Void Engine, you'll see performance complaints everywhere (I won't complain myself since I managed to run it at 720p 30fps on a laptop below minimum settings.) Apart from this, the story is nothing to write home about, rehashed themes from Dishonored 1 and few interesting characters. The game has Emily or Corvo trying to get back the empire from a cunning woman who stole it from them, and you're left to wonder how dumb both of them are if they never saw something like this coming, a plot that was three years in the making. Keep in mind that you should play the first game's DLCs if you haven't done so already as some characters return from Daud's story.
On to the good stuff: When it comes to gameplay and level design, this is a bigger and better sequel in almost everything. (Just a note here: since purchasing the game I have played it once with Corvo, doing a no-powers, no-kills, no-detections run, and then Emily, doing a kill-everything run with powers.) There are a lot more tools for stealth, such as crossbow bolts that make enemies run away and clear their alertness towards you, bolts that work like flashbombs and blind enemies temporarily, and more options for knocking out where there was only assassination previously, such as choking mid-combat and air knockouts. You now also have Emily, whose powers are much more suited for stealth, with doppelgangers, near-invisibility, and mesmerising enemies. Enemies such as the clockwork soldiers are really hard to sneak up on since they literally have eyes in the back of their heads, though you can shoot of their heads to make them blind, or rewire them. The enemy AI, however, is still fairly dumb and still rarely looks up, though it will detect you in a very short time once it does (2 seconds or less in Very Hard). The detection mechanics are still fairly weak, being based solely on line of sight and the only thing about sound which matters being whether you're crouched. The same for combat, where enemies rarely try to avoid grenades and mines. One thing to mention here is that since combat also got some upgrades from the first game, stealth still feels like it has less options.
There are now a lot more runes and bonecharms per level, as you have a lot more upgrades for each power, and new passive skills. One of these is bonecharm crafting, which allows you to destroy bonecharms to learn their upgrades and get raw whalebone to make bigger bonecharms which can store up to 4 of these upgrades, but in creating them you have a chance to corrupt them, which results in it having a downside as well. Apart from that there are black and corrputed bonecharms, whose upgrades can't be learned since they're more powerful, the corrupted ones also coming with a malus. It's a shame there aren't a lot of stealth-centric bonecharms, though. There's a lot more upgrades for equipment now as well, with arc mines and springrazors having more uses in one mine, for example, and masterwork upgrades in which you can pick one of two very powerful upgrades, some unique to either Emily or Corvo. The models for the crossbow and pistol are different for each character as well. The upgrades can be purchased throughout the black markets in most missions, and these can all be robbed, which is really great, though by doing this you won't be able to upgrade gear and buy more supplies for one or two missions.
Combat is pretty much the same stylish violence as the same one but more. Your execution moves are now more gory with chopping not only heads but limbs and torsoes, which you can then grab and throw. You can assassinate or knockout enemies while sliding. One of the new passive power trees is Reflexes, which lets you deflect projectiles with your sword like a goddamn Jedi, and slow time when you're spotted or sliding and pointing a crossbow at an enemy for the perfect headshot. It's an enhanced power fantasy with not much difficulty but immense fun, as it is still great at making you feel a sort of god of death killing everything with relative ease and style.
The level design... wow. Dishonored 2 follows a very similar mission structure in every mission: get from the sea to a mostly indoor space through fairly open streets with smaller, more closed streets and open apartments inbetween, and then the aforementioned mostly indoor space where you're supposed to eliminate your target by either murdering them or finding out a non-lethal alternative, this spanning one or two missions. This similar mission structure doesn't affect the levels negatively, as they are still excellent and have great variation, some having unique mechanics to each such as time travel, skipping the entire mission with a puzzle, the target having a body double you can only recognize with hints throughout the level, and rooms shifting as the player interacts with them. This is excellent stuff all around, and the levels are very much possible to play without powers (as you can refuse to get powers when offered, after the first mission).
Apart from this Dishonored 2 does do certain things worse than it's protagonist. The art direction is less moving watercolour-like and more realistic, and the game does lose some charm. The "big plague which can grow with how many enemies you kill" is now bloodflies instead of rats, and though their nests are visually impressive, they're mostly pushovers, and you can pretty kill their nests by running across an infested area and swinging your sword, which makes them calm down and stop attacking you. In the end you'll just kill them anyway so you can loot infested areas without having to hear an annoying buzz, and because it can give you health/mana with bonecharms. There's also the aforementioned narrative and performance.
In the end, if you liked Dishonored 1, Deus Ex or even the Thief games, this is definitely recommended as long as you can run it. It's more Dishonored and better, and with no powers it's a cool sneaker with a much inferior stealth system.

Factorio, to me, is a specialized 2D Minecraft.  My favorite things there were always automating as much as I could manage.  Mining, Crafting, etc.  Factorio is an entire game based around that.  At it's core, the premise of the game is very simple.  Build a factory to launch rockets into space.  Along the way, however, you will struggle with how to optimize your factory to produce the things you need to continue expanding, how to defend yourself against the native fauna, and the constant urge to destroy and recreate all the things you did in the beginning which now disgust your refined engineer sensibilities.  I can see why some people wouldn't like the game, but if you enjoy creative building and optimizing designs, it's definitely worth some playtime (or a LOT of playtime...).

In short, if you like looking at a system and trying to come up with a better way of doing, this game should be on the top of your must play list.

I bought this game in Feb 2015 and have literally played it hundreds of hours. The game is a bit brutal to newcomers in the beginning as the tutorial teaches you how to play, but not what everything does. For me that is/was half the fun in figuring out what things do without looking them up on a wiki.
Factorio is amazing in that you are controlling a guy that has crashed on a planet and needs to collect local resources in order to build a ship to get back home. In order to do that you'll be building factories to move things, combine things, etc.
The first 3-4 play throughs you're going to realize that you could have done something different to make things more optimized. The more optimized the factory is the better things flow. You will make mistakes and learn from those mistakes and the crazy thing is you'll keep coming back for more.
There is A LOT of content in the current state of the game. It is listed as an alpha, but wow, you can play for a good 20-30 hours on a single save before you even start to run out of things to do. If you play with the settings and make resources more scarce or the alien biters more abundant you can make the game harder as you bet better.
Currently the end game is where the game is lacking. Once you research everything in the technology tree there is little left to do and you'll usually end up creating a new save and going again.
Multiplayer is a lot of fun. It's still in its infancy, but there are a few dedicated servers available if you look in the forums and a server browser should be coming in a later version.
Overall I can't recommend this game enough. It's worth every penny and I'm so excited for Factorio to come to steam and find a wider audience.

I remember playing HW1 when I was a kid and getting destroyed.  15 years later, with an adult mind, it feels like a different game.  I know how to manage resources better, I know the strengths and weaknesses of ships better, and try to organize my fleet instead of throwing units against the enemy hoping to get a kill.
EVEN IF YOU DON'T LIKE RTS, GIVE THIS GAME A TRY.  It looks like another overcomplicated space RTS, but it's really not.  It's complicated in its own ways, but very easy to learn the basic tactics and rock-paper-scissor mechanics between all the different ships.
This isn't like other RTSs.  It's very easy to pick up and play, hard to master against real players, but the selling point is the beautiful campaigns of HW1 and 2.  Not to mention the massive battles, with fighters zipping everywhere with their glowing contrails, and massive capital ships hammering at each other with cannons and ion beems.
Good lord, it's been a long time.  It's more beautiful than I remember; with the Remastered engine, it's more than just a polished up HW2 engine.  Check out any comparison videos.
This game has gotten *BETTER* with time.  How many series/remakes can say that?

Let me be clear, this game has the full potential to really screw up. If you have a mid range PC or anything lower, dont bother. Spend your money elsewhere.
That being said, if your PC can take this game and if you dont mind occasional frame rate dips in more open areas, this is a great game. It is not better then the original, which may be my favorite game of all time, but damn does it come close.

This game acts as a straight upgrade from the original, bigger and better, even with voice-actors for the protagonists! Too bad their lines are♥♥♥♥♥♥There's literally a scene where Corvo just says "The world is full of secrets" for little to no reason other then the writers trying to be all philosiphical). That being said, some of the crap Corvo says during a high chaos playthrough will give you a chuckle due to the abruptness and absurdity of his lines. Ive no clue if that was intentional, but I liked it anyways.
Ive nothing bad to say about the gameplay. Its great. It takes what dishonored did and does it better. The powers have multiple upgrades as opposed to the one upgrade you could get in the previous game. Melee combat is fluid and the guns have a nice kick to them, plus almost all enemies pose a threat. My only wish is that there were more, but seeing as this is a stealth game I can see why they didnt want to fill the maps with enemies.
Speaking of which, the stealth is also improved upon. Enemies detect you quicker and take longer to choke out. More nonlethal options are present as well. For example, instead of just ripping out the enemies jugular you can smash their skull in to knock them unconcious. Though not a lot has changed, I think they did change the right aspects in this game.
Finally, level design is excellent, but also less excellent. In the first game, there were certain levels that seemed like a chore to me. In this game, the only level I dislike is the first level as it is rather tedious, seeing as you dont ahve any of your powers yet. Thankfully, after that each level is enjoyable, there are no levels that feel out of place. The first 5 levels are by far the weakest, though still very good. After that, each level is beyond fantastic. The Dust District presents you eith a vast array of options, while Stilton's Maner goes all Doctor Who on your♥♥♥♥♥ then comes The Grand Palace, which is absolutely dripping with atmoshpere and is a marvel to modern game design. Finally comes the final level, which is a fantastic callback to the first game. Other then a couple items out of place and one case where I managed to Time Travel my way out of the map, the level design is some of the best Ive seen in a game.
To conclude, this game has flaws. And some of them are big, big flaws. As someone who preordered this game, do some research on these flaws and then deduce whether or not you think this is worth it. For me, though initially disapointing, after a couple updates I came to truly love Dishonored 2

Since I'm nearly done with the game myself and by the end of all this, I'll have around a bit over 70 parts, here's my honest take on it.  Well since I've been a fan of the series since the PS2 days, there's a lot I can say about this game that they really improved upon.  For one, the character roster.  The roster I have to say has improved since 3 and good to see some new faces as well as similar in the previous games. I'll also add that they taken notes from Chronicles in the tag aspect since it really does help and it doesn't harm you in anyway but instead help you all the more.  You'd still have to keep your eyes on your health bar but that's a given.  The pathfinding is also a big help since Samurai Warriors is more objective based than goal based like in Dynasty Warriors.  In its own respect, Samurai Warriors 4-II gives more of a challenge since you're on the clock on the field and you'll need a partner to help cover these goals so you can survive the battle.  As for the story aspect,  I do like how the characters interact with each other more in-story than just by game itself.  The character development is in a word: beautiful. At the most I can say, it gives you a more understanding feel to the characters than in previous games where the event was more important than the characters. Now I know and from what I read from other reviews, yes it's a hack and slash and to those with a very small view to say it's repetative, the work that was put into the stages are gorgeous and the music is just stellar. Even if you might be repeating some stages, it's the point of view that's mainly important.  How he/she perceive the view of the situation and all, how it affects them..that's what make this installment different.  The skill tree reminds me of the one in FFX but simplied, and all you would need is strategy tomes to access these skills. Most being useful on the field to either bolster your attack and defense, heal or net you more experience along with bettering your innate skills, I also need to add that when you hit 1000 KOs, you do get a bit of a super effect which says a lot more than being just the strongest in the land.  I think my only gripe is how come there wasn't a stand alone story for your created characters,  I feel they shouldn't be limited to just Survival and Free mode alone, I mean it could've been done like in Chronicles where your characters are given a choice on what they think and thereby going by relationship towards their peer or ruler depending on their way of life.  It's a longshot saying this, but I hope SW4 Empires comes to Steam and like with Dynasty Warriors Empires change up on how unification be done in a more simplified tone. As a whole, would I recommend getting this game for yourself?  I'd say if you can look past it being a hack and slash and being moderately challenging for a Warriors game, then yes go for it.  Try it for yourself and I think you'll find it that it's worth getting for your library.

I only played the game for about 34 mins, and I found it to be just like the other Warrior games but the PC controls are simply the worst I've ever had to deal with. An the game doesn't even understand if a controller is plugged in. It only reads the Left Stick and the LT, RT buttons.

What to say about the game? I love it, and it hate at the same time. I've been a cult follower of Tecmo Koei and W OMEGA FORCE and the Dynasty/Samurai Warriors franchises. Simply put, I love them. The pc ports have gotten better with every installment which is nice, and they do nicely here with the amount of graphics options you can change.
Problem is on better systems when you turn the options all the way up, you get this film grain and lens flare with some saturation problems during cutscenes which really show the edges of the ps3 textures on the ps4 body textures. When using a controller, the keyboard button maps still show up instead of the controllers layout. I use a plug and play Xbox 360 controller. But thats not my main complaint of the game.
The writing with the Dynasty Warriors games have gotten better with each installment, though nothing will ever be able to beat Dynasty Warriors 5 in terms of narrative quality. As for the Samurai Warriors franchise, I feel like the writing just keeps getting worse. Not to mention this game was supposed to be more about character stories, yet in each game faction story its only about 2-3 characters and everyone else is left out and given the minor character treatment. Battles that were big in the series were narrated through with no chance of playing them, and each faction only had 5 battles to fight.
Each faction story takes what it considers historically canon in one story and butchers it in the other, and most of the time it does it to try to illicite an emotional response from the player. There is no consistency across the game whatsoever and each faction starts at a different point in time which works and doesn't work at the same time. Some characters are introduced you can't even play once and they die, and the only way you can play them is through free mode which is crap. So don't give me this bullcrap about Warriors 4-ii being about character stories, its still very much about the factions. Maybe they should look back and view Dynasty Warriors 5 as an examble for character stories, because every character on that game had a story and it was well written. This felt like a drama more than a game and every chance they had, they wanted to try to make the player feel like crap... Which really isn't the issue, its the story itself. It could of been written a lot better.
I know I should be emailing Koie or Omega Force about this, because they don't view Steam reviews, just thought I would make this aware to yall the buyers that the story is not the best of the series, or even close. I feel like Samurai Warriors 4 and its ii counterpart are the worst writing of the warriors series, with Chronicles being the best.
That being said, I don't recommend this game, but nor do I discourage people from buying it.

If the quality of games was solely based on graphics, I'd say this game was amazing. To be fair, I only bought this game because I love the original movie, and I wanted to play the "Crew Expendable" DLC. You'll notice that I didn't give a score for story. That's because I couldn't be bothered to waste any more of my time on this game. Which is too bad, as I was honestly looking forward to playing it for a long time. I was very impressed with the visuals. Not only were they beautiful, but very authentic. It sells the experience of being aboard the Nostromo. But when I got to the actual gameplay, I realized how bad the controls & game mechanics really are:
After dying several times in the vents trying to reach the other side, I gained access to the main airlock area. I'm meant to lure the Alien into the airlock, and I assume jettison it out of the ship. So I get it in there, but the game doesn't tell me what to do afterward. So I keep trying different angles, by throwing flares (which the game makes surprising annoying) and running, but the Alien only wants to follow me, and kill me. It's important to point out how difficult the controls are. They're not BAD, just DIFFICULT. This seems intentional in order to add tension and increase the "terror-factor" or whatever. However, this didn't "scare" me in any way, it just made playing the game more annoying and frustrating. So I gave up... I miss the days where the main focus of gaming was fun and entertainment, rather than frustration and wasting time.
I realize I could sit here and play for hours trying to figure it out, and eventually either come to a solution or get lucky, but that's not why I sat down to play this game. I sat down to have fun. And the bottom line is: this game is NOT fun.

This Review Will Probably Contain A Spoiler.
This game is good; but saying that isn't much of a review so I guess I'll have to flesh it out. The combat is well-fleshed out, but some would argue it feels like your character has arthritis compared to Dark Souls, the levels and boss fights are mostly well designed, and the story is there, but it isn't quite as refined or interesting as Dark Souls.
The Game is functional, coherent, well-optimized for PC, engaging, and fun. That being said I didn't enjoy it NEARLY as much as I did Dark Souls. I can't quite put my finger on it but a number of other players as well as myself have reached a consensus that  it just isn't quite as gripping as Dark Souls. It just doesn't have the same feel.
I don't want this to come off as an "It's different therefore I HATE IT" because the game is not bad by any stretch of the imagination.  The souls franchise has built their reputation as being difficult and unforgiving but fair, a fact that becomes readily appearant in EVERY advert for Dark Souls II. But for all their waving of the difficulty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I found the game much simpler and much easier. The game just seems to throw more multi-aggro at you hoping you can't handle it, and once you can, the enemies really aren't that varied mechanically speaking.
One major complaint is that the story and lore are still inaccessible, sure, but it feels like they wanted us to generate the lore for them, rather than the way did it in Dark Souls; I.E. presenting the player with numerous bits of evidence and trying to cleverly weave them together into a coherent theory that holds water.
In Dark Souls II it feels more like the devs showed up and said: "You know what would be cool? If you go through the fog gate and Dragonslayer Ornstein was there!" And the one next to him responded "How would we explain that? I mean it wouldn't make very much sense in the lore." And the first "DOESN'T MATTER, we'll just do it and let the community think of an explanation for us!"
Of course for the above example there are many fan theories, a simple youtube search yields dozens, but most of that is pure conjecture, as opposed to the Dark Souls 1 kind of conjecture: Conjecture drawing its basis from context and fact.
Of course some people will say it's like comparing apples to oranges, or even go so far as to say I shouldn't compare the two at all. But when fruit suddenly decided to be called Apple and Apple II I will compare them.
Overall I don't think the game was bad; in summary I think Dark Souls was a masterpiece. And Dark Souls II Is a decent game.
Recommendation: Try to catch it on sale, and maybe wait to see if the DLC is any good before buying it.

I finished the game for the first time on version 0.12 so some changes may have occured.
This is one of the best games I've supported in 2015. It took me 1 month to complete, as a very casual player, for a total of 64 hours. And I feel like I didn't get enough, yet! Those hours flew away like crazy :D
Exploring is a little bit boring due to the barren/repetitive world and doesn't make much sense after a while if not for the resources. But that's fine, it's not an exploration-centric game.
Fighting is fun when using a tactical approach. Trying to have an action approach is near impossible, the aliens attack so quick you'll be lucky if you get even one shot at them! Turrets (like tower defense), kiting and things like that are the best choices and they're very fun.
Researching is also fun, but it would definitely benefit from a proper tech tree and some more descriptive text, with interlocking requirements and somesuch.
Refitting/deporting industrial sectors is also fun, there's incredible room for improvement, always!
What I'm working on sometimes is optimising the infrastructure, like using less space, less buildings, less buffers, and wasting less resources and time. I enjoy this a lot, it gives room to creativity.
The time factor is the real measure of success, it is possible to do everything if you have infinite time. But doing something quickly (not placing buildings faster, but ramping up production and efficiency) is a very different thing. Sometimes it requires a lot of work to get timing right without wasting speed modules on the wrong/useless places.
A better story mode would be great, the tutorial missions are somewhat scarce on the duration side, they're quickly dispatched. Luckily, sandbox mode has a lot of settings to keep interest up. But some more things would be nice.

TL:DR Great game if you like resource management combined with base building and logistic systems; think prison architect for building but then with a character, and spacechem / infinifactory with regards to management.
Gameplay: Gather resources (manually at first, automated later) and build stuff with it! The main goal is basically survival, where you need to defend everything you build from aliens who become more aggressive overtime (nothing too zerg in the beginning, you've got time and it’s nicely balanced). Build mines to help you gather resources, build conveyor belts to transport your resources to things that use those resources and make a nice system out of it all... or don't and have chaos :D
GFX: So it’s a top down view with some good looking GFX for the kind of game it is. I THINK most of the gfx are pre-rendered sprites which have a 360 degree render pass done on them, but that definitely can’t be hold against the game.
Story: You get dropped on an alien planet where your main goal is to survive, build a base, research technology to keep you alive and build a base strong enough to sustain launching a rocket into outer space.
Pros:
- Good GFX
- Great Gameplay
- Awesome Co-op experience
Cons:
- Interfaces are sometime unclear / unclean.
- No clear tutorial yet explaining late-game stuff, it takes some time to figure out, but don't let it hold you back.
- The game is not very suited to be played more then 3-4 times, for me anyway. When you finished it once, you'll have to set your own goals, which might work for some people.

I've come to regard Ninja Theory productions as one of those rare treats that sometimes pop up and you can do nothing but obsess over it for a while. Every single time, the stories that they manage to tell suck me into a captivated bliss and I don't want to look away until it's over. But of course, I'm always sad to see them end and wish I could experience for the first time again.
ENSLAVED: Odyssey to the West is no exception.
The gameplay (action based combat and platforming) is a lot of fun with interesting mechanics, but what really drew me in was the story. The voice acting is superb, the characters feel so real to the point that you can almost taste their emotions, and the post-apacolyptic setting in which Earth has been left to the (visually beautiful) mercy of nature is a pleasure to walk through. For fear of revealing any spoilers, I won't divulge any details of the story itself, except to say that it's immensely satisfying. The ending is one of my favorites of any game I've ever played. It left me in awe... One of those endings that made me wonder what I would have done if I were in the protagonist's place.
The PC port may come with it's share of technical issues, but those are easily fixed and adjusted through a quick google search. I wouldn't let that stop you from playing this awesome game. It's one that will stick with you long after you're done playing.

Bought it because I've played Samurai Warriors 2 and loved every single character that was in the game. Since I don't own a Wii/PS3/PS4 this is my only option to play the latest installment. It attracted me since we can now change the weapon into something you really want, much easier than it was in Samurai Warriors 2. Which means I can optimised the characters I enjoy using to the fullest.
Storyline: 4/10
Every installment of Samurai Warriors, new characters are added and developed on the storyline. Being a 10th anniversary game, I hope that they added story mode for all characters. Didn't really bother me even if the older characters had PS2 graphics for their scenarios as I viewed it as a collector's item being the 1st Samurai Warriors game on PC. But they didn't. Story wise, I've predicted it weak as the characters featured didn't really play a major role in Sengoku era. I could accept that.
Characters: 5/10
What I couldn't accept is how the new character personality turn out. Head of the Il clan, apologising to every living creature on the planet in every sentence of her dialogue? Descendant of the Uesugi speaking one liners while Kanetsugu does all the talking? An Afro hair girl in netty outfit fighting with a piece of cloth? A be-spectacled guy fighting using a shield emitting laser beams? If you could accept all that, then buy the game or like me avoid using them. KT is clearly running out of personalities to create for Samurais especially with close to 60 in the roster.
Thankfully KT have been kind to still place the older characters in, which are my favourite since Samurai Warriors 2 with superior movesets making the gameplay fun.
Difficulty: 7/10
The game has 4 difficulty mode, Easy to Nightmare. Hard is like normal in previous games, while nightmare mode is a huge jump in difficulty. Unless you are using Hisahide with the only infinite combo in the game, I don't see how you can attempt nightmare mode at the start.
Combat: 11/10 (means it exceeded my expectation)
The combat is a major improvement, loads of new moves, attacks chain better, hyper attacks to reduce monotony of killing 1000 soldiers. Instead of spamming same attacks there is now a counter/parry system to retaliate by pressing button shown on screen. Some of the new features are overpowered- a single move killing 5 generals at the cost of spirit gauge and 1 musou gauge.
Controls: 8/10
The horse control went down the drain, as calling it usually ends up with a horse running in zigzag refusing to pick you up unless you stand still or beside corners of a wall.
BGM: 7/10
Fits the theme. However not my liking. The best BGM from Warriors game is in One Piece Pirate Warriors.
Online play: 6/10
The co-op is not stable at the moment this review is written, I could play with someone far from Asia but it crashes when I play with someone in Asia. Weird indeed.
Most of the game hours I have was either from falling asleep due to hectic schedule or testing game mechanics for writting guides. I don't aim to 100% everything for the reason of new abyssmal characters. I do know it will take close to a 100hrs to collect most of the weapons and max every character to optimum. I am 3/4 thru, left the characters I loath using and perhaps time to put an end to the game.
Overall it is a fun experience, a definite improvement in combat/ loot customization. Even though some say it looks like PS2 graphic, I still love it because it looks like a PS3 port to me. The DLC isn't worth collecting, not my type of weapons, the mounts aren't the strongest and the stages are just reskinned, inverted images of the storyline stages with no cutscene or dialogue. They are finally working harder to make their games gain more reception by targetting a different group of gamers.
I would give it 7/10 overall. I don't rate a game by graphics since it is acceptable and low in my priority. Quite sick of nice looking games with boring gameplay like alot of recent HD console games Squeenix is making.

This is the second installment in the Deponia trilogy. You will need to have played the first game for this one to make any sense, as it picks up exactly where the first one leaves off.
The gameplay is traditional point-and-click adventuring, which means an abundance of item-based puzzles along with the occasional skippable mini-game. It also includes standard control shortcuts such as double-clicking on arrows for instant movement, left-clicking to speed through dialogue, and ESC to skip scenes entirely.
Your character is Rufus, a sorry excuse for a human being if ever there was one, and your goal is to help him "save the world" by dealing with his brain-malfunctioning cliche of a companion, driving his friends to drink, and being at the top of PETA's most-hated list.
The game is significantly longer than the first, and involves multiple new locations to explore (i.e. wreak mayhem upon).
Some of the things I liked:
- There is a good amount of humor in the dialogue, lyrics, and situations that occur.
- Many of the puzzles were intuitive enough to not need a walkthrough, but clever enough to not be boring.
- The side characters (Doc, Bozo, etc.) were cool, and imho more interesting than the main characters.
- The overall plot was solid, and included some twists and depth that I definitely wasn't expecting.
- Platypuses.
Some of the things that bothered me:
- The pacing felt off. The start of the game is bogged down with cut-scenes, heavy dialogue, and one-room puzzles, and then the game dumps you out into a larger non-linear sandbox to explore. The juxtaposition is jarring and slightly uncomfortable. I think the first game was more successful in making the exploration feel natural.
- In order to get all of the achievements, you need to play two particularly obnoxious mini-games without skipping them. One is a quick-reflexes fighting game, and the other is a corner-the-enemy strategy game. Both are tedious, and are completely outside of the normal skill set for this genre. Neither are in any way "fun."
- Rufus is pretty unlikeable, and tbh, Goal isn't much better. They tried to give her a larger role with actual character development, but it's marred by the fact that her dialogue and actions are internally inconsistent. Even with the craziness of the main plot device, it still doesn't make sense that she would randomly forget to take key pieces of information into account, or that she would flip-flop between loving you and hating you at the drop of a hat, or that she continues to be a walking stereotype who is affected by the plot rather than driving it. There were moments of awesomeness with her character, but she really needed an overall editor.
- Was the animal cruelty really necessary?
Overall, it is a solid adventure game with a dark sense of humor and a full cast of non-heroes. If you liked the first game in the series and said "I want more of that, only with less moral fiber and more Goal", then you will absolutely love this installment. I give it 7.5 platypuses out of 10.

Factorio: One of my favourite management games ever!
So, first off, please disregard the Playtime here on Steam, I've actually put about 250 - 300 hours in game since purchasing it from their website about 2 years ago :)
So Factorio, its a management game where you're set with the task of conquering an alien planet to have your colony come down to inhabit. Its a dangerous world, and you are all alone, but you have the tools to begin automation and production on a massive factory, to build defenses such as Gun Towers and Lasers, Automation of goods via Transport Belts and Assembly Machines, and Technology, ranging from Electronic Circuits up to Trains. Research new tech to progress further and make the automation faster and more efficient. Hook up rail systems to haul more goods in, set up Robot Logistics, and so much more!
- In depth tech tree that can be branched in endless varities
- Detailed management of resource production / consumption (keep production above ;) )
- Challenging Alien enemies, to keep you on your toes and defend your factory from devastation
- Amazing soundtrack. Really captures the atmosphere.
- Completely randomized terrain, for a unique experience everytime you play!
- Did I mention you can kill alien scum with a Bazooka or a Tank? XD
- Visually, the game could be better, but its not a big issue (I'm a little biased on that)
- Auto-Save pops a window up on screen when completed (hopefully will get fixed soon)
- World Variable Conditions sometimes don't work (namely Land Segmentation)
- Could use a bit more variety in weapons / defenses.
Overall, I love Factorio, and I highly recommend at the very least, to give it a go! Its amazing, and you'll always have a fun time working out why your production is grinding to a halt Hahaha.

Since the vast majority of negative reviews here are misleading and either nitpick or make vague and uninformative complaints about failed launches, I figured I would give you guys a more comprehensive first impression of Homeworld Remastered. Before I start though, know that I haven't played the original Homeworlds and am new to the series. Also, the in-depth review will come a bit later, given that I've only played for a couple of hours.
Here's a quick summary of the game's pro's and con's.
Pros:
+ Satisfyingly simple yet beautiful visuals
+ Ease of use [I was reticent about how easy it would be to control fleets given the scope of the game and my inability to micro efficiently but the controls are spot on].
+ Audio---I can't stress this enough. Gearbox got the original developpers to contribute their original audio files—UNCOMPRESSED—for the remastered game. If you have headphones that are half decent or, ideally, have dolby 7.1, you're in for a treat. Also, the zoom level will give you access to different levels of audio. Zoomed out? You have the audio of high ranked officers and frigates. Zoomed in? You hear the dogfighting grunt screaming for his life as he's blown up.
+ Story: The narrative does a good job at not holding your hand too much. It drew me right in during the first few missions, and combined with the audio and headache free controls, nothing is really in the way of you experiencing the story without any hassles.
+Depth. Again, I can't stress this enough. Try to imagine a complicated hierarchy of ships and tiers, combine that with coordinated strikeforces which utilize altitude and formations, combined with a great two tier command system of macro and micro commands, and you get a fantastically intricate rts which flirts with becoming overwhelming but never quite gets there.
Cons:
- While the graphics are satisfying, there are certain elements that seem a little oldschool. While I know this was done to maintain the nostalgiac visuals of the original, you get some weird combination of amazing textures on the mothership with odd and clunky parts.
- The learning curve. If you're not into strategy games or are looking for something to easily jump into, this might not be the game for you. It's not a simple point and click. Like I mentioned, you have a 3d plane of combat, so you have to worry about attacks from above and below, as well as front, back and side. Also, if you weren't really into space themed games, distinguishing a corvette from a frigate from a carrier will take some memorization.
Honestly, forget these chumps who are using steam reviews as a support or troubleshooting forum. They don't post specs, probally haven't even attempted to take the most basic steps in fixing these problems, and are just firing off "Not Recommended" left and right. While I acknowledge that my experience, however seamless, won't be the same for others, I think that a certain level of patience is in order given that it's launch day. I've seen AAA titles have much more horrific launches than this gem of a game.

As a long standing supporter of Koei -even if some of their titles have made me question this time and time again-  who grew up with the original SW and DW titles for PS2, this game was a positive surprise. As DW has, in my opinion, degenerated as series has moved on, this title seems to retain the charm, challenge, and pure joy the PS2 SW instalments had.  I like playing this game, and it runs smoothly, albeit some optimisation issues remain.
However, this recommendation comes with a warning:
Is it worth the 50 euro price tag? ...no. Not for a person who is not entirely certain they like simplistic hack and slash with more or less ridiculous plot and character designs. If this is your niche, then yes, this title is a lot more deserving of your cash than other current Koei titles. Is it still worth 50 euros though? ...no. But this game is best there is for PC for the moment, unless they plan on releasing Empire titles anytime soon.
The focus is on character stories this time, reminiscent of older titles. While the stories and the in-battle events seem to lack some of the complexity and richness of the old games, it is still head and shoulders above the direction many Koei games have taken in immediate past. All scenarios are character arcs for certain characters. While I would have welcomed the earlier style of "campaign for each playable character", and holding out hope they will return to it soon, this manages to scratch that particular itch nevertheless.
The custom character creator is there, but there is not much for them to do. Options are nice and varied, albeit recycled with some models occurring as early as DW Empires, but without set custom officer campaign to use your character in this is mostly serving those of us who enjoy playing stories inside their head.
The survival mode is back, and it is surprisingly amusing. Not quite as imaginative as some of the same series, but good addition regardless for those of us who, for whatever brain damage related reason, enjoy the technical aspects of gameplay. The mode also serves as a way of acquiring strategy tomes and gold for the completionists unsatisfied with anything less than level capped characters.
Perhaps the most pleasant surprise was that of the difficulty. After insultingly easy DW 8 Xtreme Legends, I had given up hope on actually challenging Koei game being published again. However, the varied combos and level system ensure that things do not become too easy, at least not too soon. Now you have to time and plan again, something that ought to be in core of all hack and slash games. Character switch actually contributes in clearing all objectives, and the AI is smart enough to do what you ask of it, such as stop fleeing enemy officer.  As you ramp up the difficulty, this becomes a very welcome addition to player skill.
As decent as this Samurai Warriors is, there are still issues with it. First one is the already mentioned price. The game is not long enough, nor are there enough character stories, or gameplay to excuse the price. DLC are ridiculously priced across the board, albeit largely cosmetic, and hence perhaps more excusable.  What is inexcusable however is the fact what little gameplay "enhancing" DLC there is, it graduated from esteemed pay-to-win academy. Which serves no point in single-player orientated game.
Controls map nicely to Xbox controller. Problem is, that no one told the game this. I suppose one way of getting around more boring titbits of console port to PC is to replace actual command prompts with self made icons such as "press escape key" -K on keyboard in case some of you are wondering- but this is not ideal to say the least and lazy to say the truth. Partial control support also means some stuff you can only navigate with keyboard. Luckily this is limited to menus.
Repetition is mother of hack and slash gaming, but I cannot help but to feel there is tad too much of it going on here. While I initially enjoyed playing certain scenarios multiple times, just as different character on different side of events, combined together with the few story characters there is started to taste tad too much like lazy game development in the end. Future DLC may remedy this, I hope they do at least, since I feel SW 4-II has good potential, but knowing Koei I will not hold my breath.
