English and Portuguese short review.
English:
So, I had to interrupt my gameplay to come here to say it: awesome job, Koei! In my opinion, the best Warriors game ever released, in terms of gameplay mechanics! Don't be fooled by people saying it's a bad port. Graphics are really beautiful.
This game offers a huge variety of combos, seriously, much more (so much more) than in other Koei games (such as the recent Dynasty Warriors 8). You do feel like leveling up, seeing your combos getting extended, changed, more powerful! Skills and leveling system are great and easy to get acknowledged, as well as managed. Almost every detail (from attack type to mount choosing) is useful in the game. The planning is simple, but utterly effective and clear for you to see it happening.
Enemy AI is Koei pattern, but, this time, soldiers and officers attack you much more (slightly more at higher difficulties), just don't forget it's a Musou game, meaning you are the incredible warrior in the battlefield doing fantastic stuffs, a differential. There's an aggrandizement of the glory of such warriors, hence the large advantage. Look up ''Musou'' possible meanings in a  dictionary and you'll pretty much understand what this game genre is all about. Character creation is ok, few options in some categories, but more options in other categories. Music is fantastic and doesn't get badly repetitive like in other Koei titles, it's Japanese stuff, not random heavy guitars in the background.
Anyways, Story Mode is cool too (the wonderful voice acting is a big + in it), even more paired with the Character Switch system in real time, which makes the game pretty dynamic. I've always been strict towards Koei formula and such, but I must admit this game is really, really good! Played Dynasty Warriors 8? This game will lead you to another whole level!
Also, no problems with bugs, FPS and such. However, it could have more features, indeed, such as: more screen resolution options, more game modes, a better online interface, an easier way to configure buttons.
All in all, the game is worth. The game has really agradable graphics and an extremely intuitive battle mechanics.
Português:
Então, tive que interromper meu jogo pra vir aqui e dizer isto: ótimo trabalho, Koei! Na minha opinião, é o melhor jogo já lançado da franquia Warriors, em termos de gameplay, não se engane pelo fato de algumas pessoas acusarem um port ruim do jogo. Os gráficos são realmente lindos.
O jogo oferece uma variedade imensa de combos, sério, muito mais do que em outros jogos da Koei (como o recente Dynasty Warriors 8). Você consegue sentir a evolução do personagem, vendo seus combos se estendendo, mudando, tornando-se mais poderosos! O sistema de evolução e aquisição de habilidades é interessante e bem fácil de se acostumar e administrar. Sobre a batalha, quase todo detalhe (desde o tipo de ataque e a escolha da montaria) é útil no jogo. O planejamento é simples, mas muito efetivo e visível, dá pra ver as coisas acontecendo.
A inteligência artificial dos inimigos está no padrão Koei, mas, desta vez, os soldados e generais te atacam com mais frequência (um pouco mais nas dificuldades mais altas), só não se esqueça de que se trata de um jogo do gênero Musou, o que significa que você é um guerreiro capaz de feitos incríveis, um diferencial, no campo de batalha. Há um enaltecimento da glória desses guerreiros, por isso a ampla vantagem. Procure num dicionário os possíveis significados para ''Musou'' e então entenderá do que esse gênero se trata.
A criação de personagens é boa, algumas categorias têm mais opções do que outras. A música é boa e não se torna repetitiva como em outros jogos da Koei, nada de guitarras aleatórias no fundo, é tudo levado para a música oriental mesmo.
Enfim, o modo história é divertido (a ótima atuação dos dubladores é um ponto fortíssimo), ainda mais combinado com o sistema de mudança de personagem em tempo real, o que faz com que o jogo seja mais dinâmico. Sempre fui muito rígido com a Koei, principalmente sobre sua fórmula, mas tenho que admitir que este jogo é muito, muito bom! Jogou Dynasty Warriors 8? Este jogo irá lhe proporcionar uma experiência de outro nível!
Também, até agora, não tive problemas com bugs, fps e tudo mais.
Entretanto, o jogo poderia ter mais coisas, tais como: mais opções de resolução, mais modos de jogo, uma interface melhor para o modo online, uma maneira mais fácil de configurar os botões.
Enfim, o jogo vale a pena: ótimos gráficos e uma mecânica de luta extremamente intuitiva.

Commentary:
When Steam announced that they were releasing Samurai Warriors 4 on the PC, I was happy. Originally, Samurai Warriors 4 was only available on the PS3 & PS4, but I didn't have one. So, of course when they stated that it was a newly enhanced SW4, that had new features and even focused more on character storylines, I had to get it. I was unsure on spending $49.99 USD for this game, until I played my first mission. I almost instantly fell in love with the new title screen and all of the pretty anime looks to the game.
As I continued on into the game, I continued to run into problems. For example, when I called my horse instead of coming near me for my character to get on, it would run all over the place around the place and never stop moving. I also experienced the problem of the game crashing every single time I would complete a story mode campaign. I brushed these issues off because Steam just released it so there were bound to be bugs. I was just bothered by the fact that I had just spent $49.99 USD on a game that has problems with it.
Another problem I ran into was dealing with the controls. I personally used an Xbox360 controller to play the game. The game only had partial controller support, so I could only assign one action to one button on the controller. I had to try to remember that for most actions, I couldn't use my controller to complete specific actions and had to switch between using the controller and keyboard to complete actions (in the shop for example).
I rushed quickly to complete the game and found myself not even 3 days later, with all 13 (yes 13) story campaigns completed. I decided that I was going to go a step further and max out my characters to level 50 and obtain their 5th level weapons. I thought it was interesting that SW4-II still only has 5th level weapons, while Dynasty Warriors 8 has 6th level weapons, and on Steam, Dynasty Warriors 8: Xtreme Legends Complete Edition has 7th level weapons. While SW4-II, has overpriced DLC, their DLC weapons have even higher stats than the 5th level weapons you spend a lot of time trying to obtain.
Other than all of the problems listed above, I did enjoy the game. If you're a hardcore gamer, you can complete the game (story mode, character levels, and 5th level weapons) in less than a week. I would suggest that if you're desperate to get decent weapons, to wait until they have the SW4-II's DLC on sale and purchase the Weapon Set.

So I've decided to revamp this review after spending more time with the game. I'll go over everything section by section.
The story mode is fairly lackluster. In fact I've spent more time in the Castle mode than I have doing the story, and the only reason I even went through the three stories I did was so I could unlock more maps to do co-op on as well as farming for EXP and trying to get rare weapons. This game in particular focuses on one character along with a secondary and/or tertiary character depending on which campaign you pick. Usually the stories weigh more on the side of "totally bat♥♥♥♥♥♥ridiculous" with only the slightest air of historical accuracy, such as Yukimura Sanada's brother driving him to Mt. Fuji and retirement from battle, only for Yukimura to pointlessly decide to rebel yet again, which costs him his life.
Beating one story usually unlocks another. You also have to go through the stories if you wish to unlock most of the characters, though for a Koei Warriors title, this game seems to have a rather small roster, relatively speaking. I think even SW2 had more playable characters than this game did. Simply put, there's not much to say about the story. One thing that truly annoyed me is how often the game takes playable characters away from you when you're about to go to the next level of the story. You just spent all those tomes and coins powering up Ranmaru? RIP because suddenly he's now your enemy and you can't use him for the rest of the story! Stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥like that happens very often. Only after you clear a story once are you able to use anyone you want for the whole thing, but by then, why bother?
Score: 2/5
The gameplay is pretty good. Obviously it's the main reason you're here if you're interested in this game. New to this game is the "Hyper" thing, which manifests itself in the form of Hyper Attacks, and Hyper Style in terms of characters (such as Attack-oriented, Special-Oriented, Speed-Oriented, etc.) This is both useful and annoying, because the Hyper attacks make mopping up mooks much quicker, but some characters have their whole moveset revolve around it, and can become entirely useless when entering a Red Zone (kill the flag bearer to remove this effect) or when fighting Officers in general. Some stuff is also blatantly OP, such as the Spirit Musou, which just totally annihilates anything on the screen unless they're super-mega-powered up.
The combat doesn't have much depth to it. Officers 360-backflip McTwist their way out of your air juggles with alarming regularity, which makes combos pointless most of the time. You can still cheese the A.I. by forcing them to do certain moves or routines and then countering/parrying with your own move/maneuver.
Powering your characters up with the Skill Board (slightly reminiscent of FFX's Sphere Grid and in a looser sense, DW6's skill tree) is fun, but will ostensibly require much grinding to acquire the Tomes needed to "buy" upgrade slots. These Tomes can be acquired by defeating enemies in battle, completing missions, or by going through the Normal/Challenge Towers.
You can create characters again, which is great, but not without its faults. The customization isn't mind-blowing, but it's adequate for this type of game. CAW's have five unique CAW-only movesets and they can also be given any Main Officer's moveset that you have unlocked. The unfortunate thing is that these CAW's can only be played as in Free Mode or the Castle modes. There's no CAW-centered Story mode like the Ambition mode found in other Koei titles. This is a huge shame and partially eliminates incentive to even play as them, but this reviewer has, as mentioned, spent an egregious amount of time in the Castle mode, which whilst not being as fleshed out as previous versions, is still a good deal of fun.
Score: 5/5
The soundtrack is nice, but not earth-shattering. There's a few nice standouts, but overall you can easily forget many of these tracks, but that's par for the course nowadays. The battle sounds are decent and the weapon sounds are very satisfying. All spoken dialogue is in Japanese -- there are no dubs. Of course the written text is in English or perhaps whatever language you may have selected if there are other options. This adds a layer of authenticity if you're into that sort of thing, but I did enjoy the English VA from SW2 and it is missed here. I can deal with it either way.
Score 4/5
This game unfortunately, as of this review, does have some issues. Performance is usually rock-solid at 60fps with everything maxed on my Radeon HD 7870 (aka R9-270X), but there are occasional random framedrops where the framerate will drop down to low 20's for a second or two for no discernible reason. The game also is prone to random crashes. I found the crash rate dropped noticeably when I ran the game as admin and turned off my MSI Afterburner. The game still has a nasty habit of crashing when trying to play co-op. My friend and I have only managed to complete one level in co-op out of perhaps 20~ tries. It's that bad. Apparently KT are now aware of this and hopefully a patch will be rolled out to rectify this. Outside of the crashes and random framedips, the performance is pretty good.
Score 4/5
On to the final part of the review. Is this game worth the current price of admission of $49.99? No it's not. I think you can enjoy the game for sure, I know I have, but this is overpriced just like DW8 XL is on PC. The DLC is overpriced as well. You get some cool stuff, but the prices are absurd. This is a nasty trend in recent times, where EA thinks it's okay to charge $50 for their season pass for Battlefront. This should be priced at $29.99 and no higher, for what you get. If the Story Mode were more focused and didn't feel like hastily-thrown together Gaiden stories, and if CAW's had their own Campaign mode, this price could've been justified. But as it stands, unless you're the type who just HAS to max every character out stat and skill-wise, you won't be playing the game for ages. I easily spent 70+ hours on Warriors Orochi 3 three years ago. I doubt I'll do the same with this, despite enjoying the game a good deal so far.
Score: 3/5
All that said, I do still recommend this game IF you're a big enough Koei Warriors fan and you're totally cognizant of what this package includes. No idea why they didn't bring the "base" game of SW4 to PC but oh well.

Instead of the House of Representatives having the job of removing the President from power, in the Sam & Max universe freelance police have the authority to take down the president. The sheer absurdity of the situations, the spot-on jokes, and even the excellent puzzle design cemented ‘Abe Lincoln Must Die!’ as one of the greatest Sam & Max moments in history.
TellTale used to offer ‘Abe Lincoln Must Die!’ freely on its website for years, but the episode is famous on its own merit too, as it is the closest we got to the craziness of the original comics ever since the 1993 game adaptation.
Even the premise is hilariously absurd: thanks to the shenanigans of our protagonists, the United States calls for an emergency election, and the more psychotic half our duo, Max has to win it before the living statue of Abraham Lincoln takes the Oval Office.
In all other episodes, this premise alone could fill the entire content, but here it is only the first half of the ride. All along the way, we get a hefty dose of the classic Sam & Max humour, both in the banter and even in the tasks themselves.
This is also the only episode in the season that follows a traditional, linear storytelling and puzzle mechanic, except most solutions require that special kind of insane that elevates even beyond the classic adventure game logic. Their only downside is that they also need a lot of travelling, which adds more dead time to the otherwise long episode than comfortable.

The latest entry in the Samurai Warriors 4 series to come out to the West and to Steam. To my knowledge, there are four total games in this series set which are Samurai Warriors 4, Samurai Warriors Chronicles 3, Samurai Warriors 4-II, and Samurai Warriors 4: Empires. I have not played Samurai Warriors 4 or Samurai Warriors 4: Empires, but I have played Samurai Warriors Chronicles 3 so I will be making some parallels in this review.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay set out in previous Warriors games, including Dynasty Warriors, Samurai Warriors, and Warriors Orochi has vastly evolved with the coming of Samurai Warriors 4 in the form of the Hyper Attack. Hyper Attacks replace the vanilla Charge Attacks (Triangle Button for PS and Y Button for XB), which propels the character forward, performing a stylish strike that is effective for clearing waves of enemies. It quickens the pace of the game by allowing the player to clear enemies faster and adds another moveset for every character, making character variety more vast. It is ineffective against officers however, so combat against officers is standard fare.
Another gameplay addition specifically to the Samurai Warriors series is Mighty Strikes, which are more or less execution attacks that can be performed on officers when they are stunned through a button prompt. In addition to this there are Musou Counters, which counter an officer's Musou Attack by performing your own, and Perfect Blocks which are activated by pressing the correct button prompt when an enemy officer performs a Hyper Attack towards you, which stuns them and allows you to follow up with a Mighty Strike or normal attack.
The item system was also removed from this game and replaced with a skill system. Throughout the game, you will find Strategy Tomes which allows you to unlock skills for certain characters, which allows them to do certain things (increase attack, extra gold drop, extra experience drop, etc.) and increase their attributes. Every character has access to every skill and each one has a unique Epiphany skill, which once unlocked can be equipped by all characters.
New to Samurai Warriors 4, you can pick two characters to go into battle and switch between them seamlessly. The secondary character you currently are not playing as will act as another officer on the field and carry out any tasks you command them to do.
The Weapon System in this game is refreshing in the fact that you can find many weapons and fuse them together to make stronger weapons, but the main draw back to it is that you cannot choose which attributes you want to fuse in a certain weapon. In Samurai Warriors Chronicles 3, though you never find any new weapons, you did find weapon materials to upgrade your preset weapons. There was also a Blacksmith that allowed you to remove attributes that you did not want and replace them with attributes that you did want, allowing you to make your "perfect weapon" more easily. In this game, there is more RNG involved in order to create your perfect weapon.
Also to note, there are only TWO weapons available to each character: their default weapon and their rare weapon. In past Warriors games, characters normally had four weapons. This new design streamlines the experience, but I preferred to be able to build up to my third weapon and eventually unlock the fourth weapon like in the old days. Still, this is a small nitpick that should not affect the gaming experience in any way.
Character Creation returns, which was always one of my favorite parts of any Warriors game. The options for creating characters has increased quite a bit, but nothing on the level of Skyrim.
Survival Mode is a new addition to this game and comes in two types: Endless Castle and Challenges. There are four challenges, which are Trials (kill as many enemies as you can), Gold (get as much money as you can), Agility (get to the end as fast as you can), and Death (similar to Trials, but harder). The Endless Castle is what really shines here. It is the true Survival Mode, where you continue to ascend a castle with various challenges in between. For the most part, this is where the difficulty is in the game. I have found that most of the game is pretty easy with a maxed out character on Nightmare difficulty (the highest difficulty), but even a maxed out character will have trouble at the later stages of the Endless Castle. While ascending the castle, you will find various loot which carries over to your overall inventory assuming you escape the castle alive (you can leave at any floor that you want).
STORY
The story mode in this game is centered around 13 specific characters. Overall, I felt that this approach was similar to how the games used to be prior to Dynasty Warriors 4, where you pick a character and play through a story centered around them. Some stories shine and some stories fall short, so there was not much I can say about the story mode, other than they are are fairly Anime in nature. What I do wish was that they included more cutscenes instead of Event scenes.
This game DOES have the best and most fulfilling ending of any Warriors game in my opinion.
PC OPTIONS
While the game is solid, the PC options available in it are...VERY BAD. The graphical options in this game are very scarce and allows for the bare minimum of customizing your experience. There was not even an option for V-SYNC, so I was playing with screen tear for the first 5 hours of the game. In order to push out all of the graphical power of the game (and vsync which did fix my screen tearing), I had to go into my Nvidia control panel to customize everything. I feel this was a poor oversight by Koei Tecmo and if they are going to be porting games to PC, they should do it right and put it on the same level as their console releases.
DLC
HORRIBLE PRICING. Ever since Koei and Tecmo merged their DLC prices have skyrocketed, placing DLC at nearly the price of whole games. It's a good thing expensive DLC are costumes that have no effect on gameplay, but for people who do enjoy costumes this is a buzz kill.
VERDICT
Despite it's shortcomings, Samurai Warriors 4-II is a solid Warriors release for Steam. After I was able to address the initial PC options by tweaking it with the Nvidia Control Panel, the game ran fine and was very pleasing to the eyes. They are not incredible graphics on the level of say, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain, but they are more or less what you would expect from a next-gen title. If you love the Warriors games and rather play it on PC, then you should definitely consider getting this one.

A solid Warriors game and a decent port but Koei got a bit too clever with this one.
Hyper attack spamming is as mindless as it is satisfying, and it's way mindless even by musou standards.
Officers flip out of every combo. Most uppercut-style moves that lead into an air como are rendered completely useless by this change to officer AI. Not to mention combos are now more or less useless.
It's not a huge problem but officers will occasionally slow-time and try to do an attack on you that you must respond with a QTE, but the game uses completely incomprehensible generic icons for the buttons even when you are using a 360 controller so there is no where to ever do these QTEs except by memorization or luck. But there is almost no penalty for missing them as the officer will seldom even hit with the attack and it does not deal any more damage than a normal attack.
This game is also incredibly easy and grindy even by musou standards.
Horse AI is atrocious. If you call it it will reliably run past you and start charging the battlefield in circles, never to actually meet with you. This used to work reliably, Koei...
None of these are serious flaws, but they stack up, especially when the competition is DW8XLCE and OPPW3.

If you liked the Xtreme Legends versions of any of Koei's titles or you've been waiting tirelessly to see Samurai Warriors join Koei-Tecmo's lineup (much like me), then this is definitely down your alley and worth the buy. Its focus on specific characters and their own personal stories and the new playstyle with Naomasa Ii are great hooks into those who've played the original Samurai Warriors 4.
However, if you were aiming to buy this because it was advertised as the "perfect version of the title" (said title being Samurai Warriors 4), then you may want to hold off on picking it up immediately. The original factions' stories of Samurai Warriors 4 Story Mode are not included, as well as leaving out Chronicle Mode, a mode where you took your own personally created characters into Japan and have them interact with the original historical figures. The DLC is priced higher than it was previously, but this is tied to the fact that the DLC is made up of complete sets of single pieces.
Ultimately, if you love Koei Tecmo's games, Samurai Warriors, or Sengoku Era games, then I'd definitely recommend it without a doubt. However, if you were hoping for a fuller game or a Complete Edition similar to Dynasty Warriors 8, then you may want to just pick up DW8's Complete Edition. Despite being proclaimed to not be an Xtreme Legends expansion, the stripped parts of Samurai Warriors 4-II leave you feeling like it was just an Xtreme Legends expansion.

It's Homeworld 1 + 2 in classic and remastered versions.  What else can I say?  I've fired up Homeworld 1 classic and it's pretty much exactly as my existing install.  I've fired up Homeworld 1 Remastered and it's... well it's glorious.  Fairly consistent 90-120FPS with the details turned up past defaults but not maxed, it controls the same, it plays the same, and it looks much better doing it.  This is really all I wanted.
For those that don't know of this game, it's the classic 3D RTS developed by the same company that went on to make the Warhammer Dawn of War RTS games.  Homeworld bought a lot of new things to the RTS world upon release, some of which still haven't been bettered.  It's use of 3 dimensional space for positioning your units and attacking being one.  Alongside that the fleet you have created during one mission is the basis of your fleet for the next mission; meaning that careful planning from one stage to the next is essential for success.  Lack of planning and scarce resources can really bite you further into the game.
It's worth noting that micromanaging your fleet whilst not essential is advantageous; but you have at least at your desposal settings for stance (aggressive, passive, guarding), formations and basic tools such as guarding units.  Formations are cool, not only do they look good but I they can influence the encounters those units may have and their chances of success.  Though this does seem to bit different (possibly bugged) in Remastered,  you have the Classic one to compare and contrast.
In summary this is a good remastering, it polishes where needed, brings things up to date to remaing compatible with newer hardware and leaves the rest unchanged so not tarnishing the memories and reputation of the original games.
if you loved the original then this is a must, the game is a classic and the fact that they include the classics makes it all the more sweeter.

Despite giving the first
game a tentative "thumbs up" I simply cannot recommend the second game in the trilogy.
could easily have been removed from the trilogy since it does almost nothing to further the plot of the series. It features some incredibly obtuse puzzles, and a huge number of locations to explore straight from the beginning, making it confusing to know where you should be going and what you should be doing.
My main gripe with all the Deponia games (outside of the
main character, Rufus) is the gratuitous amount of completely pointless, filler dialogue you have to slog through just to complete simple tasks. Nearly every character you meet will supply you with 6+ dialogue options which will each spawn at least 15 lines of completely inane banter that does absolutely nothing to further the story or even provide mild entertainment. This
quality dialogue, like in older
games, where you actually
to click every option. Even if you ignore most of the extraneous dialogue options, often just trying to accomplish tasks will result in Rufus droning on and on and on with his signature, humorless commentary. It doesn't help that his voice is about as fun to listen to as a nursery full of teething babies with diaper rash. By the end of the game I was skipping through most of the dialogue since it added zero value to the story.
The only real point to play
is if you already own the trilogy and want to play the games in order. If not, don't bother and instead pick up an adventure game that's actually good, like one of the Special Edition
games (which, despite people's insistence on comparing them to the Deponia series, are actually nothing alike, apart from sharing a genre - and that's a good thing).

My journey on Deponia started with this second part of the trilogy. After some first hesitating steps in this world where I regretted my purchase for some minutes because I thought this kind of game would just not fit me, I simply fell in love with the whole gameplay and its setting.
The storyline itself is, well, just like the first part, very Rufus-ly. But that's what you expect, isn't it? :D
The puzzles vary in their difficulty, but even the harder ones can be solved with (sometimes a lot of) endurance and paying close attention to the scenary as to what the characters say.

I have a love-hate relationship with this game. And by that I mean I love this game, and it absolutely hates me, in the best possible way. If you like horror games and the Alien movies, get this game. Even if you don't like the movies but like horror games, get this game. (Also, what's wrong with you? Who doesn't at least like the first movie?)
The gameplay is quite good. There is some stuff I had issues with, partially due to my own idiocy but I'll also blame the game for not informing me better: your life-sign scanner makes noise, and if you have it out whilst hiding nearby enemies can hear it. I died a lot before a loading screen told me this fact (again, likely due to my own idiocy). I also spent way to much time crouch-walking, by the end I'm sure Ripley had some insane thighs, but I might just be dumb and didn't need to crouch that much.
The story is solid. Similar to
in all the right ways without being too similar. Maybe a tad predictable at times, but what isn't? However, the story is also where I feel I have some genuine complaints. There was one point where a section of you being stalked by the alien became way too long, it needed something to break it up and ease the tension a bit before throwing me back into highly stressful alien scenes. Additionally, towards the end the game begins to rely way to heavily on the "Oh you thought this was the end? Guess again!" method of drawing out a story, and after about the third "Guess again!" I was sick of it. Other than that, I enjoyed the story, and the atmosphere was incredible.
It's a good looking game. I managed to run it on the highest settings (GTX 880 and an excessive 24G RAM) and it stayed around 60fps the whole time.
I'd like to commend whoever scored this game. It is a great soundtrack, it really compliments the atmosphere and is reminiscent of the score of
. I would however, also like to punch them for making already tense gameplay even more stressful with their masterful danger music. I also had to turn the music volume down to make sure I could hear the alien's footsteps, sound is really important in this game and as much as I love the score it was way too loud on default, but that's fairly minor and inevitably down to personal taste.

About a year after it's release, I can come to a final verdict of Total War: Rome II. This was my first Total War game, so I was naive and I had no idea what exactly was going on. I pre-ordered it so I had no idea what I was getting into. Unfortunatley, my computer couldn't run it well, so I had to refrain from playing the game. Finally, with a new computer, I played the game and I was amazed. Large scale battles playing as historic empires? Groovy! I played the tutorial, sucked at it, then jumped into a campaign. I played the game on and off and during that time, I bought Total War Empire, Shogun II and Medival II. I highly enjoyed Shogun and from what I heard it had the most features in a Total War game. While I must say, the game is more streamlined, it is fun. I recommend this game for any newbies to the Total War Franchise like myself. The game has, without a doubt, gotten better as time has gone on, and the Emperor Edition fixed many of the bugs and glitches. I, myself, use mods when I play games to highten my experience, and the mods run well enough. There are many DLC, everything from factions to campaigns. I don't have much of a problem with them myself, but I can see where people get angry at DLC ♥♥♥♥♥-ing.
After all of my time I have spent with this game, I can say CA has taken their lashings from fans and critics after the, from what I have heard, terrible release and have tried their damnest to make this game better. They have released Free-LC and are dedicated to making this game to it's full potential. If you are new to the Total War Franchise, I recommend this game as a starting point. If you are a veteran, it is not as good as Shogun, but it is sure as hell better then Empire.

I wrote a negative review a while ago for this game, saying that the game "used to work but no longer does." However, I got it to work, and it ended up being fantastic. The problem was my controller. If you have the controller plugged in when you boot up the game, you get about 1 frame per second. If you plug in your controller after you start playing, it works. Now that I have played it, I can review it correctly.
The game is good.
The campaign is much higher quality than that of Just Cause 2, and it is much longer. I did enjoy the characters, cutscenes, stories, ideas, etc. and there was even some good humor thrown in. The campaign seems to take itself more seriously than the one in Just Cause 2, which I thought was a great choice on Avalanche's part.
For veteran Just Cause players, there are some "easter eggs." For example, in Just Cause 3, there is a big island in the top-right corner that replicates the one (in the same spot) in Just Cause 2 (although this one has no inhabitants). Just Cause 3's capital, Regno, has a sister city in Just Cause 2 called Bandar Baru Nipah, which I thought was awesome. In addition, just like Just Cause 2, a funny radio announcer will talk about the base that you just blew up to try to calm the dictator's people. Rico also has some throwback quotes.
The destruction in this game is total. I was constantly in awe of both how much infrastructure Avalanche had created and how much I could destroy. Blowing stuff up in this game is amazing, especially with the unlimited C4 supply.
You can be extremely creative, and there is a ton to do. There are functioning trains that you can ride up and down the mountains, and you can get cargo planes and put cars inside, then fly them high above the country. The wingsuit is very fun to play with and get better at, and the grappling system has been much improved.
The music is fantastic, and rivals Just Cause 2's soundtrack.
The country, Medici, is similar to Panau in that it is extremely diverse. There are beaches, forests, snow-covered mountains, and sea. This makes traveling around the world seem much less deja-vu than it could have been. The towns and cities are beautiful as well, making you feel like you truly are in Italy. However, I believe that Just Cause 2 has the better world; there are more cities, more easter eggs, and less of the "filler" land in Just Cause 3.
Overall, as a huge fan of Just Cause 2, I feel satisfied with Just Cause 3. The expreience has been amazing, and I think I will continue to play in this beautiful sandbox. Just make sure to unplug your xbox controller until you start to play!

Alien Isolation is a dark, old school alien game designed with the 1979 movie in mind. Heart pounding moments await you at every turn where simple decisions such as which hallway you walk through could mean the difference between life and death on Sevastopol station. This is my favorite game of 2014, and my undisputed pick for Game of the Year, with Dying Light coming at a close, but not-so-close second. 9999999/10

Alien:Isolation is a brave game, considering what the average gamer demands today. As a spin-off of the first Alien movie, the space station in which the game takes place mixes futuristic technologies and 70s stuff, while the general atmosphere of anxiety and loneliness is very true to the movie and perfectly realized with an amazing light usage. Like a true survival you have no chance to win a fight against the alien. You have to hide, reducing the noise as much as possible and only rely on your crafting abilities to survive: running will be your last card to play against such a superior specimen. Sound effects are great, your hearing being the first sense helping to evaluate your moves.
The AI is the pearl of the game: the alien will hunt you and trick you in such ways that will test your nerves, because revealing yourself will mean certain death.
There isn't any single breath you can take in this struggle. The tension will be high and constant and eventually leads to make bad decisions.
This is such a clever game, wonderfully realized within a vivid ambientation: a game not only Alien fans should play.

Samurai Warriors, or Sengoku Musou as it's known in Japan is an established series of 'hack and slash' games by Koei which are based in the Sengoku era of Japan. If you've ever played a Dynasty Warriors game you know what to expect as the two are almost identical with the exception of the cast and the locations (DW is in China, SW is Japan). Both are by Koei Tecmo and seem to use very similar engines.
The game recreates a turbulent period of history in Japan now known as the Warring States period. Battles raged all over Japan to try and unify the land and Samurai Warriors 4-II lets you take part in many of the decisive battles, using many different factions.  Each mission has a primary objective (usually defeat an enemy commander or reach an escape point) with several other objectives that can happen during the mission. It can be frantic at times, especially when multiple objectives appear within a short space of time and some of them are timed meaning you have to act fast.
The maps are laid out well but do get a little repetitive (as many of the battles were fought in the same locations). Each character has a variety of different attacks effective against different kinds of enemies, as well as having a 'Rage' system (which makes you do more damage for a short period of time) and a character specific 'Musou' attack, which is effectively a super and should be very familiar to anyone who has played Dynasty Warriors.
The game is split into a few different modes: Story Mode (clear a few missions with specific characters as their story unfolds), Free Mode (use any character on any unlocked mission), Survival Mode (ascend an endless tower that gets progressively harder) and it also has a Dojo where you can do several things like create custom characters, listen to music tracks or even read the biographies of the real-life Sengoku era warriors. The only criticism I have of Story Mode is that only a handful of characters have a story mode that involves them to any real extent so some people might be disappointed that their favourite character isn't represented much.
There is also two-player functionality, both local and co-op online. I've tested the online with a friend on the other side of the world with both of us taking turns to host and it's been flawless. No connection issues and no noticable lag whatsoever. Brilliant fun to play with a friend online; I can't comment on the split-screen as I haven't tried it.
Ultimately the game has a very simple premise; kill hundreds (or thousands) of generic grunt enemies, bring down every warlord, daimyo or rebellion you come across and try to unify Japan under your banner, whoever's that may be. As mindless as it can be sometimes, it's still a very fun game and some missions do require you to do more than just mow everything down.
I definitely recommend the game itself; the DLC however is ridiculously expensive for what it is. Unless you're desperate to see the female cast in nurse outfits, swimsuits and the like, wait until a sale to pick the DLC up. The game itself is still worth the purchase.

Biggest problem with gameplay is the difference between Corvo and Emily - the latter is MUCH more powerful and fun to play, allowing some interesting loud, stealthy, lethal AND non-lethal combos, while Corvo has the same kit as in the last game, but without the level design that utilizes that to full extent (and to be honest - Crovo's kit being rather bland and not well suited to neither stealth nor non-lethal playthroughs was one of the biggest complaints about last game).
Other problems include massive grind that block access to the crafting system (in order to craft anything powerful enough to have an actual gameplay effect I had to start New Game + and play for around 4 hours before I could do it). Then there's the hyper-perceptive enemies that have an instantly-filling alert indicator at a range that makes sense only for eagles wearing high-powered monocles, and certainly not humans.
Significantly worse than Dishonored 1's timeless and memorable levels, levels in Dishonored 2 are a lot more generic and the only memorable ones are Kalkstein's mechanical house and the mansion where you can switch between past and present in real time (
cool mechanic, I've never seen anything like this). Granted those 2 levels are leagues ahead of anything in Dishonored 1, however the bland and generic levels filling up the rest of this game overshadow those 2 flashes of brilliance.
Another issue is that levels in Dishonored 2 are not as fun gameplay-wise as in the first game. There are usually not as many ways to advance as in Dishonored 1, due to them being rather generic in nature (concrete apartment blocks, streets, more concrete buildings, more apartment blocks), you don't see as much variation in the level. For example in Dishonored 1 you could go from a small cage onto a roof, onto a flooded street, onto a makeshift outpost in collapsed district in one level. Lots of transitions both in terms of verticality and enemy positioning, and in terms of level visuals. In Dishonored 2 almost everything is on a generic street. They could have at least included some parks or factories or something with a different theme and layout. But no. Streets, apartments, and more streets. Even the observatory level felt very much like an apartment building with a street, except for the library hall.
By far the weakest part of Dishonored 2. Not only is the beginning so obviously rushed, out of place and nonsensical that it's literally cringeworthy (cringeworthy story segment in a Dishonored game!  With the same writers? How?!), but there are no memorable characters in the entire game! Like ANY. Even Kalkstein is not particularly interesting, and they all appear as nothing more than mission targets. The first game put a huge emphasis on building up characters, both friends and foes, it really made you feel like part of the world and defined well your own place in it. In this game your place is evidently slashing/choking enemies™ with the story being so bland and forgettable.
Note, that voiceacting itself is actually good, it's the plot and writing of characters that makes it all so bad. Never thought they could drop the ball so hard with one of the best elements of the first game.
This part of the game suffered least compared to the first game. There's still lots of lore to explore and find around the levels, but with the story and the levels themselves being so uninspired, the world building doesn't seem as appealing as it was in Dishonored 1. I liked the backstory of the Outsider though, I hope they expand on that a bit more later.
Overall it's a game very similar to Dishonored 1 but worse in pretty much every respect. Perhaps if they weren't so fixated on reproducing their first success, and simply used their creativity to make something in the same genre and world, this game would have turned out great. But I honestly can't be sure if Arkane really wanted to make this game, or if they were simply forced to by Bethesda in order to captialise of the first installment's major success. Whichever is the case, I can not recommend this title at full price. At 50% or less, you'll get your money's worth, especially if you play Emily, but not more than that.

I have to start out by saying, I'm not sure why the old reviews for when this first came out are at the top. Anyways, you don't need a super good rig to play this. If you know how to tweak computer graphics options (which if you are going to be a pc gamer you should know how to do), you really should have no problem. I have a Radeon R7, 8 GB ddr3, and an i5 3.0 ghz and my game plays perfectly fine at near-high performance settings (again I tweaked a few things and it worked fine). One last thing on the whole graphics/optimization "issue": if you want to know what to turn off or turn low, the developers have made very detailed descriptions of how each graphics option effects the gameplay and performance. You can also google pc gaming graphics options and you will learn all you need to know for this and any other game.
Ok, enough of the rant on that. The game was amazing. I've played it through three times. The characters are very fleshed out. Corvo has a voice now and has more of a rough and tough personality. You get most of the powers from the first Dishonored plus some new better ones. With New Game + you can use all of Corvo and all of Emily's powers.
The battle mechanics, the body physics and time manipulation are probably the most impressive use of manipulating the game world, and it is very fun. There is a ton you can do, and play around with. Look up Dishonored 2 explosive orgy if you don't believe me.
Beyond that, the coastal continet of Karnaca is a very rich, living place. The gang wars are always working against each other and you are in the middle of it all.
Unfortunately, there are not many levels. Though these levels have many different rooms and buildings to explore. There is a lot to look for and if you spend the time looking for runes and other items you will spend plenty of time in the game.
Personally, I don't feel like the story was as powerful as the first but is still engaging. If you played Witches of Brigmore for Dishonored 1 you will already know a bit of the story. There were a lot of nice nods to 1 and the DLC's. Overall, it was a satisfying game completion.
I highly recommend it. Don't let those complaints about bad customization/technical issues throw you. Besides the updates that have been released to fix most of these issues, it is very easy to tweak the graphical options to fit your computer's rig.

I was very hesitant to get this game for a number of reasons. The initial reviews weren't exactly encouraging, plus I'm not really that much of an MMO guy, I've never really understood the appeal of MMOs. In fact, the last time I've ever played an MMO was all the way back in 2006. Simply as a matter of personal preference, I'm much more interested in single-player RPGs that are rich in storytelling.
That being said, this is a review targeted towards lore nerds. I mostly play the Elder Scrolls games just for the lore. I find the Elder Scrolls universe to be fascinating, richly detailed, and refreshingly unique for a fantasy world. But I have to admit, I was honestly worried that ESO was going to be very shallow and sparse when it came to the lore. A lot of the early reviews when it first came out was about how it didn't "feel" like an Elder Scrolls game. I was worried this would apply to the lore as well, and I was expecting stories and lore that were empty, silly, and contradictory. But after hearing nothing but good news on the /r/TESlore subreddit, I gave it a shot and I'm glad to say Lawrence Schick is absolutely on point with the lore and he does an amazing job, especially with the more obsure stuff. So if you are one of those people who wants to know more about the Argonians' relationship with the Hist, or the Bosmeri Green Pact with Y'ffre, or the kalpic cycle, or more about what might have happened to cause Cyrodiil's jungles to dissapear, or get some more info on the Alessian slave revolt, definitely get this game. It's packed with some solid world-building and lore.

It is a decent game, but I just can't get into it.  If you haven't played Total War before, or only played it casually, you'll probably like it.  But as a hardcore fan who played/plays the original for probably over 2000 hours, it just doesn't hold up.  There's just too much bull****.  No family tree, no rpg elements, a baffling political system, a terrible UI in terms of immersion and gameplay, armies that can walk on water like Jesus Christ, a mechanically flawed engine, pointless naval gameplay, terrible voice acting and sound effects (including music), dumbed-down army management, most settlements not having walls, magic abilities for units......The design of this game can be summed up with the fact that you can't manually enter the amount you want to pay another faction, but it is instead scaled based on your money........
On the other hand, the game does introduce some good features.  Army traditions, realistic line-of-sight in battles, the "tactical" map, army stances, food supply, and the unit camera.  While I don't personally like the city management, it is in some ways better.
All-in-all, I just don't find it engaging or immersive.  I don't feel like I'm in the ancient world, like I did in the original.  There is still some fun to be had though, because it is Total War.  But it doesn't live up to expectations.
Just buy Rome 1 when it's on sale.  If you don't care about graphics, you'll find a mechanically better game.  It's also way more moddable than this game.
While I do appreciate the efforts of modders, the game is just simply so faulty on a hardcoded design level that mods still can't provide a satisfying experience.  I recommend watching Reynold Sanity's review, I agree with most of what he says.

If you're an old school gamer, you'll love this title. It's a throwback to the days when games where games and demanded some degree of proficiency with hand-eye coordination and strategic thought to get somewhere (not nearly as hardcore as some claim thought). However I do recommend you to first get the original Dark Souls (cheaper and just as good), and if you like that one, this one is essentially more of the same but with tighter gameplay and mechanics (you'll miss the open interconnected world but that ain't the point of the series - Demon's Souls anyone?-). Finally, some people will rant about some of the bestest story ever or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ but it's really just minimalist storytelling in a game that really benefits from it. Nothing mindblowing but if you're one of those guys that love incomplete puzzles and head scratching, this one is also for you.

A sequel that exceeds its predecessor in some ways and falls behind it in others. Dark Souls 2 presents more refined mechanics in several aspects of gameplay in comparison to Dark Souls, but its shortcomings come primarily in the form of storytelling and world building. While the original Dark Souls had great atmosphere, game-world consistency, and a well-executed bread-crumb style dark fantasy story that gave you enough information to know what your ultimate goal was without holding your hand, Dark Souls 2 seems to have taken that design strategy and turned up the intensity without much thought of if that would be a good thing or not. The story is incredibly vague up until certain points in the game and many of the ways the game areas connect don't make geographical sense in the game world. Beyond that, PvP and Co-op are complicated by the introduction of the "Soul Memory" mechanic, which ranks your matchmaking level/bracket as the sum total of souls (The in game currency for defeating enemies) you've collected, as opposed to whatever character level you decide to stop at. Beyond these complaints, the game has improved its gameplay mechanics overall, and is still one of the best options out there for a good, dark fantasy experience. Issues aside, I'd still enthusiastically recommend this game.

The game itself is a very loose interpretation of the Journey to the West tale. You're Goku and Bulma has forced you into escorting her back to her dad's house.
Combat in this game is a treat. Goku's Power Pole really feels like it has heft and density when you smack robots. You have lots of different buttons to press to perform different moves. The enemies themselves don't have much variety, but every one seems to have different attacking AI that really shines when you're fighting lots at once.
On a similar note, the animations in here are beautiful. The world is unique as well, being post-apocalyptic but allowing nature to regain control over the ruins of metropolis.
Collectaholics from the N64 days will find something to like here as well. Dragonballs strewn throughout the landscape can be used to upgrade Goku's abilities and equipment, and are also dropped from destroyed enemies.
Some issues to keep in mind: Joystick controls are not tight like a Mario game. This can eventually become an annoyance during the many platforming sections and even sometimes in combat. Also, it's yet another console port with no intuitive display options. It takes some manipulation of an .ini file before things really get rolling visually.
A few final notes: There's no challenge playing this on anything but Hard. Also, the game isn't especially long-- I've played about twelve hours at time-of-writing and have completed it, plus repeated stages several times over. Lastly, before this Premium Edition release, the preorder costumes had never been made available to everyone, so PC players once again are treated to something special.
Having completed Enslaved three separate times (once on each available platform), I've come to really enjoy it for what it is. It's earned a 7 out of 10 from me this time. I'm reminded of a paraphrased opinion I read somewhere-- Where this game is unique, it's brilliant. Where it tries to fit in with other games, it's average.
If you're still unsure, wait for a sale, but by the time you finish it you'll be another person saddened by the fact there will never be a sequel.

In 2010, "Enslaved - Odyssey to the West" came out for consoles and sold a little less than half of what the publisher had hoped for. Reasons quoted for this were that it was overshadowed by a number of other AAA titles and that there were quite some glitches. But reviews praised it, especially for its story. With a delay of 3 years, it has now been ported to PC.
"Enslaved" is very loosely based on a classic Chinese tale, "Journey to the West", and plays 150 years in the future. The planet has been ravaged by a brutal war the remainders of which are ruined desolate cities and hostile mechs that attack anyone they encounter. Humanity has scattered far and about, not only threatened by the mechs, but also by mysterious slave hunters that kidnap people without so much as a clue as to where they're taking them. Onboard a ship of slaves-to-be, Trip, a young woman with tech skills manages to escape her cell. This also opens up a way out for fellow prisoner "Monkey", a muscular loner who has subsisted in the wilderness on his own for most of his life. They manage to flee from the crashing slave ship on the last remaining escape pod, but Monkey loses his consciousness. He awakens to find that Trip has put a slave headband on him that will kill him should her heart stop. She wants to return to the community where she came from and knows she would never stand a chance all alone. So Monkey is forced to cooperate: He is the muscle that takes on all hostiles they meet, Trip is the brains with her knowledge of technology.
Gameplay consists of combat, climbing and some mini puzzles. Monkey has a staff he uses to fight with mechs and later on also shoot at ranged targets. The weapon can be upgraded in various ways using energy orbs found in the levels. Considering myself a mediocre gamer, I found fighting to be at an okay-ish difficulty once I had figured out how to block (others said combat was too easy - obviously, your mileage may vary on that). There could be more help with the controls though, special attacks are still described by giving console control pad keys.
Climbing is rather easy since one cannot fall or miss a grip point, all of which are highlighted relatively obviously. Also, in some sequences Monkey steers a hovering disc called the "cloud" over water and ground surfaces - these segments add a little speed to the otherwise pedestrian experience.
The changing relationship between the two main characters is at the centre of the plot. Thus, it's fortunate that voice acting is very good. And when, at times, not a lot is said (Monkey is not a man of many words), the finely motion-captured facial expressions convey all one needs to know. Story, characters, acting - this is where the game really shines and becomes a "page turner". Okay, well, I won't spoil the ending to you, but I think that was the one part where they could have done better. It just left me with "Hmmmmmmmmm."
Other than that, a captivating journey and definitely recommendable.

Enslaved: Odyssey to the West as an action/adventure platformer developed my Ninja Theory. Not being a very well known developer, this release was quite a surprise, and a delightful one if I may say myself.
At first glance, Enslaved appears to be quite an obscure release, with no major first party push or advertising. However, while it may lack a bit of polishing, it does contain strong mechanics, a great script, fantastic voice acting, and also a unique look to make Enslaved quite a satisfying package.
Set on a post-apocalyptic Earth, you play as Monkey, a loner who grew up in the wilds. After being captured by Slavers, Monkey is freed in the midst of another prisoner's escape. After crashing, Monkey finds himself enslaved by a young woman named Trip. Binding Monkey's fate to her using a control headband. She demands his aid to take her back home. With the control headband on, if she dies, so does he. And so the journey begins...
The colour palatte is well placed with mostly greens and browns to show the once cityscape, being taken over by lush vegetation. The character design is quite good and definitely very unique. The characters (particularly monkey) being based off of Chinese fables of the Monkey King, mixed with a futuristic setting makes for an interesting character set, and with the well done voice acting, makes for a satisfying game.
In relation to actual gameplay, there can be some hiccups. Such as some graphical issues here and there, and sometimes framerate drops. Luckily they aren't too common. Console versions are quite solid, but the PC port's keyboard and mouse controls are quite terrible, and it is very much recommended you use a XBox Controller.
Even though there are some small graphical and mechanical mishaps, Enslaved's fighting mechanics and platforming is quite exceptional. With the mix of some basic teamwork with Trip, and some puzzle solving here and there, it definitely makes for a fun experience, although quite linear. The combat is solid, although at times can be a bit boring.
The game can most likely be finished in 10-11 hours although with the Premium addition, there is an extra campaign where you get to play as Pigsy, another character within the game, which may add another couple hours, and has some new mechanics to keep the gameplay interesting.
The best part is definitely the unique story, and characters to go with it. The voice acting and facial animation keeps you captivated and invested in the characters. Even with its many flaws, it is definitely a welcome addition, and brings sometihing fresh to the gaming industry. If you can look past its flaws, Enslaved might surprise you...

Chaos on Deponia continues the adventures of Rufus and Goal. The sequel has a lot of nicely done puzzles, an amazing soundtrack, and great character development. The humour is even better than in the first game, and it's basically impossible to laught at least once every 5 minutes.

I don't believe a let a single enemy lived including civiliians because they are always running to screech for someone and set off an alarm. Note: I haven't played the first Dishonored but I do know the basics of the game. the combat is quite fun, i'd say something about how annoying it is to fight off a bunch of enemies at once but since its a stealth game i can't quite complain. The powers in the game are quite unique and cool but I literally only used Far Reach (blink for Corvo) the entire time. in rare occasions i'd use the domino power and very VERY rarley i'd use shadow walk and
only at the last two levels i used dark vision. Mesmerize and doppleganger i never touched because honestly the best thing to spend your hard earned runes on are the upgrades on your character directly. More health and mana *(idk know the name for your secondary bar) with some other upgrades for combat and ability to upgrade your jump and speed. The main villain is ok IMO, she seems more like a rejected disney princess villain than an "evil aunt; which in and of itself sounds like an evil disney villain. The main missions consist of going around lvls defeating enemies and finding bone charms and runes. they're are some neat side missions you can complete for some people you find along the way. A lot of backtracking which can be shortened with your powers. A neat black market shop you can run into along these missions and buy/upgrade your gear and among other things. Sometimes you can buy something that will reward you in the mission world. Example is a jey that unlocks a safe in an abandoned apartment building surrounded by the Swarm or the amazingly annoying big mosquitos.As in weapons they are all quite good tho you'll mainly be using Far reach or either your crossbow or pistol. A mechanical heart can help find runees and bone charms in these levels too. Overall the game on my first run was quite funm there is replay value in doing a challenging no kill playthrough and also playing the other character of which you started. Only thing that's stopping me from doing this is the incredibly TBH bland story. The levels surrounding a different "villian" where you go and kill them in the end often feel anticlimatic. Hell, half of the "crew' in the levels i killed without even knowing who they were, i just thought they were another goon i was gourging my sword into their trachea. Overall i'd give Dishonored 2 a solid 7/10, and at the time of this review it's on sale for 30 dollars, so if you need a fun stealth game, id recommend this, however if you havbe the extra cash at the time of this sale i'd buy metal gear Solid The Phantom pain.

TL:DR (up front): Imagine a TES game with every zone unlocked (yes, this game is more expansive than any previous). If you like TES, you'll love this game. You do NOT have to pay monthly to enjoy this game.
I can't compliment this game enough. When it first came out I tried the free demo and was horrified. How could they do this to my favorite game, I thought. I retired ESO and went on a long adventure through WoW. How could anything beat my love for Kalimdor, I wondered. Well, ESO went on sale and I gave it a shot. I played about a few days before realizing I absolutely needed ESO+, a monthly subscription similar to other MMORPG.
Now, let me be clear. You absolutely DO NOT need to purchase ESO+. It is possible to play the entire game without paying monthly to play. You can unlock everything without an ESO+ membership. You can play the full game without it. Yes, there are added benefits, but I met many players of significant level without it.
But I needed to buy it. Why? The aesthetics of this game are dumfounding. How on earth do they make such a visually stunning game run so smoothly as a MMO? The sound is unbelievable from the soundtrack to the ambience. Every single quest is different. You don't run to a new zone and kill 20 wolves, then 30 bears, then gather 5 herbs, to make the holy potion to kill the one boss. The quests in this game are created with the same heart and devotion of TES:oblivion and Skyrim. The characters have life. The world has life.
The social aspects of this MMO are incredible. There are no trolls. Guilds serve a purpose. By that I mean is you don't need to join a guild for leveling perks (or at all). There are PvP, PvE, RP, Social, Raid, Casual, and even Trade guilds. That's right, a group of people to band up with solely to effect the global economy to make you rich.
You truly cannot beat this game. As a long TES player, and relatively recent ESO player, I cannot recommend this game enough. If you like any TES (Morrowind or beyond) you will love this game. Once again I reiterate, you do NOT have to pay monthly to enjoy this game. I choose to because I support the developers.

KT's Warriors games are something of a guilty pleasure for me. They're constantly getting trashed by the likes of IGN, and yet the games continue to get made, and their fanbase continues to grow. I don't know what it is, but there's just something about plowing through entire armies in the flashiest way possible.
Warriors fans demand a few simple things from their games. Larger numbers of guys on screen, more characters to play as, and more creative movesets. And to that end, SW-II delivers perfectly. On top of that, the game introduces a tag in system where you can play as a second character in a completely different part of the battlefield. It's great for not only battlefield control, but for leveling up multiple characters.
...That being said, SW-II, especially our PC port has a few shortcomings. Not necessarily deal breakers, but noteworthy shortcomings I hope get improved in the next game.
While it's sort of awesome that we get to create our own characters, the feature is very limited. And with Chronicles mode from SW4 being taken out in SW4-II, I found myself not caring. In the original Samurai Warriors game, you had a campaign mode for your character where you got to pick which side you played, with future battles depending on said choices previously. If they're going to take the create a character route in the next game, I'd like to see something like this return. Otherwise, why bother?
Ah, the mighty gods SEIYUU. Mythical beings said to be able to bring fictional characters to life with the power of their holy voices, while making unworthy plebians quake in awe. Real talk: I've never understood their appeal, but forcing the game into SEIYUU mode makes it somewhat difficult to follow what's happening on the battlefield without contantly checking the subtitles-when our eyes should still be on the man-hacking....
OK, so I know that the "日本の優れたコンソール" is, and always will be KT's most comfortable platform, but christ almighty the frankenporting has got to stop. If the PS4 can handle a fully worked game, there's a good to fair chance some of our master race machines can handle the load. Hopefully KT will port us a proper current gen game. Hopefully.....
FInally, let's talk DLC. Not only is it overpriced - as is the case with most KT games, most of it adds nothing of value to the core game. If KT were to release costumes from previous SW titles, I might have bitten(alot of the character designs in SW3 were far better than SW4). As it stands now, I don't care about any of what's on offer here.
...But, like I said before: They're shortcomings, but not deal breakers. Gameplay wise, Samurai Warriors is probably KT's best title, matched only Warriors Orochi 3. Which is why despite said shortcomings, I'm still going to recommend a purchase.

The Last of Us owes a lot to Enslaved: Odyssey to the West. Not only is The Last of Us built around a burgeoning relationship between two characters who are with each other throughout their journey, like Enslaved, but The Last of Us also boasts a well-realised art style similar to Enslaved's in that it emphasises light, ruin and lush vegetation. Though also like Enslaved, The Last of Us is somewhat let down by the actual nitty-gritty of its gameplay. While Enslaved's platforming is competent, straightforward and fast, its combat very quickly becomes repetitive and frustrating - it really doesn't seem designed to cope with groups, and believe me, there are a lot of group combat scenarios. It's still absolutely worth playing, though, and while its story doesn't push the envelope in quite the same way as the story in The Last of Us, it's still an enjoyable journey with genuinely interesting characters through a stunning gameworld. Just make sure you fiddle with the graphics options in the .ini file first.

Enslaved's "green post-civilization" look is very beautiful and sets it apart. Sure, if you stop and expect some corners of the game, you'll notice a lack of tesselation, textures being on a flat tile, objects not having as many points as they should, but generally, you'll be too busy climbing or fighting to take the microscope to everything. First off, this is no open world game. Like in many climbing games, there is a high degree of linearity, but you don't feel it as much as in Remember Me or, oh shudder, I am Alive. The climbing is fun, the fighting is, for the most part, also fun, and easy mode is actually easy. The world is beautiful (and colorful), the controls are fluid and sufficiently exact (though I'm not sure I appreciate "press A+X" type controls, but you only need those if you buy certain fighting skills), and the voice acting is good. The plot is OK -- or rather, you're too busy playing the game to pay too much attention; in fact, the plot and the backstory are a bit meh and confused, and adding quasi-flashbacks in a completely different visual style was a bad decision that breaks immersion when it happens. Your character isn't the most fleshed out ever, but quite serviceable. (Unfortunately, you only get to play Monkey, the man, not Trip, his companion. There is no multi-player either, so Trip is always AI controlled. At least, she has useful skills and isn't the kind of AI that steps in your line of fire, but where she isn't dangerous due to a lack of artificial intelligence, she is as a function of the story -- she is written to get you in trouble, and while her motives are somewhat understandable, she isn't exactly likeable.)
In sum, the game feels very arcady -- big sprites, broad strokes, good fun.
I bought this at (PC) release, and am not sore for the money.

Alien Isolation is a dark, old school alien game designed with the 1979 movie in mind. Heart pounding moments await you at every turn where simple decisions such as which hallway you walk through could mean the difference between life and death on Sevastopol station. This is my favorite game of 2014, and my undisputed pick for Game of the Year, with Dying Light coming at a close, but not-so-close second. 9999999/10

Alien:Isolation is a brave game, considering what the average gamer demands today. As a spin-off of the first Alien movie, the space station in which the game takes place mixes futuristic technologies and 70s stuff, while the general atmosphere of anxiety and loneliness is very true to the movie and perfectly realized with an amazing light usage. Like a true survival you have no chance to win a fight against the alien. You have to hide, reducing the noise as much as possible and only rely on your crafting abilities to survive: running will be your last card to play against such a superior specimen. Sound effects are great, your hearing being the first sense helping to evaluate your moves.
The AI is the pearl of the game: the alien will hunt you and trick you in such ways that will test your nerves, because revealing yourself will mean certain death.
There isn't any single breath you can take in this struggle. The tension will be high and constant and eventually leads to make bad decisions.
This is such a clever game, wonderfully realized within a vivid ambientation: a game not only Alien fans should play.
93/100

Highly recommended. I'm a big fan of the first two films in the series, and Alien Isolation does an excellent job of recreating the feel of those films (kind of more Alien than Aliens, but with plenty of elements of both, and some of its own horrors thrown in).
Graphics, atmosphere, effects, level design, sound design, are all top notch. Highly deserves all the awards it got. I'm glad the alien can't hear the Steam screenshot sound going off, otherwise I would have died a lot more.

Wow. Jesus Christ, what a ride. That was, by far, the most intense experience I've ever had in a video game. It's scary, it's hard, it's frustrating, but most importantly, it's rewarding. That amazing relief you feel when you reach a save station or enter a new area, knowing you're safe, is wonderful.
Graphics: Everything looks great. Fire, lighting, characters, outer space, machinery, it's all incredibly detailed and beautiful to look at. The design is great as well. It looks just like the original movie did, but slightly upgraded (which would make sense, given the story). The game absolutely nailed the futuristic space theme.
Ambience: Definitely the best ambience I've experienced in a modern game. I find myself disappointed with most modern games' attempts at background noises, music, etc, but this one was perfectly done. The alien can be heard moving around in the vents, and the station is constantly making distant crashing noises, so you're always uneasy, knowing the station could be minutes from destruction.  It adds a whole new level of tension and constant fear that makes the game even more intense.
Story: As far as I can tell, it seems very true to the original movie. I saw the movie when I was pretty young, and none of the sequels or video games lived up to that original horrifying experience. This game created characters I genuinely cared about, a story that kept me wondering what would happen next, and had voice acting that almost brought me to tears at times.
Gameplay: This, unfortunately, is where I think the game suffers, depending on your viewpoint. While the sneaking is phenomenal, I found myself consistently frustrated with two aspects of the gameplay: the save system, and the movement speed. This game utilizes save stations, which is not always a bad mechanic (Dead Space did it quite well). However, the save stations are small, hard to find, and generally very scarce. One might argue that this adds an element of fear to the game, given that dying would be a major setback (sometimes 30 minutes of gameplay can be lost), but I believe that it makes the game much more frustrating, rather than scary or intense. I frequently found myself quitting the game because I would die and end up having to repeat 15-30 minutes of gameplay in order to get back to the part I died at, only to die yet again. This is where the movement speed comes in. Your character walks very slowly, and running is almost never a good idea because the alien will hear you. Therefore, if I want to complete a section, I have to do so very slowly, which gets tedious when you have to do it over 5 times. I found this to be extremely frustrating throughout the whole game, but luckily there were enough positive aspects that I kept coming back to it.
Overall, this game is a masterpiece. A difficult, frustrating, intense, horrifying, beautiful masterpiece. It's clear the developers put a lot of time, effort, and love into this game. If you loved the original movie like I did, this is the Alien game you've been waiting for. Buy it, play it, and love it. 10/10
