"Reckoning up the sum, the best was yet to come, for the end of part one seemed a little too coarse. To amend we'll send Rufus to attend a second chance for a decent happy-ending: a grand fling with dancing and booze and so forth..."
To put it simply, if you liked Deponia, you'll certainly like Chaos on Deponia. Part of that's because it has just as much quality in its art, characters, story, music, puzzles, etc. The other part is because it more or less follows the same motions. Rufus solves an enclosed introductory puzzle, then builds a contraption involving rockets to launch himself into the sky, winds up crashing into a vehicle which contains Goal, both plummet to Deponia, you solve a handful of major problems by solving a ton of smaller ones in a large town area, then a smaller transitional act, and finally the twisty confrontation.
And yet, despite featuring the same framework, the body is all-new. New faces, new locations, new puzzles. There's much to do and explore. So much of the world of Deponia to learn about, and a diverse and creative cast of characters to meet, all weird in their own ways.
And oh my god, the voices are so much better. I mean, the majority of Deponia's voices weren't a problem, but the Organon's certainly were. Luckily, though the voices still have the same electronic filter, the volume has been turned down from "standing beside a malfunctioning stage woofer" to "playing on a rusty seesaw". I never liked Goal or Toni's voices much in Deponia, either, but unless I'm less of a cranky old voice snob than I used to be (unlikely - I'll be a voice snob 'til the very end!), the actresses have gotten a better hang of their characters, this time around. Goal, in particular, I thought sounded very nice. And she'd have to, considering the actress now had to keep up with three or four variations of the character (each of which sounds distinct, but intentionally similar enough to be the same character). Rufus does sometimes have lines that are delivered in ways that don't seem to match the situation at hand, and I definitely caught a flubbed line here or there (which the subtitles at least got right), but even still, his V.A. does a fine job with the other 98% of his lines.
Weird translation problems do crop up from time to time, and they can have varying impacts. Chaos on Deponia was made by a German team, and it seems a little obvious here and there. For the mostpart it doesn't matter at all. On the whole, the English version of Chaos on Deponia shows an expansive understanding of the language. But there are some lines that just didn't make it through unscathed (at one point, a character asks, "What? I'm pardoned?" when he's supposed to say, "What?
pardoned?"), and some jokes seem weird in ways that suggest that they worked a lot better in their original language.
On that note, I also want to mention that Poki's folky narrative songs are more... chaotic, this time around. Maybe that was a thematic choice, based on the title. But I'll be honest, those songs were one of my absolute favorite parts of Deponia. With maybe the exception of the third song, in this game they're much harder to follow. If it weren't for the subtitles, I wouldn't have a clue what he's saying half the time, with odd rhymes, lines with way too many words, and lines that end in the middles of words. I suppose this adds to the zaniness in a way, but I still preferred the old ones better.
The puzzles are more imaginative than I had expected, even having played the first game. Where Deponia featured a borderline obsessive number of puzzles centered around washing things, the devs have put forth a much stronger effort to keep you one your toes, this time. There are some dips into moon logic territory, but even those are more to do with the problem presented (such as as a head-sized human nose sticking out of a wall as a security device), or with how extravagant the means to solving them are (the lengths Rufus goes to in order to recognize a cat door are astounding, and perhaps a little unfortunate depending on your affinity for cartoon wildlife), and maybe one or two where I wasn't sure what I was accomplishing until I had already accomplished it (ding-dong ditch comes to mind), rather than just a straight-up complete and utter lack of logic. Several puzzles are downright ingenious, though. One puzzle involving a secret knock is about as weirdly outside-the-box as it gets, and I love it in all of its fourth wall-breaking splendor.
Daedalus has struck a good balance in the difficulty. It's not as though I never got stuck. I did. In fact, I got stuck on the follow-up to that knocking puzzle simply due to a confusing sound effect. You have multiple secrets knocks which, though they should all sound different, all use the same sound effect, which made it tough to figure out how I was meant to go about solving the problem. But the vast majority of them were a joy to solve, with the game giving you just the right amount of clues necessary to understand what you're doing, without being so simplistic as to make you feel like a toddler. And there are a number of segments which take chances and break out of the typical talk to people/use items mold. You'll play an interesting take on a fighting game, compete in the weirdest form of rock-paper-scissors that I have ever seen, and take advantage of a complicated loophole in fast food pricing, among other highlights.
The puzzles are good, I like the puzzles. They're not 100% perfect but they're like 80-90% perfect. Boom, could have saved you two paragraphs of your time if I'd just written that first.
I said it about Deponia, and I'll say it again about Chaos on Deponia: the game feels like a true evolution of the old SCUMM-based Lucasarts games. Not a copy, nor even an homage. But something which could have naturally formed from Lucasarts themselves in an alternate timeline. I mean this as a great compliment. If you can stand some translational oddities, you'll find that Chaos on Deponia is a beautiful - albeit junk-strewn - world filled with strange people and creative solutions for even more creative problems. I can easily recommend picking it up. Though I of course recommend picking up Deponia, first, if you haven't. Or the recently released Complete Journey which collects the whole trilogy. If you're a fan of silly, imaginative adventures like Day of the Tentacle or cartoony ones like Curse of Monkey Island, you're in for a treat with these.

So I played the first Dishonored a while after it came out, and I thought it was an amazing game. Both the gameplay and the story were brilliant, so I had high hopes coming for Dishonored 2.
I should say now thatI tend to not be too harsh on anything, because I tend to like most things.
For me, the Dishonored 2 gameplay and map design met the same high levels as the first, and sometimes succeded it. The massive choice of how to play each level is something so nice to have in what is still a 'linear' story game. It is also very replayable, because of the versatililty of each playstyle/character/level.
My only dissapointment was the story; it wasn't bad, just quite generic and predictable. I still enjoyed it none the less, and to be honest, I think it's difficult to make a story good in a sequel, let alone better; if you try something new, it's rarely as good, but if you do the same or similar story as the first, it just feels like aremake of an old game.
So overall, still one of my favourite games and I would recommend anyone who likes singleplayer games to play it, but if you ONLY look for story in a game, well... PLay the first one!!
P.S Many people have been complaining about performance issues. I am sure they exist, so beware, but weirdly I have experienced none, and I'm on a relatively low/midrange PC.
I have a Phenom II and a GTX 960. The game ran at about 30FPS for me. So I turned off the frame counter and played the game. It was great.
after 4 playthroughs on both low chaos (don't kill much or at all) and high chaos (pretty much the opposite) I can say that I love this game.

It took nearly 20 hours to download the actual game (my wi-fi isn't the best, so this wasn't unexpected), and then upon launching the game, I was immediately greeted with a massive update to download.
That took like 2 hours or so to get to like 30%, but then it said there wasn't enough space available to continue downloading (I had over 5 gigabytes of space, so it wasn't dangerously low or anything).
I deleted a couple games, and brought my space up to 17 gigabytes (more space than I had before I'd even started the download in the first place)... And the error message STILL continued to pop up, refusing to accept that I had plenty of space to download.
I figured my only option was to close and restart the game, but upon doing so... The download had restarted.
When I finally got back onto the main menu (after that update took a couple hours to download), it refused to accept my account.
Eventually, I figured out that I had to enter the game's code into my account first (something that was never explained). And this time, when I tried to log into the game again, it said my computer was not authorized to access the game... So it sent an email with ANOTHER code.
I entered the code, and was finally able to get to the character creation screen...
And then this happened:
When I'd finally gotten into the game, I spent nearly an hour creating my character, but didn't click "create" yet because I was trying to think of a good name first.
So I went to make myself a snack (and thought of a name during that time, which was under 2 minutes), and came back to a message saying the game had kicked me due to inactivity.
All of that work down the drain.
At that point, I didn't even WANT to make a character anymore... or even play the game at all.
I'd spent a lot of time on trying to perfect my character (constantly going back and tweaking every option), and had been extremely happy with the result.
This game is the complete opposite of user-friendly.
It constantly felt like they didn't WANT me to play their game, and so were purposefully making things difficult (obviously, I know that's not really the case, but that's the impression the game gave me).
Who the hell puts an inactivity timer on a character creation screen?
And if you decided to do that (for some insane reason), why wouldn't you make that INCREDIBLY clear to the user?
Why would you NOT add a message or a PHYSICAL timer that tells you how much time you have before you'd be kicked for inactivity, and as a result, lose all of your progress?
Maybe I WILL enjoy the game once I actually play it. In fact, I probably will (I'm sure the actual game is at least decent).
However, at this point, I've currently just lost all possible interest and excitement that I previously had for the game... In fact, right now, I actively do NOT want to play the game.
It's not like I can refund the game either, since according to Steam, I've played nearly 10 hours (due to updates and such)... Despite literally not even playing for a single second.
I really wanted to try out the game, but it doesn't feel like the game WANTS me to try it out.
Everything seems to be set up in a very unclear and confusing way, and no explanations are ever provided.
This whole experience has just been irritating and infuriating...

By playing this
modern singleplayer FPS game, you get a true sense of being one in a hundred. The entire map is just filled with fairly smart AI, in groups or by themselves, hunting down the enemy. You never feel like an overpowered singularity, as you have the same weapons and vehicles as everyone else, and that's what makes it feel more immersive.
You aren't being shouted at by 8 year olds or raging through a microphone calling hax on the other team, everyone is AI and the game itself isn't even rage inducing, at least in my experience.
The best thing about this is that the map is just small enough so that you can see every individual plane, helicopter, and boat, all raining hell upon the field. However, the map is also just small enough so that it doesn't take an impossibly large amount of time to traverse half of it by foot or face another enemy group. It's just all out war, you're rarely not shooting or getting shot at, everything feels so intense, especially with planes.
When I drive a plane, I simply get so into it, I can see all the action below me as bullets rain from above and below, while chasing down another plane just to get shot down by an AA turret. There's just enough content to make it a time-killer, whether it be short 20 minute matches, or 300-man hour long wars.
As of right now, the amount of weapons are limited, bugs and glitches still happen, the AI sucks with boats, there are only 3 different maps, and the vehicles are constantly changing and getting rebalanced.
But hey, the AI is flipping amazing at piloting planes, has just the right balance of accuracy, mis-fires, and range, are able to spread out and path among the map almost similar to a real player, are great at defending, and are funny to shoot in the head when they steal that helicopter gunner spot

Initial review for posterity:

The VideoKid is a fantastic experience coming as an 80s kid myself. I enjoyed the constant references while I dodged, grinded on, and threw tapes into mailboxes. The game starts off simple enough, you have tapes that need to be delivered and you’re the guy to do it. There are other challenges thrown in as well, which makes the gameplay somewhat diverse.
The UI is clean. You have your cash earned in the top right, distance traveled in the middle and your score to the top right. Bottom left is also a pause button and a close on the right. There is no menu screen, so to adjust the sound, you’d have to either end a level or die where the sound will be at the top of the score page. Also to note, there isn’t a way to set the difficulty either in case you find yourself struggling. Score page shows your score, earned cash, movies delivered, and a way to spend that cash now.
Cash allows you to buy characters of which you’ll recognize immediately like Ferris Bueller and the Karate Kid as well as additional tricks to help boost your score on your routes. All of it costs money and quite a bit of it for the good stuff of course. So, get to landing sweet tricks on your board and these will be yours in no time.
The game starts with a goal and a route you’re to take. Unlike Paperboy, you don’t have a limit to videos you carry, you just have to land tricks, dodge obstacles, and throw videos into the red mailboxes. You can also pummel Care Bears, Alvin and the Chipmunks, and dudes who need some chill with tapes that you’ll see on benches. I personally enjoyed hitting the Fraggles myself.
There are also characters wandering the sidewalks and familiar cars on the streets to land tricks on. Hitting targets, certain characters, and getting red mailboxes consistently earns you points as well as landing tricks on cars. Stringing combos can be tricky as the setting needs to be exact for the trick to land. This was quite difficult at times since I found myself initiating the trick and then failing because of an unexpected obstacle or a Dalek.
There’s a lot going on on screen at times and it can sometimes become overwhelming trying to focus on hitting the correct mailboxes while simultaneously trying to dodge Scrooge McDuck and his damn grandkids. The are rewards for distance, a number of correct mailboxes hit in a row, tricks and combos landed as well as targets and coins gathered.
There is also a moment where you see 4 familiar green turtle open the sewers. What happens when you fall in? Yep, you skate the sewers. These little touches make the game slightly more challenging.
However, gameplay can become quite repetitive quickly. And with no way to set difficulty, some may find this game a bit too hard first time around. So, if you find yourself having a bad time, your best bet is to keep trying and work at it until you got it down to a science. Depending on what you’re hoping to achieve, you may find the gameplay lacking with this in mind.
I also found it strange there are no Steam Achievements or Trading Cards to earn for your deeds in-game. Perhaps this may be changed in the future.
The game uses WAD to move with A and D for left and W to jump. Spacebar is to throw tapes. The controls are responsive and the Video Kid jukes, jumps and throws videos on cue. Hitting mailboxes can take a few tries to get right, but once you get the mechanic down, it’s relatively simple to hit the mailboxes each time.
There is partial controller support as well if you prefer. Left thumbstick to move and jump, A to throw tapes and Y to jump. I used a wired XBox 360.
Music is fantastic and by DJ Savant. It’s upbeat enough to keep you interested, but not repetitive to the point you end up focusing more on its annoyance than the game.
The Video Kid is a cute blast from the past and I thoroughly enjoyed all the retro references. I definitely feel my age creeping up when I can name pretty much every reference in the game. :) The addictive fast-paced gameplay, the snappy controls on both KnM and controller, awesome flashbacks all work together in tandem in creating a damn good experience and a retro roller coaster.
If you can look past the lack of a menu to adjust the sound and difficulty as well as the tedium, then Video Kid is definitely one you don’t want to miss.

THE VIDEOKID
Released
PixelTrip Studios
PixelTrip Studios
Arcade
31st of January, 2017
Single-player
It’s been a while since I played a decent 3D endless runner, so THE VIDEOKID hit the right spot for me. “Runner” might be a bit of an understatement since you’re actually a skater. This is indeed a cute little title from an indie dev team at the start of their journey onto Steam. As long as you don’t mind the inherent  repetitiveness of this arcade subgenre, you’re good to go. Well, skate.
A trip down Memory Lane indeed, since the main visual diversity offered by this title comes from the multiple film and video game references it alludes, without actually naming them per se. Obviously that is just one of the many caveats imposed by copyright laws. Alas, you shall be able to easily recognize quite a few characters from the ‘80s and early ‘90s. The large pixel visual style is still pleasant on the eyes and the sounds are diversified more than enough.
The gameplay itself is somewhat lacking though. In both depth and the initial presentation. No tutorial (apart from a brief start screen that indicates which buttons to push or when), no cutscene and definitely not a very complex storyline or motivation. You’re the title’s eponymous Videokid. A silent protagonist whose apparent mission is to skillfully throw VHS tapes from a distance, while avoiding the many traffic and sidewalk obstacles that will surely get in the way. And yes, apparently the game’s goal seems to be meeting “Jessica” at the park. Now that’s something easier said than done. In the good ol’ tradition of arcades from the past (which this game really tries to emulate at least in spirit), THE VIDEOKID is hair-raisingly difficult to progress through, let alone master it. I shall not mark this as a weak point simply because I feel that such a game shouldn’t be too easy. It maintains the legacy of coin-hungry arcade machines which both forced players to focus and learn the game’s patterns and at the same gave a real sense of accomplishment for those lucky and skilled few which could best the title and reach an ever impressive highscore.
Most certainly the presence of a difficulty slider would have been welcome. In part, THE VIDEOKID is also hard because of the randomly generated obstacles which offer a new perspective and challenge every time you restart the level. And you will have to do that quite often. Distributive attention and multitasking aren’t unheard of in video games, but in this particular case you will often fail the stage by focusing too much on collecting coins (which help you unlock new outfits and items for your skater) or hitting the red mailboxes with the tapes instead of minding the road and incoming vehicles.
Videokid can aim at many objects and NPCs with grace and doing so is actually encouraged by the scoring system on the upper right side of the screen. You really can’t complain about the pacing but the gameplay itself gets boring eventually. Constantly hitting hurdles and having to restart the entire level, doesn’t help either. At least Unity Engine ensures a smooth and nicely detailed experience. The developer should definitely sweeten the deal by adding Trading Cards and Achievements in a future  update. The price tag is decent but if you’re still not convinced, buy THE VIDEOKID when it shall be inevitably bundled. I’ve decided to recommend the game for its sheer nostalgic value, if nothing more.

- Repetitive gameplay.

As for those complaining about how they think the game runs poor... well for one i have a gtx 970 and a i7 5690k with 16gb of ram  but here is the kicker, I'm running it at 1440p with 50+ fps  avg on the max settings on win 10 64bit on an ssd with out any issues. Now as far as the ram issue goes my system idles at 1.4 gb ram and playing this game it goes to ~4.5gb at an eyeball avg of 40% cpu load so....yea. And at least for me this has been constant performance from day 1 owning the game and I bought it maybe a few days after it came out.
Game is rock solid performance even on my brothers 960gtx he runs 720p at  60+fps and never encounters slowdown on 4 gb of ram on an 4 year old amd fx 8000, heck this will work just off the apu in an i7 at low settings 30 fps. As far as Ati cards go the reason their so poor on this particular game is the way they handle mass textures like explosions  where as the nvida cards are made more in mind for sudden demand in memory and particle calculations so they have a much easier time with this game so i would blame it more on the manufacture for not supporting through software in such a way that it compensates for those cards weaknesses.
But just to let you all know sometimes it can be the reverse for other games and it's not all dependent on the engine that the game runs on but the support given to that engine by that company that makes the card, it's a 2 way street. Sadly it seems that ATI still is not up to snuff with their driver support for this AAA game that's been out for a while (witch the consoles are also ATI/AMD machines). Avalanche Engine only has 5 games on it their is bound to be less support for it where as games like DOOM are based of UE4 and almost all games produced with that brand new engine run really well on most cards and their is a lot more driver support for because of all the games (
) that's like +30 games in development on this one engine.
Those of you having issues with the game their are a few steps you can take
Start the game in the lowest possible settings and slowly adjust them one by one up until you get a crash and report it to Avalanche.
validate the files through steam if your getting crashes
update your video card drivers>try the game
uninstall the game>restart>install the game>restart>try the game
uninstall your video card drivers>restart>reinstall them>restart>try the game
If it was working at one point do a system restore by going to start>search>system restore>pick a time when you know it was working.

It took nearly 20 hours to download the actual game (my wi-fi isn't the best, so this wasn't unexpected), and then upon launching the game, I was immediately greeted with a massive update to download.
That took like 2 hours or so to get to like 30%, but then it said there wasn't enough space available to continue downloading (I had over 5 gigabytes of space, so it wasn't dangerously low or anything).
I deleted a couple games, and brought my space up to 17 gigabytes (more space than I had before I'd even started the download in the first place)... And the error message STILL continued to pop up, refusing to accept that I had plenty of space to download.
I figured my only option was to close and restart the game, but upon doing so... The download had restarted.
When I finally got back onto the main menu (after that update took a couple hours to download), it refused to accept my account.
Eventually, I figured out that I had to enter the game's code into my account first (something that was never explained). And this time, when I tried to log into the game again, it said my computer was not authorized to access the game... So it sent an email with ANOTHER code.
I entered the code, and was finally able to get to the character creation screen...
And then this happened:
When I'd finally gotten into the game, I spent nearly an hour creating my character, but didn't click "create" yet because I was trying to think of a good name first.
So I went to make myself a snack (and thought of a name during that time, which was under 2 minutes), and came back to a message saying the game had kicked me due to inactivity.
All of that work down the drain.
At that point, I didn't even WANT to make a character anymore... or even play the game at all.
I'd spent a lot of time on trying to perfect my character (constantly going back and tweaking every option), and had been extremely happy with the result.
This game is the complete opposite of user-friendly.
It constantly felt like they didn't WANT me to play their game, and so were purposefully making things difficult (obviously, I know that's not really the case, but that's the impression the game gave me).
Who the hell puts an inactivity timer on a character creation screen?
And if you decided to do that (for some insane reason), why wouldn't you make that INCREDIBLY clear to the user?
Why would you NOT add a message or a PHYSICAL timer that tells you how much time you have before you'd be kicked for inactivity, and as a result, lose all of your progress?
Maybe I WILL enjoy the game once I actually play it. In fact, I probably will (I'm sure the actual game is at least decent).
However, at this point, I've currently just lost all possible interest and excitement that I previously had for the game... In fact, right now, I actively do NOT want to play the game.
It's not like I can refund the game either, since according to Steam, I've played nearly 10 hours (due to updates and such)... Despite literally not even playing for a single second.
I really wanted to try out the game, but it doesn't feel like the game WANTS me to try it out.
Everything seems to be set up in a very unclear and confusing way, and no explanations are ever provided.
This whole experience has just been irritating and infuriating...

In short, all bad reviews, all community rage etc. - was completely justified.
This is for those hard core fans of TW series who (like me) cannot help our self.
Or for some new guys who maybe don't have much experience with series, but they will like it for they own reason. I'm writing from the perspective of someone who played Medieval 1; Rome 1 / BI & Medieval 2 / Kingdoms for thousands and thousands of hours, and is completely disappointed with this long waited game.
And I want to stress that I began with Emperor Edition, which is greatly enhanced, and free of bugs. I don't know about early release, aka pre-Emperor disaster, and I'm not♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about all things Sega did before final version of game I tried in 2015-16.
I continued playing after my first review, and will probably play more of it, but ***only*** reason are workshop fan-made mods. I wanted to stress that this is the first TW game where my further engagement depends only on that. Granted, I never played Napoleon or Atilla, and I have only few hours of Empire.
In Rome 1 and Medieval 2 you wanted mods because they enhance already awesome game. Or make significant changes – like in Broken Crescent. I never tried single Rome / BI mod. Tried Medieval 2 SS mod after thousands of hours of original game.
Rome 2 without mods is simply beyond repair, and one long campaign would be more than enough for me.
- AI probably much more stupid than in Medieval 2 & Rome 1 – both on campaign and battle map
- unbelievably idiotic economy management
- buildings, unit, character and other cards (symbols you see on UI) are ugly beyond belief. Someone just made them in order to skull-**** you, and made harder to tell what is what. I won't even start ♥♥♥♥♥ing about symbols for unit action on battle-map card ("running/in melee/morale/fatigue etc.")
Only positive thing:
- You don't have to auto-resolve naval battles anymore. Empire naval battle management was allegedly terrible. In Rome – everything is OK as long as you play some Mediterranean faction with rams (boarding is clumsy at best). Granted, I haven't tried difficulties higher than Normal, but for me it goes like this: 4-6 artillery ships pounding biggest and slowest enemies; rest of fleet in crescent formation with fastest ships on wings. Ram poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Ram again. Again. Again. Chase those who rout. Ram them in the♥♥♥♥♥ Oh my god it's so fun. If you have full stack with good ships, anything but annihilation of every single enemy ship is counted as defeat. Best part is when your full stack engages enemy full stack, which is protecting full stack of transports. It's like: <3 <3 <3 I can sink 40 ships in 15 minutes <3 <3 <3  (see my Batllefleet 2 hours)
In summary:
Even for us who cannot help ourselves, and with some fairly decent fan mods, game is still worth -75% of price. That is price I paid, and anything more would be tragic waste of money.
Most DLC-s are also worth -75%, and some even -90% normal price.
But no matter how cheap you get this - you will probably be disappointed.
Despite the disastrous launch, the game is now fixed and very damn fun. Even more fun with mods such as Radious' Total War. 10/10 Euphorius Maximus

By playing this
modern singleplayer FPS game, you get a true sense of being one in a hundred. The entire map is just filled with fairly smart AI, in groups or by themselves, hunting down the enemy. You never feel like an overpowered singularity, as you have the same weapons and vehicles as everyone else, and that's what makes it feel more immersive.
You aren't being shouted at by 8 year olds or raging through a microphone calling hax on the other team, everyone is AI and the game itself isn't even rage inducing, at least in my experience.
The best thing about this is that the map is just small enough so that you can see every individual plane, helicopter, and boat, all raining hell upon the field. However, the map is also just small enough so that it doesn't take an impossibly large amount of time to traverse half of it by foot or face another enemy group. It's just all out war, you're rarely not shooting or getting shot at, everything feels so intense, especially with planes.
When I drive a plane, I simply get so into it, I can see all the action below me as bullets rain from above and below, while chasing down another plane just to get shot down by an AA turret. There's just enough content to make it a time-killer, whether it be short 20 minute matches, or 300-man hour long wars.
As of right now, the amount of weapons are limited, bugs and glitches still happen, the AI sucks with boats, there are only 3 different maps, and the vehicles are constantly changing and getting rebalanced.
But hey, the AI is flipping amazing at piloting planes, has just the right balance of accuracy, mis-fires, and range, are able to spread out and path among the map almost similar to a real player, are great at defending, and are funny to shoot in the head when they steal that helicopter gunner spot

I Picked Dark Souls 2 up during the summer sale, and got it for a pretty good deal. So far I have had a blast jollily cooperating with my friends. Now you may be asking why I don't reccomend Dark Souls 2 even though all I've said is positive things so far. Well, the answer is a game breaking addition in the latest patch (1.08). This change has completely made one of the starting classes in the game useless. The class in question is the Cleric class (which of course I happened to pick). From Software has decided to nerf all lightning spear variations to a point of utter uselessness. This nerf has caused the ammount that you can carry to be greatly (a word I don't use lightly) reduced. By default with one lightning spear attuned I could carry 11 lightning spears. Now with two atttuned I can carry a whopping 6. Oh, and did I mention that they got their damage reduced? In all the Cleric builds I've seen (including mine) lightning spears play a large role in the build. Now they're screwed. It's not like they were insanely op in PVP (Player versus Player). A nerf of this size on the lightning spears was completely uncalled for. So if you decide to buy Dark Souls 2 stay far far away from the Cleric class until they fix this, which is highly unlikely because they still haven't fixed the whole soul memory issue.

I'll preface this by saying that the first Dishonored is easily my favorite game of all time. Dishonored 2 is effectively more of the same, similar to the Knife of Dunwall DLC; new powers, new story, but doesn't feel like a new game. However, what I wanted most from Dishonored 2 was more of the same, and it certainly delivered there.
As a decidedly stealth-focused player, I thought that the new powers introduced with Emily added a lot to the gameplay. Dishonored certainly lacked in options for stealth takedowns, but this has been well improved upon in this sequel. Domino and Shadow Walk in particular give a great number of possibilities, and make the stealth gameplay feel as dynamic and interesting as the loud. To players unfamiliar with the series, the Dishonored brand of supernatural stealth is easily the best and most interesting stealth gameplay I've experienced since the original Thief games. It allows innovation and experimentation from the player in near limitless combination, and manages to stay fresh through dozens of hours of gameplay.
Having done two separate assault-style playthroughs, I have to say that I'm equally impressed with the loud gameplay. Much like the stealth part of the game, going loud allows the player to freely experiment with their gear and powers, and discover incredibly entertaining solutions to the game's obstacles. I particularly enjoyed grabbing enemies from the ground up to the rooftops, then kicking them back down with a springrazor on their backs. Again, Dishonored 2 excells in allowing experimentation and creativity.
The addition of more difficulty options and New Game+ mode have added infinitely to the replayability of the game. Playing with fully upgraded powers and gear is a whole new world of experimentation, and makes the early levels feel totally new. These features in particular make this game an improvement over the original.
The story, unfortunately, is outright bad. It's not infuriatingly stupid, but it's certainly dull. Don't play Dishonored 2 expecting to be enthralled by the characters or plot; it's just not it's strong point. However, the compelling atmosphere of the game more than makes up for this. The environments feel alive and immersive, from the sunny streets by the docks to the decrepid hallways of the almost abandoned asylum. Whatever engagement is lost in the unexciting story is compensated for by the fantastic art style, soundtrack, and level design.
Finally, the technical aspect of the game has to be mentioned. While Dishonored 2 was nearly unplayable at release, it has since become much better. However, it's still not perfect. I run most AAA games at 30 FPS on medium settings, but with Dishonored 2, I could only reach that number on the lowest settings. At four or five points in the game, particularly resource-intensive scenes drop my FPS to around 15. I would try the demo first, and see how the view of the entrance hall at the Institute affects performance. Other than that, the game runs fine; no issues with crashing, and no particularly noticable bugs.
Overall: Effectively an expansion to the first Dishonored, with excellent stealth gameplay and great replayability. Lacking in story but excelling in atmosphere. Some technical issues that should be evaluated before purchasing. Would absolutely recommend to fans of the original Dishonored.

Review by Games Fiends
Point and click adventure games run through my blood more than I’d normally care to admit. As a young kid I’d watch my stepmum tackle the Monkey Island games on the Amiga… taking great delight in the wonderful world and atmosphere they portrayed and chuckling at the fantastic humour. As I grew older, I would play other fine examples of this genre such as Full Throttle and Broken Sword. Most recently, the genre has been re-ignited thanks to TellTale Games Sam and Max franchise and of course The Walking Dead.
Chaos On Deponia establishes itself firmly in the same vein as the hallowed Monkey Island games in both tone, atmosphere and complexity of the challenges laid out before you. It doesn’t just offer an entertaining diversion for a few hours, it envelopes you in a light, bright and brilliantly realised world that is a breath of fresh air in an age of mottled brown first person shooters.
Chaos On Deponia is the second game in a trilogy which first started with August 2012′s Deponia. You play Rufus, an inhabitant of a junk world where the upper classes reside high in floating cities whilst the rest of the population slum it on the garbage filled lands and seas. Your character is an arrogant inventor of ridiculous contraptions and contrivances that occasionally (through luck more than anything else) work. The recap of the first game is a little scattershot and I felt I only picked up the detail once I’d played through a fair few hours of the second game.
That all said, it’s a testament to how much I enjoyed Chaos On Deponia that despite not having played the first title, I have purchased it from Steam and will be making sure I have the third title on order as soon as it comes out.
Firstly, the gameplay provides an engaging cerebral workout where common sense, experimentation and eureka moments all help you to move through the traditional point and click puzzle solving challenges. There is a nice mix of both delightfully obvious things you’ll need to do, some that require a bit more thought and others which are downright baffling, but once the solution is laid bare, never feels obtuse or illogical. The game starts off with a very enjoyable opening sequence where you cause a comical series of misfortunes to a poor bird as you go about the simple challenge of trying to pick up a hammer. This was a hilarious opener to Chaos On Deponia and sets the tone perfectly for the rest of the game.
Shortly after you are thrust into one of the junkyard port towns where the game really opens up. Sometimes it can be a little difficult to remember exactly what you are doing (or need to do) but that’s also a good testament to how open the gameplay is. Traipsing through the town with its cast of colourful and eclectic characters was one of the many pleasant reminders of the earlier Monkey Island games. Mini-games are neatly interspersed throughout the levels and add an extra layer of gameplay, however these can be skipped over if they prove too much of a challenge which is ideal for those who are more interested in absorbing the world and the storyline rather than spending lots of time trying to work out a puzzle sequence.
Even during the moments where I became really stuck I never got too frustrated thanks to the ability to double click from one screen to the next, which avoids having to watch your character walk from one side of the screen to the other all the time. This means that you can traverse the game areas quite quickly. Even long periods of travelling back and forth whilst you try and work out a solution to a problem never becomes patience shatteringly painful. Chaos On Deponia, despite being the second title in the trilogy, takes great care to welcome even newcomers of the series to both the game world and even the genre itself. Promising a rewarding challenge for those that want it, and as little pain as possible for those that don’t.
Graphically the game features some of the richest artwork I’ve seen in a long time. A wide colour palette and fine details adorn each screen, making progress a joyful delight as you get to admire the wonderful artistry and inhabiting characters. Having a Germanic background, the art style itself is a very abstract mix of European oddness. Some characters look like they wouldn’t be out of place in Bellville Rendez-vous, whilst others have the more conventional appearance of a Saturday morning kids cartoon character. The Deponian world is realised as a series of townships, buildings and interiors that have been constructed from recycled junk, which is reflected by the background artwork and the attention to detail. At no point do you feel like anything has been rushed in the production of this videogame series. Each screen is unique and has had the same level of care and attention lavished on it as the last.
The characters are wonderfully drawn, and although the animation isn’t fluid I didn’t find that particularly bothersome. The lack of voice syncing was a bit of a distraction during the moments where you see the characters up close during the cutscenes, and it’s only here where the artistic quality take a minor dip as they appear to be blown up from the normal character models that you control rather than original standalone artwork.
Underpinning the wonderful visuals is an equally bright and whimsical score that’s enjoyable and never too repetitious. The vocal work on the whole is largely excellent, with the dialogue not suffering as a result of the translation over from German to English. Some of the more over-excited moments of line delivery from Rufus does make the performance less convincing and slightly theatrical, the opening recap from the first game being a prime example of this. But otherwise the eccentric cast of characters are all given a unique voice with great delivery and comedic timing.
Chaos On Deponia should be an essential purchase for Monkey Island fans. A definite purchase for point and click adventure fans, and a recommended purchase for anyone else. The beautifully drawn world serves up curious but loveable characters. An entertaining story is glossed with many amusing moments. The gameplay is infused with brain wracking puzzles that challenge but don’t frustrate. The Deponia series may not resuscitate the point and click genre into mainstream popularity unlike The Walking Dead, but it serves as a strong reminder as to how good they were in the 90s heyday and how great they can be again.

Many enjoyed the second game in the series more than the first, but I'm only sort of on that boat. Many things are improved, mostly gameplay-wise, but a smaller amount is drastically deteriorated. A widespread complaint of the series is that the protagonist is a massive jerk, and not a likable jerk, but a jerk-jerk. After playing the first game, I had strongly disagreed, but slowly as more unfolds that complaint does gain far more plausabilty. I had looked toward seeing the imaginative plot develop story-wise after my time playing the first game, and unfortunately it had definitely not met those expectations. Still, it comes somewhat recommended, and it nonetheless remains an enjoyable entry to the point-and-click genre trilogy.

Chaos on Deponia (unfortunately) still follows Rufus - my most hated main character in any game series - treading unnecessary grounds between the series' first and third instalment. The plot this time around is more or less exactly the same as in Deponia: Rufus attempts to get to Elysium, hurts Goal in the process, saves Goal, then they both arrive at some sort of 'emotional finale'. The only actual tie-in with the overall story is the ridiculously unlikely romance between the two leads. There was plenty of opportunities to allow for some character development to take place here, but the developers must have thought Rufus is perfect the way he is. I doubt I am alone in thinking otherwise.
The comedy found within is more miss than hit, usually revolving around racial and gender stereotypes, slapstick, and Rufus' narcissism. Characters you meet are one-dimensional walking punchlines, only they lack actual punchlines. Often, Rufus will be painted in a good light while characters opposing him - specifically women - are seen as ♥♥♥♥♥y obstructions in a great man's journey. When that fails, crude humour comes into play in the form of dead baby animals and belittling of others. I picture the developers staring longingly through the windows of residence Monkey Island, soaking in the rain while contemplating ringing the door bell and asking for worthwhile ideas. A shame they instead resorted to the trash bin.
That being said, if you are a fan of point-and-click games, you should definitely consider giving it a shot. The gameplay is good fun, the art is gorgeous, and the English voice actors usually play their roles very well. The enjoyable musical numbers separating chapters are still present, but it's now even more painfully obvious they struggled to fit the lyrics to the songs. Sadly, all of this is not enough to warrant anything other than a red thumb.
In summary: If you find it appealing to control the bane of human existence sort of bumble from one mildly logical puzzle to the next while listening to him comment on his surrounds with punchable smugness for 8-9 hours, then by all means give this a try. I can promise if you did not like the first game, you won't find anything here to make you want to see trilogy's inevitable end.

The Videokid is an absolute throwback to the 80's.  It's a fun spin on the Paperboy games with a ton of references from the time period and maybe a bit of a Skate or Die feel.  If those all seem somewhat foreign to you then maybe a better comparison would be to modern endless runner style games.
You take control of a kid on a skateboard who is trying to meet his girl at the park.  But his pesky job of delivering VHS tapes gets in the way.  You skate along and make your deliveries while avoiding various obstacles.  Obstacles that are often references to 80's pop culture.  Maybe you need to avoid the Terminator.  Or peg some Care Bears in the head with a tape.  Drop in a sewer that you saw a few Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles drop into?  You can grind on top of cars and benches in an effort to increase your score.  Make a few extra bucks and you can unlock various characters to use along with some extra moves.
At the end of the day if you're a fan of the 80's then this might be right up your alley.  Same if you're into endless runner style titles.  If neither of those things really appeal to you then I'd give this a pass.

That took like 2 hours or so to get to like 30%, but then it said there wasn't enough space available to continue downloading (I had over 5 gigabytes of space, so it wasn't dangerously low or anything).
I deleted a couple games, and brought my space up to 17 gigabytes (more space than I had before I'd even started the download in the first place)... And the error message STILL continued to pop up, refusing to accept that I had plenty of space to download.
I figured my only option was to close and restart the game, but upon doing so... The download had restarted.
When I finally got back onto the main menu (after that update took a couple hours to download), it refused to accept my account.

And then this happened:
When I'd finally gotten into the game, I spent nearly an hour creating my character, but didn't click "create" yet because I was trying to think of a good name first.
So I went to make myself a snack (and thought of a name during that time, which was under 2 minutes), and came back to a message saying the game had kicked me due to inactivity.
All of that work down the drain.
At that point, I didn't even WANT to make a character anymore... or even play the game at all.

Maybe I WILL enjoy the game once I actually play it. In fact, I probably will (I'm sure the actual game is at least decent).

Bottom line: don't listen to all the whining over this game. It's such a HUGE game in every way that it seems to be causing a kind of disturbance ! As always there is a grain of truth to the complaints. This seems to be due to inaccurate hardware requirements published by Avalanche. JC3 requires a lot of memory (at least 16gb probably 32gb) and/or an SSD that is fast enough to load in the enormous amount of assets in the world when the engine requires them. I got away with 8gigs of memory and a fast SSD with my swap file on it:
... That's based on some proper testing, Be careful of the veritable barrage of "fixes" out there that are based on not much more than supposition. So, onto the game. As with these kind of games there's so much to offer. I tend to be drawn to ships and fast cars. The driving model is almost worth the price of entry alone ...
(
). Driving is not easy ! But incredibly exhilarating once mastered. Boats. There's a splendid ocean simulation in this game similar to what we've seen in AC: Black Flag. It's NOT a physics based system which is why its running so well on my R7 260x. At higher settings ("high" on my machine) I actually could really get a feel of being at sea, having been sailing for real. Quite a graphic design and art direction achievement. The world also feels unusually large and real when far out to sea with islands in the distance. Having been to Greece the experience was familiar. Waves grow and shrink depending on the weather and the experience of sailing along it is tactile and oddly addictive. What I'm also seeing here is new features that are more akin to Mercenaries 2: World in Flames. Winching and towing of vehicles as well as being able to load multiple vehicles into beach landing craft and offload them at a destination. With the rebels still in the stowed vehicles firing at passing enemy ships ! Key all this into the destruction model (Mattias! You've got your work cut out for you!) and we have a true MONSTER of a game here. We've seen what the Avalanche engine can do with another superb game, Mad Max. The performance is comparable to Mad Max once the larger memory/SSD requirements have been ironed out, with the game looking really very good on my AMD R7 260x/Intel i5 4690k/Asus z97-p with the settings, although not at full, tweaked for a balance between speed and graphics. So combine what JC1 and JC2 innovated, with the powerful world creation strengths of the engine that we see in Mad Max, and we get JC3. In fact its obvious the JC3 game developers were looking back at Just Cause 1, with there being a more frivolous feel here and no money system for requesting supply drops. JC3 has also had some talented designers and artists. Just take some time to look at the landscape textures and the way the vegetation is done and then compare that to Far Cry 4 and you'll see what I mean. Altogether I think JC3 is a very good example of a gaming renaissance going on now that really kicked in with Mad Max because the director applied film industry development methods to it ("work shopping"), as well as other games like AC: Black Flag (take your pick). JC3: Welcome to your own movie !

In the past the Alien game franchise has never really given gamers the opportunity to really explore the look and feel of Ridely Scott's Alien, those games stuck a pulse rifle in your hand and said go kill aliens. And while for a time the splutter of aliens was enough, it got old. Fast.
Alien Isolation delivers a fresh new take on the Alien universe, putting you right in the thick of the 1979 Alien environment. From the moment I started playing; waking up from hypersleep and taking my first footsteps around the Torrens, I immediacy knew this place. The look and feel of the game was almost nostalgic, making me feel that I was now in environment of the original Alien. The areas are well designed, and well-crafted to show a lived-in environment.
Aesthetics aside, Alien provides a unique survival challenge - not only do you just face off with the Alien but there are other hostiles to contend with. As the game advances you face more and more hostility. There are various difficulty levels that you can play through; Novice, to Nightmare Mode. Nightmare Mode I feel gave a truer sense of the intended hostility of the game, where every sound you make can grab the attention of the Xenomorph, synthetics or other hostiles on-board the decaying space station Sevastopol. There were points of the game that had me truly on the edge of my seat, and I didn't know if I would survive or be killed.
The UI is pretty minimal on all difficulties except Nightmare where there is no HUD or map. The rest of the UI; weapon / item selection is a little clunky and is done in real-time. If anything I believe this is by design to slow you down. There is a select number of item you can craft by collecting blueprints for them as the game advances, and each craftable requires specific inventory items that you will need to collect along your way. Those items as well as your motion tracker, which I think is awesomely implemented are key to surviving.
The nature of the Xenomorph's AI is pretty good. I feel the developers did a good job with the "unpredictable" AI they wrote for the game, as you never know when it will appear and hunt you down.  Save for a few scripted encounters, all of the encounters I had in the game were truly unpredictable and many times resulted in the Xenomorph eating my face.
The game is highly objective driven and while this is okay, it can distract you from exploring other areas that you may miss if you find yourself churning away at completing the goals you need to advance through the story.
As with all games there is always some pitfalls.
Alien Isolation is a game from Creative Assembly, and it is the first game I feel that is pointing is the right direction in terms of gameplay, environment and look. It is a refreshing new take on the Alien game franchise.
If you're a fan of the Alien franchise, this is one game you won't want to miss.

EDIT:
Now that I've played this game for a few hours, I can give an honest review. I will definitely say, I'm a fanboy of Dynasty warriors, but I'm not bias to it... So here's my honest opinion and review.
PROS:
- The game-play is smooth. I've been a strong Dynasty warriors player since DW4. Playing Samurai warriors really changed my gameplay experience, and to have the NPC's block and counter my attacks really take away the "1 1  2 " Attack feel. I have to change it up on a regular basis, or else I die.
- The graphics overwhelmed me a little bit; in a good way though. Although you have the graphic perfectionists, with the amount of crap on the screen, the dudes attacking, and specials all over the place, the game runs smoothly for me. And if it didn't I would turn down some of the graphics because the gameplay is straight up worth it. [I use a GTX 780 TI w/ 32GB RAM]
- The character customization felt different than Dynasty Warriors 8 Empires, but it felt good at the same time. I say that because I can't get the bad-assery everything from 5 different weapons and feel like a god. It brings a unique feel...
- The game runs smooth.
- The difficulties feel smooth in transition as well.
- The Rage system is identical from DW8, but it feels much more rewarding because when you activate it, you don't instantly get full morsou.
- The weapon system / upgrading system feels fluent, and it's awesome when you upgrade 3 weapons with different elements and have them all combine onto one weapon. Makes me excited!
- The skill tree is something I've missed since Dynasty Warriors 6. I will be playing Samurai Warriors for a LONG time.
MULTIPLAYER
- Is amazing.
- Even if a player rage-quits, you get rewarded for the progress you [And the person that rage-quit] have done.
- The "Server" is hosted by the person that invited you / accepted your invite. If there is lag, it's either the user, or the host. FYI, It's not KOEI'S fault. I think ever person in the negative box needs to understand that. I saw some people whine that the servers were laggy, and that KOEI's at fault... Yeah.. No.
CONS:
- No Chronicle mode, but I expected it. [They tweeted it, and made me sad]
-The only real gripe I have with this game, is the DLC. Off the bat, $90 + dollars. It's not a terrible gripe, because I usually buy every DLC a game has to offer if I like it [Yeah, COD... Lol]. At the same time, this is not a brand new game, and this is POST Samurai Warriors 4-2... So it's kind of expected.
If you're shopping for a new genre to play that's action packed, I highly recommend you get this game. If you're a prior dynasty warriors fan, and looking for an alternative challenge, I also recommend this game. The pace flow is different, but feels rewarding. Imagine fighting a Lu Bu doing counters for your attacks, and you end up having a "Counters" game. It's refreshing, that's for sure.
I also want to mention, you can build yourself like a god, and still push yourself to the limit to go beyond in survival mode. It's nice to feel like you can keep going and going... and have somewhat of a stat peak, and keep fighting dudes that are 1000x harder...

Q: What makes Black Mesa great?
A: It's a recreation attempt of Half-life 1 ran on the Source engine and pushed to it's limits in attempts of introducing new gameplay elements, better graphics, many puzzles to accomplish and easter eggs! While Half-life 1 Source was a disappointment of what could've been an improved version of Half-life 1, Black mesa does it best by offering that. It's also great at bringing nostalgic memories to the Half-life fanbase that played the very old GOTY beloved shooter, Half-life 1. It's still worth playing today!
Q: What's the story?
A: You play as Gordon Freeman, an black mesa scientist and a speechless character with specialized armor which is called the HEV Suit that can withstand bullets, electricity, and radiation for a limited time. You as the character and protagonist of the story Gordon Freeman, are basically late for work on conducting a test with the black mesa employees in attempts of receiving contact with extraterrestrial life with some sort of unusual crystal. Things go from positive to negative as a result regarding the aftermath of the test, and your journeys begins basically surviving and helping other fellow employees within Black mesa to safety from HECU marines and horrendous aliens. You're in for a treat of what you're about to endure next while being playing Black mesa.
Q: Is there anything positive and negatives about the multiplayer?
A: The positives of the multiplayer is that it has nice variations of weapons to pickup from maps, limited cool player customization, and a bit of fast-pace shooting elements with very nice maps. The negatives of Black mesa multiplayer is that it doesn't have a lot of players, like Half-life 2 multiplayer for instance. It's pretty much a rare occurance to encounter a lot of players, but I believe once the Xen chapter releases you may be in for a ride with people populating the servers.
Q: Should I play Half-life 1 classic first before playing Black mesa?
A: It's not really mandatory, since Black mesa is basically a recreation of Half-life 1 classic with a better engine, better graphics, and a bit of gameplay.
Q: Is Black mesa a good choice to start off before playing the rest of the Half-life games?
A: Of course. Black Mesa definitely feels like it's a recreation or an update of Half-life 1 classic, so it's safe to say that you could definitely start off with playing Black mesa first. Everything Half-life 1 classic has is transported to the game Black Mesa with updated graphics that you'll feel definitely much more satisfied with.
Q: Should I really purchase this game?
A: Well, if you're that type of person that plays games for the single player story and cool action sequences, then of course you could go right ahead and purchase the game itself. At the end of the day, it's your decision how you want to use your money on.
Q: What do you rate this game?
A: Well, I would definitely rate this game a 9 out of 10. It might increase depending how the Xen chapter is going to play out.

Borderlands 2 is pretty much endlessly replayable. I had this game for the 360 way back when it first came out (bought it day one!), and put in about 200ish hours there. Then I got it for steam, and have about 200 hours here. There's a ridiculous amount of just STUFF to do, new ways to play, funny jokes to hear (and hear again, and again...). If you don't like games with side quests that generally follow the formula of run here -> kill enemies -> run back, this isn't your game. Finally, since gear becomes obsolete so quickly, it can be frustrating when you get a really good weapon at level 34 and it's useless by level 38 (for example).
All that said, this is my favorite game of all time. It's worth picking up, especially since it's routinely on sale, and right now it's less than $9!

An elder scrolls MMO sounds perfect. And it would be, if it were anything like an elder scrolls game. Its a watered down version of skyrim. While its prety technically sound, and plays well, its just not that interesting. ESO falls to the same plague of many other online games: it feels static and guided. You dont feel like youre discovering tamriel with other people, it feels like youre running through a mmo and people are there too.
Its a decent mmo all things considered but it just wasn't what it should have been. Quests are repetetive. Not very immersive. Its a pretty cookie cutter mmo with some gimmicks to it. Writing was decent, really enjoyed the books scattered throughout, but npc interactions felt a bit overdone at times.
ESO is just not outstanding enough to recommend, given what it costs and what it very easily could have been.
If you stripped away the sluggish combat and hollow questing, you’d be left with the most gorgeous fantasy hiking simulator this side of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt.

If you are hesitant about ESO, If you are a fan of MMO's I would highly recommend giving it a chance. There are so many options within the game that there is bound to be something for you. I will attempt a short pros/cons to possibly help your decision.
Pros
-Huge amount of quest content with real voice actors
-Possible to play your way: can play any race, any class the way that suits you and it will not be wrong. There is no "right" way to play your class
-eso plus is not required to enjoy the game at all
- if you do love the game then while not neccesary the DLC is highly enjoyable and does have alot to add
- group play is not required but can add alot to the game as well as making lvling quicker
-endgame does not become boring. There is so much more than main story
- fun pvp system if thats your thing
- Add ons are easy to obtain and let you really make a HUB that you like
- crafting system is interesting and not overly "grindy"
Cons
- grouping and chat can be difficult to get into, esp with base game settings, but can be overcome easily enough with add ons
- quest tracking in base game isnt quite the best, but again add ons can easily solve this
- no auction house....can be pro or a con, there are trade guilds that you can join which are perfectly viable, but some would prefer the former, but that is a matter of opinion, you will have to decide for yourself. To me the guild based trading is fine.
- need adventures pack in order to play any race any faction, this can be frustating if you friends are on a different faction than yourself, so plan accordingly
So overall I think the pros far outweigh the cons. None of the cons are enough to lower my opinion of the game, and most all cons are easily overcome with the use of add ons.
Just a few last heads up before you decide
- eso is lore heavy, but it is still not skyrim, but whats the point of a new game exactly like one that already exist?
- eso plus is not required at all, but can add alot to the game especially after you get a good feel for it overall
-not designed to just plow through and powerlevel, the game story and other quest lines are highly interesting should play through at least once in my opinion. (there are ways to lvl fairly quickly, but can take away from overall content) to each is on

I honestly cannot stop playing this game. The amount of content in this game is astounding. I've been a Total War fan since Rome Total War and I've gotta admit, they've really improved on the whole Rome era. Everything from the units to the map look fantastic. It was a little hard to figure out the whole UI of the campaign map since they keep changing it from game to game but after a while it just felt natural. The unit cards are a litte plain and sometimes difficult to identify but there are mods out there that change them to be more appealing and identifiable. That's another thing about this game that I love: The Mod Manager. This nifty little feature allows you to download and use mods from the Steam Community to be used in the game. There are hundreds of mods for this game such as changes to units (stats, aesthetics, number, etc.) or even changes to the whole map itself. I've had a blast using the mods I've downloaded and I'm really glad that CA took the time to put this feature in so that I wouldn't have to go in and actually mess with the game code to put in mods. But, if you're not really into mods then that's perfectly fine since the game is great with or without them. I would very much recommend this game to any person who loves micro-managing and RTS games.
Overall, with the addition of the mod manager, I'd rate this game a 9/10. A lot of people have mixed reviews about this game due to the lack of multiplayer potential and content that was in the previous title. I am saddened by this because I did like having my own avatar general that I could use to play with but I was never really one for multiplayer so this feature not being in this game did not affect me as much as it did others. So if you're looking to just match up and outwit other players online then this is your game. Thanks for reading my review and I hope you enjoy the game!

Bottom line: don't listen to all the whining over this game. It's such a HUGE game in every way that it seems to be causing a kind of disturbance ! As always there is a grain of truth to the complaints. This seems to be due to inaccurate hardware requirements published by Avalanche. JC3 requires a lot of memory (at least 16gb probably 32gb) and/or an SSD that is fast enough to load in the enormous amount of assets in the world when the engine requires them. I got away with 8gigs of memory and a fast SSD with my swap file on it:
... That's based on some proper testing, Be careful of the veritable barrage of "fixes" out there that are based on not much more than supposition. So, onto the game. As with these kind of games there's so much to offer. I tend to be drawn to ships and fast cars. The driving model is almost worth the price of entry alone ...
(
). Driving is not easy ! But incredibly exhilarating once mastered. Boats. There's a splendid ocean simulation in this game similar to what we've seen in AC: Black Flag. It's NOT a physics based system which is why its running so well on my R7 260x. At higher settings ("high" on my machine) I actually could really get a feel of being at sea, having been sailing for real. Quite a graphic design and art direction achievement. The world also feels unusually large and real when far out to sea with islands in the distance. Having been to Greece the experience was familiar. Waves grow and shrink depending on the weather and the experience of sailing along it is tactile and oddly addictive. What I'm also seeing here is new features that are more akin to Mercenaries 2: World in Flames. Winching and towing of vehicles as well as being able to load multiple vehicles into beach landing craft and offload them at a destination. With the rebels still in the stowed vehicles firing at passing enemy ships ! Key all this into the destruction model (Mattias! You've got your work cut out for you!) and we have a true MONSTER of a game here. We've seen what the Avalanche engine can do with another superb game, Mad Max. The performance is comparable to Mad Max once the larger memory/SSD requirements have been ironed out, with the game looking really very good on my AMD R7 260x/Intel i5 4690k/Asus z97-p with the settings, although not at full, tweaked for a balance between speed and graphics. So combine what JC1 and JC2 innovated, with the powerful world creation strengths of the engine that we see in Mad Max, and we get JC3. In fact its obvious the JC3 game developers were looking back at Just Cause 1, with there being a more frivolous feel here and no money system for requesting supply drops. JC3 has also had some talented designers and artists. Just take some time to look at the landscape textures and the way the vegetation is done and then compare that to Far Cry 4 and you'll see what I mean. Altogether I think JC3 is a very good example of a gaming renaissance going on now that really kicked in with Mad Max because the director applied film industry development methods to it ("work shopping"), as well as other games like AC: Black Flag (take your pick). JC3: Welcome to your own movie !

TL;DR: It has it's issues. Get it on sale.
It's hard to judge this game on it's own, so I'll have to compare it to the candlestick that is Dynasty Warriors 8 on steam.
In comparison to Dynasty Warriors 8, this game falls short. There are only three game mode available: Story Mode, Free mode, and Tower Attack. Story mode is made up of a dozen story lines that have about 5 battles or so. Free mode is more or less just a free battle. Tower Attack is a timed race to the top of a tower (100 levels) which comes in standard and challenge mode. There is also a new combat attack set called hyper attacks which are huge crowd clearers and nicely break up the combat move sets so you aren't always hitting the same attack sequences. They also have added in a Spirit Charge attack move which can be used in combat to charge an enemy to break up their combo attack.
Pros:
- Story Mode has dual officer mode. Play and swap between officers you pick during combat.
- Create your own officer!
- A dozen story campaigns in campaign mode.
- Weapon/mount upgrade system is more interesting.
- Online and Local Co-op!
- New combat move set, Hyper Attacks.
Cons:
- Experienced significant visual performance issues with my PC. Random FPS drops that require exiting game to correct.
- FMV cutscens seem to be low quality.
- Not much meat to the game other than the story line. Dynasty Warriors 8 had ambition mode which was a pleasant diversion. This game offers a tower race which is interesting, but not much else to it.
- Some features are not explained sufficiently.
- Controller support is silly. You'll need to use your keyboard for some actions if you're using a controller. Since you can't do everything on the controller.
Notes:
- VO is Japanese only (english subtitles are available, but no english VO).
- Horse AI seems to be fixed. This was an issue at launch.
- Created my own steam controller config to be able to perform all game actions on the controller.
Dynasty Warriors 8 is a superior product, but this game can satisfy if you're looking to get back into the series.

Although it is more than two decades old and has been forgotten by most, Total Annihilation is still one of the best RTS games of all time. I still even have my original CD-ROM. For the base asking price of $4.99, you really can't go wrong.
The premise is simple: you start off with a single Commander unit. With this solitary unit, you must construct resource-acquiring structures that supply you with two types of currency - metal and energy, both of which are vitally important for different reasons. With this supply of resources, you must build factories that construct units such as tanks, bots, planes, ships, hovercraft, etc. At this point, the game grows in complexity as battles are fought, factions expand their territory, and new technologies become available. Oftentimes, the objective is to elimate the enemy commander(s), but this can be customized.
One of the main draws of this game for me is the extremely generous unit cap. While it is common for RTS games to have a unit cap limiting you to perhaps a few dozen units at most, Total Annihilation allows hundreds, if not thousands, of units to be on the field at any one time. If I am not mistaken, it is also possible to use a mod to remove the unit cap entirely.
Furthermore, the game has hundreds of different maps to chose from. Some are inhospitable and molten, others are freezing wastelands, while others yet are rather pleasant with lakes and rolling hills that are green with life...until the fighting begins.
There are also hundreds of units to construct, with many more available to add via mods. These units range from stealth planes to stationary cannons to laser-wielding spider robots and everything in-between.
Not only this, but there's even a campaign available if you so wish.
I could go on and on, but my point is that this game has a massive amount of content available and if you don't mind something on the older side, it is absolutely worth picking up for $4.99 (or less if you get it on sale).

In the current state i can only recommend against buying this game.
It very much feels like a (very pretty) beta that has enough technical issues to feel nearly as bad as the original.
If Gearbox manages to actually improve things i will amend this.
As it is, have a small list of problems discovered in the first 10 minutes of gameplay: The mouse has lag (even at 160 fps), there's some form of mouse acceleration at work (most noticable when scrolling to zoom in, but not when zooming out) and there's not even a sensitivity slider, with the default being very low. (Fairly important for things like rotating the camera.) Panning to the left is nearly impossible on a multi-monitor setup since the mouse is not captured in the game window. The hud on a 1920x1200 screen is small, but can be increased in size by factors 2, 3, 4. However even a factor of 2 is already too much, since every element is literally doubled in height and width.
Multiplayer is currently in beta, and makes the same mistake that killed multiplayer for the original: It forces usage of a centralized third-party service which may die at any time. There is an option for LAN multiplayer, but that is unlikely to work well on the internet.
As a postscript: Since the original version is included, it's recommended to simply play that. It also has a tiny UI, but a very sharply-designed one, and the screen is locked to 4:3, but otherwise it does not exhibit the beta-like issues of the remaster.

Distant Space (was Space Distant, but the game is massively changed since a patch that changed the name) is a fairly basic Space Invaders variant with little to recommend it, you will take on about 23 waves of very similar groups of aliens firing down at you, and at certain points fight three boss aliens.
The game is very easy, you can take a fair few hits each level, so progress is almost inevitable no matter how bad you are at these games, and when you die you will get back full health and shield, and even keep any special ammo you still have in store, so the only real penalty is having to start clearing the level from the start again. The only even slightly tough level is the final one, and even that I cleared first time (well I deliberately died once to refresh my health, so I guess technically second time)
The aliens are all similar monochrome outlines, and the bosses are just larger monochrome outlines, and pretty much every regular level plays out the same apart from the aliens follow different paths around the screen, but you just slide from side to side firing all the time without really aiming until there are only a couple left. Although the aliens have a few different variants that shoot differently, and a couple more are added into the mix as levels advance, it all feels very samey.
As mentioned there are a couple of weapon power ups you use with the right mouse button, but these are simply a double and triple fire, which are useful for quickly clearing the bulk of the aliens at the start of a level, and it is a nice change from the previous versions that you can choose to use them when you choose, but not exactly very interesting or gameplay changing.
The boss fights are fairly easy generally but long winded and tedious as every time you hit the boss it flashes with immunity for half a second or so, so you have to slowly wear them down, but as mentioned this isn't very hard to do.
Overall there is really nothing I can think of to recommend this game at this point, previous versions weren't great but at least posed a challenge that I kept coming back to try to beat every now and then, even if I should have probably spent the time playing better games, now it doesn't even have that.

Space Distant is a retro-styled version of Space Invaders.
There's not a lot to it - just the usual case of shoot down the aliens before they get you.
Some of the bigger aliens take more than one shot to kill.
Several aliens shoot diagonally.
The first boss is massive and has heat-seeking missiles
(Apparently there is a second boss - at level 15? - but I haven't got that far yet.)
Although Space Distant doesn't specify what controls the game uses, after having spent thousands of dollars on exhaustive research and private investigators, I can now reveal that they are:
Spacebar = shoot
Arrow keys = move left and right
This game is not one you would want to play over and over again.
But, then again, it has achievements, so you might want to play it a few times to get those.
It's a cheap game, just under a dollar, so you can't go too wrong with it - however, considering how basic it is, I would have thought that 50 cents would be more reasonable.
For a cheap game it's ok, but nothing more than that.
