When I bought this I put 5 hours into it over a week period and haven't played it in a month. All the game is, is hiding in a dark spot waiting for a enemy pattern to change, and sometimes getting caught and insta killed by the alien. I don't fear getting caught by the alien in the slightest bit. I fear having to reload a checkpoint and do a bunch of work over again if it catches me, and that isn't fun at all. Sometimes you craft things you use to distract enemies. Sometimes you hack a computer or wall system. Sometimes you read useless emails and logs. Every single thing I mentioned is all there is to do. I got a pistol but failed to see the point and rarely used it because what is the point when the last thing you ever want to do is draw attention since your character is beyond helpless. Here is my main complaint: if the game was dark, scary, and intense, it would be more tolerable, maybe even fun. It isn't scary save for maybe one jump scare in the 5 hours I played, and a lot of it just seems comical, like the way the androids look. Their shape, size, and look is just comical. They don't strike fear in me other than the fear of having to reload from a checkpoint if one catches me, else I get to run from them, find a room and hide in a locker, wait a minute or so, and try sneaking around them again. In other words, usually reloading a checkpoint is quicker, plus you don't lose life that way. The size and art design of all enemies and characters, scale and design of levels, and overall feel of the game just make it look soft and rounded and pleasant, rather than dreary and dreadful. It was impossible to take the game seriously even for a single second. It just looks comical to me.
Nothing about any of this so far has been more than decently fun. More of a waiting simulator than anything. I may be a action game junkie for life, but I also love slower stealth games, like Outlast or the newest Thief game. I even enjoy Deus Ex Human Revolution much better when I go stealth instead of guns blazing. But this is just agonizingly slow, not tense, not scary, and highly non-eventful especially when you have to run from something, hide for a minute or so, then come back to try to get through the section you were just at. If I ever finish it I will have to force myself.
I know I am in the minority but honestly the game just isn't tense or scary. It is more comical than anything. Plus I heard that when you get the flamethrower the game is cake after that. This game could have been done better, but imo falls short of what it should have been. TL;DR: If you're looking for a game that gives the original Alien movie a welcome and accurate reflection of what Alien games should be like, look no further. Visually stunning, great soundtrack, fantastic environments, decent AI, but slightly repetitive and supported by a life-less cast. If you can live with that you'll be in for treat!
Just as the 1979 movie, Alien Isolation presents the player with a corporate future that feels weary, exhausted and broken in ways that are all too familiar in the Alien universe created by Ridley Scott and H.R. Giger. This is a place that feels lived in, and the visuals rise to the challenge brilliantly. The lighting is superb, and the moments when a rare window offers a view of the vacuum outside are breathtaking. This is a game during which you'll spend a lot of time frozen in fear, hiding from certain death - but you're just as likely to find yourself stopped in your tracks to admire the scenery. Especially towards the last third of the game, the set pieces shine, and the sense of being alone in this massive space station really sink in, while you try to fight for your life, from androids, humans and the alien.
Gameplay wise, the game is very easy to pick up, and once you get used to the evasion mechanics and how the scanners and puzzles work it'll feel like second nature. While a controller is recommended, it works just as well with a standard keyboard & mouse combo. Occasionally, you are asked to press a number of buttons at the same time, while trying to look around if anyone is coming or hearing you. This adds to the tension, but at times just feels frustrating when you have to unlock the 20th door or switch off the 30th generator.
The crafting system, is simple, but easy to follow and enables you to create distractions against enemies in a pinch. While you will come back to it every now and then, trying to find the right materials is a bit of a chore, especially when you're already trying to stay hidden. But, they offer a sense of strategy, and they make the game "fun", especially if you try to lure raiders towards the alien or try to see what happens when you lock the shutters after thworing a molotov cocktail into a room of androids and facehuggers.
It is a long game, and on occasion you will have to do some serious back-tracking (make sure you use the motion tracker's ability to show you the shortest way to your objective, you'll thank me later!) The game's elongated feel isn't helped by the (seriously) bland supporting characters, who exist mostly to tell Ripley where to go, rather than really feeling as immersive as Sevastopol. The voice acting ranges from "fantastic" to "bland" and the character models and animation don't match up to the high visual standard set elsewhere. Doesn't mean they are bad, but they feel slow, static, misplaced.
Overall though, it is one of the best games I have played in a while, it is refreshing to see something different, something where weapons are only as useful as keeping you alive (a bit), I love the freeform AI of the alien, the tension it creates, the scale of the station, the visually stunning environments and a fantastic soundtrack - ignore the backtracking and the bland characters, just pick it up, play it, enjoy it!

I'd been playing a lot of small games before I started this one, which highlighted the contrast between an indie and AAA approach to this sort of gameplay. That contrast is primarily notable in the way story is handled; Dishonored 2 inadvertently makes a strong case against story in video games.
It's not just that the story is terrible, although I want to make it very clear that the story IS terrible; there are no recognizable beats, no memorable moments, and not a single character I cared about even a little. It almost defies the definition of a story, except I haven't yet encountered another word that sums up "long periods of other characters talking at me."
But the story's primary sin isn't how boring it is. It's that the approach to story actively inhibits the game as experience. Because the game is a fine experience, or it could be. It tells you that there's no right or wrong approach, and that'd be cool if it were true, but it also very clearly underlines that a violent approach will make the world terrible, and so if you want the "good story," you'd best play nice. Which is a shame, because all the coolest stuff in the game involves violence. The swordplay is fantastic. There are SUPER COOL ways to murder people. But you should probably just put them to sleep or teach them a lesson or make them gibbering idiots (which is better somehow, I guess?), because you don't want to create chaos and make the world awful.
There are two ways that Dishonored games disincentivize "going loud" - the story carrot, which I hate, and the chaos stick, which I like. It totally makes sense that enemies beef up their defenses if you start dropping a lot of bodies, and it almost makes more sense that there are more vermin (although really, I'm not doing THAT much killing...). But this isn't a complex RPG where there are multiple choices with divergent and often ambiguous outcomes. This is a game that gives you options, but is CLEARLY judging you for taking the fun ones.
This was the thing I didn't love about Dishonored, and since Dishonored 2 is absolutely exactly the same game, it's what I don't love about Dishonored 2. It makes play feel like a chore.
When I think about other similar games, even AAA titles, there are so many better ways to handle this. MGS V had its own terrible story, but the enemy's adaptation to your tactics was rad, and at least the story had nothing to do with your actions. Hitman has always disincentivized bloody approaches, moreso in the most recent version, because firefights are hard and being a silent assassin is cool, but again, you don't have an option to reform your targets, and it doesn't pretend it has an important story. Deus Ex, which is another series that takes its story very seriously, gives you lots of little choices, and at least gives you a financial incentive to throw out your non-lethal weapons if you're playing nice-guy. And plenty of other little indie games where you kill things give you the barest framework of story to frame the essential killing action that's the center of the game. Dishonored 2 is very much a sequence of decent experiences framed around a "dynamic" "story," and it's so much weaker for it.
Maybe the fault lies with me; the game DOES at least give me the option to skip the cut scenes, but if a game is so story-focused, I wish it would put as much energy into said story as it does into the lovely environments and (mostly skipped) gameplay.
For the record, I experienced none of the technical troubles that plagued others, and the game looks fantastic. I'd say wait for it to go on deep discount, play violently, and completely ignore the stupid story.

After seeing the torrent of disparaging and complaining reviews about Dishonored 2, I finally bought it on a half off sale. Going in, here are my specs:
ASRock Z77 Extreme4
I5-2500k @ 4.3GHz
18GB DDR3 1600MHz RAM
RX 480 OC+ Nitro (8GB)
7200RPM HDD
With such dated specs, I was afraid the game was going to run like a slug. To my surprise it ran quite acceptably with the following settings:
1920x1200 (16:10)
+5 FOV
Texture Detail: Ultra
Character Detail: Very High
Water Details: Medium
Environment Detail: Very High
Shadow Quality: High
Decal Quality: High
Fog Quality: High
PP AA: TXAA 1x
TXAA Sharpness: 10
Bloom: Yes
Camera Motion Blur: No
DoF: Yes
Lens Flare: No
Light Shafts: Yes
Rat Shadows: Yes
Bloodfly Shadows: Yes
Triple Buffering: Off
HBAO+: Yes
As you can see, mostly high, with some strategic quality culling due to dated hardware. Ran fine, mostly hitched on loading screens, but once the engine was done buffering, levels were pretty smooth I would say. Therefore, I have to say that either Arkane has fixed much of the issues plaguing the game on release, or people expect too much out of their hardware. I'm personally inclined to go with two, but who knows.
Story itself was interesting and kept me interested in the characters, which is rare since I'm quite jaded with game plots after 20 years of gaming. A few interesting and less seen mechanics were sprinkled in which I enjoyed. Didn't feel too difficult on "Hard" but the AI was sharp enough to force me to save scum quite a bit. Some sluggish controls combined with character "stickiness" to environment led to a few dozen frustrated quick loads, but the game was mostly quite good in this regard. Lots of stuff to find, plenty of filler lore to keep you busy if you swing that way. Audio design was quite brilliant which is always worth applauding, many games ignore this part but in Dishonored 2, you really get an earful of nice music and form fitting aural treats. Another aspect worthy of praise was environment design. Even though the graphics are stylized and so people have oversized heads, facial features, hands etc, the buildings and architecture over all were just magnificent to behold. Places felt as if someone lived in them. Really wonderful stuff. Going to go through the game a second time now after about 30 hours first time around, interesting to see how that changes the outcomes.
All in all, I definitely recommend this if you can get it on sale. Now, I say that as someone who is very stingy. If you generally don't mind dropping 60 bucks on some typical AAA title on launch, then you definitely want to get this game.

Prepare to die all over again, in this great sequal.
Dark Souls 2 is a great game in its own right. The game is as mysterious and wonderous as the first, if not more, with the addition of much lore that expands on the fantastic universe of Dark Souls. Many theories abound and many connections to be made, but, thats what makes the lore so much fun, eh?
As for the game itself: The graphics are beautiful, the PC port is made so much better than its predecesor, and the game is similarly punishing, as is to be expected from any of the "Souls" games. However, in my own opinion: it seems slightly easier than Dark Souls 1 (my own experiences). It seems that they removed a bit of the "grinding" from DaS1 (farming souls in Tomb of the Giants for hours, anyone?), and made the game a bit more linear (the overworld is not as interconnected as DaS1 was, barely any shortcuts / backdoors to open to get to the end of the zone easier). They also added a "Soul Memory" system that seems to be a mixed blessing for PvP purposes. I do not PvP myself, so don't take my word for it.
I didn't use (online) summon signs very much in Dark Souls 1 (mainly for fear of being invaded, I am rather bad at PvP), but I found myself using them quite a bit in 2 (I got invaded very rarely, mainly towards the end of the game, even if I was running around human most of the time). Not because the bosses are tough to beat (most seem pretty simple to understand and beat, but there are a few that are pretty annoying), but because it was just a fun aspect to the game (in my opinion). Multiplayer is much smoother to engage in, and there is also a new summon sign that lets you summon (or be summoned) to other players, even if the area boss is cleared. A nice little addition if you wanted to farm an area with some friends or something.
In addition, they generalized bonfire warping right from the get-go. A really interesting change to say the least. I remember running around the world in Dark Souls 1 for hours, just trying to farm souls for something I wanted to buy / upgrade, and running back to the NPC. It is really great to be able to warp to ANY bonfire you have activated (as opposed to only a select few as in DaS1). Also, handy recovery items have been added, in addition to the Estus Flask (which is almost non-existant in the beginning of the game).
I was sad that Pyromancy is not a class / school of magic that you can use right at the beginning (like picking the Pyromancer class from Dark Souls 1). You have to find it later in the game. But boy... it is lots of fun now, especially if you love lots of explosions.
These changes were a bit surprising, but I still found the game extremely enjoyable and difficult (yay!).
Overall, the game is a great sequal to its legendary predecesor. If you loved Dark Souls 1, or even Demon Souls, then this game is a must-play.

I think it's best to leave at the end of the first entry in the series.  Much of the interesting ideas the series presents have been explored, the characters have grown, the world is saved and there's a bittersweet note that provides some great texture and complexity.
But mostly, it's the main character Rufus.  Throughout the first game he becomes more and more insufferable.  It's endearing at first, but near the end it starts to become exhausting.  By the start of this sequel, he gets to the point of being completely intolerable.  He abandons any growth he might have attained in the first game, and devolves to even more of a jackaninny than he ever was.  While it's obvious they're trying to channel Guybrush Threepwood, it crosses some hard to define line at some point where it's just not funny anymore.  Perhaps it's when he causes even more irreversable brain damage to the woman he claims to love (in addition to the damage he'd done previously) for a lollypop.

The size and art design of all enemies and characters, scale and design of levels, and overall feel of the game just make it look soft and rounded and pleasant, rather than dreary and dreadful. I'd been playing a lot of small games before I started this one, which highlighted the contrast between an indie and AAA approach to this sort of gameplay. That contrast is primarily notable in the way story is handled; Dishonored 2 inadvertently makes a strong case against story in video games.
It's not just that the story is terrible, although I want to make it very clear that the story IS terrible; there are no recognizable beats, no memorable moments, and not a single character I cared about even a little. It almost defies the definition of a story, except I haven't yet encountered another word that sums up "long periods of other characters talking at me."
But the story's primary sin isn't how boring it is. It's that the approach to story actively inhibits the game as experience. Because the game is a fine experience, or it could be. It tells you that there's no right or wrong approach, and that'd be cool if it were true, but it also very clearly underlines that a violent approach will make the world terrible, and so if you want the "good story," you'd best play nice. Which is a shame, because all the coolest stuff in the game involves violence. The swordplay is fantastic. There are SUPER COOL ways to murder people. But you should probably just put them to sleep or teach them a lesson or make them gibbering idiots (which is better somehow, I guess?), because you don't want to create chaos and make the world awful.
There are two ways that Dishonored games disincentivize "going loud" - the story carrot, which I hate, and the chaos stick, which I like. It totally makes sense that enemies beef up their defenses if you start dropping a lot of bodies, and it almost makes more sense that there are more vermin (although really, I'm not doing THAT much killing...). But this isn't a complex RPG where there are multiple choices with divergent and often ambiguous outcomes. This is a game that gives you options, but is CLEARLY judging you for taking the fun ones.
This was the thing I didn't love about Dishonored, and since Dishonored 2 is absolutely exactly the same game, it's what I don't love about Dishonored 2. It makes play feel like a chore.
When I think about other similar games, even AAA titles, there are so many better ways to handle this. MGS V had its own terrible story, but the enemy's adaptation to your tactics was rad, and at least the story had nothing to do with your actions. Hitman has always disincentivized bloody approaches, moreso in the most recent version, because firefights are hard and being a silent assassin is cool, but again, you don't have an option to reform your targets, and it doesn't pretend it has an important story. Deus Ex, which is another series that takes its story very seriously, gives you lots of little choices, and at least gives you a financial incentive to throw out your non-lethal weapons if you're playing nice-guy. And plenty of other little indie games where you kill things give you the barest framework of story to frame the essential killing action that's the center of the game. Dishonored 2 is very much a sequence of decent experiences framed around a "dynamic" "story," and it's so much weaker for it.
Maybe the fault lies with me; the game DOES at least give me the option to skip the cut scenes, but if a game is so story-focused, I wish it would put as much energy into said story as it does into the lovely environments and (mostly skipped) gameplay.
For the record, I experienced none of the technical troubles that plagued others, and the game looks fantastic. I'd say wait for it to go on deep discount, play violently, and completely ignore the stupid story.

After seeing the torrent of disparaging and complaining reviews about Dishonored 2, I finally bought it on a half off sale. Going in, here are my specs:
ASRock Z77 Extreme4
I5-2500k @ 4.3GHz
18GB DDR3 1600MHz RAM
RX 480 OC+ Nitro (8GB)
7200RPM HDD
With such dated specs, I was afraid the game was going to run like a slug. To my surprise it ran quite acceptably with the following settings:
1920x1200 (16:10)
+5 FOV
Texture Detail: Ultra
Character Detail: Very High
Water Details: Medium
Environment Detail: Very High
Shadow Quality: High
Decal Quality: High
Fog Quality: High
PP AA: TXAA 1x
TXAA Sharpness: 10
Bloom: Yes
Camera Motion Blur: No
DoF: Yes
Lens Flare: No
Light Shafts: Yes
Rat Shadows: Yes
Bloodfly Shadows: Yes
Triple Buffering: Off
HBAO+: Yes
As you can see, mostly high, with some strategic quality culling due to dated hardware. Ran fine, mostly hitched on loading screens, but once the engine was done buffering, levels were pretty smooth I would say. Therefore, I have to say that either Arkane has fixed much of the issues plaguing the game on release, or people expect too much out of their hardware. I'm personally inclined to go with two, but who knows.
Story itself was interesting and kept me interested in the characters, which is rare since I'm quite jaded with game plots after 20 years of gaming. A few interesting and less seen mechanics were sprinkled in which I enjoyed. Didn't feel too difficult on "Hard" but the AI was sharp enough to force me to save scum quite a bit. Some sluggish controls combined with character "stickiness" to environment led to a few dozen frustrated quick loads, but the game was mostly quite good in this regard. Lots of stuff to find, plenty of filler lore to keep you busy if you swing that way. Audio design was quite brilliant which is always worth applauding, many games ignore this part but in Dishonored 2, you really get an earful of nice music and form fitting aural treats. Another aspect worthy of praise was environment design. Even though the graphics are stylized and so people have oversized heads, facial features, hands etc, the buildings and architecture over all were just magnificent to behold. Places felt as if someone lived in them. Really wonderful stuff. Going to go through the game a second time now after about 30 hours first time around, interesting to see how that changes the outcomes.
All in all, I definitely recommend this if you can get it on sale. Now, I say that as someone who is very stingy. If you generally don't mind dropping 60 bucks on some typical AAA title on launch, then you definitely want to get this game.

TL;DR: If you're looking for a game that gives the original Alien movie a welcome and accurate reflection of what Alien games should be like, look no further. Visually stunning, great soundtrack, fantastic environments, decent AI, but slightly repetitive and supported by a life-less cast. If you can live with that you'll be in for treat!
Just as the 1979 movie, Alien Isolation presents the player with a corporate future that feels weary, exhausted and broken in ways that are all too familiar in the Alien universe created by Ridley Scott and H.R. Giger. This is a place that feels lived in, and the visuals rise to the challenge brilliantly. The lighting is superb, and the moments when a rare window offers a view of the vacuum outside are breathtaking. This is a game during which you'll spend a lot of time frozen in fear, hiding from certain death - but you're just as likely to find yourself stopped in your tracks to admire the scenery. Especially towards the last third of the game, the set pieces shine, and the sense of being alone in this massive space station really sink in, while you try to fight for your life, from androids, humans and the alien.
Gameplay wise, the game is very easy to pick up, and once you get used to the evasion mechanics and how the scanners and puzzles work it'll feel like second nature. While a controller is recommended, it works just as well with a standard keyboard & mouse combo. Occasionally, you are asked to press a number of buttons at the same time, while trying to look around if anyone is coming or hearing you. This adds to the tension, but at times just feels frustrating when you have to unlock the 20th door or switch off the 30th generator.
The crafting system, is simple, but easy to follow and enables you to create distractions against enemies in a pinch. While you will come back to it every now and then, trying to find the right materials is a bit of a chore, especially when you're already trying to stay hidden. But, they offer a sense of strategy, and they make the game "fun", especially if you try to lure raiders towards the alien or try to see what happens when you lock the shutters after thworing a molotov cocktail into a room of androids and facehuggers.
It is a long game, and on occasion you will have to do some serious back-tracking (make sure you use the motion tracker's ability to show you the shortest way to your objective, you'll thank me later!) The game's elongated feel isn't helped by the (seriously) bland supporting characters, who exist mostly to tell Ripley where to go, rather than really feeling as immersive as Sevastopol. The voice acting ranges from "fantastic" to "bland" and the character models and animation don't match up to the high visual standard set elsewhere. Doesn't mean they are bad, but they feel slow, static, misplaced.
Overall though, it is one of the best games I have played in a while, it is refreshing to see something different, something where weapons are only as useful as keeping you alive (a bit), I love the freeform AI of the alien, the tension it creates, the scale of the station, the visually stunning environments and a fantastic soundtrack - ignore the backtracking and the bland characters, just pick it up, play it, enjoy it!

ROME II
Constructive Criticism
As a longtime fan of the TW series, I felt compelled to write this letter to express my concern with the direction and design of the series. Note that I am not here to complain about technical glitches or launch failures as I bought the title at a 75% discount on steam AFTER the Empire Edition update was released.
•	The philosophy of Day 1 DLC that is free when preordered is not appreciated by gamers who want to wait to see if the game is something they would be interested in buying. It’s even worse when the game is broken on launch, but I will not get into that because I am sure you have heard enough about that fiasco.
•	Also, considering that the factions in said DLC were included in the prequel (Rome I) at no additional cost, and were an iconic part of that game (Sparta) , it just feels underhanded to chop them out of the core game. It makes Rome II inferior in that regard and a sequel should never have less content than the original.
•	The Blood and Gore DLC should not be DLC, it should be a menu option that comes included in the game. I only bought it after both the game and the Blood and Gore DLC was steeply discounted (I am starting to regret it based on principle). Nothing shouts that this game was released and sold in pieces than, “ hey you bought this epic war game… wanna see the blood? Buy the DLC….”  NOT appreciated.
•	The campaign map in Rome II is not an improvement over previous titles. It is cluttered, confusing, and not easier to navigate and use. For example, the settlements that take up significant chunks of the map are just unnecessary. It isn’t cool and does not add value to the game. It’s a visual aesthetic that makes the most utilitarian part of the game (campaign strategy) more confusing. Rome I, Medieval 2, Shogun, those have acceptable maps.
•	The structure of regions and settlements is unnecessarily leveled and complex. One city per region just like Medevil 2 would be the best. It’s simple to keep track of where you are building/recruiting units.
•	The interfaces to manage the empire are so broken I don’t know where to begin.  First, the way the menus LOOK is awful. Clear/grey transparent kills the mood of managing an empire, go back to scrolls/paper something more artistic than operating system boxes.
o	Secondly, the way the menus operate logically seems haphazard. Stuff is all over the place and quite frankly should not be this foreign to someone who has played as much total war as myself.  Again, look to improve on previous titles, not scrap what was really good and make something totally new. Don’t fix what was not broken. Medieval 2 had an excellent Empire Management System.
•	The unit icons/techs/everything has this weird roman hieroglyphic style that is an eyesore. It’s hard to tell what the heck anything is. Not cool and hinders the enjoyment of the game.
•	Family tree? We need to care about our characters, see who their grandfathers were, so on so forth. It’s just a good part of the game that isn’t there.
•	Nation ranking statistics are nowhere to be found.
•	Politics feature in empire was unnecessary and in Rome II it is just confusing and not fun. I can’t stand to look at it/ Be brought to care what it is for.

So far the Deponia franchise is definitely keeping up appearances.
I played and reviewed the first game in the series and honestly do not remember having one bad thing to say about it. I’m glad to be able to say that the same goes for its sequel.
In the first review I said that with some point and click games it can be hard to follow the creators logic when it comes to item combination and puzzles, which more often than not, results in rummaging through a walkthrough at least once or twice and asking you’re self “how was I even supposed to get that?” but with these games it isn’t like that. It is consistently logically throughout the whole game and that definitely applies to Chaos on Deponia as well. Although I found this second game a little more challenging when it came to figuring out what to use with what, (it was either  a harder game or my brain was just refusing to work, which wouldn’t be surprising) I also found it quite a bit more humorous.
The sense of humour in these games is a particular part about them that I enjoy the most. The main character is as egotistical yet loveable as ever and there’s some funny references in there that make you chuckle as you play through.
Art wise, it is a beautiful as ever. Maybe even more so than last time, you can tell there was a bit of a leap in budget for the game when you switch from the first to the second. Same goes for audio, there is a huge difference when it comes to audio, it sounds a lot clearer and sharper than before, which is a nice addition to the game as a whole.
They focus a little more on water rather than land in this one, and I really liked that. There were points during the game where I couldn’t help but just think to myself, “Wow, the graphics for the water look really good.”
Of course, I have to quickly mention the chorus singers. What would the Deponia experience be without them? I love them, they are amazing. I look forward to every song between chapters.
And lastly, the achievements which I seem to like enough to have played through this game 2 and a half times. (The half because I forgot one measly achievement on my second “achievement gathering” play through.) The achievements definitely aren’t as obvious as they were in the first one, at least that’s how it seemed to me. With the first game I managed to get most of the achievements on the first play through just from general curiosity. This one I managed to miss quite a lot, which even then, although I missed a lot more, it definitely wasn’t as hard as getting all the achievements for the first one. Anyone that has played the first one would know that there was one pesky achievement to try and get, the “Droggeljug” mode achievement. When I started Chaos on Deponia I crossed my fingers and hoped so hard that there wasn’t a similar achievement in this game, and I was in luck!
All in all it is a really fun point and click game with a lot to offer. Any fan of the genre would enjoy this franchise. I have heard that a few people didn’t enjoy it because of the main characters stuck up and self-centred ways, and believe me, when I started the franchise I felt the same. But if you can get over that first hurdle in the first game, I promise you he really starts to grow on you as he progresses and grows as a character.
I have yet to play the next one, and I have no doubt that it will tie up the franchise nicely.
TL;DR : Logical item combinations, great humour, wonderful art, engaging story, an improvement audio/graphics wise from the first one, a great way to continue the series and just generally a great game for your point and click collection. Buy the series!

Deponia, the original, was varied as far as point-and-click adventure games go. There were many areas to explore. There was a good sense of progression. Maybe, there were a few puzzles in there that were a tad too cryptic, but you know, it was a memorable game simply because of how it all felt when it was over.
Choas on Deponia is memorable for the same reason, but this time, it doesn't feel good.
It feels painful.
Excrutiatingly painful.

That's just a bit too much to deal with, esspecially when the objects blend in with the background.
So this one part here at the beginning sounds, you know, pretty annoying, but at LEAST it's short, right?
No.

I don't remember the first game being like that. I remember it being fun and fair, not this overly-slow, cryptic trudge through samey diners, alleys, and laboratories.

ROME II
Constructive Criticism
As a longtime fan of the TW series, I felt compelled to write this letter to express my concern with the direction and design of the series. Note that I am not here to complain about technical glitches or launch failures as I bought the title at a 75% discount on steam AFTER the Empire Edition update was released.
•	The philosophy of Day 1 DLC that is free when preordered is not appreciated by gamers who want to wait to see if the game is something they would be interested in buying. It’s even worse when the game is broken on launch, but I will not get into that because I am sure you have heard enough about that fiasco.
•	Also, considering that the factions in said DLC were included in the prequel (Rome I) at no additional cost, and were an iconic part of that game (Sparta) , it just feels underhanded to chop them out of the core game. It makes Rome II inferior in that regard and a sequel should never have less content than the original.
•	The Blood and Gore DLC should not be DLC, it should be a menu option that comes included in the game. I only bought it after both the game and the Blood and Gore DLC was steeply discounted (I am starting to regret it based on principle). Nothing shouts that this game was released and sold in pieces than, “ hey you bought this epic war game… wanna see the blood? Buy the DLC….”  NOT appreciated.
•	The campaign map in Rome II is not an improvement over previous titles. It is cluttered, confusing, and not easier to navigate and use. For example, the settlements that take up significant chunks of the map are just unnecessary. It isn’t cool and does not add value to the game. It’s a visual aesthetic that makes the most utilitarian part of the game (campaign strategy) more confusing. Rome I, Medieval 2, Shogun, those have acceptable maps.
•	The structure of regions and settlements is unnecessarily leveled and complex. One city per region just like Medevil 2 would be the best. It’s simple to keep track of where you are building/recruiting units.
•	The interfaces to manage the empire are so broken I don’t know where to begin.  First, the way the menus LOOK is awful. Clear/grey transparent kills the mood of managing an empire, go back to scrolls/paper something more artistic than operating system boxes.
o	Secondly, the way the menus operate logically seems haphazard. Stuff is all over the place and quite frankly should not be this foreign to someone who has played as much total war as myself.  Again, look to improve on previous titles, not scrap what was really good and make something totally new. Don’t fix what was not broken. Medieval 2 had an excellent Empire Management System.
•	The unit icons/techs/everything has this weird roman hieroglyphic style that is an eyesore. It’s hard to tell what the heck anything is. Not cool and hinders the enjoyment of the game.
•	Family tree? We need to care about our characters, see who their grandfathers were, so on so forth. It’s just a good part of the game that isn’t there.
•	Nation ranking statistics are nowhere to be found.
•	Politics feature in empire was unnecessary and in Rome II it is just confusing and not fun. I can’t stand to look at it/ Be brought to care what it is for.

My experience with this game can be summed as thus: every update I found myself testing the changes, nodding in satisfaction, then quitting the game to await the next update.
Arkane knows how to make a good game. No question. But if you film an Oscar-worthy movie and the lens is smudged while filming, you can't judge what's underneath without acknowledging what's been marring your experience the entire time.
=============================
PERFORMANCE
Everyone is aware of the performance issues, and these still persist to this day. It runs much better than at launch, where it was literally unplayable, but that's because the game looks worse than before - the most noticeable change being the extremely aggressive LOD scaling. Out of the corner of your eye you notice the shapes of window frames and posters on distant buildings morphing in shape, or the furniture at the opposite end of a long hallway suddenly blinking into existence. FPS dropped to 15 when stabbing a gravehound, so they simply removed the inky visual effect that was causing the problem instead of optimizing it.
Also, Denuvo authentication is one of the longest "loading screens" of the game. Around half a minute to a full minute or more every startup.
=============================
GAMEPLAY
For the most part, gameplay is excellent and is Dishonored's strongest suit.
Dark Vision was changed to a blurry short range sonar so unlike Dishonored 1 you aren't constantly seeing blue and yellow because you had no reason not to
AI is much smarter
Nonlethal combat options are a blast
Bonecharm crafting system allows for player flexibility and "builds"
Each level feels lived-in while maintaining the duality of directive flow and open options that made the first game so good.
Emily and Corvo have distinct animations and final weapon upgrades. The animations are supremely cool.
Each level is fairly distinct, some with extremely interesting central "gimmicks." I do, however, wish the game relied less on them and had more "regular" areas.
However, under the hood lie other problems. Most of them are quality-of-life issues:
Gone are the hotkeys for journal, inventory, bonecharms, powers. Only one "journal" exists now, despite still having separate subsections.
It took months for the power wheel to be fixed. It took almost a full second after activating to pop up and be usable, breaking flow so badly I almost never used it in the first place. It's finally fixed now, but this issue was glaring and it took so long to be addressed most of us played through without it fixed.
Thrown objects don't always go exactly where your crosshair is. While this adds a layer of difficulty, it feels noticeably more clunky than in the first game.
Mana regen is pitifully slow. From using a power to fully regenerating, Dishonored 1's time is 4.7 seconds -> 3.1 seconds with Spiritual Pool. Dishonored 2's time with 4x Spiritual Pool is 6.3s -> 5.5s. The devs said they fixed this effect, but it was only made worse.
Bugs. Street speakers not playing. Dying after possessing gravehounds. An arc pylon never shutting down after pulling out its power, leaving it to either be dangerous to you to dangerous to your nonlethal playthrough. Some of these still aren't fixed.
=============================
STORY AND ATMOSPHERE
Reactivity
Great. My favorite part of Dishonored. You need to hide from a gang member to access a certain black market shop, and there are different scenarios and dialogue for if you hide, if you run into him outside, kill him outside, or kill him inside.
Emily and Corvo
Emily and Corvo are voiced. And... they don't talk enough. It's good that they're silent for most of the game, but there are times when you come across a portrait or photograph with an "Inspect" prompt. I'd love to hear Emily's thoughts on the High Overseer as see how that compares to Corvo's, or if it changes based on whether or not you accept the Outsider's Mark. Instead, all I get is the protagonist muttering the name of the person pictured. What's the point? Might as well keep them silent.
It made sense to me to play Emily first, but her story felt lackluster, like people at every turn were saying "check your royal privilege" despite my efforts to resolve everyone's problems without drawing blood. Corvo's is MUCH more interesting as a veteran of Dishonored 1.
The Outsider and The Void
I hate the new Outsider and his new voice. He felt threatening and malicious in the first game due to how calm and composed he was, and the Void felt like a strange and otherworldly place. The vignettes of Dunwall made it feel both unnatural and unnerving yet fundamentally woven into the universe. In Dishonored 2, it's just smoky blackness and sharp rocks. The Outsider is much jollier and moves around erratically, making grandiose hand gestures. They actually had a plot plot that could explain this change, but it was never addressed, so it just seems like a pointless retcon to me.
Main Plot
Dishonored's worldbuilding was always one of its appeals, and that remains true in Dishonored 2. However, the villains felt lackluster. Only the main villain has a real presence throughout the game, whereas everyone else feels introduced abruptly only to fall by your hand, all within the same mission. In Dishonored 1 everything felt personal and real. Perhaps it was because of the long intro where you interacted with most of them, or the Hound Pits's cast of characters all having different connections to your targets.
=============================
As you can see, I've played this game a LOT and have put a lot of thought into it. It was definitely worth all those hours and all that money, but the condition it was at launch and the sluggish drip-feed of support we barely get now is unacceptable. To set a precedent for future games, I can't recommend buying this unless they manage to fix all the performance issues and bugs, which doesn't seem to be happening anytime soon.

tl;dr -
I played through the entirety of JC2 on highest difficulty; spent 23 hours on it. I'm bored with JC3 after 6 hours.
I clicked "has received product for free" since I played this via family sharing from my bro's library.
It appears Avalanche Studios had a lucky hit with JC2 and don't understand what was fun about it.
JC3 is ubisoftified. They managed to make chaos boring.
The first half hour of gameplay is constant stop and go. Click for 10 seconds, watch a cutscene for 30.
The story takes itself more serious than JC2, which was over the top B movie.
The movement is still nice and it's even better with the addition of the wingsuit.
You now have tethers which you can retract. They're OP and a lot of fun initially. I thought pulling helicopters to the ground would never get old, but it does.
You have to "free" settlements by terrorizing them and destroying stuff.
A repetitive task since every settlement entails doing the same stuff over and over again.
The game has an incredible draw distance (just like JC2), yet enemies do not spawn further away than a certain (rather close) distance.
Get a sniper's gun at a base and you can't even empty the clip. The base looks empty! Move a little bit and have some soldiers spawn on you.
The enemy AI doesn't look good. The soldiers stand around letting you snipe them (supposedly they haven't seen me yet, but they also do not come to investigate any of the explosions). I once saw them shooting at a wall during a mission.
If I grapple  onto a helicopter, they shoot me with rockets before I take it over - yes they shoot their own helicopters with explosives.
I once had a soldier slowly drive his jeep into me, while we were in combat. He wanted to get to some point first before he got out and he didn't want to drive me over.
The largest base on the small island that you start on is off limits. If you go there, you get a 30m radius explosion on you every 5 seconds.
I googled a bit and it seems I'm supposed to take out some other base first (which I haven't discovered yet) to deactivate the air strikes. The game doesn't tell me this.
Regenerating health fits the game, but it's bad design to not tell the player how much HP he has left. The only indication is the saturation of the screen. Good luck guessing how many more shots you can take.
I took over an outpost by blowing up the same red objects as everywhere else and I get a "frenzy" mini game where I'm supposed to blow up the same objects with a timer and score multiplier. Talk about repetition.
Once you shoot down that last object, the base IMMEDIATELY spawns friendly forces. It's jarring and doesn't allow you to take a look at the destruction. I once took over a small outpost by accident (it only had two red destructible objects) and I'm not entirely sure whether the helicopter I took down was friend or foe (there are helicopters with red and blue colors, so you only know when it shoots at you).
You can have multiple items dropped by spending beacons (once you unlock those items), but I can't get a helicopter + guns since the guns don't spawn, yet the game does let me choose guns + a vehicle. (The game has been out 7 months now and this isn't fixed).
I once took down a huge antenna and it despawned before it hit the ground. Where's the fun in that?

I've been following Black Mesa since 2004. I downloaded the mod version when it released, and picked up the retail version during the summer sale. Recreating the original Half-Life is no easy feat, truly, and the Crowbar Collective team really outdid themselves here. The game looks, sounds, and feels like the original Half-Life (especially if you download some mods to replace the soundtrack with the original Half-Life music). However, the game suffers from a variety of problems that feel unbecoming of a retail game, and hopefully these are fixed before the final release. Most noteably, here are some of the issues I experienced during my play-through:
-Grenades to not land anywhere near my crosshair when thrown. They veer waaaay off to the right for some reason, rendering them effectively useless.
-The laser guide on the RPG only works about 1/3 of the time.
-Some shoddy design choices are carried over from the original Half-Life, and made even worse by the updated level of detail (way too many buttons are lit up but don't actually do anything), which left me scratching my head as to why they were included.
-Residue Processing still sucks. A lot. Which I guess could be seen as a negative or a positive. On the one hand, really boring and tedious level with annoying platforming puzzles. On the other hand, that's pretty faithful to the spirit of the original level. So. I'm mixed on this one.
-Lambda Core is still really ♥♥♥♥ing confusing. This is a problem that carries over from the mod release, and could easily be fixed if you made the levers we actually
to switch a bit more prominent instead of hiding them nearby a cluttered control panel
. The design of this level needs to be seriously streamlined, because in its current state it is little more than tedious and frustrating.
-The game likes to drop down to ~5-10 FPS during random sections, and will remain that way until I manage to exit a section, leading me to believe there is some sort of problem with specific rooms and their scripting or whatever it is that causes a game to dip to ~5-10 FPS for no apparent reason. It also liked to crash sometimes when I killed a bullsquid?
-The mortar launcher in Surface Tension would for some reason fire about 20 feet off from where my targets were places. It took me about 20 minutes to shoot the radio tower so I could advance.
-I really wish there was an option to disable the blood on the guns/player arms. It does not look good at all. (Although this one is more of a nitpick)
-The sounds of the MP5 is really bad.
Other than those issues though, this is a solid 110 hours of nostalgiac wish fulfillment. It remakes the original Half-Life in a way that feels both old and new, and is probably the best (and only) Half-Life game that we'll be getting for some time.
Nice game! I enjoy the new graphics so much! Keep on working on it! Please! :)
Brilliant remake of the classic Half Life! 10/10

*Note:  It still isn't fully finished at the time of my writing this, so there are some bugs to work out, and they are yet to release, but I feel like I have a fairly complete impression of the product.
Over-all rating: 10/10 - Obviously this isn't the best game ever made - this is a remake, and it is exactly the remake that everyone who loves half-life has been asking for.
Adding just enough original content into the mix to make it interesting to revisit for players of the original, but keeping it mostly as close as possibly to the original game to induce nostalgia and provide the original experience to new players - this is a total success.
Economy: 7/10 - The price is acceptable, it's not great, but it isn't bad. 20 bucks for a remake always makes you sit there and wonder if it is worth it or not - I would probably have priced it around 10 or 15 max, but I can live with the price.
Replayability: 6/10 - I doubt I'll ever replay this game. For me, it's a one-time trip down memory-lane. However, the addition of things like achievements and the new content in the game - these are all things that contribute to the replayability of this title - if not for me, then perhaps for a lot of other people. The game also features multiplayer, so there's that.
Closing statement: If you liked half-life and you liked half-life 2 as well, then chances are you will like this game at least half as much as you liked either of those games - or possibly twice as much.
It really is the original half-life game in a prettier package.
The voice-acting is so good, I could have sworn it was better than the original game and felt entirely authentic and original - the only thing that feels a bit corny is the voice acting of the "Marines" - while the script-writing for the Marines is pretty much excellent (or at least fully adequate), the actual voice-actors sound a bit too "gruntish" - but that is incidentally also how I remember them from the original Half-life game, but that is perhaps a thing they could have improved on, given the chance.
I'm not sure I like how the Male Black-Ops enemies were taken out, and the changes made to the Female Black-Ops enemies (I find them somewhat ridiculous now, compared to the original game where they were just mysterious). That has to be the ONLY thing I don't like about the game so far.
They removed the "long-jump" function, because the half-life 2 engine features sprinting which duplicates the same function, entirely without taking away from the game experience.
They also removed the flash-light power-drain. The flashlight now lasts forever. This is a significant improvement of the game over the original, because the flash-light in the original game had about 30 seconds of power... I'm sure you can see how that is ridiculous.
I'm not sure how I feel about the weapon-choices.
In some versions of half-life, the "standard" weapon of the Marines was the M16 with a grenade launcher, and in others it was the MP5 submachine-gun.
I personally - entirely - prefer the M16 variant.
I also notice the game uses the Glock 17 (I think it is) instead of the Beretta model which was featured in some versions of Half-life. I also preferred the Beretta, as it is more authentic for the time during which the game is supposed to take place.
My only remaining beef with this game would be that there are a few "scripted deaths" that you can actually prevent - except you can't. I had an experience where I saved a scientist by shooting a soldier that was going to snipe him, then the scientist panicked and ran towards a mine-field - I quickly blasted all the mines in his past, resulting in him stopping on the bare ground with no mines around, and just exploding on his own.
Obviously, the game is still in development, but things like this bugs me purely because of how finished the game feels!
Really, it is, if anything a testimony to the success of this game that I find myself complaining over such matters.

For anyone interested in games that bring back the oldschool feel of actually accomplishing something, the Dark Souls series is definitely one to look in to. Frustrating, yes, especially when at times, with each step you take forward, the game will push you several steps back. It will make you scream with frustration, but, gives you that very small (yet visible) glimmer of hope that for as long as you keep trying, victory will be yours. And beleive me, it never loses its feel (even after several playthroughs).
I've played the first one (sadly i did not finish it), and must say that the first was a lot more challenging than the second installment. Don't be fooled though, slip up once and this game will still have you for breakfast. The dark, ominous feel of the game is still pretty much there. Graphics wise, Dark Souls 2 won't disappoint, and while i may not be an expert where GPU's are concerned, i would dare say, that from an artistic point of view, the game is visually beautiful.
How about the story? Well, let's just say, that's up to you. Because depending on how much you want to explore or uncover, you'll be able to get more out of what Dark Souls 2 is, compared to others. Gameplay is as challenging as ever, as Dark Souls can present you with hundreds of different scenarios and outcomes depending on your actions (especially on how you approach the situation).
Gameplay, story, Visuals, weapons, armors, shields, combos, items, builds, magic, secrets and the special trademark difficulty of From Software - All of these combined to give gamers, who are looking for a challenge, something that will sate and satisfy their appetites for quite some time.

To begin with, I'm not good at doing reviews, but I'll try to say what I think about the game.
People say it's the worst among all "souls" games, and well, probably it is.
Still, it's the souls game I played the most, the one I've had the most fun playing, and the one that made me spend the most hours.
To be honest, I can't really tell why, maybe it's because of the balanced PVP (if you compare it to other souls games), or maybe it's because of the huge amount of builds you can make.
Or maybe it's just because it's the first souls game I played.
Dark Souls 2 is an Action RPG made by From Software (but not made by the same team that made Dark Souls 1, Demon's Souls, Dark Souls 3 and Bloodborne, that's why it looks different).
A game with an enormous amount of weapons: swords, greatswords, axes, spears, bows, bowguns, spells and so on, that allows you to play in your own way.
You can be a mage swinging giant axes onto enemies' heads, a tanky 700kg knight walking around the world dual wielding spoons, or you could just parry and kill everything you see with your bare hands.
Lots of enemies, fun bossfights (mother♥♥♥♥ing dragon), and a huge variety of places (even tho if you compare level design to other souls games, it's just the worst).
Although at the beginning of this review I said Dark Souls 2 has got the best PVP among all souls (imho), it's still got some problems. One of these is the lag, you'll see what I mean when you'll engage a fight with a player swinging his katana on the other side of the map. And there are also some OP weapons, but that's not really a problem, every weapon has weak points, just use them.
A fun coop system that allows your friend to join your world and beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of bosses together.
- PVE: 7.5/10
- PVP: 9.0/10
- Santier's Spear: -7.0/10
- Community: 5.0/10
- Overall score: Buy the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it.

Spaghetti and Meatballs
INGREDIENTS
Sauce:
2 28-ounce cans whole peeled tomatoes in juice, drained, juice reserved, tomatoes finely chopped
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
2 medium onions, peeled, halved through root end
1/2 teaspoon (or more) salt
Meatballs:
1 cup fresh breadcrumbs made from crustless French or country-style bread
1/3 cup whole milk
8 ounces ground beef (15% fat)
8 ounces ground pork
1 cup finely ground (not grated) Parmesan cheese
1/3 cup finely chopped Italian parsley
1 teaspoon salt
1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
2 large eggs
2 large garlic cloves, pressed
1 pound spaghetti
Freshly grated Parmesan cheese (for serving)
PREPARATION
For sauce:
Combine tomatoes with juice, butter, onions, and salt in large wide pot. Bring to simmer over medium heat. Reduce heat; simmer uncovered 45 minutes, stirring occasionally. Discard onions. Using immersion blender, process sauce briefly to break up any large pieces of tomato (texture should be even but not completely smooth). Season sauce with more salt and freshly ground black pepper. Remove from heat.
For meatballs:
Combine breadcrumbs and milk in small bowl; stir until breadcrumbs are evenly moistened. Let stand 10 minutes.
Place beef and pork in large bowl and break up into small chunks. Add 1 cup ground Parmesan, parsley, salt, and pepper.
Whisk eggs to blend in small bowl; whisk in garlic. Add to meat mixture.
Using hands, squeeze milk from breadcrumbs, reserving milk. Add breadcrumbs to meat mixture. Using hands, quickly and gently mix meat mixture just until all ingredients are evenly combined (do not overmix). Chill mixture at least 15 minutes and up to 1 hour.
Moisten hands with some of reserved milk from breadcrumbs, then roll meat mixture between palms into golf-ball-size balls, occasionally moistening hands with milk as needed and arranging meatballs in single layer in sauce in pot. Bring to simmer.
Reduce heat to medium-low, cover, and simmer until meatballs are cooked through, 15 to 20 minutes. DO AHEAD: Can be made 2 days ahead. Cool slightly. Chill uncovered until cold, then cover and keep chilled. Rewarm before continuing.
Cook spaghetti in large pot of boiling salted water until just tender but still firm to bite, stirring occasionally. Drain.
Using slotted spoon, transfer meatballs to platter. Add pasta to sauce in pot and toss to coat. Divide pasta among 6 plates. Top each serving with meatballs. Sprinkle meatballs with freshly grated Parmesan cheese and serve.

We all need to set one fact about this game at Launch in 2014. The Elder Scrolls Online WAS a pretty bad game. Not that it was terrible but there was an undeveloped combat system, No crime system, No player housing, Strict Zone Leveling (you need to be a certain lvl to be in a certain zone and couldnt go to other faction's zones until you become level 50 which would ruin the whole adventure part of the game and make it a grind), 3 seperate factions that cant play together (you could only play against the other factions in Cyrodil via Pvp) ,and to put the cherry on top, you would have to buy the game and pay for a monthly subscription of 15 dollars. Hell, you could write a whole 500 word essay on what WAS wrong with this game on release, and thats what angry elder scrolls fans did and sent it to Zenimax.
Now, since Zenimax had almost 3 years to work on fixing the game, ESO is like a whole new game. The combat system is improved and addicting. They added level scaling. They added a crime system. They added freedom to adventure all of tamriel and play with people from all factions. They added player housing. They even got rid of monthly subscriptions. If you are a fan of MMORPG games, then you will easily get hooked on ESO. The questing is quite enjoyable and has lore to it. There is much of tamriel to explore. You could play with friends doing pve like dungeons, trials, delves, world bosses, and pvp like battling with 24 man groups in Cyrodil. You could even just buy the game on deal just to run around tamriel seeing beyond skyrim (if your coming from skyrim) because the graphics are beautiful. Overall I highly reccomend ESO cause the developers changed a mediocre WoW knockoff to an original MMORPG and cause they care.

When I was around 14 or so, I remember heading to a friend's house where he and his brothers had a number of gaming PCs set up, all networked in and online. We would play Everquest, Counterstrike, and a number of other games into the wee hours of the morning. There was one game there that stood out to me; that game was Homeworld.
Homeworld is an amazing game. A journey through both an amazing, emotional story and wonderful gameplay. The score is driving, the visuals are breathtaking, and the whole experience is awesome.
If you played this game at original release, then I'm sure you remember the first time loading it up, hearing Samuel Barber's Angus Dei and seeing the Mothership. I know you can recall the emotion felt when the fleet returns to Kharak only to find it burning under an enemy assault. Countless memories flood forth from the mere mention of this cult jewel. Why it wasn't more popular at the time, I will never know.
A friend and I would play this title over Gameranger. We did for a good many years, actually. We would always joke about them doing an updated version of the game (if not a HW 3)...well, those jokes have become a reality. An awesome reality.
If you're a fan of the original, or curious about this game...I say go for it. It is worth every penny.
If you are new to the game, I envy you....you're about to take an amazing journey on your way home.

My analisis is based on a HARD difficulty. There are several PROs and little CONS:
PROs:
* Superb Sounds and Graphics: Very polished and optimized I've got a R9280X and after some tweaking, got to play at 45+ FPS with ULTRA Graphices. And Believe me, they're really good
* Great Atmosphere: It perfectly catches the ALIEN (first one) 80s setting. Green monitors, the keystrokes of the keyboard, even the Characters. Also lights and darkness are great.
* Fear: You always are at a disadvantage and you feel like prey all the time. The alien is an always present figure, either if you see it or not.
* Story and Character: The story is really good, it picks up some in between Alien and Aliens. Amanda is very like his mom, a really strong character, but more in a Lara Croft 2013 tomb raider.
CONs:
* Length and backtrack: At some point of the game if you want to get the achievements and stuff, you got to do a LOT of backtrack. And I mean A LOT (2+ hours) which can be frustrating on several locations with the Alien lurking around.
* Difficulty: At some points you are way over your head and it depends mostly on luck that anything else. There are only a few, but can be daunting.
If you like a true survival horror experience, a character you care about and to scare the s..t out of you, go for it, without hesitation. But be prepare for a challenge. If you are more of a FPS player (or faint of heart!) try anywhere else

Dishonored 2 improves on the standards set by it's predecessor and adds it's own unique style in the form of a new playable character. While playing as Corvo is largely the same as Dishonored 1, Emily adds some unique abilities that give players a wider range of options in how they play each level. Speaking of the levels: the level design in this sequel far surpasses that of the original game. Each level feels like it's own living world and changes game-play up with a cool new mechanic. Levels feel bigger this time around and have more areas to explore. Every single building is open to exploration with apartments full of treasure to find and surprises that affect the story. Some of the big baddies are a bit lackluster, but their surroundings make up for it by giving you endless options for dealing with each enemy, whether you choose the sneaky, non-lethal route, or any of the multitude of brutal murderous ones. Overall, I highly recommend this game to those who enjoyed the first Dishonored.

To begin with, I'm not good at doing reviews, but I'll try to say what I think about the game.
People say it's the worst among all "souls" games, and well, probably it is.
Still, it's the souls game I played the most, the one I've had the most fun playing, and the one that made me spend the most hours.
To be honest, I can't really tell why, maybe it's because of the balanced PVP (if you compare it to other souls games), or maybe it's because of the huge amount of builds you can make.
Or maybe it's just because it's the first souls game I played.
Dark Souls 2 is an Action RPG made by From Software (but not made by the same team that made Dark Souls 1, Demon's Souls, Dark Souls 3 and Bloodborne, that's why it looks different).
A game with an enormous amount of weapons: swords, greatswords, axes, spears, bows, bowguns, spells and so on, that allows you to play in your own way.
You can be a mage swinging giant axes onto enemies' heads, a tanky 700kg knight walking around the world dual wielding spoons, or you could just parry and kill everything you see with your bare hands.
Lots of enemies, fun bossfights (mother♥♥♥♥ing dragon), and a huge variety of places (even tho if you compare level design to other souls games, it's just the worst).
Although at the beginning of this review I said Dark Souls 2 has got the best PVP among all souls (imho), it's still got some problems. One of these is the lag, you'll see what I mean when you'll engage a fight with a player swinging his katana on the other side of the map. And there are also some OP weapons, but that's not really a problem, every weapon has weak points, just use them.
A fun coop system that allows your friend to join your world and beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of bosses together.

Does it have a potential? - yes. Is it good and stable in it's current release? - no. It says I have ~50 h on it. I have actually played much more on the pirated version, before deciding to support the devs.
Pros:
+ There are two different gamemodes. Vanilla (base game, doesn't get updates often) and V2 (is more similar to Rust). The second one is more up to date, seems to be more balanced and overall seems to run better.
+ There are cars, motorcycles and four-wheelers. Some servers have kits to make it easy for you to get them. Usually you will have to farm pieces to make your vehicle functional.
+ Game is not as harsh as Rust. If you are not into PvP, on death you will only loose resources that you have in your inventory. You will keep all your equiped gear and weapons if you are not infamous. If you are into PvP, you will notice that there is a unique "infamous" system which I mentioned earlier. If you have it, you are basically marked as a bandit and you will drop random equiped gear after death.
+ Colorful and good looking graphics.
+ Nice base building system. (Similar to Rust).
+ Different biomes, with different resource nodes and more or less, different aggresive animals. (Only skin changes, not the model.)
Cons:
- Guns are NOT balanced at all. People will bunny-jump near you and shoot you with a shotgun using only one round. (Because when you jump, its accuracy becomes better? What? Yes.) Assault rifles have the same accuracy as bolt action rifles. You just need to get used to it. (Balanced? Nope), same goes for the pistol, but for a lower damage output. Bolt action seems to be in overall, most balanced.
- Optimization. Oh boy, you will lag a lot. (More frequent in "community servers") This will be especially noticable in close, face to face fights. :) (Most people try to abuse it, they will jump around and with added server/game lag you will most likely be on the other side of the stick). Prepare your nerves and attidude that this is just an unfinished game and♥♥♥♥♥♥does happen.
- Animals, I have been playing this game for two years and they still seem to be some what bugged. It is not as bad as it used to be, but they will try to make your day miserable. (In V2 most animals will run from you, in vanila they will attack you and if you are into PvP, get prepared to be overhelmed.)
- Raiding. There are no secure doors in hurtworld. Doesn't matter how though your base is, doors only require one C4 to be destroyed. My suggestion: if there is /sethome command in the server, use it and just teleport back to your home when you leave (have an exit on the 3rd floor or something). Do NOT build wooden houses. Please. Unless you aren't planning to keep your precious resources there and just want to rp. (Which I would not recommend).
- Cheaters, exploiters, hackers. you name it. You will encounter them. Wallhacks and aimbots (usually aimbots accure in PvP based servers) are there and people using them are not punished. (additional note, usually russians do it. Damn commies.)

This game is very enjoyable. I have played several of the Elder Scrolls games in the past, and this game does a great job of making it feel like an actual Elder Scrolls game. As an MMO, It is also pretty good. I have played just about every MMO out  there. This game has a very good Action Combat system that requires you to block attacks, dodge telegraphed attacks, and so on. I believe it is much better than the typical point and click attacks and auto attacking/cooldown combat of the past; it feels much more involved, like you are able to turn the tide of the fight yourself. So, a few areas to talk about:
Graphics: The graphics are quite nice. It has a nice styalized look to it. The environment is very nice to look at, with very many locals to explore. The characters and armors, weapons, attacks, powers, magic, all look impressive.
Exploration: There is a vast world to explore, with many areas from the previous games, and more that have never been explored in grand detail like this before. They are adding more regions with the new DLC, and if memory serves correct, I believe you have to own the DLC to actually explore the regions, but there is plenty of map to explore, anyways.
Story: The story is the typical fantasy trope that all fantasy titals nowadays have: The world is doomed from gods, or something, and you are the one to stop it. The story itself kind of takes a backseat to the rest of the quests. Just like Slyrim and Oblivion befroe it, the side quests are the real draw to the game. The cool thing is, you can see some characters from some of the other Elder Scrolls games and lore that you hear about, as well.
Experience/Leveling: The game, when it first released, was very difficult to level. The combat was difficult to engage in because of the difficulties of the leveled enemies. This has been fixed, thankfully. You can now get experience for just about everything you do: exploring, smithing, tailoring, fighting, questing, fishing, etc. There is no shortage of opportunities for finding experience. Leveling can be tedious, like any other game, but is most certainly worth it in the long run, if you have the patience.
Music/Sound: The theme music is once again composed by Jeremy Soule, who has worked with the previous Elder Scrolls games since Morrowind. The rest of the score is compsed by Rik Schafer and Brad Derrick, who make an ambiance with the music, but nothing to be listening to on your own. I just turn the music off and listen to my own music, which is just fine. The sounds are very detailed as well. There are these cool Sky-Anchors that are portals from one world to the other that release these creatures in to Tamriel, and the sound that it makes when it spawns is quite menacing. Another thing to note is that every quest in the game is completely voice acted, which is a feat within itself. The voice acting is not too bad either; the voice of the Prophet is really nice and almost Shakespearean.
All in all, I would highly recommend this game to anybody who loves the series and MMO's. There is no monthly subscription, once you buy the game, it is yours. The game runs very well as well. To be quite honest, I am unable to think of anything as a con in the current state. Buy the game and try it for yourself. I believe that you will ike it.

UPDATE: Tried to run Homeworld 2 Remastered, game won't launch. Score updated appropriately.
I've only had a brief time with the game but here's my initial experiences/opinions from playing the Homeworld 1 Remastered campaign:
First the bad;
1) Controls not rebindable. Tried with several keys on one command, and half a dozen different commands after and even clearing the keys from commands before attempting to add new ones results in an error message blocking you from rebinding ("the key is already in use as "command"").
2) First mission glitched, skipped initial objective rendering the mission impossible to finish. Restarted mission to try again, all going well until told to capture drone with salvage ship, whereupon my fighters (set on aggressive mode, as per the previous objective instructions) sped half way across the map to kill it before my salvage ship got there, resulting in another failed mission. Third time's the charm and I finally finish it.
3) Second mission goes well. Apart from a brief issue getting my ship to behave, which I suggest was my fault, the mission went smoothly, enemy ships were fought,♥♥♥♥♥♥exploded, all went well.
4) Third mission again bugged. Told to kill one assault frigate and capture the other with salvage ship. Salvage ship will approach the frigate but refuses to interact with it, no matter how much damage I deal first. Thought I might be missing a ship but the research menu shows no further research to be made.
5) Sound for weapons firing keeps cutting out. Looks like a sound channels issue but even after bumping it from the default (apparently 0, but obviously not otherwise there'd have been no sound) to 100 the problem persists.
6) Lighting issues, you can rotate the camera to blatantly see the sun in the background but the side of an object facing you is still brightly lit up, while it has shadows around the edge (as though your camera is a brighter light source than the sun. It's a little nitpick but it bugs the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me nontheless.
Now the good;
1) The remastered textures are pretty, even on moderate settings and zoomed in far the game looks amazing.
2) The cutscenes are great too.
3) Having Homeworld 2's UI in the Homeworld 1 campaign is a blessing, probably the best design decision they've made overall. I really can't stress how great this is.
4) The new music is spectacular, that opening cutscene where the mothership undocks has some great music.
5) Alt-F4 works.
Finally, the ugly;
1) There's no game speed option. I can't remember if the classic Homeworld had it or not but not having one in a more modern game is just plain silly. Resource collectors can take upwards of 2-3 minutes to grab a handful of resources (often only enough for one or two ships or a single research project) and can't be sped up. Any game that puts me in a situation where I'm actively flicking through a magazine while playing is not winning brownie points.
2) There are 4 UI scale options (not on the options screen, but rather the pause (F10) screen. It's a nice feature to have but at size 2 the UI's group panel (where you assign tactics and formations) is too small to read and at size 3 it takes up about two-thirds of the screen space and leaves you a tiny rectangle in the middle to play with. This could be solved quite easily with more granular options like a slider instead of just 4 settings.
All that said; it's Homeworld - they're great games and nothing will change that.
Overall: I can't recommend it. It feels like an old game dragged kicking and screaming into the modern era, which is equal parts good and bad (mostly good, thankfully) but the bugs and glitches had me reaching for Alt-F4 after only two and a bit missions of the campaign. Typically the start of a game is more polished than the end (simply because it has more time with the playtesters) and if the quality of the first three missions is anything to go by the rest of the game must be an absolute trainwreck.
Add in the fact that the multiplayer is still in beta, which is a broad definition these days anyway, while the game is billed as a full release and you've got something that stinks of being rushed out the door to take advantage of a rapidly depopulated release window.
Sorry Gearbox but you've blown it pretty hard at release.

I really liked Alien: Isolation, for the first 6 hours. It had the atmosphere and a certain feel to it, even if it never approached being scary. However, a little more than half way through the game, a thing happens that totally changes the tone and the goal of the game. At this point, the "spooky" direction the story was heading in was all to clear and I was proven right when after a few levels, the game returns to its original tone in a move that makes little sense even within the universe and there are new additions that only exist to frustrate.
A big problem with the game is just how much backtracking there is. There's one portion of the game, where you enter a room, which has a usable object you clearly need to go back for, then go across the hall (dodging the alien the whole time), just so you can go back to the room and then back across the hall. If anything, Alien: Isolation's biggest problem is that it is not scary, but frustrating. There was one section of the game, where you open a door and if you're not ready, you can get automatically killed over and over; sometimes by fault of the physics engine and not your own.
The reason the Alien in this game was never scary is simple. It has 3 modes of attack.
1. Hiding in the vents, waiting for you to walk under it or waiting for a gun to fire so it can come out.
2. Is leashed to you, has to be within a certain distance, and appears through no fault of your own because of a scripted scene to "raise tensions".
3. "I'm going to kill you mode". This is by far the worst of the 3 modes because it practically throws a stealth based survival horror attempt out the window as you pass silently through each room, only for the Alien to pop in and screw around for a bit. There was one moment half way through the game, where I just watched the Alien stumble about the room (unable to find me) for 15 minutes. Because it was leashed to me, the AI knew I was in the room, but it never came close to catching me. This is not scary and all you can do in these moments is just wait for it to go away, just so it can reappear out of the same vent less than a minute later. There is no skill involved in avoiding it and it just turns into a frustrating mess.
If the Alien crawled on the ceiling or over cover, it would have been scary as you would be forced to change positions and hide under things, rather than just walk in circles around a chest high wall. However, the team involved wanted to keep the game as close to the original movie as possible and in doing so broke some well established canon.
The only other problem with the game is that the campaign is far too long and isn't remotley fulfilling. You never feel like you're making progress because the game never gives you a sense of achievement. Every time you sucessfully do something, there is no reward. Its especially frustrating when most missions is designed like God of War or Bioshock, in that it should be a linear corridor, but you need to go on a fetch quest through a long series of rooms just to open the door.
