A video game adaptation that understands why the Alien series started so strong and perfectly recreates its horror and science fiction atmosphere.
Having been a huge fan of the first Alien movie, the atmosphere and immersion this game provides were exactly what I had been craving. The very slow and drawn out start, the mystery about the aliens as well as the corporate interests and the nature of humans, and the fear of being hunted by a unpredictable and unstoppable creature. But enough about the film.
The game itself is mostly a stealth game where you constantly need to be out of sight or else you will be spotted and swiftly ended. The alien is not your only threat, though, as there are some humans still aboard the Sevastapol space station who are desperate enough to kill to survive, as well as some faulty androids that will resort to violence to complete their mission. These separate enemies are not only a threat to you but to each other and getting them to interact is definitely recommended in some cases, but often you are better off not bothering any of them if possible.
There is a bit of crafting in the game to help you distract enemies, heal yourself, or, if need be, to kill. Lower difficulties offer resources abundantly while the higher difficulties make them scarce. Lore is spread about in the form of text documents and audio tapes usually found on computer terminals which can also be explored some other time in the pause menu and provide a good insight into the events that occurred prior to your arrival. The story itself is good and is well paced throughout the game but if you remember the films, you know what to expect. Personally, I did not care much for the ending, but I feel the destination is nowhere near as satisfying as the journey in this game.
The game is great but it is not perfect. There are a few bugs that are not game breaking but definitely hamper the immersion. Amanda, your character, sometimes screams at seemingly random places because whatever system that is supposed to trigger a scream at a cue is bugged. After you acquire the flamethrower, the audio will sometimes bug so the sound of the fuel in the canister sloshing around can be heard every way you move. Animations are sometimes messed up if you travel to places the story doesn't intend for you be. While not a bug, if you activate a quick time or moment where you only have camera control, the field of view will revert to the default 45 and switch back to your set field of view after it ends, which is quite noticeable. Also, the only level design problem to be found is that some of the save station placements are a little too plentiful in some areas and a little too sparse in others. Other than that, the game runs perfectly fine and none of the technical issues hinder progress.
What really sold me on the experience was the attention to the little details and the audio. Like how the motion tracker does not work well in vents or through certain large objects like android storage chambers. How the sticky notes and pictures inside lockers and on terminals are not all the same. One corpse had a magazine stuffed down the throat like the android tried to do in the first movie. The dust on your motion tracker is visible in the light. The quick time events for small tasks were timed just long enough to add tension to your actions. All of the sound effects which emulated the films or created for this were just right for the setting of a 70's vision of the future. The scenes where you don an astronaut suit. This game just had atmosphere in spades.
For a video game based on the first Alien films, this is what we had wanted all along.

Easily one of the scariest horror games I've ever played, and one of the best games I've ever played in general. Every fan of horror needs to play this.
This game will not hold your hand. There are no automatic savepoints. Just the mere act of saving is frightening by itself, because you can be killed while in the middle of the process.
You have to be cautious and calculate your odds of survival at every turn in the game. Just turning a corner in a hallway could spell your end. You can hide in vents, but the Alien is unpredictable and will sometimes randomly enter them and find you. The Motion Tracker is an awesome feature that lets you track if and where the Alien is nearby, but even THAT needs to be used with caution as the beep noise it makes can reveal your location to the Alien.
I dare to say that this game is a masterpiece. I honestly didn't find any fault with it whatsoever. Creative Assembly should be applauded for making such a fantastic game and loveletter to the Alien franchise. I was totally immersed and spooked the whole way through. That's not something I say often about licensed games. If there was only one licensed game you played in your entire lifetime, make it this one.  You won't regret it.

Dishonored 2 is a great sequel to what was my personal favorite in 2012.
It takes place several years after the first game and Emily Kaldwin is the Empress of the Isles. Her father, Corvo, the player character in the first game, continues his role as Royal Protector. Dunwall has prospered under her reign, however, a serial killer with the name "Crown Killer" has been brutally murdering critics of Emily, leading many to believe her and her father are the culprit. During a ceremony celebrating Jessmine's life, Emily's mother, a witch by the name of Delilah Copperspoon and the Duke of Serkonos, Luca Abele, barge in and Delilah claims to be Jessamine's older sister and the rightful heir to the throne. The coup is successful and, depending on who you decide to play as, either Corvo or Emily are turned to stone. I chose to play as Emily.
Emily escapes her house arrest and flees Dunwall on a ship with Meagan Foster, heading south to Karnaca in the Serkonos region. It is here that Emily will find out and get to the bottom of who the Crown Killer is, who is behind the conspiracy to usurp her leadership.
It's a classic stealth game with an incredibly developed world and lore to go with it. The graphics are generally great, the world design of the buildings are classically Victorian. The somewhat steampunk/industrialist technology continues, especially with Jindosh's home. It's just a great game really. Depending on what choices you make, the game's ending can also be drastically different.
I will say that PC performance can vary. I turned off v-sync in game and opted to use AMD driver's v-sync. I also turned off Bloom in game as it just wasn't that great and really detered performance at some points. Otherwise, I hadn't had too many issues.
9.4/10

I wanted to celebrate and share my love for the HL series with my girlfriend. The 'remake' of HL, Black Mesa, was obviously where she should start the journey.
She's an avid gamer, yet I found her constantly annoyed at this classic masterpiece of FPS. Why?
There's a ton of dominant bugs that require you to input commands in the console to nullify them. I'm talking enemies that are stuck, scientists who's tie do the helicopter, scripts not triggering untill you find out why they don't trigger by reading the walkthrough, etc. This game came out of Early Access too early, its super buggy.
Half Life 1 was, back then, a masterpiece of level design. Black Mesa attempts to stay faithful to it but end ups delivering the levels in an annoyingly old fashioned way. Jumping on tiny ledges and doing acrobatic♥♥♥♥♥♥like it was designed for CSGO crouch-jump pro's is too prevalent for it to be fun after the millionth time, it's like the design itself requires you to be a pro at HL1/2 before you've even started it.
After playing through the game for hours, my gf forgot most of the story and I had to remind her she blew up Area 51 and is now trying to escape. She reminded herself she was playing this for HL2, asking me if it is really a better game.
Black Mesa was originally a free community service. I understand and respect monetizing the mod, but in exchange for that I do expect extra effort. The ultimate FPS classic is now a frustrating journey of bugs and backtracking, and the fact that the Xen level is STILL missing after YEARS sadly leaves me no choice but to give this mod a thumbs down.
Apart from the scenes in Black Mesa, basicly apart from the intro, the game is more blasphemy than homage. I'm sad that the first person I tried to show the awesomeness of Half Life in a supposedly 'improved' jacket, quit the game after 75% because of it being a buggy and frustrating experience.

After putting nearly 400 hours into this MMO, I have to say that returning was one of the best choices I've made in awhile. Zenimax has created an amazing game where there's always something to do. ESO is a massive semi open world game where you can play however you want. There is so much to try and experience, from huge PvP battles, castle sieges, group dungeon content, soloing and adventuring throughout Tamriel, playing the amazing DLC such as Thieves Guild and Dark Brotherhood, which add new skill lines and epic campaigns.
Everything players have wanted has been pretty much added such as player housing with the homestead update, and a fun crime/theft system. You can become a werewolf, vampire, play as a thief or assassin, take on the role of a healer, tank, or DPS, while also customizing and theorycrafting each piece of your build for the best performance, such as going stamina or magicka, Dual Wield, 1H, Bows, Staves, the combat customization is endless and makes for a fun endgame.
Questing is interesting with a fully voice acted game, and every NPC has a unique voice. With the One Tamriel update, you can now quest where ever you want, at any level, with no restrictions. Everything scales to you, so you can experience every factions campaign or quest at any zone you feel like questing in at any time. Questing with others is also possible, by sharing quests and completing them together.
After hitting the levelcap, you continue to progress via champion points, elevating your characters power further as you gain XP by doing end game content.
Gearing is done in this game by grinding for drops, or crafting gear, which requires researched traits. You can create and wear so many different mixes of sets to fit your specific needs. Certain sets are great for magicka users, some are great for thieving, others are made for stamina builds, some are for PVP, with lots of other sets with all different purposes.
ESO has regained its spot as my top MMO very quickly with all Zenimax has done to improve the game lately. If you're looking for an MMO to immerse yourself into and have a great time, there's no other I could reccomend.

I have only played a few skirmish matches so take this with a grain of salt, especially with the numerous bugs that are apparently still in the game. Gearbox have a bit of a♥♥♥♥♥♥track record in my book so I was sceptical.
Well the game looks and feels great and is an absolute nostalgic blast. Once you hear the Ion beams and the delightfully nonchalant battle chatter (a welcome distraction from the try-too-hard cliché military gruff stuff we are used to nowadays) you feel right at home. Controls still hold up, though I would've wished a middle mouse button camera panning. It's a nice throwback to when RTS wasn't about unit spam or superhuman micro capabilities.
The visuals are neat. Seing HW1 in this fidelity is a treat, HW2 also looks nicer but the leap isn't that big comparatively. Ship damage is still just pre-rendered 2d sprites but even those got increased resolutions. FOV is also cool but really gimmicky. Overall performance is decent, could be better though seeing as this isn't exactly cream of the crop visually despite all enhancements. This is still a 15 year old engine at its heart.
Negatives are that the AI wasn't improved and is still kind of dumb. They'll get stomped even if they keep up with your economy. Also the UI scaling doesn't affect the ever obnoxiously large sidebar.
Overall a recommended buy, for the ability to play this on current systems alone.

I don't usually write public reviews, but this game and series are probably my go-to in terms of single player.
Setting/Feel:
How does a game about dead things with mostly stationary enemies (Before aggro of course) seem so alive? Well it honestly doesn't, but it does set the feel really well. While not being the definition of graphics, it does know where it wants to go and hits damn near its mark. With a theme around dark, dead and the afterlife, you will get the feels (Especially if you are a first time player) If you are a first time player, I suggest starting from Demon's Souls and working up the ladder, although I personally feel Demon's Souls to be a bit outdated at this point, if you can handle older games, its worth it. (This will also require a console, if you can't get it, Dark Souls 1 is still fairly relevant.)
Gameplay:
Not to be confused by multiplayer!
While the game is usually labeled "Hard" or "Difficult" its more a play on learning and trial and error. If you don't use your hints and tools to their fullest, you will die and die and die again. Though, that's fine, because that's where the trial and error come in! Both are fine ways to play, but end up looking tough. (That's also why DkS1 Zealots think this game is easy, its just because they are too good.) Luckily, in this game, their is no real trial and error forcefulness (Such as Seath from 1, yeah, none of that♥♥♥♥♥♥ though a bunch of really tough optional bosses take the place of that.
- I should also add that this game rewards hit and run tactics and baiting -
Playstyle:
I wanted to add this to "Gameplay", but I felt I had more to say on this topic. This game is an RPG, it goes without saying that you get to customize your character. Though, unlike most ARPGs, Dark Souls 2 really hands you a more than full plate when it comes to weapons, armor, shields, weapon styles and 3 types of magic. Most of which are completely unique. That's before you even fully decide on a stat build. Its quite wonderful to build a character and then test it out too! Multiplayer ho!
Multiplayer:
With most modern games, you can't survive such a wonderful system of playstyle without the ultimate test. Most times, players are either praising or raging when it comes to online and to be honest, its usually both. I personally love the PvP, the community (The community of long term players, there are always trolls. Alas, thus is the life of the net!) are really nice and understanding too. I once flat out called them bad for complaining rather than adapting and they DIDN'T get mad at me. I was so proud. That is another thing, in this game, you will always be faced with something you do not understand, much like the PvE, you will need to adapt and learn! You would be surprised how many people cannot understand that.
Though, PvP isn't the only aspect of this game's multiplayer! You can also summon friends (Assuming that you are of similar level and Soul Memory(Soul Memory is hard to explain, its basically your total amount of souls gathered)) or randoms to help with areas and bosses. Some people even use this function to fight other players in "unfair" circumstances. It should be noted that it is very easy to trip on your friend if attacking near each other. Use that to your advantage!
Verdict:
While I didn't cover everything (Such as lore, I highly suggest VaatiVidya on youtube for that stuff! :P) I will still be factoring in everything. Even my personal experience. (I have 37 hours as of this review, it should be noted that I have beaten the game twice and racked up at least 100 hours on my PS3 as well)
The way I rate: 1 being♥♥♥♥♥♥poop), 5 being par and 10 being godly, I give Dark Souls 2 an 8.5.
People will disagree with me, reviews are generally opinionated, but I tried to put in as many facts as I could. The reason this game didn't go further to a perfect score is because it isn't perfect. Feel free to point out flaws in my review as well, I apprietiate feedback!

, please contact me-

This game has been a major part of my childhood since the first day I witnessed my dad playing it. He played it at work after hours with his coworkers, and I loved watching him play skirmishes at home. Eventually, he let me take a stab at it, and I quickly fell in love. Even though this game came out in 1997, it still brings a level of fun and strategy that isn't seen in many games that came after it. I still come back to it every once in a while, though not nearly as often as I used to, and relive the fun of crushing the filthy Core with endless waves of Flash tanks and Brawler planes. In recent times, my dad has stopped playing, and my younger brother never had as much fun with it as I did, but I still like to play a few matches here and there. I'm a purist when it comes to this game, and the most additional content I've installed has been the 3.1c patch and final 6 official Cavedog units. Sadly, this game takes a bit of work to get running smoothly on Windows 10, but it is WELL worth the effort. For the Commanders before me, and those who will follow in my footsteps, good luck out there, and may the Arm Rebellion live free forever!

The performance is still not perfect unfortunately. I found out that there is some major issue when it comes to vsync and locking framerate to 60. Vsync would obviously lock to 30fps as soon as you drop below 60. But if you turn it off and lock the framerate to 60 you will experience disgusting amount of screen tearing. Turns out that if you set the fps lock to higher than 60 then the screen tearing is mostly gone and the game all of a sudden started to run almost 2x better than with locking it to 60 (although there are still some areas that do drop fps when you start looking at them).
So, after these few latest patches + unlocking the fps (I'm still baffled how locking to 60 causes issues) the game is pretty enjoyable.
Few things I didn't like such as having to press shift again to stop sprinting (I am used to crouching to cancel running but this time you enter a slide) and sometimes I would have issues going through small gaps because the game auto lowers you while in crouch to pass through but sometimes it doesn't let you through.
Graphically this game can look stunning, but also the enemies are really hard to spot sometimes since everything has this bland neutral tone and especially in later leves certain enemies just blend with the background.
Gameplay wise it plays out just like Dishonored 1. Everything is there with addition to crafting runes which just led to stacking bunch of useful effects up to 4 times.
All in all, now that majority of performance issues are resolved and once my dumb♥♥♥♥♥realized that somehow locking higher than 60fps fixes the game I can actually recommend this game.

Just Cause 3 (abbreviated as JC3) offers a fun and explosive experience powered by its well-crafted physics engine.  Fans of JC2 are going to love this game.  The game delivers cheesy, yet adrenaline-pumping action backed by a great soundtrack and spectacular visuals.  However, the game still has a few inexcusable flaws which must be addressed.
The Just Cause series is quite the oddball when it comes to gameplay.  I would describe it as GTA on steroids.   The game is packed with over-the-top action, a recurring characteristic for the franchise.
Among the new and improved gadgets in the players arsenal lies the wingsuit.  The wingsuit was a major selling point in my opinion as not only is it a new and welcome addition to the Just Cause series, but also because the game pulls off its mechanics with flying colours.  Being quick to learn yet hard to master, the wingsuit rewards players who have mastered it with quick and angile escapes an most importantly, a hell of a ride.  The wingsuit is incredibly fun to use and the players will find themselves using it frequently.
JC3 offers a vast open world free for players to destroy to their heart's content.  The game does have a few minigames to keep players occupied.  Wingsuit, driving and piloting are core of the game's side activities.  Each of these challenges unlock the next tier of abilities for the player.  The type of ability depends on the type of challenge you complete.  For example:  Driving challenges will award you with additional modifications for a player-spawned vehicle, while wingsuit challenges offer wingsuit upgrades such as airbrakes and faster wingsuit deployment times.
JC3 is a no-brains game, if you're looking for something smart, you're looking at the wrong game.  There is only one solution to every problem:  Blow it up.  Quite frankly, that's the meat of the game.  Players will find themselves moving from one spot to another as they make their way around town.  The player can 'recapture' towns for the local folk by tearing down anything related to the government.  Objects which should be blown up are marked with red stripes, an indicator of what you should be trying to tear down in order to recapture the town.
Aside from the regular weapons, the player also has access to the Just Cause flagship grappling hook.  The player fires tethers from the wrist-mounted grappling hook, which they can use to zip at lightning speed towards the target object or attach one entity to another, pulling the two towards each other.  JC3 brings more improvements to the grappling hook, allowing players to manually control the tension of the tether using the "Shift" Key.  The grappling hook is a versatile and destructive tool which the players are encouraged to experiment with.
However, the game's strong point is also its weak point.  By saying so, I mean that the game's ridiculously silly physics and rather brainless approach to every situation makes the game feel extremely shallow.  The game is dumb, but it doesn't mean it isn't fun.  The most damaging part of the game is how repetitive it can be.  Players who go into the game with the sole intention of completing one objective as efficiently as possible will find themselves going through routine patrols around the town, searching for propaganda to tear down with the grappling hook and finally destroying a list of objects at the local police station.  This mind-numbing process is repeated in every single town and it's disappointing to say the least.
My favourite wingsuit is also to blame for ruining the gameplay.  JC2 saw a respectable use of vehicles as driving from one location to another was faster than using the parachute.  JC3 falls flat on its face in terms of its driving mechanics.  Cars feel stiff, sluggish and seem to be glued to the ground, making the wingsuit the go-to choice for travelling.  It's a pity that the vehicles are given no attention as each one seems to have its own unique interior with great engine sound effects as well, an aspect of the series which has been scrapped despite its popularity in previous installments.
The player assumes control of Rico, an experienced "spy" (more like explosives expert) returning to his home in Medici after his retirement.  At first, he's happy to be at home, but he spots something.  No...could it be?  Another dictator has seized control over the country!  This one sounds exactly like Hitler and looks like Stalin, unfortunately I don't remember the bloke's name so I'll call him Stitler.  With the help of his friends in Medici, Rico must bomb every town and destroy all facilities to regain control over his beloved country.  Hooray for terrorism!
The story is far from the series' strong suit and I was not expecting any quality story of any sort.  However, I still expect at least some form of a story from a game asking for $60.  Come on, JC2 received criticism for its forgettable, awkward and rather pointless story.  Had Square Enix made any effort at all to at least improve the game's story, I'd have given it a higher score.  However, the game still doesn't provide any incentives for the player to progress through the already-shallow story.
Square Enix believes that by putting a thick-accented Italian aptly named 'Mario' into the game, they've improved the story.  Even though this 'Mario' character does have his moments, it certainly cannot compensate for the neglected story.  I can't blame the developers, though, as the nature of the game itself seems to restrict any smart or witty story-telling.  So I understand, nice try.
JC3 showcases up-to-date graphics, a souped-up physics engine built for fun and destruction models which do nothing short of enhancing the game's experience.  Medici has a gorgeous landscape reminiscent of Sorrento in Italy.  The design of the cars as well as the game's sountrack, which uses tunes from an acoustic guitar as its backbone, all combine together to set a great atmosphere for the game's location and sets the theme perfectly.  The game is far from heavy and is all about toying around and having fun.  Explosions are phenomenal as they give both satisfying audio and visual feedback.  Explosions go off with satisfying pops and light up the area in a magnificent extravaganza of fire.  The graphics are only disappointing for vehicles, which seem to have a surprisingly low texture quality.  Fortunately, this isn't immediately noticeable and does not detract from the game's experience.
The shadows are at their best when the sun is out.  Everything is well-lit and warm light is cast on the environment.  Medici's abundant sunflower fields can be driven through, flattening flowers and allowing players to leave behind symbols in the field.  Rico's attire is also well-designed.  Unlike JC2 in which Rico was known under the handle "Scorpio", bearing a red scorpion on his shirt - JC3 gives Rico a casual, yet well-equipped outlook.  Rico's harness hooks up to his grappling hook tether, freeing both his hands, and his unprofessional outfit fits in well with the whole retirement theme of the game.  Better still, the game runs at a rock solid 60fps on high settings for me, great optimization.
The visuals completely make up for JC3's lackluster story and is what keeps the game enjoyable.
Despite the neglected story and repetitive gameplay, JC3 is still loaded with fun for casual and hardcore players alike.

The character selection at the beginning of the game may have been a pointless addition and the gameplay systems stay eerily similar to the previous game in most other aspects, but Dishonored 2 has some of the best level design ever both in stealth games and immersive sims. It is stunning how close “The Clockwork Mansion” came to realize the idea of a mad scientist lair with moving walls and robot enforcers that seemed like utter CGI bullshot territory in the game’s first trailer. Meanwhile, “Edge of the World” perfectly introduced the new setting in Karnaca while being an impressively open-ended level, and “A Crack in the Slab” had a design centered around time travel that was expertly positioned at a point in the game where the usual game mechanics started to wear thin. The biggest issue with the game by far is its similarity to the previous game in the series, and this issue is probably exacerbated by my chosen playstyle of lingering on levels, exploring every inch, taking out every enemy with non-lethal means and staying undetected. It is an exceptional and remarkable game in many ways, but I really wish that they took larger steps to switch up the formula, like Mankind Divided did.

I only played about half of the game, so the other half I watched via walkthroughs. But I did find that using the flamethrower was the easiest method to simply "win" the game.
The first "intro" I saw to this game had a part where someone from the game said "the items you use can be used to distract the alien, but become less effective the more you use them." Finding out that the flamethrower guarantees the alien doesn't kill you is quite saddening, since I had hoped the alien would find a way to counter you just running through the game. This is assuming you wait the alien out, as there are quite a few points where you can simply wait long enough and the alien simply leaves; so there's no need to use the flamethrower most of the time, which means more ammo for later.
If you're looking for a fun horror game, there are times that it is 10/10 and times where it's 5/10 or worse. The only thing that is scary in the game is the alien, and it is only the threat about 50% of the time-which brings me to the second but most important qualm I have with this game:
"Alien: Isolation" is a name that makes you think you're alone against an alien, a wonderful setting for a horror game. When I learned there are other humans or androids on board I was considering how that could go. If there are a few, then it can greatly benefit the game. You're about to be shot by a human who's losing his mind or an android that somehow became faulty, but the alien kills them and saves you. But there's only a few seconds of respite, as the alien isn't going to focus on a dead body when it saw another living thing nearby as well. So learning that the alien is only somewhat present in the game and that humans account for a major protion of the troubles you have is quite disappointing.
It makes it much worse when non-alien enemies don't pose any serious threat. Androids are so slow that a little prior planning can save you almost entirely from them ever getting near you. Humans are so fragile that a few revolver or shotgun shots will put them down for good. Yet this goes without mentioning that a single noisemaker or gunshot can call the alien, making it a powerful weapon for you. Factoring in that the alien eventually leaves and doesn't return without other noises, this becomes a one-shot-kill for all enemies in the game. Why have a gun fight when an invincible alien can kill everyone at the cost of one gun shot?
Overall I'm disappointed I bought this game. The handling (gameplay) and implementation are poor, to say the least. Though the graphics and story are intruging.

After a troubled past, ESO got a chance to redeem its self. How well did it do?
ESO is an MMO, this needs to be said right away. Although it has Elder Scrolls in the title, do not expect an Elder Scrolls game. This is a fully-fledged MMO with an Elder Scrolls setting. You can expect all the story and lore that makes Elder Scrolls fascinating, but you most certainly cannot expect anything resembling Elder Scrolls combat, weapon levelling, armor levelling or character levelling. So many people went into this expecting Skyrim part two, and they were heavily dissapointed. Wether this is on the game's marketting behalf or their own ignorance is up for debate. Now that that is out of the way, let's talk about some more game-related matters. This isn't a conventional MMO by any means, and there are many things that make it unique. Abilities are not timed, and therefor, you have no cooldown on any of your hotbar moves. Instead, ESO incorporates a Magicka bar management, your abilities will consume Magicka, which regenerates when you aren't spamming moves. As expected, when your Magicka is too low, you'll need to get M1 spamming. Depending on how you like your MMOs, this is either a positive or negative, but I found it greatly enjoyable, allowing for faster paced combat and less of a focus on strafing. The game is primarily split into two paths, those being Stamina and Magicka. Stamina is for tanky individuals who want to be dishing out constant damage while remaining safe, and Magicka is for spell-based classes who want to dish out heals, buffs, summoning or sorcery.
The game begins, as expected, with character creation. Depending on which one of the 9 base-game races you pick, you'll be thrown into a different allegience. This will determine where you spawn in the world, and what quests you will start off is. But very soon, you'll realise why this game is called "Tamriel Unlimited". You can go where you want. Whenever you want. The base game is about 4 to 6 times the size of the Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, and it is all free to you. You can't explore all of Tamriel however, as large portions of it are either still in developement or locked behind DLCs. This is a little dissapointing at first, but you can get the main DLCs very cheap, and it never stunts your exploration. For an MMO, you'd expect this game to be based on raids only. This is not the case. You can expect enormous, sprawling cities all over the place. The world is extremely detailed for this type of video game. Most MMOs, and all Elder Scrolls games tend to have sub-par voice acting, but Elder Scrolls fixes this. You can expect some amazing voice acting by professionals like Michael Gambon and John Cleese. Aside from this, even the randomers you will meet have very nice voice acting, to the point where they feel like real people in a real world, despite being in an MMO, and also an Elder Scrolls title. Honestly, I enjoyed the world building greatly, to the point where it felt as though they had taken any other Elder Scrolls world and put an MMO in it. This is highly impressive stuff. The questing, for the most part, is good, and you can expect a departure mostly from generic fetch quests, and more of a focus on combat-involved quests and puzzles. If you're interested, the game also has an entire country which acts as one enormous PvP arena, which essentially acts as a war between the three factions, complete with castle sieges and no-nonsense duking it out. This can go very large scale, and it opens up to you once you reach level 10, which could actually take a while, as levelling is both rewarding and hard. Past level 5, you'll notice an enormous increase in XP cost for the next level. This makes every level gained that more satisfying.  If you can think of an MMO build, this game most certainly has one, which you can approach in whatever way you want, providing you have sufficient points to unlock perks, which are obtained by finding sky shards in the open world, or simply completing quests. The game is absolutely overflowing with Elder Scrolls lore, and you can expect to find loads of books on the matter, if it interests. All this is made only better by the game's looks. Graphics do not make a game, but this is definately one of the most pretty MMOs out there, writhing with detailed atmosphere and high graphical quality. The world is definately the strongest part of the game.
Elder Scrolls Online wasn't always this open and dandy. However, the game has worked hard to please the customer for the most part. The Tamriel Unlimited update has to be one of the most impressive updates I've ever seen in video gaming. Before this update, you were limited to your faction's worldspace, leaving you stuck to a third of what you could be exploring. The game has also improved on the levelling system, as you can do any quest whenever you want, and enemies will always match your level, improving on what ESO used to be. One thing threatenning the future of this game is the DLC. It is a little bit daunting how many chunks of Tamriel are missing. While you have more than enough questing and exploring to do already, I feel as though we can expect alot more DLC in the future, locking these chunks behind more and more paywalls. I hope this isn't the case, as it would be a dis-service to the customers. Everyone wants to go back to Skyrim, the White-Gold Tower and Vvardenfell, two of the latter being already locked behind DLCs. You can already expect this with most MMOs to begin with, but I feel as though it is about to reach its limit, and too many more DLCs could scar the game. Let's hope not, for the future of our enjoyment, and the longetivity of the game.

So, I don't usually write reviews so soon after installing the game, but this game is just so good I had to write about it.
No More Room in Hell is a very simple zombie survival game. Choose a server based on the mode you want to play in (PVP deathmatch, PVZ story objective, PVZ waves, or PVZ dodgeball). A brief explanation of all the modes:
PVP Deathmatch: Jump in, pick your primary weapon, pick your secondary weapon, and go shoot everyone else. Plays just like any other FPS, but without all the crazy HUDs and abilities and all that. Usually has infinite ammo.
PVZ Story Objective: Jump in at the start with a number of other players and complete the objectives you are given while trying to stay alive. Numerous zombies stand in your way. You must find your own weapons in the level, and ammunition is limited, so AIM FOR THE HEAD! Otherwise, be very precise with your melee attacks. Objectives in this mode often involve going through the level past many zombies to the very end where you must contact the military/government/somebody to come and rescue you. If you jump in during the middle of a group playing, you will usually have to wait until they all die before you can play as well, which may take a little while depending on skill level.
PVZ Waves: Jump in and fight back the zombie hordes for as long as you can. Sometimes you are given infinite ammunition, sometimes it is limited. If it's limited, AIM FOR THE HEAD! Game ends once everyone dies or you kill all the zombies.
PVZ Dodgeball: This is an odd mode, and I still don't quite understand it. Most of the time you simply spawn into a gymnasium split down the middle with a metal fence, and you have to fight the zombies on your side. I think that as you kill more zombies, you get more money to buy weapons from the vendors in the gym, but I could be wrong. I wouldn't recommend this mode because it can get boring very fast.
And now for the pros and cons:
PROS:
-Story/objective mode can get very addicting. You could spend hours either playing or watching your remaining fellow survivors  struggle to the finish.
-Graphics are actually fairly good. Thumbs up.
-Zombie A.I. is well-polished. Most of the zombies are really slow, though the children zombies are fast and short, and there are some adult zombies that can run. Some zombies also have broken legs, so watch your ankles! Something may be biting them.
-Story/objective mode actually makes you tense and feel like it is a real-life zombie situation. Usually you can't respawn, so all your effort has to be put forth then and there. It's so stressful but so fun when you keep worrying about conserving your ammo.
-Turning into a zombie is a thing (as I have encountered oh so many times)! If one of the zombies bites you, you'll soon start to notice orange veins appearing on the edge of your screen. As a minute passes by, more veins appear and your vision gets much darker. After I think 2 minutes, you can't see anything but darkness and veins, and your body flops over. Your corpse then comes back to life as a runner zombie (controlled by an A.I.). You can fight off the infection by using a certain type of pills, but the effects will come back within another 2-3 minutes. In a group, it ultimately becomes a big choice of whether they should kill the infected person or risk continuing in hopes of finding pills. You also have the option to kill yourself if you have a loaded gun. Just press K and then left mouse button if you are willing to sacrifice your life for the safety of the group.
-Community is mostly friendly and willing to work together to achieve a goal. In the story/objective servers, many players are very willing to make friends and joke around with complete strangers, all in the name of good fun.
CONS:
-Melee system is incredibly hard to master. You have to get down a good system of picking the right weapon when given the option (crowbar or hatchet work best) and then carefully striking the zombie while it is alone, pushing it away using V, and then backing up. Repeat this process until you can defeat them all. Unless if you have it mastered, either let the more experienced players take control or hang in the back of the group with a loaded gun to provide back-up in case someone else gets hurt.
-There are many (well, not "many", but quite a few) servers dominated by non-English speaking players. Usually they are either Spanish-speaking or speaking a language of Eastern Europe/Russia. I guess this is a PRO if you are from one of those areas and/or can speak those languages. But for solely English-speakers, it can be difficult to communicate as a team with other people.
-Community is mostly friendly, except in the PVP Deathmatch servers. In almost every one of these servers, you will find several of the stereotypical FPS "MLG 4/20 BLAZEIT 360HEADSHOTNO-SCOPE MUDAFUKA" guys. Not the friendliest of people, and not the best to hang out with.
ALSO, some tips for you guys just so that you are better at the game when you jump in:
--If you haven't figured it out already, AIM FOR THE HEAD! Not only is it a quicker kill, but you conserve lots of ammo if you go for the short range headshots. Most guns will give one-shot headshots. Some pistols require two shots, and then the military zombies may need up to five shots to the head before dying.
--Use the melee technique I mentioned: lead the zombies away from each other, strike, push, back-up, repeat.
--Work as a team. You'll accomplish things faster.
--Travel in at least groups of two, preferably three. That way, you always have someone's back and someone has yours. Separation from the group can easily get you killed.
--These last two are the most important tips. If you are infected, shout out to your team immediately to see if anyone has pills. If someone does, they will most likely give it to you. If they don't and you know there's no chance of finding more pills, kill yourself at once. If you have nothing to kill yourself with, ask a team member and they will almost always reply with a few quick taps of a crowbar.
--If someone else is infected and they shout out for pills and you have some which you aren't using, give the pills to them. It will be worth having another person around for a few minutes, and you're not infected so why would you need them? Also, if you notice someone's player name (an indicator of health) is slowly turning towards the red end of the color spectrum (i.e. yellow, orange, and red), give them pills. If you don't have any, kill them immediately, because asking the whole team will take too much time. Make sure that when the person dies, their body goes into rag-doll physics. This means they are dead for good. If the body goes into a kneeling-falling animation, the person will come back to life as a zombie and you need to take action immediately.
Overall. an absolutely awesome game.

Total Annihilation (1997) is a must-play, classic RTS title by Chris Taylor! Two factions, the ARM and the CORE, fight to ensure the complete destruction of the other in multiple story campaigns and battle tactics scenarios. In a skirmish match, your key unit is the Commander, which constructs units in real time using nanolathe technology. Destroy the enemy Commander to defeat the opposing army. This is one of the first RTS games to emphasize the importance of macromanagement in tandem with micromanagement.
This game has great replayability. Although I have few hours logged on the Steam version, I have played through every campaign at least twice before buying it on Steam, once on medium difficulty and once on hard. During my medium playthrough, I had logged in a word document over fifty hours of my attempt at a speed run (which does not include failed attempts). Sometimes it is hard to believe that it was released 20 years ago because of its 3D sprites and map layouts, which were way ahead of its time. Total Annihilation is the inspiration for Supreme Commander, also developed by Chris Taylor, which also has a big following.
Don't miss out on this gem.

This is a fun free RPG with real-time combat.
The difficulty level is geared towards casual gamers; save points are plentiful and your health regenerates over time. There are a few tougher boss battles but they can be played on an easier difficulty level if you wish (I played on the Normal difficulty without problems).
There is also a crafting system which is simple but effective. There are a few mini-games; for example one is a spoof of Pac-Man. There are also some very easy puzzles to add variety to the combat.
Graphics are not AAA quality; this an indie game made using RPG Maker. I know a lot of people immediately dismiss RPG Maker games (because, let's face it, so many of them are bad). But in this case it's probably the best, most innovative use of RPG Maker I've seen, and the graphics are more than suitable for what the developer is trying to accomplish.
The game is mostly linear so it's basically impossible to get lost.
The plot is one of the game's strongest points. At first it seems to be a pretty straightforward quest in which a young girl (Senia) is looking for her missing sister. But as more of the plot is unveiled through short cutscenes and flashbacks things get a lot more sinister. Eventually you start to question the very basis of what you thought was your quest. At the very end the plotline branches (with savepoints nearby being nice enough to warn you!) and there are three possible endings. It took me about six hours to complete every optional quest and get all three endings.
Unfortunately English is not the author's main language. So expect some spelling and grammar issues with the translation.
For some reason the game starts out in windowed mode. After looking in the Settings screen I saw that pressing F5 and F6 can adjust the screen. I played in full screen mode and did have a few brief instances of choppy frame rates, but overall the game ran well on Windows 7 64 bit and I encountered no bugs.
The soundtrack consists of numerous catchy tunes.
I enjoyed Eternal Senia. If you're not a stickler for graphics and you like ARPGs with a strong emphasis on story and gameplay it's well worth checking out!

If you are new to the series - buy it. (I would recommend playing Rome I first, before you play Rome II.) That is how I did it, coming relatively late to the series, it will more than wet your appetite for more.
In fact I spent £600 building a PC specifically for this game. Bought it 6 months after release so when I did it was in a very good state, it is now in an excellent condition. You do not need the most powerful or insane computer to run this game, even integrated graphics n a laptop will allow you to play it, of course though at a poorer fps and visual quality. Running an EVGA GTX 760 (not over clocked) and i7 4690 I can run this game on ultra settings for the majority of settings, with fps averaging around the 60fps mark without any major drops even with 6000-8000 soldiers on screen etc.
If you have played TW games before you will find some aspects of previous games (in particular Rome I), missing - buy it on sale, but buy it. Some of the criticism is fair, some is still aimed at how the game was a year ago. Give it a go, on sale for $10, you can't really go wrong.
Following a poor release where the game came out too early - I believe on the behest of SEGA, Creative Assembly could have taken the money (highest number of pre-orders for a Total War game) and run; moving onto the next in the series (Attila) and forgot all about this game and it's issues. They didn't and deserve credit, not for the state of the game on release (again I beleive SEGA) but for spending over a year, probably with many unpaid overtime hours, applying 17 patches and listening to the community in terms of resolving the issues with pathfinding and balancing issues as just two examples.
The community for this title, and all the games in the Total War series is massive and expert, considering it is a fairly niche title. This includes some incredible modders creating mods ranging from basic skins, to campaign mods which are of course free; some of which are as good if not better than the official DLC campaign packs, to complete overhaul mods. One of the best communities for any game out there, adding additional quality in most aspects and gameplay to what is, now, a seriously enjoyable and immersive game. It is also absolutely beautiful to look at. Nothing beats looking at your Legions of Roman infantry (even vanilla) as you prepare to battle it out to the death.
Rome I has certain aspects which are, surprisingly missing from this sequal. Those missing aspects are not game breaking but it is curious why they have been left out. Such as unit collision (different engine but for me the biggest disapointment) and a distinct family tree which gives you a reason to care for which general is which. This has been improved in the ''Emporer Edition'' with a more in-depth political system, meaning the more power your family holds within your faction the more likely the other families will see you as a threat and begin a civil war to attempt to retake power from you. Still not as engaging as in previous titles in my opinion, but a step in the right direction.
The core mechanics of raising and training an army of hand-to-hand combat troops and taking them into battles is here, with a huge variety of troop types in vanilla many many more if utilising mods and the game, it looks great, although using the Warscape Engine, it has some problems with collision in comparisson to the original. This has been improved on, but it still has the same core problem - only 1 soldier will fight 1 other soldier, no other combatant can intervene.
Personally, I enjoy every battle I take my troops into, even if the A.I, which, again, has been improved on as much as can be expected, can be easily beaten at times. (It is A.I after all, it in 2014 will never compete with a human player, and there is no reason to even expect them to for a second). Hike up the difficulty if this is frustrating for you, add mods to increase the length of battles if again that is an issue.
I am a single-player focussing on campaigns, not having fought a multiplayer battle or co-op/versus campaign even once, just not my thing, I cannot comment from pesonal experience, although having watched many videos of multiplayer battles, there is a huge multiplayer community, with many great players and many who just enjoy the battles win or lose. You will find the vast majority are just looking for a good, fun battle and are not the type of idiots you would find in more ''popular'' titles such as call of duty etc. I have got hours and hours of fun even without the multiplayer aspect of the game.
If you enjoy history (albeit not 100% historically accurate), if you like the sound of leading 6000+ individual soldiers from archers, to elephants, from Caesar's Roman Legionairies to Leonidas' Spartan Warriors, from Barbarians to to Spartacus' slave rebellion this is the game for you.
Outside of battle you must develop your technology trees, run and control your provinces and cities while maintainig order and making money, building alliances or declaring war and destroying other civilisations, this game is for you, like it is for me.
If new to the series, again I would recommend starting with the original - Rome I, then pick this game up. Ignore the nay-sayers and experience it for yourself. Check out the ''Total War Centre'' for an idea of just how huge the community is and have a look at some of the mods available on the Steam Workshop, many made by experienced modders and whole teams of modders.

Meanwhile, “Edge of the World” perfectly introduced the new setting in Karnaca while being an impressively open-ended level, and “A Crack in the Slab” had a design centered around time travel that was expertly positioned at a point in the game where the usual game mechanics started to wear thin. The biggest issue with the game by far is its similarity to the previous game in the series, and this issue is probably exacerbated by my chosen playstyle of lingering on levels, exploring every inch, taking out every enemy with non-lethal means and staying undetected. It is an exceptional and remarkable game in many ways, but I really wish that they took larger steps to switch up the formula, like Mankind Divided did.

Is Dishonored 2 a great stealth game? Definitely. Level design here is good at its worst and phenomenal at its best. Attention to small detail both in visual design and gameplay, pleasant reactivity, all of it builds up to present a memorable world. Two playable characters to choose from, each with unique powers, new game+ options, replay value is high indeed.
Does it have a story? Yes, it does... I guess? With its key moments often feeling hilariously rushed (traditional coup out of nowhere! vintage Dishonored!). It is also, apparently, heavily based on Brigmore Witches dlc for the original game, which I didn't play. At least the support cast of villains and vigilantes is fairly colourful.
Is it still, at this point, a shabby port? Evidently it is. It ran acceptable-ish for me on 1070, with some annoying texture/shadow popping in here and there, but a lot of people still struggle with running it well.
And now that we're done with the rubbish questions, let's answer a real one:
As you know, or will know in a moment (patience!), early on in Dishonored games you're granted the Heart artifact (see, patience paid off! But what a masterful use of foreshadowing on my part, eh?). Aside from irrelevant to the present prosecutorial topic uses, the Heart serves to tell you secrets. Point it at anyone
, right click and learn of this person's most shameful deeds! And what do you do with this knowledge? Why, you prosecute, swiftly and relentlessly! This is your chance to be Miles Edgeworth on a rampage! Being judgemental is a tremendously popular pastime after all, try it out!
There're some exceptions to this common rule. The Heart cannot read the hidden thoughts of:
A) Dogs. Because, obviously, all dogs are saints and keep no dark secrets, as canine author of this most marvelous review can testify.
B) Mechanical soldiers, but those murderous clockwork beauties look highly trustworthy anyway.
C) Rats and bloodflies, because they're terrible bores.
Of course, in a decadent society that Dishonored 2 portrays, almost everyone is guilty of some misdeed or other. And so it falls to you to serve some justice, preferably poetic and in style.
This dock worker sabotaged a ship with murderous intentions? Guilty! Off into the canal waters he goes, then!
This officer tests out fancy torture devices on prisoners? Guilty! Let's test this springrazor contraption on him!
This lady murdered her father's dog? Double guilty! Beware the anger of a gentle corgi. Knock the murderous lass over a balustrade by throwing an unconscious dog at her (the dog volunteered, I assure you)!
This guard kicked a neighbour's child? Well now, I hardly see anything wrong with that, I don't like kids myself. Pass.
Some additional examples of the Heart's insights:
"He tied the baker and covered him with confectioner's glaze. Then he let the rats do the rest." - guilty of squander, there're starving children on the streets who could've used a bite of a delicious glazed baker.
"He cuts off an ear from each victim. Right ear for men, left ear for women." - guilty of sexism, clearly both ears should be cut off regardless of gender.
"He makes sure the guilty ones don't make it back out on the streets. And he always thinks they're guilty." - guilty of being a goddamn copycat.

Dishonored 2 is absolutely worth the sixty dollars. In my opinion, it's worth a lot more, too. D2 is the sequel to what is certainly my favorite game, hands down. Now, I know what everyone's thinking; "Oh, it's a sequel. Probably much lower quality." And to that I say, "GTFO." Dishonored 2 has problems, I won't say it doesn't. It doesn't have fantasitic framerate, the AI is buggy (sometimes) but EVERYTHING is made up for in the gameplay, the story, the characters everything.
To start, the story. D2's story isn't the best story in video games, it is easily comparable to the first game's on some level, but it is more than formidable. The main story is based, cleverly, on the decisions of one of the characters who is player controlled in the DLCs, Daud, the Assassin Leader. The main characters of D2 were never aware of Daud's actions, so you know more than the main characters, which is fun. Plus, just before the final level, there's a great callback to that exactly.
To continue, the characters. There are two main characters in D2, Emily and Corvo. In the previous game, you played as Corvo and were tasked to save Emily when she was eight (This explanation isn't doing it justice, play the d*** game). So when you get to the part of the story in which you have to choose between the two of them, you're torn. I ended up playing Corvo, but I've played through it with both of them a couple of times. Personally, I prefer Emily's powers over Corvo's, but, and it may sound edgy, Corvo's executions are so brutal and powerful even if Emily's are more exotic. Anyway, They're both so very endearing (and fully voiced!).
Finally, for the pros, the gameplay. The last game was most definitley fantastic, with the choices you could make and the paths you could take, and D2 only expanded upon all of the best characteristics that worked so well for the first game. In only nine expansive levels, Arkane built thousands of possiblities, each more enticing than the last. If you have or buy the game any time soon, make a save file and experiment! Explore the level to the fullest, even if it means killing everyone. Just revert the save if you're doing low chaos. The gadgets are what I wish I had had in Dishonored, and the new powers are just as interesting and crazy.
Flaws. Only one really comes to mind, and that is the ending. It's a good ending to a great story, but it's not satisfying. To summarize my feelings, there are a bunch of choices throughout the game you can make that'll change the ending, and that is most definitely a good thing, but the cutscene that the game drops off on is like a thin patchwork quilt. All of your choices are spat back at you by the Outsider and given their consequences, but not in order of significance. In fact, not really in order of anything, it feels somewhat random.
*Edit: One thing I neglected to elaborate upon is the graphics. I have an Nvidia GTX 970, and I get a steady 50-60, but during big fights, it can get noticably lower. Only on very high settings of course.
Conclusion: Buy it.  999/10. (would be 1000/10 if the ending was better.)

I only played about half of the game, so the other half I watched via walkthroughs. But I did find that using the flamethrower was the easiest method to simply "win" the game.
The first "intro" I saw to this game had a part where someone from the game said "the items you use can be used to distract the alien, but become less effective the more you use them." Finding out that the flamethrower guarantees the alien doesn't kill you is quite saddening, since I had hoped the alien would find a way to counter you just running through the game. This is assuming you wait the alien out, as there are quite a few points where you can simply wait long enough and the alien simply leaves; so there's no need to use the flamethrower most of the time, which means more ammo for later.
If you're looking for a fun horror game, there are times that it is 10/10 and times where it's 5/10 or worse. The only thing that is scary in the game is the alien, and it is only the threat about 50% of the time-which brings me to the second but most important qualm I have with this game:
"Alien: Isolation" is a name that makes you think you're alone against an alien, a wonderful setting for a horror game. When I learned there are other humans or androids on board I was considering how that could go. If there are a few, then it can greatly benefit the game. You're about to be shot by a human who's losing his mind or an android that somehow became faulty, but the alien kills them and saves you. But there's only a few seconds of respite, as the alien isn't going to focus on a dead body when it saw another living thing nearby as well. So learning that the alien is only somewhat present in the game and that humans account for a major protion of the troubles you have is quite disappointing.
It makes it much worse when non-alien enemies don't pose any serious threat. Androids are so slow that a little prior planning can save you almost entirely from them ever getting near you. Humans are so fragile that a few revolver or shotgun shots will put them down for good. Yet this goes without mentioning that a single noisemaker or gunshot can call the alien, making it a powerful weapon for you. Factoring in that the alien eventually leaves and doesn't return without other noises, this becomes a one-shot-kill for all enemies in the game. Why have a gun fight when an invincible alien can kill everyone at the cost of one gun shot?
Overall I'm disappointed I bought this game. The handling (gameplay) and implementation are poor, to say the least. Though the graphics and story are intruging.

Just Cause 3 (abbreviated as JC3) offers a fun and explosive experience powered by its well-crafted physics engine.  Fans of JC2 are going to love this game.  The game delivers cheesy, yet adrenaline-pumping action backed by a great soundtrack and spectacular visuals.  However, the game still has a few inexcusable flaws which must be addressed.
The Just Cause series is quite the oddball when it comes to gameplay.  I would describe it as GTA on steroids.   The game is packed with over-the-top action, a recurring characteristic for the franchise.
Among the new and improved gadgets in the players arsenal lies the wingsuit.  The wingsuit was a major selling point in my opinion as not only is it a new and welcome addition to the Just Cause series, but also because the game pulls off its mechanics with flying colours.  Being quick to learn yet hard to master, the wingsuit rewards players who have mastered it with quick and angile escapes an most importantly, a hell of a ride.  The wingsuit is incredibly fun to use and the players will find themselves using it frequently.
JC3 offers a vast open world free for players to destroy to their heart's content.  The game does have a few minigames to keep players occupied.  Wingsuit, driving and piloting are core of the game's side activities.  Each of these challenges unlock the next tier of abilities for the player.  The type of ability depends on the type of challenge you complete.  For example:  Driving challenges will award you with additional modifications for a player-spawned vehicle, while wingsuit challenges offer wingsuit upgrades such as airbrakes and faster wingsuit deployment times.
JC3 is a no-brains game, if you're looking for something smart, you're looking at the wrong game.  There is only one solution to every problem:  Blow it up.  Quite frankly, that's the meat of the game.  Players will find themselves moving from one spot to another as they make their way around town.  The player can 'recapture' towns for the local folk by tearing down anything related to the government.  Objects which should be blown up are marked with red stripes, an indicator of what you should be trying to tear down in order to recapture the town.
Aside from the regular weapons, the player also has access to the Just Cause flagship grappling hook.  The player fires tethers from the wrist-mounted grappling hook, which they can use to zip at lightning speed towards the target object or attach one entity to another, pulling the two towards each other.  JC3 brings more improvements to the grappling hook, allowing players to manually control the tension of the tether using the "Shift" Key.  The grappling hook is a versatile and destructive tool which the players are encouraged to experiment with.
However, the game's strong point is also its weak point.  By saying so, I mean that the game's ridiculously silly physics and rather brainless approach to every situation makes the game feel extremely shallow.  The game is dumb, but it doesn't mean it isn't fun.  The most damaging part of the game is how repetitive it can be.  Players who go into the game with the sole intention of completing one objective as efficiently as possible will find themselves going through routine patrols around the town, searching for propaganda to tear down with the grappling hook and finally destroying a list of objects at the local police station.  This mind-numbing process is repeated in every single town and it's disappointing to say the least.
My favourite wingsuit is also to blame for ruining the gameplay.  JC2 saw a respectable use of vehicles as driving from one location to another was faster than using the parachute.  JC3 falls flat on its face in terms of its driving mechanics.  Cars feel stiff, sluggish and seem to be glued to the ground, making the wingsuit the go-to choice for travelling.  It's a pity that the vehicles are given no attention as each one seems to have its own unique interior with great engine sound effects as well, an aspect of the series which has been scrapped despite its popularity in previous installments.
The player assumes control of Rico, an experienced "spy" (more like explosives expert) returning to his home in Medici after his retirement.  At first, he's happy to be at home, but he spots something.  No...could it be?  Another dictator has seized control over the country!  This one sounds exactly like Hitler and looks like Stalin, unfortunately I don't remember the bloke's name so I'll call him Stitler.  With the help of his friends in Medici, Rico must bomb every town and destroy all facilities to regain control over his beloved country.  Hooray for terrorism!
The story is far from the series' strong suit and I was not expecting any quality story of any sort.  However, I still expect at least some form of a story from a game asking for $60.  Come on, JC2 received criticism for its forgettable, awkward and rather pointless story.  Had Square Enix made any effort at all to at least improve the game's story, I'd have given it a higher score.  However, the game still doesn't provide any incentives for the player to progress through the already-shallow story.
Square Enix believes that by putting a thick-accented Italian aptly named 'Mario' into the game, they've improved the story.  Even though this 'Mario' character does have his moments, it certainly cannot compensate for the neglected story.  I can't blame the developers, though, as the nature of the game itself seems to restrict any smart or witty story-telling.  So I understand, nice try.
JC3 showcases up-to-date graphics, a souped-up physics engine built for fun and destruction models which do nothing short of enhancing the game's experience.  Medici has a gorgeous landscape reminiscent of Sorrento in Italy.  The design of the cars as well as the game's sountrack, which uses tunes from an acoustic guitar as its backbone, all combine together to set a great atmosphere for the game's location and sets the theme perfectly.  The game is far from heavy and is all about toying around and having fun.  Explosions are phenomenal as they give both satisfying audio and visual feedback.  Explosions go off with satisfying pops and light up the area in a magnificent extravaganza of fire.  The graphics are only disappointing for vehicles, which seem to have a surprisingly low texture quality.  Fortunately, this isn't immediately noticeable and does not detract from the game's experience.
The shadows are at their best when the sun is out.  Everything is well-lit and warm light is cast on the environment.  Medici's abundant sunflower fields can be driven through, flattening flowers and allowing players to leave behind symbols in the field.  Rico's attire is also well-designed.  Unlike JC2 in which Rico was known under the handle "Scorpio", bearing a red scorpion on his shirt - JC3 gives Rico a casual, yet well-equipped outlook.  Rico's harness hooks up to his grappling hook tether, freeing both his hands, and his unprofessional outfit fits in well with the whole retirement theme of the game.  Better still, the game runs at a rock solid 60fps on high settings for me, great optimization.
The visuals completely make up for JC3's lackluster story and is what keeps the game enjoyable.
Despite the neglected story and repetitive gameplay, JC3 is still loaded with fun for casual and hardcore players alike.

Having played this for dozens and dozens of hours when I was younger, experiencing the Remastered Collection is an absolute treat. No more modern military shooters or the same racing games done countless times before, the Age of Space is back! And having one of the finest space RTS games ever, remastered for a whole new generation to experience solidifies itself as an absolute must own.

I played the old Homeworld 2 and instantly fell in love, this new iteration is no exception. Everything from the graphics to the controls are crisp and wonderful to behold. I have played all sorts of RTS games from Age of Empires to Civ 5 to Star Wars Empire at War. However, this game keeps your attention better than any of them I feel. That constant fear of an attack from above or below, as the 3D plane allows, keeps you on your toes. There are always more layers to this game so that you will never get bored, and if you somehow do, it allows mods! Hardcore RTS players will enjoy the depth of strategy and casual players, like myself will also find this to be quite enjoyable. 10/10

At first i wasn't really impressed by this game. There's a larger then average learing curve, long waits for respawn, and servers where players aren't working together or know what to do in objective can really leave a bad impression.
What worked best for me and improved my overall experience was learning the ropes in a unlimited ammo/respawn server. It was fun to blast zombies left for dead style but that isn't how the game is supposed to be played and soon the novelty wore off. Thats when i jumped back to the "classic" style and with my newfound knowlage on how to play my enjoyment of the game was leaps and bounds more then when i started.
Some other tips for new players.
1) Work together and communicate.
2) If you don't have the gun...leave the ammo for someone that does.
3) Keep a backup melee weapon.
4) Press "c" to bring up compass and current objective
5) Save a bullet...infected players can kill teamates when they turn (press "k" to take the easy way out if your infected)
6) Bandages are for when your bleeding/medkits for when your grayed out/pills for when your infected.
7) Conserve resources!
8) Don't clog doorways...players are solid(ish) you will be sitting targets.
9) Watch out for children....
Over all...would i recomend this game? HELL YES! It takes a bit but it growns on you. I see many more hours to be had in this game....btw you know the games free right?!

The Dark Souls games can be described as two brothers. They both are nice guys, but Dark Souls 2 is the brother who spends a bit more time than his older brother trying to look nice, but is a little bit shallow in comparison. He's a good kid, really. He just spends a bit too much time focusing on himself and appearances as well as his family name rather than being who he could be.
Dark Souls 2 has plenty of flaws, just like the original did, but the problems are largely different. Dark Souls 1 suffered from a large number of technical problems that could be largely solved through a bit of tweaking and modding. Dark Souls 2 fixes most of these problems, yet sort of piggybacks off the original's success for it's own, if that makes sense. It just feels a bit more shallow. A little easier. A little less uninspired. And that's a shame.
The game is still a Souls game, and if you come from the other Souls games (namely Dark Souls) you will probably enjoy it. But I think it's safe to say it won't blow you away like the original.

I've been playing Dark Souls 2 for roughly 2 months now, and I have to say in complete honesty, this game was a massive dissappointment. The boss fights are no where near as memorable or as interesting as the first game's. In short, there were too many situations where you face multiple bosses at a time and this ineviatably lead to playing a long and monotonous waiting game with the attack cycles. The boss designs also came off as incredibly lazy to me with many of the bosses  simply being large, armored huminoid creatures wielding oversized weapons (Sentinels, Smelter, Pursuer, Velstadt, Dragonriders, Flexile, Looking Glass, etc). The developers also seem to have placed no regard in balancing enemy strengths and weaknesses with the most notorious being the number of enemies in an area vs the power of each individual enemy. This pretty much just encourages players to run past everything or employ cheap, unfun strategies (lightning spears all day everyday). PvP as of now is a complete joke, and literally every other player I've come across is wearing Havel's and just RB spams some variant of an embued Greatsword. Finally, many of the elements in this game feel incredibly reused and the elements of the game that were supposed to change gameplay dynamics such as torches, incorporation of life stones and the adaptability stat had little if any impact from my experience. Still, while this game was a dissappointment in terms of the high bar the previous souls games had set, it is by no means a terrible game as evidenced by the 100+ I played it. It still retains many of the things that makes a Souls game a Souls game and overall, I'd give Dark Souls 2 a 7/10.

I can't even begin to explain how disappointing this game was.
From Software, all you had to do was fix connecting to other players, and add proper 60FPS to the game. Not only are those things STILL broken, and not to mention we learn more and more every day about how terrible the implementation of 60fps is in the game, but you also had to ruin almost everything else that made the original game fun.
The near perfect hitboxes of the first game? Completely gone, and now you can guarantee dying every so often for the dumbest things.
The fair balance of rolling? Also gone. It baffles me how any developer could think that tying i-frames to a stat was a good idea. The point of having a fixed amount of i-frames was so players could actually GET GOOD at dodging and KNOWING when they would be invincible during a roll instead of having near-zero invincibility at low levels and then having a hard time to adjust once they did have a good amount of i-frames in their rolls.
The realistic movement? Once again, gone. Welcome the new floaty movement that feels like you're always ice skating instead of walking on solid ground. Oh and also the way equipment weight affects movement is ridiculous as well, making you look like a bouncing balloon instead of an actual person.
Now on to weapons. Not only have the movesets been worsened, but now it feels like you're swinging a foam sword instead of having any actual weight behind it. They clearly did not use mo-cap for this game, or in the case that they did use it, made  terrible use of its advantages.
The world map makes no sense whatsoever, and the interconnectivity from the first game is non-existant. It's all straight pathways from now on. Not only this, but none of the areas are as good as the original game's environments. They are incredibly inconsistent and far from grounded and realistic.
Alright, now the enemies. You thought it would get better from here in the review right? WRONG. Humanoids humanoids humanoids EVERYWHERE. No originality whatsoever. But that isn't a huge deal, you know what is though? The fact that the game throws wave after wave of AWFUL enemies in groups of 4 to 5 enemies at you because "LEL DERK SULZ IS HERRRD" instead of putting you against 1 or 2 difficult enemies that have interesting fighting styles. It also sucks that almost every single enemy in the game has a 'one-shot' move in which you get stuck in a dumb animation where all you'll find to say is "How in the f*** did he grab me? I WAS 3 METERS AWAY!". All in all your deaths from these enemies with the smarts of a zombie will always leave you flabbergasted as to how you actually died.
Finally, the bosses. Ohhh how great it was when you first encountered O&S, and later when you fought Artorias. The bosses were hard at first, but all you needed to do was adjust to their attacks and switch up strategies. They had unique fight styles which engaged the players and every death felt like it was YOUR fault instead of leaving you screaming at the monitor about how unfair the Ancient Dragon's attacks are. But that's not it, the game applies the same logic to bosses that they apply to enemies. It's no longer a fair fight where you can focus on the boss. No. Now the game puts you against MORE than one boss at a time, all with their own ridiculous hitboxes just for your enjoyment. Oh, and they are almost all humanoids too, and none of them are remarkable from the rest.
I could probably go into how terrible the lore and story is in Dark Souls 2, but I think just remembering how poor this game was has left enough disappointment in me for today.
