Is Dishonored 2 a great stealth game? Definitely. Level design here is good at its worst and phenomenal at its best. Attention to small detail both in visual design and gameplay, pleasant reactivity, all of it builds up to present a memorable world. Two playable characters to choose from, each with unique powers, new game+ options, replay value is high indeed.
Does it have a story? Yes, it does... I guess? With its key moments often feeling hilariously rushed (traditional coup out of nowhere! vintage Dishonored!). It is also, apparently, heavily based on Brigmore Witches dlc for the original game, which I didn't play. At least the support cast of villains and vigilantes is fairly colourful.
Is it still, at this point, a shabby port? Evidently it is. It ran acceptable-ish for me on 1070, with some annoying texture/shadow popping in here and there, but a lot of people still struggle with running it well.
And now that we're done with the rubbish questions, let's answer a real one:
As you know, or will know in a moment (patience!), early on in Dishonored games you're granted the Heart artifact (see, patience paid off! But what a masterful use of foreshadowing on my part, eh?). Aside from irrelevant to the present prosecutorial topic uses, the Heart serves to tell you secrets. Point it at anyone
, right click and learn of this person's most shameful deeds! And what do you do with this knowledge? Why, you prosecute, swiftly and relentlessly! This is your chance to be Miles Edgeworth on a rampage! Being judgemental is a tremendously popular pastime after all, try it out!
There're some exceptions to this common rule. The Heart cannot read the hidden thoughts of:
A) Dogs. Because, obviously, all dogs are saints and keep no dark secrets, as canine author of this most marvelous review can testify.
B) Mechanical soldiers, but those murderous clockwork beauties look highly trustworthy anyway.
C) Rats and bloodflies, because they're terrible bores.
Of course, in a decadent society that Dishonored 2 portrays, almost everyone is guilty of some misdeed or other. And so it falls to you to serve some justice, preferably poetic and in style.
This dock worker sabotaged a ship with murderous intentions? Guilty! Off into the canal waters he goes, then!
This officer tests out fancy torture devices on prisoners? Guilty! Let's test this springrazor contraption on him!
This lady murdered her father's dog? Double guilty! Beware the anger of a gentle corgi. Knock the murderous lass over a balustrade by throwing an unconscious dog at her (the dog volunteered, I assure you)!
This guard kicked a neighbour's child? Well now, I hardly see anything wrong with that, I don't like kids myself. Pass.
Some additional examples of the Heart's insights:
"He tied the baker and covered him with confectioner's glaze. Then he let the rats do the rest." - guilty of squander, there're starving children on the streets who could've used a bite of a delicious glazed baker.
"He cuts off an ear from each victim. Right ear for men, left ear for women." - guilty of sexism, clearly both ears should be cut off regardless of gender.
"He makes sure the guilty ones don't make it back out on the streets. And he always thinks they're guilty." - guilty of being a goddamn copycat.

Dishonored 2 is absolutely worth the sixty dollars. In my opinion, it's worth a lot more, too. D2 is the sequel to what is certainly my favorite game, hands down. Now, I know what everyone's thinking; "Oh, it's a sequel. Probably much lower quality." And to that I say, "GTFO." Dishonored 2 has problems, I won't say it doesn't. It doesn't have fantasitic framerate, the AI is buggy (sometimes) but EVERYTHING is made up for in the gameplay, the story, the characters everything.
To start, the story. D2's story isn't the best story in video games, it is easily comparable to the first game's on some level, but it is more than formidable. The main story is based, cleverly, on the decisions of one of the characters who is player controlled in the DLCs, Daud, the Assassin Leader. The main characters of D2 were never aware of Daud's actions, so you know more than the main characters, which is fun. Plus, just before the final level, there's a great callback to that exactly.
To continue, the characters. There are two main characters in D2, Emily and Corvo. In the previous game, you played as Corvo and were tasked to save Emily when she was eight (This explanation isn't doing it justice, play the d*** game). So when you get to the part of the story in which you have to choose between the two of them, you're torn. I ended up playing Corvo, but I've played through it with both of them a couple of times. Personally, I prefer Emily's powers over Corvo's, but, and it may sound edgy, Corvo's executions are so brutal and powerful even if Emily's are more exotic. Anyway, They're both so very endearing (and fully voiced!).
Finally, for the pros, the gameplay. The last game was most definitley fantastic, with the choices you could make and the paths you could take, and D2 only expanded upon all of the best characteristics that worked so well for the first game. In only nine expansive levels, Arkane built thousands of possiblities, each more enticing than the last. If you have or buy the game any time soon, make a save file and experiment! Explore the level to the fullest, even if it means killing everyone. Just revert the save if you're doing low chaos. The gadgets are what I wish I had had in Dishonored, and the new powers are just as interesting and crazy.
Flaws. Only one really comes to mind, and that is the ending. It's a good ending to a great story, but it's not satisfying. To summarize my feelings, there are a bunch of choices throughout the game you can make that'll change the ending, and that is most definitely a good thing, but the cutscene that the game drops off on is like a thin patchwork quilt. All of your choices are spat back at you by the Outsider and given their consequences, but not in order of significance. In fact, not really in order of anything, it feels somewhat random.
*Edit: One thing I neglected to elaborate upon is the graphics. I have an Nvidia GTX 970, and I get a steady 50-60, but during big fights, it can get noticably lower. Only on very high settings of course.
Conclusion: Buy it.  999/10. (would be 1000/10 if the ending was better.)

A good stealth/action game, with quite solid and addictive gameplay mechanics.
Gameplay: 9/10 - Fun most times, frustrating every once in a while, where the platforming lets it down in places. There is almost no improvement upon Dishonored 1's gameplay (possibly because it was already great on gameplay).
Level design: 7.5/10 - Levels feel deep and multi-layered. Misses a lot of verticality in a most missions and some missions feel incredibly linear. Overall though, most levels are good, encouraging attention to detail and planning.
Graphics: 7/10 - Nothing new, apart from some more detailed long-distance views compared to Dishonored 1. The art style is great, but it's mostly a copy-paste of the 4-year-old game that came before it.
Sound: 9/10 - Sound is a very important part of this game, as it is necessary to guide you through the missions (especially on Stealth gameplay). The voice-acting is TOP NOTCH with amazing voice actors and a great variety of NPC dialogue/monologues. The music was just ok, apart from the main theme which captures the atmosphere well.
Story: 7/10 - Story is mediocre and most of the time feels like a copy of the first game. The only saving grace is the replayability offered by 2 protagonist playthroughs and that your choices matter. The after-taste though leaves much to be desired, as it feels like they could have done A LOT MORE with the story, 4 years after the original.
Characters: 9/10 - Your decisions matter, you connect with characters and you feel like they influence your decisions as much as you do theirs. That goes for all allies and most enemies, but one let-down is the main antagonist, which feels very generic as a main villain.
Overall: 8/10 - If you played the 1st one and loved it, you will love this one as well. If you are new to the series, watch a lot of gameplay and reviews before getting it, as it is not for everyone. Overall, it was great fun, but lacking in 1 or 2 areas (like the story) compared to the 1st one. A very solid entry to the series nevertheless.

It's like the people behind Bioshock and Thief had a baby!... probably because that's exactly what it is.
It really does play like the Bioshock folks made a scifi mod to Thief. All the technical stuff is the same. The characters look exactly like Thief characters in slightly different clothes--same shrink-wrapped appearance and everything. The sound design is similar, and not just because the Thief himself, Stephen Russell, voices a secondary character. The robots sound alike, the movement noises are the same, right down to that satisfying "BRANG!" you get when you jump on something metallic. You can mantle onto things too high to jump onto, although I can't remember that ever adding much to gameplay.
The gameplay is all Bioshock, including (spoilers ahoy) a mystery voice who assumes an identity to gain your trust only to betray and try to murder you and fight you in the final boss battle. You're also a (mostly) silent protagonist, like Jack and Delta from Bioshocks 1&2. There's audio logs scattered everywhere. You go around thwapping people with your wrench. There's ghosts to be found periodically, although just like the ghosts in Bioshock they don't really add much to the story.
Unfortunately... I didn't really like this game. I know, I know, it's a classic, designed by the creators of two of the best franchises in gaming history. And I loved Bioshock. I loved Thief. I just didn't love this. The levels want to be open and sprawly like in Thief but still want a mostly linear story like Bioshock. This ends up translating to a lot of keycard puzzles and a LOT of backtracking. Unlike Bioshock, where the levels are interesting and colorful, most of the levels in this game are the same bland white and grey (once you've turned the gamma up--the game gets really dark and confusing from time to time). It's easy to get lost because everything looks alike and the enemies respawn. There's a lot of junk you can pick up, which lead me to discard some things I actually needed for puzzles and meant I spent even more time wandering aimlessly around levels.
There weren't any diversions, like Bioshock's Little Sister rescues, and there weren't many times where I felt Thief-type exploring let to anything of interest. The story was pretty much System Shock 2.0 (there's a shock to the system, huh). By the end of the game there was no fun in stabbing giant muscly bird monsters with coat-rack looking crystals anymore. I was just hanging around to finish the story. And then the final battle was solved by hacking a few things and then picking off Shodan's health with my pistol. It was a slog and I wasn't a fan.
For what it's worth, though, it does run very well. Unlike the Thief games I didn't have to do any tinkering to see the cutscenes, and the only bug I found was when my arm would detach, causing me to be sprinting around, fleeing from hybrids, while my arm was still hanging out on the other side of the map, uselessly punching the wall.

I love the Elder Scrolls games, I started back in the day with Daggerfall and have been a fan ever since. ESO is a game that took me by surprise when it was announced. I didn't expect an MMO to ever be a thing in the IP, maybe co-op stuff but never on this scale. I waited a long time to finally get into it as I already had played the beta and kind of felt it was lacking alot of things that a good MMO needs "okay" would describe my feelings at that point.
With that said, the game is quickly losing it's charm. The game moves along at a decent pace, TES games were never about getting things fast, or becoming a god aftert 3 hours, but the leveling in ESO seems artificially stunted. Maybe it's the low(ish) level cap, maybe it's something else. It feels wrong to me though.
Questing is decent, nothing special, typical MMO stuff. Can't complain too much here.
Audio is hit or miss with certain things being dead on but combat lacks that PUNCH that makes it feel brutal.
Now on to why I truly loathe this game at this point, which honestly saddens me.
Crafting, the time it takes to do research, 6 hours? Seriously!? Is this a damn mobile game, did I accidentally log in to Clash of Clans, this is stupid as hell honestly two hours would have been perfect. A general playtime length for the average player to maybe knock out 2 items in a session and log off. I get with the system they used it doesn't really have a whole lot of things to really "research" so they padded it out. Another dumb idea to artificially lengthen the game.
The monotany of this game shines the more and more I play it, it drives me crazy. Solo is just way to easy to do, and group content is sorely lacking anything of mention. PVP is a joke, seriously, the worst MMO PvP I have ever played and I have a big list of MMOs dating back to EQ1.
I really hope the upcoming patches and ideas ZeniMax talked about at E3 will make this game more usefull than just a soundtrack for taking naps at my desk which is basically all it is now.

The short of it: grognard vote of approval.
The long of it: Homeworld (its demo, in fact) was the first game I installed on my first computer. I've kept at it constantly through the years. The Remastered edition does contain Homeworld and Homeworld 2, they are as good as ever, and this is reason enough for a thumbs up.
The Remastered edition adds a lot of visual improvements, and some gameplay modifications as well. The awesome Homeworld story is brought into the Homeworld 2 engine - some players might choose this opportunity to experience it, since you can now issue orders while the game is paused, and thus deal with the more hectic moments of space combat.
Apart from more detailed textures, 3D models, lightning system, here are some pros and cons at a glance:
PROS:
- the gameplay tried to remain faithful to the original
- game runs well
- good sound quality
- everything said in cinematics has a subtitle, including the launch game-engine cinematic
- good first day support (got a game update immediately after my first crashed, which got fixed)
- you can pit Kushan against Hiigaran, or any of the 4 factions of the two games in skirmish
- it is fun
CONS:
- though technically impressive, the visual aspect of the game needs some more polishing and fitting together
- some HW1 ships don't work well yet, like Hive Frigates
- HW1 Salvage Corvette numbers are now drastically limited; doing the campaign junkyard style seems doubtful
Nitpicking:
- The starting cinematic ends with the view centered on the Resource Collector; however, due to the orientation of the camera, the backdrop is outer space, rather than Kharak, as was in the original game. I feel this disrupts the narratively important visual repetition of Kharak (multiple times in the starting cinematic, then contrasted in mission 3), and I would like the developer to 'fix' the narrative element back.
Bottom line: good, fun games, done in the spirit of the old and improved upon. Still need a few patches.

I can't even begin to explain how disappointing this game was.
From Software, all you had to do was fix connecting to other players, and add proper 60FPS to the game. Not only are those things STILL broken, and not to mention we learn more and more every day about how terrible the implementation of 60fps is in the game, but you also had to ruin almost everything else that made the original game fun.
The near perfect hitboxes of the first game? Completely gone, and now you can guarantee dying every so often for the dumbest things.
The fair balance of rolling? Also gone. It baffles me how any developer could think that tying i-frames to a stat was a good idea. The point of having a fixed amount of i-frames was so players could actually GET GOOD at dodging and KNOWING when they would be invincible during a roll instead of having near-zero invincibility at low levels and then having a hard time to adjust once they did have a good amount of i-frames in their rolls.
The realistic movement? Once again, gone. Welcome the new floaty movement that feels like you're always ice skating instead of walking on solid ground. Oh and also the way equipment weight affects movement is ridiculous as well, making you look like a bouncing balloon instead of an actual person.
Now on to weapons. Not only have the movesets been worsened, but now it feels like you're swinging a foam sword instead of having any actual weight behind it. They clearly did not use mo-cap for this game, or in the case that they did use it, made  terrible use of its advantages.
The world map makes no sense whatsoever, and the interconnectivity from the first game is non-existant. It's all straight pathways from now on. Not only this, but none of the areas are as good as the original game's environments. They are incredibly inconsistent and far from grounded and realistic.
Alright, now the enemies. You thought it would get better from here in the review right? WRONG. Humanoids humanoids humanoids EVERYWHERE. No originality whatsoever. But that isn't a huge deal, you know what is though? The fact that the game throws wave after wave of AWFUL enemies in groups of 4 to 5 enemies at you because "LEL DERK SULZ IS HERRRD" instead of putting you against 1 or 2 difficult enemies that have interesting fighting styles. It also sucks that almost every single enemy in the game has a 'one-shot' move in which you get stuck in a dumb animation where all you'll find to say is "How in the f*** did he grab me? I WAS 3 METERS AWAY!". All in all your deaths from these enemies with the smarts of a zombie will always leave you flabbergasted as to how you actually died.
Finally, the bosses. Ohhh how great it was when you first encountered O&S, and later when you fought Artorias. The bosses were hard at first, but all you needed to do was adjust to their attacks and switch up strategies. They had unique fight styles which engaged the players and every death felt like it was YOUR fault instead of leaving you screaming at the monitor about how unfair the Ancient Dragon's attacks are. But that's not it, the game applies the same logic to bosses that they apply to enemies. It's no longer a fair fight where you can focus on the boss. No. Now the game puts you against MORE than one boss at a time, all with their own ridiculous hitboxes just for your enjoyment. Oh, and they are almost all humanoids too, and none of them are remarkable from the rest.
I could probably go into how terrible the lore and story is in Dark Souls 2, but I think just remembering how poor this game was has left enough disappointment in me for today.

Before I get too nasty, I need to preface with the fact that this game is definitely worth your time: just play this before playing Dark Souls 1, or you might be dissapointed. This is a good game, but not a good sequel. And before the excuse of different directors is brought up, it still could've been better. In this game, they decided to try and make it harder, because, naturally, a sequel to a game bent on being difficult should be harder. I agree with that, but in turn of making it as rewarding as the first game, they decided to make it harder in an unfair way, ESPECIALLY the closer you get to the endgame. There are enemies that are harder to beat than the bosses they protect, on top of the enemies being put in situations that make death nearly inevitable until they stop respawning (I'm talking to you, Shrine of Amana...). Some people complained about the spike in difficulty at Ornstein and Smough in Dark Souls 1, but the difficulty from there on was smoothly rising. In Dark Souls 2, however, the difficulty is EVERYWHERE! For some people, it was the build they were trying to make, but that was on top of the enemies that could insta-kill you anyway. All that aside, I'll be blunt, the ending sucked♥♥♥♥♥cheeks. I mean, really? In Dark Souls 1 *(SPOILER)* you could become the new Lord of Cinder, or become a Lord of Darkness. THAT WAS AWESOME!!! In the new game, you just become the new king and sit in a sealed chamber until the door closes... *(END SPOILER)* That sucks in comparison. It's just not worth it. Not to mention, the final boss is SO EASY. If you run around the room, hit (blank) a couple of times along the way, they die easily! It isn't a good ending at all. With a lack of luster for ideas on top of a new harder difficulty with your payoff being another runthrough of the game at a HIGHER difficulty, it's not necessarily the best game in comparison to the last two Souls games being better. However, it is still a little fun and is worth your time. Play this game first, then play the other two to see how it pales in comparison.

Indeed the best use of the Alien franchise in gaming history - and one of my new favorites in the survival horror genre.
Atmospheric and engrossing, this has to be one of the most nerve-wrecking games I have ever played - well done to the developers for the design choices they made. One element of this is the save point system: while many have complained about it, I feel the game would not have been nearly as intense had you been able to save anywhere. An unscripted AI dishing out insta-kills aboard a cramped space station, where every action, sound and movement you make could be your last, is enhanced 10-fold by the fact that you have to get to a save point or lose your progress. No matter how many times I may have died in a specific scenario, it always had me coming back to find another strategy. The subtle beeping sound of a save point in the distance will become your favorite tune. There are times you will literally hold your breath while hiding in a cabinet - with the alien beastie strolling by, looking to dirt-nap someone.
The game recreates the original movies tension and environment, and adds to the story nicely. Nothing major here in terms of twists and turns in the plot, but it is entertaining enough to keep the whole package together. We're in it for the gameplay and suspense, and it's thrills in all respects.
Entertaining to the end - freaky as hell - highly recommended. 9/10

The game is beautiful, from beginning to end. It's plenty scary as well. The reason I couldn't get into it mostly came down to the atmosphere it cultivates. It's all about making you feel as powerless as possible. You have weapons, but even 5 hours into the game, they're pretty much just for show. If things get really desperate, you could waste 90% of your extremely limited ammo killing one of the robots that make up the huge majority of this game's bad guys, but that usually just ends up attracting more of them.
I'm not knocking this game for what it is, because i knew about it going in...i guess i just thought i'd have more fun in it. I love horror games, but stuff like Dead Space is more my thing. Basically, I want to face the monsters/aliens/whatever, but I want to have a chance to fight my way through them. If that's the way you feel too, I wouldn't buy this one.
This is a stealth game. I don't mean that in the way that games like "Splinter Cell" use it. This game is extremely unforgiving, and I never encountered an enemy that couldn't easily kill you if a mistake was made. If caught, trying to run and hide can make things worse, because there is no shortage of enemies here, and you'll most likely run into one while trying to escape another.
If you like games like Amnesia, Slender, or any of the other horror games that rely on making you as defenceless as possible to amp up the tension and scares, you will LOVE this game.
It's well made, it's beautiful, it's what Alien games always could have been...it just wasn't for me.

Anyway, if you're into Alien at all, or sci-fi stealth/survival games, you should definitely give this a go.

But anyway, on to the game itself;
Single Player was OK, but honestly seemed to rely more on the fact that Kevin Spacey was there than much else. At its core its your generic shoot 'em up gameplay as you blast though a level until you reach the finish line. The "twist" in the story is more or less forced on you, and the game really showcases its lack of grey as it turns your old allies in to Nazis over like, 1 day. And apparently you don't now seem to care you're now killing people you worked with for several months/years. The stealth is pretty much your standard "follow the leader", so there's very little of that. Graphics wise, it's not all that great, you can tell they've ported this straight from the consoles. In fact in one instance I tried to lower the graphics settings because I was getting some FPS lag, it caused a bluescreen and upon rebooting my PC, it had to validate the files were still working. Furthermore, the cutscenes have a tendency to freeze, and since they interlace the cutscenes with loading screens you can't skip them, so it's like watching a broken VCR.
Overall, the story is lack lustre, but doesn't leave you on as big of a cliff hanger as Ghosts did (but still leaves you with a very clear open ending showing this story is going to be continued). Like most of the CoD campigns, it feels like the effort wasn't directed here and it has no feel of replayability. If you're a sort of person that gets games for their story, then this isn't a strong reason to get this game.
Anyway, on to the co-op mode now. Co-op originally started as Exo-Survival, which was pretty much just MW3 survival, but with a few small differences. Despite this, it still felt quite fun. Esspecilly the classes and unique scorestreaks you could use. But it sort of lost some lustre as it was of course, still just survival from MW3. And thin it got worse. Then they added "Exo-Zombies". At first, I was hoping they'd do their own spin on it, and have their own version of it for a different spin of this mode. I was wrong. Exo-Zombies literally only exists to feed off all the people that like Zombies in Treyarch games by making it exactly the same as Zombies, but with the added useage of Exo-suits. Overall, nothing original here. Only worth playing if your MW3 or WaW/BO/BO2 isn't working. Or if you feel like playing surivial/zombies but on one of SHG's maps.
And finally, the main seller of any CoD game; the multiplayer. Now this can be a very hard and subjective thing to judge. I mean some people just look at a negative review and just go "You only think it's bad because you are bad". Well in this case, I can say that's not completly the case. I do get a few good games in, and I'm currently pulling a positive K/D to anyone that gives a rats♥♥♥♥♥♥about K/D. But anyway, to the actual review. Well first we should start with the most obvious issue; Dedicated Servers. We were promised dedicated servers, and they never came. Just another show of how the companies put the consoles before the PC. And don't get me wrong, I don't really buy in to this whole "PC master race" malarcky, but if you're going to make a game for PC, then make it 'for' the PC, don't just port the intended console version over. And then there's the weapon balance, and frankly SHG shot themselves in the foot with the weapon balance, however they must have done it with the Atlas 45 since they didn't even notice they'd ♥♥♥♥ed it up. The main issue with the weapon balance is all the supply variants. And some of those are given such pathetic buff to nerf ratios that even nerfing the base gun does nothing. Per example, the Obsidian Steel gains a 3 shot kill out to a fairly long range, while only gaining a small hipfire increase, a minor recoil increase (mitigated by a grip) and a RoF drop of only 50 RPM. Genrally, the most popular guns in MP are the Bal-27 and ASM1, and genrally, it'll be their +Damage varaints, the Obsidian Steel and Speakeasy. As someone that genrally uses the HBRa3 and IMR, I can say they're not completly bad, but it's still pretty much the same weapons over and over again. And on the topic of consistant weapons, the maps have once again been built with only 1 tactic in mind; rushing. Now I know CoD has always suited a "Run 'n' gun" play style, and that's what makes it so popular. But I loathe that these maps have been built specifically for rushing. When we compare it to MW2 maps, there was variety. There was long range combat on Afghan, there was mid-range combat on Underpass, and there was still some CQC action on Skirow (spelt wrong since that's apparently a naughty word on Steam). AW mpas just feel like they've been built for CQC, with the off mid-range sightline. And of course, if you try to use the sightline with a mid-range weapon, you just called a camper and hacker and everythign under the sun just because you killed a rusher. And of course, add in the exo-suits and you basically have Halo bunny hopping on steroids.
And as an added bonus. The community reception. Now, i don't mean Community as in us, I mean how SHG dealt with the community, because frankly your commmunity makes up most of your game, esspecially if you want it to last, or if you want people to buy all your micro-DLCs (which by the way, did I mention the consoles get a micro-DLC to get supply drops but us on PC don't?). Frankly, SHGs community support has been appalling. I mean, any points AW may have still saved for a rating, I'd knock off for their community interaction. Firstly, most of the things they said would happen didn't. You can look though these reviews and look at ones several months old, and see the issues are still relevant. In my once experiance, I had to debate with the support team for 4 months, just to get 1 hour of double XP. And frankly, the only people they seem to care about are the people making revenue of their game on YouTube. So you might see people like Ali-A and Drift0r praising the game, because they're getting paid for it, and SHG know that so it's them they're keeping happy. But then you look at all the people that aren't getting paid for it, and aren't as powerful free advertisement simply being ignored. A good example is all of us leaving negative reviews, since like I said above, our issues ahve yet to be responded to. And then there's the Call of Duty Wiki (~1 million views a week) and CharlieIntel who never get any acknowledgement from SHG despite the fact they're both huge CoD communties (and trust me, we have tried contacting them).
So in short. The campaign is medocre and predicatable, the co-op mode is nothing more than copy-paste, and the multiplayer is just a bombshell made to panda to those that will actually praise the game instead of listen to criticism. And as far as SHG is concerend, this review means nothing because I don't have millions of subscribers on YouTube.
Edit: Another thing that makes me somewhat sad. Is while many of the reviews are funny, many people leave "Recommended" reviews, with nothing more than silly comments that don't reflect the games issues. This leads to incorrect percentages.

Even though I've not played these games for long so far, I can tell this is exactly what I wanted and was buying. Gearbox didn't dissapoint this time with this flawless remastering of a classic. These game's mechanics still hold up to this day and with updated graphics it leaves all other current RTS of this kind. It's very hard to describe the feeling you get when you combine nostalgia with a great game and then polish it to this level of sheen. This should be an instant purchase for past lovers of these games. Newcomers should also try these if they are fans of RTS games. The controls are smooth and intuitive. They work well for 3d navigation in 3d space. The HUD is relatively easy to navigate as well. My only complaint about the HUD is the upgrading and building menus. Those I have always considered somewhat clunky. Large scale space combat in these games is fun and cinematic. These games also feature a great soundtrack fit for space exploration. The added workshop compatibility for mods just makes this package too sweet to ignore. Can't wait for someone to redo Cataclysm and put it on there. All in all, a solid buy even at full price. It should be noted that I even dislike RTS games for the better part, but would place this game solidly on a top 10 games of all time list.

To put it bluntly, Dishonoured 2 is a more than worthy successor to one of best stealth games of all time. Taking place 15 years after the original, the empress of the isles, Emliy Kaldwin is overthrown by none other than Delilah Copperspoon, the main villian of dishonoureds two fantastic DLC's. Thus it is up to Emily or her father Corvo to take back the throne by going to karnaca, where Delilahs insidous allies lurk and taking them out, how you see fit. First off, the gameplay has been shined to a mirror sheen, combat is fast-paced and suprisingly difficult, seriously, a new player taking on a small group of enemies is basically suicide without a proper plan of action. The combat is shown of the best any time you fight one of the clockwork soldiers, which is one of the best enemy types i've had the joy of fighting in any game ever.
Movement is also overall a lot smoother and many peoples biggest complaint has been fixed: there is now non leathal combat, with almost every attack, from counter attacks to drop assassinatons getting a non-leathal version. Level design is also the same high standard as the original with many paths open for reaching your goal, with the trio of levels "Edge of the world", "The good doctor" and "The clockwork mansion" being the highlights for me. Even the powers and bonecharm systems got updated, with each power having it's own mini upgrade tree instead of just a level 1 and a level 2 and being able to craft your own bonecharms and the introduction of black bonecharms.
The replay value is high on this one aswell, with the two different characters getting completely different powers and even their gun and crossbow being different. There is also choosing low and high chaos playthroughs that effects someparts of the levels as well as the overall ending and choosing if you want the outsiders mark or not, meaning that you would have to play the game 8 different times to see everything it has to offer.

When I first completed Dark Souls 2, I had to take a step back and really think about what made this game enjoyable. Was the reverse difficulty curve of the game a refreshing change or a nuisance that messes with the core Dark Souls formula? Was the lore as mysterious and intriguing as the first game, or was it living in its predecessor's shadow too often to be able to breathe on its own? I came to the conclusion that whatever Dark Souls 2 could have been is something that's only on my mind as I slog through the beginnings of the game. What it is now, as an overall game experience, is really all that mattered to me by the end of the game and I wouldn't have devoted my many hours into it if that hadn't been true.
Dark Souls 2 lives up to reputation, if not high expectation. It's bigger, meaner, and every bit as satisfying to complete as the first game. It improves in most aspects such as UI and combat, and the changes are noticeable and incredibly helpful. Finally you'll be able to target different body parts of a boss rather than tackling the awkward camera movements of the previous center-only target focusing system. The world is much larger and more varied than DS1 so expect a long journey of expletives and controller-throwing, but also one of awe and breathtaking inspiration depending on location you're in. There's a lot to say when it comes down to the improvements of the game, but you should really see yourself to avoid spoilers.
I'll emphasize that Drangleic isn't Lordran, so don't go in expecting Dark Souls 1: 2.0. Rather, expect Dark Souls 1: Reimagined. You'll worry less about what could have been, and you'll start enjoying what's currently being offered.

With that said, the game is quickly losing it's charm. The game moves along at a decent pace, TES games were never about getting things fast, or becoming a god aftert 3 hours, but the leveling in ESO seems artificially stunted. Questing is decent, nothing special, typical MMO stuff. Can't complain too much here.
Audio is hit or miss with certain things being dead on but combat lacks that PUNCH that makes it feel brutal.

Crafting, the time it takes to do research, 6 hours? Seriously!? A general playtime length for the average player to maybe knock out 2 items in a session and log off. This game aged a little roughly, from a graphics perspective; but the story and gameplay are still as compelling as ever. I actually never played System Shock 1 or 2 before playing this on Steam. And I have to say, I had a great time. This game has chilling themes and tense moments, as you are caught in a battle, raging between a horific hivemind of alien, psychic, artificially-enhanced flesh and a mechanical AI that is hell-bent on becoming the universe's next goddess.
The gameplay provides a lot of skill points for your stats, but they are limited. You will need smarts and strategy to build a character that matches your playstyle. But there are a lot of options, playstyles, and tactics to help you beat the game. However, a word of advice: While you should certainly not be afraid to experiment with any of the psychic powers, I advise not starting this game with a psychic/magic-power focused character until you are on your second playthrough or just want a challenge. Some of the psychic abilities are almost completely useless, so knowing which ones are good and which ones are bad for your style is crucial to your success with a mage-build. That being said, play the game how you like. But do be mindful that, true to classic games, System Shock 2 will NOT pull punches and will smack you around if you aren't careful.
Even so, this game was a lot of fun and still lives as a testament when challenge and choices were actually valued in games.

Story:
We play as Senia, a young girl who’s climbing the Tower of Eternity to find her sister. That the best short summary I can give without going into spoilers.
Lets get the bad out of the way, I think it needs a better translator. What story that was translated is good and I’ll be saying good things later, but there some little bits here and there that bother. I shouldn't care that Senia calls Magaleta sis but sometimes it just doesn’t sound right when I’m reading it. And second is the fairy. Now there isn’t anything  wrong with the character itself but outside of gameplay, she barely does anything to the story and I forgot she was around.
Now for the good. While we don’t know the full relationship between the two leads, we do get flashbacks that explore how they meet and why they care so much about each other. I was getting pretty invested in by the end of the story.
Gameplay:
The game is an action RPG with a very simple battle system where you just have touch an enemy to kill them. you can get four moves to help with combat and two can be used to find secret with one being a dash and the other being a range attack and the other two are useful attacks that hit lots of enemies.
Now while these are fun to use, the enemies are ridiculously easy to beat and you might not get a dent when you fight them, which is a shame since some of the enemies are pretty fun to fight like the magic users and the ones that charge at you. Oh my gosh, this game was AMAZING! The dev worked hard to make this game both smooth in gameplay yet challenging, and I was not disappointed. It doesn't take extremely long to play, around 5 or 6 hours, but those are 5 or 6 hours you wil not regret.
One of the big things that stood out to me was the regular enemy battle style. I like not having to enter sepereate battle scenes every time I run into an enemy but just running into them until they die (It's more satisfying than it sounds). Some enemies are fairly static, but others have special abilities or moves that require you to strategize as well. Despite not having a full-on RPG-style battle mode, armor and weapons are still important, and I enjoyed trying to gather enough materials to collect all of them. I think having a hierarchy of making one piece of equipment require the next one down allowed for actual progress in the game as opposed to just getting the highest-ranked equipment from the start, which is a smart move.
The boss battles were challenging, too, and are different than regular enemy encounters. They do have a battle mode where you are trapped in one area, and they are the most challenging parts of the game. This game also had multiple endings, which I always like in a game. Each game ending was special, and in one of them you get an extra boss! All I can say is that I died a few times trying to defeat her. The rest is spoilers. ;)
The plot was not shabby, either. It starts out giving you a classic plot line, but more is revealed as the game goes on, which leads to interesting plot twists that create a unique story from the lost-person-must-save-them archetype. The plot also leaves the endings alone, in the sense that there isn't a bias over which choices you should make at the end. Either choice is acceptable, but they lead to completely different endings, as opposed to them not mattering. It's relieving after playing some games where the choices lead to generally the same ending.
I HIGHLY recommend this game to the casual gamer or the general RPG fan. Someone looking for hardcore Final Fantasy- style gameplay will not get that here, although those people may still enjoy the game. This is a beautifully well-rounded game that, in my opinion, has an almost perfect balance of everything. It's amazing that it's free, so give it a try.

Broforce. Okay, this one is going to be a bit 'one the one hand', 'on the other hand', but stick with me and I will explain all.
Before I get into the details, I would like to note that I recommend this game. I've enjoyed it a lot, and I hope to keep enjoying it. If you're interested, I say go for it. But maybe wait until it's on sale. Read on to find out why.
Broforce's Unique Selling Point is the character-switching mechanic: every time the player 'rescues' a prisoner, the player takes on a different character, or 'bro', lovingly modelled on ultra-masculine action movie heroes. These are unlocked as the game progresses, and there is a fair amount of variety once a decent number have been unlocked. And that can be problematic.
With so many different character types, each with their own combat and movement style, there is an element of 'the luck of the draw' when it comes to getting the right character for the situation at hand. A character who fires rockets horizontally may not suit a moment which calls for the one who shoots streams of bullets directly downwards, or drops dynamite, or fights with rapid-fire punches or swordplay. In fairness, on that last point, melee characters feature some kind of ranged attack tied to the 'melee attack' key (paradoxically), but there are times when the 'Blade' and 'Neo' knock-offs just aren't as useful as their longer-range counterparts. Enduring several ill-fated attempts in a row before the ideal character turns up isn't unusual, and this is especially true of boss fights. I've wasted plenty of time attempting to punch my way through a boss level before the bro who can manipulate time finally showed up and finished the fight in seconds flat. Even in less extreme cases, there's more to worry about: planning a strategy is almost impossible when the next available bro might turn out to be a dud. The choice is sometimes between rescuing the hostage and gaining an extra life in the process, but risking a dissatisfactory bro-change, or ignoring the hostage but passing up that valuable extra life. And when the game gets tough, those lives are like gold dust. During one particular boss fight (to which I shall return shortly) I several times received an excellent bro from the spawn point, but had to immediately release a hostage to gain a vital extra life, getting a lesser bro for my troubles. In the middle of a boss battle, switching into a shoddy bro can be even worse. Finish this incredibly punishing fight with the character who charges directly into the enemy who's pummelling me with fireballs? Whatever you say, Broforce.
Spawn points are an issue as well. You wouldn't think it at the start of the game, they seem to be everywhere, but there are crucial points where they are most needed. I probably won't be finishing the boss fight to which I alluded before, as it  is comprised of at least 3 sections, with no way to properly save, quit, and return to the game between sections, which can take a long time due to trial-and-error and the aforementioned bro-switching roulette game. There ARE points at which this can be done, but apparently no-one thought to implement this during one of the most time-consuming sequences in the game.
The save point issue is one of several examples which gives the impression - perhaps incorrectly - that not enough thought has been put into the game's design. Glitches, there are. At least once I have beaten a boss by ending up INSIDE the enemy, and simply shooting from within, when I'm sure this wasn't the intention. The camera can get a little confused sometimes, and characters ending up embedded inside terrain is unusual but not unheard-of. Most infuriatingly, terrain which is designed to dissolve into thin air when stepped on by a player character will sometimes dissolve as the character spawns, leaving empty chasms that are difficult or impossible to cross. Perhaps this is being worked on, but the list of irritations eventually becomes annoying.
Broforce is basically a good game: good central concept, neat sense of humour, with enough variety to keep the player on their toes. Unfortunately, its problems weigh it down, making it exceeding annoying at times.
Ultimately, I advise that you put this game on your wishlist and buy it when it goes on sale. The reduction in price seems to me a fair exchange for the game's flaws.

Total Annihilation.
Damn.
This game was my childhood. I remember sitting on my Dad's lap and we'd build up our army together and then nuke the CORE to pieces. Those were the days.
Total Annihilation is a Real-Time Strategy game. You start off with one 'Unit', your Commander, and slowly build up your army of planes, vehicles, mechs, boats, hovercraft, etc. For a game that is 20 years old this year this is STILL in my opinion the greatest RTS game of all time. This is the type of game that despite the graphics being massively outdated, and only 1.1GB big (not even that), it's still feels full of content. The maps are HUGE and there's lots of variety. The Units all have their own jobs and characteristics. There's a campaign too, and also, if you can figure out how to get it to work, a multiplayer. At the time of writing this review it only says I have 2.1 hours on record, but to be truthful I probably have hundereds outside of Steam. This game is truly one of my favourite games of all time and I HIGHLY reccomend it to anybody who's into the Supreme Commander series. This is similar to Planetary Annihilation in that it was made by a few of the same people, but from what I've heard from Planetary Annihilation, despite being more modern, better in graphical design and including much more content, THIS is the game you want. Trust me.
Thanks for reading my review of Total Annihilation. I really hope you buy this game; it's truly a masterpiece.

To put it bluntly, Dishonoured 2 is a more than worthy successor to one of best stealth games of all time. Taking place 15 years after the original, the empress of the isles, Emliy Kaldwin is overthrown by none other than Delilah Copperspoon, the main villian of dishonoureds two fantastic DLC's. Thus it is up to Emily or her father Corvo to take back the throne by going to karnaca, where Delilahs insidous allies lurk and taking them out, how you see fit. First off, the gameplay has been shined to a mirror sheen, combat is fast-paced and suprisingly difficult, seriously, a new player taking on a small group of enemies is basically suicide without a proper plan of action. The combat is shown of the best any time you fight one of the clockwork soldiers, which is one of the best enemy types i've had the joy of fighting in any game ever.
Movement is also overall a lot smoother and many peoples biggest complaint has been fixed: there is now non leathal combat, with almost every attack, from counter attacks to drop assassinatons getting a non-leathal version. Level design is also the same high standard as the original with many paths open for reaching your goal, with the trio of levels "Edge of the world", "The good doctor" and "The clockwork mansion" being the highlights for me. Even the powers and bonecharm systems got updated, with each power having it's own mini upgrade tree instead of just a level 1 and a level 2 and being able to craft your own bonecharms and the introduction of black bonecharms.
The replay value is high on this one aswell, with the two different characters getting completely different powers and even their gun and crossbow being different. There is also choosing low and high chaos playthroughs that effects someparts of the levels as well as the overall ending and choosing if you want the outsiders mark or not, meaning that you would have to play the game 8 different times to see everything it has to offer.

I grew up with Half Life, Half Life 2, Portal etc... as a young man now I am saddened to see there will never be Half Life 3; This comes close enough. In my opinion, the original has its own replayability value (for instance I'm weird and sometimes I like the way really old graphics look) And since I remember simpler, dumbed down areas mimicked in Black Mesa, the "nostalgia" isn't along with me for the ride QUITE as much as I thought it'd be, simply because there's so much detail in Black Mesa it feels like I'm playing a new game. Some areas however, such as the blast pit, Surface Tension and Lambda Core remind me they were faithful all along. It's Half Life 1.5, and it's freaking awesome.
Gore effects are updated from HL2, and gibs have returned from the original in the form of full body dismemberment, and oddly enough you can interact and even toss around the arms, legs, torso, etc... I found the blood staining the gloves and gun cool as well, adding a bit of realism and closeness. Everything looks crisp and clear, with few jagged textures for the most part. I felt the soldiers to be a bit... accurate with their firearms, to an annoying degree yet this pushed me to strategies that made simple firefights dragged out battles of tactic and guile. All the set pieces are there, all the enemies remember and environments that made us think.
I think it has some technical issues, but what game doesn't these days? It's like saying medication has side effects. Black Mesa holds up both as a magnificent remake and its own game, being perhaps as close as we'll ever get to a Half Life 3. Just can't wait for Xen!
On a sidenote is it too much to ask to just take the head crab zombies, give Gordan the damn portal gun, and make Half Life 3 the culmination of the best gameplay elements from Portal, Left for Dead, and of course Half Life and make the game? I don't think we'd be that hard to please

So I am the first person to say "shame on you!" when developers release a game as 'Early Access' and then spend YEARS waiting to actually release it.
This, however, is the one exception.
I played the mod that this game released as back when it first came out. I remember coming home from work so excited to finally be able to download it and the torrent was being downloaded by so many people around the world it took hours to get and I never had time until the following day to finally get it installed. I was BLOWN AWAY by how amazing of a job they did.
The paid version of the game caught a LOT of flak when it released because people were complaining that you shouldn't have to pay for a mod. What they didn't realize in the midst of all that complaining were two things:
A) You don't have to buy it. Wanna play the mod? Keep playing the darn mod.
B) The mod is just that...a mod for Half-Life 2 that won't ever get updated again. The paid version came about after Valve realized how AMAZING of a job they did, as aforementioned, and allowed them to use the latest Source engine so they could update and complete their title.
Why did Valve allow this? This mod first started off as a project to remake Half-Life on the Source engine since the official Half-Life Source was such a disappointment. Valve wouldn't let them use the word Source in the title of the mod for whatever reason. Perhaps they were offended, perhaps not. Regardless, they clearly realized how wrong they were and owned up to it. Maybe there is more to that story but what matters is that one of the geatest video games of all time was EXPERTLY remade using the latest Source engine and is almost complete.
I won't say this about any other 'Early Access' title but you seriously need to buy this because it is so good that the original Half-Life has been put to bed.

Before we begin, a word of warning: This game is not for the faint of heart. I have been a fan of the horror genre all my life, read many books, watched tons of films, but none managed to pull my fear strings as hard as Alien: Isolation.
So with that out of the way, let me tell you why this review is different compared to all the reviews I have done before. I wrote fragments of my impressions and thoughts on a notepad as a played through the game and used them as the basis of my review. It breathes more life into the review in a sense. Hope everyone finds it interesting!
This game, Alien: Isolation, is based on the late 70’s cult classic sci-fi horror flick: Alien. There have been numerous games based on the franchise, but only by name, which is pretty much the case for all movie licensed games sadly. However, Isolation is a different beast entirely. Where previous Alien games used the license just as a name to cover a lackluster game, this however is the most faithful recreation of the Alien universe or any film to game for that matter. It flawlessly manages to capture the very essence of the Alien franchise while harnessing the power of this interactive medium to further suck you into Ridley Scott’s sci-fi nightmare beyond the proficiency of films.
You play as Amanda Ripley, the descendant of Ellen Ripley. Amanda has been working for a mega corporation called Weyland-Yutani for a while now. Her main purpose for working with them was because the corporation had ties with the disappearance of her mother some 15 years ago. She finally gets a break which hopefully will shed some light to the answers she is looking for.
When it comes to gameplay, there is just one important thing the game emphasis more than anything else: is to Survive. All the impressive sound and visual design aren't just there for the sake of immersion, finally, they actually serve as very important gameplay systems. You need to keep your senses in full capacity because of the all the different kinds of dangers that are lurking all around the space station. Because of the desperate situation, many of the people over there who managed to keep themselves alive formed various groups in order to work together and try to survive. Unfortunately, that means they tend to keep it to themselves and will consider anyone outside of their group hostile, like yourself. It is suicide to go head to head against them if they outnumber you, so you need to carefully plan out what you are going to do. Will you take them on all by yourself? Will you try to sneak past them with the help of your gadgets and wits? Or will you take the help of the Alien by throwing a noise bomb which as expected emits a lot of noise for the Alien to swoop down from above and kill everything in the vicinity. You can also manipulate the machines in the station to give you an edge by hacking into the systems. The hacking mini-games are fun very well grounded to the world design around you.
Then there are creepy androids or better known as Working Joe. They are basically a very simple version of synthetic humans in the Alien universe. Now, you never can trust robots no matter how friendly they appear to be at first, the same rule applies here. Some of the Joes are malfunctioning which is causing them to savagely kill any human that is not obeying the exaggerated rules planted into their head. What is even worse, they robots don’t go down easily and can take some serious punishment before it kneels over and dies with the same hollow look as if nothing happened. Yes, the Joes are perhaps the creepiest thing you will encounter in the game, more so than the Alien I felt. Something about their dead emotions, their stern attitude and the way they look at you with those dead eyes and talk in equally empty voice is very unsettling!
Going further up the top of the food chain we have, the Alien: it is unbeatable, unkillable and once it sees you there is a very good chance you are dead. So it is very important to make sure such a situation never even happens in the first place. In order to do that, you need to stay hidden as much as you can. Ripley is an engineer and just like her mom, a true survivor who can make the best out of the given situations. She can hide in lockers; hack terminals to alter some of the security systems around the space station to make new escape routes; use her extensive engineering skills to craft tools and gadgets like flash bang, Molotov cocktail, etc. to give her a better fighting chance and make it through. Despite all this help, it does not make your time any easier with the Alien lurking about, because the thing is…you are never safely hidden.
You are constantly being haunted most of the game by this vicious, hideous, merciless creature. That is 20 hours of constant tension and that is not even the only thing you need to worry about, the environment is very unpredictable and changes in hostile ways as the story progresses. So take a deep breath and hope you won’t break while you playing.
The presentation can be summarized in one word: outstanding! The gorgeous lighting effects are some of the best I've seen and most effectively utilized like a horror game should. The way lights reflect when you point your flashlight around metal constructs like ventilation shafts, and further reflects back and radiates by bouncing off the surrounding metal plates, an effect called radiosity, is very hard to pull off in video games. This further gets complicated very easily when the surrounding surfaces where the light bounces off each other is made up of different materials, as different materials absorb light in different ways thus radiates differently. As you can you imagine, it is very computationally expensive to calculate such variables and thus many game out there do their best to fake this effect. However, the smart folks at Creative Assembly wouldn’t settle for anything less than realistic. They managed to find ways to achieve realistic light scattering and reflecting without bogging down hardware using a very impressive engine they made in-house for the game.
According to science, even though visual memory is the most prominent form of memory, it is the memory that is recorded through sound that evokes the most powerful of emotions. So for a horror game, audio is incredibly important, if not more than the visuals. Well then, lucky for us, Creative Assembly completely nailed it here. This game has probably the most advanced sound design I've heard in gaming. It is there not just to create the hollow atmosphere, but it is probably the best tool at your disposal to survive. With you being inside of an aluminum shell, every sound is more pronounced than it normally is. The sound of thudding metal of something big and hulking by the vents and ceiling right on top of you can be very scary, but at the same time it gives you the opportunity to hear you're foes and make decisions: which is to either fight or flee (just flee when the sound is too heavy!).
It is amazing to think a lifelong RTS developer like Creative Assembly managed to make a survival horror game in the truest of the definition. I would like to end by saying that I loved every bit of my time at Sevastopol. I would love to return to it again but…definitely not anytime soon!

I have a problem: I am compelled to buy half-complete early access titles in the Survival-Crafting Open World PVP genre. It's like a curse, in which my wallet and my happiness must suffer. So naturally, I wanted to give Hurtworld a try. I was compelled to.
I logged into a server and immediately encountered a neutral player trying to shoo me from his gathering area. He threw his spear at me, missing, all the while communicating to me with voice chat to go away. Point taken, I high tailed it out of there half-naked and with nothing to my name. A couple nights later I had established some basic tools but died of hypothermia. I have not died since. You learn to prioritize resource gathering and craftables, to keep a campfire at the ready for the harsh cold nights. I encountered friendly players, who offered some spare leather or had a kind word in passing. But I also encountered my first hostile player, who tried to coerce me into dropping all my logs. I refused and he chased me with his bow. I turned on him, spear in hand, and wacked him over the head. He didn't like that. I chased him off with my stick and very suddenly a blinding dust storm kicked up. He complained about not being able to see and I used that opportunity to get away -- even though I was the one chasing him. It felt great, as a new player, to be able to defend myself against others. And even better to see how the environment had protected me and given me cover. Cool.
A few hours of gameplay later and I have claimed a plot of land, clothed myself, crafted a back pack, built a small home, stocked up my storage container, created tier 2 tools, and am ready to explore. I feel I have met small milestones and there is a sense of accomplishment and survival. I have hunted and gathered my way to basic comfort and survived the few hostile players.
What the future holds, I am uncertain. I'd like to believe I cannot progress through the game so quickly. I'd like to believe great dangers lurk where great rewards lie, but I have not explored far enough yet.
Here's what I do know: The game is fun, it is a solid title for Early Access, the community isn't totally filled with jerks (at least not on the server I joined), and I can only hope the developers expand on this game as I want more of it.
-Pros-
+While it is an EA title, it feels like a solid game with a full feature list. Highly playable.
+Runs smoothly, no crashes, high frame rates
+Combat is adequate
+Survival takes some effort and thought during the first couple hours
+Basic resources continue to be useful
+Player community
+I not YET encountered a cheater
+The server I play on is not full when I want to play
+Its fun
+You keep your tools when you die, but drop your resources
+HUD is clutter free
-Cons/Other Thoughts-
-Hypothermia is a bit harsh
-Overheating mechanic is ridiculous. I'd understand if you overheat from the desert sun. But instead you overheat from being near your campfire or firepit, which is required for cooking food and smelting ores. It is ridiculous that I can't be anywhere inside my house while the firepit is going or I will start to overheat. Overheating can very well kill you. This could turn into an interesting mechanic if water is required to cool down from the hot desert or player must find shade or equip special gear. Tedius, but could be interesting. As it is right now its downright annoying.
-Some resources will appear at a certain distance away, but will not be there when you approach, and may reapper after wandering around a bit. Similarly, the LOD on creatures is questionable. Bors can look a bit like logs at a distance because they are boxy until you get close enough for their details to be clear. And sometimes they won't appear at all until right up next them. Minor bugs.
-Building a home is nice, but needs some work. There are no stairs or ladders. And you do not get any of your resources returned when you destroy something you've built. Certain resource requirements make no sense.
-Crafting menus could be improved on, but not really a con. They work as intended.
Overall, for 20$ I am enjoying the game and look forward to playing more of it.

Ravenfield is like a single player only mix between Battlefield, Unturned, the sandbox battles of Mount and Blade and some TABZ thrown in for good measure. While a campaign is planned, the current sandbox mode is fantastic on its own, pitting you against another team for control of respawn points. The main gamemode is a bit of Domination from Call of Duty, with the number of respawn points you control filling in a points meter at the top of your screen. You can defend a single point and never lose it, but if you have 1 and the enemy has 5, you're going to lose. The interesting thing about the sandbox style is that once the game "ends," you can still keep playing, you just get notified of which team won and then it keeps going on forever. There's vehicles (tanks, jeeps, ATVs, boats, planes and helicopters), gadgets (grenades, health and ammo kits, launchers, etc) and a decent amount of weapons for being in early access. There's also 4 secret weapons that for some reason the AI are allowed to use at any time, but I've had some trouble getting them to stay in my loadout screen after closing the game. Overall it's all you really need to entertain yourself if you like pure gameplay, no story, no anything other than constant fighting. There's also no-respawns TDM gamemode called spec ops and another one that I don't know anything about because I've been so entertained with the default conquest style gamemode.
One big draw is the "active ragdoll physics." The game models may look like they're from Totally Accurate Battle Simulator but don't be discouraged, your movement is just like in any other FPS and your aim is elastic-y like a ragdoll but it's quite comfortable to use. The ragdoll physics become active when you fall, swim, get caught in an explosion or get shot enough and it's surprisingly great for the gameplay. When being shot by powerful guns, or a lot with weak guns, you'll obviously take damage but at a certain point you'll ragdoll and fall down. Explosions that aren't close enough to hurt you may still knock you over and so will near misses from heavy machine guns, but without hurting you. (also there's no fall damage, which is good for pilots) The ragdolling adds a second penalty beyond death, which is occupying your attention. You can't do anything as a ragdoll and this is a fate worse than death, literally. Rather than respawning with full health and armor in a matter of seconds, you stay where you are, not rearming and respawning and you're taken out of the fight, not for the time it takes to respawn but until you can get on your feet and stay that way. Stun grenades and heavy machine guns make it so that a single soldier can defend a position against 5 or more, even knocking them over through cover, taking them out of the fight without giving them their ammo and health back and letting them spawn where they can get a vehicle to take vengeance, and of course that applies to you too. If that's not enough depth, the AI can be knocked down but not out, meaning you can't easily tell if someone's dead or alive. You have to decide between wasting ammo and time shooting every body you come across, or risking a bullet in the back when a dead soldier turns out to have fallen out of a helicopter or tripped on some splash damage.
There may not be a ton of content so far, but the game is easily worth the money and absolutely worth your time, especially with planned Steam Workshop support. There's night versions of each map to add some variety and if you enter the beta branch you can play the old version of one map (it's basically a totally different map), bringing the level count up to 5.
Pros-
Great replay value if you can make fun for yourself in a sandbox
Really solid combat
Interesting and unique ragdoll system
Vehicles are simple but easy to control, feeling just like Battlefield.
Active developer with updates being released often.
Cons-
There may not be enough content for some people, particularly in the map department. If you're worried about this, consider waiting for more levels or workshop support so you don't get tired of the game too soon.
Vehicles aren't too well balanced, tanks feel a bit weak with any of the launchers being able to destroy one and having ammo to spare. Helicopters are glass cannons and the missile boats are titanium cannons.
Overall 9/10 game, it's really fun and deserves a spot in your library.

Broforce is one of the best "retro shooters" of the modern age.
It embraces the fast paced action and difficulty of 90s games, such as Metal Slug, while still feeling fresh and new.
The game makes fun of the american partiotism and machism, and you play as a wide variety of characters, the "BROS", which are caricatures of male and female action movies stars.
Rambo, Terminator, Ellen Ripley, Robocop, Chuck Norris ecc...there are a lot.
The best thing about the game is that you spawn each time as a different character, after dying or getting a new life, so you´'ll always play as a different hero, keeping the gameplay fresh.
All the heroes have different weapons, traits, abilities and special attacks, and most of them are very fun to play, but there are a cuple ones that are completely useless and not up to the task (such as Indiana Bro).
A unique feature of this game is the destructable environmets. Every single block of the level can be destroyed, and that increases the tactical planning, encouragin the player to dig tunnels and demolish structures.
Before approaching the game you have to know it starts easy but gets quite hard at the end.

- Addictive Gameplay
- Many Levels
- Perfect Difficulty
- Super fast paced action
- Many fun characters to play with

- Destructable environments
- Variety

My experience with this game can be summed as thus: every update I found myself testing the changes, nodding in satisfaction, then quitting the game to await the next update.
Arkane knows how to make a good game. No question. But if you film an Oscar-worthy movie and the lens is smudged while filming, you can't judge what's underneath without acknowledging what's been marring your experience the entire time.
=============================
Everyone is aware of the performance issues, and these still persist to this day. It runs much better than at launch, where it was literally unplayable, but that's because the game looks worse than before - the most noticeable change being the extremely aggressive LOD scaling. Out of the corner of your eye you notice the shapes of window frames and posters on distant buildings morphing in shape, or the furniture at the opposite end of a long hallway suddenly blinking into existence. FPS dropped to 15 when stabbing a gravehound, so they simply removed the inky visual effect that was causing the problem instead of optimizing it.
Also, Denuvo authentication is one of the longest "loading screens" of the game. Around half a minute to a full minute or more every startup.
=============================
For the most part, gameplay is excellent and is Dishonored's strongest suit.
However, under the hood lie other problems. Most of them are quality-of-life issues:
=============================
Great. My favorite part of Dishonored. You need to hide from a gang member to access a certain black market shop, and there are different scenarios and dialogue for if you hide, if you run into him outside, kill him outside, or kill him inside.
Emily and Corvo are voiced. And... they don't talk enough. It's good that they're silent for most of the game, but there are times when you come across a portrait or photograph with an "Inspect" prompt. I'd love to hear Emily's thoughts on the High Overseer as see how that compares to Corvo's, or if it changes based on whether or not you accept the Outsider's Mark. Instead, all I get is the protagonist muttering the name of the person pictured. What's the point? Might as well keep them silent.
It made sense to me to play Emily first, but her story felt lackluster, like people at every turn were saying "check your royal privilege" despite my efforts to resolve everyone's problems without drawing blood. Corvo's is MUCH more interesting as a veteran of Dishonored 1.
I hate the new Outsider and his new voice. He felt threatening and malicious in the first game due to how calm and composed he was, and the Void felt like a strange and otherworldly place. The vignettes of Dunwall made it feel both unnatural and unnerving yet fundamentally woven into the universe. In Dishonored 2, it's just smoky blackness and sharp rocks. The Outsider is much jollier and moves around erratically, making grandiose hand gestures. They actually had a plot plot that could explain this change, but it was never addressed, so it just seems like a pointless retcon to me.
Dishonored's worldbuilding was always one of its appeals, and that remains true in Dishonored 2. However, the villains felt lackluster. Only the main villain has a real presence throughout the game, whereas everyone else feels introduced abruptly only to fall by your hand, all within the same mission. In Dishonored 1 everything felt personal and real. Perhaps it was because of the long intro where you interacted with most of them, or the Hound Pits's cast of characters all having different connections to your targets.
=============================
As you can see, I've played this game a LOT and have put a lot of thought into it. It was definitely worth all those hours and all that money, but the condition it was at launch and the sluggish drip-feed of support we barely get now is unacceptable. To set a precedent for future games, I can't recommend buying this unless they manage to fix all the performance issues and bugs, which doesn't seem to be happening anytime soon.

I'm new to the PC side of gaming, and Dark Souls II is something that I had previously experienced on the PS3 back in March, however after thoroughly enjoying the game (and series in general) I decided to pick up the game for the PC to see what all the hype around it was about. Let me tell you... Dark Souls II on the PC is BY FAR the definitive edition of the game, so much so that i question why I ever played it on console.
The sheer boost in framerate (It runs at a solid 60fps without dropping a frame) makes the game so much more enjoyable, I actually found this helping me in terms of being able to dodge roll through enemies attacks more easily. Honestly, looking back to the PS3 version of the game, I wonder how it even got released, the textures are full 1080p on the PC compared to the almost oily unsmooth look of them on console, and I think the overall boost in quality really allows the player to fully appreciate the level of detail that From Software put into this world. Anything from the large-scale bosses that tower above you, to the way your shadow reacts when standing near a bonfire, it's truly magnificent.
Another massive plus in my opinion is that the game tends to be running extremely well on a large range of rigs, which is the complete polar opposite to the original Dark Souls on Steam which, despite Durante's DSFix is still known for being one of the worst PC ports known to man. My machine set everything to Medium by default however despite the game's Steam Page recommending a GTX 750 or equivalent to run this game well, I immediately cranked the graphics settings up to maximum with including AA, AO and Vsync and have yet to see the game drop a single frame on my GTX 650 Ti. This is such a great incentive to pick up the game on PC rather than your 8 year old console hardware.
Even though I hate the stereotype of 'PC Master Race', on this occasion I have to say props go to From Software for being able to deliver such a phenomenal experience to the fans of the souls series, and i hope they continue into the future retaining this standard of quality in their products. Roll on the DLC! :D
