Before we begin, a word of warning: This game is not for the faint of heart. I have been a fan of the horror genre all my life, read many books, watched tons of films, but none managed to pull my fear strings as hard as Alien: Isolation.
So with that out of the way, let me tell you why this review is different compared to all the reviews I have done before. I wrote fragments of my impressions and thoughts on a notepad as a played through the game and used them as the basis of my review. It breathes more life into the review in a sense. Hope everyone finds it interesting!
This game, Alien: Isolation, is based on the late 70’s cult classic sci-fi horror flick: Alien. There have been numerous games based on the franchise, but only by name, which is pretty much the case for all movie licensed games sadly. However, Isolation is a different beast entirely. Where previous Alien games used the license just as a name to cover a lackluster game, this however is the most faithful recreation of the Alien universe or any film to game for that matter. It flawlessly manages to capture the very essence of the Alien franchise while harnessing the power of this interactive medium to further suck you into Ridley Scott’s sci-fi nightmare beyond the proficiency of films.
You play as Amanda Ripley, the descendant of Ellen Ripley. Amanda has been working for a mega corporation called Weyland-Yutani for a while now. Her main purpose for working with them was because the corporation had ties with the disappearance of her mother some 15 years ago. She finally gets a break which hopefully will shed some light to the answers she is looking for.
When it comes to gameplay, there is just one important thing the game emphasis more than anything else: is to Survive. All the impressive sound and visual design aren't just there for the sake of immersion, finally, they actually serve as very important gameplay systems. You need to keep your senses in full capacity because of the all the different kinds of dangers that are lurking all around the space station. Because of the desperate situation, many of the people over there who managed to keep themselves alive formed various groups in order to work together and try to survive. Unfortunately, that means they tend to keep it to themselves and will consider anyone outside of their group hostile, like yourself. It is suicide to go head to head against them if they outnumber you, so you need to carefully plan out what you are going to do. Will you take them on all by yourself? Will you try to sneak past them with the help of your gadgets and wits? Or will you take the help of the Alien by throwing a noise bomb which as expected emits a lot of noise for the Alien to swoop down from above and kill everything in the vicinity. You can also manipulate the machines in the station to give you an edge by hacking into the systems. The hacking mini-games are fun very well grounded to the world design around you.
Then there are creepy androids or better known as Working Joe. They are basically a very simple version of synthetic humans in the Alien universe. Now, you never can trust robots no matter how friendly they appear to be at first, the same rule applies here. Some of the Joes are malfunctioning which is causing them to savagely kill any human that is not obeying the exaggerated rules planted into their head. What is even worse, they robots don’t go down easily and can take some serious punishment before it kneels over and dies with the same hollow look as if nothing happened. Yes, the Joes are perhaps the creepiest thing you will encounter in the game, more so than the Alien I felt. Something about their dead emotions, their stern attitude and the way they look at you with those dead eyes and talk in equally empty voice is very unsettling!
Going further up the top of the food chain we have, the Alien: it is unbeatable, unkillable and once it sees you there is a very good chance you are dead. So it is very important to make sure such a situation never even happens in the first place. In order to do that, you need to stay hidden as much as you can. Ripley is an engineer and just like her mom, a true survivor who can make the best out of the given situations. She can hide in lockers; hack terminals to alter some of the security systems around the space station to make new escape routes; use her extensive engineering skills to craft tools and gadgets like flash bang, Molotov cocktail, etc. to give her a better fighting chance and make it through. Despite all this help, it does not make your time any easier with the Alien lurking about, because the thing is…you are never safely hidden.
You are constantly being haunted most of the game by this vicious, hideous, merciless creature. That is 20 hours of constant tension and that is not even the only thing you need to worry about, the environment is very unpredictable and changes in hostile ways as the story progresses. So take a deep breath and hope you won’t break while you playing.
The presentation can be summarized in one word: outstanding! The gorgeous lighting effects are some of the best I've seen and most effectively utilized like a horror game should. The way lights reflect when you point your flashlight around metal constructs like ventilation shafts, and further reflects back and radiates by bouncing off the surrounding metal plates, an effect called radiosity, is very hard to pull off in video games. This further gets complicated very easily when the surrounding surfaces where the light bounces off each other is made up of different materials, as different materials absorb light in different ways thus radiates differently. As you can you imagine, it is very computationally expensive to calculate such variables and thus many game out there do their best to fake this effect. However, the smart folks at Creative Assembly wouldn’t settle for anything less than realistic. They managed to find ways to achieve realistic light scattering and reflecting without bogging down hardware using a very impressive engine they made in-house for the game.
According to science, even though visual memory is the most prominent form of memory, it is the memory that is recorded through sound that evokes the most powerful of emotions. So for a horror game, audio is incredibly important, if not more than the visuals. Well then, lucky for us, Creative Assembly completely nailed it here. This game has probably the most advanced sound design I've heard in gaming. It is there not just to create the hollow atmosphere, but it is probably the best tool at your disposal to survive. With you being inside of an aluminum shell, every sound is more pronounced than it normally is. The sound of thudding metal of something big and hulking by the vents and ceiling right on top of you can be very scary, but at the same time it gives you the opportunity to hear you're foes and make decisions: which is to either fight or flee (just flee when the sound is too heavy!).
It is amazing to think a lifelong RTS developer like Creative Assembly managed to make a survival horror game in the truest of the definition. I would like to end by saying that I loved every bit of my time at Sevastopol. I would love to return to it again but…definitely not anytime soon!

(*Personal opinion* Things that could have saved Hurtworld) The devs should have tweaked and created more content for version 1. Simple things like random creature spawn locations, clothing coloring (to differentiate players since everyone looks like Ronald McDonald), adding new weapons and food resources.
I really miss what this game USED to be. Fingers are crossed that the devs get their heads on straight and listen to the community instead of assuming what the players want. We don't want Rust, if we wanted Rust then we would play Rust.

I. Love. This. Game.
I've been playing this game since it was in Beta 4 on itch.io, and it's been my go-to game for when I'm bored since then--and that is said as an absolute compliment! There are so many things I like about the game: it's simple, it's singleplayer, it's got a ton of stuff to do, it's still in development (more on that later), and it's so, so fun. I will play this game for hours, and never get bored. There's so many combinations of things to do that you never get bored. When you get tired of flying planes you start sniping. When you get tired of sniping, you run with the Patriot (my personal favorite gun). And when all else fails, you start killing your teammates with rockets and grenades!
Now, I've seen on the Community page of the game that many people think the game isn't worth $15. And I will be honest: in its current state, it's not. But it's Early Access, which means it's an investment. You buy it now for, admittedly, too much, and you get to play it through its development until it's worth as much as you paid for it, and often times more. I love Early Access games, especially with developers like SteelRaven7, who is constantly updating the game. I truly believe that this game will one day be worth more than $15, so I had no issue paying that much for it now--I bought it without hesitation the day it came out on Steam.
Now, nobody can argue that the game is perfect right now. Go to the Community page and you'll see post after post of bugs, glitches, mistakes, and possible improvements for the game. Off the top of my head, right now, I can probably think of several dozen things this game needs to have no be cosidered anywhere near complete: more maps, more game modes, modding, a Campaign Mode, better AI, more weapons, more detailed maps, countless tiny details to improve general gameplay---plus a ton of bug fixes. But the great thing is that SteelRaven7 has already said he would address many of these things. Archipelago is costantly being updated to be better, along with the other maps, and almost every week a bug fix comes out. It just takes time.
So if you're reading this now, and are considering purchasing the game, just do it. I guarantee that you won't regret it. If your patient and enjoy this type of game, you will have a ton of fun playing it. And also: don't pirate the game. That's not cool. It's $15, and if you want it that bad, just buy it legally. SteelRaven7 is the only developer--one person!--who is making this game, and he has spent so much time and energy doing so. If you want the game to go anywhere, get the game from Steam, and save yourself the headache of getting a virus in the proccess. And good luck fighting those pesky reds!  :)

Beats out even the original Deus Ex as the best "immersive sim" game ever made. Even after almost two decades the gameplay still holds up and the depth of the mechanics is insane, with many different playstyles and character builds possible. The hostile, claustrophobic atmosphere will have you constantly tense; you're never safe so there's never a dull moment.

The only thing that doesn't hold up today is the graphics. Even at the time of its release it was by no means a beautiful game, especially when compared to Half-Life which came out the same year. But this isn't a true downside because the SS2 community has released many texture packs and other visual improvements, not to mention unofficial patches which fix minor bugs or inconsistencies. So definitely pick those mods up from SS2's PCGamingWiki page, and the game will look as good as it feels to play.
Overall I can't recommend this game enough. I've been coming back to it time and time again for more than fifteen years and still haven't tired of it.

I loved this game, as I did the first.  To the people who have complained about the hardware issues, I experienced zero hardware problems, and was able to run the games at max settings on my PC with an NVIDIA GTX 1080, and an NVIDIA GTX 970.
There were a lot of improvements on the game mechanics over the first game, such as being able to knock people unsconcious from the front, from above, and in the middle  of combat.  There were a lot of new additions in weapons, such as explosove bullets, frenzy bolts, and sticky bombs.  I really liked Emily's powers, and it had a very different playstyle than Corvo's.  I haven't even had a chance to try all of Emily's powers out and I have played 50 hours already.
The graphics were gorgeous, and I stopped at several moments to just take in some of the scenery.  The environmental story telling was neat as well, there was a lot of individual self-contained stories in some of the buildings or scenes that draws you into the world.  The civilian interactions are much better in this game, as not every person you see is an enemy.  There are several marketplaces and shops scattered about Karnaca that you can walk among.
The gameplay itself is....pretty much the same as Dishonored 1.  There are some really neat levels, for instance Aramis Stilton's Manor, where you can SPOILER ALERT
.  If you enjoyed Dishnored 1, then you WILL enjoy this game.  Some of the levels are better, some of them are not, but overall I think it's a bit more polished.
There's also a lot of replay value.  There's at the very least four playthroughs, high and low chaos as both Emily and Corvo (and they are different enough in playstyle to warrent that, at least in my opinion).  It took me about 30 hours or so to get through the first playthrough (because I took my time), so you would definietly get your money's worth if you evalute it at a dollar an hour.
Overall, I really loved this game, and I loved the first one.  It didn't dissappoint me at least.

EDIT: Crash bugs right now if you have texture size turned way up. The classics are working fine for me. By the way, you must download the DLC to be able to play the campaigns in the remastered edition. Issues thread:
Let me tell you something about homeworld (1+2 AND the lost game, homeworld cataclysm). Even 15+ years later, it's still the gold standard for 3D RTS. Here's a few big points:
Very intuitive controls. Movement control is a simple two step, where the first sets horizontal movement, then *optionally* holding shift or click and drag for height. I've yet to see another 3D RTS which even comes close to how quickly and simply that I can give move orders in a 3D space, even though mice and monitors are 2D devices.
Extremely helpful *contextual* visual indicators. When in the process of giving a move order, a lot of supporting information for movement then pops up. For example, to show how high other ship's height are above yours in the 3D battlespace, an ecliptic disc is drawn centered on your ships in the move order interface, and vertical lines are drawn from that disc to those other ships. It GREATLY aids in plotting the movement order so you can order your ships to intercept over long distances. Once the move order is given, all of this goes away so there isn't information overload.
Battles actually take place in 3D space as well. Skilled players WILL use height to flank from above and below to avoid being subjected to a full broadside of guns. Fighters zoom around ships without regards to direction, attacking from multiple angles. This isn't "2.5D" as I would call it, you NEED to use height, especially with fighters.
Two camera modes. One is the standard battle camera, which you spend most of your time in for orders in a small area, and a strategic camera, which is an "at a glance" of the battlespace with a LOT more information and large map wide movement. The space bar is the simple key to switch between them.
In the story, you must be somewhat careful of losses (but it's not so bad that it inhibits gameplay). Every mission brings the resources, ships, and research that you have from the previous missions. You are quite literally a nomadic fleet. Resources on each map are *not* regenerative, even in multiplayer, so grab what you can! Think starcraft in terms of resources: it's plentiful, but resources will run out in a prolonged battle.
The story itself: It's of loss and sacrifice, hope and victory. It's quite a roller coaster of emotion.
Soundtrack: Very "spacey" feel that is well designed to suit each mission. Plus, mission 3 on HW1 had the best freaking use of a classic choir song (Agnus Dei - Adagio for strings) I've ever heard.
My only regret: the source code to HW:Cataclysm is lost. There's no remastering it. It's not considered canon, but it was still fun playing as the mining faction's ship "Kun-Laan" and fighting the galactic cancer known as "The Beast".
EDIT: Made a grammar mistake, fixed. Kun-Laan is the mining faction's ship, but I forgot to mention that their faction name is "Somtaaw"

Okay everybody, I JUST finished playing this game and I must say... wow. I'm still shaking and my face is red from the adrenaline (I know, I'm a crybaby bedwetter but whatever). Xenomorphs were always something that freaked me out so when I heard that there was going to be a survival horror game like Outlast starring the freaky things, I knew I had to play it.
I read up on every aspect of it and followed it for months. Once I had finished my gaming rig, I bought it. It truly was a great game for me and I have a lot to say about it, so let's get into the good, the bad and the ugly (the ugly is about glitches that I experienced but you may not).
GOOD:
-Runs smoothly on my meh PC (I have a GPU from 2013 but it's still a pretty good rig)
-Great visuals that SCREAM 1970's future at the top of their lungs
-Good voice acting, including new clips from the actors from Alien
-Sound direction is top notch and includes countless hours of music from the real movie
-Alien A.I. is smart and realistic (even on normal difficulty). This really is the perfect organism...
-Crafting system is symplistic but adds a great amount of detail to the game
-Pacing was good (for me it only lasted 16 hours but I've heard some people say 20-24)
-Story makes sense canonically and does the job nicely
-All rooms are recognizable and you will know when you're backtracking (which never really felt like a chore)
-Good emotional moments peppered throughout the game
-The saving in this game is controlled by YOU. There are many save points across the station which can be heard by the slight 'beep' they make. Most of the time you can only save at these stations. This can be a little annoying at times, but if you're smart and stealthy this won't be a problem
-Fun survival mode with good DLC to keep you plaing long after you finish the campaign
BAD:
-Sometimes Alien A.I. is too good and won't leave you the ♥♥♥♥ alone so that you can complete your objective even in the earlier missions
-Some missions feel a bit like padding, one that recurrs quite often is this;
"Go get this item for me."
"Oh, doors locked, go find the passcode."
"Oh, power's out, go find the generator to turn the computers on to get the passcode to open the door to get the item for me."
(Seriously, why does NOTHING work on this station)
-There are a couple of cheap deaths in the later missions put in place to extend the play time (you can not thesibly react to some of them on your first try)
UGLY:
-The funniest glitch that happened to me was when a frozen Alien model came sliding out of a vent next to me and just stayed there. It disappeared after a while though :D
-Invisible objects sometimes happened such as transit cars, computer terminals and even the alien (that one was terrifying when it happened) but these were few and far between
-There were slight graphical glitches like sliding down a ladder instead of climbing down, symbols on a keyboard twitching around and other small stuff but again these happened rarely
Overall, I have to say this was an AMAZING game. For any fan of the Alien franchise I must ask you one question. Why don't you have this game yet? For everyone else, I must recommend it. My final verdict as a fan and as an outsider is as follows.
FAN: 9.5/10
OUTSIDER: 8.5/10

This game simply oozes 90's charm, from gameplay to experiencing the limitations.
A lot of people who are not long time RTS fans will probably get turned off by this game, just from looking at it.
I do, however, encourage people to play this game.
This game is still to this day years, decades even, ahead of it's time.
From the notion of destroyed unit husks blocking unit movement, to the sheer scale of how powerful simple units can be.
And for once in an RTS I actually feel like an Experimental unit, is Experimental.
The Krogoth is an amazing unit that, while yes, does take a long time to build, can dish out serious firepower, however unlike Experimental units of today it is not Nigh-on invincible, and can die reletively easily, but can quickly pave the way for an army.
The one big downside to the Krogoth is that only the CORE can build it, so if you're the ARM, you might want to build up your artillery.
Although you'll probably never reach the point of actually building the Krogoth since it does take a considerable amount of time to build.
The game also has a booming soundtrack, composed by the one and only Jeremy Soule, who also composed the music for Elder Scrolls, Guild Wars and other hit/Cult Classic titles.
Very few composers such as Soule actually still compose today.
Frank Klepaki is one such artist, alough his Command and Conquer work, will probably still be his best.
The only game that I could recommend to ever coming close to TA, is probably Dark Reign, and even that doesn't come anywhere near the level this game produced.
Pros:
-The game is quite fluid, and offers quite a great deal of control over your units.
-The future setting works in its favor instead of against it (Even to this day).
-The music is masterfully crafted to suit the game's tone and ambition.
-The art is quite unique and no 2 units look the same.
-One of the very few RTS of its time to use more than 1 resource and be balanced
-Maps are expertly crafted so that no one position feels, acts, or is the same.
-Terrain actually plays a role in the game's combat.
-Buildings actually have a wide degree of rotation (For the most part).
Cons:
-The game's flidity can be hindered by unexpected obstacles (UI, terrain, etc.).
-While the art is incredibly unique, I do understand that it is a bit dated, namely how units and structures act.
-Having 2 resources also means having more to protect in specific locations.
-Asymmetry can lead to many problems on some of the maps, such as spawns.
-Terrain is nice, but the tiniest of bumps can make a well planned base fall apart (So be very careful and wary)
-Yes buildings have a surprising amount of rotation, however construction buildings can only be placed one way with minor rotation when placed.
The game also came with a map editor and a ridiculous player system, both of which were not great.
Building maps was a chore, and had many placement issues.
The player count required 4 extra copies if you wanted to take advantage of all 8 player slots.
TA Kingdoms improved on both of those features, but was unfortunately the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child, to many people, of the franchise.
Although I quite liked Kingdoms, I just feel like it had too many units, and could have been better.
Overall I give Total Annihilation a 10/10.
Not even the flaws can keep me from loving this Masterpiece of "Ahead of its time" technology.

There's really too much to say about this game, and perhaps Total War in general, for a short review here, so instead I will leave you with this:
Rome II in its current state is a halfway-decent game, particularly if you're new the series, but is otherwise a giant let-down for old fans of the franchise.  I personally find its combat fun, but it's relatively simplistic.  I find the city- and empire-building to be sub-par, even compared to its predecessors.  The "RPG" elements they tried to add are a joke.  Its politics and economics are nearly non-existent.  Its faction and unit variety, always my favorite part of games, including Total War, just aren't there.  The AI, as always, is bad.
If you're still interested and can pick the game up for cheap, I wouldn't blame you.  But the amount of bad decisions and killed expectations is too much for me.  I have no hope for Atilla, and not much more for the next Total War.

This game is really good. Visually and thematically, it's got a wonderful art style, great steampunk ambiance, awesome lore and world building. The same guy who does Garret's voice in the first three Thief games voices Corvo this time, and he feels EXACTLY like Garret. It's so cool, and it makes playing as Corvo almost feel like a proper new Thief game.
The gameplay is really tight and refined - more polished than the first game - but I also find it to be a bit too easy because of the incredibly powerful arsenal of magic powers available to both Corvo and Emily (and either of them can use the other's powers in New Game +, making that mode even easier). You can make the game more difficult by bumping the difficulty up to Very Hard, mainly because that makes your mana replenish more slowly and nerfs the power of mana potions, so you'll actually have to ration your spell usage somewhat. One cool thing is you can tweak and modify every difficulty modifier. Things like the aforementioned potion/mana variables, and enemy response time can be changed in the game's very extensive difficulty customization menu.
I don't enjoy this game's story and setting as much as those of its predecessor. Karnaca is very well done and probably more artistically accomplished and inspired than Dunwall. But Dunwall in the first game had a certain special something, a horrific-yet-captivating and immersive atmosphere that Karnaca just doesn't quite live up to somehow. The plot compares even less favorably, being a carbon copy of Dishonored 1's story, but without the operatic twists and sense of urgency.
What's here is still really quite excellent and a triumph of game design. I just wish it were mechanically more difficult and had more narrative thrust to it. I'd give it an 8.5/10.
Edit: I probably sound more negative than I mean to. It's just that I tend to notice and nitpick at flaws the more something approaches perfection. This is a wonderful game that you should definitely purchase. It's got high replay value for at least three playthroughs, too (once each for Corvo and Emily, then either for New Game +).

Homeworld is a space strategy game that redefined the RTS genre, and remains today as the only game that did it right. A deep and thrilling story (30 missions over 2 campaigns), powerful and anomalous music, and a very unique style of play. A true space opera!
Even though games are nearly 15 years old now, the mechanics and gameplay don’t feel outdated. Instead, they are still unmatched by any other space RTS that have released since. The three dimensional environment requires a whole new level of thinking when it comes to strategy.
Now let’s talk about the remaster and a company that actually put some effort into a remake.
This was crafted with the assistance and guidance of the original creators as well as the help of a passionate fan community.
- Complete overhaul of the games engine
- Significantly upgraded visuals, including high-res textures and models
- Up to 4k resolution
- Sound and music overhaul
- Upgraded cut-scenes with clean artwork and some new 3d animations
- Redesigned UI for HW1 (from HW2 which also got an update)
- Mod compatibility and workshop support
- Compatibility with newer operating systems
- Combined Multiplayer between both games
As you can see, they put a considerable amount of effort into this remastered version of Homeworld and that's why I totally think it’s worth the price tag, unlike any other HD remake out on Steam. You also get both of the original games with this package, which were previously hard to get ahold of, and they are even updated to be playable on modern operating systems.
If you enjoyed Homeworld 1/2 or other real time strategy games, you should strongly consider giving this a try, as it really an experience that is unmatched to this very day! Let’s show the industry that there is still demand for strategy games like this, so that we can expect more in the future!

A fun, unassuming game, Eternal Senia impressed me more than I thought it would.
*Before I talk about anything, I want to mention that the soundtrack is phenomenal.  It really makes you realize how important music can be to the overall experience.*
The game and story are both short and sweet.  The story itself hits a soft spot for me, so I'm probably biased, but all things considered it's not especially unique or noteworthy on it's own.  It's good, but not unique, let's say.
Likewise, the base combat is also incredibly simple; run into enemies to deal damage.  Unfortunately, this means that you're spending a lot of time doing essentially very little, just moving from boss fight to boss fight.  The boss fights are much more spectacular, and legitimately challenging, considering how the rest of the game plays, but are also where some of the problems with the combat design present themselves.
Things like hit stun, lingering hitboxes, and occassionally hard to read attacks can make some of the fights frustrating, especially on hard mode.  The boss fights frequently morph into a psuedo bullet hell style of game, but the game doesn't necessarily handle well enough to prevent you from dying to things in ways that don't feel particularly fair.

Dark Souls II is a good game, but it's one you need to start with an open mind. Going in with preconceived notions that you may have gained from Dark Souls will end painfully (hello there, rolling i-frames, meet my new friend adaptability). Even if you're a veteran of the original, be prepared to die. A lot. A-whole-♥♥♥♥ing-lot. The new engine and deadzone on character movements will throw you off at first, but eventually you'll grow accustomed.
The game's world, Drangleic, has some beautiful areas and interesting bosses, but aesthetically I would say it loses out to Dark Soul's Lordran. Instead of having a bunch of interconnected areas that all loop together, areas are sequenced into branches and paths. The bosses range from fantastic to absolutely lame, and you may even see a few familiar faces if you're a Dark Souls player.
Co-op is fantastic (though Soul Memory may or may not cause you some limitations, depending on how you play) and connecting to your friends is much easier now. With the Name-Engraved Ring (an ingame item), you'll never have to worry about being summoned by XxSephiroth420quickscopezxX instead of your friends! Just make sure you're in compatible Soul Memory ranges! Aside from that, though, co-op is largely unchanged from Dark Souls, aside from now phantoms can use their own Estus. The Sunbros are still around and if you only want to be summoned for a little bit, you can do that too with the Small White Soapstone.
PvP is fundamentally good, but can be ruined by its players from time to time. Be prepared to meet lots of heavy-armored buff-stacking folks with fast rolls, be prepared to be riddled with Lightning Spears the moment you're summoned to duel in another host's world, be prepared for hackers and most importantly, be prepared for people doing gimmick/cosplay/fashion builds: they're usually pretty ♥♥♥♥ing good at the game. Note that while not all the things I described are bad things, they're all a part of the broth in the soup that is Dark Souls II.
I don't consider myself a fanboy, far from it. I have more reservations than I'm comfortable admitting when it comes to this game. However, From Soft has shown that they do keep track of their community and at the very least do work towards balancing PvP (which is a Sisyphusian task in itself), so I give them credit for trying. I think the game is worth a shot, and I look forward to how future patches change the pace of the game. I'd say something about Soul Memory, but this is a review, not a ♥♥♥♥ing dissertation. You'll have to make up your own mind on that one.

One of the best games I have ever played, hands down. I lie you not, this is by no means an overexaggeration.
Let me start off by countering the most common misconception about this game. Many people claim that Dark Souls series has no lore hence no actual proper storyline - that is far from true, both the lore and a very well written, unique storyline are there but they are not given to you on a plate - you have to be able to look for all the small hints that are spread throughout the game. Because of this, the game's world, the so called Drangelic, is surrounded by this mysterious, dark aura. If you lack the wits to put two and two together, you will discover only a small portion of the game's storyline. You have to be able to connect the dots and all the pieces out there (the overall feeling while struggling through the harsh world of Dark Souls reminded me of The Walking Dead TV series which I absolutely love).
That being said, while the story of the game is of very high quality, it is by no means its main, most appealing trait (at least to me that is). The game's combat system and level of difficulty are unlike anything I have ever experienced when it comes to single player games. Compared to all the other games that are being released these days, Dark Souls 2 is the most challenging thus rewarding, by FAR. There are COUNTLESS bosses in this game, each and every one with unique, complex mechanics and stunning visuals (I will refrain from spoiling but some of the abilities that the bosses use in this game left me simply speechless. Same goes for the bosses themselves).
And that is not all. Multiplayer is also present but not as a separate mode - it is strongly linked to the single player experience,  allowing us to interact with players as we progress through the game's main storyline. Let me explain - after first few hours or so, you will obtain an item that will allow you to summon other players, the so called phantoms, into your world. Something to keep in mind though - remember that defeating bosses in Dark Souls on your own will grant you the biggest satisfaction. With phantoms (other players) at your side, some of these fights are simply not as challenging. Your world can also get invaded by the so called 'dark spirit' - an evil entity i.e other player that came to your realm with one sole purpose - to kill you and make you lose your souls. The adrenaline rush I experienced while PvPing in this game is undescribable.
The game's replay value is also something worth mentioning. After beating the game for the first time, you will unlock NG+ which stands for New Game Plus (and after beating NG+, NG++ and so forth). Going into NG+ will make the game even more challenging at certain aspects, pushing you to your limits even further. New enemies will lure around every corner, waiting for the perfect opportunity to leap at you from behind and deal a killing blow. As far as I know, the current limit one can reach is NG 10+ but don't hold me to that.
Dark Souls 2 has one downside though - it was designed for consoles and the default controls for PC are somewhat lacking thus it is recommended that you get an XBOX 360 PC game controller. Don't get me wrong, the game is definitely playable with the use of mouse and keyboard if you set up your keybinds properly but playing on a console pad feels so much better.
If you find this game to be too hard for you, give it some time. You are supposed to die numerous times, that is the way of Dark Souls. I can tell you with an uttermost confidence that you will fall in love with the game and won't be able to get your hands off it. After spending over 200 hours in Dark Souls, I am pretty sure that I will come back to this title over and over again.
PROS:
+ The game is extremely hard in comparison to other games released these days and thus feels very rewarding.
+ Numerous unique enemies (including the bosses with stunning looks and differing abilities).
+ The story is well written and quite interesting.
+ The game is sorrounded by this mysterious atmosphere, it is dark and creepy hence feels very mature.
+ While this game is definitely not a sandbox, there are tons of secrets for you to explore making it far from linear. Ther is no such thing as a minimap and the exploration feels very satisfactory.
+ Game's audio is of a very high quality, the voice acting is quite solid, same goes for the amazing soundtrack.
CONS:
- It pains me that this game was initially released for consoles. This might come as controversial but I can't comprehend why people buy consoles these days. I mean I I know whey they do but it is so silly of them - PCs are better in every aspect. Anyway, lets not stair away from actually reviewing the game. As I have mentioned earlier, controls for PC are somewhat lacking.
- Graphics are below average - don't get me wrong, some of the bosses look absolutely stunning, same goes for certain locations in the game. The problem is, the game engine makes them look quite... oldish (I can't say bad cause they definitely do not look bad).. Did you see the Witcher 3 trailer? Compare these graphics to Dark Souls, the gap is colossal. Suprisingly, the game engine for Dark Souls 2 is quite new (at least according to the game developers). To me, it seems like they slightly revamped the original DS1 engine, nothing more.
Final Verdict: This year's best game without a doubt, 9.5/10 is a note I am giving to Dark Souls 2, the 0.5 being reserved for a truly perfect game (and Dark Souls 2 comes as close as it gets).
So what are you waiting for? If you haven't played Dark Souls 2 yet and consider yourself a fan of the RPG genre, waste no time and seek souls... larger, more powerful souls. Seek the king. THAT IS THE ONLY WAY! Lest this land swallow you whole. As it has so many others.

Okay everybody, I JUST finished playing this game and I must say... wow. I'm still shaking and my face is red from the adrenaline (I know, I'm a crybaby bedwetter but whatever). Xenomorphs were always something that freaked me out so when I heard that there was going to be a survival horror game like Outlast starring the freaky things, I knew I had to play it.
I read up on every aspect of it and followed it for months. Once I had finished my gaming rig, I bought it. It truly was a great game for me and I have a lot to say about it, so let's get into the good, the bad and the ugly (the ugly is about glitches that I experienced but you may not).
GOOD:
-Runs smoothly on my meh PC (I have a GPU from 2013 but it's still a pretty good rig)
-Great visuals that SCREAM 1970's future at the top of their lungs
-Good voice acting, including new clips from the actors from Alien
-Sound direction is top notch and includes countless hours of music from the real movie
-Alien A.I. is smart and realistic (even on normal difficulty). This really is the perfect organism...
-Crafting system is symplistic but adds a great amount of detail to the game
-Pacing was good (for me it only lasted 16 hours but I've heard some people say 20-24)
-Story makes sense canonically and does the job nicely
-All rooms are recognizable and you will know when you're backtracking (which never really felt like a chore)
-Good emotional moments peppered throughout the game
-The saving in this game is controlled by YOU. There are many save points across the station which can be heard by the slight 'beep' they make. Most of the time you can only save at these stations. This can be a little annoying at times, but if you're smart and stealthy this won't be a problem
-Fun survival mode with good DLC to keep you plaing long after you finish the campaign
BAD:
-Sometimes Alien A.I. is too good and won't leave you the ♥♥♥♥ alone so that you can complete your objective even in the earlier missions
-Some missions feel a bit like padding, one that recurrs quite often is this;
"Go get this item for me."
"Oh, doors locked, go find the passcode."
"Oh, power's out, go find the generator to turn the computers on to get the passcode to open the door to get the item for me."
(Seriously, why does NOTHING work on this station)
-There are a couple of cheap deaths in the later missions put in place to extend the play time (you can not thesibly react to some of them on your first try)
UGLY:
-The funniest glitch that happened to me was when a frozen Alien model came sliding out of a vent next to me and just stayed there. It disappeared after a while though :D
-Invisible objects sometimes happened such as transit cars, computer terminals and even the alien (that one was terrifying when it happened) but these were few and far between
-There were slight graphical glitches like sliding down a ladder instead of climbing down, symbols on a keyboard twitching around and other small stuff but again these happened rarely
Overall, I have to say this was an AMAZING game. For any fan of the Alien franchise I must ask you one question. Why don't you have this game yet? For everyone else, I must recommend it. My final verdict as a fan and as an outsider is as follows.
FAN: 9.5/10
OUTSIDER: 8.5/10

At the time of this review, I've put 114.4 hours into Tyto. In the interest of disclosure - I received the base game as a gift from a friend, though I purchased the DLC on my own.
I've been with the game a long time - I believe shortly before the Himylan DLC came out, through to the current Cretacious DLC. In that time there's been a lot of growth and a lot of care (even the odd spot of free content), and while it's still not perfect, it's a lot of fun and it's been money more than well spent.
The game recieves bugfixes/hotfixes and has developers active on the forums, so if you encounter an issue it's actually worthwhile reporting - even if it takes some time and a couple fixes to entirely sort some of the stickier issues. It's the sort of developer support and communication you wish every dev could do. The game has definitely felt better and better as time has gone on, with improvements to a number of areas both large and small.
The core gameplay is essentially food chain 'management', and as expected of a real food chain it can be quite sensitive and mutable. You manage within a biodome, so while there won't be populations of animals 'moving in' from other areas to fill a niche, that's fine since you're placing new populations yourself in the first place and as you learn an ecosystem more thoroughly, you'll gain a better insight into the various consumers and producers, making it easier to get the results you want. You begin with one section of the biodome and some basic 'starter' flora and fauna, along with a decomposter (which consume detritus). As time goes on you earn 'coins' which are used to unlock new sections or other consumers and producers (this isn't a microtransaction, don't worry). If you wish you can start a new biodome of the same type, and all your unlocks will be available save for biodome sections (you can start fresh with a new profile if you want to crawl your way up from scratch, and it's quick and painless to switch between profiles if you want to keep older ones).
This makes it quite easy to try out different playstyles, which is itself a lot of fun. You will have moments of horror as you realize a lone deermouse population was underpredated, has reproduced well beyond control, and swathes of land begin to lose their vegetation as the vermin run rampant until they burn themselves out and die en masse from starvation. You'll see tropical rainforests grow an evolving canopy over time as trees grow and die. Given enough time you can let a single tree grow into a dense forest.
The DLC is also worthwhile. Every ecosystem comes with its own plants, animals and decomposters, the ecosystems do play out differently. The biodomes are also larger in the dlc.
There are some minor caveats. Pollinator and decomposter populations don't produce new population 'spawns' like normal plants and animals (which do have reproductive and life cycles modelled), meaning the only way to increase their population 'spawns' is manually introducing them yourself. For most of the game this really isn't important; it's an abstraction that lets you focus on the real meat of the game. However this also means that (at the time of this writing; the devs are still trying to make it work), most insectivores (which aren't numerous in the game to begin with) run a pretty good risk of causing ecosystem damage or even collapse due to how rapidly many breed and the simple fact that they share the prey role - which, in a diverse ecosystem, can make it easy for them to gain the needed momentum, which basically means you won't be using them beyond very early stages if you even choose to use them at all. There's also no flying animals (aside from moths and bees; some birds which don't fly are in the game if you must have birds), and a couple plants are (currently) bugged and don't quite reproduce right.
But these are ultimately fairly minor complaints in the grand scheme of things (and they may not always hold true). The real fun has been in things like creating a self sustaining food chain, or watching a buffalo herd grow from a handful of individuals to one much larger... or annihilating a food chain with an apocalyptic level of snakes. Typical gameplay is deliberate, even slow with pacing but has fast forward and time advancing options and you can even let the game 'advance' between play sessions for up to a year of gametime, which makes for a mellow experience. The engine was even recently updated to UE4 for improved visuals and stability.
Highly recommended.

Every time you level up you get 1 skill point which you can spend for skills of course. Another way to get skill points is from collecting 3 skyshards which automatically turn into a skill point. You can find sky shards in specfic places within a zone, they'll have a huge beam of light reaching the sky from them, pretty hard to miss lol. Best to look them to bolt straight for them when going to a new zone.
There's also weapon skill trees of, one-handed and shield, two-handed, dual wielding, destruction (magic damage staff), restoration (healing magic staff) their skill trees work just like the class skills they get experience and can "morph" into other skills when LV4 etc
Get this, any class can equip any weapon or kind of gear of light, medium or heavy armor. You can be a heavy armored sorcerer or a healing based nightblade, i love the variety this allows
There's crafting and gathering as usual for an MMORPG but the gathering spots don't glow, no markers for them, you'll actually need to keep an eye out of where they are when exploring which i love. As for crafting very simple straightforward, just refine your materials and add more of them for whatever you're gear you're crafting to suit said level. Higher tier crafting requires special items that will increase the "RNG" percentage of your resolve. Nice you can make it be 100% if you put effort into it then just getting screwed over like every other crafting system by RNG even if you did everything right >_>"
The game has an excellent sense of exploration, you'll gain exp from being in a new section of a zone. I always looked at the map of said zone feeling the need to check out various points to see what this town like place of what quest could be in store for me. There aren't any quest markers all right there from the start on the map, you'll have to be within range for the game to keep track of a discovered quest. So its just another reason to force you to look every where to find everything and it is all worth it, rewards galore y'all my goodness. There will be highlights on the map saying to discover the problem with said section of the zone so really its asking you to find the quest giver for it to fix it, decent hint.
no idea what end game is like, just that there's PVP sieges apparently which you have access at LV10, look for it in your menu and takes you to a different zone for it
The cash shop is full of mounts, costumes, not sure if its P2W but based off what ive seen of it doesn't seem like it currently but the in-money needed to get a mount is a ton, better off just buying one with real money. I have yet to aquire a mount, just been running on foot, i don't mind it.
honestly i'm not a fan of the elder scrolls main title games and i love this game surprisingly, even reading the quests and like crafting and gathering, those 3 things i just do not do in other MMORPGs ever, thats how good it is for me. Sorry this was so long for a "first impressions" :S

An old time classic that still holds up pretty well. With the exception of UI flaws this game is actually able to stand the test of time. Which is quite rare for a RTS game. It'll run on Windows 10 too but some things need to be installed first.
So what can you expect? It's an RTS with infinitive resources that needs to be balanced. Metal and Energy. While you have a stock amount of metal and Energy this will quickly go away if you can't keep up with the demand and when it hits bottom things will take far longer to build.
The two sides have similar units on Tier 1 but on Tier 2 they vary a bit. But most units can be useful later on. Arm are the best looking though. Just a fact.
With mods installed you can build up to 1000 per player but that generally just crashes the game so keep to 500 per player. The AI can't really handle this amount either as they'll do stupid things like building 100 Metal extractors instead of Moho Mines on a metal planet.
You'll also get conga lines of enemies towards your base and these lines can be pretty long and pretty big. For instance with 1000 units on that line is just one long line from the enemy base to my base. Or rather to the range of my turrets.
There are plenty of unit mods for this game and you'll be needing some programs in order to use them all. But there is still a limit on how many you can have.
If you decide to play online you can limit how many units the AI can build of certain things and this can be used to stop them from building a ton of useless structures. Could be a way to make it more of a challenge too.

Still to this date this game still hold up with one of the beast base building design ever made. This game has endles time of fun with modded units to just playing standed. I can still remember the days i was a kid playing this late at night trying to kill the other players base's. This game can turn into eather a 2 hours game or 5 days later. This game is worth anything steam charges. I would still buy it.

Ravenfield is basically a singleplayer version of Battlefield multiplayer. The maps are large, and most have many different vehicles to use to gain the advantage. It is early access, so a lot should be added in the coming months (campaign, map builder, more maps, etc.).

+ Physics are entertaining (dead bodies flying in the air are pretty great)
+ Not a serious FPS, so it can be funny at times
+ Great alternative if you cannot or do not want to play multiplayer FPS's
+- Early Access: Limited content right now, but it sounds like a lot is going to be added soon
+- Can be buggy sometimes, but this is excusable considering it is early access
+- Price is high for right now, but more content is being added

- No multiplayer
Overall, I would highly recommend this game, especially if you are a person who either has crappy wi-fi and gets annoyed with multiplayer FPS's, enjoys large scale battles in video games or has fun experimenting with AI. It's a little pricey for right now, but even since I bought it a few days ago, I have seen improvements.

This game is really good. Visually and thematically, it's got a wonderful art style, great steampunk ambiance, awesome lore and world building. The same guy who does Garret's voice in the first three Thief games voices Corvo this time, and he feels EXACTLY like Garret. It's so cool, and it makes playing as Corvo almost feel like a proper new Thief game.
The gameplay is really tight and refined - more polished than the first game - but I also find it to be a bit too easy because of the incredibly powerful arsenal of magic powers available to both Corvo and Emily (and either of them can use the other's powers in New Game +, making that mode even easier). You can make the game more difficult by bumping the difficulty up to Very Hard, mainly because that makes your mana replenish more slowly and nerfs the power of mana potions, so you'll actually have to ration your spell usage somewhat. One cool thing is you can tweak and modify every difficulty modifier. Things like the aforementioned potion/mana variables, and enemy response time can be changed in the game's very extensive difficulty customization menu.
I don't enjoy this game's story and setting as much as those of its predecessor. Karnaca is very well done and probably more artistically accomplished and inspired than Dunwall. But Dunwall in the first game had a certain special something, a horrific-yet-captivating and immersive atmosphere that Karnaca just doesn't quite live up to somehow. The plot compares even less favorably, being a carbon copy of Dishonored 1's story, but without the operatic twists and sense of urgency.
What's here is still really quite excellent and a triumph of game design. I just wish it were mechanically more difficult and had more narrative thrust to it. I'd give it an 8.5/10.
Edit: I probably sound more negative than I mean to. It's just that I tend to notice and nitpick at flaws the more something approaches perfection. This is a wonderful game that you should definitely purchase. It's got high replay value for at least three playthroughs, too (once each for Corvo and Emily, then either for New Game +).

Stability/Engine/Polishing:
At launch the game was rather unplayable for older systems and even better ones had their issues with the graphics engine.
There are still one or two bugs in the game that you may come across. They can mess up a perfect stealth mission.
One is that enemies once saw me straight through a wall, another one is after loading a save game, a guard on the other end of the street got alerted and ran straight up to me (happened 3x with the same save file)
Other than that the game is working well.
Graphics:
Now with my brand new GTX1070 I maxed out all graphic settings (and removed motion blur and depth of field, because I don't want those) the game plays well and looks good, with the little exception that everything seems dark, even outside during daytime it's some times hard to see anything and the nightvision skill doesn't help there at all since it's just there for spotting things, not actually seeing better. Nightvision makes things even worse since it puts a red'ish film over your screen and makes everything look the same.
Sound:
It sometimes behaves a little weird but in general it's a nice experience.
Sound can be dampened through obstacles and works fine with 5.1 surround systems.
The only thing I don't understand is why I stop hearing what NPCs say if I stand up from crouching and hear them again when I crouch again.
Gameplay:
The controls sometimes turn out to be iffy and get me killed a lot.
For example it happens all the time that I suddenly can't crawl under a table or through a little window anymore, leaving me trapped outside in the open as NPCs come my way.
It also happened at least once that I stand in front of a climbable window and when pressing space I don't climb but just jump vertically.
I often end up doing something weird when using Far Reach. For example I try to teleport myself up to a window and end up breaking the glass of the door I'm standing next to and kissing the doorframe instead of going to the window.
Level Design:
(spoiler)
The environment is rich of details and the maps are usually reasonably big.
There are huge ammounts of hidden items that can help you through the game.
Story:
The story is full of mysteries and things slowly come together as you progress through the game.
There is a lot of sideinformation to collect and some alternate outcomes of the stories.

Broforce is one of the best "retro shooters" of the modern age.
It embraces the fast paced action and difficulty of 90s games, such as Metal Slug, while still feeling fresh and new.
The game makes fun of the american partiotism and machism, and you play as a wide variety of characters, the "BROS", which are caricatures of male and female action movies stars.
Rambo, Terminator, Ellen Ripley, Robocop, Chuck Norris ecc...there are a lot.
The best thing about the game is that you spawn each time as a different character, after dying or getting a new life, so you´'ll always play as a different hero, keeping the gameplay fresh.
All the heroes have different weapons, traits, abilities and special attacks, and most of them are very fun to play, but there are a cuple ones that are completely useless and not up to the task (such as Indiana Bro).
A unique feature of this game is the destructable environmets. Every single block of the level can be destroyed, and that increases the tactical planning, encouragin the player to dig tunnels and demolish structures.
Before approaching the game you have to know it starts easy but gets quite hard at the end.
Pros:
- Stylish 16-bit graphics
- Addictive Gameplay
- Many Levels
- Perfect Difficulty
- Super fast paced action
- Many fun characters to play with
- Lovely irony
- Destructable environments
- Variety
Cons:

I've dabbled a bit in the game. Completed the main story, played through the Sky Fortress DLC and now I plan on jumping into the new Mech DLC.
Personally I've really enjoyed the game and never had problems when it comes to memory leaks or random crashing. I'm running an i7 3770k and an EVGA 980 ti SC, so that could contribute to why I have no issues running. But most of these negative reviews are because their system componets are sub par and they probably expected the game to run at a smooth 60 fps on ultra. If you don't have good parts then you won't be able to play, welcome to the world of PC gaming. If it's truly that bad then just play on a console, it would probably work better for you there anyway.
Now then, on to the actual gameplay review (Which is what these reviews are for)
The gameplay can be a bit wonky in some places, I mostly noticed it around melee and trying to grapple some enemies. But that's normal Just Cause gameplay and wouldn't feel the same without it. The car handling mechanics are miles ahead of what they used to be. Bigger explosions and a lot more toys to play with. The Glider suit feels improved as well, as far as handling goes, you can also wingsuit across the entire island if you're good with that grapple hook. Lotta newly added vehicles and aircraft bring a lot of new fun to the table. I didn't have any issues when it came to story or side missions, the glider trials can be a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥though.
TL:DR - Overall I'd say this is a nearly perfect game with some minor hiccups here and there. Gameplay wise it's what you'd expect from Just Cause, widespread chaos and destruction (The Bavarium Nuke launcher is tons of fun >.>)
If your system cannot handle the game then don't rate it negative, either buy a better system or go to consoles for budget playing. This is a great game for those of us who can handle it.

The bottom line is, if you're the type that get's bored easily and can't enjoy slower paced games, this probably won't appeal to you, this isn't action packed and generally the satisfaction you'll get from it is from watching the flora/fauna interactions and watching a biome succeed. Total War: Rome II Emperor Edition
Long review, if you want a detailed analysis of this RTS, keep reading! Not for the impatient. I've owned this game since release, this review is up to date.
+A wide variety of units available to each faction, including spearmen/hoplites, sword wielding troops, archers, vicious war dogs, cavalry and even war elephants. Topple the enemy cities with onagers and balistae or storm them with ladders and siege towers!
+ The battles in this game are great. Command thousands of men at once and watch the raw brutality of combat unfold. People can be impaled or even decapitated (with the blood DLC pack). The battle AI is improving with every patch (there's been a lot since release) and they acknowledge your flanks, making counter-moves.
+ Very nice graphics on extreme settings.
+ Many new features which take the Total War series in a different direction. However, this does have some massive down sides which I'll explain later. Balancing food input and public order is one of the central challenges of the game like always. The interface has changed entirely and feels unique. Armies can now level up as they gain experience and acquire new abilities. There's also different victory conditions such as cultural and economic. In addition, there's been changes to city management with a new province system. Owning every town within a province unlocks access to an edict, which can increase the tax rate, food output and happiness or wealth from the province in question. There's many more tweaks I can discuss, but for simplicity's sake I won't delve deeper.
+ Creative Assembly has consistently worked to resolve issues with bugs since the day of release and continue to do so, in conjunction with giving the playerbase free DLC. The amount of support they've given everyone is outstanding to be honest. Many developers would've given up, but they stuck it out for an entire year to ensure this game was as awesome as they envisioned initially.
+ Technology tree which unlocks new buildings, units and benefits when research is completed. This is somewhat different for each faction, which gives a feeling of uniqueness.
+ The campaign map of Europe and the Middle East is once again smaller than Empire: Total War, but an improvement on Total War: Shogun 2's small map size.
+ Multiplayer custom battles for competitive players and co-op mode to play campaigns with friends.
- After several months of not playing the game, I realised when I returned that my main issue with Total War: Rome II Emperor Edition is that it tries to be something it's not. It's not Civilization V, it's Total War. The new interface, provinces, food balancing and construction system are NOT like traditional Total War. The game feels completely different. You have to read every minor detail about a building to know what it does, it becomes a complex and confusing task just to build your empire. It's a very NEW approach to Total War, the game is practically unrecognisable in terms of previous titles in this regard. YES I got used to it, and it's OK, but that's all it is. It's Meh, indifference. I would greatly prefer a typical Total War game like Shogun 2 or Empire: Total War.
- There's a lot of micro-management. I appreciate the ability to level up my armies, giving them various traits to fulfill the roles I want them to complete. BUT, across many armies, agents and generals this becomes a somewhat monotonous, annoying chore.
- Removal of some old features which people enjoyed, such as family trees and seasonal effects (these effects can be seen in the expansion DLC exclusively). There's no good reason this couldn't be kept for the main game. Creative Assembly have decided to be sell-outs and put these into the latest Total: War game "Attila" instead which funnily enough, is around $45...
- While the battles can be cool, there's a lot of management involved which means you often don't get to engage in the conflicts by watching it up close. Animations can sometimes be difficult to see as well, the AI soldiers have trouble executing them properly.
- There have been some patches in the past which aren't save-game compatible (what I mean by this is that the game still works and most patch fixes are implemented instantly, but some won't take effect until you start a new campaign).
- DLC expansions are excessive, a blatant cash-in by Creative Assembly. They really don't offer anything extra compared to the main game, just different scenarios, factions and time periods, with some fresh units. I can't justify the price on most of these, as they're a rip off, but I purchased two that had their prices slashed significantly. I can vouch that even though Caesar in Gaul wasn't much different to Rome II, it was still pretty fun. If you're interested, pick them up when cheap.
Overall Score: 7.5/10
Total War: Rome II Emperor Edition is a fun, turn based real time strategy game that will last hundreds of hours. I do recommend it but it's an unusual entry into the series, if the developers just adhered to their traditional Total War formula, I feel this game could've been SO much better. Alas, it just doesn't feel right..It's still good and well worth the price (even when not on sale).

There are 4 classes in the game, Templar (healer tank), Nightblade (Rogue), Sorcerer, and Dragon Knight (magic base tank). Within each of these classes they have 3 skill trees, each skill gains experience and when it's LV4 you can use a skill point to "morph" it to new skill that either does more damage or can heal/support buff and it starts at LV1 again. Each time you "morph" that same skill it takes longer and longer for it to level up.
Every time you level up you get 1 skill point which you can spend for skills of course. Another way to get skill points is from collecting 3 skyshards which automatically turn into a skill point. You can find sky shards in specfic places within a zone, they'll have a huge beam of light reaching the sky from them, pretty hard to miss lol. Best to look them to bolt straight for them when going to a new zone.

If you liked the previous Dishonored game, you will like this new installment. If you didn't, the game hasn't changed significantly and you probably won't enjoy your time in Karnaca.
Mechanically it's more of the same. Sneak around and avoid detection or commit brutal slaughter (or anything inbetween the two extremes). Use the powers the Outsider gives you to get an advantage over your enemies and take out the target for each level. Like in part one, if you go on a rampage the levels become more desolate and you will encounter more enemies. It does feel like the guards are more clever this time around. They will get suspicious when their mates start disappearing and respond a lot better to any sounds you cause. There also seem to be far more alternative paths. I really like the more intricate level designs compared to Dishonored 1.
For me the most interesting path has been playing Emily without powers. Just refuse the Outsider's mark, and you get to play a game more like Thief. You have more money left for gadgets, but you will need to study the environment more carefully for paths that can be taken without the use of said powers. Even more so if you are going for zero detection.
The PC version of the game isn't perfect. Performance is so-so, though I disagree with some of the harsh criticisms on how good or bad the game looks. The graphics are stylized, just like in part one, so do not expect photorealism. Just use the game's recommended setting, and you should be fine. It won't look like the screen shots, though. Not sure what they used for that. On my system (2,7 GHz i7, 16GB Ram, GTX 980M 4GB, 1920x1200) that put me at medium settings. Framerate is more important than graphical effects, in my opinion. There are a few graphical glitches here and there if you know where to look, but not enough to spoil the fun.
Also expect to fail and reload regularly as the game fails to interpret controls or the AI looks through walls. The choke command is very hit-and-miss at certain angles. Another particular anoyance is that after loading a save game the AI will go into alert state and suddenly change paths. This sometimes makes your quicksave useless. Adding insult to injury, the autosave will then save after combat, so be sure to press escape immediately if things go wrong ad reload. Worst case, you will be redoing large sections of a mission as you curse the inept save feature. Did anyone actually test this?
At almost 40 hours in and still not done playing, I'd say the game is worth its price, and I would heartily recommend it to anyone who likes these types of stealth games. Just don't expect to set the graphics to the maximum settings. Particularly not at 4k.

Alien Isolation is a stealth/horror game (ala: Amnesia and Outlast) with a few major differences... You are constantly being hunted by the Xenomorph, almost nothing is scripted and your in space (where no one can hear you scream!). Now there are small scripted segments to move the story along but for about 85% of the game you are runing/hiding from, and outsmarting an incredibly well crafted monster. The audio (with the exception of the voice acting) is great and the lighting is hands down the best I have ever seen in a game period. The Alien "AI" is impressive and unpredictable to a point where I stopped getting frustrated and gradually got more and more impressed. While you can take the offensive strategy with other humans and "Working Joes" (robots), your only chance with the Alien is to waste resources temporarily causing it to flee or staying invisible. And when it runs away because of your attack you better think of something fast cause it's coming back with an attitude. This game is also a massive fan service. If you like horror, stealth or the original Alien movie then this is for you.
Pros:
*Lighting
*Unpredictable Xenomorph
*Audio
*Attention to detail staying faithful to the source material.
*Very few bugs (I experienced none)
*Game length
*Story
Cons:
*Certain areas (A very small number of them) can feel "bottlenecked" making progression very difficult due to being forced into a room (Usually to activate a cutscene or something).
*Human npc AI can go from impressive to questionably suicidal pretty quickly.
*Voice acting is average at best...

EDIT 9/3/2016
I'm changing my review since last year.
I still love this game, but I think I like it more now. Not only because I have a more powerful PC that can comfortably max out this game, but because I'm now doing something different than last year. Last year, although my review was very possitive, I really couldn't enjoy this game past Chapter 6, since I found it insanely difficult due to the unpredictable nature of the game and its A.I.
Let me tell you one thing: If you hide and wait trying to read your enemy's movements, you are playing the game wrong. This is a game that rewards boldness. Yes; you might get killed by the Xeno, but it's going to be much less.
This game is unlike any other modern game where it will hold your hand even in lower difficulties. this is a different kind of thing. YOu got to survive, but move forward. trust your instincts, the lighting, your ability to stay calm and how you read the motion tracker. Do this right and you'll find yourelf with one of the best horror/sci-fi games ever made since Dead Space.
Pros:
-Graphics (playing on ultra with a i5 K series 4.2ghz and a GTX 970)
-Optimization (even my old rig with a i5 3.0ghz and a GTX 750ti could get 60fps on medium/high)
-Sound
-Music (you'll learn to hate those violins)
-Gamplay
-Atmosphere
-Story
-Faithfulness to the source (for early 80's kids like me, this is a nostalgia trip)
-Controls (It's your choice, but I feel this plays better with Xbox One controller, despite being a FPS game)
-A.I (Xeno)
Cons:
-Some people give up on this game without trying a different strategy (myself included last year)
-Objectives are a bit hard to track sometimes, even if they show on the map. that is part of the game's mechanics though.
If you play it right by thinking fast and being bold, and this game will amaze you. Play it wrong by chickening out or doubting and it will punish you severly.

I went into Black Mesa with very high expectations, and was quite satisfied, but was also to a degree dissapointed. Anyone who has never played the original Half-Life will likely get more enjoyment out of this game as going through this area is first for them. For those who have already finished the original Half-Life...you best come prepared. You are not in Kansas anymore. This isn't the same Black Mesa you went through nearly 20 years ago, as the levels have been changed slightly, with stronger and tougher enemies, and slightly more difficult puzzle and platforming segments.
Anyway, let's start with what I like about the game. First of all, the game is gorgeous; anyone who's played the original Half-Life will likely be blown away by how the level of detail the Black Mesa Research Facility has changed drastically, sporting some impressive character and level design, making this particular fan very excited about how the later parts of the game are going to look. For those of you wondering- Yes, this game does run on the most recent version of the Source Engine. Along with the attractive visuals, the sound design also takes a tad of a step up. Characters and creatures no longer sound like thier dialogue was recorded on an old cassete tape, with creatures sound appropriately terrifying, and the ambience doing a great job to constantly set a  dynamic, suspenseful stage for the players, something that I felt the original Half Life lacked in some areas. Control-wise, well...it's Half-Life. The game still plays the same, if not better than it did nearly 20 years ago, with ladders much safer to navigate being the only real change.
Now let's talk about what I DIDN'T like about the game. First of all, some of the enemies have either been given new attacks or beefed up to the point where their encounters at times feel grueling and frustrating. Along with that, some enemies come at you with new and devasting attacks (notably the bullsquid's spreadshot attack), are harder to kill, do much more damage to you, and unless you're an amazing dodger, expect to get hit and killed...alot. Why is that? Because some of the (largely unchanged) weapons you are given have been noticeable nerfed, and all of which have decreased max ammo for some stupid reason, making fighting these alien scum slightly harder than it needs to be. The machine gun now only has 30 rounds instead of 50, more spread, and you can only carry 3 grenades instead of 10. The shotgun is way to slow, making timing those double blasts and reloads a chore towards the end of the game. Also, the order you get the weapons in is very confusing for those who played the original Half-Life, as even the trademark crowbar is a challenge to get in the beggining areas of the game. And last but not least, some of the levels have added platforming and puzzle sequences, some of which are fun and pratical, with one in particular being a clever throwback to Half Life 2, and others that are just plain infuriating and unnecessary.
With these complaints aside, It's important to remember that this is still an early access game, and has yet to be finished. Needless to say, let's hope Crowbar Collective really gets thier act together with fixing the game according to feedback provided by the community as well as myself, along with revealing the exciting final levels of the game. As of right now, I'll gladly rate this game 8 Headcrabs out of 10. Giving the fans back the arsenal they know and love, taking out some of the unnecessary puzzle/platforming segments, and making the enemy's attacks a tad easier to dodge will go along way into making this modern remake of the Classic Half-Life a glorious return to a highly revered classic.

You have been transported back to 1998 and after summer school swimming you would first watch your friend's lawyer law firm dad play total Annihilation. You thought first, "Well, this isn't [Command and Conquer: Red Alert]" is what you would had thought. No, this is some sort of rule defying CPU magic that could only happen on a Hewlett Packard running Windows 98. There on the screen were fully rendered 3D polygons with basic bit textures, with full working shadows and particles that you could see. Robots were expected to be scouts and ambushers, vehicles were to be the ground spearhead, aircraft had a role in providing support, but wait the ships at sea or the riverbanks might need a world from you. This was not a 2D plane that had grid square movements and spacing, this was close to real life when war was not fought with sprites, but with real 3D modeling of both the unit and environment.
Tanks robots and ships will attempt to shoot aircraft with all weapons when attacked by them.
Subs stay underwater when firing torpedos.
Everything land and sea leaves a wreckage.
Audio is not stuck in 16 bit audio but uses the CD as the audio.
Nukes and missile defenses were a real game changer.
And all the things that you had then, all started with nothing but a single unit known to as your avatar commander.
You could build anything, everywhere, all the time.
You can make anything, anywhere, every time.
You can fight anything, any time, all the time.
Somehow, somewhere, you are thinking about anything that can possibly be absolutely perfect in 1998 only to top it off with a soundtrack composed by Jeremy Soule.
My youth.

The predecessor to Supreme Commander.  This is one of those few games that is still playable today, it has a big variety of units from land, sea, and air to choose from and can change the outcome of the game.  The units are 3D modeled on a 2D interface, and there are units that the TA community have built that can be inserted into the game to increase the types of units and structures that you can build.  A person/persons put together a mod that can be used with TA that makes changes to the games interface and includes new units and defense structures to make the game more interesting.   There are those people that will complain about the graphics, but the graphics are still fine, you can tell what the units are supposed to be and there is still detail on the units themselves, it's not like they are just flat Atari tanks and planes moving around.  I own many RTS games, this is still one of the best ones out there that has good balance and a slew of things to make, not to mention the patrol system is still ahead of many modern games.  One of the cool things of today is that this game can be played using huge maps and 1000+ units/buildings and still run great due to todays processors.  If you enjoy huge battles that will force you to make various things to win, then this is a game for you, but if you like your star craft and like to build few things and rely on specific units, then you best stick to your star craft type games.
