How I Spent My Summer Vacation Aboard Sevastopol Station: Hiding in a locker, under a table, and shooting androids.
This is a completely new kind of game for me, and for all of us. It's similar to Dishonored (which the devs have admitted to gleaning inspiration from) in that it has a lot of the same gameplay mechanics and stealth-emphasis, but unlike Dishonored and Aliens: Colonial Marines (the less said about that game, the better), you're put up against a considerable threat that you can NOT defeat, which I guess is where a lot of the fear comes from.
It's like "The Ant Bully": "What'cha gonna do about it, Xeno? Nothing! Because I'm strong, and you're small!"*
Except now the tables have turned. A:CM got us so used to blazing through Aliens, but with this beautiful, horrifying, high-definition monster casually prancing around the station (his walk reminds me of Steve Urkel's; every time he walks past me I want to crank up the tunes and dance with him), it makes you realize how helpless you are, which I suppose is what they keep telling people. It isn't Call of Duty, so if you fancy spitting out as much lead as possible then go play Aliens: Colonial Marines; but if you want to try something different or try and ease into the horror genre - the TRUE horror genre, then this is a good choice. I know a lot of these reviewers always complain about how you "die all the time", but in all honesty you don't. I'm playing on the hardest difficulty, and although it isn't by any means easy, it's not like the Alien has heat vision or something and can see you hiding in a locker from across the station. Play this game cautiously, don't sprint around, don't act like the lone gunslinger, don't hide in lockers (only use them if you're in an area with absolutely nowhere to hide), and don't get the impression that, "Oh, I get a gun in this game so that must mean I can pwn the Alien."
Fellow Aliens fans or people who might get hooked into the fascinating backstory of this franchise also have additional things to be gained, for this game has some really, really interesting elements that it adds to the story. The Arious motion tracker, for example, can actually be seen on advertisements, where its intended usage is in pest control, which makes some sense. So it's just things like that, those little things that make it more fun, and less of a game where, "Oh, I'm on a random space station and all I have to do is hide from an unkillable Alien, and then I'll win somehow."
So overall, for fans of this genre and/or series; buy it and you won't have a whiff of regret. For Call of Duty fanboys and people on low-end computers, you almost certainly won't enjoy this. If you decide to disregard a mixture of common sense, your own instinct, and a friendly warning, and you're unhappy with the purchase, then you're idiots.

Unless nostalgia rules your life, I'd have to say pass on this game (unless it's on sale or free).
It's not that it's a bad game per se; rather, it hasn't held up over time.
The main things about Total Annihilation (specifically, the Steam version) that make me not want to recommend the game are listed below:
• The available screen size is very limited compared to modern successors. It makes finding enemy units firing from far off screen very difficult, and base management as well.
• The command interface is split across several pages, and is non-intuitive compared to modern games but also compared to some of its contemporaries (Age of Empires, Warcraft 2, Command & Conquer: Red Alert, etc.)
• The unit movement and structure placement is very finicky -- once again, this is based upon my comparisons to modern RTS games of its kind, but watching a robot spend several (5+) seconds walking into a wall isn't as entertaining as you might think.
• Also, I felt that several of the campaign missions are very unbalanced, but your opinion may differ on this point.
Therefore, it was a good game during its heyday when it was fresh and introduced new and novel features to RTS games, but I can't recommend it now.

It's alright, really.
Maybe not worth full price, but pretty alright. The main issue with Dishonored 2 is that it exists because Dishonored 1 sold well, so they made a new story to go with the new game. It doesn't exist because they already had more story that they wanted to build a game around.
A second issue is that there's such an incredibly minor difference between playing Emily or Corvo that you're unlikely to ever really notice it(especially in New Game + where they both have access to each others' powers), and that the difference between high and low chaos is far less tangible than in Dishonored 1.
In fact, the real complaints here aren't that Dishonored 2 is an outright bad game, just that it's not quite as good as the first. Less interesting scenarios, less interesting level design, less dramatic final mission, no actual interesting reveals for the story(it's all as it seems from the get-go, while Dishonored 1 had an actual surprise or two), less pay-off for choices made(several options for mission resolutions have all of one line of easily missed dialogue, and in one case it's the more involved and complicated method of resolution which has no payoff, weirdly enough. Not sure if it smells of lacking ideas or lacking time...).
I wouldn't mind more games in the Dishonored setting, but I feel like it'd benefit if they took a step away from the stealth game schtick for the next installment or two, just until they had enough good ideas to make it worth another shot. Maybe an RPG or some sort of turn-based squad tactics, I can see the world having the space for either.
All in all, it's really not going to blow your mind, but if you liked the first game a lot, this probably won't be a waste of your time and money.
PS: Why even have water-specific abilities when the game has so little actual water? Feels like a leftover from the first game which had somewhat more aquatic navigation options.

INCREDIBLE!  A true survival horror game.  Very cenimatic, eerie, and engrossing.  Isolation feels, looks, and runs like a sequel to the original Alien movie, and thats pretty much what it is.  Everything about this game is perfect, gameplay, crafting, stealth, AI, you name it.  The alien is absolutely the most terrifying thing about the game.  It is smart, it is deadly, and it is incredibly scary to encounter (especially since you can't kill it.  If it sees you, you're probably already dead.)  If you like the Alien series, or just sci-fi horror, this is the game for you.

An accessible, aesthetically consistent and gorgeous game marred by the very entity in its title: the Alien.
To clarify, if the Alien's actions weren't so deeply rooted in the player's every movement, this game would be a glowing example of a horror/survival horror hybrid. The survival horror parts, namely the engagements between you and other humans (or synthetics) are very well balanced: resources are scarce, and avoiding combat is advisable, but if you must get into a scrape, you can expend your resources to survive and move forward regardless.
However, as soon as it moves into the pure horror part of the game, namely the Alien sections (they are nearly two-thirds of the game, by the way), the game falls flat very quickly. Creative Assembly have done a bang-up job presenting the Alien as something to be afraid of again, and during your first real encounter with the organism you will inevitably feel some fear and thrill as it literally stalks you out as its prey. However, make no mistake, the thrill quickly becomes frustration and annoyance when you realize that this horror game is incredibly unforgiving.
To start with, the save system is simply awful. Not in the sense that it's unusable, but in the fact that the game has no autosaves (save for a single, privileged section I can recall). If the game does not give you a save point, or you simply miss one trying to avoid the Alien, then you'd better have your wits about you and stay sharp, knowing that if you die, it's *all* the way back to your previous save. This makes avoiding the Alien less of a fun experience and more of a tense, unpleasant chore.
When you start thinking about the word "chore", you see that it fits into a lot of what the game devolves to. Depending on your difficulty setting, you may find yourself sitting anywhere from a few to a few dozen minutes on a locker, eyes glued on your motion tracker waiting for the Alien to recede back into a vent. You can only spare a few moments to relax and advance however, as less than a minute later, the Alien, on any difficulty setting, may be back on the ground and on your tail. This is actually pretty exhilarating the first couple of times you have to sit through it, but once you realize that you're barely making any sort of progress, it again brings back the concept of sitting through a lecture or doing a chore.
It's a shame too, because Sevastapol station clearly had a lot of care put into it during development, but often times there's little chance to explore, take in the view or even catch your breath... because of the Alien. He is simply obsessed with you and will not spare any expense to hug you to death back to your last save.
It doesn't help that the game sometimes deals you a bad hand on the hiding mechanics. On any difficulty setting, the Alien has a chance to lean in on your hiding places, prompting you for a split second to hold your breath and lean back (this is never introduced as a tutorial, and feels like a cheap "gotcha!" move by the developers) in order to avoid the Alien. Why is it though, based on the unpredictable A.I. of the Alien, that he doesn't check any other locker besides the one you're in? Of course, if you get caught, there is no chance to fight back, it's back to your last save.
It is highly advisable that you do *not* play this game on the difficulty the developers intended you to play it, which is Hard, as stated by them. If you're looking for a thrilling, frightening experience, and not a really stagnant, boring one, I would not recommend anything past Easy. I personally started on Hard and found that the Alien is just simply too active and aggressive. Too often I found myself sitting on lockers idly and inching ever so slower for the game to allow any sort of tension to build. The Alien simply does not let you simmer in your own fear, making every encounter with him meaningless and anger-inducing instead of interesting and frightening.
The game controls fine and is very well animated, with plenty of good-looking contextual actions and setpieces. It looks fantastic as far as lighting and wall textures go (something difficult to pull out without proper knowledge of bump-mapping), and runs silky 60-frames smooth even on an old machine like mine, marred by a GTX 760 and i7 2600k. This cannot be understated: the game never failed to impress me as far as visual prowess is concerned.
As far as a game involved in the Aliens storyline is concerned, this game is actually very accessible and I had no trouble getting into it, even though I've never watched a movie in the franchise. It explains itself well enough and requires nearly no background information to be enjoyed. It arguably overstays its welcome, being actually quite a sizable game, with a fair bit of backtracking. It felt like it could've easily had about two to four hours less content and it would still justify its price tag, but I shan't argue for games with less content in them.
This game is fantastic in every way, except for its horror part. I would completely recommend a purchase, but unfortunately, the Alien simply drags the experience through the mud. Not even on Novice is it fun to engage with such a brutal, unforgiving mechanic, and if you're playing on Hard, I really do feel for you.

It's hard to really figure out just where to start with a serious review of this game.
I suppose I'll start negatively:
Whatever you do, don't play the first game, and then this one, back to back if you expect a familiar experience. Yes, the feel and the atmosphere of the games, as well as the story, all feel similar and not overly different, but a lot of mechanics have been changed and swapped around. Some for the better, but some for worse too.
The gameplay is a lot heavier this time around, and a whole lot of things aren't as they used to be. Your character is nowhere near as nimble right off the bat, as rolling and moving - even fighting and using items, are all determined by stat values. Effectively this means that to a new player, you can expect your first playthrough to be much harder than an NG+ run, if only because it's very different.
Would I suggest playing this game before Dark Souls 1, or without having any intention to play it at all? Well, no. Not if you have any interest in storytelling - This games story doesn't make an awful lot of sense to begin with, and without knowing the first game, many of the 'Aww yeah!' moments won't take effect and the game might feel far more stale.
The postive things?
All in all this game is a beautiful visiual experience, and while arguably being more 'accesible' to newcomers of the series, and generally less demanding of the player, it's still a nice and challenging game that takes a step back from many of the overused mainstream-gaming tropes that we see these days.
It doesn't come with a difficulty setting, bu the game offers enough variety and optional content to give 'hardcore' gamers a run for their money while still easing new souls-players into the game without being as 'unfair' as the first game might have seemed to many.
The game is less punishing, which might sound like a bad thing at first, but actually, being less punishing makes it far more punishing. Dark Souls 2 has a strange way of easing you into this state of confidence where you'll make a casual blunder that ends up costing you dearly - And the magic of the Souls-series takes effect: It was your own fault.
All in all, expect hours of fun and frustration, a lot of epic moments, a lot of shouting at your monitor, and every now and then, a cheap and undeserved death because of poor or lazy game design.

Alright, to start, i love games that focus on the ecosystem, love them, but i give a negative review on this game, with so little time actually playing, is because its sloppy. heres my list in no particular order
1. flying bugs stay where they are, dont fly around, dont land on things, just magically pollinate everything from their stationary position
2. ground bugs dont leave their nest, just simply move around it a circle, kinda magically floating around it as a flat image, they also magically eat waste from there stationary positions
3. bugs neither breed nor eat or be eaten (from what i can tell) you can have an entire population of decomposers that never die out
4. plants cant overpopulate, the point of an ecosystem is that even plants can wipe out other plant species and are all competing for water and sunlight, which brings me up to my next issue
5. water isnt a resource, nothing requires water, main example is the desert biome in the first open spot, there is no readily available water, all the animals should be dying of dehydration
6. animals dont have nests, burrows, homes, nothing has shelter, why dont the rabbits have burrows? everything just kinda wanders around there ittybitty territory, munching on whatever and sleeping wherever, its nonsensicle, my rabbits are just being eaten while they sleep
7. animals are dumb, you have a preditor walking around, you dont walk up to it and say hey
8. the "territories" concept, this is a good mechanic, but it doesnt do realisism justice, animals territories are constantly shifting, a hunter moves into an area, prey moves elsewhere, hunters run out food, they look elsewhere
9. fungus grows randomly, but mostly directly where you placed them they'll clump up, they'll kinda grow around dead things, but not much
10. lastly, its just overly simple, everything is simplified, and i feel they simply couldve done more with it
overal, its very lacking, and really i wouldnt complain so much about this stuff if this games main focus wasnt on a realist ecosystem, if we are supposed to be controling the dome, we should be controling things like wind, tempeture, water, sun exposure, maybe geomorphing the land to form it into whatever kind of ecosystem we are aiming for, and then have it so we are simply releasing seeds into the wind or even directly planting them, and then watch the plants grow and spread overtime, releasing animals into it, watch them find safe places to burrow or build a nest, watch them migrate around the dome looking for food and avoiding preditors, watch them over eat the plants, or watch the plants dry out the water or over populate, trees blocking the sun of smaller plant life that grew under them and dying off, fungus dying off because they have nothing to feed off of, watch preditors compete for territory, watch wolves hunt in packs, and cougars hunt solo, the ecosystem is so much more complex then what we have here, the game needs concepts like cover, water requirements, nests, sun exposure, make the animals more dynamic instead of eating sleeping and dying

It's alright, really.
Maybe not worth full price, but pretty alright. The main issue with Dishonored 2 is that it exists because Dishonored 1 sold well, so they made a new story to go with the new game. It doesn't exist because they already had more story that they wanted to build a game around.
A second issue is that there's such an incredibly minor difference between playing Emily or Corvo that you're unlikely to ever really notice it(especially in New Game + where they both have access to each others' powers), and that the difference between high and low chaos is far less tangible than in Dishonored 1.
In fact, the real complaints here aren't that Dishonored 2 is an outright bad game, just that it's not quite as good as the first. Less interesting scenarios, less interesting level design, less dramatic final mission, no actual interesting reveals for the story(it's all as it seems from the get-go, while Dishonored 1 had an actual surprise or two), less pay-off for choices made(several options for mission resolutions have all of one line of easily missed dialogue, and in one case it's the more involved and complicated method of resolution which has no payoff, weirdly enough. Not sure if it smells of lacking ideas or lacking time...).
I wouldn't mind more games in the Dishonored setting, but I feel like it'd benefit if they took a step away from the stealth game schtick for the next installment or two, just until they had enough good ideas to make it worth another shot. Maybe an RPG or some sort of turn-based squad tactics, I can see the world having the space for either.
All in all, it's really not going to blow your mind, but if you liked the first game a lot, this probably won't be a waste of your time and money.
PS: Why even have water-specific abilities when the game has so little actual water? Feels like a leftover from the first game which had somewhat more aquatic navigation options.

This game on it's surface is everything we've wanted in an overhauled Rome. Appropriate culture names with their own unique troops and cultural nuances that had to be mastered in order to defeat your neighbors. A more realistic rise to power path in which regional rivals had to be defeated and an empire formed before you were truly ready for conquest on a global scale. At it's campaign map level this game seemed like the apex of the Total War series. A much more steady AI who actually engaged in diplomacy (as much as a game solely about war should allow). Economic and cultural decisions and technology. A long with a new provincial development system that allowed for major and minor settlements to be developed instead of mega cities. Giving your civilization a more spread out and realistic feeling. Agents work well and are pretty useful though not over powered. Armies have more options to how they move and what they can do.
However, once you get into the battle map the game completely goes to hell. Every culture has it's strengths on the battlefield. The AI should be programmed to those strengths. It isn't. Skirmish Calvary has to be micro-managed. Heavy Infantry lacks sustainability and missile troops seem to pelt one and other with marshmallows and feathers. On top of that not a single culture who apparently all want mega empires are actually willing to fight for it. The moment that Brutus takes an arrow to the face everyone one else panics and runs. Heavy infantry, pike and phalanxes which should be able to stand there and fight even as they take causalities, quiet frankly don't. Along with the cowardly lion AI it's all apparently completely un-drilled. It is near impossible to adjust battle lines as moving unit blocks doesn't move to the position or formation you want them too with out extreme micro-managing, and by moving they expose themselves to attack which they will promptly run away from. Also because in addition to all of this already whacked out shenanigans the AI army flat out sprints at you. So if you do by accident position a unit out of place you won't have the time to reposition it before the enemy army marches the mile gap between the forces in 30 seconds. In short battles are resolved in 5 minutes and are messier then running mascara on emotionally distraught individual. While battles are a messy affair they are also well planned before the messy up close phase. The new battle AI doesn't give you the opportunity to do that. It simply rushes at you and piles in. Two minutes later after frantic clicking both armies are running away from each other and the one who runs away less wins.
TL;DR: The Battle AI is a disaster.
If Rome was built by legions with motto's like First to Advance, Last to Retreat that legion certainly isn't modeled in the game.

Having played TW:M, TW:M2, TW:E, and TW:S2, I would say the TW:R2 is a very good game from many angles, but still not my favourite.
The game has the best graphics yet, and the new maps are excellent.  There are changes aimed at making it a deeper experience - introducing political parties for example.  There are new agents, that wield new powers.  Overall it is a very good game.
Some of the annoyances come from playing other titles in the series and perhaps having hard time adapting to changes.  I think the agents are too powerful and I tend to spend more time managing them than my armies.  The number of armies themselves is limited, and it is not possible to recruit garrisons.  Buildings and improvements come with negative effects which makes the management a bit more challenging.  These are some of the changes in the game, which often leave me frustrated, but I must admit they add to the complexity.  It is no longer to simply spawn huge armies and march across the map.
I recommend this title to all fans of the series.  In wost case there are plenty of mods to fine tune your gameplay.

After 200+ hours of gameplay i think i can write an honest review.
As far as class goes, they are all fun with the right build. Some more than others.
After messing with my own builds i searched for info on more precise builds and with a few tweaks of my own i found the game far more entertaining.
Starting out can seem a little tedious, but if you persist and take the time to process the mass amounts of information thrown at you then you will enjoy the game.
Between quests, lore, skills, gear, pvp, guilds, dlc etc..... there is an enormous game just waiting to be explored.
Once you get the basics and start to level up to the point of completing the campaign, you get the option to complete the quests from the other factions.
Then you have the dlc's. I must admit that i have not spent much time doing dlc stuff or even pvp but that's how big this game is.
At this time i don't even have a guild. Playing solo has actually been quite enjoyable. Guilds are the way to go but if you enjoy solo play it is very possible and as fun as you want it to be.
Personally i don't have as much time to play ESO as i would like and some of the guilds enforce fee's so i just haven't bothered with them yet.
Quests and exploration blend together and before you know it you have cleared a complete map area.
With the help of a few Addons for Skyshards etc... you can explore at you leisure, and gather ingredients, wood etc.. so that when you hit your next town you can bank what you wanna keep and top up with potions, learn new traits etc...
There is just so much to keep you occupied in ESO.
Graphically, ESO is beautiful. The maps are well designed and clutter is almost minimal in parts, but with a decent PC and good internet connection you could find yourself staring at the horizon for a moment before setting off on another adventure.
Yes, some of the quests are not exactly exciting and there are a few very small issues, but ESO is an awesome way to pass the time. Solo or otherwise.
This is a game everyone should have in their library. :)

I have very much loved the souls series since I started with Demons Souls. Dark Souls 2 doesn't entirely dissapoint, but it does have some problems.
-First I will say all that I found good.
The PC port was much better than in Dark Souls 1. I didn't think that 1s was too bad, so I whent back to play it today, and it was tough to get back into it for me.
It overall looks better, in my opinion. It's much less dreary, even though that was kind of a plus for the first one.
The gameplay is much smoother, since the framerate stays near 60 instead of 30. This makes gameplay much more pleasurable.
I found I liked the new healing system better than in 1s, I feel like it fits better.
All of the fresh new things like new places and weapons/armor are a nice new experience to play through.
-Now I'll say some of the things I didn't like...
The world doesn't feel as connected as it was in dark souls one, and there arent really many, if any, open areas. Most areas are fairly small, fairly linear, and fairly enclosed. There are still plenty of branching paths, but overall I wouldve appreciated a more connected feel.

-All in all, I still really like this game. I like what From has done for the most part, and I realise it must of been hard to capture the magic that the first game had. It is still a very enjoyable game, it just might get old after finishing it once or twice, but I hope the dlc will be good, even though it will cost money when I don't have much. Before recently acquiring this title as part of the developer's across-the-board sale, I have never played it, in fact, I had never heard of it. So, my review is not coloured by nostalgia or sentimentality of any kind.
SS2 is a pioneer design that combines the rudiments of FPS gameplay with RPG mechanics. The game has a wide array of groundbreaking features, and you can clearly see that this franchise was a heavy influence on the BioShock series, made years later. The storyline is solid, and introduced seamlessly into the game, without the use of cutscenes or other clumsy forms of exposition. The voice acting is excellent, the atmosphere and AI sound effects are just right, and the user interface is smooth. The enhanced graphics make this game appealing to the modern audience and effectively overcome the technological barriers to enjoyment.
The fact that the original release of this game was so vastly overshadowed by the competing Quake 2 speaks to the sad reality of the lowest common denominator, and shows that many gems are not appreciated in their time.
The story incorporates a lot of fascinating science fiction elements, with a little twist of cyberpunk for the ladies. Psionic abilities, cyberware hacking, puzzles, and even basic alchemy add a variety not seen in many titles from this era.
The RPG character development mechanics grant this title a good amount of replayability. You can hone abilities that best suit your style of play, and the rewards you will receive are highly satisfying. You will need to be every bit as strategic in how you advance your character as you are in every other aspect of the gameplay, as whatever improvements you make will quickly be matched pound for pound.
Not only the tools you are given, but the ability to use and maintain those tools, are essential to the outcome. Each character class has strengths and weaknesses that drastically alter the strategy of the game. No matter which class you choose, you will often find that the abilities you don't have are the ones you need the most.
When you finish this adventure (if you make it) you will feel like you have really achieved something. Nothing in this game is given without being earned, and you need to develop skills to match the challenges, even if you are playing in wuss mode. To succeed in this game, you need to utilize all of the skills and resources available to you. You need to exercise situational awareness, tactical and management skills, and pay attention to seemingly insignificant details.
This is a excellent Steam version of an absolute classic that plays like a top. Highly recommended to anyone.

System Shock 2 is gaming history. Being the spiritual predecessor to Deus Ex, it already featured an astonishingly deep RPG/FPS experience regarding gameplay mechanics, full voice acting with lots and lots and lots of audio logs and one of the best horror atmospheres I've seen in the last 20 years.
System Shock 2 doesn't look pretty anymore and it plays quite unwieldy from today's perspective. The story, gameplay itself and especially the superb atmosphere are more than worth revisiting it though. Actually, even someone who never played it back in the day will most likely get quite a lot of enjoyment out of it by installing some mods to overhaul the visuals. Personally I used the mod-pack floating around within the Steam discussions here and it worked like a charm.
If you are one of those people that enjoyed any of the Deus Ex games or Bioshock  1/2, System Shock is how it all began. To this day, it is and will remain one of my favourite games of all time and it felt actually quite awesome to revisit it so many years after I last played it.
Even although it's old, it was updated by Nightdive in a way that it supports resolutions up and beyond 4k flawlessley as well.

Total Annihilation is one of the true classics of the RTS genre, and IMHO, a must-own for any strategy fan. While parts of it can feel dated today, the basic mechanics, gameplay, and the epic score still hold their own nearly 20 years later. I first bought this game barely a month after release, back in the beforetime of 1997, and it's been perpetually on my favorite games of all time list since then. At a time when Starcraft was dominating the RTS market, Total Annihilation was providing an alternative to the small scale clickfest style of gameplay that Starcraft ushered in, offering large maps, epic battles, physics-based combat, and some truly memorable moments. Why throw a dozen marines at something when you can command a hundred-plus giant robots and tanks to obliterate everything in their path?
The game definitely had and still has its faults - players unfamiliar with the game are going to be confused by the relative sameness of some of the units, and the sheer numbers of them available to build. It also featured an active use economy; the first of its kind that I'm aware of - I personally love it, but it does entail quite a learning curve from the classic Dune II/Age of Empires "spend it when you build it" model. Some of the larger maps are also not for the faint of heart - while eventually outdone by Supreme Commander, the larger TA maps can take literally hours of multiplayer slug-matches to end a game, particularly once you bump up the unit count to something a modern computer can sink its teeth into.
In the end though, it's said that an amateur thinks in terms of strategy, while a professional thinks in terms of logistics - and that's absolutely the case here, where you can spend yourself into inaction, or use the shattered remains of your opponents' armies to fuel your own war machine.

This game deserves much more recognition. Emphasis and the MUCH.
GREAT character development, wide variety of monsters and monster art, GREAT artwork, AWESOME storyline, AMAZING soundtrack, and a simple yet VERY CLEAN combat and upragding/crafting system. The game flows well enough to the point where you're actually trying to find flaws with it as someone would a $60 game. The only couple falws I'd complain about are the run-into-enemy combat, and mini bosses (that drop upgrade shards). Running into the enemy is a great idea for a simple pixel-game but debris/destrucible objects should be included. There were times I didn't know when to simply run into something, or smash the spacebar. Mini bosses should also be mobile within their area, and given an attack pattern. Same as their smaller versions would be fine but going the extra mile to give them a totally different arsenal would be the cherry on top. You could kill it by simply using skills, and waiting for your mana to refresh without taking damage. THE FOLLOWING PARAGRAPH IS MY EMOTIONAL ATTACHMENT TOWARDS THIS GAME AND NOT EXACTLY PART OF THE REVIEW FOR THIS GAME.
I say all this in retrospect to the fact that THIS GAME IS FREE. Not the buggy/glitchy, hardly-any-content kind of free game, but the kind of free game that makes you want to personally thank the developer(s) for pouring their heart and soul into such a masterpiece and sharing it with the rest of us. All this becomes apparent as you delve into the game with the developer(s) as you explore the bonus area they leave behind for players that finish the game. It's obvious that a lot of passion went into this game and that the developer(s) loves what they do. It's games like these that rekindle my love for gaming and drive my appreciation for it. Games like LoL, R6S, and even GW2 have become my go-to games that have left me feeling stressed, and empty afterwards. It's games like these that adhere to the very aspect of gaming; filling their players with joy, tension, sadness, guilt, sympathy, curiosity, and a sense of purpose.

I recently got this game from a buddy of mine, a little over a week and a half or so ago. Ever since he introduced me to this amazing game, I've dumped nearly 130 hours into it!
I love Dark Souls II. It is absolutely fabulous! The character creativity seems like it could never end! Every time I start up a new game, I think of how I want this new character to be played. Perhaps, this time I'll use a character that uses a bow and daggers, or maybe I'll be proud knight with heavy armor wielding sword-and-shield. I even have the option of going berzerk with two ultra greatswords and just smashing things (which is fun as hell)! There's even different types of magic that a player can use to melt down their enemies!
The world seems like it almost never ends! On my first playthrough, everytime I came across a new area, my mind was blown! Some of the areas in the game look absolutely stunning! The Gutter is one of my favorite places, but oh man does that place annoy me. The Gutter is a dark underground place that feels slightly enchanting, but you know there is danger everywhere. It is a really short area and you have to either take your time to push through it, or just sprint past everything and risk dying on several occasions! Another area in the game that looks beautiful, is The Shrine of Amana. I HATE that place. The wizard guys have infinite range on their homing missiles and there's always at least two or three of those guys firing at you constantly! If you step in the wrong spot, you'll get jumped by some nasty hairless thing that makes dodging the missiles much more dreadful. Even though the area tore me to shreds, this was the place in the game where I just said "this place looks amazing"!
There's not much for me to dislike about this game. I've replayed it multiple times already, and I'm sure I can keep going for awhile. It's so addicting and hard for me to turn away from. I mainly dislike soul memory. It just doesn't seem very effective as a way to play against people, or play with friends. A different system that is easier to use seems in order.
I also slightly dislike the areas in the distance. Go look past the ocean in Majula. Way out there looks terrible doesn't it? Yeah I wish that seemed more realistic, and less like a static painting hanging on the games wall.
Overall I'd give this game a solid 9/10! It's very addicting, gives a nice challenge, and has plenty of things in the game to discover!

Dark Souls 2 sticks to the old formula of Demon's Souls and Dark Souls. That is a good thing because this formula has the perfect balance of skill. The deaths in this game teaches you how to play the game. Every mistake you make can cost you your souls.
I've played Demon's Souls and Dark Souls a lot and Dark Souls 2, did feel a little easy for me seeing as though I've already learnt most of my mistakes with this gameplay formula from past souls games.
The story is based on a dark fantasy gameworld like all souls games and is very easy to ignore but still proves to have an in depth story and narrative that supports the players actions.
Apart from the dark story the gameplay is where it's at. The gameplay of Dark Souls 2 is an amazing balance of skill and I highly recommend it. I also love the online features in Dark Souls 2 which has saved me a couple of times. Helping people defeat bosses has always been my way of restoring my humanity and max health and coop is a bonus. I do like to challenge myself and use the optional Bonfire Ascetic to make enemies in levels harder and I am very impressed it does not just make enemies harder. I was in an abandoned encampment with undead pigs, the small kind and as soon as I burned the Bonfire Ascetic into the bonfire to increase difficulty I was attacked by huge monster boars and red phantoms.
Customisation is my favourite, I'd spend a lot of time seeing which clothing and armour would suit me in combat without slowing me down and look aethetically good. So many weapons to go with but in the end my main weapon was the Claymore and Drangleic Sword, with the Havel's Greatshield.
The map works just like Dark Souls. It is amazing to figure out the various paths you can take and where each paths leads. The maps is one of the best parts of Dark Souls 2. Also a very good thing is that there is fast travel between any bonfire right at the start of the game.
It took me 60 hours to complete my first playthrough and I still have a lot of things to do.
I highly recommend this game.

Black Mesa is probably one of THE BEST Source games I've ever played, the graphics are on par with any current-gen game on the market, the story is Half-Life with some extra details to better fit it into the world, the soundtrack (available on ITunes) mixes HL with HL2 along with the composer's personal touch to create a unique audio experience, and the Black Research Facility has been made a believable and nearly inhabitable location. This game is superior in every way to the highly unstable and buggy Half-Life Source. It may not be a complete game, and bugs still remain, but with the Xen update coming soon, and even without it, it has a lot of potential and is definitely worth a buy.

Black Mesa is obviously a recreation of the revolutionary first person shooter Half-Life, recreated on the Source engine, with massively improved graphics, gameplay changes and ect, although it sticks to the original story.
Black Mesa has a massively improved appearance from Half-Life, as well as a completely new soundtrack, not originally playing Half-Life I can't make comparisons to the original gameplay, however this is a well made mod, considerable as a triple-A title.
Fortunately for Black Mesa, I can't see many downsides, however there are a few.
One of my biggest ones is the Grenade throwing, it's realistic, as in the grenade originates from Gordon's right hand (or maybe left with flipped viewmodels), and shares CS:GO's short or long throw mechanics, but in corners this can prove to be tricky.
Another issue is some parts CAN BE very difficult.
My only other issue with it is it is missing Xen... However that will be a free update, and shouldn't be too long now, so it might be worth your time to wait.
Black Mesa seems like something VALVe would make, level design is slightly off point, but otherwise it's fantastic and definitely worth your money, especially considering it's cheaper than many other games.

Ahh system shock 2... Heard lots of good things about this game and having played bioshock and loving it to pieces, I decided to give this game a try. Starting the game, I didn't have a very good first impression of it. The mechanics felt dated (i.e. navigating through inventory, ability, audio log, etc. slots felt clunky) and I was overwhelmed by the number of things I can do in varying my playstyle, I'll talk abt this in more detail afterwards. However, after having played it a few hours, I was blown away by the atmosphere and the creepiness started sinking in. Once I got more familiar with the game mechanics, it started to become really fun and I got really invested in the game. I think some ppl who hvnt played a lot of old-school PC games would feel the same way I did and I am glad that I gave the game a chance to prove my prior judgments wrong.  OK then, enough dillydallying on the surface, I'd like to talk abt the game in more detail.
So, to start off, I'd like to address gameplay which is the key element of this game. If you've played bioshock, you'd probably b familiar with the term "adam", the equivalent of "adam" in this game are "cyber modules". These cyber modules allow the player to invest on certain skill sets, psychic abilities, weapon upgrades, etc. which help give variety to your playstyle. I made the mistake of not investing on my psychic abilities which many have deemed to be the more satisfying route but  still got a lot of enjoyment out of prioritizing weapon upgrades. The thing is, halfway through the game, I thought that I would invest in psychic abilities (aka PSI powers) later on in the game and there's this particular piece of equipment (called a "PSI amp") that is required  for PSI power usage. So, I decided to drop the PSI amp in order to economize on inventory slots  so that I could carry more weapons, thinking that i would find another PSI amp later on in the game. I ended up not finding another PSI amp and wasted my inventory slots on too many weapons.
Now, this brings me to another aspect of the game. The reason why I was economizing on inventory slots was because I was keeping weapons which were not yet equippable due to factors like being made from an unknown specimen or not having enough weapon skill points to use the weapon. This brings me to yet another feature of this game, the "technical skills" aspect. These skills include hacking, maintenance, research, repair, etc. Now, when we encounter an unknown specimen, we are required to do "research" on it  before being able to make use of it. Usage ranges from being able to use it as a weapon to inflicting more damage on an enemy from where the specimen stemmed from. Not only does doing research sometimes require a certain research level (upgraded by using cyber modules) but, it also requires the use of certain chemicals to aid in this research process. There are multiple storage rooms which store a various array of these chemicals and u'd need 1 or 2 of a particular chemical to proceed with the research. However, some storage rooms might not have the particular chemical you are looking for and sometimes you may end up having to backtrack just to look for that one chemical that you left in a storage room that u found hours ago.
Although some may deem the above mentioned example a drawback, I actually think this is a great example of how much ur gameplay can deviate just from prioritizing on doing research on weapons. It shows that u really hv to choose wisely on how u wanna spend ur cyber modules and on how u wanna go about playing the game. Another interesting aspect of the game is how ur weapons can deteriorate and get broken after several uses. This is where the maintenance and repair skills come in. In order to prevent a weapon from breaking, you'll have to use a disposable maintenance tool which also requires a certain maintenance skill level to use. But upon breaking it, you can also try repairing it either by using ur repair skill(which consumes ur nanites; nanites is the currency in this game and can be used to revive and/ or heal urself, purchase healing items & ammo, etc.) or by using an auto-repair unit. I am only scratching the surface and already you can see how cohesive and broad the rpg elements are and how they build up to create such an amazing system. There's more to talk about regarding gameplay but I'll leave everything else a surprise for anticipating players.
Another thing to mention is the atmosphere. I recently played resident evil hd remastered and tho I did enjoy d experience, I didn't feel a sense of dread and fear while playing it. I'd have to say otherwise for this game which is pretty amazing considering the fact that the graphics are pretty dated and yet I still got spooked by those polygonal creaturesXD The sound effects added with the cryptic lines aimed at the player sent chills down my spine and since the game doesn't pause when u'r looking through your inventory, ability, audio log, etc. slots, it gets nerve-wrecking when u'r trying to just listen to your audio logs or arrange your items from fear of being attacked while you're caught off-guard.
So, do I recommend that you go buy this game?? Definitely! Depending on ur luck, u might not enjoy ur first playthrough of this game but once u've gotten familiar with the gameplay elements, im sure u'll have a blast playing it! After hearing what ppl had to say about the game getting better and better after each playthrough, I will definitely go play this again sometime in the near future!

I finally got around to finishing it. It's easily become one of my favorite games of all time. System Shock 2 holds it's atmosphere brilliantly high with some of the best sound design I've ever heard in gaming period. The lighting and claustrophobic design of the ship sells it as well. The graphics, while being dated, don't honestly negate the atmosphere much for me. If anything, it's kind of enhanced because of the lighting itself and the sound. It makes the low poly models of the enemies more surreal and threatening, strangely enough. Old as this is, the challenge that comes along with the classic tropes of survival horror, ala, inventory management, spending ammo on your targets wisely meshes well here. This is one of the few games that actually managed to frighten me pretty much all the way through, on the story, atmosphere, and gameplay, since it weaves together incredibly well. It's also really replayable! It's much more open in it's gameplay choices than in Bioshock, and I'd even say that I enjoy the story here, and the cyberpunk aesthetic even more, and yet that game was a home run. This.. is a grand slam.
Let me just say this though - if you're going into this game blind, have patience. It's not as cryptic as some old games are, it has all the tools you need to get through it without a walkthrough, just let yourself sink into the atmosphere of it and you'll have a great time. It's not for everyone. BE SURE TO PUT POINTS INTO HACKING THOUGH!
Now, get ready, soldier, wake up on the Von Braun and the Rickenbacker, something has gone terribly wrong.. ..someone will guide you though.

Played it first in 2017, it holds up. Give it a couple of hours and you'll find yourself hooked.
This game flawlessy combines FPS action, RPG elements, horror and unique story telling in a way that I haven't really seen in a game before (excluding Bioshock). Even compared to Bioshock, I like this better, mostly because of the amazing atmosphere - the ship you're exploring and slowly finding the story of (by listening to audiologs) feels absolutely desolate and abandoned. I think the ambient sound effects contribute the most to this, followed by the fantastic level and art design.
The gameplay is satisfying and even by the end of the game you'll find yourself challenged by the enemies (though I feel this can change depending on which way you spec your character). It can be hard at first to decide where to spend your points in / what upgrades to get but I feel the game encourages experimentation. I myself have played a Navy character specializing in standard weapons and hacking. There's also the possibility of going the PSI route ('magic' powers) or Marine (heavy weapons).
Story-wise there's not much to say - you will find everything through audiologs scattered throughout levels. I love games that are not hand-holdy Hollywood park rides and that require the player to put all the pieces togheter. The story in this game is one of the main reasons it kept me going forward. It goes without saying that the antagonist is very well written and, compared to other video game big bad guys, actually scary.
There are a couple of things I wish were done better - in some missions I did feel a bit lost, not knowing where to go. A better map would have helped. The weapons degradation is also a bit extreme.
All in all, a great game that I'm glad I got to finally play. Can't wait for the System Shock remake and SS3.

What a game!
God knows how much CRT radiation I soaked up while glued to this game back at the turn of the century.
Total Annihilation has finally made the jump to Steam, so I'm back for more play. I'm still damn impressed that this game from '97 supported widescreen (16:9) aspect ratios straight out of the box (Quite literally so, I remember first buying this game when it came in a cardboard box).
Things that I remember impressed me about Total Annihilation back in 1999:-
• 3D units
• You could start forest fires
• The ability to mine rocks for metal and harvest trees for surplus energy
• The messy aftermath of significant battles (big battles left a big mess, metal wreckage of hundreds of destroyed units would litter large portions of the map)
• You could often recycle the metal from the wreckage of destroyed units
The explosions in-game are also awesome, and will gratify most action junkies. When your units get destroyed, the explosions are screen-shaking, audibly thunderous, polygonal chunks of shrapnel debris hurtle through the air all over the place.
When your commander unit is destroyed, it triggers an enormous nuclear explosion that causes significant 'splash damage', therefore when you sense an inevitable defeat you have an opportunity to rage quit in a kamikaze-esque enemy-destroying nuclear blaze of glory.
If you like RTS games, science fiction and playing with nuclear weapons, you should check this game out.

It starts very solid due to good level design, but in the middle interactive narrative is so non-generic the alien, that it turns into comics-level crossover "rocketeer and Raiden versus aliens". Thankfully final chapters go back to generic aesthetics so it returns to normal state. A fun, bright, colourful, and extremely cute take on the ranching genre of games with just a liiittle twist of first-person survival and crafting peppered in.
Here's the premise - you wake up on a far away and mostly deserted planet, not because your spaceship was shot down by a myserious threat or anything dire; you're here by choice because you wanted to ranch slimes. This planet is full of happy little slime critters that have, for lack of a better description, very valuable poo, and you're here to make use of them. You'll spend most of the gameplay exploring the world, capturing rare and unique slimes, gathering new foods for them, and trying to make your little slice of the planet into the neatest little slime farm in the quadrent, with little asides as the protagonist gets sentamental letters from home and reads up on her new discoveries. It's not completely without danger, but Slime Rancher is overall a very peaceful, quirky, fun romp that will leave you smiling from ear to ear.
I highly recommend Slime Rancher to anyone who enjoys the ranching genre (like Stardew Valley or Harvest Moon games) as well as folks looking for a more serene survival-ish game with less emphasis on building and folks who just want something a little peaceful and fun in general.

Dark Souls 2 is an amazing game that is significantly improved over its predecessor. Graphical performance is no longer hindered by a default 30 frames per-second that 2011's Dark Souls suffered both on consoles and PC.
However what lacks in Dark Souls 2 is the inner-connectivity between its various regions that the original Dark Souls did a great job with. Bonfires which serve as the game's waypoints are more numerous and closer to each other which makes Dark Souls 2 more forgiving than it was in the original. This may disappoint some fans of the series.
There is a heavier focus on Covenants in Dark Souls 2 which is the series' version of playable factions. Any covenant can be joined at any one time which a player can level up in to unlock stronger spells and unique weapons by fulfilling specific requirements for each covenant. Each covenant in Dark Souls 2 serves a different style of player archetypes that is either focused on PvE, PvP and player co-op.
New Game Plus mode returns in Dark Souls 2. After completing the story players have the option of replaying the game keeping most of their gear but substancially raising the difficulty of enemies; adding new mobs and attack patterns.
Dark Souls 2 story takes place centuries after the first Dark Souls game. NPC monologue is fantastically well written but the overall story is largely unchanged. The player assumes the role of an undead and like many of Dark Souls 2's inhabitants you're cursed and tasked with the mission of finding a cure.
Along the player's journey across Drangleic he or she will come in contact with various NPCs which each have their own unique set of dialogue that gives the player more information about Drangleic's backstory and what may have happened during the time between the original Dark Souls and Dark Souls 2.
You should try Dark Souls 2. Really impressive graphics and pretty tough to play but enjoyable

Believe it or not, this is my first Half-Life game (Just got into PC gaming). This game below me away and made me fell in love with the Half-Life series.
What I liked:
I love how the game starts from survival horror to an action first person shooter once the marines arrives. The music is fantastic! (one of the best soundtracks in gaming history) It's starts off creepy but gets more hype and action packed later on (my favorite being surface tension 4).
This game is difficult! This isn't one of those "handholding" modern games. No, you have to use your brain to solve puzzles and know what weapon is best for certain enemies. The marine AI is brutal, some will chase you down while others will flank you (mark my words, you're gonna die a lot for your first time).
I loved how the crow bar fromed, the speed of the crowbar is so fast that it will prevent enemies from meleeing back. This makes the crowbar a very useful weapon. (It doesn't work for bull squids, zombies, houndeye, barnacle, and possibly the alien controller unfortunately)
What I Dislike:
I dislike how the game wasn't finished. You only get the Black Mesa levels but not Xen, but the developers are planning on releasing Xen this summer.
I dislike how the health system worked, I wish the suit energy would regenerate itself instead of having to find suit power. This makes you focus on two heal percentage instead of one.
The Verdict: I love this game to death! It's my favorite steam game and one of my top 5 favorite games of all time! I would highly recommend it to FPS fans or single player fans.

and tend to be in groups, while some may decide to stray off from the rest and flank from another route. Because of this, and how you can even pair up with them in a few select vehicles, allows for many interesting battles and games. One simple move by joining your fellow soldier in an attack helicopter can open up an objective for the rest of your team to take, which can help you begin securing the rest of the map.
I'm impressed especially at how even your own teammates as well as the opposing team will have different weapon choices. One of my favorite moments of this is when I joined a crew of soldiers inside of a jeep, and as we got out at an objective, I was equipped with a scoped rifle
, and my other teammates either had regular rifles, or had something for suppressing fire and or to take out vehicles. It just makes the battles really interesting since they'll change every time.
Before you start up a map, you are given the option of a team to join, whether you want it to be day or night time, if you want vehicles or not, reverse mode (not sure what that does), and a slider to decide how you want the teams balanced (more or less soldiers on a team). There are also 2-3 gamemodes, however I haven't really tested them out besides the normal one, in which you try to take all of the capture points. Pros:

Neutral:
-no save everywhere,you're tied to save stations

Cons:
-a few cheap deaths,sometimes it comes down to blind luck
-a few textures are not as nice as the rest
-human opponents are more often just annoying rather than a challenge

Overall Alien Isolation is an amazing game when you consider it for what it is,that is a frightening experience that throws you against an alien and an hostile space station with little means to actually fight back.
The tension while you are chased by the alien or other hostiles,the frantic scrambling to try and find an hiding place while trying to understand where your enemy lies,trying to manage your ammo/item counts...all into an universe recreated to firmly follow what we saw in the '79 movie.
Sure it's not a game for everyone,its not action oriented,its pacing can get lost at times,sometimes it might be frustrating...but it's basically the best Alien game to date and one of the few I genuinely found unnerving,I fully recommend it.

I have to say, Eternal Senia was a pleasant little game. For a free Action RPG, it's not bad! The music is very good, the controls are smooth, and it didn't overstay its welcome!
However, free or not, it does still have a few flaws I feel should be addressed. The English translation was pretty iffy. There were multiple times where it seemed like a literal translation of the original script, which led to plenty of typos and awkward wording. It never made it hard to understand the general idea of what was being said, but it still could've been better. I also noticed that a majority of the enemies could be dealt with by simply holding a direction and waiting for the battle to end. It made combat pretty dull outside of boss fights and the few instances where enemies actually attacked you.
Possibly the worst offenders of this issue with the combat were the Elite enemies. These enemies require you to have all of your equipment at "Elite" status or higher to fight them, though there's really no need for this. They never attack you if you only use skills to damage them, so you can just whale on them with your skills, and wait for them to die with no repercussions. It was very odd that normal enemies could be considered a bigger threat than these supposedly challenging opponents.
Still, this game has the potential to be something great, and while merely having potential doesn't make a game good, it was still an enjoyable experience. Should a sequel be made, I do hope that it addresses these problems, and results in a better experience. I did enjoy my time with Eternal Senia, and in the event the developer is reading this, I wish you the best of luck in your future endeavors!
To everyone else, give it a shot! You've nothing to lose from a monetary perspective, and it might just surprise you!

this game is really fun to play but of course there is always space for improvements ut if you follow the discussion page on this game you can see that the developers are always taking in ideas and creating a better everything in game
Although this game is fun to play, your progress sure goes slowly when you start since you have to wait for more plants to grow, animals to reproduce, babies to mature, so it ends up in a lot of waiting. But after getting in to the game unlocking more animals,plants and areas the game really begins to move faster as you decorate and plan were things will go on your biome

So, you just place colonies of plants and animals and watch them prosper or die out, and get "XP" each month based on biodiversity. Pretty simplistic game. For the price, I do recommend it, but there's a lot of room for improvement. I would have preferred more/better features even if that would have changed the price. Just a short list of things that could have been better:
Graphics. They are OK. They could have been beautiful.
Sounds.
Energy system (planting something drains energy that slowly trickle back). It just adds waiting times. I don't see the point in it at all. Waiting/idling is not good in a game.
There are no layers for vegetation. So if you place grass, you can't place bushes or trees there.
Grass is not available in all biodomes (the ground is still green though).
Placing vegetation is sometimes tricky, could have been made a lot better to get thicker vegetation. I don't see the benefit in placing 6 tufts of grass in fixed location rather than sowing an area, specially since those 6 tufts share "HP".
Biodomes are a bit small even if you unlock more stages. But then again, the energy system makes it a chore to fill even one.
Controls are...well, they are OK, but could have been better. I mostly find myself getting an aerial view of things and staying there.
Filtering system, more than the basic plant/animal/detritus remover.
So again, at the price, yeah I recommend it. But I do wish for a better game.

I´m happy I bought & played Alien Isolation because this is truly a great survival horror game, not only something which manages to recreate Alien and stay authentic to the source material to an almost insane degree, that they even bothered with limiting themselves with props available during the late 70s for when modelling the environments, converting videos to VHS so that they could create the distortion effect and then converting it back, managing to convince the actors from Alien to come back and do some fan service in recording some audio for logs in the main missions and reimagining a few scenes from the original Alien for a few DLCs.
It has the ambience, the atmosphere, the mood, the music the tension, the quirks and even character flaws of the original Alien, with only very little character development which can be, if we are being generous, subtle at best.
For instance, Amanda Ripley is seen by some, like Yahtzee, to be a very forgetful character, mainly reacting to things happening. This is to a large part true, but this is true even of Ellen Ripley in the movie.
When I generously look at scenes from Alien Isolation, I can appreciate the subtle ways Amanda deals with some situations,
These are small examples of the different ways you are reminded of how Amanda is related to Ellen, and they can be appreciated, but it is understandable that some demand more character development, though I am happy that most people still behaved semi rationally or reasonably panicked on Sevastopol station, horror movies aren´t exactly known for their likeable cannon fodder you can relate to and think to yourself that you might have done the same thing in their situations - Alien being one of the rare exceptions, so again it recreates that sense of the people still trying their best and even having some good plans, but still failing infront of the unstoppable alien terror.
These are the ways I liked the plot, the creators obviously tried to hit many of the themes from the movie, with some spacewalks, some explorations which made sense in the plot but still was clearly put in because of how much the devs wanted to have as much from Alien as possible, and as an alien fan I did appreciate the game just taking the movie and expanding upon it.
Also liked that the Working Joes Androids were creepy cheap knock-offs from WY, but also that it had a good android almost like Bishop, breaking the familiar stereotype of all human technology being black-or-white evil to the core.
The weakest part is the ending. It is a cliffhanger with a QTE event. QTEs are practically nonexistent in the game. Now it is clear from all the passion put in, the attention to detail, the lovingly crafted atmopshere and effort behind the execution, that the devs in Creative Assembly are fans, and they wanted to set out to make the alien game they always felt the movies deserved, and they had the core ideas, the resources and they knew how to set up the game, but I get the sense that it didn´t occur to them that one day, their passion would come to an end, that they would need to wrap things up, it seems like they were so immersed in creating the game that when it came time to have the story arc discussed and get some of that closure, either they didn´t know how to address it, or they were reluctant to contemplate the prospect of closing it.
Enough about the story.
Gameplay is very reliant on the atmosphere, on multiple factors coming together, not one gimmick, though arguably if someone wanted to suggest the game having a gimmick it would be the AI, but I don´t think that argument works, since the AI also works alongside the other elements, the dynamic sound system, the lighting, and the vulnerability of the player versus the unstoppable alien, the ingredients create the scenes when they all come together.
I was unsure if I´d like a game where I cannot kill the alien, where I am vulnerable and need to rely on hiding and hoping the alien doesn´t see me, or else dying on the spot. But I do like it, it makes sense, the tension is fun and for the most part the encounters with the alien work with a logic; the alien has senses, it listens and looks around, and the player needs to be aware about their own noise levels and line-of-sight, this makes it easier to accept when you´ve been sloppy and the alien gets a scent of you and kills you, as you can look back and understand what went wrong, less arbitrary videogame logic and more grounded rules the system works with. And doing something right also felt more rewarding, I didn´t feel like I gained the system, or found any loopholes in the AI pathing system to exploit, but the reasoning and work inside the laws the game operates within payed off.
The game does have some bugs, I fortunately avoided many, but I did run into some afterimages of tools and weapons floating in midair, fixed by switching back-and-forth to them, and the Alien sometimes did get stuck in vents, though I "fixed" it by poking the alien, promptly dying for displaying my concern for the ungrateful git.
You have tools available, and they do serve some purpose, even at either distracting hostiles or killing them, though the alien you can at best fend off for a moment. Direct contact with hostiles is discouraged.
The Alien AI is something I´ve been fascinated by, it can be quite unpredictable at times, have freedoms of movement and choices in where to go and what to do, and the devs knew that to evoke the unknown terror of the Alien as seen in the original movie, it needed to have some degrees of unpredictability and emergent behaviour. So it hunts, stalks, or goes away, and shows up, sometimes at surprising moments.
and
Graphically the game looks gorgeous. It runs on my laptop, an intel core i7-4710HQ 2.5GHz, 12GB RAM, Nvidia GT840M 2GB Windows 8.1, with settings at a mosaic of ultra and off settings (motion blur, depth of field and chromatic aberration I can do without in games) on an acceptable resolution of 1280x720 at 60fps for 80~% of the time. Had no problems so feels like a good port (especially since it allowed me to tailor what options to enable). The lighting, the sound, the environments, all are made with such care for the source material, that you will feel like you are walking along sets of the original movie, heck, buy the Crew Expendable DLC and you do get to walk around the Nostromo.
The Alien is magnificent, its movements, behaviour, the way it looks, all worthy of such an iconic creature by H.R. Giger.
This is a game true to the movies, and true to one of the best of films in horror scifi.

If you ever looked outside, saw how nature did things and thought 'I could probably do better than that, nature. You suck at your job.', then this is the game for you :P
In all seriousness, though. I didn't regret buying it, even though I have a relatively firm grasp on how ecosystems work. It also lets you experiment with things you really, really shouldn't do in actual nature. Unleash hordes of rabbits on an unsuspecting grassland. Release the hounds (or something close enough) on your biome to spice things up, or to cut down on the aforementioned rabbits. Find out how long it takes 50 groups of rabbits to starve to death after they ate everything even remotely plant shaped. Or try to find just the right balance between plants, herbivores and carnivores to let nature take its course without everyone starving in the long run.
There is a tutorial for the basics, but the art of creating a biodome that essentially works on its own is something that requires a lot of learning, experimenting and, most likely, failure. You can have a lot of fun tinkering with your biome, or just flying over it and watch the various animals do their thing, or literally watch the grass grow. As for the pacing... this is not really a game you play full time - your biome will not really need you too often, unless things are solidly out of balance. I find there is more to do when a biome starts out, as I try to arrange all my plants to some degree. Once life is placed, it is out of your control. Plants will flower, fruit and reproduce on their own, animals will go and eat their way through the foilage or their fellow species... Leave it on while you do things that are not your homework, or check in between sessions of other games as the devs suggested. If you want to micromanage every aspect of your biome, you might be disappointed. However, if you have an interest in nature and enjoy seeing (or seeking) the small changes since you last visited your biome, then I really recommend buying.

I've sunk in enough hours into the game, and have experienced both aspects of PvE and PvP quite evenly. Is Elder Scrolls Online a perfect game? No, of course not, not in any sense of the word. But it is a game that shows promise and initiative that other MMORPG's are not providing, such as WoW or FF XIV. This game started as one of the WORST MMO's I have ever played, with damn near no content, and numerous bugs and glitches. Here we are, several years later. The game pulled itself out of the dirt and surpassed any and all expectations from it, so much that it holds nearly as many active players as WoW currently does, and growing.
PROS:
-Hours and hours and hours of content, both PvE and PvP
-Fun, engaging combat system, not to complex, but not mind numbing either, you will be kept on your toes.
-Beautiful art design, worthy of an Elder Scrolls I.P.
-AMAZING Soundtrack, on par with that of Skyrim and Oblivion
-Non-Toxic community (Mostly)
-Huge variety of playstyles, class builds, and weapon choice
-Compelling storyline, as well as DLC storyline
-Great voice acting, phenomenal for that of an MMORPG
-Not pay-2-win
CONS:
-Minor bugs and glitches
-Have to grind a good amount if you want to get into end game content
-DLC is somewhat on the pricy side, unless you just go with sub time
-Stability issues in PvP
-Certain monster sets make others seem irrelevant, only 4-5 sets primarily used for META.
-PvP gets far less love than the PvE content. Numerous balancing issues, slowly but surely being improved, but still there as of now.
Final Thoughts:
All in all nothing is truely game-breaking for me to get me to stop playing. Every time I log in there seems to be something for me to do, whether it be do dailies, dungeons, PvP, make alts, go back and work on my crafting, or work on many of the complex quests they offer in the DLC. This game is my favorite MMORPG, and one of my favorite games of all time, I rank it far above WoW or FF XIV, as the game does not feel like a chore to complete, rather than a living, breathing Elder Scrolls world that was there far before you arrived, and will continue to be there after you are gone. I highly reccomend playing this game if you are a fan of MMORPGS, or a fan of the Elder Scrolls lore.
Final Verdict: 9/10, Excellent.

This game will give you a real kick in the♥♥♥♥♥for the first hour or so, but after that it's a matter of learning your enemies and how to approach different siutations.
There's a fair amount of back-tracking and key hunting, but it's not the bad kind, and gives you incentive to learn the different decks of the ship and leave markers around and on the map screen to remember where to go. No area in this game is ever really obsolete, as gear and research chemicals are not uniformly spread, and your inventory cannot hold everything.
There's also a pretty decent amount of lee-way when playing the game as far as character design goes, each type of weapons having their own playstyle as well as pros and cons associated with them. That said, it's not recommended to put a ton of points into heavy weapons right off the bat, you won't see your first grenade launcher for about 2-3 hours into the game. I'd recommend avoiding guides however, since it's part of the game to figure things out on your own, and creating your own story.
The controls and menus are responsive and make sense once you get used to them, however make sure your movement keys are bound properly. When I first started, my movement keys were w-z-c-x to move, a and d to turn left and right, and s to crouch. This is not fun to use, and I recommend changing the controls to something a human can use.
All in all, it's a 8/10 game. I just wish it was longer, there was more customization of your character, and more interactablility in the environment, otherwise I have no real complaints. I mean, it's a game that is almost as old as I am, so by that standard this thing is a master piece, but we have to rate things by how they stand up now.

The highest praise I can give this game is that it's how I
Half-Life. If you put this in front of me in another ten years, I might not even realise that I wasn't playing the original game.
The Source engine used by Black Mesa is showing its age in some respects - levels load frequently, many models (especially the humans!) are slightly odd-shaped, and the physics can be really unpredictable. It's a little grating when you come from a more recent game - especially considering that this game is still being worked on - but it's still a long way ahead of the game it remade.
This would be a fine way to experience Half-Life for the first time, but it stands up even better as a way to re-experience the original. The game was full of fond memories of the original (and some not-so-fond ones - I'm looking at you, assassins), especially as I came across new areas, weapons, enemies or game mechanics for the first time. Again.
I'm not sure if I'm looking forward to the Xen levels or not. The game holds up well without them, but they certainly weren't a highlight of the original Half-Life.

There were also a few glitches in the game, at least on my end, which I've chopped down to my pc not being the most powerful out there, so I'm gonna let those slide.
All in all I will give this game a 9/10.

While the transformation into a 3d shooter may be the biggest leap this franchise has taken, it has significant drawbacks. That isn't to say it's all bad, though.
Positive:
+ Kevin Spacey (let's just get that out of the way)
+ Extreme fast-paced combat. All the different exo-movements and jumps you can perform make the learning curve on this title steeper than other CoD titles. Dodging bullets is a thing now. Kills are fast and action is everywhere. There's never a dull moment.
+ Weapon variants add a new meaning to choosing a weapon, provided you unlock the good ones. You earn supply drops containing variants every 45 mins or so (and advanced supply drops at level 20, 30, 40, and Prestige). Hunting new variants for your favorite guns will definitely keep you playing a few more games.
+ Armor customization is actually pretty fun. You earn armor pieces the same way as weapon variants, and there are some pretty crazy outfits out there. Having a full set of an armor type equipped will give you a 5% bonus to earned XP.
+ Quite a selection of weapons, which all function differently. Not all are great but most are usable or fun.
Negative:
- Everything about the campaign (minus Kevin Spacey). Completely uninspired and repetitive. Although CoD multiplayer has always been the highlight of the series BO2 set a new standard for CoD campaigns which AW just doesn't live up to. Also, combat in the campaign doesn't prepare you at all for the craziness of multiplayer.
- Terrible port. In my experience, crashes are abundant compared to other games with similar graphics. High-end PC's might not have a problem though.
- Every game mode except Team Deathmatch and (occasionally) Mosh Pit are dead. No one joins. So if you're looking to play CTF, S&D, Infection, and most other game modes, forget about it. TDM and MP games are sparce unless it's peak hours, too.
All in all, I can't recommend the game. As the PC CoD community grows Activision will be forced to make better ports but that day is not today. It's a shame because the gameplay is actually extremely fun - but a terrible campaign and lack of games other than TDM and MP make the PC version of AW not worth the price.

Rapid Review after two full Playthroughs as both characters with both High/Low endings.
Pros:
-Faithful Sequel to the Original Game
-Gameplay remains intact with improvements
-New Powers
-Two Characters to choose from
-Great Story Length
-Fun action via High Chaos
-Complex thinking via Low Chaos
-Connected Lore between Games, tons of new Lore
-3 Total Endings (1 Hidden)
-No Powers Option
-Playing HUDless is really fun
-Custom Difficulty Mode
-New Game+ (Unlocks access to Powers from BOTH Characters)
-Chapter Select
Cons:
-Very Hard not challenging enough
-Voice Actors can fall flat sometimes
-Music via Musicians is cut off abruptly via directional viewing
-Parry/Counter Attack is limit of Swordplay
-Not all gadgets feel needed when Sword and Bow/Gun do the work faster
-Emily's powers feel weaker compared to Corvo
-Dialogue is roughly similar between characters, only changing via Low/High Chaos playthroughs
-Few Performance issues, hit or miss on whether these affect you
TL;DR - If you liked and enjoyed Dishonored 1 then this game is what you are looking for in a sequel. If you had no interest in the franchise or didn't enjoy the first game, it's okay.
